Flow-cytometry quantification of T-cell subsets found expansion of circulating CD4+ T lymphocytes expressing surface DR, suggesting their activation; low natural killer cells and CD8+ T-lymphocyte levels. Urine immunofixation electrophoresis was negative. Ig-replacement therapy was started but not pursued by the patient.
Ten months later (May 2016, age 25) she was hospitalized for a 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. CRP, lactate dehydrogenase and beta2-microglobulin levels were 40 mg/L, 340 U/L (NR 5-240 U/L) and 3.53 mg/L (NR 1.2-2.5 mg/L), respectively. As shown in Table 1, hypogammaglobulinemia, CD19+ B lymphopenia and low peripheral CD8+ T-cell count persisted but without T activation, as assessed by HLADR-positivity. CT scans visualized bilateral diffuse infiltrates, ground-glass opacities and large nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis revealed Pneumocystis jiroveci cysts with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (4,000 copies/mL); high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids were prescribed. Searches for other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, Cryptococcus and Aspergillus species, were negative. At that time, her bone-marrow biopsy was normal.
Despite appropriate antibiotics and clinical improvement, thoracic CT scans revealed worsened dense infiltrates (Figure 1(a)), pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly and nodular lesions of both kidneys (Figure 1(b)). A new bronchoscopy with biopsies found CD20+ large lymphomatous cell infiltration (Figure 2) in bronchi. Those large atypical lymphoid tumor cells were CD10-BCL-6- and MUM1+BCL-2+, with an 80% Ki-67-proliferation index on immunolabeling. EBV, as assessed by in situ hybridization with an EBV-encoded small RNA probe, was diffusely positive in about 80% of tumor cells (Figure 2). The FISH assay for MYC gene rearrangement (MYC FISH DNA Probe, Split Signal, (Y5410), Dako, Locus 8q24) was negative. EBV-positive DLBCL with a nongerminal center phenotype was diagnosed without bone-marrow infiltration. Circulating EBV-DNA was positive (2,430,000 IU/mL). DLBCL treatment consisted of RTX, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone. Even with EB viremia becoming negative, she developed fever, cytopenias, liver damage and neurological manifestations, as a consequence of her prominent bone-marrow hemophagocytosis. Unfortunately, she died of multiorgan failure at age 25.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old woman in long-term remission from primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) 3 years after rituximab therapy presented in July 2015 with a 3-day history of high fever (39.2 °C), chills, myalgias, lower abdominal pain, and vomiting, followed 10 months later by a 15-day history of low-grade fever, weight loss, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Treated in June 2012 with 4 weekly infusions of rituximab (375 mg/m^2) and IVIG for relapsing anti-GPIIb/IIIa+, anti-SSA+ primary ITP, the patient remained infection-free until July 2015 (age 24), when she presented with acute febrile agranulocytosis and Campylobacter jejuni bacteremia. Ten months later (May 2016, age 25), having declined maintenance immunoglobulin replacement for persistent pan-hypogammaglobulinemia and complete B-cell aplasia, she presented with 15 days of fever, weight loss, dry cough, and dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary ITP diagnosed in 2008, treated with prednisone, IVIG cycles (2009–2012), and rituximab (June 2012, 375 mg/m^2 × 4) with baseline pre-rituximab mild lymphopenia (0.513 × 10^9/L).
subjective.review_of_systems: July 2015: fever, chills, myalgias, lower abdominal pain, vomiting. May 2016: 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: July 2015 admission: temperature 39.2 °C, normal physical exam. May 2016 admission: low-grade fever and progressive respiratory distress, later developing hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, liver failure, and neurological deterioration.
objective.routine_investigations: July 2015: CRP 114 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L), AST 144 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, ALP 389 IU/L, GGT 698 U/L, agranulocytosis (WBC 4.9 × 10^9/L, ANC 0.02 × 10^9/L), Hb 14.5 g/dL, platelets 46 × 10^9/L; blood and stool cultures grew Campylobacter jejuni; negative HIV-1/2; profound hypogammaglobulinemia and 0% circulating CD19+ B cells with reduced NK and CD8+ T cells. May 2016: CRP 40 mg/L, LDH 340 U/L (normal: 5–240 U/L), beta2-microglobulin 3.53 mg/L (normal: 1.2–2.5 mg/L), and plasma EBV-DNA 2,430,000 IU/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: July 2015 bone marrow aspirate showed maturation-arrested hypoplastic granulopoiesis; thoracoabdominal CT was normal. May 2016 chest CT showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and nodules; BAL was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and PCR (4,000 copies/mL) and negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, CMV, Cryptococcus, and Aspergillus. Subsequent repeat CT showed worsening pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral renal nodules; repeat bronchoscopy with bronchial biopsy revealed an EBV-positive (EBER+ in 80%, MYC-negative) non-germinal-center diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL: CD20+, CD10-, BCL-6-, MUM1+, BCL-2+, Ki-67 80%) complicated by fatal bone marrow hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections were excluded on BAL, and the patient was diagnosed with unmasked common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) / persistent post-rituximab B-cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia complicated sequentially by Campylobacter jejuni septicemia with agranulocytosis (cured with ceftazidime/gentamicin and 2 weeks of amoxicillin-clavulanate), Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treated with high-dose TMP-SMX and steroids), and fatal EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with hemophagocytic syndrome despite R-CHOP chemotherapy.

raw_case_text: A 73-year-old male patient presented to the Pulmonary Medicine OPD with chief complaints of fever, difficulty in breathing, palpitations, and increased frequency of urination since the last 5 days. The fever was low grade in nature and was associated with evening rise of temperature. He also complained of passing blood in urine along with dribbling of the same. He was a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus and pulmonary tuberculosis since last 10 years and 2 years, respectively. Detailed history revealed that he had taken antitubercular drugs for 6 months and left by himself months back. There was no history of HTN or any other comorbidities. On examination, he was febrile; heart rate was 86 beats/min; respiratory rate was 27 breaths/min; blood pressure was 100/60  mm Hg; and oxygen saturation was 91% while breathing room air. The patient had pallor and bilateral pedal oedema. Respiratory system examination revealed crepitations on the right side of the chest. Other systemic examinations did not reveal any significant findings. The total leukocyte count was 8795/mm3 with 70% neutrophils and 18% lymphocytes. His fasting and postprandial blood sugar levels were 185  mg/dl and 439  mg/dl, respectively, whereas HbA1c was recorded as 8.5%. Sputum samples were sent for Gram stain, acid-fast bacilli stain, culture, and KOH mount. AFB stain and GeneXpert was done, both of which came negative. KOH mount revealed branching filament-like structures, which were confirmed by modified acid-fast staining as Nocardia spp. The sputum sample was also cultured on blood agar and it revealed white, dry colonies with rough surface after 48 hours of incubation. These colonies were identified by MALDI-TOF as Nocardia araoensis with a confidence interval of 1.50. He was started on Tab Trimethoprim-Sulphamethoxazole for a period of 15 days. On follow-up after a period of 15 days, the patient had improved symptomatically.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old diabetic male with a history of defaulted pulmonary tuberculosis treatment presented with a 5-day history of low-grade evening fever, dyspnea, palpitations, urinary frequency, dribbling, and gross hematuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 5 days prior to outpatient pulmonary presentation, the patient developed low-grade fever with evening temperature rise, shortness of breath, palpitations, increased urinary frequency, terminal dribbling, and hematuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 10 years; diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years prior, for which he took anti-tubercular drugs for 6 months before self-discontinuing; no hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for evening fever, dyspnea, palpitations, frequency, dribbling, and hematuria.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, HR 86 bpm, RR 27 breaths/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, SpO2 91% on room air, pallor, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and right-sided chest crepitations on auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 8,795/mm^3 (70% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes), fasting blood glucose 185 mg/dL, postprandial blood glucose 439 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.5%. Sputum conventional Ziehl-Neelsen AFB stain and GeneXpert MTB/RIF were both negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Sputum KOH wet mount and modified acid-fast staining revealed branching filamentous acid-fast bacilli; 48-hour blood agar culture grew dry, rough, chalky-white colonies identified by MALDI-TOF MS (score 1.50) as Nocardia araoensis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Active pulmonary tuberculosis relapse was ruled out by negative sputum Ziehl-Neelsen AFB stain and GeneXpert MTB/RIF, and modified acid-fast staining, blood agar culture, and MALDI-TOF MS confirmed pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia araoensis in a poorly controlled diabetic patient (HbA1c 8.5%). He was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 15 days with symptomatic improvement at follow-up.

raw_case_text: Written informed consent was obtained from the patient. A 20-year-old man who presented with 2 month history of fever was admitted in our hospital on 8 October 2016. Without obvious cause, the patient had repeated chills and fever 2 months ago and the highest temperature raised to 39 C. He passed bloody stools and got abdominal pain during hospitalization. Physical examination was non-remarkable. Blood examination revealed 10.42 x 109 white blood cells/L, with 69.40% neutrophils and 16.17% lymphocytes. HIV antibody, immunochemistry, dengue antigen, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, influenza A, and influenza B antigen were all unremarkable. Chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan showed ileocecus of ascending colon, and transverse colon showed diffuse thickening of the wall. The most obvious was in the transverse colon, which was considered as inflammation. On 13 October 2016, colonoscopy showed multiple segmental colon ulcers, which was considered as Crohn's disease or tuberculosis (Figure 1(a) and (b)). Pathology showed that there were a lot of acute and chronic inflammatory cells infiltration in lamina propria, submucosa, and muscle layer, and there were multiple granulomatous lesions without obvious caseous necrosis. In addition, the possibility of intestinal bacterial infection, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), intestinal tuberculosis, lymphoma, histoplasmosis, and other diseases were excluded. It tended to be Crohn's disease, but tuberculosis was not excluded (Figure 2). The CTE of the small intestine showed that ileocecus and distal ileum were thickened and strengthened obviously after injection, so that the patient was conformed to Crohn's disease (Figure 3(c) and (d)). From 8-25 October, we gave him antibiotic treatments. Taking small intestinal computed tomography enterography (CTE), colonoscopy, and pathology into consideration, he was diagnosed as Crohn's disease and given glucocorticoids and immunosuppressant therapy from 20 October. After 5 days of treatment, the patient still had repeated fever, and the anti-infection treatment was upgraded to imipenem. However, his symptoms still have not improved. Therefore, we rechecked the colonoscopy. On 30 October, IBD was considered by colonoscopy, but it was not confirmed (Figure 1(a) and (b)). Meanwhile, tuberculosis was not excluded. Sample of intestinal biopsy was sent to our hospital and the Southern Hospital of Southern Medical University for examination. In the oral report of intestinal pathology in our hospital, the microbes with positive Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining were examined, which were also seen in the intestinal pathology on 13 October. Therefore, we thought that we made a wrong diagnosis. Pathology reported that distal ileum, ascending colon, transverse colon, and sigmoid colon mucosa were infiltrated by a large number of tissue cells that had a large number of blue purple granules. Special staining showed purple blue particles with positive PAS staining and Gomori's Methenamine-Silver (GMS) staining. It was considered to be histoplasmosis. On 7 November, Southern Hospital Pathology Consultation Report described that a large number of tissue cells and multinuclear giant cells were seen in the lamina propria of ileum mucosa, and fungal spores were found in tissue cells, so that he was diagnosed as talaromycosis (Figure 4). On 8 November, immunologic testing showed that CD3 cells accounted for 17.40%, CD4 cells accounted for 11.50%, CD8 cells accounted for 4.10% and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 2.8. According to the pathology consultation report, he was finally diagnosed as talaromycosis. A treatment of itraconazole 0.2 g twice daily for a long term was given to him. The temperature dropped to normal and bloody stools disappeared after anti-fungal treatment for 5 days. We knew that he used to have a history of taking methamphetamine many times between July and August after inquiring about his medical history again. He reviewed colonoscopy in the hospital again on 17 January 2017. The examination results suggested that the intestinal inflammation subsided.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old man presented on October 8, 2016, with a 2-month history of recurrent chills and high fever (up to 39 °C), complicated after admission by abdominal pain and hematochezia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to hospital admission, the patient experienced unexplained recurrent fevers (up to 39 °C) and chills, and subsequently developed abdominal pain and bloody stools during hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Subsequent detailed history revealed repeated methamphetamine use between July and August 2016.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, chills, abdominal pain, and bloody stools.

objective.physical_examination: Unremarkable physical examination on admission; febrile up to 39 °C.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 10.42 × 10^9/L (69.40% neutrophils, 16.17% lymphocytes); negative HIV antibody, dengue antigen, HBV, HCV, and influenza A/B antigens. T-cell subset analysis (November 8) showed CD3+ 17.40%, CD4+ 11.50%, CD8+ 4.10%, and CD4/CD8 ratio 2.8.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest/abdominal CT and small-bowel CT enterography (CTE) showed diffuse mural thickening and hyperenhancement of the distal ileum, ileocecal region, ascending colon, and especially the transverse colon. Colonoscopies (October 13 and October 30, 2016) revealed multiple segmental colonic ulcers initially misdiagnosed as Crohn's disease vs. intestinal tuberculosis. Re-evaluation and specialist pathology consultation (November 7) of the ileal and colonic mucosal biopsies demonstrated massive lamina propria infiltration by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells packed with PAS- and GMS-positive intracellular fungal spores/yeast-like organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Intestinal tuberculosis and Crohn's disease were ruled out after glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and imipenem failed, and PAS/GMS staining with reference pathology review of the ileocolonic biopsies confirmed disseminated intestinal talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei). Initiation of long-term oral itraconazole (0.2 g BID) achieved defervescence and cessation of hematochezia within 5 days, with complete mucosal healing confirmed on follow-up colonoscopy on January 17, 2017.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old middle-age gentleman, who was otherwise fit and well, presented with persistent high-grade fever for more than ten days duration associated with intermittent productive cough of whitish sputum. He also had arthralgia and myalgia. He denied any hemoptysis, night sweats, shortness of breath, or pleuritic chest pain. He did not have any constitutional symptoms such as loss of weight or appetite. He was previously diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) where he completed a total duration of 9 months of anti-TB therapy. During this course of therapy, he had recurrent admissions for empyema thoracic, where a chest tube drainage and prolonged antibiotic therapy were needed. He was a nonsmoker and was doing a rural job, in the form of farming for a living. He denied alcohol consumption and the usage of recreational drugs.
On examination, he appeared tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/minute. His other vital signs were normal. There were reduced air entry and vocal resonance with the presence of stony dullness on examination on the lower zone of the right lung. There was a skin lesion over the face and scalp which resembles seborrhoeic dermatitis. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.
In terms of blood investigations, he had leucocytosis (WCC of 14.9 x 109/L) and thrombocytosis (platelet count of 609 x 109/L), with significantly raised inflammatory markers (ESR of 102 and CRP of 137.4). A sputum acid-fast bacillus was scanty 1+, and the sputum mycobacterium culture was negative. Hepatitis and HIV screenings were negative. Chest radiography showed consolidative changes with mild to moderate pleural effusion on the right side (Figure 1). The pleural analysis shows the exudative picture with protein ratio (pleural protein) : (serum protein) = (3.3 g/L : 77 g/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio (pleural LDH) : (serum LDH) = (3317 U/L : 315 U/L). Cytology was sent and no malignancy detected, and an acid-fast bacillus was also negative. Skin biopsy was taken and showed Paecilomyces species. CT thorax was performed and revealed a multiloculated collection within the right hemithorax depicting a thickened enhancing wall which joins at the margins of the collection to form the split pleura sign. This is associated with the compression atelectasis surrounding it (Figure 2).
The patient was referred to a cardiothoracic surgeon, and right thoracotomy and decortications were done in February 2016. The findings from the operation are thickened cortex measuring 0.8 cm plastered to the surface of the right lung with small pus collection. Tissue culture and sensitivity were sent and reported as Gram-positive and thin branching filaments. Modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining reported as many branching of acid-fast bacilli which is consistent with the morphology of Nocardia species. And it is sensitive to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (Bactrim). He was started on IV imipenem 500 mg QID and oral Bactrim 4/4/3 tablets TDS total for 4 months. After completed treatment, the patient was getting better and no more shortness of breath and cough. Repeated CT thorax noted no more pleural effusion or empyema (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male farmer presented with a >10-day history of persistent high-grade fever, intermittent cough productive of whitish sputum, arthralgias, and myalgias.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with over 10 days of unremitting high fever, productive cough with white sputum, joint pains, and muscle aches.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and completed 9 months of anti-TB therapy, complicated during treatment by recurrent admissions for thoracic empyema requiring chest tube drainage and prolonged antibiotics. Non-smoker, non-drinker, farmer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, productive cough, arthralgia, and myalgia; negative for hemoptysis, night sweats, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, anorexia, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Tachypneic (RR 24 breaths/min) with otherwise normal vital signs; stony dullness to percussion, reduced air entry, and decreased vocal resonance over the right lower lung zone; seborrheic dermatitis-like facial and scalp skin lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 14.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 609 × 10^9/L, ESR 102 mm/h, CRP 137.4 mg/L, negative viral hepatitis and HIV screens, and scanty 1+ sputum AFB smear with negative sputum mycobacterial culture. Facial/scalp skin biopsy grew Paecilomyces species. Chest X-ray showed right lower lung consolidation and a mild-to-moderate right pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracentesis yielded exudative fluid (pleural:serum protein 3.3 g/dL : 77 g/L; pleural:serum LDH 3,317 U/L : 315 U/L) negative for malignant cytology and standard AFB smear. Thoracic CT demonstrated a multiloculated right pleural collection with thickened enhancing visceral and parietal pleura ('split pleura' sign) and compressive atelectasis. Right thoracotomy and decortication (February 2016) removed a 0.8 cm thick pleural peel and purulent collection; surgical tissue Gram stain and modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain revealed Gram-positive, partially acid-fast thin branching filaments, and culture isolated trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-susceptible Nocardia species.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Active tuberculous empyema relapse was excluded by negative sputum and pleural mycobacterial cultures, and intraoperative pleural tissue culture and modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining from the right thoracotomy/decortication confirmed right thoracic empyema caused by Nocardia species in a post-TB patient. Following surgical decortication, he completed a 4-month antibiotic regimen of intravenous imipenem (500 mg QID) and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (4/4/3 tablets TID), achieving complete clinical and CT resolution of the empyema.

raw_case_text:
Scenario 2: an 83 year old elderly man presented to our hospital with low grade fever and productive cough of one-week duration and shortness of breath of 3 days duration. He also reported an episode of streaky hemoptysis and a background history of treatment for a sputum-confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, 19 years previously. There was a recent history of a self-limiting sore throat and generalized body weakness. He was hypertensive and diabetic but reported good drug compliance. He had presented at the early stage of community transmission of COVID-19 infection within the country with strong consideration given to its likelihood. However, he had been screened for COVID-19 through RT-PCR test from nasopharyngeal and throat swabs obtained at an accredited outside laboratory which returned negative; the result of which he made available at the time of admission to our facility. The remarkable findings on clinical examination were tachypnoea (respiratory rate of 36/minute), poor room air oxygen saturation of 90%, tachycardia (pulse rate of 100/minute) and systemic hypertension (blood pressure of 165/96mmHg). All initial laboratory blood panels were within normal limits except for borderline elevation in serum creatinine of 1.6mg/ml (normal: <1.5mg/dl) and low estimated glomerular filtration rate of 45.5ml/min/1.73m2 (normal: >90ml/min/1.73m2) indicating low renal reserve.
The chest radiograph done on admission revealed dextrocardia with features of multiple consolidations in both lung fields demonstrating peripheral disposition. There was no evidence of pleural or pericardial effusion (Figure 5). A 12-lead electrocardiogram revealed features of left ventricular hypertrophy and left axis deviation with sinus tachycardia. Two-dimensional trans-thoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with good biventricular systolic function (left ventricular ejection fraction {EF} of 65% and Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion {TAPSE} of 2.5cm).
Given the negative COVID-19 test, the clinical diagnosis of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia was made with a differential diagnosis of reactivated pulmonary tuberculosis. He was commenced on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy according to hospital infectious disease protocol for community-acquired pneumonia as well as other supportive therapy, including corticosteroids and anticoagulants. Consideration was also given to commencement of a trial of empirical anti-tuberculous therapy because of his past medical history. However, his clinical condition remained poor, necessitating further imaging evaluation with chest computed tomographic (CT) scan on the 5th day of admission (12th day from the onset of illness) which revealed diffuse ill-defined ground glass densities in both lungs with multiple peripherally-distributed non-enhancing peri-bronchovascular consolidations especially in the lower lobes. There was bilateral pleural thickening with mild cardiomegaly (CTR=54%), rightward cardiac apex, and bovine branching pattern of a rightward aortic arch consistent with dextrocardia. The liver was located on the left and the spleen on the right, in keeping with a situs inversus (Figure 6). These imaging findings heightened suspicion of COVID-19 viral pneumonia, especially as there was a prevailing surge in community-transmitted cases at the time. The patient was transferred to the hospital isolation facility with repeat throat and nasal swabs sent for the COVID-19 test, which returned positive after five days. The patient made a full recovery from the infection and was discharged home after 16 days in the isolation centre after two subsequent consecutive COVID-19 RT-PCR tests had returned negative. No hospital staff among the primary contacts of this patient was reported to be infected with COVID-19 after contact tracing and isolation.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old man with situs inversus totalis presented with a 1-week history of low-grade fever, productive cough, streaky hemoptysis, and generalized weakness, and a 3-day history of shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Preceded by a self-limiting sore throat, the patient developed 1 week of low-grade fever, productive cough, an episode of streaky hemoptysis, and generalized weakness, followed 3 days prior to admission by progressive dyspnea. An outpatient nasopharyngeal/throat SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR test obtained prior to admission was negative.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sputum-confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis treated and cured 19 years prior; congenital situs inversus totalis with dextrocardia; hypertension and diabetes mellitus with good medication adherence.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for low-grade fever, productive cough, streaky hemoptysis, dyspnea, sore throat, and generalized weakness.

objective.physical_examination: RR 36 breaths/min, SpO2 90% on room air, pulse 100/min, BP 165/96 mmHg, and dextrocardia.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood panels were normal except for mildly elevated serum creatinine at 1.6 mg/dL (normal <1.5 mg/dL) and reduced eGFR of 45.5 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (normal >90 mL/min/1.73 m^2). Pre-admission outpatient SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR was negative. Admission CXR showed dextrocardia and multifocal peripheral bilateral lung consolidations without effusion. 12-lead ECG showed LVH, left axis deviation, and sinus tachycardia; TTE showed concentric LVH with LVEF 65% and TAPSE 2.5 cm.
objective.advanced_workup: Day-5 chest CT (day 12 of illness) demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and peripheral non-enhancing peribronchovascular consolidations predominantly in the lower lobes, bilateral pleural thickening, mild cardiomegaly (CTR 54%), dextrocardia with a rightward bovine aortic arch, and abdominal situs inversus (left-sided liver, right-sided spleen).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Reactivated pulmonary tuberculosis was considered in the differential but excluded when repeat nasopharyngeal/throat swabs sent after the characteristic day-5 chest CT returned positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR, confirming COVID-19 pneumonia in an elderly patient with situs inversus totalis and remote cured TB. Managed in isolation with broad-spectrum antibiotics, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, and oxygen support, he recovered fully and was discharged after 16 days following two consecutive negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR tests.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 59-year-old male from Dammam, Saudi Arabia with a history of HIV for 15 years, who was non-compliant to HIV treatment for five years. The patient last visited the HIV clinic in December 2020 and blood tests showed a viral load of 9340 copies per mL. Furthermore, this person had a history of HBV (immune to hepatitis B due to natural immunity), chronic non-treated HCV, diabetes mellitus type II for three years, hypertension (HTN), smoking and active drug abuse for heroin and alcohol, chronic kidney disease stage III, and a previously treated cervical spine abscess with internal fixation surgery. The patient was prescribed tenofovir and emtricitabine; no antiretroviral resistance screening test was performed, and we could not obtain lymphocyte subset results. Prior to emergency department (ER) admittance, the patient had three months history of progressive neck pain, and sudden weakness in the upper and lower limbs the day before presenting to the ER; however, they experienced no numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. The results of the patient's physical examination, blood pressure and other vital signs were normal, and neuromuscular examination results were unremarkable. However, laboratory blood test results revealed a high white blood cell (WBC) count, decreased hemoglobin level (Hgb), and high platelet count (Plt). The patient's serum creatinine level was 2.54 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen was 45 mg/dL. Notably, there were elevated levels of inflammatory markers, such as procalcitonin and C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A brain computed tomography (CT) revealed chronic small vessel disease, with a number of lytic lesions on the patient's first cervical vertebra.
Seven days post admission, the patient experienced fever (38.8 C), in addition to persistent and uncontrolled high blood pressure; however, a physical examination showed no evidence of limited movement or mobility. Prior to receiving blood culture results for sepsis testing, vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics were empirically prescribed. The patient received a complete work-up, and was tested for complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, and blood and urine cultures.
The septic workup results showed a high WBC count and high levels of inflammatory markers, including CRP and procalcitonin (Table 1). 
We incubated one set of blood culture vials in a BacT/Alert Virtuo system (BioMerieux, France) for 5 days, according to the internal policies and procedures of the microbiology laboratory at King Fahd Hospital of the University. After 72 hours of incubation, one of the two blood culture vials flagged positive, and direct Gram staining showed Gram-positive bacilli. Subsequently, the blood culture vials were sub-cultured on sheep blood, MacConkey, chocolate, and anaerobic Brucella agars.
After 48 hours incubation at 37 C, there was no growth present on sheep blood, MacConkey's, and chocolate agars. However, there was bacterial growth on anaerobic Brucella agar (Figure 1). We used Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight-mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS) (VITEK MS; bioMerieux) and the Knowledge Base database (version 3.0) with a confidence value of 99.9% to identify Clostridium paraputrificum. Antibiotics-susceptibility tests for anaerobic organisms were not available in our routine diagnostic laboratory; therefore, we depended on 2022 Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) cumulative data, which showed that Clostridium was sensitive to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole antibiotics. Urine analysis results were normal, and the urine culture showed no growth. 
Forty-eight hours following treatment with vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics, the patient clinically improved, the fever subsided, and blood cultures showed no growth. All subsequent cultures were negative, but inflammatory markers remained high. On day 12 of admission, the patient experienced sudden cardiac arrest due to reflex arrhythmia caused by atlantoaxial subluxation and passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, presented to the emergency department with a 3-month history of progressive neck pain and a 1-day history of sudden-onset upper and lower limb weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive neck pain over the 3 months prior to presentation, followed by acute onset of weakness involving both the upper and lower extremities the day before emergency department admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV infection for 15 years with non-compliance to antiretroviral therapy for 5 years (last HIV clinic visit in December 2020 showed a viral load of 9,340 copies/mL; lymphocyte subset results were unavailable and no antiretroviral resistance screening was performed). Past history also includes resolved hepatitis B virus infection (natural immunity), chronic untreated hepatitis C virus infection, type 2 diabetes mellitus for 3 years, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage III, previously treated cervical spine abscess with internal fixation surgery, smoking, and active heroin and alcohol abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or weight loss prior to presentation. Prescribed home medications included tenofovir and emtricitabine (non-compliant).

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs including blood pressure were normal, and physical and neuromuscular examinations were unremarkable. On hospital day 7, the patient developed fever (38.8 °C) and persistent uncontrolled hypertension without limited movement or mobility.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests showed elevated WBC count, decreased hemoglobin, elevated platelet count, serum creatinine 2.54 mg/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL, and elevated procalcitonin, CRP, and ESR. Urinalysis was normal. Repeat septic workup on day 7 showed persistently elevated WBC count, CRP, and procalcitonin.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT demonstrated chronic small vessel disease and multiple lytic lesions involving the first cervical vertebra (C1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: 59-year-old male with longstanding poorly controlled HIV infection (prior HIV-1 viral load 9,340 copies/mL) complicated by C1 lytic vertebral lesions and healthcare-associated sepsis caused by Clostridium paraputrificum bacteremia. One of two blood culture vials incubated in the BacT/Alert Virtuo system flagged positive at 72 hours with Gram-positive bacilli; subculture grew strictly anaerobic colonies on Brucella agar at 48 hours, identified by MALDI-TOF MS (VITEK MS, 99.9% confidence) as Clostridium paraputrificum (sensitive per CLSI cumulative data to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole). Urine culture showed no growth. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were initiated on day 7, resulting in defervescence, clinical improvement, and clearance of subsequent blood cultures within 48 hours, though inflammatory markers remained elevated. On hospital day 12, the patient suffered sudden cardiac arrest secondary to reflex arrhythmia from atlantoaxial subluxation and passed away.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old woman was admitted to our emergency department with a subacute onset of mild confusion and left hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 4/5). She was fully alert and orientated, complaining about headaches (Visual Analogic Scale 7/10). She had no history of drug abuse or cigarette smoking.
Pre- and postcontrast computed tomography (CT) scans of the brain [Figure 1] revealed a 2 cm diameter hypodense nodular lesion in the right thalamus with perilesional edema causing moderate mass effect, with colliquative features inside. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pre and post contrast [Figure 2] confirmed a right thalamic nodular lesion measuring 25 x 22 mm, with perilesional edema. The nodule appeared hypointense on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences, isointense on T1-weighted and reg-diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences. The nodule and associated edema resulted in ipsilateral ventricular compression. In the coronal sections [Figure 3], there was an irregular postcontrast enhancement, especially along the nodule walls. Was also visible an inner enhancing nodule, which should have raised the suspicion of parasitic infection [Figure 3, Panel C].
The clinical presentation (without any known history of immune suppression) and the neuroimaging features of the solitary brain lesion primarily suggested a brain tumor, even if other diagnostic hypotheses could not be rejected.
Considering the deep location in an eloquent area, it was decided to perform a neuronavigated stereotaxic biopsy [Figure 4]. Preoperative planning was conducted using three-dimensional reconstruction to simulate the surgical trajectory and avoid functional areas and tracts (StealthStation S8; Medtronic, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA) [Figure 4].
A coronal trajectory was used passing lateral to the lateral ventricle wall. Histopathology revealed extensive areas of necrosis, vascular thrombosis phenomena and aspects of vasculitis with lymphohistiocytic and granulocytic infiltrate at the level of the vascular walls. Rounded structures containing eosinophilic corpuscles inside the infiltrate were found, suggesting a protozoal infection, and allowing the diagnosis of cerebral toxoplasmosis [Figure 5].
The immediate postoperative course was uneventful without complications. Nevertheless, in the following days, the patient presented with fever and abdominal pain with rapid clinical worsening and septic shock. Therefore, the patient was then transferred to intensive care unit. A total-body CT scan revealed multiple abscesses (liver, kidney, and thyroid gland), intestinal walls thickening, and pleural effusion [Figure 6].
Due to the septic shock and the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis, the patient was evaluated by the infectious disease specialist, who initiated the treatment of toxoplasmosis and performed a serologic test which revealed an HIV infection.
Despite therapy, due to HIV-related immunosuppression, the patient suffered multiorgan failure and died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a subacute onset of mild confusion, left hemiparesis, and severe headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed subacute mild confusion accompanied by left-sided weakness and headache rated 7/10 on the Visual Analog Scale prior to admission, with no known prior history of immunosuppression.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known past medical history of immunosuppression. Negative history of cigarette smoking or illicit drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache (VAS 7/10) and left-sided weakness.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was alert and oriented with mild confusion and left hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 4/5).
objective.advanced_workup: Pre- and post-contrast brain CT revealed a 2 cm hypodense nodular lesion in the right thalamus with colliquative internal features and perilesional edema causing moderate mass effect. Pre- and post-contrast brain MRI confirmed a 25 x 22 mm right thalamic nodular lesion appearing hypointense on T2/FLAIR and isointense on T1/DWI, with irregular peripheral ring enhancement, an inner eccentric enhancing nodule, perilesional edema, and ipsilateral lateral ventricular compression. Neuronavigated stereotactic biopsy (StealthStation S8) of the right thalamic lesion demonstrated extensive necrosis, vascular thrombosis, vasculitis with lymphohistiocytic and granulocytic infiltration of vessel walls, and rounded structures containing eosinophilic corpuscles diagnostic of protozoal infection. Following subsequent postoperative deterioration with fever, abdominal pain, and septic shock, a total-body CT scan revealed multiple abscesses in the liver, kidney, and thyroid gland, intestinal wall thickening, and pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated and cerebral toxoplasmosis unmasking previously undiagnosed HIV infection, complicated by septic shock and multiorgan failure. Initial neuroimaging differential of solitary primary brain tumor was ruled out by stereotactic brain biopsy histopathology confirming Toxoplasma gondii protozoal corpuscles, and subsequent infectious disease evaluation with HIV serology confirmed underlying HIV infection. Despite targeted anti-toxoplasmosis therapy and intensive care unit support, the patient progressed to refractory septic shock and multiorgan failure secondary to severe HIV-related immunosuppression and died.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old male patient was admitted to a tertiary public hospital in Sao Paulo city, Brazil, with a history of fever, fatigue, weight loss, disseminated skin lesions, low urine output, and mental confusion progressing over three months. The patient received outpatient treatment for thoracic herpes zoster and was diagnosed with HIV infection three weeks earlier but decided not to initiate antiretroviral therapy. At hospital admission, upon physical examination, he was afebrile and dehydrated, with a blood pressure of 109/72 mmHg, pulse rate of 130 beats/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Mental confusion was observed (Glasgow Coma Scale - GCS = 14). The lung sounds were clear upon auscultation, the abdomen was innocent, and there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy, but diffuse maculopapular and crusty skin lesions were noticed (Figure 1A). Laboratory results showed hemoglobin = 13.9 g/dL, white blood cell count = 6,500/mm3, platelet count = 82,000/mm3, C-reactive protein = 26.1 mg/dL, creatinine level = 4.0 mg/dL, sodium concentration = 127 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase = 5,782 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase = 342 U/L, alanine aminotransferase = 340 U/L, total bilirubin = 3.9 mg/dL (direct bilirubin = 3.4 mg/dL), international normalized ratio = 1.71, triglycerides = 324 mg/dL, and ferritin > 100,000 ng/mL. Serologic diagnosis of HIV-1 infection was confirmed, CD4 count was 4 cells/mm3, and HIV-1 viral load was 1,749,163 copies/mL. The chest computed tomography (CT) showed unspecific findings (Figure 1B). The brain CT scan and the cerebrospinal fluid were normal. The abdominal CT scan showed no hepatosplenomegaly, but some retroperitoneal, periaortic, and interaortocaval lymph node enlargement was identified. On day 1, the sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score was 8, and septic shock with multiorgan dysfunction (acute renal failure, metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure, and coagulopathy) was diagnosed.
The primary care team initiated volemic expansion, and ceftriaxone was administered empirically. Yeasts suggestive of Histoplasma spp. were observed in the cytoplasm of macrophages of a routine peripheral blood smear (Figure 1C). On day 2, the patient was transferred to the ICU and required supplemental oxygen (1 L/min). Amphotericin B deoxycholate was initiated. On day 3, the SOFA score was 14 and the patient's clinical condition progressed with reduced level of consciousness (GCS 10) and refractory septic shock, requiring high doses of vasopressors, corticosteroids, mechanical ventilation, and hemodialysis. Yeasts suggestive of Histoplasma spp. also were observed in the cytoplasm of macrophages in the bone marrow and skin samples (Figure 1D) on days 3 and 7, respectively. Hemophagocytosis was not observed in the bone marrow. After four weeks of incubation, peripheral blood and bone marrow samples cultures revealed Histoplasma spp. Aerobic, anaerobic, and mycobacterial blood and bone marrow cultures were all negative. In addition, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay, mycobacterial cultures, and acid-fast bacillus smear from tracheal secretion were negative. The patient stayed in the ICU for 32 days, receiving empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy and frequent blood and platelet transfusions. Treatment with amphotericin B was extended to 23 days (20 days with amphotericin B deoxycholate and 3 days with liposomal amphotericin B). Antiretroviral therapy was initiated on day 10. After progressive clinical improvement and most laboratory test results returned to normal, the patient was discharged from the hospital with no need for dialysis and an early follow-up in the outpatient clinic of our hospital. Eight months after the discharge, he is fully active and able to perform all pre-hospitalization activities without restrictions. The recent laboratory results showed mild abnormality of kidney function (creatinine level = 1.3 mg/dL), CD4 count = 180 cells/mm3, and HIV-1 viral load < 40 copies/mL. In addition, the patient is maintaining regular use of darunavir/ritonavir, dolutegravir, lamivudine, prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Advanced HIV-1 infection (confirmed by positive HIV-1 serology, baseline HIV-1 viral load 1,749,163 copies/mL, and CD4 count 4 cells/mm3) complicated by severe disseminated histoplasmosis presenting with septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction (SOFA score 8 on day 1, rising to 14 on day 3 with GCS 10, acute renal failure, hepatic failure, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathy).
