assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary and nodal EBV-positive low-grade (Grade 1–2) lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG) secondary to newly diagnosed advanced HIV infection (confirmed by positive HIV serology in November 2022, plasma HIV RNA 363,000 copies/mL, CD4+ count 150 cells/mm3, and blood EBV DNA 23,627 copies/mL). Cytotoxic immunochemotherapy was deferred to avoid infectious complications, and the patient was treated solely with co-formulated bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Within 3–4 months of ART initiation, her plasma HIV viral load became undetectable, CD4+ count recovered to 494 cells/mm3, blood EBV DNA declined to 3,116 copies/mL, and chest CT showed marked regression of pulmonary nodules. Complete clinical, spirometric, and radiological remission on ART monotherapy was achieved by October 2023 and sustained through May and December 2024 without requiring immunochemotherapy.

raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with gradual onset dyspnea accompanied by cough and fever. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to smoking (20 packs/year) and HIV infection without any follow-up or treatment, diagnosed three years prior during hospitalization for pulmonary actinomycosis. He did not have any recollection of when the transmission occurred.
On admission, his vital signs included blood pressure of 110/56 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, and SpO2 of 82% (room air). He was conscious, with a Glasgow coma scale ranking of 15 (ocular response four points, verbal response five points, motor response six points), without changes in pupil size or shape. Other notable findings during the physical exam included white lesions on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx, compatible with oral candidiasis, and papular lesions in the healing phase in his back (Figure 1). No lymphadenopathy was noted. He was sarcopenic, weighing 50 kg. Lung auscultation revealed scattered crackles. The neurological exam was normal, and no meningeal signs were present.
Arterial blood gas (oxygen at two liters/minute) showed pH 7.45, PaO2 73 mmHg, PaCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, and lactate 1.1 mmol/L, with an alveolar-arterial O2 gradient of 77.9 mmHg. Admission's laboratory notable findings included leukocytes 4.5 x 103/microL (lymphocytes 0.6 x 103/microL), LDH 330 U/L, and C-reactive protein (CRP) 7.9 mg/dL (Table 1). The patient had 1 CD4+ cell/uL (normal 410-1590 cells/uL), a T-helper/suppressor ratio of 0, and an HIV viral load superior to 92,000 copies. Additional serologic studies for syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania, and Hepatitis B and C virus were negative. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella urine antigen tests were also negative.
A high-resolution chest CT scan revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities (Figure 2). Since the patient was a person living with HIV without any follow-up or treatment and the imaging studies were suggestive of PCP, empirical trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (250/1250 mg three times a day) and prednisolone (40 mg twice a day on the first five days, followed by 40 mg once a day in the next five days and 20 mg once a day on the following ten days) were started. BAL (Figure 3) fluid analysis was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (by PCR), Cryptococcus neoformans (by culture), and multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli (by culture). Additionally, liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg daily) plus flucytosine (1250 mg four times a day) and meropenem (1000 mg three times a day, directed to Escherichia coli) were added. Blood cultures collected were also positive for Cryptococcus neoformans.
Three days after admission, the patient started with headaches, nausea, vomiting, and lethargy, and a head CT scan was performed, showing hypodense areas in the left gangliocapsular region with mass effect (Figure 4A-4B). Cerebral MRI confirmed the presence of tumefactive lesions in the head of the right caudate nucleus and in the head and body of the left caudate nucleus, with hypersignal in T2. These lesions were compressing the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles (Figure 5A-5B) and were suggestive of cryptococcomas.
A lumbar puncture was performed (with an opening pressure of 21 cm H2O), yielding positive results for Cryptococcus neoformans, both antigen (titer >1:1024) and culture. Second and third lumbar punctures (opening pressure <20 cm H2O) were done on days 7 and 14 of treatment. Its results can be observed in Table 2.
Due to the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis, the initiation of ART was deferred due to the risk of IRIS. Liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine were administered for two weeks until the cultures were negative, followed by consolidation therapy with fluconazole (800 mg once a day). Regarding PCP, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was maintained for 21 days, followed by secondary prophylaxis (160/800 mg thrice a week).
In the fourth week of hospitalization, the patient experienced a decreased level of consciousness, with a Glasgow coma scale of 10 (ocular response of three points, verbal response of two points, and motor response of five points), accompanied by vomiting, dizziness, headaches, right hemiparesis, and mixed aphasia. Emergent cerebral CT showed left gangliocapsular hyperdensity, compatible with hemorrhagic transformation following ischemic stroke, with ipsilateral intraventricular bleeding and hydrocephalus (Figure 6A-6B). He was subsequently transferred to the neurosurgery unit, where his condition deteriorated, not having surgical conditions and ultimately culminating in the patient's demise.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man with untreated HIV infection presented to the emergency department with gradual-onset dyspnea, cough, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed gradually progressive shortness of breath accompanied by cough and fever prior to emergency department admission. He had been diagnosed with HIV infection 3 years earlier during a hospitalization for pulmonary actinomycosis but had never engaged in HIV follow-up or antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 3 years prior (ART-naive and lost to follow-up); prior hospitalization for pulmonary actinomycosis 3 years ago; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) secondary to a 20-pack-year smoking history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea, cough, fever, weight loss/sarcopenia, and oral thrush; developed headache, nausea, vomiting, and lethargy on hospital day 3.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: blood pressure 110/56 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, and SpO2 82% on room air; conscious and alert with GCS 15 and normal pupils. General exam showed severe sarcopenia (weight 50 kg), white plaques on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx consistent with oral candidiasis, and healing papular lesions on the back without peripheral lymphadenopathy. Chest auscultation revealed scattered crackles; baseline neurological exam was normal without meningeal signs. In week 4, he deteriorated to GCS 10 with right hemiparesis and mixed aphasia.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ABG (on 2 L/min O2) showed pH 7.45, PaO2 73 mmHg, PaCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, lactate 1.1 mmol/L, and A-a O2 gradient 77.9 mmHg. Blood tests showed WBC 4.5 x 10^3/µL (lymphocytes 0.6 x 10^3/µL), LDH 330 U/L, and CRP 7.9 mg/dL. Serologies for syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania, HBV, and HCV, as well as urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigens, were negative. Blood cultures grew Cryptococcus neoformans.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 1 cell/µL (reference 410–1,590 cells/µL) with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0. Chest HRCT revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by PCR, Cryptococcus neoformans by culture, and multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli by culture. Head CT and brain MRI on day 3 demonstrated T2-hyperintense tumefactive lesions (cryptococcomas) in the right caudate head and left caudate head/body compressing the frontal horns with left gangliocapsular mass effect. Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 21 cm H2O and positive CSF Cryptococcus neoformans antigen (titer >1:1024) and CSF culture (clearing on repeat LPs at days 7 and 14 with opening pressure <20 cm H2O). Week 4 emergent head CT revealed a left gangliocapsular hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke with intraventricular hemorrhage and hydrocephalus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Advanced untreated HIV/AIDS (CD4+ count 1 cell/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0, plasma HIV viral load >92,000 copies/mL) complicated by simultaneous Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, disseminated cryptococcosis (cryptococcal fungemia, pulmonary cryptococcosis, cryptococcal meningitis, and bilateral caudate cryptococcomas), multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli pneumonia, and oral candidiasis. Treatment included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (250/1250 mg TID for 21 days followed by 160/800 mg thrice weekly prophylaxis) with a 21-day prednisolone taper for PCP, meropenem (1,000 mg TID) for MDR E. coli, and induction liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day) plus flucytosine (1,250 mg QID) for 2 weeks until CSF sterilization followed by fluconazole consolidation (800 mg/day), with ART deferred due to high risk of fatal CNS IRIS. In the fourth week of hospitalization, the patient suffered a fatal left gangliocapsular ischemic stroke with hemorrhagic transformation, intraventricular extension, and obstructive hydrocephalus, and died after neurosurgical evaluation deemed him inoperable.

raw_case_text:
In March 2023, a 43-year-old Chinese male presented to the fever clinic with a one-week history of fever (peak temperature 39.8  C) and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. He had no significant medical history and denied corticosteroid or immunosuppressive drug use. On admission, the patient's vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 119 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, blood pressure 112/69 mmHg, and body temperature 38.5C. Laboratory tests showed normal white blood cell count (6.72 x 109/L; reference range, 3.5-9.5 x 109/L) but elevated neutrophil ratio (77.5 %; reference range, 40-75 %) and C-reactive protein (78.9 mg/L; reference range, 0-8 mg/L), liver function tests were within normal limits: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (32IU/L, reference range, 9-50 IU/L), Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (40 IU/L, reference range, 15-40 IU/L).
Following evaluation at the fever clinic, he was admitted to the infectious disease department. Laboratory results revealed a positive HIV antibody test, the Jiaxing Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Jiaxing CDC: responsible for disease surveillance and public health management at the municipal level) confirmed the positive result, further laboratory tests revealed a CD4 count (163.4 cells/muL, reference range, 324.60-1274.70 cells/muL) and viral load (153,270 copies/mL, reference range, < 20 copies/mL). Enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed low-density areas in the right lobe of the liver, with a CT value of approximately 30 Hounsfield Unit (HU) and peripheral ring enhancement observed after the administration of contrast material, suggestive of an abscess (Fig. 1, panel A).
The patient had a persistent high fever, prompting ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of the hepatic abscess (PLAD), which yielded a large amount of pus. Bacterial culture of the drained fluid (aerobic and anaerobic) and pre-antibiotic blood cultures (four bottles: 2 aerobic, 2 anaerobic from bilateral arms; three positive: both aerobic, left anaerobic) identified Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhi: identified by biochemical tests (API 20E) and confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS). Using broth microdilution (MIC) and Kirby-Bauer (zone diameter) methods per CLSI 2023 guidelines, the isolate demonstrated susceptibility to: ceftazidime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), cefepime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (MIC <= 1/19 mug/mL), piperacillin-tazobactam (MIC 8 mug/mL), and aztreonam (MIC <= 1 mug/mL). Antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone 2000 mg every 24 h was initiated. However, despite continuous drainage of the liver abscess and targeted anti-Salmonella therapy, the patient continued to have a fever and gradually developed dyspnea. Chest and abdominal CT scans (on the 14th day of hospitalization) showed enlargement of the liver abscess and rupture into the pleural space (Fig. 1, panel B).
Further inquiry into his medical history revealed that the patient had a history of diarrhea and abdominal pain two months before presentation, which resolved spontaneously without treatment, and He originated from an amebiasis-endemic region in China and denied special social history.
Unfortunately, no hospitals or laboratories in southern China currently offer amoebic serological testing. Given the patient's pleuropulmonary involvement and CT findings suggestive of abscess rupture into the pleural space, an ultrasound-guided thoracentesis was performed (on the 14th day of hospitalization), which yielded 1500 mL of a "fish sauce-like" fluid, on the 16th day of hospitalization, mNGS of both pleural and liver abscess drainage fluids detected sequences of Entamoeba histolytica. Additionally, mNGS of the liver abscess drainage fluid revealed sequences of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhi) and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhimurium (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhimurium), then, rapid wet mount microscopic examination of additional liver drainage from drainage tubes fluid revealed unicellular organisms with pseudopods, suggestive of amoebic trophozoites (Fig. 1, panel C)
Combining findings from microscopic examination of the drainage fluid, microbiological culture, radiological imaging, and mNGS results, the diagnosis was confirmed as an amoebic liver abscess complicated by concurrent Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Typhimurium bacterial liver abscesses. Although gastrointestinal endoscopy was recommended by the medical team due to the patient's prior intestinal symptoms, the patient declined further evaluation. However, the possibility of intestinal amoebic infection could not be ruled out. Consequently, the patient was treated with a 10-day regimen of metronidazole (750 mg every 8 h), 26-day ceftriaxone (2000 mg once daily), and paromomycin (500 mg three times daily, initiated 16 days after admission for a 10-day course.) to eradicate cysts in the intestinal lumen.
After treatment, the patient's symptoms resolved, and he was discharged in stable condition. Based on the antibiotic susceptibility testing of the Salmonella Typhi isolate from the aspirate culture, the patient continued oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for four weeks after discharge until inflammatory markers normalized completely and follow-up imaging confirmed complete resolution of the abscess.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old Chinese male presented to the fever clinic in March 2023 with a 1-week history of high fever (peak 39.8 °C) and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week prior to presentation, the patient developed high fevers peaking at 39.8 °C accompanied by right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Further history revealed a self-limited episode of diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 months before presentation that resolved without treatment.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical history; originated from an amebiasis-endemic region in China. Denied prior corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever (39.8 °C), right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and subsequent inpatient dyspnea; history of diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 months prior.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: temperature 38.5 °C, heart rate 119 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 112/69 mmHg.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed normal WBC count (6.72 x 10^9/L; reference 3.5–9.5 x 10^9/L) with elevated neutrophil percentage (77.5%; reference 40–75%), elevated CRP (78.9 mg/L; reference 0–8 mg/L), normal ALT (32 IU/L; reference 9–50 IU/L), and normal AST (40 IU/L; reference 15–40 IU/L). Rapid wet-mount microscopy of hepatic drainage fluid on day 16 revealed motile unicellular trophozoites with pseudopods.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 163.4 cells/µL (reference 324.60–1,274.70 cells/µL). Admission contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated right hepatic lobe low-density lesions (~30 HU) with peripheral ring enhancement consistent with liver abscess, treated with ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage. Repeat chest and abdominal CT on hospital day 14 (performed for persistent fever and new dyspnea) revealed enlargement of the hepatic abscess with transdiaphragmatic rupture into the right pleural cavity, prompting ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielding 1,500 mL of 'fish sauce-like' fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Polymicrobial hepatic abscess (Entamoeba histolytica co-infection with Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi and Salmonella enterica serotype Typhimurium) complicated by transdiaphragmatic rupture and right pleuropulmonary empyema in a newly diagnosed HIV-positive 43-year-old male (confirmed by Jiaxing Municipal CDC positive HIV antibody testing, plasma HIV viral load 153,270 copies/mL [reference <20 copies/mL], and CD4 count 163.4 cells/µL). Pre-antibiotic blood cultures (3 of 4 bottles) and initial hepatic pus cultures isolated Salmonella Typhi (identified by API 20E and MALDI-TOF MS; susceptible per CLSI 2023 to ceftazidime MIC <=1 µg/mL, cefepime MIC <=1 µg/mL, TMP-SMX MIC <=1/19 µg/mL, piperacillin-tazobactam MIC 8 µg/mL, and aztreonam MIC <=1 µg/mL), while day 16 metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of pleural and hepatic drainage fluids detected Entamoeba histolytica, Salmonella Typhi, and Salmonella Typhimurium (corroborated by wet-mount amoebic trophozoites). Treatment consisted of percutaneous hepatic and thoracic drainage, IV ceftriaxone 2,000 mg daily for 26 days, metronidazole 750 mg every 8 hours for 10 days, luminal eradication with oral paromomycin 500 mg TID for 10 days (started day 16), and a 4-week post-discharge course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, achieving complete clinical, biochemical, and radiological resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 35 year old Caucasian female was found to be infected with HIV1 in 1989, when she tested after heterosexual exposure. She was put on zidovudine in 1995, when her CD4 lymphocyte count steadily declined. She took the drug intermittently until 1997, when she was still asymptomatic, with CD4 lymphocytes <100/muL and a high HIV1 viral load (>500 000 copies/mL). In July 1997, she started her first line HAART regimen including stavudine 30 mg twice a day (bid), lamivudine 150 mg bid and indinavir 800 mg 3 times a day. At that time her body weight was stable, her body shape was lean and preserved, with a body mass index (BMI) of 18.3. Adherence and response to treatment were optimal; she reached undetectable viremia (< 400 copies/mL) and a >200/muL CD4 lymphocyte gain by the 12th week of treatment. Since April 1998, the patient complained about remarkable breast size increase, fat accumulation at waist, and a fat pad grown over her lumbar spine. The pad was 7 x 10 x 3 cm in size by July, 1998. At that time indinavir was replaced with ritonavir/saquinavir 400/400 mg bid due to renal stones. Rapidly progressive, severe lipoatrophy at limbs, buttocks and face ensued in the following months, together with a further increase in size of her fat pads. HIV1 viremia remained constantly undetectable; metabolic parameters were normal throughout follow-up, with an isolated abnormal value of triglycerides (306 mg/dL) in August 1998. Adherence to treatment was full until April 2000, when the CD4 lymphocyte count was >500/muL. The patient was offered a simplified regimen, which she refused, preferring a sharp interruption of HAART. At that time, she did not allow us to take pictures. After interrupting HAART, HIV1 viremia rebounded to lower than baseline, remaining <100 000 copies/mL (mode, 25 000 copies/mL) thereafter. CD4 lymphocyte counts declined very slowly; the patient remained asymptomatic, regularly attending her follow-up visits. Her metabolic parameters, including triglycerides, remained within the normal range at all further checks. She decided to carry on without any treatment for over 4 years, until July 2004, when the CD4 lymphocyte count had dropped to 84/muL. Pads of fat accumulation at waist had reverted to nearly normal appearance; the lumbar pad was no longer appreciable; breasts were still enlarged, although to a lesser extent (Fig. 1a). At variance, lipoatrophy was still well evident; the patient admitted partial improvement at upper extremities, whereas she found no improvement at all for buttocks (Fig. 1b) and legs (Fig. 1c and 1d). Her BMI had dropped to 17.3. The patient was offered a new HAART regimen including nevirapine 200 mg bid, tenofovir diproxil 300 mg once a day and lamivudine 150 mg bid; adherence was full until her last visit, on December 23th, 2004, with a CD4 lymphocyte count of 250/muL and a viral load of 1250 copies/mL.
Our observation provides pictorial evidence that severe combined lipodystrophy in our patient was only partially reversible, even under the ideal condition of a long lasting and safe interruption of HAART. Recent reports indicate that the loss of CD4 lymphocytes during treatment interruptions is frequently rapid in patients with a Nadir CD4 lymphocyte count <200/muL and a high rate of cell gain under treatment, irrespective of the level of CD4 lymphocyte count at the interruption of HAART. In spite of that, our patient could safely carry her interruption on for over 4 years, remaining asymptomatic throughout the period, with >200 CD4 T-lymphocytes/muL until late in 2003. She did eat a light and balanced diet; she reported taking L-carnitine (5 grams/daily) since June, 2000, until June, 2001, whereas she denied taking any other drug or supplement possibly interfering with lipid metabolism thereafter. Under these extremely favourable circumstances, sites of lumbar and waist fat accumulation reverted to nearly normal appearance, whereas breasts showed partial improvement (Fig. 1a). Such a clear-cut reversal of fat accumulation has not been reported in controlled trials investigating the efficacy of therapy switches, probably because of persistent interference with lipid metabolism caused by the new antiretroviral drugs.
Severe lipoatrophy at buttocks and legs, instead, was unchanged both on patient's and on our judgment (Fig. 1b, 1c and 1d). Although it is plausible that instrumental measurements at the affected sites might have detected partial improvements, our observation suggests that the loss of peripheral adipose tissue caused by HAART may not be fully reversible after treatment interruption, even in the long run.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old Caucasian woman with HIV-1 infection presented with progressive central fat accumulation (breast enlargement, increased waist circumference, and a dorsocervical/lumbar fat pad) and severe peripheral lipoatrophy of the face, limbs, and buttocks following combination antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with heterosexually acquired HIV-1 in 1989 and treated intermittently with zidovudine monotherapy from 1995 to 1997, she initiated first-line HAART in July 1997 (stavudine 30 mg BID, lamivudine 150 mg BID, and indinavir 800 mg TID) at a lean baseline BMI of 18.3 kg/m2. By April–July 1998, despite optimal viral suppression, she developed marked breast hypertrophy, central abdominal fat accumulation, and a 7 x 10 x 3 cm lumbar spine fat pad. After switching indinavir to ritonavir/saquinavir (400/400 mg BID) in July 1998 due to nephrolithiasis, she developed rapidly progressive severe lipoatrophy of the extremities, buttocks, and face alongside further enlargement of her central fat pads. In April 2000 (with CD4 >500/µL), she elected a complete structured treatment interruption for over 4 years until July 2004.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed in 1989; indinavir-induced nephrolithiasis in July 1998.
subjective.review_of_systems: Asymptomatic for HIV-related opportunistic illnesses throughout follow-up; reported central adiposity (breasts, waist, lumbar pad) and peripheral lipoatrophy (face, arms, legs, buttocks). Took oral L-carnitine (5 g/day) from June 2000 to June 2001.

objective.physical_examination: Baseline BMI in July 1997 was 18.3 kg/m2. By July 1998, she had marked breast enlargement, increased waist adiposity, a 7 x 10 x 3 cm lumbar fat pad, and progressive severe facial, limb, and gluteal lipoatrophy. By July 2004 (after >4 years off HAART), her BMI was 17.3 kg/m2; the lumbar fat pad had completely resolved, waist fat accumulation had reverted to near-normal, and breast enlargement had partially regressed, whereas severe lipoatrophy of the buttocks and legs remained unchanged (with only mild subjective improvement in the upper limbs).
objective.routine_investigations: Fasting metabolic parameters remained within normal limits throughout follow-up except for a single isolated triglyceride elevation of 306 mg/dL in August 1998.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was <100/µL prior to HAART (July 1997), increased by >200/µL by week 12, reached >500/µL at HAART interruption in April 2000, remained >200/µL until late 2003, declined to 84/µL in July 2004, and recovered to 250/µL by December 23, 2004.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HAART-associated severe mixed lipodystrophy syndrome (central lipohypertrophy and peripheral lipoatrophy) in a 35-year-old woman with chronic HIV-1 infection (baseline July 1997 HIV-1 viral load >500,000 copies/mL and CD4 <100/µL; undetectable <400 copies/mL on stavudine/lamivudine/indinavir and ritonavir/saquinavir; rebound viremia mode 25,000 copies/mL [<100,000 copies/mL] during a 4-year treatment interruption from April 2000 to July 2004). Prolonged 4-year HAART interruption demonstrated complete reversal of the lumbar fat pad and waist fat accumulation and partial reduction of breast hypertrophy, but irreversible peripheral lipoatrophy of the buttocks and lower extremities. When her CD4+ count declined to 84/µL in July 2004, she was restarted on a thymidine-analogue-sparing and protease-inhibitor-sparing HAART regimen of nevirapine 200 mg BID, tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg QD, and lamivudine 150 mg BID, achieving a CD4+ count of 250/µL and HIV-1 viral load of 1,250 copies/mL by December 2004.

raw_case_text: A 32-year-old male with HIV presented with a 1-month history of pruritic erythematous scaly patches on the scrotum, groin, and thighs, progressing to painful pustules and erosions in the preceding 4 days. The patient was 174 cm in height and weighed 68 kg. Previous mycological examinations of the scrotum and inguinal regions, conducted at multiple healthcare facilities, consistently yielded negative results. History revealed routine use of "Huoli 28 Disinfectant" (containing benzalkonium chloride) for soaking flat-angle underwear due to HIV-related hygiene practices. Laboratory investigations revealed an HIV viral load below the lower limit of quantification (<1.0E+2 IU/mL). The patient is currently maintained on oral lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine combination therapy.Initial misdiagnosis as eczema showed partial response to corticosteroids but rebounded severely upon discontinuation. Dermatological examination revealed symmetrically distributed dull-red patches, erosions, and pustules involving the scrotum, inguinal regions, and thighs (Figure 1a). A close-up view of the eruption on the right thigh is shown in Figure 1b. Histopathology of thigh lesions revealed hyperkeratosis, granular parakeratosis, granular basophilic keratohyalin granules, intra-corneal pustules, and mild dermal lymphocytic infiltration (Figure 2a). Dermoscopy of the thigh revealed a faint reddish background with relatively uniform dotted and globular vessels, accompanied by mild scaling (Figure 2b). Mycological examination of the scrotum and inguinal region was negative, while direct microscopy of the thigh lesion was positive for fungal elements; culture subsequently identified Candida albicans (Figure 2c). Concurrent CD4+ lymphopenia was observed (CD4+ count: 320 cells/muL; CD4+/CD8+ ratio: 0.58). The present case exhibited the following features: prior exposure to benzalkonium chloride, involvement of intertriginous areas, peripheral parchment-like desquamation, histopathological findings of keratohyalin granules within the stratum corneum, and Candida species isolation on fungal culture. Based on these collective findings, the patient was diagnosed with GP with concomitant candidiasis. Tinea corporis and tinea cruris are common dermatoses in people living with HIV and were therefore key differential diagnoses in this case. The patient was not diagnosed solely with these conditions for the following reasons: repeated mycological examinations of the scrotum and inguinal regions:conducted at multiple hospitals including our institution:were negative; Candida species were only isolated from a culture of the thigh lesion during the current presentation. Notably, the most severely affected area was the medial thigh, a site consistently in close contact with the patient's boxer shorts, which likely led to increased and prolonged exposure to benzalkonium chloride residues. The medial thigh, subjected to the most intense and prolonged exposure to benzalkonium chloride, consequently sustained the greatest compromise to its skin barrier function. This local vulnerability, compounded by the systemic immunosuppression associated with HIV infection, created a permissive environment for secondary candidal infection at this specific site.The cutaneous lesions resolved completely following an 8-day course of intravenous compound glycyrrhizin (60 mL once daily) combined with cessation of benzalkonium chloride exposure.The healing process was documented with serial clinical photographs capturing the daily progression of the cutaneous lesions from days 1 to 8 (Figure 3a-h), along with the follow-up assessment on day 27 (Figure 3i). To allow for more detailed observation, close-up views of the right thigh were obtained, documenting the daily evolution of the skin lesions from days 1 to 8 post-treatment (Figure 4a-h), as well as the follow-up assessment on day 27 (Figure 4i). Notably, on day 2, after fungal microscopy returned positive, topical naphthifine and ketoconazole cream was applied but subsequently discontinued due to reported stinging sensation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 1-month history of pruritic erythematous scaly patches on the scrotum, groin, and thighs that progressed over the preceding 4 days to painful pustules and erosions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, the patient developed pruritic erythematous scaly plaques in his scrotal, inguinal, and thigh regions. He had been misdiagnosed at outside clinics with eczema (with transient partial response to topical corticosteroids followed by severe rebound upon discontinuation) and had multiple negative outside mycological smears of the groin and scrotum. Four days prior to presentation, the lesions progressed to painful pustules and erosions. History revealed routine soaking of his boxer-brief underwear in 'Huoli 28 Disinfectant' containing benzalkonium chloride.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV infection stably maintained on combination antiretroviral therapy; routine exposure of underwear to benzalkonium chloride disinfectant.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for inguinal/scrotal/thigh pruritus, pain, pustules, and erosions. Home medications: oral lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine. Experienced local stinging upon application of topical napftifine-ketoconazole cream.

objective.physical_examination: Height 174 cm, weight 68 kg. Dermatological examination revealed symmetrically distributed dull-red erythematous patches, peripheral parchment-like desquamation, erosions, and pustules involving the scrotum, bilateral inguinal folds, and medial thighs (most severe on the medial thighs contacting his underwear).
objective.routine_investigations: Direct potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture of the scrotum and inguinal folds were negative, whereas direct fungal microscopy of the medial thigh lesion was positive for fungal elements and culture isolated Candida albicans.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 320 cells/µL with a CD4+/CD8+ ratio of 0.58. Dermoscopy of the right thigh lesion showed a faint reddish background with uniform dotted and globular vessels and mild scaling. Skin biopsy histopathology of the thigh lesion demonstrated hyperkeratosis, granular parakeratosis with retained basophilic keratohyalin granules in the stratum corneum, intracorneal pustules, and mild dermal lymphocytic infiltration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Benzalkonium chloride-induced granular parakeratosis (GP) complicated by secondary cutaneous Candida albicans infection in a 32-year-old male with virologically suppressed HIV infection (plasma HIV viral load <1.0 x 10^2 IU/mL, CD4+ count 320 cells/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.58 on lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine). Primary tinea cruris/corporis was excluded by repeatedly negative dermatophyte microscopy and cultures, while GP was confirmed by benzalkonium chloride exposure history and pathognomonic retained stratum corneum basophilic keratohyalin granules on histopathology. Topical napftifine-ketoconazole cream was discontinued on day 2 due to local stinging; the patient was treated with immediate cessation of benzalkonium chloride disinfectant exposure and an 8-day course of intravenous compound glycyrrhizin (60 mL once daily), achieving complete resolution of all cutaneous lesions by day 8 and sustained clearance at day 27 follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old male patient with HIV infection was referred to our department due to recurrent fevers and bilateral axillary masses. The patient was diagnosed with HIV infection in December 2011 and initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) with the following regimen: zidovudine 300 mg every 12 h, lamivudine 300 mg once daily, and nevirapine 200 mg every 12 h. On February 21, 2012, because of hepatotoxicity, the regimen was modified to zidovudine 300 mg every 12 h, lamivudine 300 mg once daily, and lopinavir/ritonavir 500 mg every 12 h, and the viral load suppression was below the lowest detectable limit. Since 2013, he presented recurrent fever, with body temperatures of 38.5 C-39 C, and accompanied by generalized aches and fatigue, coughing, abdominal pain, diarrhea, axilla lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Improvement can be achieved with antimicrobial and symptomatic treatment in private clinics. The fever recurred every 2-3 months and lasted for approximately 4-10 days each time. In 2015, a bone marrow biopsy was performed at other medical facilities with suspicion of lymphoma, and this diagnosis was excluded. Since 2017, he has been admitted to the Department of Hepatology multiple times. The abnormal test results during several hospitalizations are shown in Figure 1. Additionally, Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) antibodies tested positive. Other tests showed no abnormalities, including cytomegalovirus (CMV)-DNA and CMV antibodies, hepatitis B virus antibodies, hepatitis C virus antibodies, autoimmune hepatitis antibodies, brucella antibodies, and bone marrow smears and cultures, as well as blood cultures. Chest CT revealed nodular shadows in the middle lobe of the right lung and multiple nodular high-density shadows in the lower lobes of both lungs. Abdominal CT showed multiple enlarged lymph node shadows in the abdominal cavity, bilateral axillae, and mediastinum, raising suspicion of lymphoma. Despite undergoing numerous examinations, a definitive diagnosis has yet to be established. Key observations included reductions in hemoglobin and platelet counts during fever, accompanied by elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and serum amyloid A (SSA). When the persistent high fever did not respond to treatment, dexamethasone 10 mg was administered via intravenous drip once daily for 3-4 days, which resulted in symptom relief. The patient was hospitalized almost every month. Each time the patient experienced disease flare-ups, the CD4+ T-cell count was markedly reduced. However, following remission, the count increased during ART follow-up (Figure 2). In April 2020, the patient was transferred to our department for further treatment. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) in blood showed that he was infected with KSHV (555 sequence reads). Positron emission tomography/computer tomography (PET/CT) suggested that lymphoma was very likely to be suspected. A biopsy of the right axillary lymph node was conducted, which showed follicular hyperplasia accompanied by conspicuous vascular proliferation in the interfollicular zones, with extensive plasma cell infiltration (Figure 3). Immunohistochemistry confirmed predominantly follicular zone cells CD20(+) and CD79a(+); germinal centers CD10(+), Bcl-6(+), Bcl-2(-), and Ki-67(+, about 80%); follicular dendritic cells CD21(+) and CD23(+); interfollicular zone cells mostly CD2(+), CD3(+), CD5(+), and Ki-67(+, about 20%); and plasma cells MUM1(+). Unfortunately, due to the rarity of the disease and the inexperience of clinicians and pathologists, a specific diagnosis remains elusive. He was given symptomatic treatment with blood transfusion, human albumin infusion, glucocorticoids, and anti-infection. Due to recurrent anemia, the antiretroviral regimen was adjusted to include raltegravir. During this period, his viral load remained below the lower limit of detection. In July 2020, he was transferred to another hospital for hospitalization due to a fever, and during hospitalization, mNGS in blood was reviewed again, which showed that he was infected with KSHV (8327 sequence reads) and EBV (283 sequence reads). Pathological diagnosis showed that the (left cervical lymph node) Castleman's disease was considered. Immunophenotypic analyses showed CD3 (T cell, +), CD20 (B cell,+), CD79alpha (B cell, +), CD21 (FDC network, +), CD43 (T cell, +), CD10 (follicle center, +), BCL-2 (follicle center, -) BCL-6 (follicle center, +), Ki67 (follicle center about 90% +, perifollicle about 30% +), CD30 (few, +), Pax-5 (B cells, +), ALK1 (-), MUM1 (few +), CyclinD1 (few +), CD5 (T cells, +), CD19 (+), CD22 (+), KSHV (+), actin (vasculature,+), and PD-1 (+), IgG4 (few, +). Molecular pathology results: EBER (+). The final diagnosis for the patient was KSHV-MCD. The treatment involved sodium phosphonate (60 mg/kg/d, intravenous drip, once every 8 h),ganciclovir (5 mg/kg/d for KSHV and EBV, lasting 14 days), rituximab (375 mg/m2 once weekly for 4 weeks), combined with thalidomide (50 mg, once daily) for 1.5 years. The patient responded well to treatment and showed no recurrence at the 3-year follow-up. The diagnostic and treatment flowchart for the case is presented in Figure 4. Detailed post-treatment follow-up reports are provided in Figures 1 and 2 and in Table 1.
(a) Each time the patient experienced disease flare-ups, the CD4+ T-cell count was markedly reduced. (b) Following remission, the count increased during ART follow-up.
(a) Hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification x40. The lymph node architecture is preserved, showing prominent follicular hyperplasia with clearly defined follicular structures and interfollicular regions. (b, c) Hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification x100. Follicular hyperplasia accompanied by conspicuous vascular proliferation in the interfollicular zones, with extensive plasma cell infiltration.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old HIV-positive male was referred in April 2020 with a 7-year history of recurrent episodic high fevers and bilateral axillary and generalized lymphadenopathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV in December 2011 and virologically suppressed on ART, the patient began experiencing recurrent 4-to-10-day febrile flares (38.5–39.0 °C) every 2–3 months starting in 2013, accompanied by generalized myalgias, fatigue, cough, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Outside bone marrow biopsy in 2015 excluded lymphoma, and from 2017 onward he required nearly monthly hospitalizations for febrile flares with cytopenias and acute-phase elevations that transiently responded to 3–4 days of IV dexamethasone (10 mg/day) before relapsing.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in December 2011, initially treated with zidovudine 300 mg q12h, lamivudine 300 mg QD, and nevirapine 200 mg q12h, switched on February 21, 2012 due to nevirapine hepatotoxicity to zidovudine 300 mg q12h, lamivudine 300 mg QD, and lopinavir/ritonavir 500 mg q12h (later modified to include raltegravir due to recurrent anemia).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent high fevers (38.5–39.0 °C), generalized aches, fatigue, cough, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and axillary masses. Home medications: antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, lamivudine, lopinavir/ritonavir, later adjusted to raltegravir-based ART).

objective.physical_examination: Febrile during flares (38.5–39.0 °C) with bilateral axillary and cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Disease flares were characterized by recurrent drops in hemoglobin (anemia) and platelet counts (thrombocytopenia) accompanied by markedly elevated CRP, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and serum amyloid A (SAA). EBV antibodies were positive; CMV DNA/antibodies, HBV/HCV antibodies, autoimmune hepatitis antibodies, Brucella antibodies, and blood and bone marrow cultures were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell counts dropped markedly during each febrile flare and rebounded during remissions on ART. Chest CT showed nodular opacities in the right middle lobe and bilateral lower lobes; abdominal CT and FDG-PET/CT demonstrated widespread hepatosplenomegaly and bilateral axillary, mediastinal, and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy. Right axillary lymph node biopsy (April 2020) and left cervical lymph node biopsy (July 2020) demonstrated preserved nodal architecture with follicular hyperplasia, prominent interfollicular vascular proliferation, and dense interfollicular plasma cell infiltration; immunohistochemistry and molecular pathology showed CD20+/CD79a+/Pax-5+ B-cells, CD21+/CD23+ follicular dendritic networks, germinal center CD10+/BCL-6+/BCL-2- (Ki-67 ~80–90%), MUM1+ plasma cells, HHV-8/KSHV (+), and EBER (+).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus-positive multicentric Castleman disease (KSHV-MCD) with EBV co-reactivation in a 44-year-old male with virologically suppressed HIV infection (plasma HIV viral load persistently below the limit of detection on lopinavir/ritonavir- and subsequently raltegravir-based ART). Diagnosis was confirmed by peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detecting KSHV (555 reads in April 2020; 8,327 KSHV reads and 283 EBV reads in July 2020) and definitive lymph node histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirming KSHV-positive, EBER-positive plasmacytic/vascular Castleman disease. Treatment with intravenous foscarnet (sodium phosphonoformate 60 mg/kg/day divided q8h) and ganciclovir (5 mg/kg/day) for 14 days, four weekly infusions of rituximab (375 mg/m2), and oral maintenance thalidomide (50 mg daily for 1.5 years) alongside raltegravir-based ART achieved complete clinical and hematological remission with no recurrence over 3 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old male with adjustment and developmental disorders presented with rapidly progressive neurological symptoms and altered consciousness over 10 days, which prompted transport from a preceding hospital. He had no history of prior opportunistic infections. Findings of the systemic evaluation suggested meningitis and led to the diagnosis of pneumonia, for which empirical antibacterial therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin was initiated. Initial serological testing, prompted by his background as a man who has sex with men, was positive for HIV antigen/antibody and syphilis, prompting transfer for suspected acute HIV with neurological complications.
Upon arrival at our hospital, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13 (eyes, 4; verbal, 3; motor, 6). His vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min on 3-L/min nasal cannula oxygen; peripheral oxygen saturation, 94%; heart rate, 78 beats/min; blood pressure, 136/100 mmHg; and temperature, 36.9 C. Physical examination revealed cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and nuchal rigidity, suggesting meningeal irritation.
Initial laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 9600/muL, severe lymphopenia (lymphocyte 0.8%; 77 cells/muL), and a subsequent CD4+ count of 5.5%, indicative of profound immunosuppression consistent with advanced HIV/acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). The C-reactive protein level was 1.22 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis showed mild hypoxemia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed high opening pressure (23 cmH2O), low cell count (2 cells/muL), elevated protein level (69 mg/dL), and low glucose level (23 mg/dL). Computed tomography (CT) revealed mild lateral ventricular enlargement and diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, suspicious for pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) (Figure 1). Syphilis and suspected PCP were diagnosed. Due to suspicion of severe pneumocystis pneumonia, empirical therapy with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and aqueous prednisolone was initiated in the emergency room. The treatment of suspected PCP was prioritized, leading to the deliberate delay of induction antifungal therapy despite meningitis concerns and consideration of DC.
  Cryptococcus neoformans  was rapidly identified on CSF analysis on hospital Day 1 (Day 1), leading to a diagnosis of DC. Prompt antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine) was subsequently initiated. However, his condition rapidly deteriorated within 10 h. By 18 h, he developed severe hypoxemia (P/F ratio~100), requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. He then sustained two cardiopulmonary arrests, the second necessitating VA-ECMO. The subsequent post-cardiac arrest syndrome was characterized by a no-flow time of 0 min and a low-flow time of a maximum of 17 min. Broad-spectrum antibacterial coverage (meropenem and vancomycin) was initiated for presumed sepsis. The patient also developed severe disseminated intravascular coagulation requiring aggressive transfusion (red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma, ~20 units each on Day 3 due to persistent tracheal bleeding). A CT scan was obtained, which revealed no surgical bleeding source. However, severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, splenic infarction, hepatic ischemia, and extensive bilateral atelectasis were observed (Figure 2A-D). Elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin I level, 12,015 pg/dL; creatine kinase-MB level, 245.5 ng/dL) indicated substantial myocardial damage. Echocardiography revealed severely impaired cardiac function (ejection fraction 10%-20%, diffuse hypokinesis, and pericardial effusion). By Day 4, his neurological prognosis was deemed poor, leading to a transition to palliative care. The patient died on Day 6 of hospitalization.
Postmortem examination revealed cryptococcal infiltration within the myocardial interstitium and capillaries, accompanied by microemboli (Figure 3A). Other findings included severe softening of the brainstem and cerebellum (Figure 3B) and organ necrosis, for example, the liver and spleen (Figure 3C,D). Based on the postmortem findings, the final diagnoses included AIDS, DC, and post-cardiac arrest syndrome, likely due to myocardial microemboli from fungal elements and thrombi.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male was transferred with a 10-day history of rapidly progressive neurological symptoms and altered consciousness alongside pneumonia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 days preceding transfer, the patient developed rapidly worsening altered mental status and meningeal symptoms along with pneumonia (initially treated empirically with ceftriaxone and azithromycin at an outside hospital). Outside screening prompted by his history as a man who has sex with men returned positive for HIV antigen/antibody and syphilis, leading to urgent transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of adjustment and developmental disorders; no prior opportunistic infections. Sexual history notable for men who have sex with men (MSM).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for altered consciousness and respiratory dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: On arrival: Glasgow Coma Scale score 13 (E4V3M6), temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 136/100 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with SpO2 94% on 3 L/min nasal cannula oxygen. Physical examination revealed cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and nuchal rigidity.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed WBC 9,600/µL with profound lymphopenia (0.8%, absolute lymphocyte count 77 cells/µL), CRP 1.22 mg/dL, mild hypoxemia on ABG, and positive HIV Ag/Ab and syphilis serologies. Following cardiopulmonary arrest on day 1, cardiac biomarkers were markedly elevated (troponin I 12,015 pg/dL, CK-MB 245.5 ng/dL) and severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) developed.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell percentage was 5.5%. Head and chest CT on admission showed mild lateral ventriculomegaly and diffuse bilateral ground-glass pulmonary opacities. Lumbar puncture revealed elevated opening pressure (23 cmH2O), acellular/pauci-cellular CSF (2 cells/µL), elevated protein (69 mg/dL), low glucose (23 mg/dL), and rapid identification of Cryptococcus neoformans on hospital day 1. Post-arrest echocardiography demonstrated severe biventricular/left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF 10–20%, diffuse hypokinesis, and pericardial effusion), and whole-body CT showed severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, splenic infarction, hepatic ischemia, and bilateral atelectasis. Postmortem autopsy histopathology demonstrated disseminated cryptococcal infiltration and fungal microemboli/thrombi within the myocardial interstitium and capillaries, brainstem/cerebellar encephalomalacia, and hepatic/splenic necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (positive HIV Ag/Ab combo, CD4+ 5.5%, ALC 77/µL) complicated by fatal disseminated cryptococcosis (cryptococcal meningoencephalitis and cryptococcal myocarditis/myocardial fungal microemboli), neurosyphilis/syphilis co-infection, and suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Initial emergency department prioritization of suspected PCP with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids delayed antifungal initiation until hospital day 1, when CSF analysis confirmed Cryptococcus neoformans and liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine were started. Within 18 hours, the patient progressed to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ~100), suffered two cardiopulmonary arrests requiring veno-arterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) and massive transfusions (~20 units each of RBCs and FFP for DIC/tracheal hemorrhage) alongside meropenem and vancomycin, and died on hospital day 6 after transition to palliative care on day 4.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis C virus coinfection presented with an atypical pharyngeal lesion. He had a history of intravenous drug use and cigarette smoking. He had recently recorded a CD4+ T-cell count nadir below 100 cells/muL due to self-cessation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Three months prior to the lesion appearing, he had been recommenced ART, which included emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir.
A small plaque-like lesion was first noted near his right lower wisdom tooth. As the lesion resembled oral hairy leukoplakia, he was treated with courses of valaciclovir and aciclovir while the lesion relapsed and remitted. After four months, his CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 340 cells/muL and HIV replication was fully suppressed, but this was accompanied by growth of the thick, white, well-circumscribed, exophytic plaque to cover the left tonsil, along with uvula enlargement, a change in voice quality, a dry cough, and bilateral otalgia. There was no lymphadenopathy nor systemic symptoms.
The patient had mild eosinophilia (0.46 x 109/L) with normal levels of other leucocytes. Syphilis serology was negative. A CT scan (Figure 1) demonstrated that the lesion extended from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx. He was commenced on amoxicillin/clavulanic acid orally with no change in the lesion. A left tonsillar biopsy was performed which was complicated by postoperative hemorrhage.
Microscopic examination (Figures 2(A), 2(B), 2(C), and 2(D)) of the tonsil revealed a dense inflammatory cell infiltrate consisting largely of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. There was exocytosis of eosinophils into the overlying squamous mucosa and vascular proliferation comprising of numerous thin-walled capillary-sized vessels arranged in a lobular pattern. Foci of necrosis were present, some of which were centered around blood vessels, but there was no vasculitis. The B- and T-cell markers were of a benign mixed pattern, excluding a lymphoproliferative process.
The biopsy demonstrated a reactive process with unusual areas of necrosis, although no opportunistic infection was identified: no fungi were seen on the methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff stains; the Warthin-Starry stain for spirochetes was negative; no acid-fast bacilli were seen; and Cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and LMP1 for Epstein-Barr virus immunoperoxidase stains were negative. The vascular proliferation and eosinophilia were most consistent with angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia; however, the vessels lacked the classic cobblestone endothelial lining, and the location in the tonsil was not typical. The presence of eosinophilia, along with the clinical picture, distinguishes this from pyogenic granuloma, which is seen on the oral mucosa but is characterized by a classic red polypoid appearance.
Despite various treatments including antibiotics, antivirals, and surgical debridement, the lesion continued to wax and wane, but after 48 months, it resolved completely, possibly due to immune control.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old man with HIV and hepatitis C virus co-infection presented with a persistent, enlarging white exophytic tonsillar and oropharyngeal plaque, uvular swelling, voice change, dry cough, and bilateral otalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following self-cessation of antiretroviral therapy and a CD4+ nadir <100 cells/µL, the patient restarted ART (emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir) 3 months prior to first noticing a small plaque near his right lower third molar. Initially treated with courses of valaciclovir and aciclovir for presumed oral hairy leukoplakia with waxing and waning behavior, over the ensuing 4 months—coinciding with immune recovery to a CD4+ count of 340 cells/µL and full HIV viral suppression—the lesion expanded into a thick, white, well-circumscribed exophytic plaque covering the left tonsil with uvular enlargement, dysphonia, dry cough, and bilateral referred ear pain, unresponsive to oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV and hepatitis C virus co-infection; history of prior ART interruption with CD4+ nadir <100 cells/µL; history of intravenous drug use and cigarette smoking.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pharyngeal mass sensation, altered voice quality, dry cough, and bilateral otalgia; negative for fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. Home medications: emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir.

objective.physical_examination: Oropharyngeal examination revealed a thick, white, well-circumscribed exophytic plaque covering the left palatine tonsil accompanied by uvular enlargement, without cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count showed mild eosinophilia (0.46 x 10^9/L) with normal remaining leukocyte subsets. Syphilis serology was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had risen from a nadir of <100 cells/µL to 340 cells/µL. Neck CT demonstrated a mass lesion extending from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx. Left tonsillar biopsy (complicated by postoperative hemorrhage) demonstrated a dense reactive polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with mucosal eosinophilic exocytosis, lobular capillary-sized vascular proliferation (lacking cobblestone endothelium), and perivascular necrosis without vasculitis. B- and T-cell immunohistochemistry showed a benign polyclonal mixed pattern, and special stains/immunoperoxidase for GMS, PAS, Warthin-Starry (spirochetes), AFB, CMV, HSV, and EBV LMP1 were all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Atypical reactive angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia (ALHE)-like naso-oropharyngeal lesion associated with immune reconstitution following ART re-initiation in a 35-year-old male with HIV/HCV co-infection (suppressed HIV viral load and CD4+ T-cell recovery from <100 to 340 cells/µL on emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir). Lymphoma, syphilis, fungal/mycobacterial infections, HSV, CMV, EBV oral hairy leukoplakia, and classic pyogenic granuloma were excluded via histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and negative special stains. Despite trials of oral antibiotics, antivirals, and surgical debridement, the lesion waxed and waned before achieving complete spontaneous resolution after 48 months of sustained immune control on ART.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old male with no family history of autoimmune diseases or thrombotic events and no chronic degenerative diseases began experiencing his current condition on June 9, 2025, at approximately 8:30 a.m. Upon waking up, presenting with sudden onset paresthesia in the upper and lower extremities of the left side of the body, lasting approximately two hours. The initial symptoms were accompanied by muscle stiffness in the left side of the body, generalized weakness, paresthesia in the left side of the face, and predominantly distal dysesthesia, with preserved consciousness and speech. He therefore went to the emergency department, with initial vital signs of blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, heart rate 88 beats per minute, saturation 94% in ambient air, and temperature 36.2 degrees.
Neurological evaluation of the left lower extremity revealed hyperreflexia, increased muscle tone, and a positive Babinski sign, consistent with left upper motor neuron (UMN) syndrome. He had a strength of 3/5 on the Daniels scale in his left upper limb and 3/5 in his left lower limb, with decreased fine sensitivity in the ipsilateral upper limb. His initial National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 12 points, corresponding to a moderate neurological deficit, and his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15.
Due to suspicion of a stroke, a plain computed tomography (CT) scan of the skull was performed, which revealed an ischemic cerebrovascular accident in the right parietal lobe, including the semioval center (Figure 1). Given the time elapsed since the onset of symptoms exceeding 4.5 hours, the patient was not a candidate for intravenous thrombolysis, nor did he meet the imaging or clinical criteria for mechanical thrombectomy. The neurology department expanded its investigations to determine the etiology of the stroke in this young patient. A carotid Doppler ultrasound was requested and showed no significant atheromatous plaques, but did reveal findings consistent with vertebrobasilar insufficiency. The transthoracic echocardiogram showed no septal defects, valvular heart disease, patent foramen ovale, or cardiometabolic sources. Blood tests were uneventful, with a lipid profile showing triglycerides 158 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 52 mg/dL, and HDL cholesterol 15 mg/dL, and a coagulation profile showing prothrombin time (PT) 12 seconds and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 28 seconds. 
Given the patient's age, the absence of associated risk factors, and the suspicion of a prothrombotic state, markers for autoimmune diseases were requested, with positive results for lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies (Table 1), which led us to suspect primary antiphospholipid syndrome as the cause of the stroke. Viral serology tests are requested for hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The HIV test is reactive, so viral load and Western Blot tests are requested for confirmation, confirming the presence of infection with a viral load of 1,117,549 and a CD4 count of 23 cells/microl, which tested positive for human immunodeficiency virus type I (Table 1).
Treatment begins with high-intensity statins, antiplatelet agents (acetylsalicylic acid), anticoagulants based on vitamin K antagonists (VKA), prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, as well as antiretroviral therapy and physical rehabilitation to enable the patient to resume basic and instrumental activities of daily living. Confirmation of antiphospholipid antibody positivity was performed at 12 weeks (Table 2). The INR targets are monitored very closely, as they are currently not on target. Currently progressing well and undergoing multidisciplinary follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presented to the emergency department on June 9, 2025 with sudden-onset left-sided facial, upper, and lower extremity paresthesias, left-sided muscle stiffness, and left hemiparesis upon awakening.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At approximately 8:30 a.m. on June 9, 2025, upon waking, the patient experienced sudden-onset paresthesias and predominantly distal dysesthesias involving the left face and left upper and lower extremities lasting ~2 hours, accompanied by left-sided muscle stiffness and weakness with preserved consciousness and speech. He presented to the emergency department more than 4.5 hours after symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic degenerative diseases; family history negative for autoimmune diseases or thromboembolic events.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left hemibody paresthesia/dysesthesia, stiffness, and weakness; negative for loss of consciousness or aphasia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, SpO2 94% on room air, and temperature 36.2 °C. Neurological examination showed GCS 15, NIHSS score of 12, left upper and lower limb motor strength of 3/5 (Daniels scale), decreased fine touch sensation in the left upper limb, and a left upper motor neuron syndrome with left lower extremity hyperreflexia, spastic hypertonia, and a positive left Babinski sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests showed triglycerides 158 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 52 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 15 mg/dL, PT 12 seconds, and PTT 28 seconds. Autoimmune prothrombotic workup was positive for lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies (confirmed positive on repeat testing at 12 weeks). Viral serologies were negative for HBV and HCV and reactive for HIV. Carotid Doppler ultrasound showed no significant carotid atheroma but suggested vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 23 cells/µL. Non-contrast head CT demonstrated an acute-to-subacute ischemic stroke in the right parietal lobe involving the centrum semiovale. Transthoracic echocardiogram excluded valvular disease, septal defects, patent foramen ovale, or cardioembolic sources.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute right parietal ischemic stroke (NIHSS 12) secondary to antiphospholipid syndrome (persistent lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin positivity confirmed at 12 weeks) unmasking previously undiagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (confirmed by reactive HIV screening, positive HIV-1 Western blot, plasma HIV-1 viral load of 1,117,549 copies/mL, and CD4+ T-cell count of 23 cells/µL). Because presentation exceeded the 4.5-hour window and thrombectomy criteria, acute reperfusion was not performed; he was initiated on high-intensity statin therapy, aspirin, vitamin K antagonist (VKA) oral anticoagulation with close INR monitoring, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, antiretroviral therapy, and physical rehabilitation, with favorable functional recovery on multidisciplinary follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old male with a history of HIV (diagnosed in 2015) presented to our emergency department with abdominal pain. Over the past 2 weeks, he reported flu-like syndrome, spiking fevers, chills, abdominal pain, daily diarrhea, 10 lb weight loss, dyspnea on exertion, and sudden appearance of tender, growing, non-pruritic skin lesions starting on the back and spreading to the face, trunk, and extremities. The patient also reported tender, crusted sores on his lip with associated dysphagia. He denied recent travel, sick contacts, or drug use. He was last sexually active (male partner) using protection approximately 1 year prior to presentation.
Physical examination showed scattered umbilicated plaques with an erythematous border and central necrosis, present on the face, trunk, and extremities (Fig. 1a, b). There was erosion of the lips with yellow fibrinous tissue. There was a large, ulcerated, indurated verrucous plaque of the gluteal crease and surrounding white papules and erythema (Fig. 1c). During the hospital course, the patient continued to have intermittent fevers but remained hemodynamically stable.
Punch biopsy of the left arm showed thickened cells with viral cytopathic changes. In situ hybridization was positive for monkeypox (Mpox) infection. Biopsy of the perineum showed ulcerated, hyperplastic skin with hyper/parakeratosis. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) was identified by immunohistochemistry and Mpox by in situ hybridization. Herpes simplex virus (HSV)/varicella zoster virus swab of the lower lip erosions showed HSV-1. Wound culture of the gluteal abscess was positive for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Respiratory pathogen polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panel detected adenovirus and rhinovirus/enterovirus.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed para-aortic (Fig. 2a) and external iliac (Fig. 2b) lymphadenopathy, and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed enlarged, centrally necrotic inguinal, internal iliac, and perirectal lymph nodes with no evidence of visceral involvement. Inguinal lymph node biopsy revealed an atretic appearing lymph node with a small focus of spindle cell proliferation associated with slit-like vasculature and red blood cell extravasation, morphologically consistent with KS and confirmed by immunoreactivity for HHV8 in the spindle cells adjacent to the CD34+ vasculature (Fig. 3a). A large necrotic area was observed in the same lymph node (Fig. 3b) with the necrotic cells showing abundant in situ hybridization for Mpox (Fig. 3c). Excisional biopsy of the right cervical lymph node (3 cm) showed focal involvement of KS with granulomatous (many non-necrotizing, few necrotizing) inflammation, supportive of abscess and granulation tissue with acute inflammation. Pancytokeratin stain was negative. Positive acid-fast bacilli were occasionally observed. The background lymph node appeared atretic with patchy plasmacytosis. HHV8+ plasmablasts were scarce.
PCR analysis for HHV8 viral load was 90,600 copies/mL maximum. HIV viral load was 67,300 copies/mL and CD4 count was 21 cells/muL. Laboratory studies showed elevated ferritin (2,528 ng/mL at maximum), C-reactive protein (143 mg/L at maximum), globulins (5.6 g/dL maximum), neutropenia (0.09 x 103 cells/muL minimum), and low hemoglobin (6.0 g/dL minimum). Inflammatory markers were elevated, including IL-2 receptor (1,737 pg/mL maximum), IL-6 (100 pg/mL maximum), and IL-10 (212.4 pg/mL maximum). Screenings for tuberculosis, cryptococcus, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Chest CT revealed pulmonary embolism (PE), and bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
Bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir (Biktarvy) 50-200-25 mg daily was initiated at admission. The patient was treated for Mpox with 600 mg tecovirimat twice daily. Hydroxyzine 10 mg as needed was prescribed for pruritus, and MediHoney wound gel was applied to crusted nodules to facilitate wound healing. Valacyclovir 1,000 mg twice daily was given for HHV8 suppression. Valganciclovir 450 mg twice daily was prescribed for CMV infection. MRSA infection was treated with linezolid 600 mg twice daily, later changed to daptomycin 10 mg/kg daily. Incision and drainage and diverting loop colostomy were performed for his gluteal abscess. His PEs and DVTs were managed with a heparin drip, later changed to apixaban 5 mg twice daily.
Approximately two months after initial presentation, the patient's cytopenia and intermittent fevers resolved. The HHV8 viral load decreased to 22,300 copies/mL and then to 3,600 copies/mL 1 week later prior to discharge. HIV viral load decreased to 54 copies/mL. Inflammatory markers IL-2 receptor, IL-6, and IL-10 also decreased to 935 pg/mL, 4.1 pg/mL, and 11.8 pg/mL, respectively. The patient was discharged with antimicrobials, ART, and wound care instructions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old HIV-positive male presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of abdominal pain, spiking fevers, chills, daily diarrhea, 10-lb weight loss, exertional dyspnea, painful crusted lip sores with dysphagia, and disseminated tender umbilicated skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 weeks preceding presentation, the patient developed a flu-like illness with spiking fevers, chills, abdominal pain, daily diarrhea, a 10-lb weight loss, dyspnea on exertion, painful crusted lip erosions causing dysphagia, and non-pruritic tender skin lesions that began on his back and spread to his face, trunk, extremities, and gluteal cleft.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection in 2015. Denied recent travel, sick contacts, or illicit drug use; last sexual contact was protected intercourse with a male partner approximately 1 year prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for spiking fevers, chills, 10-lb weight loss, abdominal pain, daily diarrhea, dysphagia, exertional dyspnea, lip sores, and disseminated tender skin plaques.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable with intermittent fevers. Cutaneous and mucosal examination revealed scattered umbilicated plaques with erythematous borders and central necrosis across the face, trunk, and extremities; lower lip erosions covered by yellow fibrinous exudate; and a large ulcerated, indurated verrucous plaque in the gluteal crease surrounded by white papules, erythema, and a gluteal abscess.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation showed severe anemia (hemoglobin nadir 6.0 g/dL), severe neutropenia (ANC nadir 0.09 x 10^3 cells/µL), hypergammaglobulinemia (globulins peak 5.6 g/dL), elevated ferritin (peak 2,528 ng/mL), elevated CRP (peak 143 mg/L), and elevated inflammatory cytokines: soluble IL-2 receptor (peak 1,737 pg/mL), IL-6 (peak 100 pg/mL), and IL-10 (peak 212.4 pg/mL). Lower lip swab was positive for HSV-1; gluteal abscess wound culture grew MRSA; respiratory pathogen PCR panel detected adenovirus and rhinovirus/enterovirus; screenings for tuberculosis, Cryptococcus, Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, and Toxoplasma were negative. Bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound demonstrated deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 21 cells/µL. Chest CT revealed pulmonary embolism (PE); abdominal CT and pelvic MRI demonstrated para-aortic, external iliac, and centrally necrotic inguinal, internal iliac, and perirectal lymphadenopathy without visceral masses. Left arm punch biopsy showed viral cytopathic changes positive for mpox by in situ hybridization (ISH); perineal biopsy showed mpox ISH positivity and CMV immunohistochemistry positivity. Inguinal and right cervical (3 cm) lymph node biopsies demonstrated nodal Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8+ spindle cell proliferation with CD34+ slit-like vascular spaces) co-localized with extensive mpox ISH-positive necrosis and occasional acid-fast bacilli.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Advanced uncontrolled HIV/AIDS (plasma HIV viral load 67,300 copies/mL, CD4+ count 21 cells/µL) complicated by severe disseminated mpox (cutaneous, perineal, and necrotizing lymphadenitis), nodal Kaposi sarcoma with HHV-8 viremia (plasma HHV-8 PCR peak 90,600 copies/mL), mucocutaneous CMV and HSV-1 co-infections, MRSA gluteal abscess, adenovirus/rhinovirus respiratory co-infection, and deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism. Management included initiation of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Biktarvy 50/200/25 mg daily), oral tecovirimat 600 mg twice daily for mpox, valganciclovir 450 mg twice daily for CMV, valacyclovir 1,000 mg twice daily for HSV-1/HHV-8, linezolid 600 mg BID transitioned to daptomycin 10 mg/kg daily plus incision/drainage and diverting loop colostomy for the gluteal MRSA abscess, MediHoney wound care, and IV unfractionated heparin transitioned to apixaban 5 mg BID for PE/DVT. After 2 months, fevers and cytopenias resolved, HIV viral load fell to 54 copies/mL, HHV-8 viral load declined to 3,600 copies/mL, and inflammatory cytokines normalized (sIL-2R 935 pg/mL, IL-6 4.1 pg/mL, IL-10 11.8 pg/mL), allowing hospital discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old married male, office worker,diagnosed with HIV in 2011 (baseline CD4+ count: 84 cells/microl; initial viral load undocumented), was initially treated with AZT/3TC/NVP. He switched to bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide in May 2022. In March 2022, he developed painless lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions, with the largest node being chestnut-sized, firm, smooth, and mobile. There was no fever, erythema, discharge, or skin adhesion. The patient did not seek medical care initially.
On June 18, 2022, he presented to Tianjin Second People's Hospital with mildly enlarged cervical nodes. A biopsy on June 22 suggested reactive hyperplasia. PET-CT on June 29 revealed widespread lymphadenopathy with elevated FDG uptake, based on diffuse, symmetric nodal uptake and absence of focal destructive lesions, including bilateral cervical (max SUV 11.03), axillary (max SUV 10.03), thoracic, abdominal, and inguinal nodes(Figure 1). Although lymphoma was suspected, inflammatory changes were considered more likely. The patient received treatment with glucocorticoids. and was discharged with follow-up advice.
He returned on July 4 with new-onset fever (up to 39.5  C), fatigue, anorexia, chest tightness, dyspnea, and progressive lymph node enlargement. Repeat lymph node puncture again indicated reactive proliferation. Bone marrow biopsy with histopathological examination and flow cytometry, which showed no lymphoma infiltration. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of lymph node tissue detected HHV-8 and EBV. Symptoms improved with anti-infective and glucocorticoid therapy, and he was discharged after lymph node regression. On August 27, he was readmitted with recurrent high fever and worsening lymphadenopathy, prompting referral to our hospital.
Physical examination at admission showed enlarged, firm, non-tender, mobile lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions:the largest being egg-sized:without erythema or ulceration. Vital signs were stable, and systemic examination was otherwise normal.
Lab tests showed a CD4+ count of 435 cells/microl, CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.44, and undetectable HIV viral load. Notable findings included thrombocytopenia (85x109/L), mild anemia (Hb 118 g/L), and elevated inflammatory markers: ESR 69 mm/h, CRP 68.33 mg/L, and IL-6 21.86 pg/mL. Liver and kidney function were normal. Syphilis serology was positive (TPPA+, RPR 1:2). EBV IgG positive, EBV DNA negative. Chest CT suggested possible lymph node space-occupying lesions. Abdominal CT revealed splenomegaly, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and a cystic lesion in the right inguinal region.
After the results of the puncture biopsy could not confirm the diagnosis, a resection biopsy was eventually performed to make a definite diagnosis. Excisional biopsy of cervical and inguinal nodes confirmed the diagnosis: histology showed follicular hyperplasia with mantle zone expansion exhibiting an "onion-skin" pattern, vascular proliferation, and HHV-8 positivity on immunohistochemistry. These findings supported HHV-8+ multicentric Castleman disease, plasma cell type (Figures 2, 3).
The patient was diagnosed with HIV-associated HHV-8+ multicentric Castleman disease and latent syphilis. Treatment began on September 22, 2022, with four weekly cycles of rituximab (375 mg/m2) and etoposide (100 mg/m2). Syphilis was treated with benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units IM weekly for three weeks).Persist in using bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for HIV treatment.
A follow-up PET-CT scan in January 2023 revealed significant therapeutic improvement, characterized by a marked reduction in the size and number of lymph nodes across all previously involved regions, along with substantially decreased FDG uptake (SUVmax 2.52, mean 1.76), indicating an excellent treatment response (Figure 4). Throughout 36 months of continuous monitoring, the patient has maintained sustained complete remission with no evidence of disease recurrence (Table 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old married male office worker with HIV presented with a 5-month history of progressive generalized lymphadenopathy and a 2-month history of recurrent high fevers (up to 39.5 °C), fatigue, anorexia, chest tightness, and dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In March 2022, the patient noticed painless, mobile, chestnut-sized cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. In June 2022, initial fine-needle/core biopsy suggested reactive hyperplasia and FDG-PET/CT (June 29, 2022) showed diffuse hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy (cervical SUVmax 11.03, axillary SUVmax 10.03), transiently improving with glucocorticoids. On July 4, 2022, and again on August 27, 2022, he was hospitalized with recurrent high fevers up to 39.5 °C, fatigue, anorexia, chest tightness, dyspnea, and progressive nodal enlargement to egg size.
