subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection in 2011 (baseline CD4+ count 84 cells/µL), treated initially with zidovudine/lamivudine/nevirapine (AZT/3TC/NVP) and switched in May 2022 to bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent high fever (up to 39.5 °C), fatigue, anorexia, chest tightness, dyspnea, and generalized painless lymphadenopathy. Home medication: bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were stable on admission; physical examination revealed multiple enlarged (up to egg-sized), firm, smooth, mobile, non-tender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes without overlying erythema, ulceration, or skin adherence.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 118 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 85 x 10^9/L), normal hepatic and renal function, elevated ESR (69 mm/h), elevated CRP (68.33 mg/L), and elevated IL-6 (21.86 pg/mL). Syphilis serology was positive (TPPA positive, RPR titer 1:2); EBV IgG was positive with negative plasma EBV DNA.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 435 cells/µL with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.44. Baseline FDG-PET/CT showed diffuse symmetric hypermetabolic cervical, axillary, thoracic, abdominal, and inguinal lymphadenopathy; chest and abdominal CT showed nodal enlargement, splenomegaly, and a right inguinal cystic lesion. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry excluded lymphoma, while lymph node mNGS detected HHV-8 and EBV. Excisional biopsy of cervical and inguinal lymph nodes confirmed HHV-8-positive multicentric Castleman disease (plasma cell type), demonstrating follicular hyperplasia with 'onion-skin' mantle zone expansion, interfollicular vascular proliferation, plasma cell sheets, and HHV-8 immunohistochemical positivity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HIV-associated HHV-8-positive multicentric Castleman disease (MCD, plasma cell variant) and concurrent latent syphilis in a 65-year-old male with virologically suppressed HIV infection (undetectable plasma HIV viral load, CD4+ count 435 cells/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.44 on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide). Confirmed via excisional cervical and inguinal lymph node histopathology, HHV-8 immunohistochemistry, and nodal mNGS after two prior needle biopsies showed nonspecific reactive hyperplasia. Starting September 22, 2022, he was treated with four weekly cycles of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2) plus etoposide (100 mg/m2) alongside intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units weekly for 3 weeks for latent syphilis) and continued bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Follow-up PET-CT in January 2023 demonstrated marked nodal regression and metabolic resolution (SUVmax reduced from 11.03 to 2.52), and the patient maintained complete remission over 36 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 48 year-old black female presented at the Medunsa Oral Health Center with a large swelling of the left side of her face, and proptosis of her left eye (figure 1). The facial mass was firm and immobile. The nasolabial furrow was obliterated by the swelling, the nose was displaced to the right and the tumour was fungating from the left nostril. Intraorally, there was a large soft tissue mass growing from the maxilla, and extending from the left side across the midline. A large portion of this mass was necrotic (figure 2). The patient stated that the facial swelling had rapidly enlarged over the previous month, and that she had recently lost the sight of her left eye. Because of language and cultural difficulties in communication, we could not determine why she had not received medical attention before our consultation.
Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen from the intraoral mass showed a neoplastic plasma cell tumour. The densely packed tumour cells were mainly plasmablasts with prominent nucleoli (figure 3). Aspiration of bone marrow from the femur demonstrated plasmacytosis (9% of the myelogram) without an increased number of blasts. The plasma cells were preponderantly mature with occasional binucleated forms. A trephine biopsy of bone marrow was not done, so the clonality of the plasma cell population could not be determined. Erythropoiesis was reduced.
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation showed IgG kappa monoclonal protein. Both serum IgG (35.89 g/L, reference range 7.00 - 16.00) and kappa light chain (8.4 gr/L, reference range 0.6 - 1.3) were elevated. The patient was HIV-seropositive with a CD4+ T cell count of 41 x 10-6/L, and the percentage of CD4 lymphocytes was 9.06. There was normocytic normochromic anemia, lymphopenia, and a high platelet count. Serum calcium and creatin levels were normal. A skeletal survey excluding the head showed no abnormalities. Ophtalmological examination confirmed blindness of the patient's left eye.
Computed tomography revealed a large soft tissue mass measuring 12 cm x 12 cm that had caused destruction of the left maxillary ethmoid sinus, the sphenoid sinuses and the left nasal cavity, and extended intra-cranially into the anterior cranial fossa (figure 4) The intra-orbital tumour mass caused severe proptosis of the left eye (figure 5). The mass involved the left nasopharynx, as well as the parotid and masseteric spaces and the buccal tissues on the left side. The left submandibular space and the floor of the mouth were also affected by the tumour (figure 6). The mandible appeared normal but had been displaced, without evidence of osteolytic or sclerotic lesions. The tumour mass appeared heterogeneous with hypodense areas of necrosis (figure 7). Bilateral enlarged cervical lymphnodes were evident at various levels of the radiographic cuts.
A diagnosis of myeloma was made and the patient was referred to the regional hospital where she died 5 days later from respiratory complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old Black female presented with a 1-month history of a rapidly enlarging left facial and intraoral maxillary swelling, left ocular proptosis, and recent left eye blindness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the month preceding consultation at the Medunsa Oral Health Center, the patient experienced rapid enlargement of a firm left maxillofacial and intraoral mass that displaced her nose, obliterated the left nasolabial fold, fungated through the left nostril, and caused severe left eye proptosis and complete loss of vision in the left eye.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical records available due to language and cultural communication barriers.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for rapid left facial swelling, nasal obstruction/fungating mass, intraoral necrotic mass, and left visual loss.

objective.physical_examination: Extraoral examination revealed a large, firm, immobile left facial mass obliterating the left nasolabial sulcus, displacing the nose to the right, fungating out of the left nostril, and causing severe proptosis and confirmed blindness of the left eye. Intraoral examination revealed a large, extensively necrotic soft-tissue mass arising from the left maxilla and extending across the hard palate midline.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests demonstrated normocytic normochromic anemia, lymphopenia, thrombocytosis, and normal serum calcium and creatinine. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation revealed an IgG kappa monoclonal paraprotein with markedly elevated serum IgG (35.89 g/L; reference 7.00–16.00 g/L) and elevated kappa light chains (8.4 g/L; reference 0.6–1.3 g/L). Extra-cranial skeletal survey showed no other osteolytic lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 41 x 10^6/L (CD4% = 9.06%). Head and neck CT demonstrated a heterogeneous 12 x 12 cm necrotic soft-tissue mass destroying the left maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses and left nasal cavity, extending intracranially into the anterior cranial fossa, intraorbitally causing severe left proptosis, and invading the left nasopharynx, parotid, masseteric, buccal, submandibular, and floor-of-mouth spaces with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Incisional biopsy of the intraoral mass revealed densely packed neoplastic plasmablasts with prominent nucleoli, and femoral bone marrow aspiration showed 9% plasma cells (predominantly mature with occasional binucleated forms) and reduced erythropoiesis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Aggressive maxillofacial plasmablastic multiple myeloma (IgG kappa monoclonal gammopathy with 12 x 12 cm sinonasal/maxillary/intracranial/orbital plasmablastic tumor and 9% marrow plasmacytosis) in a newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS patient (HIV-seropositive, CD4+ T-cell count 41 x 10^6/L [9.06%]). The patient was referred to the regional tertiary hospital for oncologic and HIV management but died 5 days later from respiratory complications.

raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old HIV-positive man, who had been treated at our hospital since 1995 for HIV, hepatitis C, and hemophilia, had profuse diarrhea (6-8 episodes/day), fever as high as 39.9 C, and 10 kg of body weight loss in 5 weeks. Laboratory findings included hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, pseudocholinesterase 2,099 U/L, HIV-DNA virus count 500 copies/mL, CD4+ lymphocyte count 29 x 106/mL, and C-reactive protein 76 mg/L. Stained colon tissue samples, bone marrow punch, and liver biopsy showed abundant acid-fast bacilli. Endoscopic findings on colonoscopy were multiple polypoid lesions approximately 5 mm in size in the transverse and sigmoid colon.
Microbiologic analyses included culture for mycobacteria (liquid media: BACTEC 460TB or MGIT [Becton, Dickinson and Company, Cockeysville, MD] and solid media produced in-house, all media without supplementation of mycobactin) from at least 21 specimens (blood, urine, sputum, biopsy, feces) over a 3-year period. Of these, eight specimens (blood, feces, and biopsy) were positive for mycobacteria in liquid media after 6 to 16 weeks of incubation. Subcultures remained negative on Lowenstein-Jensen slants but after approximately 4 weeks became positive on mycobactin-supplemented Middlebrook slants with colorless dysgonic colonies. Microscopic examination of these colonies showed acid-fast bacilli (Figure 1).
For species identification, AccuProbe assays (Gen-Probe, San Diego, CA) for M. avium complex were performed on liquid media, all yielding strong positive results. However, repeated attempts to perform drug-susceptibility testing in the liquid BACTEC 460TB system were unsuccessful because of insufficient growth of the control. Since M. avium complex usually grows very well, the primary identification was questionable. Thus, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for the amplification of a part of the mycobacterial gene coding for the ribosomal 16S RNA and additional sequencing was performed from two positive cultures. The resulting sequence was compared with those stored in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database, showing the signature sequence of M. avium/M. paratuberculosis, which is identical for both species and confirmed the AccuProbe results. For further differentiation between M. avium and MAP, PCR targeting the insertion sequence IS900 (primer: IS900-1: 5  TGTTCGGGGCCGTCGCTTAG; IS900-2: 5 -CGTTCCAGCGCCGAAAGTAT), which is present only in MAP strains, was done with the two most recent positive cultures. This assay showed clearly positive results from the two cultures tested and the MAP type strain, while the M. avium strains remained negative (Figure 2).
Because acid-fast bacilli were identified in biopsy specimens, treatment was started with ethambutol, ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, and rifabutin. Initially, no clinical improvement was observed, and the patient's weight loss and daily fever of 39C -40 C continued. When ciprofloxacin was replaced with levofloxacin, progression of the infection appeared to stop. However, the patient died from cardiorespiratory failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old HIV-positive man with hemophilia presented with a 5-week history of profuse watery diarrhea (6–8 episodes/day), high fever up to 39.9 °C, and a 10 kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 5 weeks prior to evaluation, the patient developed profuse diarrhea (6–8 stools daily), persistent high spiking fevers up to 39.9 °C, and a 10 kg unintentional weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated at the hospital since 1995 for HIV infection, chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and hemophilia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for profuse diarrhea (6–8 times/day), high fever (39.9 °C), and 10 kg weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (up to 39.9–40.0 °C) and cachectic following a 10 kg weight loss over 5 weeks.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, pseudocholinesterase 2,099 U/L, and CRP 76 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ lymphocyte count was 29 cells/µL. Colonoscopy revealed multiple ~5 mm polypoid lesions across the transverse and sigmoid colon. Histopathological staining of colonic mucosal biopsies, bone marrow punch biopsy, and liver biopsy all demonstrated abundant acid-fast bacilli.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) infection (involving blood, colon, liver, and bone marrow) in a 36-year-old man with hemophilia, chronic hepatitis C, and advanced AIDS (CD4+ count 29 cells/µL, HIV viral load 500 copies/mL). Eight of 21 clinical specimens (blood, feces, and tissue biopsies) grew mycobacteria in liquid media (BACTEC 460TB/MGIT) after 6–16 weeks that failed to grow on standard Löwenstein-Jensen slants but formed dysgonic colonies on mycobactin-supplemented Middlebrook slants; definitive identification of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis was confirmed by positive MAC AccuProbe, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and positive MAP-specific IS900 insertion sequence PCR. Initial quadruple therapy with ethambutol, clarithromycin, rifabutin, and ciprofloxacin failed to control his daily 39–40 °C fevers and wasting; substituting levofloxacin for ciprofloxacin halted clinical progression, but the patient ultimately died of cardiorespiratory failure.

raw_case_text:
In August 2005 a 43-year old woman with known HIV infection since 1998 presented in the emergency department with post-prandial abdominal pain and important weight loss (10 kg) over 4 months. HIV infection was treated since 2000 with a HAART including didanosine, lamivudine and abacavir. At admission her absolute CD4 count was 279/mm3 and HIV viremia 270,000 copies/ml. Diffuse lymphoadenopathy, splenomegaly and ascites were observed associated with biochemical abnormalities of the liver parameters: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were 1.5 times upper normal range, alkaline phosphatase (AP) twice and gamma-glutamyltransferase (gammaGT) four times above normal values. There was neither alcohol intake nor toxic exposure; screening was negative for viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HDV, HCV and HEV), CMV and EBV, autoimmune hepatitis (antinuclear antibodies, antiactin antibodies and total serum immunoglobulins), Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis and schistosomiasis. A thoraco-abdominal CT scan showed mediastinal and axillar lymphadenopathies, pulmonary nodules and a heterogeneous liver parenchyma with signs of portal hypertension (esophageal varices, ascites and splenomegaly). A transjugular liver biopsy revealed a slightly abnormal portal pressure gradient (8 mmHg wedge gradient) and the histology described normal parenchymal architecture with a minimal portal fibrosis and sinusoidal infiltration of mainly T lymphocytes (CD3+). A lymphoproliferative disease was ruled out by flow cytometry of peripheral blood lymphocytes, intranodal lymphocytes (axillar lymphnode biopsy) and of liver infiltrating lymphocytes. At this point our hypothesis pointed towards a miliary tuberculosis with lung and peritoneal involvement. In the ascites fluid the polymorphonuclear count was low (PMN, <250 cells/mm3) as also the albumin (10 gr/l) and protein level (9 gr/l) with a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of 2.6 pointing towards portal hypertension. However, the cultures of the ascites fluid tested positive for M. tuberculosis and treatment was started with rifampin, isoniazid (INH) and ethambutol for six months and thereafter bitherapy with INH and rifampin (based on the antibiogram) for additional seven months. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy evidenced grade I esophageal varices. For the viral breakthrough of HIV, HAART was changed to tenofovir, efavirenz, atazanavir and ritonavir. The patient was dismissed from the hospital but presented seven, eight, ten and 12 months later severe esophageal variceal bleedings treated with endoscopic band ligation and slerotherapy and beta-blockers (propanolol).
In September 2006 she was admitted again for bilateral leg swelling and important ascites with very low proteins (7 gr/l, serum albumin 30 gr/l, serum-to-ascites albumin gradient SAAG of 2.3). Liver function tests were still abnormal: AST and ALT 1.5 ULN, AP 2x ULN, gammaGT 4x ULN and diminisched Factor V (50%). An abdominal CT scan and MRI showed large volume ascites, splenomegaly and portal-systemic collaterals. The portal vein was patent. A second transjugular liver biopsy revealed again minimal portal fibrosis without significant inflammation. On the reticulin stain a typical nodular rearrangement of the parenchyma with atrophic periportal and regenerative centrolobular plates was compatible with NRH (Figure 1). In addition, fibrous material was occluding portal veins in several portal tracts pointing towards HIV-associated obliterative portopathy.
Hence, in the context of HIV infection, we suspected a hypercoagulable state with micro-thrombosis in the distal portal veins causing NRH. A thrombophilia work-up (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, factor II G20210A mutation, factor V Leiden mutation, anti-thrombin, protein C and protein S) showed low level of free protein S antigen (37% normal > 55%). An anticoagulant treatment with vitamin K antagonists (VKA, acenocoumarol) aiming at an INR of 2.0-3.0 was introduced. However, the anticoagulant treatment with VKA was difficult to regulate with highly variable INR, which was repeatedly infra-therapeutic. In November 2006 she presented another variceal bleeding (with an INR at 1.7) controlled by band ligation, ascites and progressive cachexia (BMI 15.6). HIV infection was again uncontrolled and treatment was changed to tenofovir, emtricitabin, lopinavir and ritonavir. Thus, in February 2007 the patient was listed for LT with a MELD score of 14. To bridge until LT a TIPS was placed. Four weeks after the TIPS placement, the anticoagulant treatment with VKA was still extremely difficult to manage with unsatisfactory INR levels. Low platelets counts, factor V level, and fibrinogen (2.1 g/l) together with high D-dimers were suggestive of a persistent consumption coagulopathy and an ongoing thrombotic process. For these reasons, anticoagulant treatment was switched to LMWH in March 2007 for the next two months. With this treatment, the factor V levels increased, D-dimers normalized and fibrinogen increased (to 6.5 g/l); this was all highly suggestive of efficient anticoagulant treatment (resumed in Figure 2). In May 2007 anticoagulant treatment was switched back to VKA and INR could be maintained between 2 and 3. In the following months ascites and lower leg edema disappeared, the nutrition state improved considerably, and finally the patient was removed from the LT waiting list. While writing this report the patient was well with a BMI of 21.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old HIV-positive woman presented in August 2005 with a 4-month history of postprandial abdominal pain and 10 kg weight loss, followed by recurrent esophageal variceal hemorrhages and refractory ascites in 2006.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV in 1998 and treated since 2000 with didanosine, lamivudine, and abacavir, the patient presented in August 2005 with 4 months of postprandial abdominal pain, 10 kg weight loss, ascites, splenomegaly, and diffuse lymphadenopathy. Ascitic fluid culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and she was treated for 13 months with anti-tubercular therapy alongside a switch of HAART to tenofovir, efavirenz, atazanavir, and ritonavir. However, at 7, 8, 10, and 12 months post-discharge she suffered severe recurrent esophageal variceal hemorrhages, and in September 2006 was readmitted with bilateral lower extremity edema and large-volume refractory ascites.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 1998; exposure to didanosine, lamivudine, and abacavir since 2000; tuberculous peritonitis diagnosed in August 2005. Denied alcohol intake or hepatotoxic exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for postprandial abdominal pain, 10 kg weight loss (cachexia with BMI 15.6 kg/m2 by November 2006), recurrent hematemesis/variceal bleeding, abdominal distension, and bilateral leg swelling. Home medications included didanosine, lamivudine, and abacavir initially, switched to tenofovir, efavirenz, atazanavir/ritonavir, and propranolol.

objective.physical_examination: August 2005 examination showed diffuse peripheral lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and ascites. September–November 2006 examinations revealed bilateral lower extremity edema, tense ascites, and progressive cachexia (BMI 15.6 kg/m2, later recovering to 21 kg/m2).
objective.routine_investigations: August 2005 and September 2006 liver enzymes showed AST and ALT 1.5x ULN, ALP 2x ULN, and GGT 4x ULN, with Factor V reduced to 50% in September 2006. Viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV, HEV), CMV, EBV, autoimmune hepatitis serologies (ANA, anti-actin, immunoglobulins), Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, and schistosomiasis workups were negative. Thrombophilia workup revealed free protein S deficiency (37%; normal >55%) and subsequent consumptive coagulopathy (low platelets, low Factor V, fibrinogen 2.1 g/L, and elevated D-dimer). Ascitic fluid analysis showed low PMNs (<250/mm3), low total protein (7–9 g/L), and high SAAG (2.6 and 2.3 g/dL) with August 2005 ascitic culture positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission (August 2005) CD4+ T-cell count was 279 cells/mm3. Thoraco-abdominal CT and MRI showed mediastinal/axillary lymphadenopathy, pulmonary nodules, heterogeneous liver parenchyma, patent portal vein, splenomegaly, portosystemic collaterals, and large-volume ascites. Upper GI endoscopies showed grade I esophageal varices progressing to recurrently bleeding varices requiring band ligation and sclerotherapy. Flow cytometry of blood, axillary lymph node biopsy, and liver biopsy excluded lymphoma. First transjugular liver biopsy (August 2005) showed wedge hepatic venous pressure gradient of 8 mmHg, minimal portal fibrosis, and sinusoidal CD3+ T-cell infiltration; second transjugular liver biopsy (September 2006) with reticulin staining demonstrated nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and fibrous obliterative portal venopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HIV- and didanosine-associated non-cirrhotic portal hypertension secondary to nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH), obliterative portopathy, and acquired free protein S deficiency (37%) with portal microthrombosis, alongside resolved tuberculous peritonitis, in a 43-year-old woman with HIV infection (August 2005 HIV viral load 270,000 copies/mL and CD4 count 279/mm3; regimen modified in August 2005 to tenofovir/efavirenz/atazanavir/ritonavir and in November 2006 to tenofovir/emtricitabine/lopinavir/ritonavir). Tuberculous peritonitis was treated with 6 months of rifampin, isoniazid, and ethambutol followed by 7 months of isoniazid and rifampin. Recurrent variceal hemorrhages and refractory portal hypertension (MELD 14) were managed with endoscopic band ligation, propranolol, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) placement in February 2007 as a bridge to liver transplantation listing, and a 2-month course of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) in March–May 2007 (which normalized D-dimers, raised fibrinogen to 6.5 g/L, and stabilized INR 2.0–3.0 upon transition back to acenocoumarol), resulting in complete resolution of ascites and edema, nutritional recovery to BMI 21 kg/m2, and removal from the liver transplant waiting list.

raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old married male, graduate, with stable premorbid personality traits, without any genetic loading, non-addict, normotensive, non-diabetic developed aberrant behaviour for the first time. This led to irregularities and inattentiveness at work, increasing global withdrawal, emotional aloofness, irritable and impulsive outbursts, neglect of personal hygiene and personal care, delusion of reference, fragmentary persecutory delusion, impaired judgement and insight for illness. The altered behaviour persisted for more than 6 months when he suddenly developed profound psychomotor retardation, inability to speak, tremulousness while walking and held anything that he came in contact with. He did not communicate any depressive symptom. His condition progressed to complete immobility with abnormal postures and mutism, and he needed assisted feeding. Response to strong noxious stimuli were absent although spontaneous movements were present. Although he slept most of the time, he nevertheless looked alert with his eyes chasing objects during the waking phase.
There was no history of fever, lymphadenopathy or diarrhoea. No history of head injury, seizure or ear discharge was reported.
He was diagnosed as a case of functional catatonia and was referred to our centre.
General examination was within normal limits. There was no cutaneous lesion, oral thrush, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary tuberculosis was not evident both on clinical and radiological examination.
Higher function examination revealed an extreme degree of hypokinesia, mutism and catalepsy for more than 30 seconds. He looked conscious, vigilant with positive eye-tracking movements, and loss of apparent condition-avoidance response. Orientation, attention, concentration, memory and judgement could not be commented upon due to mutism. His affect was blunt without weeping or laughing spells (no pseudobulbar pattern). Cerebellar signs could not be tested; mild motor ataxia was present. There was no sensory-motor deficit but bladder and bowel incontinence was present. A syndromic diagnosis of catatonia was made. The patient was subjected to a battery of investigations. Routine blood and urine examination, hepatic and renal function tests were within normal limits except mild iron deficiency anaemia; serum B12 and HbAIC levels were within the normal range. The optic fundus was normal. CSF pressure and biochemical parameters were normal and the VDRL test was negative. X-ray chest and USG abdomen were normal. CT scan revealed a single non-enhancing hypodense lesion in the left frontal cortex and mild cerebral atrophy for his age (Fig 1).
After 7 days of hospitalization, the patient revealed positive grasp, rooting and glabellar tap reflexes, and right hemiparesis (grade III). At that point, considering the focal cerebral damage, he was categorized as a case of akinetic mutism. The patient was found to be positive for HIV-1 and -2, which was confirmed by the Western blot test. The total leucocyte count was 4990 cells/cmm, lymphocytes were 16%, the absolute lymphocyte count was 800 cells/cmm. The absolute CD3+ T lymphocyte count was 528 cells/cmm. The absolute CD4+ T helper cell count was 339 cells/cmm (normal range 337-1690 cells/cmm). Analysis was done using the flowcytometry method. MRI, done after 5 days of CT scan, revealed multiple, confluent, non-enhancing, discrete, asymmetric, subcortical white matter lesions, maximum in the frontoparieto-occipital and cerebellar regions without mass effect (Figs 2-5). Ante-mortem brain biopsy was not feasible.
A final diagnosis of PML in AIDS was made for inducing the state of akinetic mutism.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old married male graduate was referred for a 6-month history of progressive social withdrawal, paranoid delusions, and aberrant behavior culminating in acute mutism, profound psychomotor retardation, and immobility.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 6 months prior to referral, the previously well-adjusted patient developed work irregularities, inattentiveness, emotional aloofness, global withdrawal, irritable/impulsive outbursts, self-neglect, and delusions of reference and persecution. He then acutely progressed to profound psychomotor retardation, mutism, gait tremulousness, compulsive grasping, abnormal posturing, complete immobility requiring assisted feeding, and urinary/fecal incontinence, leading to an initial outside diagnosis of functional catatonia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stable premorbid personality; normotensive, non-diabetic, no substance abuse, and negative family history of psychiatric or genetic illness. No prior head trauma, seizures, or ear discharge.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for behavioral changes, mutism, immobility, and urinary/fecal incontinence; negative for fever, lymphadenopathy, diarrhea, or communicative depressive symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: General physical examination was normal without cutaneous lesions, oral thrush, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Initial neuropsychiatric examination demonstrated extreme hypokinesia, mutism, catalepsy (>30 seconds), blunted affect, mild motor ataxia, urinary/fecal incontinence, and preserved visual tracking with absent conditioned avoidance to noxious stimuli. On hospital day 7, examination evolved to show positive primitive reflexes (grasp, rooting, and glabellar tap) and grade III/V right hemiparesis consistent with akinetic mutism. Fundoscopic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood and urine tests, hepatic and renal function, serum vitamin B12, and HbA1c were normal except for mild iron-deficiency anemia. Total leukocyte count was 4,990 cells/mm3 with 16% lymphocytes (absolute lymphocyte count 800 cells/mm3). Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Flow cytometry showed an absolute CD3+ T-lymphocyte count of 528 cells/mm3 and an absolute CD4+ T-helper count of 339 cells/mm3 (reference 337–1,690 cells/mm3). Lumbar puncture showed normal CSF pressure and biochemistry and negative CSF VDRL. Initial head CT showed a single non-enhancing hypodense lesion in the left frontal cortex with mild age-inappropriate cerebral atrophy; brain MRI performed 5 days later revealed multiple confluent, discrete, asymmetric, non-enhancing subcortical white matter lesions without mass effect predominantly involving the frontoparieto-occipital and cerebellar regions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) secondary to newly diagnosed HIV-1 and HIV-2 co-infection (confirmed by positive HIV-1/2 screening and confirmatory Western blot test, ALC 800/mm3, CD4+ count 339 cells/mm3, and characteristic multifocal non-enhancing subcortical white matter demyelinating lesions on brain MRI), initially masquerading as schizophrenia/psychosis and functional catatonia before evolving into organic akinetic mutism with right hemiparesis and frontal release signs.

raw_case_text: A 5 1/2-year-old HIV-infected boy presented with recurrent fever and cough since 2 years, recurrent diarrhea and vomiting since 6 months and generalized pruritis and abdominal pain since 15 days. He had taken ATT 2 years ago for 6 months. His father was a prisoner and was diagnosed to be HIV-infected 2 years back. His mother was also diagnosed to be HIV infected a year back. Thus, the child seemed to have acquired the HIV infection vertically. He was immunized till date. On examination, he was malnourished (weight=10 kg, <5th centile and height=96 cm, <5th centile). He had pallor, multiple mobile nontender cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphnodes with oral thrush. On systemic examination, he had mild splenomegaly. Other systems were normal. His investigations showed hemoglobin of 11.4 g/dl, white cell count of 7,200/mm3 and ESR of 62 mm at end of 1 h. X-ray chest showed bilateral hilar congestion. Mantoux test was negative. Liver function and renal function tests were normal. His enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was repeated, which was positive. A baseline CD4 count of 161 cells/mm3 was detected, with a CD4 percentage of 7.98%, suggestive of severe immunosuppression. He was started on three drugs; ART consisting of Stavudine, Lamivudine and Efavirenz. He had a weight gain of 2 kg within 1 month of starting ART and his lymphadenopathy regressed. However, his cough and pruritis persisted. A repeat X-ray chest showed a right-sided lower zone pneumonia. A Mantoux test performed at this time was negative. He was treated with antibiotics but the pneumonia did not subside, and thus he was started on ATT to which the pneumonia responded. Three months after start of ATT, he developed left cervical matted rubbery lymphadenopathy (4 cmx4 cm) that did not subside with antibiotics. Fine needle aspiration of the cervical adenopathy was carried out, which showed caseous granulomas. Drug compliance with ATT was confirmed. A wedge biopsy of the node was carried out, which again confirmed tuberculosis, and then the child was started on six-drug ATT. Subsequently, within 1 week, he developed severe sepsis with intestinal obstruction and was hospitalized. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple splenic lesions, a large liver lesion, encasing retroperitoneal lymphnodes, large right pelvic lymphnodes and a large right inguinal lymphnode with a large presacral mass (6.8 cmx5.08 cm) with intrasacral extension into the spinal cord suggestive of lymphoma [Figure 2]. However, before any intervention could be started, the child expired the following day. A postmortem lymph node biopsy was performed, which showed round cell tumor that was found to be a B cell lymphoma on immunophenotyping.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5.5-year-old HIV-positive boy presented with a 2-year history of recurrent fever and cough, a 6-month history of recurrent diarrhea and vomiting, and a 15-day history of generalized pruritus and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child experienced recurrent fevers and cough for 2 years (having completed a 6-month course of anti-tuberculosis therapy 2 years earlier), recurrent diarrhea and emesis for 6 months, and generalized pruritus and abdominal pain for 15 days prior to presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Vertically acquired HIV infection (father was a prisoner diagnosed with HIV 2 years prior; mother diagnosed with HIV 1 year prior); completed a 6-month course of anti-tuberculosis therapy (ATT) 2 years prior; immunizations up to date.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fever, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, generalized pruritus, abdominal pain, and severe failure to thrive.

objective.physical_examination: Severely malnourished (weight 10 kg [<5th percentile], height 96 cm [<5th percentile]) with pallor, oral thrush, multiple mobile non-tender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes, and mild splenomegaly. Three months after restarting ATT on ART, he developed a 4 x 4 cm matted rubbery left cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline labs showed hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, WBC 7,200/mm3, elevated ESR (62 mm at 1 hour), normal liver and renal function tests, negative Mantoux tuberculin skin test (at baseline and repeat), and positive repeat HIV ELISA. Baseline chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar congestion; repeat chest X-ray at 1 month showed right lower zone consolidation/pneumonia.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 161 cells/mm3 (CD4% = 7.98%). Fine-needle aspiration and wedge biopsy of the 4 x 4 cm matted left cervical lymph node confirmed caseous necrotizing tuberculous granulomas. Subsequent abdominal and pelvic CT (performed during acute decompensation with sepsis and intestinal obstruction) revealed multiple splenic lesions, a large hepatic mass, encasing retroperitoneal, right pelvic, and right inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a 6.8 x 5.08 cm presacral mass with intrasacral spinal canal extension. Postmortem lymph node biopsy and immunophenotyping confirmed B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Vertically acquired pediatric HIV/AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, baseline CD4+ count 161 cells/mm3 [7.98%]) complicated by pulmonary and paradoxical/unmasking cervical lymph node tuberculosis and rapidly fatal high-grade intra-abdominal/presacral B-cell lymphoma. Following initiation of triple antiretroviral therapy (stavudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz), the child gained 2 kg in the first month, was started on first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (ATT) for antibiotic-refractory right lower lobe pneumonia, and was escalated at 3 months to six-drug ATT after biopsy confirmation of caseating cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis. One week later, he developed fulminant sepsis and acute intestinal obstruction from disseminated B-cell lymphoma (confirmed by postmortem nodal biopsy and immunophenotyping) and died the following day.

raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old German Caucasian truck driver presented to the ophthalmologist with unilateral visual loss. Upon eye examination, visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 0.02 in the left eye (normal visual acuity = 1). Fundoscopic examination showed swelling of the optic disk and serous retinal detachment in the left eye (Figure 1, upper image). Slit lamp exam did not reveal any additional pathology. Therefore, the diagnosis of unilateral papillitis was retained. Additionally, oral ulcers and thrush were identified (Figure 2, upper left image), hence an HIV test was ordered. HIV-serology was positive and the patient was referred to the infectious disease department of the University Hospital of Giessen.
Regarding his medical history, the patient had been asthenic and anorectic for 7 weeks and had lost 12 kg. He received a course of oral antibiotics (3 days of azithromycin) three weeks prior to presentation due to sinusitis. He had a burning pain when swallowing, but no other complaints. Apart from sinusitis no pre-existing medical conditions were known. The risk factor for HIV infection was MSM contacts.
On admission the patient had a mild fever of 38.5 C but the other vital signs were normal. Clinical examination was unremarkable except for a moderately enlarged liver and oral ulcers. In addition to the oral lesions, multiple painless, hard-edged ulcers and oedematous swelling were found on the penis and scrotum (Figure 2, upper right image). No anal lesions were present. Signs of fluid overload such as peripheral oedema were absent. No abnormalities were found upon neurological examination, there being no signs of meningismus.
Serum laboratory values on admission showed increased inflammation markers C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and procalcitonin, moderately elevated liver enzymes, moderate hypoalbuminemia and severe hyponatremia (Table 1). Moreover markedly reduced levels of Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH), thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) were noted, indicative of a centrally-induced hypothyroidism. Creatinine and uric acid levels were subnormal. Urine analysis revealed high osmolality and sodium, consistent with the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH).
Laboratory diagnosis of syphilis in this patient included serology and a Real-Time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) assay against the polA gene of Treponema pallidum . Serologic tests revealed a reactive Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR)-titer of 1:32, a T. pallidum haemagglutination assay (TPHA) titer of 1:2560 and positive T. pallidum IgM and IgG immunoblots (recomBlot, Mikrogen, Germany). The RT-PCR detected the presence of T. pallidum DNA in the swabs from oral and genital lesions, but not from the anal swab. All other bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures of this patient were negative. Surrogate markers of the HIV infection showed a viral load of 2 x 105 c/ml and a CD4 count of 191/mul. Additional virological studies revealed chronic HBV and HCV infection with viral loads of 55 c/ml (12 IU/ml HBV-s-NAT) and 107 IU/ml (HCV-NAT).
CSF analysis indicated increased blood-brain-barrier permeability with an elevated white blood cell count of 6/mul (normal <4/mul) and protein level of 0.59 g/l (normal <0.45 g/l). No blood contamination was detected (red blood cell count <1/mul). The T. pallidum IgG immunoblot from the cerebrospinal fluid was also positive showing the presence of additional and higher-intensity bands compared to the serum sample. This indicated intrathecal antibody production and suggested neurosyphilis. HIV load in CSF was 2 x 104 c/ml, while PCR based testing for JC Virus (JCV), Herpes Simplex Virus 1/2 (HSV 1/2), Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) and Cytomegalovirus (CMV) were negative.
Sonography found a normal thyroid size and structure, however, a discrete reduction of the perfusion was noted. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed generalized lymphadenopathy, moderate enlargement of liver and spleen, and extension of the genital oedema to the lower abdominal wall (Figure 2, lower image). Cerebral Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) including pituitary imaging showed no abnormalities apart from sinusitis. Of note, no signs of elevated intracranial pressure were detected. CSF pressure was not measured during lumbar puncture.
The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g/d for 14 days due to a reported allergy to penicillin. Prednisolone at 50 mg/d (tapering scheme over 4 weeks) was added on the recommendation of the ophtalmologist in order to treat papillitis. Fluconazole was included for oesophageal thrush, and trimethoprim-sulfomethoxazole for pneumocystis prophylaxis. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) was started after completion of ceftriaxone. Because of the high viral load in the CSF, a regimen with a high CNS Penetration-Effectiveness rank was chosen, consisting of Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r), Tenofovir (TDF), Lamivudine (3TC), Zidovudine (AZT).
A therapeutic response to syphilis treatment was observed with normalization of sodium levels (Figure 3), healing of oral ulcers and improvement of the patient's general condition within one week. TSH levels normalized within 3 weeks without any additional specific thyroid treatment, whereas T4 and T3 remained low for longer (Table 2). Visual acuity also improved markedly from 0.02 to 0.2 and papillitis was no longer present after 3 weeks of treatment (Figure 1, lower image).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old German Caucasian male truck driver presented with acute unilateral left visual loss, a 7-week history of asthenia, anorexia, and 12 kg weight loss, and burning odynophagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to an ophthalmologist with unilateral left visual loss and oral thrush/ulcers and was referred to the infectious diseases department after testing HIV-positive. Over the preceding 7 weeks, he had experienced profound fatigue, anorexia, a 12 kg weight loss, and burning pain on swallowing, and had received a 3-day course of oral azithromycin 3 weeks earlier for sinusitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent sinusitis 3 weeks prior; no other known prior medical conditions. Sexual history notable for men who have sex with men (MSM) contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left visual loss, 7-week asthenia, anorexia, 12 kg weight loss, and burning odynophagia. Reported drug allergy to penicillin.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, temperature was 38.5 °C with otherwise normal vital signs and euvolemic fluid status (no peripheral edema). Ophthalmologic exam showed visual acuity of 0.8 (right eye) and 0.02 (left eye), normal slit-lamp exam, and left optic disc swelling with serous retinal detachment (unilateral syphilitic papillitis) on fundoscopy. Mucosal and genital exam revealed oral candidiasis, oral mucosal ulcers, and multiple painless indurated chancres with edematous swelling of the penis and scrotum (no anal lesions). Abdominal exam showed moderate hepatomegaly; neurological exam was normal without meningismus.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs demonstrated elevated CRP and procalcitonin, moderately elevated hepatic transaminases, moderate hypoalbuminemia, severe hyponatremia with low serum creatinine/uric acid and elevated urine osmolality and urine sodium diagnostic of SIADH, and central hypothyroidism (markedly decreased TSH, T4, and T3). Syphilis testing showed reactive serum RPR (1:32), TPHA (1:2560), positive Treponema pallidum IgM and IgG immunoblots, and positive T. pallidum polA real-time PCR from oral and penile/scrotal ulcer swabs (anal swab negative). Viral testing revealed chronic HBV (55 copies/mL; 12 IU/mL) and HCV (10^7 IU/mL) co-infections. Thyroid ultrasound showed normal gland size with mildly reduced perfusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 191 cells/µL. Thoraco-abdominal CT showed generalized lymphadenopathy, moderate hepatosplenomegaly, and genital edema extending to the lower abdominal wall. Brain and pituitary MRI showed sinusitis without pituitary mass or intracranial hypertension. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 6/µL; normal <4/µL), elevated protein (0.59 g/L; normal <0.45 g/L), intrathecal Treponema pallidum IgG antibody production on CSF immunoblot, CSF HIV viral load of 2 x 10^4 copies/mL, and negative CSF PCRs for JCV, HSV-1/2, VZV, and CMV.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Malignant early/secondary syphilis and neurosyphilis (presenting with unilateral left papillitis/serous retinal detachment, multiple persisted oral/penoscrotal chancres, SIADH, and central hypothyroidism) co-occurring with newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV viral load 2 x 10^5 copies/mL, CSF HIV viral load 2 x 10^4 copies/mL, CD4+ count 191/µL), esophageal candidiasis, and chronic HBV/HCV co-infection. Due to penicillin allergy, neurosyphilis and papillitis were treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g/day for 14 days plus a 4-week oral prednisolone taper (starting at 50 mg/day), alongside fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, and subsequent initiation of high-CNS-penetration ART (lopinavir/ritonavir, tenofovir, lamivudine, and zidovudine). Serum sodium and oral ulcers normalized within 1 week, and within 3 weeks endogenous TSH normalized without hormone replacement and left eye papillitis resolved with visual acuity improving from 0.02 to 0.2.

raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old male, presented with complaints of fever and extensive rashes on the skin of the face and the neck, ulcerations and erythema of the conjunctiva and the oral cavity and difficulty in swallowing, of ten days' duration. The past medical history of the patient revealed that he had been diagnosed with HIV infection (HIV-1) eight months back. He was initiated on HAART therapy (zidovudine 300 mg + lamivudine 150 mg + NVP 200 mg) a month back when the viral load was 1, 09,000 copies/ml. The patient was also on anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) (rifampacin 150 mg, isoniazid 300 mg) and vitamin supplements for the past three months. The patient was well-oriented and on examination, had hyperpyrexia, generalized, maculopapular and bullous eruptions on the neck, face and the trunk [Figures 1 and 2]. Intraorally, the patient was completely edentulous and had multiple oral ulcers of the buccal mucosa, soft palate and buccal vestibule. The ulcers were hemorrhagic and tender on palpation. Hemorrhagic erosions were also seen on both the upper and lower lips [Figures 1 and 2]. Ophthalmic examination showed acute conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhages. There was no history of previous hypersensitivity reaction to drugs. The pruritis involving the oral and the ocular region was followed by vesicles and ulcerations four days after the initiation of HAART therapy.
The laboratory investigations at the time of admission to our referral centre showed a CD4 count of 470 cells/microliter (normal range 200-1347 cells/microliter), total white blood cell (WBC) count was 4860-cells/cu mm (normal range 4000-11000 cells/cu mm), hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl (normal range 12-17 g/dl) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 36 mm/h (normal range 0-14mm/h). The platelet count was 208 x 109/L (normal range 137-367 x 109/L) and random blood glucose was 186 mg/dl (normal range 80-120 mg/dl). Urine analysis and serum chemistry were within normal limits. A chest radiograph of the patient did not show any active tuberculous lesion.
On the basis of the history and clinical presentation a diagnosis of SJS was made. As the first line of treatment HAART was discontinued and the patient was administered intravenous 5% dextrose and 2 ml dexamethasone (4 mg/ml). Supportive therapy with oral topical anesthetic gel (lignocaine 2%) for the oral ulcers was prescribed. The ocular lesions were managed with dexamethasone (0.1%) eye drops and crusting dry lesions were managed with liquid paraffin. The skin and the oral lesions healed over a period of two weeks. The patient was subsequently followed up and after 12 weeks the oral mucosal lesions resolved completely [Figures 3 and 4].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 10-day history of fever, extensive facial, neck, and truncal blistering skin rash, ocular redness, hemorrhagic oral and labial ulcerations, and dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV-1 infection 8 months prior and treated with anti-tuberculosis therapy for 3 months, the patient was initiated on HAART (zidovudine 300 mg + lamivudine 150 mg + nevirapine 200 mg) 1 month prior to presentation. Four days after starting HAART, he developed oral and ocular pruritus that rapidly progressed over the next 10 days to high fever, generalized maculopapular and bullous skin eruptions, acute conjunctivitis, painful hemorrhagic oral and lip ulcers, and severe dysphagia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed 8 months prior (baseline viral load 109,000 copies/mL 1 month prior); pulmonary/systemic tuberculosis on anti-tuberculosis therapy for the past 3 months. No prior history of drug hypersensitivity.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, oral/ocular pruritus, dysphagia, painful oral/lip ulcers, ocular redness, and blistering skin rash. Home medications: zidovudine 300 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, nevirapine 200 mg (started 1 month prior), rifampicin 150 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, and vitamin supplements.

objective.physical_examination: Well-oriented and hyperpyrexic. Cutaneous examination revealed generalized maculopapular and bullous eruptions over the face, neck, and trunk. Ophthalmic examination showed bilateral acute conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhages. Intraoral examination revealed an edentulous patient with multiple tender hemorrhagic ulcerations across the buccal mucosa, soft palate, and buccal vestibule, along with crusted hemorrhagic erosions on the upper and lower vermilion lips.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests showed WBC 4,860 cells/mm3 (normal 4,000–11,000), hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL (normal 12–17), platelets 208 x 10^9/L (normal 137–367 x 10^9/L), elevated ESR 36 mm/h (normal 0–14 mm/h), random blood glucose 186 mg/dL (normal 80–120 mg/dL), and normal urinalysis and serum chemistry. Chest X-ray showed no active tuberculous lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 470 cells/µL (normal 200–1,347 cells/µL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Nevirapine/HAART-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) with severe mucocutaneous and ocular involvement in a 50-year-old male with HIV-1 infection (prior viral load 109,000 copies/mL, admission CD4+ count 470 cells/µL) and concurrent anti-tuberculosis therapy. Management consisted of immediate discontinuation of HAART (zidovudine/lamivudine/nevirapine), intravenous fluid hydration (5% dextrose), systemic intravenous dexamethasone (2 mL of 4 mg/mL), topical 2% lignocaine anesthetic gel and liquid paraffin for oral/lip ulcerations, and topical 0.1% dexamethasone ophthalmic drops for conjunctivitis. Cutaneous and oral lesions healed within 2 weeks, with complete resolution of all mucosal lesions confirmed at 12-week follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An eight-year-old girl presented with painful blisters on the skin of 40 days duration. She also had fever with chills, cough, dyspnoea, and severe headache for the past one month. She had suffered from chickenpox four months back, which resolved uneventfully. She was anemic, and had stunted growth. Chest examination revealed bilateral crepitations. She also had neck stiffness.
Multiple painful and tender vesicles and bullae of varying size were seen all over the body, predominantly over the acral areas. Few bullae were hemorrhagic. Warty excrescences were seen overlying some blisters. Oral erosions were noted. The skin lesions started as tiny vesicles [Figure 1], which evolved into larger bullae, some of them were hemorrhagic [Figure 2]. Thereafter, they progressed to form warty excrescences [Figure 3], and finally resolved with varioliform scars. New lesions continued to appear, even as the older ones healed. Oral erosions were also present. There was no dermatomal grouping of the skin lesions.
Due to the unusual morphology of the lesions, enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV was done, which turned out to be positive. Western blot for HIV was also positive. Her parents were HIV negative. There was no history suggestive of sexual abuse. No possible explanation could be offered for the HIV positivity of the child, other than frequent, and possibly unsafe intramuscular injections in the past.
Tzanck smear from the blisters showed multinucleated giant cells [Figure 4]. Histopathology of the early vesicle revealed typical features of varicella blister, and that of late warty lesions showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis without the classical features of viral blister.
Chest x-ray showed pneumonitis, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytosis. Complete hemogram was normal except for dimorphic anemia. Her CD4 count was 41, blood VDRL was nonreactive, and serum IgG and IgM for HSV-1 and HSV-2 were negative. Serum IgM for VZV was negative, but IgG for VZV was positive in very high titre.
The patient was started on antiretroviral therapy comprising three drugs: stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine. Intravenous acyclovir in the dose of 10 mg/kg body weight was administered for three weeks. There was dramatic improvement with complete resolution of the skin lesions, meningitis, and pneumonitis. At the end of third week, acyclovir was stopped and the patient was discharged. However, the blisters promptly recurred within two weeks. This time oral acyclovir was started with the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, and the lesions subsided again. At present, the child is on antiretroviral therapy and oral acyclovir with the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, for the past three months. Her general condition is improving, but the occasional vesicle still continues to appear. It has been planned to continue acyclovir with the same dose till her CD4 count improves substantially.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old girl presented with a 40-day history of painful generalized skin blisters and a 1-month history of fever with chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having recovered uneventfully from primary varicella (chickenpox) 4 months earlier, the child developedcrops of painful vesicles and hemorrhagic bullae 40 days prior to presentation that evolved into hyperkeratotic warty excrescences and varioliform scars while new blisters continued to erupt. For the 1 month preceding admission, she also experienced fever with chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary chickenpox 4 months prior; history of stunted growth and frequent, potentially unsafe intramuscular injections in the past. Both parents tested HIV-negative, and there was no history of sexual abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful/hemorrhagic skin blisters, oral erosions, fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.

objective.physical_examination: Anemic and growth-stunted child with nuchal rigidity and bilateral pulmonary crepitations on auscultation. Mucocutaneous examination revealed oral mucosal erosions and generalized non-dermatomal painful vesicles, hemorrhagic bullae, overlying verrucous/warty excrescences, and varioliform scars predominantly distributed over the acral extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete hemogram showed dimorphic anemia with normal leukocyte and platelet counts. Blood VDRL and serum HSV-1 and HSV-2 IgG/IgM were negative; serum VZV IgM was negative while serum VZV IgG was strongly positive in very high titer. Tzanck smear of blister fluid demonstrated multinucleated giant cells. Chest X-ray showed bilateral pneumonitis.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 41 cells/µL. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis consistent with viral meningitis. Skin biopsy histopathology of an early vesicle showed classic intraepidermal varicella viral blistering, whereas biopsy of a late verrucous lesion demonstrated hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated chronic verrucous/bullous varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection complicated by VZV pneumonitis and aseptic lymphocytic meningitis unmasking horizontally acquired pediatric AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, confirmatory HIV Western blot, CD4+ count 41 cells/µL, high-titer VZV IgG, and multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear). The child was initiated on triple antiretroviral therapy (stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine) plus intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) for 3 weeks, achieving complete resolution of skin lesions, pneumonitis, and meningitis. When cutaneous vesicles recurred 2 weeks after stopping IV acyclovir, long-term suppressive oral acyclovir (80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses) was instituted alongside ART, maintaining clinical control at 3-month follow-up pending substantial CD4+ recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old Thai girl presented at a provincial hospital with fever, oral ulcers, disseminated papular lesions and multiple joint pain for 4 weeks. Twelve weeks before this admission, she was diagnosed as a case of perinatal HIV infection after presenting with disseminated herpes zoster infection and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). At that time, her CD4+ cell count was 7.2% or 39 cells/mm3. Plasma HIV-RNA level was not obtained. She was started on GPOvirS30  (a fixed drug combination of stavudine 30 mg, lamivudine 150 mg and nevirapine 200 mg) 1 tablet twice daily and PJP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Eight weeks after starting ART she developed fever, multiple oral ulcers, disseminated papular lesions over the face, body, and extremities, and severe pain in many joints. The symptoms did not respond to many kinds of oral antibiotics and she was referred to Chiang Mai University (CMU) Hospital.
Upon admission to CMU Hospital, the physical examination revealed high-grade fever. Multiple painful ulcerated lesions were found on the lip and oral mucosa. Generalized non-pruritic erythrematous papules and nodules with central umbilication were found over the face, body, and extremities (Figure 1). Marked swelling, warmth, and tenderness of many joints, including right shoulder, wrist, metacarpophalangeal, knee, and ankle joints were also noticed. Neither lymphadenopathy nor hepatosplenomegaly were found. Her laboratory results are shown in Table 1. CD4+ cell count was 11% or 51 cells/mm3. Plasma HIV-RNA level was < 50 copies/mL. Chest roentgenogram was normal. Roentgenograms of both wrists and ankles showed multiple round radiolucent defects of the bones (Figure 2). Skin biopsy showed necrotizing histiocytic granuloma formation with neutrophilic infiltration in the upper and reticular dermis. Tissue sections from skin biopsy stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain revealed numerous intracellular and extracellular, round to oval, elongated, thin-walled yeast cells with central septation (Figure 3). No organism was observed in the bone marrow aspirate specimen. The hemoculture, bone marrow culture, and skin culture revealed no evidence of P. marneffei or other fungus. Blood was also sent for mycobacterial culture with negative results. Serum cryptococcal antigen was negative. The diagnosis of disseminated P. marneffei infection from unmasking IRIS was made.
The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B at a dosage of 0.7 mg/kg for 2 weeks along with paracetamol and ibuprofen, followed by oral itraconazole at a dosage of 5 mg/kg twice daily orally. She responded well to treatment. Her fever, skin lesions, and joints pain gradually resolved. She was discharged with a plan to complete a 10-week course of oral itraconazole therapy followed by the maintenance therapy with oral itraconazole at a reduced dosage of 5 mg/kg daily. Her skin lesions and joints pain resolved after 4 weeks of antifungal treatment, and itraconazole was discontinued after 4 months of maintenance treatment. After 1 year of therapy, she had gained 4 kg weight without recurrence of P. marneffei infection. Her repeated CD4+ cell count had risen to 21.1% or 269 cells/mm3. Her plasma HIV RNA level was undetectable (< 50 copies/mL).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old Thai girl with perinatally acquired HIV presented with a 4-week history of high-grade fever, painful oral ulcers, disseminated umbilicated papular skin lesions, and severe polyarthralgia/polyarthritis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Twelve weeks prior to admission, the patient was diagnosed with perinatal HIV infection (baseline CD4+ count 39 cells/mm3 [7.2%]) after presenting with disseminated herpes zoster and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and was initiated on fixed-dose stavudine 30 mg / lamivudine 150 mg / nevirapine 200 mg (GPOvirS30) twice daily plus TMP-SMX prophylaxis. Eight weeks after starting ART (4 weeks prior to admission), she developed persistent high fever, multiple painful oral ulcers, disseminated facial/truncal/extremity papular lesions, and severe polyarticular joint pain and swelling that failed multiple outpatient oral antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Perinatally acquired HIV infection diagnosed 12 weeks prior; recent disseminated herpes zoster and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia 12 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, painful oral and lip ulcers, generalized non-pruritic umbilicated papules, and severe polyarthritis (right shoulder, wrists, MCPs, knees, and ankles). Home medications: GPOvirS30 (stavudine 30 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, nevirapine 200 mg BID) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

objective.physical_examination: High-grade fever on admission without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Mucocutaneous examination revealed multiple painful ulcerated lesions on the lips and oral mucosa and generalized non-pruritic erythematous papules and nodules with central umbilication across the face, trunk, and extremities. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrated marked swelling, warmth, and tenderness of the right shoulder, bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, knees, and ankles.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum cryptococcal antigen was negative; blood, bone marrow, and skin fungal cultures and blood mycobacterial cultures were negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Bilateral wrist and ankle radiographs demonstrated multiple well-defined round radiolucent osteolytic bone defects.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 51 cells/mm3 (11%; up from 39 cells/mm3 [7.2%] at baseline, and rising to 269 cells/mm3 [21.1%] at 1 year). Bone marrow aspirate microscopy was negative for organisms. Skin biopsy histopathology (H&E, PAS, and Grocott methenamine silver stains) demonstrated upper and reticular dermal necrotizing histiocytic granulomas with neutrophilic infiltration and abundant intracellular and extracellular round-to-oval elongated yeast cells with characteristic central transverse septation diagnostic of Penicillium (Talaromyces) marneffei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated Penicillium (Talaromyces) marneffei infection with multifocal osteolytic bone lesions and polyarthritis presenting as unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) 8 weeks after initiating stavudine/lamivudine/nevirapine in a 14-year-old girl with perinatal HIV infection (plasma HIV-RNA <50 copies/mL, CD4+ count rising from 39 to 51 cells/mm3; confirmed by central-septated yeast cells on PAS/GMS-stained skin biopsy). She was treated with intravenous amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) for 2 weeks plus paracetamol and ibuprofen, followed by oral itraconazole (5 mg/kg twice daily for 10 weeks, then 5 mg/kg once daily maintenance for 4 months) while continuing ART. Her fever, skin lesions, and arthritis completely resolved within 4 weeks, and at 1-year follow-up she had gained 4 kg with no recurrence, an undetectable HIV viral load (<50 copies/mL), and a CD4+ count of 269 cells/mm3 (21.1%).

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old male presented to us with acute increase in bilateral neck swelling since 5-6 days, neck pain, fever, and weight loss.
Patient had first noticed the swelling 2 months ago. It started as multiple neck swellings which were initially small. He did not take any treatment for it. Later on he was admitted for altered sensorium. His serology for HIV was positive andfine needle aspiration cytology of swelling was suggestive of tuberculosis. CD4 count was 48 cells/mm. Magnetic resonance imaging of brain was normal. He was given category 1(2HREZ+4HR) under RNTCP and Anti Retroviral antiretroviral therapy (3TC+d4T+EFV), with septran and fluconazole for prophylaxis against pneumocystis carinii and fungal infections. He improved symptomatically after the drugs were started, even though there was no appreciable change in the number and size of swelling.
After about 2 months of treatment there was acute aggravation of complaints for which the patient presented to us. There was a history of increase in size of swelling during the past 1 week. On examination of the neck swellings, there were multiple, discrete, firm, mobile, tender, nonwarm, nonreducible, nonpulsatile swellings on both sides of the neck involving all lymph node groups [Figure 1, 2]. The swellings were of different sizes ranging from 2 to 12 cm in maximum dimension. There was no enlargement of any other lymph node groups in the body. Ultrasonography of the neck revealed multiple bilateral enlarged conglomerated nodes in levels 2, 3, 4, and 5. Chest X ray was normal. Sputum examinations of two morning samples were negative for acid fast bacilli. CD4 count was 100 cells per cubic millimeter of blood.
At this stage considering the fact that in spite of treatment with ATT+ART, the patient had presented with increase in size of neck swelling, we were considering a differential diagnosis of infection with drug-resistant bacilli, infection by MOTT, and IRD.
Tablet prednisolone 25 mg once daily was added to his treatment and it was tapered over a period of 3 weeks. The swelling gradually became soft; skin over swelling became tense and red. About 100 cc pus was aspirated from neck swelling and sent for mycobacterial culture and sensitivity. AFB culture report (BACTEC/L-J) was suggestive of M. avium complex (MAC) on the basis of NAP (rho-nitro-alpha-acetyl amino-beta-hydroxy-propiophenone) and morphology. AFB culture and sensitivity report showed sensitive to all first line drugs. The patient had a diagnosis of AIDS, he was on antiretroviral therapy with increase in CD4 count and worsening of preexisting disease; hence, the diagnosis was IRD.
Along with category-1 ATT and ART, azithromycin and ciprofloxacin were added for MOTT. Patient was kept on fortnightly follow-up. At the time of sending this publication the patient had completed 4 months of treatment and the patient is symptomatically better with marked reduction in size of the swelling [Figure 3].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male on anti-tuberculosis and antiretroviral therapy presented with a 5-to-6-day history of acute painful enlargement of bilateral neck swellings, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient first noticed multiple small neck swellings 2 months prior to presentation, followed by an admission for altered sensorium where he was diagnosed with HIV infection (CD4 count 48 cells/mm3) and cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis by fine-needle aspiration cytology (with normal brain MRI). He was started on RNTCP Category I anti-tuberculosis therapy (2HREZ/4HR), antiretroviral therapy (lamivudine, stavudine, and efavirenz), cotrimoxazole, and fluconazole with initial symptomatic improvement. However, after 2 months of combined therapy, he experienced an acute 1-week flare of painful, rapidly enlarging bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection and cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis diagnosed 2 months prior (baseline CD4 count 48 cells/mm3; normal brain MRI).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bilateral neck pain and swelling, fever, and weight loss. Home medications: lamivudine, stavudine, efavirenz, Category I ATT (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Septran), and fluconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Neck examination revealed multiple discrete, firm, mobile, tender, non-warm, non-reducible, non-pulsatile bilateral cervical lymph node enlargements involving all cervical nodal levels (measuring 2 to 12 cm in maximum dimension), which subsequently softened with overlying tense erythematous skin yielding ~100 mL of pus upon aspiration. No extra-cervical lymphadenopathy was present.
objective.routine_investigations: Two morning sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Chest X-ray was normal. Neck ultrasonography demonstrated multiple bilateral enlarged conglomerated lymph nodes across cervical levels II, III, IV, and V.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat CD4+ T-cell count had doubled from 48 cells/mm3 at baseline to 100 cells/mm3. Aspiration of ~100 mL of pus from the suppurative cervical lymph nodes with mycobacterial culture on BACTEC and Löwenstein-Jensen media identified Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC / MOTT) based on NAP test and colony morphology, with susceptibility to all first-line anti-TB drugs.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Paradoxical/unmasking mycobacterial immune reconstitution disease (IRD / IRIS) with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC / MOTT) suppurative cervical lymphadenitis in a 35-year-old male with AIDS (CD4+ count rising from 48 to 100 cells/mm3 after 2 months of lamivudine/stavudine/efavirenz and Category I anti-tuberculosis therapy). Management included a 3-week tapering course of oral prednisolone (starting at 25 mg once daily), therapeutic pus aspiration (~100 mL), continuation of Category I ATT and ART, and addition of azithromycin and ciprofloxacin for MAC coverage, resulting in marked regression of the cervical lymphadenopathy and symptomatic recovery at 4-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old housewife presented with multiple, large, ulcerative lesions all over the body of 1-month duration. She did not give any history of genital lesions before the onset of skin lesions. Concomitant symptoms of headache, fever, myalgia and leucorrhea were present. She also gave a history of two spontaneous miscarriages for which she had not taken treatment and has not had contact with her husband since 6 months. Her husband, a lorry driver had multiple extra and premarital contacts. He was diagnosed as having HIV 2 years ago and was initiated on antiretroviral therapy. He was currently being treated for chancroid as well, due to many genital ulcers that he presented to us with.
On examination, the patient was febrile. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple, ulcerative, crusted lesions on the face and extremities [Figures 1 and 2]. Erosions were present on the lips and genital mucosa as well. Palms [Figure 3] and soles showed multiple annular lesions with central pigmentation. The axillary, epitrochlear and inguinal lymph nodes were enlarged, tender and rubbery in consistency.
Initial laboratory investigations revealed leucocytosis, with predominance of polymorphs and an elevated ESR. VDRL was reactive (1:128 dilution) and HIV-1 was positive (ELISA). Western blot assay for P24 antigen was also found to be positive. Pus culture from the ulcerated lesions grew Staphylococcus aureus which was highly sensitive to newer quinolones. CSF analysis showed no abnormalities of raised intracranial pressure, pleocytosis or elevated proteins. CSF VDRL was nonreactive in our patient.
VDRL of the patient's partner was found to be positive in 1:64 dilution. We initiated treatment with Benzathine penicillin G 24 lakh units intramuscularly as a single dose following which the partner was lost to follow-up.
Skin biopsy of the rupioid lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with ulceration, dense lymphocytic infiltrate at mid-dermal level on 20x magnification [Figure 4] and plasma cell infiltrate with obliterative vasculitis on 40x magnification [Figure 5].
Since the patient gave history of intense headache and fever we considered an impending CNS involvement and hence treatment was initiated with procaine penicillin 1.2 million units daily for 3 weeks intramuscularly, and we also took the advantage of admitting the patient in our hospital. She was also given a course of oral antibiotics to eliminate the S. aureus. Patient started responding to treatment and all her cutaneous lesions healed completely in 3 weeks [Figures 6 and 7]. Patient also showed leukoderma colli around her neck. She was discharged and referred to a HIV center for HAART therapy. Monthly VDRL titers were done, and there was a four-fold decrease in the titers. Follow-up after 6 months showed no evidence of relapse, with a nonreactive VDRL and positive TPHA.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old housewife presented with a 1-month history of multiple large ulcerative and crusted skin lesions across her body accompanied by severe headache, fever, myalgia, and vaginal discharge.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding month, the patient developed widespread large ulcerative, crusted rupioid skin lesions over her face, extremities, palms, and soles along with lip and genital mucosal erosions, intense headache, fever, myalgia, and leukorrhea, without preceding primary genital chancres.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of two untreated spontaneous miscarriages. Marital/sexual history notable for no sexual contact for 6 months with her husband (a long-distance truck driver with multiple pre- and extramarital partners who was diagnosed with HIV 2 years prior on ART, currently treated for chancroid, and found to have a positive VDRL titer of 1:64).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized crusted skin ulcers, lip/genital erosions, severe headache, fever, myalgia, and leukorrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile on admission. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple large rupioid ulcerative and crusted plaques over the face and extremities, annular lesions with central hyperpigmentation on the palms and soles, mucosal erosions on the lips and genitalia, and subsequent leukoderma colli around the neck. Lymphatic examination revealed enlarged, tender, rubbery axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed polymorphonuclear leukocytosis, elevated ESR, reactive serum VDRL (titer 1:128), and positive HIV-1 ELISA. Pus culture from the ulcerated skin lesions grew quinolone-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed normal opening pressure, cell count, and protein, and nonreactive CSF VDRL. Skin biopsy histopathology of a rupioid lesion demonstrated pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with ulceration, a dense mid-dermal lymphocytic and plasmacytic infiltrate, and obliterative endarteritis/vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Malignant syphilis (lues maligna) with secondary Staphylococcus aureus superinfection unmasking newly diagnosed HIV-1 infection (confirmed by positive HIV-1 ELISA, positive p24 antigen Western blot, serum VDRL 1:128, and obliterative plasmacytic vasculitis on skin biopsy; overt neurosyphilis excluded by normal CSF and negative CSF VDRL). Due to intense headache and fever raising concern for impending CNS invasion, she was hospitalized and treated with intramuscular procaine penicillin (1.2 million units daily for 3 weeks) plus oral fluoroquinolones for S. aureus superinfection, resulting in complete healing of all cutaneous lesions within 3 weeks. She was referred to an HIV center for HAART initiation, and at 6-month follow-up showed no relapse with a nonreactive serum VDRL and positive TPHA.

raw_case_text:
A 38 years-old moderate hemophiliac A male patient was diagnosed to be co-infected with HIV (Subtype B, CCR5+) and HCV (Subtype 4), both transmitted by a blood transfusion received in 1982 during hip surgery for a fracture. Diagnoses of these infections were respectively ascertained in 1988 and 1998.
Since 1989, he received different lines of anti-retroviral treatment (ART) then HAART (Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy) with poor compliance, voluntary interruption until 2008, and correct compliance since then. A 215S mutation of the HIV virus reverse transcriptase, which induces resistance to the anti-retroviral drug azidothymidine was consequently identified. His HCV infection (Metavir score A0A1-F1F2 determined by biopsy and checked regularly by noninvasive markers of hepatitis inflammation/fibrosis) was never treated. Moreover his hepatic assessment, as observed with L-aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT), L-alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) and gammaGT gamma-glutamyltransferase markers is not so much disrupted (Figure 1A).
The patient received prosthesis of the left eye in 1996 after a paintball accident and a hip replacement in 2011 for osteo-necrosis known since 1982. None of these surgeries were accompanied by infectious side effects. Indeed, over these 30 years and despite an extremely low number of T lymphocytes, the patient displayed neither opportunistic infections, nor HIV-related cancer, nor HCV-hepatitis damages. In 1989 his initial CD4+ T-cells count was 196/mm3 and since 1995 remains between 5 and 59/mm3 (Figure 1B).
