A 54-year-old Hispanic male who was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), and AIDS-related cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma (KS; affecting his nose, back, and left leg) 1 year earlier was seen by his primary care physician (PCP) with cough and exertional dyspnea. He was empirically treated with amoxicillin, but failed to show clinical improvement. During a follow-up visit to his PCP, he was noted to be hypoxemic on room air and was sent to our hospital emergency department for further evaluation.
At the time of his initial HIV diagnosis 9 months earlier, he was found to have a CD4 count of <20 (500-1,600) with 2% (25-65%) CD4 cells. Following the diagnosis, he was started on appropriate prophylactic therapy for opportunistic infections as well as highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Unfortunately, he consistently demonstrated a lack of adherence to his medications. One month after the initial HIV diagnosis, he was noted to have systemic KS involving the pulmonary tree and bone marrow following presentation with hemoptysis and pancytopenia. Both processes were biopsy-proven. His HAART regimen was adjusted, and his symptoms and cell counts subsequently improved. He also underwent multiple cycles of chemotherapy with doxorubicin for the visceral involvement of KS.
In the emergency department, he was found to be hemodynamically stable with a low-grade fever and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest revealed a large pericardial effusion, but did not show any focal pulmonary infiltrates or evidence of pulmonary embolism. In light of these findings, he was admitted to the intensive care unit for closer monitoring. Concerns regarding poor adherence to his medications were again raised.
On the second day of his hospitalization, a transthoracic echocardiogram was done and revealed a large anterior and moderate posterior pericardial effusion with evidence of early pericardial tamponade. A CT scan of the chest also showed the pericardial effusion (Fig. 1). He underwent a pericardiocentesis, and 900 cc of bloody fluid was aspirated. A pericardial tube was placed, and this drained an additional 300 cc of bloody fluid. Laboratory examinations including serologic tests for acute EBV and CMV viral infections were negative. Pericardial fluid bacterial, fungal, and acid fast cultures were negative. Pericardial fluid cytology was also negative. However, the pericardial fluid cell count was compatible with hemopericardium. At that time, he had a viral load of 1,395 copies/ml, with a CD4 count of 113 (500-1,600). Multiple follow-up echocardiograms performed during the hospitalization showed stable small residual pericardial effusion, prompting removal of the pericardial tube on the fifth day of hospitalization. Given his stable disease and absence of recurrence of the effusion, treatment with anti-inflammatory agents was deferred. He was discharged on the sixth day with instructions for close follow-up visits with transthoracic echocardiogram and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan.
The follow-up PET/CT (Figs. 2-4) scan done after 2 months of discharge showed FDG avid areas in the right paratracheal (SUV of 9.8) and subcarinal (SUV 5.6) tissues representing pericardial involvement of KS. The scan also showed FDG avid areas in the left upper abdominal quadrant. It, however, failed to show any pulmonary tree or bone marrow involvement. A repeat PET/CT (Figs. 5, 6) done after 3 months to monitor the progression of the disease showed diminished metabolic activity in the previously seen right paratracheal and subcarinal regions with SUV up to 3.9 compared to 9.8 on the previous scan. There was also no subdiaphragmatic involvement.
In light of the improved appearance of the lesions, resolution of the pericardial effusion, and improved medication adherence, the patient was continued on the same HAART regimen with close monitoring, and the lesions were attributed to KS.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old Hispanic male with AIDS and previously diagnosed cutaneous, pulmonary, and bone marrow Kaposi sarcoma was referred to the emergency department by his primary care physician for persistent cough, exertional dyspnea, and room-air hypoxemia unresponsive to oral amoxicillin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 1 year earlier (9 months prior per timeline) with advanced HIV/AIDS (baseline CD4 count <20 cells/µL [2%]) and cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma (nose, back, and left leg), followed 1 month later by biopsy-proven pulmonary and bone marrow KS treated with HAART and multiple cycles of systemic doxorubicin, the patient had a history of poor medication adherence. He presented to his primary care physician with cough and exertional dyspnea that failed empirical oral amoxicillin and was referred to the ED after pulse oximetry demonstrated hypoxemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS diagnosed 9–12 months prior (nadir CD4 count <20 cells/µL [2%]) with chronic non-adherence to HAART and opportunistic infection prophylaxis; biopsy-proven cutaneous, pulmonary, and bone marrow Kaposi sarcoma treated with multiple cycles of doxorubicin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, exertional dyspnea, and low-grade fever. Poorly adherent to prescribed HAART and OI prophylaxis.

objective.physical_examination: In the ED, the patient was hemodynamically stable with a low-grade fever and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air.
objective.routine_investigations: Acute EBV and CMV serologies were negative. Pericardiocentesis and pericardial drain fluid analysis (1,200 mL total bloody fluid: 900 mL initial aspirate + 300 mL drain output) confirmed hemopericardium with negative bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures and negative malignant cytology.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 113 cells/µL (reference 500–1,600 cells/µL). Chest CT and transthoracic echocardiogram (day 2) revealed a large anterior and moderate posterior pericardial effusion with early cardiac tamponade and no focal pulmonary infiltrates or pulmonary embolism. Outpatient FDG-PET/CT at 2 months post-discharge demonstrated FDG-avid pericardial/mediastinal Kaposi sarcoma involvement in the right paratracheal (SUVmax 9.8) and subcarinal (SUVmax 5.6) regions and left upper quadrant without pulmonary or marrow activity; repeat PET/CT at 5 months showed marked metabolic regression (SUVmax reduced from 9.8 to 3.9) and complete resolution of subdiaphragmatic uptake.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pericardial Kaposi sarcoma presenting with large hemopericardium and early cardiac tamponade in a 54-year-old male with AIDS (admission plasma HIV viral load 1,395 copies/mL, CD4+ count 113 cells/µL) and prior cutaneous, pulmonary, and bone marrow KS. Acute tamponade was successfully managed with therapeutic pericardiocentesis and 5-day pericardial catheter drainage (1,200 mL total bloody effusion with negative infectious cultures) alongside reinforced adherence to his existing HAART regimen without additional cytotoxic chemotherapy or anti-inflammatory agents, achieving durable resolution of the pericardial effusion and marked metabolic regression of mediastinal/pericardial KS lesions on serial PET/CT.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old man presented with right scrotal hardening and swelling, accompanied by inguinal pain and flank soreness, for 3 months. An off and on fever was also noted. Right epididymitis was the initial impression, and oral antibiotics of Cephalexin were prescribed. The symptoms persisted after treatment. An ultrasound examination showed heterogeneous echogenicity of the right testis, suggesting a testicular tumor. A further pelvic computed tomographic scan revealed enlargement of the right testis estimated to be 4.5 x 4.0 cm in dimension, with heterogeneous enhancement, suspected of being a testicular tumor (Fig. 1a). No abdominal lymphadenopathy was found. Serum tumor markers, including alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), were within normal limits. A right radical orchiectomy was performed under the impression of a testicular tumor.
On gross examination, the testis revealed an ill-defined, gray to tan, soft-tumor-like lesion measuring 3.3 x 3.2 x 2.6 cm (Fig. 1b, c). Histologically, the lesion disclosed dense lymphoplasma cell and histiocyte infiltration in the interstitium, as well as spindle cell proliferation (Fig. 2a, b, c). There were small foci of foamy histiocyte aggregation and microabscess formation in the lesion (Fig. 2d). Some of the blood vessels revealed obliterative vasculitis (Fig. 2e). The seminiferous tubules revealed atrophic change (Fig. 2f). There was no well-formed granuloma or caseous necrosis in the lesion. The inflammatory process had also partially affected the epididymis and spermatic cord.
A panel of histochemical stains and immunohistochemical (IHC) stains was performed. IHC staining of CD68 (1:250; Biocare) and CD163 (1:50; Leica) proved a histiocytic nature. The spindle cells were focally positive for smooth muscle actin (1:50; DAKO), but negative for ALK (1:200; NOVO) and CD21 (1:100; Cell Marque), suggesting a myofibroblastic origin. No significant immunoglobulin G4 -positive plasma cell infiltration was seen (IgG4, 1:800; Invitrogen). No microorganisms were demonstrated by acid-fast, periodic acid-Schiff, Grocott-Gomori methenamine-silver stains, or Gram's stain. IHC with a rabbit polyclonal antibody against Treponema pallidum (dilution 1:100, Biocare Medical, Concord, CA, USA) displayed some spirochetes in the cytoplasm of histiocytes (Fig. 3a), highly suggestive of syphilitic orchitis.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for the T. pallidum DNA polymerase I gene using paraffin-embedded tissue was done. Positive control was applied using an anal biopsy specimen previously diagnosed as syphilis proved by immunohistochemistry and serology. A semi-nested PCR using the primers of TPmod-F1 (5'-GTGTGCACTGGGCATTACAG-3'), TPmod-F2 (5'-TGAAGCTGACGACCTCATTG-3'), and TP mod-R1 (5'- GTCTGAGCACTTGCACCGTA-3') targeted a different region of the T. pallidum DNA polymerase I gene (Fig. 3b). Direct sequencing proved positivity for T. pallidum, which confirmed the diagnosis of syphilitic orchitis.
The patient underwent further serology tests postoperatively. An anti-human immunodeficient virus (HIV) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and Western blot tests were positive. However, serology tests for syphilis, including both Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA), demonstrated false-negative results. At that time, the patient had a low CD4 count (72 cells/mm3) and a low CD4/CD8 ratio (0.07).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive right scrotal hardening and swelling, right inguinal pain, flank soreness, and intermittent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 3 months prior to presentation, the patient experienced painless-to-achy induration and enlargement of his right hemiscrotum accompanied by right inguinal pain, ipsilateral flank soreness, and intermittent fevers. Empirical outpatient oral cephalexin for presumed right epididymitis failed to relieve his symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previously known medical history prior to surgery.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right testicular mass/swelling, right inguinal pain, flank soreness, and intermittent fever.

objective.physical_examination: Hardened, enlarged right testicular mass on scrotal palpation.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative serum tumor markers—including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)—were all within normal limits. Scrotal ultrasound showed heterogeneous echogenicity of the right testis. Postoperative serologies were positive for HIV by ELISA and confirmatory Western blot, while both serum VDRL and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) tests were falsely nonreactive.
objective.advanced_workup: Postoperative CD4+ T-cell count was 72 cells/mm3 with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.07. Pelvic CT revealed a 4.5 x 4.0 cm heterogeneously enhancing right testicular mass without abdominal lymphadenopathy. Right radical orchiectomy specimen showed an ill-defined 3.3 x 3.2 x 2.6 cm gray-tan mass; histopathology demonstrated dense interstitial lymphoplasmacytic and CD68+/CD163+ foamy histiocytic infiltration, microabscesses, SMA-positive/ALK-negative myofibroblastic spindle cell proliferation, obliterative vasculitis, and seminiferous tubular atrophy (negative AFB, PAS, GMS, Gram, and IgG4 stains). Anti-Treponema pallidum polyclonal immunohistochemistry revealed intracellular spirochetes within histiocytes, and semi-nested PCR and direct sequencing of the T. pallidum DNA polymerase I gene (polA) confirmed Treponema pallidum.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Seronegative tumefactive syphilitic orchitis mimicking testicular malignancy and unmasking advanced HIV/AIDS (confirmed postoperatively by positive HIV ELISA and Western blot, CD4+ count 72 cells/mm3, and CD4/CD8 ratio 0.07). Despite false-negative serum VDRL and TPPA serologies (attributed to profound HIV-induced B-cell/humoral dysfunction or prozone/immunodeficiency phenomenon), definitive confirmation of Treponema pallidum orchitis was established on the radical orchiectomy specimen via obliterative endarteritis histopathology, anti-T. pallidum immunohistochemistry, and semi-nested polA PCR with direct DNA sequencing.

raw_case_text:
A 46 year-old African-American woman with HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy (ART) presented to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) from a community health center in Washington, DC, for further evaluation of elevated LAEs. Her baseline CD4 cell count was 420 cells/mm3 and her LAEs were normal prior to starting ART (Figure 1). Five months after initiation of ART with the fixed-dose combination pill of efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine, routine laboratory evaluation revealed a mild increase in her serum alkaline phosphatase (AP) to 207 U/L (normal < 116 U/L). Her AP briefly normalized before increasing again, followed by progressive increases in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) over the next year. Her CD4 cell count increased to 1,100 cells/mm3, with suppression of her HIV viral load from 62,000 copies/mL (log 4.8) to <50 copies/mL within the first 3 months of ART and remained stable thereafter.
On evaluation at the NIH, she complained of mild right upper quadrant pain and denied any other symptom. She reported a family history of scleroderma. She denied known drug allergies, over-the-counter medication use, herbal or dietary supplementation, alcohol abuse or illicit drug use. Screening laboratories showed elevation in her LAEs with AST 244 U/L, ALT 287 U/L, AP of 659 U/L, and gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT) of 607 U/L (Figure 1). Serum total bilirubin peaked at 1.7mg/dL (direct bilirubin 1.3mg/dL). Viral hepatitis serologies, hepatitis B DNA PCR and hepatitis C RNA PCR were negative. Serum iron and ceruloplasmin and alpha-1 antitrypsin levels were normal.
Autoantibody testing was remarkable for a positive ANA, greater than 12.0EU (negative < 1EU, positive > or = 1EU, strongly positive > or = 3EU) and a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody, greater than 0.6U, (negative <0.1U). Anti-smooth muscle antibody and anti-liver-kidney microsomal antibody were negative. Serum copper was elevated slightly above the upper limit of normal (173 mcg/dL, normal <145 mcg/dL). Subsequent laboratory testing revealed hypergammaglobulinemia (serum IgG 5,250 mg/dL, normal <1730 mg/dL), positive anti-centromere (>8.0 U, negative <0.1U) and anti-double stranded DNA (799 IU/mL, normal <30 IU/mL) antibodies. SCL-70 antibodies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and triple-phase CT scan of the liver were normal.
Percutaneous liver biopsy showed chronic cholestatic liver disease with marked inflammatory activity, bile duct injury, and periportal and perivenular fibrosis consistent with primary biliary cirrhosis (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry staining for cytokeratin 7 was performed using anti-cytokeratin 7 antibody from Dako (clone OV-TL-12/30 at 1:400 dilution) and the Ventana Ultra View detection system. Based on this histology and supporting laboratory findings of hypergammaglobulinemia, positive anti-nuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, the patient was diagnosed with primary biliary cirrhosis and autoimmune hepatitis overlap syndrome.
Treatment was initiated with oral prednisone (30mg daily for 7 days, then 20mg daily) and ursodiol (13-15 mg/kg daily). She continued efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine. After one month of treatment, prednisone was tapered with concomitant initiation of azathioprine (150mg daily). Her LAEs improved over the next year (Figure 1). Elevated IgG fraction declined. Her CD4 count has remained stable, and she is in excellent clinical condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old African American woman with HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy was referred to the National Institutes of Health for evaluation of mild right upper quadrant abdominal pain and progressive cholestatic and hepatocellular liver enzyme elevations.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: With normal baseline liver-associated enzymes (LAEs) and a CD4+ count of 420 cells/mm3 prior to starting fixed-dose efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine, the patient developed a mild alkaline phosphatase elevation (207 U/L) 5 months after ART initiation, followed over the ensuing year by progressive marked increases in alkaline phosphatase, GGT, AST, and ALT alongside mild right upper quadrant discomfort, while achieving full HIV viral suppression (<50 copies/mL) and robust CD4 recovery to 1,100 cells/mm3.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection well controlled on efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine. Family history notable for scleroderma. Denied alcohol abuse, illicit drug use, over-the-counter medications, or herbal/dietary supplements.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mild right upper quadrant abdominal pain; negative for jaundice or other constitutional symptoms. Home medication: fixed-dose efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine. No known drug allergies.

objective.routine_investigations: NIH laboratory evaluation showed AST 244 U/L, ALT 287 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 659 U/L (normal <116 U/L), GGT 607 U/L, peak total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL), and slightly elevated serum copper (173 µg/dL; normal <145 µg/dL). Viral hepatitis serologies, HBV DNA PCR, HCV RNA PCR, serum iron, ceruloplasmin, and alpha-1 antitrypsin were all normal/negative. Autoimmune workup revealed marked hypergammaglobulinemia (serum IgG 5,250 mg/dL; normal <1,730 mg/dL), strongly positive ANA (>12.0 EU; strongly positive >=3 EU), positive anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA >0.6 U; negative <0.1 U), positive anti-centromere antibody (>8.0 U; negative <0.1 U), and elevated anti-dsDNA antibody (799 IU/mL; normal <30 IU/mL), with negative anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had increased from 420 cells/mm3 pre-ART to 1,100 cells/mm3. Triple-phase liver CT was normal. Percutaneous liver biopsy with cytokeratin 7 (CK7) immunohistochemistry demonstrated chronic cholestatic liver disease with florid interface/lobular hepatitis, bile duct injury, and periportal and perivenular fibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Autoimmune immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (autoimmune IRIS) manifesting as primary biliary cirrhosis / autoimmune hepatitis (PBC/AIH) overlap syndrome in a 46-year-old African American woman following robust CD4+ T-cell reconstitution (from 420 to 1,100 cells/mm3) and HIV viral suppression (from 62,000 to <50 copies/mL) on efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine. Confirmed by percutaneous liver biopsy showing combined bile duct injury and marked interface hepatitis alongside AMA >0.6 U, ANA >12.0 EU, anti-dsDNA 799 IU/mL, and IgG 5,250 mg/dL. She was treated with oral ursodiol (13–15 mg/kg/day) and oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 7 days, then 20 mg daily for 1 month before tapering) transitioned to maintenance azathioprine (150 mg daily) while continuing efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine, achieving normalization of liver enzymes and IgG levels and stable CD4 counts over 1 year of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old male presented with a rapidly enlarging swelling in the right anterior palatal mucosa measuring 5.6 cm x 4.5 cm with white coating, moderately painful, and bled upon touching [Figure 1]. This swelling was present since last 2 months and growing exponentially. He had visited a local dentist with this swelling for which antibiotics and analgesics were prescribed for few days but did not get any relief.
The patient was a nonsmoker, and his medical history did not reveal other relevant information. The extraoral examination did not show any facial asymmetry and cervical lymphadenopathy. Results of laboratory testing showed hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cell, and platelet counts within normal range. On intraoral examination, the swelling had not crossed the midline and appeared to be pedunculated, afebrile, nonfluctuant. Teeth associated with the swelling, i.e., all premolars and molars on the right side of the upper jaw were noncarious, nontender, and nonmobile. The swelling did not have an ulcerated surface and palpation revealed a soft consistency. The first impression of the lesion suggested clinical characteristics of benignancy suggesting pyogenic granuloma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, peripheral ossifying fibroma, and even pleomorphic adenoma as differential diagnosis. Radiographic investigations were noncontributory as they showed mild bone loss which is usually seen in relation to reactive hyperplastic lesions.
An incisional biopsy of the lesion was submitted for pathologic examination. Histopathologic sections revealed an atypical lymphocytic infiltrate consisting of large, lymphoid cells with pleomorphic nuclei, numerous atypical mitoses, and infiltrative pattern of tumor cells. These atypical round tumor cells showed vesicular nuclei having cleaved appearance with the presence of 2 or more nucleoli [Figure 2]. Neither peripheral capsule nor Reed-Sternberg cells were seen. Immunohistochemical (IHC) studies were performed with appropriate positive and negative controls on the incisional processed tissue. IHC analysis using streptavidin-biotin protocol was performed with antibodies: CKAE1/AE3, CD3, CD5, CD15, CD20, CD30, CD56, CD68, CD99, leukocyte common antigen (LCA), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), synaptophysin, HMB-45, S-100, MPO, MUM1, and p80NPM/ALK. Tumor cells showed strong positivity with CD30 and LCA, and EMA positivity was seen only in 50% of tumor cells [Figure 3]. Negative stain was identified for CK, CD3, CD5, CD15, CD20, CD56, CD68, CD99, synaptophysin, HMB 45, S-100, MUM1, MPO, and p80NPM/ALK.
The patient was referred to Oncology Department where further laboratory and imaging tests were performed. ELISA tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C were done. Serology of the patient came out to be strongly positive for HIV based on ELISA, negative for hepatitis B and C. Further evaluation of his seropositivity by Western blot confirmed ELISA results of HIV. CD4 cell count had dropped down to 120. Full body scan to rule out the presence of any other malignancy associated with AIDS was performed. No associated malignancy or metastasis was detected on imaging. There were also no associated lymphadenopathies.
R-EPOCH infusion chemotherapy was started for the patient in the Oncology Department with one cycle every 3 weeks for a total of six courses. HAART therapy (efavirenz + tenofovir + emtricitabine) was also initiated orally. Despite consecutive follow-up, unfortunately, the patient did not cooperate and after three cycles of chemotherapy, the patient was lost. However, it was observed during a follow-up period of chemotherapy that the swelling had decreased in size. Although, even after incisional biopsy the swelling had reduced but the remarkable reduction in size was seen after chemotherapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male presented with a 2-month history of a rapidly enlarging, moderately painful, easily bleeding mass on the right anterior hard palate.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 2 months, the patient noticed an exponentially growing swelling on the right anterior palatal mucosa that bled on contact and failed to improve after a short course of oral antibiotics and analgesics prescribed by a local dentist.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; non-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful, bleeding right palatal swelling; afebrile.

objective.physical_examination: Extraoral exam showed no facial asymmetry or cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral examination revealed a 5.6 x 4.5 cm pedunculated, soft, non-fluctuant, non-ulcerated mass covered by a whitish pseudomembrane on the right anterior palatal mucosa not crossing the midline, with adjacent right maxillary premolars and molars non-carious, non-tender, and non-mobile.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC (hemoglobin, hematocrit, WBC, and platelets) was within normal limits. Dental radiographs showed only mild alveolar bone crest resorption. Viral serologies were negative for HBV and HCV and strongly positive for HIV by ELISA.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 120 cells/µL. Whole-body staging imaging showed no distant metastases, synchronous malignancies, or systemic lymphadenopathy. Incisional palatal biopsy histopathology demonstrated a diffuse infiltrative proliferation of large pleomorphic lymphoid cells with cleaved vesicular nuclei, multiple prominent nucleoli, and frequent atypical mitoses without Reed-Sternberg cells; immunohistochemistry was strongly positive for LCA (CD45) and CD30, positive in 50% of cells for EMA, and negative for p80 NPM/ALK, CD3, CD5, CD15, CD20, CD56, CD68, CD99, MUM1, MPO, CK AE1/AE3, synaptophysin, HMB-45, and S-100.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary oral/palatal ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL: CD30+, LCA+, EMA+ in 50%, ALK-, CD20-, CD3-) unmasking previously undiagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, confirmatory HIV Western blot, and CD4+ T-cell count of 120 cells/µL). The patient was initiated on oral HAART (efavirenz, tenofovir, and emtricitabine) and systemic R-EPOCH infusion chemotherapy planned for 6 cycles every 3 weeks; the palatal lymphoma mass regressed markedly over the first 3 cycles of chemotherapy before the patient was lost to follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old African American female developed a painless iris mass in the right eye for 10 months. She had a vertically transmitted human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection since birth. As a result of poor compliance, the most recent CD4 count was 27 cell/mm3 without previous opportunistic infections. HIV viral load was 60,261 copies/mL. The patient had been taking antiretroviral drugs (nevirapine, zidovudine, and lamivudine) and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole at the time of visit.
She complained of blurred vision in the right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70 OD and 20/25 OS. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy in the right eye revealed an oval, yellowish, highly vascularized iris mass with 6 mm horizontal diameter and 10 mm vertical diameter extending from the 4:00 to 11:00 positions (Figure 1). Multiple iris pigment epithelial cysts were found adhering to the posterior iris surface. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the left eye and dilated ophthalmoscopies of both eyes demonstrated no significant findings. Gonioscopy showed a tumor occupying the entire iris surface and obstructing the temporal anterior chamber angle. The anterior surface of the tumor adhered to the corneal endothelium. Ultrasound biomicroscopy revealed a hypoechoic mass coalesced with iris stroma and multiple underlying posterior iris pigment epithelial cysts (Figure 2). The largest diameter was 5.6 (horizontal) and 9.3 mm (vertical) by ultrasonic measurements. Since the tumor was confined within the iris tissue with ciliary body extension, an iridocyclectomy was performed to remove the entire mass. The neoplastic lesion that was removed was solid with homogeneous gray-white cut surfaces.
Histology revealed the specimen consisting of iris tissue with an attached tumor mass. The tumor lesion consisted of plump-shaped and epithelioid-appearing cells containing mildly pleomorphic, vesicular nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli, and ill-defined eosinophilic cytoplasm. Vague fascicular arranging pattern was observed. Mitotic count was ~8/10 high-power fields (HPF). Tumor necrosis was not found. Because of its epithelioid shape, tumors with such morphology, eg, malignant melanoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, and EBV-SMT were included in the lists of differential diagnoses with immunohistochemical studies which were performed accordingly. The neoplastic cells were strongly reactive to smooth muscle actin but negative to cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S-100, desmin, epithelial membrane antigen, and HMB-45. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded ribonucleic acid revealed a positive reaction in most regions of the tumor (Figure 3). The final diagnosis was, therefore, concluded as "EBV-associated SMT".
At 14-month follow-up, the patient was free of disease. The visual acuity was 20/25 OD (Figure 4).
This study was approved by the Ramathibodi Hospital, Mahidol University Ethic committee. Written, informed consent was obtained from all subjects and the study adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old African American female with vertically transmitted HIV infection presented with a 10-month history of a painless right iris mass and blurred vision in her right eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 months prior to presentation, the patient developed a progressively enlarging painless mass on the iris of her right eye accompanied by right ocular blurred vision. She had a history of poor adherence to her prescribed antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Vertically transmitted HIV infection since birth with poor ART compliance; no prior history of opportunistic infections.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painless right iris mass and blurred vision OD; negative for ocular pain or systemic opportunistic symptoms. Home medications: nevirapine, zidovudine, lamivudine, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70 OD and 20/25 OS. Right eye slit-lamp biomicroscopy and gonioscopy revealed a 6 x 10 mm oval, yellowish, highly vascularized iris mass extending from the 4:00 to 11:00 clock hours, adhering anteriorly to the corneal endothelium, obstructing the temporal anterior chamber angle, and associated with multiple posterior iris pigment epithelial cysts. Left eye slit-lamp exam and bilateral dilated fundoscopy were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) of the right eye demonstrated a 5.6 x 9.3 mm solid hypoechoic mass coalescing with the iris stroma with ciliary body extension and underlying posterior iris pigment epithelial cysts.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 27 cells/mm3. Complete surgical excision via right iridocyclectomy yielded a solid homogeneous gray-white tumor; histopathology showed plump epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in vague fascicles with vesicular nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, ~8 mitoses/10 HPF, and no necrosis. Immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization demonstrated diffuse strong reactivity for smooth muscle actin (SMA) and EBV-encoded RNA (EBER ISH), with negative staining for AE1/AE3, S-100, desmin, EMA, and HMB-45.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary iris/ciliary body Epstein-Barr virus-associated smooth muscle tumor (EBV-SMT) in a 14-year-old adolescent with advanced vertically acquired HIV/AIDS (CD4+ count 27 cells/mm3, plasma HIV viral load 60,261 copies/mL on zidovudine/lamivudine/nevirapine). Confirmed by iridocyclectomy histopathology, strong SMA positivity, and diffuse EBER in situ hybridization positivity (excluding amelanotic melanoma and carcinoma). Following complete surgical resection via iridocyclectomy and continuation of antiretroviral therapy, the patient remained recurrence-free at 14-month follow-up with right eye visual acuity improved to 20/25.

raw_case_text: A 76-year-old man was admitted to the emergency room after being found disoriented by his family. He experienced episodes of fever (38-39.5  C) in previous days. There were no other complaints including headache or seizures. His prior history included an HIV-1 infection diagnosed 10 years before, pulmonary tuberculosis, hypertension and hyperthyroidism. His medications included zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, tiamazol, and captopril. The last laboratorial results showed a CD4 cell count of 668 cells/mm and HIV viral load < 50 copies/mL. At admission, the physical examination showed a patient in good general conditions, moderately dehydrated and pale, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. The neurological exam showed disorientation in time and space with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14. The rest of the examination was normal. Laboratorial tests showed leukocytosis with left shift and no other alterations. A brain computed tomography scan showed a single low attenuation lesion with a uniform ring enhancement in the left temporal region (Fig. 1A). At this moment, empiric treatment for toxoplasmosis with parenteral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5/ 25 mg/ kg twice a day) was initiated. Seven days later, the patient's level of consciousness worsened, presenting disorientation and confusion. At this moment, after a review of the prior images, the hypothesis of bacterial or mycobacterial brain abscess was considered and ceftriaxone (2 g twice a day) and metronidazole (500 mg three times a day) were started. A lumbar puncture showed 1 cell/dL, 56 mg/dL of glucose, and 40 mg/dL of proteins. The cerebrospinal fluid direct exam and bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria cultures were all negative. The latex agglutination test for Cryptococcus neoformans,Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitides andHaemophylus influenzae type B, and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for these bacteria as well as for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were also all negative. Blood cultures performed by automated microbiology growth and detection system for aerobic, anaerobic and fungi resulted negative. The patient underwent trepanation, and drainage of the lesion was performed. Purulent material was obtained and sent to culture, which resulted in the growth of methicillin-sensitive S. aureus. Anti-Toxoplasma treatment was discontinued and antibiotic scheme was changed to oxacillin (2 g six times a day). The patient received eight weeks of this medication, improved progressively, clinically and radiologically (Fig. 1B-C) and was discharged to home. The patient underwent dental examination, with no evidence of dental infection. At transesophageal echocardiography the valves and left atrium were free of thrombi and vegetations, and there was no evidence of infection in thechest radiography and also in the abdominal ultrasound. In the daily assessment, measures of capillary glycemia were normal. Despite intensive efforts, no predisposing condition leading to the brain abscess, including trauma or surgery, intravenous drug use, skin or soft tissue infection, empyema, lung or intraabdominal abscess, bacterial endocarditis, dental infection, sinusitis or mastoiditis, were identified.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old HIV-positive man was brought to the emergency room after being found disoriented by his family following several days of fever (38.0–39.5 °C).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the days preceding emergency room admission, the patient experienced intermittent fevers ranging from 38.0 to 39.5 °C before being discovered disoriented in time and space by family members.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed 10 years prior (well controlled with most recent CD4+ count 668 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load <50 copies/mL); previously treated pulmonary tuberculosis; hypertension; hyperthyroidism. No history of trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use, endocarditis, dental infection, sinusitis, or mastoiditis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recent fevers (38.0–39.5 °C) and acute disorientation; negative for headache or seizures. Home medications: zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, thiamazole (methimazole), and captopril.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, moderately dehydrated and pale, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable in good general condition. Neurological examination revealed disorientation to time and place with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 14 and no focal motor deficits. Dental examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed leukocytosis with a left shift and normal daily capillary blood glucose. Automated aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal blood cultures were negative. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 668 cells/mm3. Brain CT demonstrated a solitary low-attenuation lesion with uniform ring enhancement in the left temporal lobe. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed 1 cell/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, protein 40 mg/dL, and negative Gram/AFB/fungal stains, cultures, latex agglutination, and PCRs for Cryptococcus neoformans, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed normal valves and left atrium without vegetations or thrombi. Following surgical trepanation and abscess drainage on day 7, purulent aspirate culture grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cryptogenic solitary left temporal lobe methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) brain abscess in a 76-year-old man with virologically suppressed HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, CD4+ count 668 cells/mm3 on zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz). Initial empiric parenteral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5/25 mg/kg BID) for presumed cerebral toxoplasmosis, followed on day 7 by empiric ceftriaxone (2 g BID) and metronidazole (500 mg TID) for worsening confusion, were replaced after neurosurgical trepanation and drainage isolated MSSA by an 8-week course of intravenous oxacillin (2 g six times daily), resulting in complete clinical and radiological resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old married male with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) who was a shopkeeper by profession presented with skin lesions on both lower limbs for past 9 months. It was associated with mild itching and pain. There were no complaints of joint pain or redness of eyes. The patient was diagnosed with HIV in 2007 and first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) (tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz) was started in 2009. He developed severe fatigue, weight loss, cough, and dyspnea, and CD4 count dropped to 50 cells/mm3 with plasma viral load of 157 copies/ml, 11 months ago in March 2015. Due to treatment failure, he was then put on second-line ART (abacavir, lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir) and his CD4 count increased to 204 cells/mm3 with plasma viral load of 38 copies/ml in September 2015. The present skin lesions started 2 months after initiation of second-line ART. Patient also had history of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) in 2007 when his CD4 count was 213 cells/mm3, and Herpes Zoster in 2012 when CD4 count was 78 for which treatment was taken.
On general examination, patient was moderately built and nourished, and his vitals were within normal limits. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple well-defined nontender hyperpigmented papules and nodules on both ankles, dorsum of bilateral feet and soles [Figure 1a-c]. Inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. There were no lesions elsewhere in the body. Hair, nail, and oral mucosa were normal. No ocular or systemic abnormality was noted.
Differential diagnoses considered were Kaposi's sarcoma and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) related infection including cutaneous TB. His routine blood investigations showed hemoglobin 11.5 g%, total leukocyte count 4300/mm3; and differential count neutrophil 70%, lymphocytes 28%, eosinophils 1% and monocytes 1%, and platelets 287,000/mm3. Liver function tests and renal function tests were normal. Mantoux test, serological tests for syphilis (VDRL, TPHA), hepatitis B and C, and anti-nuclear antibodies were negative. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Biopsy taken from the nodular lesion on dorsum of left foot showed a diffused dense infiltrate in reticular dermis with mild fibroplasia. The infiltrate consisted of neutrophils and histiocytes with scattering of lymphocytes and plasma cells. The infiltrate surrounded small thickened vessels and extended extensively into the interstitium. Small amount of neutrophilic nuclear dust was also present within the infiltrate [Figure 2]. Overlying epidermis and dermoepidermal junction were largely spared. These features were suggestive of EED. Patient was started on oral dapsone 100 mg/day and then increased to 200 mg/day to which he is responding gradually.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old married male shopkeeper with AIDS presented with a 9-month history of mildly pruritic and painful hyperpigmented papules and nodules over both lower extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV in 2007 and started on first-line ART (tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz) in 2009, the patient experienced immunological failure in March 2015 (CD4 count 50 cells/mm3, viral load 157 copies/mL) with fatigue, weight loss, cough, and dyspnea, prompting switch to second-line ART (abacavir, lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir). Two months after starting second-line ART (9 months prior to presentation, as his CD4 count rose to 204 cells/mm3), he developed persistent mildly itchy and painful papules and nodules over both ankles, dorsal feet, and soles.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS diagnosed in 2007; pulmonary tuberculosis in 2007 (at CD4 count 213 cells/mm3, treated); herpes zoster in 2012 (at CD4 count 78 cells/mm3, treated); switched from first-line TDF/3TC/EFV to second-line abacavir/lamivudine/atazanavir/ritonavir 11 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for lower extremity skin nodules with mild pruritus and pain; negative for arthralgias or ocular redness. Home medications: abacavir, lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir.

objective.physical_examination: Moderately built and nourished with normal vital signs. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple well-defined, non-tender, hyperpigmented papules and nodules symmetrically distributed over both ankles, the dorsum of both feet, and the soles, without inguinal lymphadenopathy or mucosal, nail, hair, or ocular lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, WBC 4,300/mm3 (70% neutrophils, 28% lymphocytes, 1% eosinophils, 1% monocytes), platelets 287,000/mm3, and normal liver and renal function tests. Mantoux test, VDRL, TPHA, HBsAg, anti-HCV, and ANA were all negative. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had increased from 50 cells/mm3 in March 2015 to 204 cells/mm3 in September 2015. Skin biopsy from a left dorsal foot nodule demonstrated a spared epidermis/dermoepidermal junction and a dense diffuse reticular dermal infiltrate of neutrophils and histiocytes with scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust), mild fibroplasia, and thickened small dermal vessels diagnostic of erythema elevatum diutinum (EED).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Erythema elevatum diutinum (EED) presenting 2 months after initiation of protease-inhibitor-based second-line antiretroviral therapy (abacavir, lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir; CD4+ count rising from 50 to 204 cells/mm3, plasma HIV viral load 38 copies/mL) in a 47-year-old male with AIDS. Kaposi sarcoma and cutaneous tuberculosis were ruled out by characteristic leukocytoclastic vasculitic/fibroplastic dermal histopathology. Oral dapsone was initiated at 100 mg/day and titrated to 200 mg/day alongside continued second-line ART, resulting in gradual regression of the acral nodules.

raw_case_text:
A 49 year old man presented with chronic headache in 2013, on a background of HIV diagnosed in 1987.
In the early 2000s his CD4+ T cell count was at a lifetime nadir of 70 cells/mul, plasma HIV RNA 5   35 log, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 4   69 log. At that time he had cognitive impairment consistent with HIV associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) with an MRI brain showing multifocal grey and white matter hyperintensities. CSF was normal including negative PCR for JC virus (JCV) DNA, but a right frontal lobe biopsy showed oligodendrocyte nuclei with viral inclusions, prominent reactive astrocytes including bizarre forms, and was strongly positive for JCV DNA by PCR. HIV associated encephalitis was also present (Anders et al.).
He commenced HAART for the first time with efavirenz, lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine, and stavudine (the latter two later switched to raltegravir for tolerability), with consequent CD4+ T cell count rise to over 300 cells/mul. He was clinically stable but required institutional care due to poor cognition that did not improve with HAART.
By 2013 his CD4+ T cell count had been over 500 cells/mul for 7 years, and HIV RNA had been undetectable for a decade. Annual MRI brain scans since 2008 (Figs. 1, 2 and 3) showed progressive white matter atrophy, and since 2010 asymptomatic fluctuating contrast enhancement without mass effect, in both cortical grey and subcortical white matter.
Examination when he presented with headache in 2013 revealed a new right inferior quadrantanopia, preexisting cognitive impairment, mild upper limb action tremor, and impaired tandem gait. CD4+ T cell count was 648 cells/mul. CSF was bland; cryptococcal antigen and HIV RNA were undetectable. However CSF JCV DNA was detected (below 30 copies/mL, the lower limit of quantification of the assay), using primers targeting the VP2 gene. The sequenced 131 base pair PCR product was a 93 % match to JCV CPN1 strain using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool. MRI brain showed increased subcortical signal hyperintensity and cortical enhancement in the left posterior temporal lobe extending into the parieto-occipital region (Fig. 3). He was diagnosed with possible recurrent PML.
His headache spontaneously improved only to recur several months later. An MRI showed new enhancing lesions in the left temporoparietal grey and subcortical white matter. Serial MR spectroscopic studies showed increasing choline and myoinositol in these regions with markedly reduced N-acetylaspartate implying ongoing gliosis of the subcortical U-fibres. CSF again showed low JC viral load. A stereotactic-guided biopsy of the left temporoparietal lesion was performed within a month of presentation, and repeated six months later because of the unusual findings, with essentially the same result. The patient has shown no clinical progression on history or examination since the biopsies. MRI has not been repeated.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old man with a 26-year history of HIV-1 infection and treated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) a decade earlier presented in 2013 with recurrent chronic headaches and a right visual field defect.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV in 1987, the patient had presented in the early 2000s (at nadir CD4 count 70 cells/µL) with cognitive impairment and biopsy-proven right frontal lobe PML and HIV encephalitis; he was started on HAART and achieved CD4+ counts >500 cells/µL for 7 years and undetectable plasma HIV RNA for 10 years, though residual cognitive impairment required institutional care. Annual surveillance brain MRIs since 2010 showed asymptomatic fluctuating cortical and subcortical contrast enhancement, and in 2013 he presented with chronic relapsing headaches.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed in 1987 (lifetime nadir CD4+ count 70 cells/µL, baseline plasma HIV RNA 5.35 log10 and CSF HIV RNA 4.69 log10); biopsy-proven right frontal PML and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) / encephalitis in the early 2000s, stably treated with HAART (efavirenz, lopinavir/ritonavir, and raltegravir [switched from lamivudine/stavudine]).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic relapsing-remitting headache, baseline cognitive impairment, visual field loss, and mild gait unsteadiness. Home medications: efavirenz, lopinavir/ritonavir, and raltegravir.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination in 2013 revealed a new right inferior quadrantanopia, baseline cognitive impairment, mild bilateral upper limb action tremor, and impaired tandem gait.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count in 2013 was 648 cells/µL (maintained >500 cells/µL for 7 years). Lumbar puncture CSF was acellular/bland with undetectable CSF HIV RNA and negative cryptococcal antigen, but ultra-low-level CSF JC virus (JCV) DNA (<30 copies/mL) was amplified using VP2 primers (131-bp product showing 93% sequence identity to the JCV CPN1 strain). Serial brain MRI and MR spectroscopy demonstrated progressive white matter atrophy and new fluctuating cortical grey and subcortical white matter contrast enhancement in the left posterior temporal and parieto-occipital lobes, with elevated choline and myoinositol and markedly reduced N-acetylaspartate indicating active subcortical U-fiber gliosis. Two stereotactic biopsies of the left temporoparietal lesion (performed 6 months apart) confirmed chronic/smoldering inflammatory PML/gliosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Late relapsing/smoldering inflammatory progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) with JCV CPN1-like variant detection (<30 copies/mL in CSF) occurring after 10 years of sustained HIV virological suppression and robust immune reconstitution (CD4+ count 648 cells/µL on efavirenz, lopinavir/ritonavir, and raltegravir). Confirmed by serial CSF VP2 PCR/sequencing, MR spectroscopy, and two stereotactic left temporoparietal brain biopsies; the patient remained clinically stable without neurological progression on continued HAART following the biopsies.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old male presented to our institution complaining of a 1-month history of abdominal pain. His medical history was significant for HIV (diagnosed 18 years ago), KS, and chronic left-leg edema secondary to pelvic infiltration of KS, compressing the common femoral and superficial femoral veins for which he previously received chemotherapy (paclitaxel, doxorubicin, and then gemcitabine) and electron beam radiation. The patient also noted worsening abdominal distention, which he attributed to his worsening abdominal pain. In addition to his abdominal distension, he gave a history of unintentional 4.5 kg (10 lbs) weight loss over a 1-week period and bilateral lower-extremity edema that was worse on the left side. He also complained of progressively worsening dyspnea, nausea, intermittent pyrexia as high as 38.3 C (101 F), anorexia, rhinorrhea, and malaise for 2 days prior to admission. He admitted to being compliant with his current antiretroviral regimen, which included raltegravir, ritonavir, and the combination abacavir/lamivudine/zidovudine.
On admission, his blood pressure was 113/77 mm Hg, pulse 97 beats per minute, temperature 36.5 C (97.7 F), respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and pulse oximetry 99% (room air). Physical examination was significant for generalized abdominal distension on inspection, decreased frequency of bowel sounds, and generalized tenderness to palpation without any rebound tenderness or guarding. He had bilateral flank dullness to percussion, positive shifting dullness, and fluid thrill. There was no cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal adenopathy. HIV serology showed an absolute CD4 count of 261 cells/microl and a quantitative HIV-1 RNA level of 220 copies/ml. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was significant for moderate-volume abdominal ascites prominently seen in the perihepatic region extending into the right paracolic gutter without any evidence of bowel obstruction (fig. 1). His ascites rapidly reaccumulated within 48 h after the initial paracentesis.
His initial ultrasound-guided paracentesis yielded 1,365 ml cloudy, yellow ascitic fluid. Analysis of the ascitic fluid was positive for a large number of atypical lymphoid cells. Flow cytometry cytospin showed pleomorphic, large lymphoid cells with large nuclei, multiple prominent nucleoli, and deeply basophilic cytoplasm with a plasmacytoid appearance. Polymerase chain reaction showed clonal B cells, and HHV-8 immunostain revealed positive nuclear staining (fig. 2), which confirmed the diagnosis of PEL. The cell block preparation revealed multiple malignant lymphocytes (fig. 3).
Given his Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score of 1, he was promptly started on DA-EPOCH as we were optimistic of a good outcome. His ascites gradually improved and did not recur on follow-up visits after 4 cycles of DA-EPOCH.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old HIV-positive male with a history of Kaposi sarcoma presented with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain and abdominal distension, a 1-week history of 4.5 kg (10-lb) weight loss, and a 2-day history of dyspnea, nausea, intermittent fever up to 38.3 °C, anorexia, rhinorrhea, and malaise.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the month preceding admission, the patient experienced progressively worsening generalized abdominal pain and abdominal distension, accompanied by a 4.5 kg weight loss over the prior week, asymmetric bilateral lower extremity edema (left worse than right), and 2 days of worsening dyspnea, nausea, anorexia, rhinorrhea, malaise, and intermittent fever up to 38.3 °C (101 °F).
subjective.past_medical_history: 18-year history of HIV infection (adherent to raltegravir, ritonavir, and abacavir/lamivudine/zidovudine); cutaneous/pelvic Kaposi sarcoma complicated by chronic left femoral vein compression and left leg lymphedema/edema, previously treated with systemic paclitaxel, doxorubicin, gemcitabine, and electron-beam radiotherapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for abdominal pain, abdominal distension, 4.5 kg weight loss in 1 week, asymmetric leg edema, dyspnea, nausea, anorexia, intermittent fever (38.3 °C), rhinorrhea, and malaise. Home medications: raltegravir, ritonavir, and abacavir/lamivudine/zidovudine (Trizivir).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: blood pressure 113/77 mmHg, pulse 97 beats/min, temperature 36.5 °C (97.7 °F), respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and SpO2 99% on room air; ECOG performance status 1. Abdominal examination revealed marked distension, hypoactive bowel sounds, diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding, bilateral flank dullness, shifting dullness, and a positive fluid thrill, along with chronic asymmetric left-predominant lower extremity edema and no peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission absolute CD4+ T-cell count was 261 cells/µL. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated moderate-volume perihepatic and right paracolic ascites without bowel obstruction or solid lymphomatous masses. Ultrasound-guided paracentesis (1,365 mL cloudy yellow fluid, rapidly reaccumulating within 48 hours) with cytology, cell block, flow cytometry, PCR clonality, and immunohistochemistry revealed numerous large pleomorphic plasmacytoid lymphoid cells with deeply basophilic cytoplasm, multiple prominent nucleoli, clonal B-cell Ig rearrangement by PCR, and positive nuclear HHV-8 immunostaining.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Peritoneal extracavitary/classic HHV-8-positive primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) presenting with rapidly reaccumulating malignant ascites in a 47-year-old male with well-controlled HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV-1 RNA 220 copies/mL, CD4+ count 261 cells/µL on raltegravir, ritonavir, and abacavir/lamivudine/zidovudine) and prior pelvic Kaposi sarcoma. Confirmed via ascitic fluid cytology, clonal B-cell PCR, and nuclear HHV-8 immunohistochemistry. Prompt initiation of systemic dose-adjusted EPOCH (DA-EPOCH) chemotherapy alongside continued ART resulted in complete resolution of ascites without recurrence after 4 cycles.

raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old boy was referred to our hospital for persistent fever, cough and weight loss for 3 weeks duration. He had previously consulted in a peripheral hospital where a chest X-ray was normal and a treatment for acute bronchitis was prescribed (thiamphenicol and clavulanic acid and amoxicillin).
On admission, he was conscious but in respiratory distress, with dyspnoea, and polypnea of 56 cycles/min, the heart rate was 108beats/min and temperature of 38.7 C. He presented a hepatomegaly, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. He was admitted in the paediatric intensive care unit. A thoracoabdominal sonogram showed a left liver lobe abscess. A chest and abdominal computer tomography scan (CT scan) was requested to further characterize the liver abscess. It showed bilateral pleuropneumopathy, a diaphragmatic collection thru the larrey's aperture, hepatosplenomegaly, and minor ascites [Figures 1-4]. The amoebic serology was normal. He was placed on IV antibiotic (amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, and gentamicin). A review of the scan films made us suspect a pericardial effusion or amediastinal abscess. A rightmediastinal drainage was done and evacuated 500ml of frank greenish pus. There was no improvement with that regimen. The antibiotic was changed to ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/24 h, metronidazole (mg/kg/24 h) and gentamicin (5 mg/kg/24 h). The child was further stabilized with a blood transfusion for severe anaemia. The evolution was marked by no improvement after 3 days and he was more ill, the preoperative American Society of Anesthesia (ASA) was in class V. He then underwent a thoracotomy and a pericardiectomy at day 4 from admission. Twolitres of frank pus were removed from the pericardium. Two drains were left in place. AT J3 after the surgery, he remained febrile, the culture of the pus growed Staphylococcus aureus, and the HIV serology requested after counselling of the mother was positive. Based on the antibiogram, gentamicin was stopped and ciprofloxacin was started. At J9 post-operatively the temperature subsided and the hemodynamic parameters improved, but there was a persistent purulent drainage. AT J13, he was stable, a corticotherapy was introduced to decrease the fibrosis and drains were removed. The chest radiograph showed a persistent bilateral lower lobe infiltrate and a mild cardiomegaly. The cardiac sonogram showed a thickened pericardium, but no pericardial effusion and no valvular anomaly. AT J24, he was discharged home with per os ciprofloxacin and iron treatment. The steroids were stopped. He was seen in the out-patient department 1 week after and was doing well. He was again seen 1 month after discharged. The confirmation HIV testing was still positive, the Cluster determination (Lymphocytes T4) [CD4] count was 14 cells/ml. He was placed on antiretroviral drugs associated to cotrimoxazole. The child was referred back to his hospital were the mother was a nurse. After counselling, the mother admitted being on antiretroviral treatment for many years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old boy was referred with a 3-week history of persistent fever, cough, and weight loss, presenting in acute respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 3 weeks prior to referral, the child experienced persistent fever, cough, and weight loss that failed to improve after outpatient treatment for presumed acute bronchitis (thiamphenicol and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, with a normal initial chest X-ray) at a peripheral hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable prior medical history reported at admission; post-diagnosis counseling revealed that his mother (a nurse) was HIV-positive and had been on antiretroviral therapy for many years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3-week fever, cough, weight loss, and acute dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: On admission to the PICU, the child was conscious but in severe respiratory distress with tachypnea (56 breaths/min), tachycardia (108 beats/min), and fever (38.7 °C). Cardiovascular and abdominal examination revealed jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hepatomegaly (ASA physical status class V prior to thoracotomy).
objective.routine_investigations: Severe anemia requiring packed red blood cell transfusion; negative amoebic serology; positive HIV serology (confirmed 1 month post-discharge). Pericardial/mediastinal pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Postoperative day 13 chest X-ray showed persistent bilateral lower lobe infiltrates and mild cardiomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count at 1-month post-discharge follow-up was 14 cells/mL. Thoracoabdominal ultrasound and thoracoabdominal CT demonstrated a left hepatic lobe abscess, bilateral pleuropneumonia, an anterior diaphragmatic/mediastinal collection extending through Larrey's space, massive purulent pericarditis, hepatosplenomegaly, and mild ascites. Initial right mediastinal drainage evacuated 500 mL of frank greenish pus, and day 4 open thoracotomy and pericardiectomy evacuated 2,000 mL of frank pericardial pus. Postoperative day 13 echocardiogram showed pericardial thickening without residual effusion or valvular abnormality.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Staphylococcus aureus left hepatic lobe abscess complicated by transdiaphragmatic rupture through Larrey's space causing anterior mediastinal abscess and massive purulent pericarditis with cardiac tamponade, unmasking vertically acquired pediatric HIV/AIDS (confirmed by repeat positive HIV serology and CD4+ T-cell count of 14 cells/mL). Managed with initial mediastinal drainage (500 mL pus), day 4 open thoracotomy and pericardiectomy (2 L pus evacuated), blood transfusion, short-course adjunctive corticosteroids (started day 13 to prevent constrictive pericardial fibrosis), and targeted antimicrobial therapy switched from amoxicillin-clavulanate/gentamicin and ceftriaxone/metronidazole/gentamicin to ciprofloxacin based on S. aureus susceptibility. Discharged on postoperative day 24 on oral ciprofloxacin and iron supplementation, and subsequently initiated on antiretroviral therapy and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis at 1-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old Hispanic man from Mexico presented with pain and swelling of the right foot for 1 year. His medical history was only remarkable for latent TB diagnosed 9 months prior to presentation and was prescribed isoniazid for 9 months, but only 2 months was completed by the patient for unknown reasons. The pain in his right foot had been increasing in intensity and began to hinder his ambulation, thus leading to a visit to the emergency room. The pain was throbbing in nature, localized to the right foot, and was exacerbated by walking and movement of the ankle. The patient was unable to bear weight on his ankle. He denied any trauma, insect bites, or recent travels. Review of systems was negative for dyspnea, cough, sputum production, chest pain, pleurisy, fevers, chills, or night sweats. He did, however, report a 20-pound weight loss over the past 6 months.
On physical examination, inspection of the right foot showed no erythema, pallor, lesions, or discharge. The right foot was warm to touch and tender, especially along the lateral portion of the dorsum of foot. There was decreased range of motion secondary to pain and edema that extended from the mid-foot up to the ankle. Pedal pulses were intact, and there were no signs of trauma or infection. The remainder of his physical examination, including the lungs, was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies revealed the following values: white blood cell (WBC) count 10.8 (normal 4.8-10.8 thousands/mL); hemoglobin 10.5 (normal 14-18 g/dL); hematocrit 31 (normal 42-52%); platelets 172,000 (normal 130,000-400,000); serum sodium 130 (normal 135-145 mmol/L); serum potassium 4.6 (normal 3.5-5.1 mmol/L); serum chloride 94 (normal 98-107 mmol/L); serum bicarbonate 25 (normal 22-29 mmol/L); Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) 17 (normal 6-20 mg/dL); serum creatinine 0.96 (normal 0.7-1.2 mg/dL). Liver function tests were all within normal limits, except for elevated alkaline phosphatase of 584 (normal 40-129 u/L). On admission, HIV screening was positive which was confirmed with western blot assay. HIV viral load was found to be 76,168 copies (normal <175) and CD4 count was 89 (normal 490-1,740 cells/microL). Admission chest x-ray was suggestive of miliary TB (Fig. 1a).
The patient was admitted and placed in respiratory isolation. CT demonstrated a diffuse pattern of nodules throughout both lungs, also suggestive of military TB (Fig. 1b). Radiography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right foot and ankle revealed significant destruction of the navicular cuneiform joints with associated osteomyelitis compared to initial imaging 1 year prior (Fig. 2a and b). Differential diagnosis at the time of admission included septic arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, aseptic necrosis, and TB osteomyelitis. Serological investigations revealed the following: C Reactive Protein (CRP) 5.24 (normal <0.5 mg/dL); Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 100 (normal 20 mm/h); uric acid 6.4 (normal 3.4-7.0 mg/dL); Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) 248 (normal 135-225 units/L); Anti-Nuclear Antibodies (ANA) negative; anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (CCP) <16 (normal <20); Rheumatoid Factor negative; and Quantiferon-TB Gold positive. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) sputum smears and cultures were negative. On discussion with an infectious disease consultant regarding initiation of anti-TB chemotherapy, it was recommended that treatment be started after a tissue diagnosis has been obtained. A fluoroscopy guided bone biopsy of the right first cuneiform was performed which revealed severe acute and chronic mycobacterial osteomyelitis with numerous AFB (Fig. 3). Furthermore, cultures were positive for mycobacterium TB and it was sensitive to all anti-TB drugs. Anti-tubercular chemotherapy was initiated after tissue diagnosis was obtained. Highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) was started 2 weeks later due to the increased risk of immune reconstitution syndrome (IRIS). The patient was found to have iron deficiency anemia and subsequently started on iron supplementation. During the course of the hospital stay, he started having fevers with a T-max of 102.7 F along with watery diarrhea associated with non-specific abdominal pain and oral thrush. He was empirically started on vancomycin, cefepime, bactrim, and fluconazole for possible septic arthritis, pneumonia, Pneumocystis pneumonia infection, and oral candidiasis. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral contrast revealed diffuse colitis and metronidazole was added to therapy. All blood, sputum, and urine cultures were negative, including toxins for Clostridium difficile. Eventually the fevers and diarrhea resolved; however, his renal function began to deteriorate. Vancomycin was discontinued and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was switched to atovaquone. Renal function quickly improved with hydration and the change in drug regimen.
Our patient had a positive clinical response to medical therapy with a decrease in the pain and swelling of his right foot and ankle in 2 weeks time. Upon discharge, his ambulatory dysfunction resolved and he was walking with the assistance of a cane. Follow-up with 3 months of anti-TB treatment, repeat chest x-ray showed significant improvement from the previously seen miliary TB pattern (Fig. 4). His viral load was undetectable and CD4 trended up. One year after discharge the patient was ambulating without any assistance. Follow-up chest x-ray and MRI of his right foot showed no pulmonary abnormalities and significant improvement of the navicular and first and second cuneiforms of the right foot, with the bones appearing relatively normal (Fig. 5). His total anti-TB therapy duration was 9 months of rifabutin, which was used instead of rifamycin during his therapy. After HRZE therapy (isoniazid, rifabutin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for 2 months, patient received 7 months of isoniazid (INH)/rifabutin treatment. His HAART treatment consisted of protease inhibitor (PI)-based therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old Hispanic man from Mexico presented to the emergency department with a 1-year history of progressively worsening throbbing right foot pain and swelling that prevented weight-bearing, alongside a 20-lb weight loss over 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding year, the patient experienced progressive throbbing pain and swelling of his right mid-foot and ankle exacerbated by movement until he could no longer bear weight. Nine months prior to presentation, he had been diagnosed with latent tuberculosis and prescribed a 9-month course of isoniazid, but he discontinued therapy after only 2 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: Latent tuberculosis diagnosed 9 months prior (completed only 2 of 9 prescribed months of isoniazid). Denied trauma, insect bites, or recent travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right foot/ankle pain, swelling, inability to bear weight, and 20-lb weight loss over 6 months; negative at presentation for dyspnea, cough, sputum, chest pain, fevers, chills, or night sweats (subsequently developed inpatient fever to 102.7 °F, watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and oral thrush).

objective.physical_examination: Right foot examination revealed warmth, edema extending from the mid-foot to the ankle, marked tenderness over the lateral dorsum of the foot, and pain-limited ankle/foot range of motion with intact pedal pulses and no overlying erythema, skin breakdown, or purulent drainage. Lungs and remaining initial physical exam were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed WBC 10.8 x 10^3/mL (normal 4.8–10.8), hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL (normal 14–18), hematocrit 31% (normal 42–52%), platelets 172,000/µL, sodium 130 mmol/L (normal 135–145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 94 mmol/L (normal 98–107), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, BUN 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase 584 U/L (normal 40–129 U/L) with otherwise normal LFTs, CRP 5.24 mg/dL (normal <0.5), ESR 100 mm/h (normal 20), uric acid 6.4 mg/dL, LDH 248 U/L (normal 135–225), iron-deficiency anemia, negative ANA, anti-CCP (<16), and RF, and positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold. Sputum AFB smears and cultures, blood/urine cultures, and stool C. difficile toxin were negative. Admission chest X-ray showed a diffuse miliary pattern.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 89 cells/µL (normal 490–1,740 cells/µL). Chest CT confirmed diffuse bilateral miliary pulmonary nodules; abdominal/pelvic CT during inpatient diarrhea showed diffuse colitis. Right foot/ankle radiographs and MRI demonstrated severe osteolytic destruction of the naviculocuneiform joints and osteomyelitis of the navicular and cuneiform bones. Fluoroscopy-guided bone biopsy of the right first cuneiform revealed acute and chronic necrotizing mycobacterial osteomyelitis with numerous acid-fast bacilli, and bone culture grew pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Tuberculous osteomyelitis and septic arthritis of the right naviculocuneiform joints with concurrent miliary pulmonary tuberculosis unmasking newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV screening, confirmatory Western blot, plasma HIV viral load 76,168 copies/mL, CD4+ count 89 cells/µL, and right first cuneiform bone biopsy AFB smear and culture positive for pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Following bone biopsy confirmation, the patient was initiated on a 9-month rifabutin-based anti-tuberculosis regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifabutin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol followed by 7 months of isoniazid and rifabutin), with protease-inhibitor-based HAART initiated 2 weeks later to minimize IRIS risk, plus fluconazole for oral thrush, metronidazole for colitis, and atovaquone (switched from TMP-SMX and vancomycin after transient acute kidney injury) for PCP prophylaxis. By 3–12 months of follow-up, his HIV viral load was undetectable, miliary lung nodules resolved, right foot MRI showed near-complete bony healing, and he was ambulating independently without assistance.

raw_case_text: A 19-year-old male presented to our medical clinic in mid-2009 with complaints of acne, hair loss, and difficulty in getting up from sitting position with evidence of proximal muscle weakness. He had been recently diagnosed with dermatomyositis based on his clinical features of elevated creatine kinase levels, typical skin changes, and electromyography (EMG) pattern consistent with dermatomyositis. His medications at the time included prednisone, methotrexate, folate, and vitamin D. He was sexually active with both male and female partners with inconsistent use of condoms. Subsequently, he had multiple clinic visits between 2010 and 2011 for complaints of sore throat, fever, chills, anal pain, anal itching, and anal discharge. During this time, he was treated for oral candidiasis, scabies infestation, syphilis, and condyloma acuminata. He refused HIV testing, claiming that he was tested negative elsewhere. In early 2012, he consented for HIV testing. HIV ELISA and western blot were positive, with a CD4+ cell count of 182 cells/microL and HIV RNA copies of 1,337,310 copies/mL on diagnosis. He was started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). After initiation of HAART his CD4+ count gradually increased to 346 cells/microL and HIV-1 RNA copies decreased to 462 copies/mL within 2 months. At this time, he started having frequent flares of dermatomyositis. His dermatomyositis had been fairly well controlled on prednisone and methotrexate before initiation of HAART. He was switched to a combination of prednisone and azathioprine, then with mycophenolate mofetil, all with poor response. In June 2013, he was started on monthly intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), to which he initially had a fair response but ultimately required reintroduction of methotrexate and increased doses of prednisone to control the dermatomyositis flares. Despite this regimen, he had another dermatomyositis flare in 2014. In mid-2015, he presented to the emergency department with complains of diffuse muscle pain, chest pain, and shortness of breath on exertion. His last dose of IVIG was a week before presentation. His active medications were prednisone 60 mg daily, methotrexate 40 mg once a week, IVIG once a month, and Atripla. On physical examination, he had mild heliotrope rash on eyes, chest wall tenderness, neck, and proximal muscle weakness on both upper and lower limbs. Critical laboratory findings included creatine kinase of 1,145 IU/L, aspartate transaminase of 400 IU/L, and alanine transaminase of 220 IU/L. Because of the refractoriness of therapy, a muscle biopsy was done which confirmed the clinical diagnosis of dermatomyositis (Fig. 1a and 1b). He was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone at stress doses with prompt improvement in overall muscle strength. He was discharged to follow up as an outpatient for rituximab therapy. He continues to take HAART and follows up in Infectious disease clinic. At the time of this report, the patient's latest helper CD4 counts was 320 cells/mcL and HIV-1 ultrasensitive RNA <20 copies/mL 02/8/2016. The patient is yet to follow up at the rheumatology clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male with dermatomyositis and subsequently diagnosed HIV-1 infection presented with recurrent refractory dermatomyositis flares (proximal muscle weakness, diffuse myalgias, heliotrope rash, chest pain, and exertional dyspnea) following antiretroviral-induced immune reconstitution.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with dermatomyositis in mid-2009 (well controlled initially on oral prednisone and methotrexate), the patient had multiple visits in 2010–2011 for oral candidiasis, scabies, syphilis, and anal condylomata before consenting to HIV testing in early 2012. Within 2 months of starting HAART (Atripla), as his CD4+ count rose from 182 to 346 cells/µL and HIV-1 RNA fell from 1,337,310 to 462 copies/mL, he began experiencing frequent severe flares of dermatomyositis refractory to azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, monthly IVIG, methotrexate (40 mg weekly), and high-dose prednisone (60 mg daily), culminating in a mid-2015 emergency department admission for diffuse myalgia, chest pain, and exertional dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Dermatomyositis diagnosed in mid-2009; HIV-1 infection diagnosed in early 2012; history of oral candidiasis, scabies, syphilis, and perianal condyloma acuminata in 2010–2011. Sexual history notable for inconsistent condom use with male and female partners.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for diffuse muscle pain, proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope eyelid rash, chest pain, and exertional dyspnea. Home medications in mid-2015: efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir (Atripla), prednisone 60 mg daily, methotrexate 40 mg weekly, monthly IVIG, folate, and vitamin D.

objective.physical_examination: Mid-2015 emergency department examination revealed a mild bilateral periorbital heliotrope rash, anterior chest wall tenderness, and symmetric neck flexor and bilateral upper and lower extremity proximal muscle weakness.
objective.routine_investigations: Mid-2015 flare labs demonstrated markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK 1,145 IU/L), AST 400 IU/L, and ALT 220 IU/L. Baseline electromyography (EMG) in 2009 had shown a classic myopathic/inflammatory dermatomyositis pattern.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 182 cells/µL at HIV diagnosis in early 2012, rose to 346 cells/µL within 2 months of HAART initiation, and was 320 cells/µL in February 2016. Skeletal muscle biopsy performed in mid-2015 confirmed active dermatomyositis with perifascicular atrophy and inflammatory myopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Autoimmune immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) manifesting as severe, treatment-refractory exacerbations of pre-existing dermatomyositis following HAART-induced CD4+ T-cell recovery (CD4+ rising from 182 to 346 cells/µL and HIV-1 RNA suppressed from 1,337,310 to <20 copies/mL on Atripla, confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, Western blot, and 2015 skeletal muscle biopsy).
