subjective.history_of_present_illness: In July 2022, the patient was diagnosed with SLE, lupus nephritis, and polyserositis (SLEDAI score 20) after presenting with facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension, cough, and white sputum. She was treated with glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone, prednisone), cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), hydroxychloroquine, and four infusions of belimumab (480 mg initiated July 22, 2022 through September 29, 2022), which improved her symptoms and allowed tapering of glucocorticoids and MMF. In October 2022, she developed herpes zoster infection followed by occasional chest tightness and mild dyspnea prior to her scheduled fifth belimumab dose on November 1, 2022.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus nephritis and polyserositis diagnosed in July 2022; history of reported glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency; herpes zoster infection in October 2022.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath; negative for noticeable cough or expectoration in November 2022. Home medications included tapered prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine sulfate, and belimumab.

objective.routine_investigations: WBC count and CRP were normal. HIV serology and anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies were negative. Serum beta-D-glucan, galactomannan, cryptococcal capsular antigen, tuberculosis antibody, Candida IgG antibody, and Candida antigen tests were all negative. Serum immunoglobulins showed decreased IgG at 5.44 g/L (reference 8–18 g/L), normal IgA at 1.16 g/L (reference 0.9–4.5 g/L), and decreased IgM at 0.64 g/L (reference 0.84–1.32 g/L). Repeat G6PD enzyme testing was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subset analysis revealed CD4+ T-cell count 332/µL (reference 180–324/µL), reduced CD8+ T-cell count 646/µL (reference 1185–1901/µL), and markedly depleted NK cell count 16/µL (reference 200–587/µL). Chest CT (November 1, 2022) demonstrated diffuse bilateral patchy, nodular, and flocculent ground-glass opacities across all lung lobes, alongside nodules and cavitary lesions in the dorsal segment of the left lower lobe. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) next-generation sequencing (NGS), fungal culture, and PCR were performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary co-infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii and Talaromyces marneffei in an HIV-negative immunocompromised 52-year-old woman with SLE receiving belimumab and immunosuppressive therapy. Definitive confirmation was achieved via BALF metagenomic NGS detecting Pneumocystis jirovecii (178,940 sequence reads) and Talaromyces marneffei (7,480 sequence reads), positive BALF P. jirovecii PCR, and positive BALF fungal culture isolating T. marneffei, while HIV and anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies were negative. The fifth dose of belimumab was discontinued, and SLE maintenance was adjusted to prednisone 5 mg/day, mycophenolate mofetil 0.75 g/day, and hydroxychloroquine 0.2 g/day. T. marneffei was treated with voriconazole (0.6 g/day on day 1, then 0.4 g/day), and P. jirovecii pneumonia was treated initially with clarithromycin 1.8 g/day for 1 week due to historical G6PD deficiency concern, then switched to sulfamethoxazole after normal G6PD activity was confirmed. Repeat chest CT after 1 month demonstrated marked radiographic improvement, and the patient remained stable on outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 50s male patient with cough, bloody sputum expectoration, slight fever and slightly visible body rashes at the thoracoabdominal junction (Figure 1A) presented to Zhejiang Provincial People's Hospital on July 6, 2021 because of pulmonary shadow found in physical examination of local hospital for more than half a year. The patient had been healthy and had not been infected with HIV in the past but had a 30-year history of smoking. After admission, the physical examination was completed. The body temperature was 37.6 C, pulse rate was 105 times/min, respiration was 20 times/min, blood pressure was 101/68 mmHg, and the breath sound was coarse through auscultation of both lungs. The results of the initial laboratory examination are shown in Table 1. In addition, we also monitored the laboratory test indicators of patients during hospitalization (Figure 2A-D). Chest computed tomography (CT) showed pulmonary solid mass in the right upper lobe with apical bronchial occlusion, patchy infiltration and irregular thickening of local interlobular septum. There were multiple nodules, patchy and cord infiltration in the right lower lobe with fuzzy boundary, irregular thickening of interlobular septum and adjacent pleural thickening. Fibrous foci and tiny nodules were seen in the left lower lobe, presenting with a right pleural effusion (Figure 3A; July 8th). 
No cancer cells were found in fibrobronchoscopic fluid, pleural effusion or pulmonary masses and no abnormal cells were seen by bone marrow biopsy. The histopathological results of the right pulmonary masses showed multifocal areas of consolidation with fibrous polypoid tissue, alveolar epithelium and vascular hyperplasia in the alveolar cavity. A large number of lymphocytes, plasma cells, phagocytes and neutrophils were infiltrated in the lung tissue, and the pulmonary septum was widened, which suggested that chronic active inflammation of lung tissue with parenchymal lesions and bronchiolitis obliterans with organized pneumonia (BOOP) (Figure 1B-F).
Tuberculosis screening laboratory demonstrated negative acid-fast staining in a suppurative inflammatory background with plentiful neutrophils and macrophages, which preliminarily ruled out the infection of Mycobacterium (Figure 4B). Blue fluorescent fungal spores were observed in the dark field indicating fungal infection by fungal fluorescence staining of sputum (Figure 4C). Gram staining of alveolar lavage fluid showed that deeply stained fungal spores were detected (Figure 4D). Scattered, slightly asymmetric and typical double-helical broom-like fungal hyphae with short, smooth walled, ellipsoidal, mono-verticillate penicillium conidiophores were observed under oil lens after gently touching scotch tape to the colonies and staining with lactophenol cotton blue (Figure 4E). Fungal culture of BALF revealed colonies with temperature-dependent dimorphic growth character, which showed yeast-like fungi producing soluble red pigment at 28 C and mycelia at 37 C in CANA, PDA and SDA (Figure 4F). Single band PCR amplification for internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region in genomic DNA of the clinical isolate was observed after electrophoresis (Figure 4A). The nucleotide sequences of the 563-bp ITS including the 5.8S rRNA and 26S rRNA gene were verified and utilized to perform phylogenetic analysis by the Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (MEGA) software version 11 through the minimum-evolution method as reported in the previous literature. A phylogenetic tree was constructed utilizing the sequence of Talaromyces marneffei ZJPPH1 (GenBank number: ON287261.1) from the isolate of this study along with 53 available sequences with the highest homology retrieved from GenBank. The nucleic acid sequence of the present isolate revealed 99.62% similarity with Talaromyces marneffei strain AMC PM002 (Figure 5).

subjective.chief_complaint: A male patient in his 50s presented on July 6, 2021 with cough, bloody sputum expectoration, low-grade fever, a thoracoabdominal rash, and a pulmonary shadow noted for over 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A pulmonary mass/shadow had been detected on routine examination at a local hospital more than 6 months prior to presentation; he subsequently presented with cough, hemoptysis/blood-streaked sputum, mild fever, and a faint thoracoabdominal rash.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no history of HIV infection; 30-year history of cigarette smoking.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, bloody sputum, mild fever, and thoracoabdominal skin rash.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: temperature 37.6 °C, pulse 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure 101/68 mmHg. Cutaneous inspection showed a faint rash at the thoracoabdominal junction. Chest auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV testing was negative. Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining was negative against a suppurative background of neutrophils and macrophages, whereas sputum fungal fluorescence staining revealed blue fluorescent fungal spores.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (July 8, 2021) demonstrated a solid mass in the right upper lobe with apical bronchial occlusion, patchy infiltrates, and interlobular septal thickening; multiple nodules and patchy/cord-like infiltrates with adjacent pleural thickening in the right lower lobe; fibrous foci and tiny nodules in the left lower lobe; and a right pleural effusion. Cytology of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, pleural effusion, and lung mass as well as bone marrow biopsy were negative for malignancy. Right lung mass histopathology showed multifocal consolidation with fibrous polypoid tissue, alveolar epithelial and vascular hyperplasia, dense lymphocytic/plasmacytic/neutrophilic/macrophage infiltration, and bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP) changes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary talaromycosis with secondary bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP) in an HIV-negative male smoker. Definitive pathogen confirmation was achieved via Gram stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) showing deeply stained fungal spores, BALF culture on CANA, PDA, and SDA media demonstrating thermal dimorphism (yeast-like colonies with soluble red pigment at 28 °C and mycelia with mono-verticillate penicillium conidiophores on lactophenol cotton blue staining at 37 °C), and 563-bp ITS rRNA PCR amplification and sequencing (strain ZJPPH1, GenBank ON287261.1) showing 99.62% sequence homology with Talaromyces marneffei strain AMC PM002. Malignancy and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection were ruled out.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old male patient, a native and resident of Guangxi, China, was admitted to our hospital with a 1-month history of fever, coughing with expectoration, dizziness, headache and gait imbalance for 9 days. He was a smoker and had no history of organ transplants, leukemia, diabetes and autoimmune disease.
Basic laboratory workup revealed increased levels of leukocytes (10.12x 109/L), lymphocytes (3.55x 109/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 46mm/h). The CD4+ T-cell count was 1181 per mm3 (561-1,137 per mm3), and NK cell percentage was 33.56% (9.5-23.5%). The anti-HIV antibody was negative, and the absolute neutrophil count, IgG, IgM as well as C-reactive protein were all within normal limits. A chest computed tomography (CT) showed multiple high-density patches of shadows in both lungs (Figure 1A). Brain CT showed a cerebral infarction in the right occipital lobe, and brain enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an irregular lesion measuring up to 3.5 cm x 2.5 cm x 3.2cm. (Figure 1B). T. marneffei isolated from sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) culture (Figure 2A), while blood cultures were negative. After receiving antifungal treatment with voriconazole (0.2g twice daily), the patient's fever, coughing and expectoration symptoms improved 1 week later. However, he presented with progressive neurological symptoms characterized by exacerbating headache and bilateral visual impairment. As a result, the patient underwent a craniotomy for resection of the lesion.
Histological examination of brain tissue revealed no evidence of malignancy but suggested the presence of a chronic brain abscess with Gram-positive filamentous bacilli (Figure 2B). The diagnosis of Nocardia brain abscess was confirmed by the identification of Nocardia farcinica in purulent fluid culture, while testing for TM yielded negative results. Subsequently, the patient was diagnosed with brain nocardiosis and pulmonary talaromycosis. We initiated anti-infective therapy with oral sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (SMX 0.8g and TMP 0.16g three times daily) and moxifloxacin (0.4g once daily). With the implementation of the aforementioned treatment, there was a significant improvement in his symptoms including headache, gait imbalance and vision loss in both eyes, as well as complete resolution of the intracranial mass (Figure 1C). Serum sample was obtained to test the detection of AIGAs through an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kit (USCN Life Science Inc., Wuhan, China) according to the manufacturer's protocols. We found that he had a high positive titer (15460ng/mL) and the positive titer value was based on our previous study.
After 1-month treatment, CT scan showed improvement in lung lesions (Figure 1D), and there was no change in brain MRI. AIGAs turned negative (3021ng/mL) after 3 months. Overall, SMX-TMP and moxifloxacin were administered for 9 months, and the voriconazole was for 12 months. No relapse of either nocardia brain abscess or pulmonary TM infection had been observed during 18-month follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male from Guangxi, China, presented with a 1-month history of fever and productive cough, and a 9-day history of dizziness, headache, and gait imbalance.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever and productive cough 1 month prior to admission, followed 9 days prior to admission by progressive neurological symptoms including dizziness, headache, and gait instability.
subjective.past_medical_history: Smoker; native and resident of Guangxi, China. Negative history of organ transplantation, leukemia, diabetes mellitus, or autoimmune disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, productive cough, dizziness, headache, and gait imbalance.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological clinical course included gait imbalance, worsening headache, and subsequent bilateral visual impairment prior to craniotomy.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline blood tests showed leukocytosis (10.12 x 10^9/L), lymphocytosis (3.55 x 10^9/L), elevated ESR (46 mm/h), negative anti-HIV antibody, and normal absolute neutrophil count, serum IgG, serum IgM, and CRP. Blood cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological workup revealed a CD4+ T-cell count of 1,181 cells/mm3 (reference 561–1,137 cells/mm3) and elevated NK cell percentage of 33.56% (reference 9.5–23.5%). Chest CT demonstrated bilateral patchy high-density pulmonary consolidations. Brain CT showed a right occipital lobe infarction, and contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed an irregular 3.5 x 2.5 x 3.2 cm intracranial mass lesion. Following craniotomy and lesion resection for worsening headache and bilateral visual impairment, brain biopsy histopathology excluded malignancy and demonstrated a chronic brain abscess containing Gram-positive filamentous bacilli.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody (AIGA)-associated immunodeficiency (HIV-negative) complicated by disseminated co-infection with pulmonary Talaromyces marneffei and Nocardia farcinica brain abscess. Sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cultures isolated Talaromyces marneffei, purulent intracranial abscess fluid culture isolated Nocardia farcinica (while brain tissue was negative for T. marneffei), and serum ELISA confirmed high-titer anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (15,460 ng/mL). Initial voriconazole (0.2 g twice daily) improved fever and cough within 1 week; after craniotomy resection of the brain abscess, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP 0.16 g / SMX 0.8 g three times daily for 9 months) and oral moxifloxacin (0.4 g once daily for 9 months) were added alongside a 12-month total course of voriconazole. The patient achieved complete resolution of headache, gait imbalance, vision loss, pulmonary lesions, and the intracranial mass, with AIGA titers turning negative (3,021 ng/mL) at 3 months and no relapse over 18 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
The patient is an 83 years-old, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-negative, Caucasian male, with a history of recurrent nasal bleedings since childhood, recurrent gingival bleedings, frequent cutaneous hematoma after minor traumata, which were attributed to ITP diagnosed at age 52 years, splenectomy at age 52 years for the ITP, coronary heart disease resulting in two myocardial infarctions at age 52 years, corticosteroids for ITP since age 53 years, steroid-induced diabetes mellitus since age 53 years, requiring insulin since age 78 years, arterial hypertension since years, hyperlipidemia since age 53 years, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty at age 62 years, aortocoronary bypass grafting at ages 64 and 75 years, atrial fibrillation since age 68 years, cataract surgery at ages 71 and 74 years, bilateral carotid artery stenosis requiring stent implantation at age 72 years, a 6-fold stent placing for coronary stenoses at age 75 years, bilateral hypoacusis since age 78 years requiring hearing devices bilaterally and sensori-motor polyneuropathy since age 78 years. Since age 82 years, he also noted a mild cognitive decline and non-specific visual impairment and started to use a stick for walking and a walker since two weeks prior to admission. His family history was positive for diabetes mellitus and short stature in his mother. From age 68 years until admission, he was taking phenprocoumon.
He was admitted at age 83 years because of chronic tiredness, dyspnea, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain. Blood chemical findings showed leucocytosis with a maximum value of 38.8/nL (n, 4.0-9.0/nL) on hospital day (hd) 3, thrombocytopenia with a minimum value of 4/nL (n, 150-450/nL) on hd 15 and hd 18, renal insufficiency, and elevated C-reactive protein with a maximum value of 34.7 mg/dL (n, <= 0.6 mg/dL) at hd 3 (Table 1). There were also elevated glutamate-oxalate transaminase, glutamate pyruvate transaminase, and lactate dehydrogenase (Table 1). Creatine-kinase was normal throughout hospitalization. There was slight hypocalcemia (Table 1) and elevation of ferritin to 3817 ng/mL (n, 30-400 ng/mL). Thyroid function parameters were indicative of hyperthyroidism. The HbA1c was 7.4% (n, <= 6%). X-ray of the lung revealed multiple reticulonodular infiltrates up to one cm in diameter over both lungs with predominance in the left lower lobe, a pleural effusion in the horizontal interlobar fissure, and an encapsulated effusion in the right-sided diagonal interlobar fissure. X-ray of the lung five weeks earlier had been normal. A CT-scan of the thorax showed an 11x7 cm, enhancing mass lesion in the right upper lobe with central and peripheral necrosis and multiple irregularly contoured hyperdensities over both lungs (Fig. 1). Sputum cultures grew Nocardia sp.
Clinical neurologic examination revealed slight dysarthria, dysphagia, bilateral ptosis, bilateral hypoacusis, postural tremor, left-sided dysdiadochokinesia, weakness for hip extension bilaterally (M5-), reduced tendon reflexes on the upper limbs and absent tendon reflexes on the lower limbs, diffuse wasting, stocking-type sensory disturbances bilaterally, and ataxic stance. He was able to walk with a walker. MRI of the cerebrum showed a hyperintense, enhancing lesion of 4 mm in diameter in the cranial part of the cerebellar vermis (Fig. 2). Additionally, there were small hyperintense lesions in the occipital deep white matter and subcortically bilaterally (Fig. 2). Lumbar puncture was recommended, but contraindicated due to ITP. No manifestations of nocardiosis other than in the lung and cerebrum were detected.
For ITP, the patient received prednisolone 50 mg/d until hd 9. For the general infection, he initially received amoxicillin between hd 2 and hd 4. From hd 4 to hd 7, he received caspofungin and between hd 5 and hd 7 piperazillin. Meropenem was started on hd 8 and maintained until hd 45. He had never developed fever during the entire hospitalization. After dismissal, the patient was switched to a long-term therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol. Shortly after admission, oral anticoagulation was stopped because of severe thrombocytopenia of 4,000/nL (Table 1). Since hd 23, corticosteroids had to be restarted because of deteriorating ITP (Table 1). His therapy at dismissal included danazol, furosemide, pantoprazole, atorvastatin, metoprolol, enalapril, amiodarone, prednisolone, folic acid, and insulin in addition to the antibiotic. At the three month follow-up, dimension of the pulmonary lesions had regressed. On the contrary, the cerebral lesions had progressed despite trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol, promting a switch to sultamicillin and then to meropenem. Unexpectedly, the patient died from acute myocardial infarction shortly thereafter. Autopsy excluded a pulmonary malignancy as the underlying cause of nocardiosis and confirmed that antibiotic therapy was not effective in eradicating the cerebral infection, although cerebral tissue cultures were negative for Nocardia sp.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old Caucasian male presented with chronic fatigue, dyspnea, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, and progressive gait instability requiring a walker over the preceding 2 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive chronic tiredness, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain leading to hospital admission, superimposed on a 1-year history of mild cognitive decline and visual impairment and a 2-week requirement for a walker.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) diagnosed at age 52 (treated with splenectomy at age 52 and chronic corticosteroids since age 53); steroid-induced diabetes mellitus since age 53 (insulin-dependent since age 78); coronary artery disease with two myocardial infarctions at age 52, PTCA at age 62, CABG at ages 64 and 75, and 6 coronary stents at age 75; arterial hypertension; hyperlipidemia; atrial fibrillation on phenprocoumon since age 68; bilateral carotid artery stenting at age 72; bilateral cataract surgery at ages 71 and 74; bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and sensorimotor polyneuropathy since age 78. Family history positive for maternal diabetes mellitus and short stature.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fatigue, dyspnea, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, mild cognitive decline, visual impairment, and gait difficulty; negative for fever throughout hospitalization. Home medication prior to admission included phenprocoumon, prednisolone, and insulin.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile throughout hospitalization. Neurological examination revealed mild dysarthria, dysphagia, bilateral ptosis, bilateral hypoacusis, postural tremor, left dysdiadochokinesia, mild bilateral hip extension weakness (MRC 5-), reduced upper limb reflexes, absent lower limb reflexes, diffuse muscle wasting, bilateral stocking-distribution sensory loss, and ataxic stance (ambulatory with walker).
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed marked leukocytosis (peak WBC 38.8/nL on hospital day [hd] 3; reference 4.0–9.0/nL), severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 4/nL on hd 15 and 18; reference 150–450/nL), renal insufficiency, elevated CRP (peak 34.7 mg/dL on hd 3; reference <=0.6 mg/dL), elevated AST, ALT, and LDH, normal CK, mild hypocalcemia, elevated ferritin (3,817 ng/mL; reference 30–400 ng/mL), biochemical hyperthyroidism, HbA1c 7.4% (reference <=6%), and negative HIV testing. Chest X-ray showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates (up to 1 cm, left lower lobe predominant) and interlobar pleural effusions (compared to a normal chest X-ray 5 weeks prior). Sputum cultures isolated Nocardia species.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated an 11 x 7 cm enhancing right upper lobe mass with central and peripheral necrosis and bilateral nodular hyperdensities. Brain MRI revealed a 4 mm enhancing hyperintense lesion in the superior cerebellar vermis and small bilateral occipital subcortical/deep white matter hyperintensities (lumbar puncture was contraindicated due to severe ITP). Bone marrow/autopsy excluded underlying pulmonary malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary and cerebral nocardiosis (confirmed by sputum culture isolation of Nocardia sp., 11 x 7 cm necrotic right upper lobe mass on chest CT, and 4 mm enhancing cerebellar vermis lesion on brain MRI) in an HIV-negative 83-year-old asplenic male on long-term corticosteroid therapy for chronic ITP. Phenprocoumon was discontinued due to severe thrombocytopenia (4/nL), and after initial empiric amoxicillin, caspofungin, and piperacillin, he was treated with intravenous meropenem from hospital day 8 to day 45 alongside prednisolone and danazol for ITP, followed by discharge on oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole maintenance. At 3-month follow-up, the pulmonary lesions regressed but the cerebral lesions progressed on MRI despite TMP-SMX, prompting switches to sultamicillin and meropenem; the patient died shortly thereafter from an acute myocardial infarction, with autopsy confirming absence of lung malignancy and persistent cerebral lesions with negative postmortem brain cultures.

raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old girl, offspring of a family who recently moved from Yemen to the United States, presented with symptoms of abdominal pain, polyuria and polydipsia, which had started a few weeks ago. The severity of the abdominal pain, described as dull, diffuse, and present for a long time, had increased in the past 2 days. The patient was reported to have had a protuberant abdomen since birth, which had shown no change in the recent past. She had frequent voidings that worsened over the last few weeks. She had a very good appetite. Ingestion of fluids was reported as adequate. The patient was born full term and had had no perinatal problems, but was developmentally delayed (talked and walked at age 4 years). At 8 years of age, she was diagnosed to have diabetes mellitus (DM) in Jordan by routine blood tests that showed a high blood sugar. Hypertension was diagnosed a few years later. The parents were told that the prognosis was poor. No treatment was offered for DM or hypertension. Breast development and pubic hair were noticed at age 9 years and axillary hair and body odor - at age 11 years. She had increased facial and body hair, but the age at which this was noticed was not clear. The patient had not yet started her menstrual periods. She had a history of poor dental hygiene and poor vision. The family history revealed a consanguineous relationship (distant cousins) between the father and mother who were otherwise healthy. The patient has three sisters and one brother who are all reported to have no medical problems. There is no family history of congenital or metabolic diseases. A review of the symptomatology is listed in Table 1, and the findings on physical examination are given in Table 2. Vital signs at presentation were: pulse: 98/min, blood pressure: 144/84 mmHg, respiration: 20 /min, afebrile. She weighed 40.3 kg (5th percentile for age, -1.7 SD) and her height was 144 cm (under the 3rd percentile, -2.25 SDS), her body mass index(BMI) was 19.4 kg /m2 (0.00 SD). The pertinent features were: absence of subcutaneous fat in the extremities, face, trunk and hands; prominent muscles; looking much older than her stated age; dysmorphic features; developmental delay; hepatosplenomegaly; poor vision; enophthalmus; and arthropathy. There was no evidence of retinopathy. Laboratory data are listed in Table 3. Her serum glucose was 393 mg/dL and there was no metabolic acidosis. Given the history of fever and hepatosplenomegaly, screening for human immunodeficiency virus, Hepatitis A, B, C, and tuberculin test were done, and were all negative. Imaging studies demonstrated striking organomegaly involving the liver, spleen, and kidneys. Stool impaction was evident on X-ray. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed hepatomegaly, enlargement of the main portal vein, numerous splenic varices, and splenomegaly indicating a mild degree of portal hypertension. Radiograms showed mottled bones. Echocardiogram revealed aortic insufficiency and left ventricular hypertrophy. Chromosomal analysis specifically for mutation of 11q13 and 9q34 is not yet completed.
The clinical features and laboratory data of this patient suggested a diagnosis of congenital lipodystrophy, and more specifically of BSCL2. She was started on an insulin regimen of 1 unit/kg/day and increased up to 6 units/kg/day (300 units daily). Her present insulin regimen includes glargine (100 units) at bedtime and aspart (40-60 units) before each meal. Given the risks of liver toxicity associated with metformin, metformin was started at 250 mg once a day and gradually increased to 500 mg twice a day. Liver function tests were monitored every 6 weeks. Even with combined insulin and metformin therapy, her blood sugar has remained in the 200-500mg/dL range. Her hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), which was 12.2% at diagnosis, had improved to 10.6% over a 6-month period. She is encouraged to do more physical activity. She was also started on ergocalciferol and calcium for vitamin D deficiency. The carious teeth were extracted. For persistent proteinuria and nephromegaly, a kidney biopsy was done that showed IgA nephropathy. She was placed on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor for persistent proteinuria and hypertension. Her blood pressure has normalized on antihypertensive medication. Portal hypertension has been monitored closely as these patients are at risk for esophageal varices.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old girl who recently emigrated from Yemen to the United States presented with a several-week history of worsening polyuria, polydipsia, and diffuse abdominal pain that intensified over the preceding 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a lifelong protuberant abdomen and chronic dull abdominal pain that acutely worsened 2 days prior to presentation, accompanied by several weeks of worsening polyuria and polydipsia despite a voracious appetite and adequate fluid intake.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born full-term without perinatal complications; global developmental delay (walked and talked at age 4 years); untreated diabetes mellitus diagnosed in Jordan at age 8 years and untreated hypertension diagnosed several years later; premature adrenarche/thelarche (breast and pubic hair at age 9, axillary hair at age 11), hirsutism, primary amenorrhea at age 14, poor vision, and severe dental caries. Born to consanguineous parents (distant cousins) with four healthy siblings.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for abdominal pain, abdominal distension, polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, hirsutism, primary amenorrhea, poor vision, and joint stiffness/arthropathy.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: pulse 98/min, blood pressure 144/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, afebrile; weight 40.3 kg (5th percentile, -1.7 SD), height 144 cm (<3rd percentile, -2.25 SD), and BMI 19.4 kg/m2 (0.00 SD). Physical findings included generalized absence of subcutaneous adipose tissue across the face, trunk, limbs, and hands, prominent muscular hypertrophy, acromegaloid/progeroid facial appearance, dysmorphic features, enophthalmos, developmental delay, massive hepatosplenomegaly, arthropathy, poor visual acuity without diabetic retinopathy, and extensive dental caries.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission serum glucose was 393 mg/dL without ketoacidosis; baseline HbA1c was 12.2% (improving to 10.6% at 6 months); vitamin D deficiency and persistent proteinuria were present. Screening tests for HIV, Hepatitis A, B, and C, and tuberculin skin test were all negative. Abdominal X-ray showed fecal impaction and skeletal radiographs showed mottled bone density; abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, dilated main portal vein, and splenic varices consistent with mild portal hypertension.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated aortic insufficiency and left ventricular hypertrophy. Percutaneous renal biopsy performed for persistent proteinuria and nephromegaly confirmed IgA nephropathy. Genetic testing for 11q13 (BSCL2/seipin) and 9q34 (AGPAT2) mutations was initiated.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Berardinelli-Seip congenital generalized lipodystrophy type 2 (BSCL2, HIV-negative) complicated by severe insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus (baseline glucose 393 mg/dL, HbA1c 12.2%), arterial hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, aortic insufficiency, hepatosplenomegaly with mild portal hypertension, vitamin D deficiency, and biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy. Management included high-dose basal-bolus insulin therapy titrated up to 6 units/kg/day (300 units/day: insulin glargine 100 units nightly plus pre-meal insulin aspart 40–60 units), metformin titrated to 500 mg twice daily with 6-weekly LFT monitoring (reducing HbA1c to 10.6% at 6 months), ACE inhibitor therapy (normalizing blood pressure and treating IgA nephropathy/proteinuria), ergocalciferol and calcium supplementation, dental extractions, and ongoing surveillance for portal hypertension.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old man presented to the emergency department with pleuritic chest pain, a swollen and painful right knee, and weight-bearing difficulty. Accompanying this was hip and back pain after a fall. This occurred on a background of unexplained progressive weight loss of 40 kilograms over the past 2 years, poor appetite, fever and drenching night sweats, increased susceptibility to infection, and intravenous drug use. He had a 16-year history of hepatitis C (HCV; genotype 3), which remained untreated due to noncompliance and poor clinic attendance. He had been a well-built professional boxer of 96 to 100 kilograms for most of his adult life; however, his admission weight was 60.61 kilograms. This was a loss of approximately 63% of his total body weight. His relevant medical history includes postoperative pulmonary embolism, disc prolapse, mild depression, and a family history of adult polycystic kidney disease. The relevant surgical history includes osteomyelitis and amputation of the third digit of the right hand, and multiple fracture repairs. Systems review was unremarkable. He has a complicated social history including a troubled upbringing, intravenous heroin use up to 1 gram per day, experimentation with most illicit drugs, a significant criminal history, and participation in an opiate substitution programme. He does not smoke tobacco or drink alcohol. 
On examination, the patient appeared acutely unwell, although vital signs were normal. He appeared cachectic, had sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, poor dentition, extensive tattoos, and had track marks in the cubital fossae and groin. There was rib and mediastinal tenderness with no masses. Right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness was noted on palpation, with hepatomegaly 6 centimetres below the costal margin. Nontender lymphadenopathy was present in the upper left jugular nodes and bilaterally in the groin. A warm, right knee effusion was also apparent. There were no signs suggestive of infective endocarditis or chronic liver disease. Respiratory, cardiovascular, thyroid, and neurological examinations were unremarkable. 
Initial blood biochemistry revealed a noncritical normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 102 g/L), raised CRP, elevated calcium (2.57 mmol/L), and low albumin (23 grams/L). A thyroid function test detected 18 picomols/L of free T4 (normal range 7-17 pmols/L). This was assumed to be a transient reactive elevation rather than the cause of such significant weight loss. Liver function tests, blood cultures, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation profile, alpha-fetoprotein, vasculitic screen, iron studies, vitamin B12, urate, and globulins were all within normal ranges. Hepatitis C serology was reactive with an IgG response. forth generation antigen/antibody assay was performed twice, four weeks apart, to determine HIV positivity; however, both tests returned negative. The patient's history revealed that previous HIV tests were also negative, and as such a Western blot analysis was not performed. Hepatitis B serology was consistent with immunisation. Polymerase chain reaction found the patient to be reactive to cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein Barr virus (EBV), but human herpes virus 8 was not detected. Although blood IL-6 levels could have been used as a marker of systemic inflammation, C-reactive protein was chosen instead as per hospital policies. A computerized tomography of the chest and abdomen found enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes and lytic lesions in T8 and T9. There was no splenomegaly, and the liver architecture was unchanged. 
A computerized tomography pulmonary angiogram, chest X-ray, and cardiac troponin I were requested to exclude pulmonary embolism, rib fracture and pneumothorax, and myocardial infarction. All were normal. The right knee joint was aspirated, and fluid analysis showed methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus which was treated as septic arthritis with intravenous flucloxacillin and vancomycin. Following spiking fevers over the next few weeks in hospital, a transoesophageal echocardiogram was performed to exclude infective endocarditis from a septic arthritis-induced bacteraemia. 
At this point, the patient was clinically suspected to have lymphoma or multiple myeloma, and further investigations undertaken were to exclude either. beta-2 microglobulin and LDH levels were normal, no monoclonal band was detected on serum and urine protein electropheresis, and flow cytometry showed normal subpopulations of B cell and T cell lineages. A bone scan showed further destructive thoracic lesions but did not confirm its extent. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed T8 to T11 osteomyelitis with epidural involvement indenting on, but not compressing, the spinal cord. Lymphoma and multiple myeloma were excluded by bone marrow biopsy. 
The diagnosis of multicentric plasmacytic Castleman's disease was histologically confirmed by an excision biopsy from an inguinal lymph node. Macroscopically, the specimen was a circumscribed ovoid nodule measuring 30 x 22 x 10 mm with a central blackish area. Microscopically, no malignant cells, Reed Sternberg cells, or their variants were seen. This was confirmed by two separate laboratories. Also noted were distinct hyaline deposits, prominent paracortical expansion by sheets of plasma cells, and subcapsular and interfollicular neutrophilic bodies. HHV-8 was not detected in this sample. 
A four-week rituximab regime was chosen as the primary treatment for this patient. Steroid treatment was also being considered as adjunct therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male former professional boxer presented to the emergency department with pleuritic chest pain, a painful swollen right knee with inability to bear weight, and hip and back pain following a fall, superimposed on a 2-year history of 40 kg weight loss, fevers, and drenching night sweats.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented acutely after a fall with pleuritic chest pain, hip/back pain, and an acute right knee effusion impairing ambulation. Over the preceding 2 years, his weight had progressively fallen from his baseline adult boxing weight of 96–100 kg to 60.61 kg (~40 kg loss), accompanied by anorexia, recurrent fevers, drenching night sweats, and frequent infections.
subjective.past_medical_history: 16-year history of untreated chronic hepatitis C virus infection (genotype 3); prior postoperative pulmonary embolism, intervertebral disc prolapse, mild depression, right third digit osteomyelitis requiring amputation, and multiple fracture repairs. Family history of adult polycystic kidney disease. Social history notable for active intravenous heroin use (up to 1 g/day), polysubstance use, opiate substitution program participation, and non-smoker/non-drinker status.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 40 kg weight loss over 2 years, anorexia, fevers, drenching night sweats, pleuritic chest pain, back/hip pain, and right knee pain/swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely unwell and cachectic (weight 60.61 kg) with normal initial vital signs, sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, poor dentition, extensive tattoos, and cubital/inguinal injection track marks. Musculoskeletal and systemic exam showed rib and sternal/mediastinal tenderness, a warm right knee effusion, right upper quadrant tenderness with hepatomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin, and non-tender left upper jugular and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 102 g/L), elevated CRP, hypercalcemia (2.57 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (23 g/L), mildly elevated free T4 (18 pmol/L; reference 7–17 pmol/L), reactive HCV IgG, protective HBsAb, positive blood CMV and EBV PCR, negative HHV-8 PCR, and two negative fourth-generation HIV Ag/Ab combo assays performed 4 weeks apart. LFTs, renal function, blood cultures, troponin I, beta-2 microglobulin, LDH, serum/urine protein electrophoresis, vasculitic screen, and chest X-ray were normal. Right knee arthrocentesis grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiogram and transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) were normal (excluding PE and infective endocarditis). Chest/abdominal CT, bone scan, and spine MRI revealed enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes and destructive T8–T11 vertebral osteomyelitis with epidural extension indenting the spinal cord. Peripheral blood flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy excluded lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Excisional inguinal lymph node biopsy (30 x 22 x 10 mm) confirmed HHV-8-negative multicentric plasmacytic Castleman disease, demonstrating hyaline deposits, paracortical sheets of mature plasma cells, and subcapsular/interfollicular neutrophilic aggregates without Reed-Sternberg or malignant cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HHV-8-negative, HIV-negative multicentric plasmacytic Castleman disease (confirmed by excisional inguinal lymph node histopathology and two negative 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab assays 4 weeks apart) complicated by MSSA right knee septic arthritis and T8–T11 vertebral osteomyelitis with epidural extension in a 46-year-old intravenous drug user with untreated genotype 3 HCV, CMV, and EBV co-infections. MSSA septic arthritis and vertebral osteomyelitis were treated with intravenous flucloxacillin and vancomycin, and a 4-week regimen of intravenous rituximab (with adjunctive corticosteroid consideration) was selected as primary therapy for multicentric Castleman disease.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old male was referred for blurred disk margins and possible papilledema from his optometrist. He was visually asymptomatic. He had been seen in a hematology-oncology clinic one month prior for swollen groin lymph nodes that were noted to be reactive, but of unknown etiology. He had not had any previous STDs, genital lesions, penile discharge, or rash.
On exam, visual acuity was 20/25+ OD and 20/20- OS. Ishihara color plates were 11/11 OU. He had a trace afferent pupillary defect OS. Intraocular pressures were 12 OD and 18 OS. He had asymmetric disc edema, greater in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography showed a retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) average thickness of 188 microns OS with concentric circumferential elevation and an average RNFL thickness of 118 OD with inferonasal elevation (Figure 1).
Brain MRI and MRV with and without contrast were unremarkable, without mass lesions or venous occlusion. He underwent a lumbar puncture which showed a normal opening pressure of 18 cm H2O, normal protein, and glucose, and 72 white cells/mm3, predominately lymphocytes. Within 2 weeks of presentation, he developed headaches and eye pain, especially when bending over. Repeat examination showed worsening disc edema in the right eye and enlargement of the blind spot on visual field testing. Because his presentation was not consistent with papilledema, orbit MRI was performed, which showed increased optic nerve sheath fluid, especially posterior to the globes (Figure 2) and contrast enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths. Since the clinical and imaging findings appeared consistent with optic perineuritis, he was tested for secondary causes. He tested positive for syphilis with a rapid plasma reagent (RPR), with a titer of 1 : 128. FTA-ABS measured for confirmation was also positive. HIV testing was negative. He was placed on IV Penicillin 3,000,000 Units every 4 hours for 14 days. Repeat testing two weeks after antibiotic treatment showed marked improvement in both his symptoms and the extent of disc edema (Figure 3). Visual field testing also improved after antibiotics, with resolution of the enlarged blind spot (Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old visually asymptomatic male was referred by his optometrist for evaluation of bilateral blurred optic disc margins, followed within 2 weeks by headache and ocular pain worsened by bending over.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially referred for asymptomatic bilateral optic disc edema detected on routine optometric exam, the patient developed headaches and eye pain exacerbated by bending forward within 2 weeks of presentation, accompanied by worsening right optic disc edema and blind spot enlargement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Evaluated in a hematology-oncology clinic 1 month prior for reactive inguinal lymphadenopathy of unknown etiology. Denied any history of sexually transmitted infections, genital ulcers, urethral discharge, or skin rash.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially asymptomatic; subsequently positive for headache and positional eye pain; negative for vision loss, genital lesions, or rash.

objective.physical_examination: Initial ophthalmic examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/25+ OD and 20/20- OS, Ishihara color vision 11/11 OU, a trace left relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), intraocular pressures of 12 mmHg OD and 18 mmHg OS, and asymmetric bilateral optic disc edema (left greater than right initially, with worsening right disc edema and blind spot enlargement at 2 weeks).
objective.routine_investigations: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed average retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness of 188 µm OS with concentric elevation and 118 µm OD with inferonasal elevation. Syphilis serology was strongly reactive with serum RPR titer 1:128 and positive confirmatory FTA-ABS; HIV serology was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI and MR venography (with and without contrast) were normal without mass or venous sinus thrombosis. Dedicated orbital MRI demonstrated increased fluid within the optic nerve sheaths posteriorly and perineural contrast enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths bilaterally. Lumbar puncture revealed a normal opening pressure of 18 cmH2O, normal CSF protein and glucose, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis of 72 WBCs/mm3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Bilateral syphilitic optic perineuritis / neurosyphilis in an HIV-negative 41-year-old male, confirmed by serum RPR titer 1:128, positive FTA-ABS, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (72 cells/mm3) with normal opening pressure (18 cmH2O), and bilateral optic nerve sheath enhancement on orbital MRI. Treated with intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G (3,000,000 units every 4 hours for 14 days), resulting in marked resolution of headaches, ocular pain, optic disc edema, and visual field blind spot enlargement within 2 weeks post-treatment.

raw_case_text:
A 47 year-old-man, human immunodeficiency virus negative, with a recent diagnosis of central nervous system lymphoma presented with perianal skin lesions and nonbloody diarrhea. The skin lesions began as nodules that progressed to a roughened plaque and in the minority, ulceration. The lesions began eight weeks prior to presentation, were multiple, scattered in the perianal area and upper thigh bilaterally, and three centimeters at the widest diameter (Figure 1). A more distinct lesion with irregular border was present over the sacrum consistent with a decubitus ulcer. The patient had been diagnosed with a CNS lymphoma six weeks prior to admission when he presented to another hospital with lower extremity weakness, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence, and was found to have a L1-L2 intramedullary spinal mass. He had emergent surgical resection of the mass and was treated with high-dose dexamethasone and further radiation therapy. He was additionally found to have a right temporal lobe mass that was resected and pathology was consistent with a B-cell lymphoma with T-cell infiltration. He had no other significant past medical history or immunocompromising condition. The lower extremity weakness persisted and primarily confined him to bed. For ongoing fecal incontinence and the nonhealing sacral decubitus ulcer, he ultimately had a diverting colostomy. Two weeks prior to presentation, his bowel movements became more liquid in consistency and increased in frequency. He denied abdominal pain. The perianal skin lesions were not painful, but the initial loss of sensation from the compressive spinal mass had not recovered. He remained on a dexamethasone taper and was transferred to this hospital for further evaluation for chemotherapy. His complete blood count was notable for a normocytic anemia, and his liver function tests for an elevated alkaline phosphatase. An excisional biopsy of one of the skin lesions from the upper thigh was obtained and sent for pathological examination.
Sections of the pathological specimen revealed a dense neutrophilic crust with numerous bacteria distributed in varying sized aggregates, and the underlying epidermis was acanthotic with artefactual subepidermal clefting. However, the superficial dermis demonstrated a distinct perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and the endothelial cells were markedly enlarged (Figure 2). Some endothelial cells contained magenta-colored nuclear inclusions consistent with cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection which was confirmed by a positive CMV immunostain (Figure 3). Stains with periodic acid-Schiff and for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient was treated with intravenous ganciclovir at five mg/kg every twelve hours for 21 days followed by transition to valganciclovir. A serum CMV viral load was 16,400 copies/mL at treatment initiation and was undetectable after four weeks of treatment. The diarrhea resolved within two weeks, and the skin lesions had completely healed at the time of switch to valganciclovir. Based on pathological findings and response to treatment, the diagnosis of cutaneous CMV was made. The primary mode of pathogenesis was thought to be local inoculation from fecal shedding. The diarrhea appeared to be a manifestation of CMV colitis, but given the commitment to CMV treatment and the response to therapy, no further investigation was performed. Unfortunately, the patient later died secondary to complications of an intracranial hemorrhage at the site of the temporal lobe resection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old HIV-negative man with recently diagnosed central nervous system lymphoma presented with an 8-week history of multiple perianal and bilateral upper thigh nodular-to-ulcerative skin lesions and a 2-week history of watery non-bloody diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six weeks prior to transfer, the patient presented to an outside hospital with lower extremity paraparesis, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence from an L1–L2 intramedullary spinal mass and a synchronous right temporal lobe mass (both surgically resected and confirmed as B-cell lymphoma with T-cell infiltration), managed with high-dose dexamethasone, cranial/spinal radiotherapy, and a diverting colostomy for fecal incontinence and a sacral decubitus ulcer. Eight weeks prior to presentation, painless nodules appeared over his perianal area and bilateral upper thighs that progressed to roughened plaques and ulcers (up to 3 cm), and 2 weeks prior to transfer he developed frequent watery non-bloody diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary CNS B-cell lymphoma involving the L1–L2 spinal cord and right temporal lobe diagnosed 6 weeks prior, status post surgical resections, radiation therapy, high-dose dexamethasone taper, and diverting colostomy; sacral decubitus ulcer; paraplegia/bedbound status.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painless perianal/thigh plaques and ulcers, sacral ulcer, persistent lower extremity weakness and saddle anesthesia, and 2 weeks of watery diarrhea; negative for abdominal pain. Home medication: tapering oral dexamethasone.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple scattered 3 cm roughened plaques and ulcerated nodules across the perianal region and bilateral upper thighs, alongside an irregular sacral decubitus ulcer. Neurological exam showed persistent paraparesis and saddle anesthesia from the prior L1–L2 spinal cord lesion.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count showed normocytic anemia; liver function tests showed elevated alkaline phosphatase; HIV testing was negative. Baseline serum CMV viral load was 16,400 copies/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional biopsy of an upper thigh cutaneous lesion revealed an acanthotic epidermis with a dense superficial dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and markedly enlarged dermal endothelial cells containing characteristic magenta intranuclear inclusions that stained strongly positive on anti-CMV immunohistochemistry (PAS and AFB stains were negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous perianal/thigh cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (arising via local fecal inoculation prior to colostomy) and presumed CMV colitis secondary to high-dose corticosteroid immunosuppression in an HIV-negative 47-year-old man with CNS B-cell lymphoma. Confirmed by dermal endothelial CMV intranuclear inclusions, positive CMV immunohistochemistry on thigh skin biopsy, and baseline plasma CMV viral load of 16,400 copies/mL. Treatment with intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 21 days) followed by oral valganciclovir resulted in resolution of diarrhea within 2 weeks, complete healing of cutaneous lesions by day 21, and an undetectable serum CMV viral load at 4 weeks; however, the patient later died from an intracranial hemorrhage at his prior right temporal lobe resection site.

raw_case_text:
The patient was an 88-year-old man of Mediterranean descent, with a history of cirrhosis and underlying HBV infection. At the time of presentation in the clinic, he complained of generalized weakness and fatigue over the last month. Physical examination revealed icterus of the skin and sclera, as well as abdominal distention, owing to the presence of ascitic fluid without any detectable hepatosplenomegaly.
The peripheral blood count showed macrocytic anemia (Hb: 11,6 g / dL, MCV: 108,0 fL), thrombocytopenia (PLT: 113 x 103/ muL) and normal WBC count and differential. In particular, the exact values were as follows: WBC: 4,0 x 103/ muL, Neut.: 72%, Lymph.: 18%, Mono.: 9,0%, Eosino.: 1,0%, RBC: 3,09 x 106/ muL, Hb: 11,6 g / dL, MCV: 108,0 fL, MCH: 37,6 pg, and PLT: 113 x 103/ muL. His serum profile provided the following results: Gluc: 105,0 mg / dl, UREA: 32,0 mg / dL, CREAT: 0,88 mg / dL, SGOT: 223,0 U / L, SGPT: 155 U / L, T-Bil.: 7,0 mg / dL, Bl-Bil.: 3,0 mg / dL, gamma-GTP: 50 U / L, ALP: 165 U / L, LDH: 241 U / L, Prot: 7,4 g / dL, Alb: 2,1 g / dL, CK: 183 U / L. The biochemical examination of the collected peritoneal fluid revealed: Gluc 111 mg / dL, Prot: 2,2 g / dL, Alb: 0,65 g / dL, LDH: 1590 U / L, Chol: 7,0 mg / dL, and Trigl: 16 mg / dL.
Abdominal Ultrasound-Sonography (US) demonstrated liver cirrhosis and massive ascites. Computed-Tomography (CT), which was carried out later confirmed the ascites, although with no visible peritoneal implants. Furthermore, no pathological lymphadenopathy was detected by the obtained CT-scans.
Paracentesis was performed, yielding a large amount (800 ml) of ascitic fluid that was subsequently sent for cytological evaluation. After centrifugation of the sample, the sediment was used for ThinPrep preparation as well as for routine preparation, with direct smearing stained with both Pap and Giemsa. The remaining sediment was used for cell block preparation, using the plasma-thrombin method and standard H and E staining.
The Thin Prep material consisted of abundant large-sized malignant cells, with a moderate amount of basophilic cytoplasm, which were arranged singly. Most of them had a single nucleus, but occasionally, bi-nucleated or multinucleated cells were also seen. The nucleus had coarse chromatin pattern, irregular nuclear outlines, and a single or multiple prominent nucleoli. A high mitotic activity, with abnormal mitoses was present, and a large number of apoptotic bodies as well as nuclear debris were additionally seen [Figures 1a and 1b].
The immunophenotypic profile of the tumor was determined by standard immunoperoxidase methods using paraffin sections from cell block material. The primary antibodies used were: AE1 / AE3, EMA, Vimentin, Melan A, MPO, Fascin, Perforin, Bcl-6, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD15, CD20, CD30, CD34, CD43, CD45 (LCA), CD45RO, and CD138 antigens. In addition, anaplastic lymphoma kinase 1 (ALK-1) protein, TIA-1, LMP-1, and HHV-8 (Latent Nuclear Antigen-1; LANA-1) were also investigated. Antigen retrieval was performed using ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA)-based solution (CC1). The primary antibody, secondary antibody, and avidin-enzyme conjugate were then visualized using the precipitating enzyme diaminobenzidine (DAB). The detailed immunocytochemical list of the antibodies used in our case is depicted in Table 1.
A possible Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection was excluded using the EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in situ hybridization test in cell block material. On the contrary, the infection with he Hepatitis B virus was further confirmed with the identification of the HBV-DNA. Moreover, sediment from the ascitic fluid was examined using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method to detect any clonal rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene (IgH). Moreover, we checked for gene rearrangement in the T-cell receptor. In particular, and in more detail, the methods used are described below and the obtained results are shown in the attached figures.
Molecular analysis was performed using the IdentiClone IgH Gene Clonality Assay kit (CE-IVD, InVivoScribe Technologies, USA). The DNA was extracted and amplified by primers that target the conserved framework of the variable (V) regions, the conserved joining (J) regions, as well as the diversity and joining regions, according to the manufacturer's instructions. The DNA quality was tested by the Specimen Control Size Ladder Mix, which contains multiple oligonucleotides targeting the housekeeping genes [supplied with the Kit, Figure 3].
The presence or absence of clonal T-cell Receptor Gamma chain gene rearrangements was evaluated using the IdentiClone TCRG Gene Clonality Assay (CE-IVD, InVivoScribe Technologies, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions, as mentioned earlier.
The PCR products were analyzed in agarose gel electrophoresis, followed by non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), in the presence of positive (clonal) and negative (polyclonal) controls [Figures 4-6].
A bone-marrow aspirate showed no evidence of lymphoma. The serological investigation revealed the following results: HbsAg: (+), Anti-Hbc: IgG(+), Anti-Hbe: (-), HbeAg: (+), Anti-Hbs: (-), Anti-HCV: (-), and Anti-HIV: (-).
The final diagnosis that was based on both cytological and immunocytochemical findings, in conjunction with the appropriate molecular workup, was indicative of primary effusion lymphoma with aberrant T-cell expression. The patient unfortunately died one week after the final diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 88-year-old man of Mediterranean descent with hepatitis B virus-related cirrhosis presented with a 1-month history of generalized weakness, fatigue, jaundice, and progressive abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding month, the patient experienced progressively worsening generalized weakness, fatigue, cutaneous and scleral icterus, and abdominal distension due to massive ascites.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-month generalized weakness, fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal distension.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous and scleral icterus and marked abdominal distension with massive ascites without palpable hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, MCV 108.0 fL, MCH 37.6 pg, RBC 3.09 x 10^6/µL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 113 x 10^3/µL), and normal WBC (4.0 x 10^3/µL; 72% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 1% eosinophils). Serum biochemistry showed glucose 105.0 mg/dL, urea 32.0 mg/dL, creatinine 0.88 mg/dL, AST (SGOT) 223.0 U/L, ALT (SGPT) 155 U/L, total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, GGT 50 U/L, ALP 165 U/L, LDH 241 U/L, total protein 7.4 g/dL, albumin 2.1 g/dL, and CK 183 U/L. Viral serologies were positive for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg, and serum HBV DNA, and negative for anti-HBs, anti-HBe, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV. Ascitic fluid biochemistry (800 mL paracentesis) showed glucose 111 mg/dL, protein 2.2 g/dL, albumin 0.65 g/dL, markedly elevated LDH 1,590 U/L, cholesterol 7.0 mg/dL, and triglycerides 16 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed cirrhosis and massive ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT confirmed liver cirrhosis and massive ascites without peritoneal implants or pathological lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow aspirate was negative for lymphoma. Ascitic fluid ThinPrep cytology and cell-block immunocytochemistry demonstrated large pleomorphic malignant lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and brisk atypical mitoses positive for HHV-8 (LANA-1), CD45, CD30, EMA, CD138, Perforin, and aberrant T-cell markers (CD3/CD4/CD5/CD43/CD45RO) and negative for EBER ISH and B-cell surface markers. IdentiClone PCR clonality assays on ascitic cell DNA confirmed clonal rearrangements of both the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) and T-cell receptor gamma (TCRG) genes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HHV-8-positive, EBV-negative peritoneal primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) with aberrant T-cell antigen expression and dual IgH/TCRG gene rearrangements in an HIV-negative 88-year-old Mediterranean man with HBeAg-positive HBV cirrhosis. Confirmed by ascitic fluid cytology, HHV-8 LANA-1 immunocytochemistry, and molecular PCR clonality studies, without solid nodal or bone marrow involvement. The patient deteriorated rapidly and died 1 week after final diagnosis.

raw_case_text: A 42-year-old man presented with a six-month history of nonbloody diarrhea associated with the clinical triad of fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Anti-Leishmania antibodies serological tests (indirect immunofluorescence title 1 : 640 and rapid test with the recombinant k39) were positive. The diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis was firmed by the detection of amastigotes in a bone marrow aspirate smears. Because of upper gastrointestinal symptoms (mild dysphagia and vomiting), an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed, revealing in duodenum the presence of erosions coated with fibrin, plates of enanthema, and thickened pleats with small whitish spots distributed diffusely. In a tissue fragment obtained by biopsy, the duodenal mucosa showed villous enlarged and filled with numerous histiocytes packed with intracytoplasmic round structures with morphology suggestive of amastigotes of Leishmania spp. The patient received liposomal amphotericin B, 4 mg/kg of body weight during 5 days with complete improvement of visceromegaly, fever and recovery of white blood cell and platelets counts. After treatment and hospital discharge, diarrhea and anemia persisted, and his condition continued to deteriorate. Four months later the patient was admitted once again to hospital with worsening diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte imbalance. Blood tests revealed a normochromic normocytic anemia, profound hipoalbuminemia (1.9 g/dL), and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/1 hour). Laboratory examinations also revealed low serum folic acid and iron levels. Both vitamins were replaced and nutritional support was beginning. This time, an extensive search for parasites in stool microscopy was done and eggs of S. mansoni were identified on stool microscopy. The patient was treated with praziquantel 60 mg/kg of body weight. After four weeks, diarrhea remained unchanged, and his condition continued to deteriorate with anorexia and weight loss. Abdominal computer tomography showed mild splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and a normal liver size. There was mild dilatation of intestinal loops of the colon. A bone marrow aspiration was also performed showing only reactive changes and no Leishmania amastigotes. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) assessment on whole blood and bone marrow samples showed positive results using the ribosomal RNA small subunit gene (SSU rRNA) from Leishmania spp. as DNA target. Patient's lymphocyte counts were TCD4+: 539/mm3, TCD8+: 503/mm3 e TCD3+: 1,094/mm3. A colonoscopy was normal. Despite the absence of symptoms of upper gastrointestinal system, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, and it showed the presence of diffuse pallor in stomach and duodenum with swollen appearance without ulceration. Duodenal mucosa histopathology showed the persistence of amastigotes, as four months before (Figure 1). The immunohistochemical study confirmed the presence of numerous immunolabeled amastigotes forms of Leishmania (Figure 2). Tests to detect anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies, a protozoan also endemic in Brazil and with tropism for the gastrointestinal tract, and the anti-HIV testing were negative. The patient was treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate, 0.8 mg/kg of body weight for 30 days, and diarrhea resolved completely within two weeks. Two months after the end of treatment the patient had reached its normal weight and normalized erythrocyte levels. The plasmatic levels of IFN-gamma and IL-10 were measured before and after treatment by sandwich-enzyme-linked immuonosorbent assay, as previously described. The results were expressed as picograms per milliliter (pg/mL) based on a standard curve. IFN-gamma was undetectable before and after treatment, while IL-10 levels decreased from 36 pg/mL at initial evaluation to 16.3 pg/mL (55% reduction) after amphotericin treatment and clinical improvement.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of chronic non-bloody diarrhea, fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, mild dysphagia, and vomiting, followed 4 months after initial therapy by severe relapsing diarrhea, dehydration, anorexia, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 6 months of non-bloody diarrhea, fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, mild dysphagia, and vomiting; duodenal biopsy and bone marrow aspirate confirmed visceral and duodenal leishmaniasis, and a 5-day course of liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day) resolved his fever, splenomegaly, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. However, his diarrhea and anemia persisted, and 4 months later he was readmitted with severe watery diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, profound hypoalbuminemia, anorexia, and progressive weight loss that failed to improve 4 weeks after praziquantel therapy for concomitant Schistosoma mansoni.
subjective.past_medical_history: Visceral and duodenal leishmaniasis diagnosed 4 months prior to readmission; intestinal schistosomiasis (Schistosoma mansoni).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic intractable non-bloody diarrhea, fever (initial), mild dysphagia/vomiting (initial), anorexia, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: febrile with splenomegaly. Readmission 4 months later: dehydrated, cachectic/wasted, and pale with mild splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial serologies were positive for anti-Leishmania antibodies (IIF titer 1:640 and rK39 rapid test). Readmission labs showed normocytic normochromic anemia, profound hypoalbuminemia (1.9 g/dL), elevated ESR (120 mm/1st hour), metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalance, low serum folate and iron, negative anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies, and negative anti-HIV serology. Stool microscopy on readmission identified Schistosoma mansoni ova. Plasma cytokine ELISA showed undetectable IFN-gamma before and after therapy and elevated IL-10 (36 pg/mL initially, decreasing by 55% to 16.3 pg/mL post-treatment).
objective.advanced_workup: T-lymphocyte subset counts at readmission were normal: CD4+ 539/mm3, CD8+ 503/mm3, and CD3+ 1,094/mm3. Initial bone marrow aspirate showed Leishmania amastigotes; repeat bone marrow aspirate at 4 months was microscopically negative but positive for Leishmania spp. SSU rRNA by real-time qPCR in both whole blood and bone marrow. Abdominal CT at readmission showed mild splenomegaly, normal liver size, mild colonic loop dilatation, and no lymphadenopathy; colonoscopy was normal. Initial and 4-month repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with duodenal biopsy and immunohistochemistry demonstrated swollen, pale, eroded duodenal mucosa with villi packed with histiocytes containing abundant Leishmania amastigotes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Chronic relapsing duodenal and visceral leishmaniasis with severe malabsorptive enteropathy and concurrent Schistosoma mansoni co-infection in an HIV-negative, immunocompetent 42-year-old man (CD4+ count 539/mm3, negative HIV and Chagas serologies), driven by an antigen-specific Th1 defect / elevated IL-10 (36 pg/mL) response. Confirmed by persistent duodenal mucosal Leishmania amastigotes on histopathology/immunohistochemistry and positive blood/bone marrow SSU rRNA qPCR after initial 5-day liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day) and praziquantel (60 mg/kg). Retreatment with a 30-day course of intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate (0.8 mg/kg/day) plus iron, folate, and nutritional supplementation achieved complete resolution of diarrhea within 2 weeks, a 55% reduction in plasma IL-10 (to 16.3 pg/mL), and full restoration of body weight and hemoglobin at 2 months post-treatment.

raw_case_text:
A 61-year-old woman with well controlled diabetes visited our clinic in March 2009 for ocular pain and visual impairment of the left eye persisting for 2 weeks. In another clinic, she had been diagnosed with proliferative diabetic retinopathy of both eyes and cystoid macular edema of the left eye. She had received an inravitreal injection of bevacizumab (Genetech, San Francisco, CA, USA) in the left eye 3 weeks prior and panretinal photocoagulation in both eyes 2 weeks before her visit to our clinic. After treatment, she had used an anti-glaucoma agent because of increased intraocular pressure of the left eye.
At presentation, vision of the left eye was hand motion only. Slit lamp examination demonstrated 4+ cells and hyphema in the anterior chamber and iris neovascularization. Funduscopy revealed dense vitritis and retinal vascular obliteration. Ocular ischemia was suspected through fluorescein angiography which revealed arterial filling delay. No abnormal findings were observed in carotid Doppler sonography which was performed to rule out ocular ischemic syndrome. Examination of the right eye was unremarkable except diabetic retinopathy and scarring from panretinal photocoagulation. Further detailed examination was needed to draw the diagnosis and treatment plan but dense vitritis disturbed further evaluation. As a result, a pars plana vitrectomy was performed. During the vitrectomy, necrotizing retinitis with dense retinal whitening and hemorrhage along the inferotemporal vascular arcade was observed, suggestive of infectious retinitis (Fig. 1). The undiluted vitreous sample acquired by vitrectomy was analyzed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR; Q-CMV real time complete kit, Nanogen Advanced Diagnostics, Turin, Italy) and cultured for herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicellar zoster virus (VZV), and CMV. To rule out other etiologies of infectious retinitis, vitreous was also analyzed by staining and culture for bacteria and fungus.
Blood tests did not show any immune dysfunction and complete blood count was normal. CD4 and CD8 cells counts were also within the normal range, 522 and 275 cells/microL. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antigen and antibodies were negative. Her serum CMV IgG level was 244.5 units (range of nonreactive <6.0 AU/mL) and IgM was negative. Although the CMV antigenemia test showed positive results (9/20,000 cells) using the Biotest CMV Brite kit (Biotest Diagnostics, Denville, NJ, USA), there were no other clinical manifestations of CMV infection except retinitis.
While the culture for CMV was negative, PCR for CMV DNA was positive in the vitreous and negative in peripheral blood, confirming the diagnosis as CMV retinitis. The others including HSV and VZV were negative in the vitreous and blood. Neither bacteria nor fungus were observed by staining and culture.
The patient underwent intravenous administration of ganciclovir (2.5 mg/kg/12 hr), a half dose reduction because of renal insufficiency. Necrotizing retinitis with retinal whitening and iris neovascularization had markedly decreased, but obliterated vessels were sustained without recovery of nonperfusion. After 17 days of administration, intravenous treatment was discontinued. During the follow-up period of 12 months, there has been no recurrence of retinitis, but her left eye could not perceive light because of optic nerve atrophy and retinal ischemia due to obliteration of retinal vessels.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old woman with well-controlled diabetes mellitus presented in March 2009 with a 2-week history of left ocular pain and severe visual loss following recent intravitreal bevacizumab injection and panretinal photocoagulation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed at an outside clinic with bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy and left cystoid macular edema, the patient received an intravitreal injection of bevacizumab in her left eye 3 weeks prior to presentation and bilateral panretinal photocoagulation 2 weeks prior to presentation, followed by topical antiglaucoma medication for elevated left intraocular pressure. Over the 2 weeks preceding referral, she experienced progressive left ocular pain and severe vision reduction to hand motion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled diabetes mellitus with bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy and left cystoid macular edema; recent left intravitreal bevacizumab injection (3 weeks prior) and bilateral panretinal photocoagulation (2 weeks prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left eye pain and severe visual loss; negative for systemic symptoms of cytomegalovirus disease. Home medications included diabetes medications and topical antiglaucoma drops.

objective.physical_examination: Left eye visual acuity was reduced to hand motion only. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed 4+ anterior chamber cells, hyphema, and iris neovascularization; fundoscopy and intraoperative examination during pars plana vitrectomy demonstrated dense vitritis, retinal vascular obliteration, and necrotizing retinitis with dense retinal whitening and hemorrhage along the inferotemporal vascular arcade. Right eye examination showed proliferative diabetic retinopathy and panretinal photocoagulation scars.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count was normal; HIV antigen and antibodies were negative. Serum CMV IgG was elevated at 244.5 AU/mL (nonreactive <6.0 AU/mL), serum CMV IgM was negative, peripheral blood CMV DNA PCR was negative, and blood CMV pp65 antigenemia (Biotest CMV Brite) was weakly positive (9/20,000 cells). Fluorescein angiography showed left retinal arterial filling delay, while carotid Doppler ultrasonography was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell counts were normal at 522 cells/µL and 275 cells/µL, respectively. Diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with undiluted vitreous fluid real-time PCR (Q-CMV kit) was positive for CMV DNA and negative for HSV and VZV, while vitreous viral, bacterial, and fungal cultures and stains were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Unilateral left cytomegalovirus (CMV) necrotizing retinitis with occlusive retinal vasculitis following intravitreal bevacizumab injection in an HIV-negative, systemically immunocompetent 61-year-old diabetic woman (CD4+ count 522/µL, CD8+ count 275/µL; confirmed by positive vitreous CMV DNA PCR with negative HSV/VZV PCR and negative bacterial/fungal cultures). She was treated with a 17-day course of renal-adjusted intravenous ganciclovir (2.5 mg/kg every 12 hours), resulting in marked regression of retinal whitening and iris neovascularization without recurrence over 12 months of follow-up, though the left eye progressed to no light perception due to optic atrophy and retinal vascular obliteration.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old woman presented with decreased visual acuity associated with white retinal lesions in both eyes. A history of pneumonia of unknown aetiology closely preceded the deterioration of vision. Five years previously the patient was diagnosed with follicular non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (December, 2004). She underwent eight cycles of combination chemotherapy that included cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine and prednisone with later addition of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab. The patient was in remission for 19 months. Following a relapse with involvement of the retroperitoneal lymph nodes (February, 2007), rituximab and 90Y-ibritumomab tiuxetan were administered. A second relapse occurred 22 months post radioimmunotherapy (April, 2009). Four combination cycles of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and mitoxantrone were then undertaken leading to partial remission. Subsequent therapy included rituximab administered once per month for four months and once every third month thereafter. No further relapses were experienced from April, 2009 to April, 2010.
At presentation (April, 2010), her best-corrected Snellen visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/12 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. There were large keratic precipitates and a mild anterior chamber cellular reaction present in both eyes (Figure 1). Examination of the fundus revealed bilateral findings of moderate vitreous opacities, pale optic discs, retinal necrosis with retinal infiltrates, several hemorrhages in the posterior pole and areas of peripheral retinal atrophy. Some vessels displayed extensive white sheathing providing them with the appearance of frosted branch angiitis (Figure 2).
