objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 17,500 cells/µL; 83.6% neutrophils, 1.8% bands, 1.8% atypical lymphocytes; peaking at 22,000 cells/µL inpatient) and HbA1c 8.8%. HIV serology, serum cryptococcal antigen, blood cultures, and urine cultures were all negative. Unroofed bulla fluid Gram stain revealed yeast forms without bacteria, and wound culture grew pure Cryptococcus neoformans. Bedside forearm ultrasound showed no subcutaneous abscess.
objective.advanced_workup: CT scans of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis and lumbar puncture CSF analysis (including CSF cryptococcal antigen) were completely negative for disseminated or CNS cryptococcosis. Right forearm MRI confirmed superficial cellulitis without deep abscess or necrotizing fasciitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary cutaneous cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans) of the right forearm resulting from direct traumatic wood inoculation in an HIV-negative 56-year-old man immunosuppressed by chronic high-dose prednisone (>=50–100 mg/day) and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.8%), with disseminated and meningeal disease excluded by negative serum/CSF cryptococcal antigens, negative blood/urine cultures, and normal pan-CT. Because intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day) provoked reproducible infusion-related chest pain, he was treated with surgical epidermal unroofing, topical Pluronic antimicrobial dressings (polymyxin/nystatin/nitrofurantoin), a 14-day course of ampicillin-sulbactam transitioned to amoxicillin-clavulanate for suspected superimposed bacterial cellulitis, prednisone tapering, and a 6-month course of oral fluconazole (12 mg/kg/day stepped down to 8 mg/kg/day), achieving complete wound healing within 3 months and no relapse or dissemination at >6 months.

raw_case_text:
Patient is a 25-year-old woman from Guinea-Bissau, West Africa, and was admitted with an 18-month history of dorsal back pain, asthenia, and significant weight loss followed in the last 8 months by loss of the ability to walk.
On her physical examination she presented with three skin lesions (two ulcerated and one nodular) involving the right subclavicle region and other two lesions on her left thigh (one ulcerated and the other in a healing phase) (Figures 1 and 2); her neurological exams exhibited an ASIA A paraplegia with a sensory level at D4. Patient was anaemic with hemoglobin of 11,2 g/dL with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 75 mm/h and a C-reactive protein of 5,26 mg/dL. Gamma globulin level was 44 g/dL and blood chemistry evaluation was normal. HIV and primary immunodeficiency testing were negative. A chest X-ray revealed an enlarged mediastinal shadow (Figure 3), and the spinal computed tomographic scan showed a large anterior and paravertebral abscess from D1 to D10 with significant compression and osteolytic lesions of vertebral bodies with a kyphotic deformity (Figure 4). Spinal magnetic resonance revealed significant compression of the spinal cord at the kyphotic apex and angulation of the column, anterior and paravertebral epidural abscess consistent with spondylodiscitis (Figure 5).
Bone biopsy revealed granulomatous inflammation with few acid-fast bacilli. Skin biopsy of the lesions (Figure 6) revealed acanthosis and pseudoepitheliomatous, hyperplasia of the epidermis, and necrosis foci surrounded by a histiocytic and lymphocyte infiltrate with giant cells on the dermis, consistent with tuberculosis with negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain. The patient was started on quadruple antituberculosis drug regimen together with pyridoxine and steroids, with a progressive clinical improvement, including healing of the skin lesions. One month later, anterior surgical debridement and posterior arthrodesis of the spine were performed. Blood and urine cultures including cultures for mycobacteria all proved negative. Cultures of the material collected through bone biopsy revealed M. tuberculosis. The patient fulfilled 15 months on antituberculosis medication and a favorable outcome was reported with complete recovery of neurological deficits.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old woman from Guinea-Bissau presented with an 18-month history of dorsal back pain, asthenia, and significant weight loss, complicated over the preceding 8 months by complete paraplegia and multiple ulcerating skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 18 months prior to admission, the patient developed progressive thoracic back pain, asthenia, and marked weight loss, followed 8 months prior to admission by complete loss of ambulation and ulcerative/nodular skin lesions over the right infraclavicular area and left thigh.
subjective.past_medical_history: Native of Guinea-Bissau, West Africa; no known prior medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic thoracic back pain, asthenia, weight loss, paraplegia, and chronic ulcerating cutaneous nodules.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed three right infraclavicular lesions (two ulcerated, one nodular) and two left thigh lesions (one ulcerated, one healing). Neurological examination demonstrated complete paraplegia (ASIA Impairment Scale grade A) with a T4 (D4) sensory level.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL), elevated ESR (75 mm/h), elevated CRP (5.26 mg/dL), hypergammaglobulinemia (44 g/L), normal serum chemistry, and negative HIV and primary immunodeficiency workups. Blood and urine mycobacterial and bacterial cultures were negative. Chest X-ray showed a widened mediastinal shadow.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine CT and MRI demonstrated extensive osteolytic vertebral destruction from T1 to T10 (D1–D10) with severe kyphotic angulation, a large anterior paravertebral and epidural abscess, and severe spinal cord compression at the kyphotic apex. Vertebral bone biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with scanty acid-fast bacilli and grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis on culture; skin biopsy showed epidermal acanthosis, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and dermal necrotizing granulomas with Langhans giant cells (Ziehl-Neelsen negative) consistent with cutaneous scrofuloderma/metastatic tuberculous abscess.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Extensive thoracic Pott disease (T1–T10 tuberculous spondylodiscitis and paravertebral/epidural abscess causing ASIA A paraplegia) with disseminated cutaneous tuberculosis (scrofuloderma/tuberculous gumma) in an HIV-negative, immunocompetent 25-year-old woman from Guinea-Bissau, confirmed by vertebral bone biopsy AFB microscopy and culture isolation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. She was treated with quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy (completed for 15 months), pyridoxine, and systemic corticosteroids, followed 1 month later by anterior spinal surgical debridement and posterior spinal arthrodesis, achieving complete cutaneous healing and full recovery of neurological function and ambulation.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 50-year-old white male, previous smoker (he smoked for 30 years, 45 pack-years, quitting 8 years ago), who worked in an underground emerald mine for 20 years, until 9 years ago, without proper use of personal protective equipment. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated with rifampin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide for 2 months, followed by rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months, 11 years ago.
He attends a pneumology outpatient clinic due to silicosis and, as of 2013, a high-resolution computed tomography of the thorax already showed structural lung sequelae.
During follow-up, he developed a worsening of cough and expectoration pattern. Two sputum samples were positive for acid-fast bacilli [(+) and (++), resp.], and presumptive treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis was initiated with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Mycobacteria culture was not performed at this moment. However, at month 5 of treatment, already in the continuation phase with rifampin and isoniazid, and despite correct medication intake and a slight improvement of symptoms, sputum bacilloscopy remained positive. A thorax computed tomography revealed large pulmonary opacities in the upper lobes of both lungs, with intermingled air bronchograms and calcifications, bilateral diffuse nodular infiltrates with areas of pleural thickening, and nodular interstitial infiltrate associated with ground glass opacities in the posterior segment of the inferior right lobe, as well as cavitations with thick walls, suggesting an active inflammatory process (Figure 1). Blood tests revealed a normal hemogram and renal and liver functions, and HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C serologies were negative.
Sputum cultures were then performed and two were positive for NTM; while awaiting the identification of the species, empiric treatment with streptomycin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, and rifampin was instituted for Mycobacterium avium, the most frequently NTM isolated in our community. The patient had a greater improvement of his symptoms.
The species identification was performed by the Tuberculosis Bacteriology Laboratory from the Professor Helio Fraga Reference Center (Rio de Janeiro), the National Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory, using genetic sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene. The NTM species isolated was Mycobacterium sherrisii. The treatment regimen was once again adjusted, with the replacement of rifampin with rifabutin, inclusion of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), and suspension of streptomycin after 2 months. A sensitivity test was not performed.
Currently, the patient is at month 9 of treatment, with only an occasional nonproductive cough, and with negative sputum bacilloscopies and cultures, which have been performed monthly, since month 2 of treatment.
It is our plan to complete 12 months of treatment with rifabutin, clarithromycin, ethambutol, and TMP-SMX, as of the first negative culture.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old white male former underground emerald miner with silicosis presented with worsening chronic productive cough and persistent sputum acid-fast smear positivity despite 5 months of standard first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Followed in a pulmonology clinic since 2013 for occupational silicosis and post-tuberculosis structural lung sequelae, the patient developed worsening cough and sputum expectoration with two positive sputum acid-fast bacilli smears (+ and ++). He was treated presumptively for recurrent pulmonary tuberculosis with 2 months of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol followed by 3 months of rifampin and isoniazid with good adherence, but at month 5 his sputum AFB smear remained persistently positive.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupational silicosis from 20 years of underground emerald mining without personal protective equipment (stopped 9 years prior); treated pulmonary tuberculosis 11 years prior (2RHZ/4RH); former heavy smoker (45 pack-years over 30 years, quit 8 years prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic cough and expectoration.

objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, renal function, and liver function tests were normal; serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were all negative. Serial sputum bacilloscopies were positive for acid-fast bacilli (+ and ++) prior to and at month 5 of standard anti-TB therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT at month 5 of standard TB therapy demonstrated large bilateral upper-lobe conglomerate pulmonary masses with air bronchograms and calcifications, bilateral diffuse nodular infiltrates with pleural thickening, right lower lobe posterior segment ground-glass and nodular infiltrates, and thick-walled cavitary lesions. Two sputum mycobacterial cultures grew non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), definitively identified by the National Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory via 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Mycobacterium sherrisii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cavitary pulmonary Mycobacterium sherrisii disease superimposed on occupational silicosis and prior post-tuberculosis lung sequelae in an HIV-negative 50-year-old male, confirmed by two positive sputum cultures and 16S rRNA gene sequencing after failing 5 months of standard first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy. Initial empiric NTM therapy with streptomycin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, and rifampin was tailored upon species identification to a 12-month regimen of rifabutin, clarithromycin, ethambutol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (with streptomycin discontinued after 2 months), achieving sustained monthly sputum smear and culture conversion from month 2 onward and clinical resolution by month 9.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 77 year-old Hispanic male who initially presented to the emergency room with a 6-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, cough productive of yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, worsening fatigue and weight loss of 10 lbs. On admission, he denied fever, chills, chest pain, sick contacts, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure and history. His past medical history was significant for Non-Hodgkin follicular B cell lymphoma (NHL) diagnosed in 1997, treated with Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin and Prednisone (RCHOP) three times. Last treatment was completed 1 year prior to presentation. He also had biopsy-confirmed cutaneous Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS), identified within the same year of presentation, treated with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 20 mg/m 2 once every 21 days for two cycles.
On admission, he had a low grade fever and was tachycardic. His physical exam was remarkable for a 2 cm firm, non-tender, mobile right submandibular lymph node. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. He was grossly anasarcic with 4 (+) pitting edema of the lower extremities. He also had multiple violet, non-tender skin lesions localized to the lower extremities, mainly around the medial aspect of his ankles and anterior thighs bilaterally.
His labs revealed a normal cardiac panel, a white blood cell (WBC) count of 8,100/mm 3 with no leukocytosis. Manual differentiation of the white blood cells showed 28% neutrophils, 48% lymphocytes, 17% monocytes and 5% eosinophils. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative for infections. Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. 
A chest X-ray done on admission showed a right lung consolidation consistent with pneumonia thus the patient was started on empiric vancomycin 1gm every 12 hours and piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5gm every 8 hours for a duration of 8 days. A computerized axial tomographic (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, showed numerous nodular opacities throughout each lung which were suspected to be consistent with KS as well as small pleural effusions in both lungs ( Figure 1).
Despite completing a course of antibiotics for pneumonia, his symptoms did not improve. A follow-up CT scan of the chest demonstrated that the bilateral pleural effusions had worsened ( Figure 2). Patient underwent a thoracentesis of the larger effusion in the right lung which showed a sero-sanguineous and exudative fluid based on chemistry analysis. Histopathology failed to demonstrate malignant cells.
A bronchoscopy was also performed, revealing diffusely hyperemic and edematous mucosa of the lower airways with mucopurulent secretions ( Figure 3). Biopsy was not performed at this time given concern for endobronchial bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) stains and cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi or acid fast bacilli. Pneumocystis jiroveci PCR and fluid cytology were also negative but PCR for HHV-8 showed 5800 DNA copies/mL. The patient had a HIV p24 rapid antigen test done which was negative.
After two weeks of supportive treatment, the patient's symptoms began to improve. He continued to have numerous indurated confluent lesions on his body and face consistent with KS. His pulmonary symptoms were thought to be due to disseminated KS. Following significant discussions with the patient and his family regarding the poor prognosis of his disease, he decided not to undergo any further antineoplastic treatments and eventually was discharged home with hospice.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 77-year-old Hispanic male with a history of follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma and cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presented to the emergency room with a 6-week history of progressive exertional dyspnea, productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, worsening fatigue, and a 10-lb weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 6 weeks preceding admission, the patient developed progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion, productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, fatigue, and a 10-lb weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 1997, treated with three courses of R-CHOP chemotherapy (last completed 1 year prior to presentation); biopsy-confirmed cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma diagnosed earlier in the same year and treated with two cycles of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (20 mg/m2 every 21 days).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for exertional dyspnea, productive cough, intermittent hemoptysis, fatigue, and 10-lb weight loss; negative for reported fever, chills, chest pain, sick contacts, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, low-grade fever and tachycardia were present. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm firm, mobile, non-tender right submandibular lymph node, gross generalized anasarca with 4+ bilateral lower extremity pitting edema, multiple non-tender violaceous cutaneous plaques/nodules over the bilateral medial ankles, anterior thighs, trunk, and face, and initially clear lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission WBC count was normal at 8,100/mm3 (28% neutrophils, 48% lymphocytes, 17% monocytes, 5% eosinophils), cardiac biomarkers were normal, and urinalysis and urine culture were negative. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae. Rapid HIV p24 antigen/antibody testing was negative. Admission chest X-ray showed right lung consolidation.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT demonstrated numerous bilateral pulmonary nodular opacities and bilateral pleural effusions that worsened on repeat chest CT despite antibiotic therapy. Right thoracentesis yielded serosanguineous exudative pleural fluid with negative malignant cytology. Bronchoscopy revealed diffusely hyperemic, edematous lower airway mucosa consistent with endobronchial Kaposi sarcoma; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures, Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR, and cytology were negative, whereas BAL quantitative HHV-8 PCR was strongly positive at 5,800 DNA copies/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Classic/iatrogenic HIV-negative disseminated cutaneous and pleuropulmonary Kaposi sarcoma (confirmed by violaceous mucocutaneous/endobronchial lesions, progressive bilateral nodular infiltrates and serosanguineous exudative pleural effusions, and BAL HHV-8 viral load of 5,800 DNA copies/mL with negative HIV p24 test) complicated by concurrent bacteremic Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia in a 77-year-old male previously treated with R-CHOP for follicular B-cell lymphoma. Although an 8-day course of intravenous vancomycin (1 g q12h) and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q8h) treated his pneumococcal bacteremia, his pleuropulmonary Kaposi sarcoma progressed; following goals-of-care discussions regarding poor prognosis, the patient declined further cytotoxic chemotherapy and was discharged home with hospice care.

raw_case_text:
In March 2014, a 47-year-old woman was hospitalized at the Bernhard Nocht Clinic (Hamburg, Germany) with chills, nausea, and fever (temperature <40 C). The patient had a history of intravenous drug use (cocaine and benzodiazepines) and was currently enrolled in a methadone substitution program. She also had chronic hepatitis C virus infection that was successfully treated with pegylated interferon-alpha, ribavirin, and boceprevir. The patient had a sustained virologic response and negative results for hepatitis C virus RNA at follow-up without progression to liver fibrosis or cirrhosis.
At admission, her peripheral blood leukocyte count was 6.6 x 103 cells/muL, and her C-reactive protein level was increased (29 mg/L [reference value <5 mg/L]). Other routine serum and urine chemical test results were unremarkable. HIV-1/2 infection was not detected. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Soft tissue abscess was not observed, but the patient admitted having injected cocaine and unknown crushed tablets intravenously the day before admission. Toxicologic screening showed highly increased levels of benzodiazepine (>5,000 ng/mL) and cocaine (>1,000 ng/mL) (reference values <20 ng/mL for both substances). Three blood cultures were collected before empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g 1x/d) was given on day 1.
The next day, the patient's condition deteriorated. Her leukocyte count increased to 27.6 x103 cells/muL, and C-reactive protein level increased to 112 mg/L. She was highly febrile and became hypotensive and tachycardic, which are compatible with severe sepsis. The patient responded rapidly to fluid substitution, became hemodynamically stable, and did not need vasopressors. Antimicrobial therapy was changed empirically to meropenem (1,000 mg 3x/d) on day 2.
After 18 h of culture incubation, microbial growth was detected in 3 aerobic blood culture bottles inoculated at admission. Gram staining showed gram-negative rods, and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization/time-of-flight mass spectrometry fingerprinting with direct sample deposition without extraction (Bruker Daltonim GmbH, Bremen, Germany) identified A. ursingii (score 2.19). A BLAST search (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST) of partial 16S rRNA gene sequence was performed by using a taxonomy browser (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) and showed 99% identity with the A. ursingii type strain NBRC110605 (GenBank accession no. LC014147.1).
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by using Vitek 2 (bioMerieux, Nurtingen, Germany). Results showed susceptibility to imipenem (MIC <0.25 mg/mL), meropenem (<0.25 mg/mL), gentamicin (<1 mg/mL), and ciprofloxacin (<0.25 mg/mL) and resistance to ceftriaxone (32 mg/mL).
The patient became afebrile the next day, her clinical symptoms improved, and laboratory parameters of inflammation returned to reference values. Follow-up cultures remained negative. A transesophageal echocardiogram was unremarkable, without any evidence of infective endocarditis. Antimicrobial drug therapy was continued for 10 days before discharge. At follow-up 2 months later, the patient had no symptoms and was attending group-counseling sessions to maintain drug abstinence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presented in March 2014 with acute fever (<40.0 °C), chills, and nausea 1 day after injecting cocaine and crushed tablets intravenously.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One day after injecting cocaine and unknown crushed tablets intravenously, the patient presented to the Bernhard Nocht Clinic in Hamburg with acute high fever, chills, and nausea. On hospital day 2, she acutely deteriorated with high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and marked leukocytosis consistent with severe sepsis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of intravenous drug use (cocaine and benzodiazepines), currently enrolled in a methadone maintenance program; history of chronic hepatitis C virus infection cured (sustained virologic response with negative HCV RNA and no cirrhosis) following pegylated interferon-alpha, ribavirin, and boceprevir therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, and nausea; negative for local soft-tissue abscess.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: febrile (<40.0 °C) without soft-tissue abscesses. On hospital day 2: highly febrile, hypotensive, and tachycardic (responding rapidly to intravenous fluid resuscitation without vasopressors).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission WBC was 6.6 x 10^3 cells/µL and CRP was 29 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L), surging on day 2 to WBC 27.6 x 10^3 cells/µL and CRP 112 mg/L. Routine serum/urine chemistry and chest radiograph were normal; HIV-1/2 testing was negative. Urine/serum toxicology screen showed markedly elevated benzodiazepines (>5,000 ng/mL; reference <20 ng/mL) and cocaine (>1,000 ng/mL; reference <20 ng/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was normal without valvular vegetations or infective endocarditis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Community-acquired Acinetobacter ursingii bloodstream infection and severe sepsis following intravenous injection of cocaine and crushed tablets in an HIV-negative, HCV-cured 47-year-old female intravenous drug user. All three aerobic blood culture bottles drawn on admission flagged positive at 18 hours with Gram-negative rods identified by MALDI-TOF MS (score 2.19) and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (99% identity to A. ursingii type strain NBRC110605, GenBank LC014147.1). Vitek 2 antimicrobial susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to ceftriaxone (MIC 32 mg/L)—explaining clinical failure on day 1 empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g daily)—and susceptibility to imipenem (MIC <0.25 mg/L), meropenem (MIC <0.25 mg/L), gentamicin (MIC <1 mg/L), and ciprofloxacin (MIC <0.25 mg/L). Escalation on day 2 to intravenous meropenem (1,000 mg three times daily for 10 days) and IV fluid resuscitation resulted in defervescence within 24 hours, negative follow-up blood cultures, and full recovery at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
The 80-year-old male patient complained of hoarseness and a stinging sensation in his throat for approximately six months and was then transferred to our clinic. The endoscopic larynx examination revealed a lesion that completely infiltrated the epiglottis and reached the right aryepiglottic fold. It was vegetating, pink and purple in color, multilobular, fragile, and shaped like a bunch of grapes and was covering the bleeding airway passage (Figure 1).
Before arriving at our clinic, a punch biopsy was done and suggested a diagnosis of Kaposi's sarcoma. The patient reported that he used to smoke approximately fifty packs of cigarettes per year but had not smoked in the last five years. He had no history of systemic disease or infection. Nothing was remarkable in routine blood analyses. ELISA tests for HIV-1, HBV, and HCV were negative. A positron emission tomography (PET-CT) showed that no other areas were affected. The case was discussed by our hospital's head-neck cancer committee and a surgery decision was made. A tracheotomy was performed under local anesthesia before the operation due to respiratory distress and endotracheal intubation difficulty. The direct laryngoscopy showed that the mass was limited in the supraglottic area, had invaded the entire left aryepiglottic fold and one-third of the front right aryepiglottic fold, and completely covered epiglottis. The laryngeal ventricle, vallecula, arytenoids, interarytenoid area, and glottic and subglottic areas were intact. The mass was found to be bleeding and fragile.
An epiglottectomy was conducted with a diode laser and partial resection was performed on the aryepiglottic folds (Figure 2).
In the histopathological examination of the mass, a tumoral mass consisting of fusiform cells under the surface epithelium was observed in preparations stained with hematoxylin-eosin (Figure 3). Some of the fusiform cells constituted slits and bundle structures involving erythrocytes (Figure 4). After staining the tumoral tissue with common CD31, the diagnosis of Kaposi's sarcoma was made and an apparent nuclear HHV-8 positivity was observed (Figures 5 and 6). When the pathological piece was analyzed, surgical borders were found to be positive. The patient was referred to the radiation oncology department for radiotherapy treatment (RT). The patient was disease-free after one year of follow-up and 33 RT sessions.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 80-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of progressive hoarseness and a stinging sensation in his throat.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 6 months preceding referral, the patient experienced persistent dysphonia and pharyngeal stinging, and an outside punch biopsy of a supraglottic laryngeal mass suggested Kaposi sarcoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of systemic disease or chronic infection; former heavy smoker (~50 pack-years, quit 5 years prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 6-month hoarseness, throat stinging, and acute airway/respiratory distress prior to surgery.

objective.physical_examination: Endoscopic and direct laryngoscopy revealed a fragile, bleeding, multilobular, grape-bunch-like pink-to-purple vegetating mass completely infiltrating the epiglottis, the entire left aryepiglottic fold, and the anterior third of the right aryepiglottic fold, obstructing the supraglottic airway while sparing the vallecula, arytenoids, ventricles, glottis, and subglottis.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were normal; ELISA serologies for HIV-1, HBV, and HCV were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Whole-body FDG PET-CT demonstrated isolated supraglottic laryngeal involvement without nodal or distant metastasis. Following awake local-anesthesia tracheotomy, diode laser epiglottectomy, and partial aryepiglottic fold resection, histopathology and immunohistochemistry demonstrated subepithelial sheets of spindle (fusiform) cells forming erythrocyte-filled vascular slits with strong CD31 positivity, nuclear HHV-8 positivity, and positive surgical margins.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary isolated supraglottic laryngeal HHV-8-positive Kaposi sarcoma in an HIV-negative, HBV/HCV-negative 80-year-old male (confirmed by CD31+ and nuclear HHV-8+ spindle-cell histopathology and staging PET-CT). Managed with preoperative tracheotomy, transoral diode laser epiglottectomy and partial aryepiglottic fold resection, and adjuvant external-beam radiotherapy (33 fractions) for positive microscopic surgical margins, achieving complete disease-free remission at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
In July of 2015, a 63-year-old man with 9-month history of nephrotic syndrome was admitted to Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital because of multiple subcutaneous abscesses with intermittent fever for 20 days. Twenty days prior to admission, 2 subcutaneous abscesses presented on his left lower limb.
The subcutaneous abscesses then sequentially spread from the primary infection to the right dorsal hand, the chest wall, the abdominal wall, the left elbow, and the right lower limb. The abscesses appeared as firm and nonfluctuant masses initially, then they gradually grew up and manifested as tender, fluctuant, and erythematous nodules. They were 0.5 to 5 cm in diameter. Some abscesses ruptured and oozed yellow pus. The patient also developed intermittent chills and fever up to 39.7 C. The patient had been admitted to another hospital 15 days before. He was empirically treated with levofloxacin, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and surgical drainage there. After half a month with no improvement, he was transferred to our hospital.
Medical history: The patient was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome 9 months ago, and mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis was confirmed by renal biopsy. He was initially treated with oral methylprednisolone (48 mg/d) and got a remission. Subsequently, his renal disease was stable with a creatinine clearance of 104 mL/min and minimal proteinuria (220 mg/24 h) under low-dose methylprednisolone (8 mg/d). He had developed diabetes after receiving steroids 7 months before this admission. At that time, he also got pneumonia and recovered with empirical antibiotic treatment. He had a history of hypertension and chronic HBV infection. The patient's social and family history were not remarkable.
Physical examination: On admission, T (temperature) 39.5 C, PR (pulse rate) 80/min, RR (respiratory rate) 14/min, BP (blood pressure) 120/81 mm Hg. More than 10 scattered subcutaneous abscesses were found (Figure 1A), and some ruptured or incised abscesses (Figure 1B) with yellowish purulent discharge were observed. The cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.
Lab test: A complete blood count showed a white blood cell (WBC) of 17.5 x 109/L with 88.4% neutrophils. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 97 mm/h , Procalcitonin 0.340 ng/mL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 130.00 mg/L . 24 h urine protein: 0.22 g. Serum markers of HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis (TB) were all negative. Serum HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBe were positive. Immunology: Antinuclear antigen (ANA), anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA, anti-SSB and anti-Scl-70: negative. Serum levels of IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE were within normal limits. Serum C3 0.85 g/L , serum C4 0.33 g/L, anti-O: 119.00 IU/ML and serum rheumatoid factor (RF) <9.75 IU/ML. Subset of lymphocytes was almost normal: CD3+ 85.04%, CD4+ 45.01%, CD4+/CD8+ 1.13, CD8+ 39.90%, natural killer (NK) cells 7.97%, CD19+ 5.93%. Immunoelectrophoresis results were normal and M-protein was negative. Liver function tests and the chest radiograph were negative. Ultrasound on sites of abscesses: Subcutaneous anechoic lesions. Blood culture was performed, but it did not yield growth of any bacteria after incubation. In addition, HBsAg and HBeAg staining were both negative on the renal biopsy. There were some infiltrated lymphocytes, but no granulomas were found. Moreover, nocardia was not found on the renal biopsy by wade fite staining
Treatment: The multiple abscesses were incised and drained. Before identification of the pathogen, we used meropenem empirically. Meanwhile, culture of pus was ordered. All of the pus cultures, which were aspirated from 5 different complete abscesses, presented Nocardia consistently, and gene sequencing (Figure 2) confirmed that they were all N. brasiliensis. Further investigations for disseminated disease, including computed tomography of the chest and the brain, were negative. According to drug susceptibility testing, linezolid and TMP-SMX were employed as antibiotic therapy. In addition, the immunosuppression treatment was not halted at the time of nocardia presentation. After 1 week's treatment, his fever resolved. Three weeks later, the abscesses disappeared, and the incisions or wounds had healed (Figure 1C). The WBC and neutrophils count also went down. After 4 weeks of hospitalization, he was sent home on a 6-month course of oral TMP-SMX therapy. He remains well off all treatments, without recurrence. The clinical course is summarized in Figure 3.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome on oral methylprednisolone presented in July 2015 with a 20-day history of multiple spreading, painful subcutaneous abscesses and intermittent high fever up to 39.7 °C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Twenty days prior to admission, two firm nodules appeared on his left lower extremity and sequentially spread to his right dorsal hand, chest wall, abdominal wall, left elbow, and right lower extremity, enlarging into >10 tender, fluctuant, erythematous abscesses (0.5–5 cm) that ruptured and drained yellow pus, accompanied by chills and intermittent fevers up to 39.7 °C. Fifteen days of empiric levofloxacin, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and surgical drainage at an outside hospital failed to control the infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Biopsy-proven mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis presenting as nephrotic syndrome 9 months prior (remitted on oral methylprednisolone 48 mg/day, maintained on 8 mg/day with CrCl 104 mL/min); steroid-induced diabetes mellitus and resolved pneumonia 7 months prior; hypertension; chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for >10 painful, purulent subcutaneous nodules/abscesses and high fever (39.7 °C) with chills. Home medication: oral methylprednisolone 8 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: temperature 39.5 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and blood pressure 120/81 mmHg. Cutaneous exam revealed >10 scattered tender, fluctuant subcutaneous abscesses (0.5–5 cm), several ruptured or incised with yellowish purulent discharge, across the left and right lower limbs, right dorsal hand, left elbow, chest wall, and abdominal wall. Cardiopulmonary and neurological exams were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 17.5 x 10^9/L with 88.4% neutrophils), ESR 97 mm/h, procalcitonin 0.340 ng/mL, CRP 130.00 mg/L, 24-hour urine protein 0.22 g, normal liver function tests, positive serum HBsAg, anti-HBc, and anti-HBe, and negative HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Scl-70, RF (<9.75 IU/mL), and serum M-protein. Serum IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, C3 (0.85 g/L), and C4 (0.33 g/L) were normal. Blood cultures were negative; chest X-ray was normal; soft-tissue ultrasound showed subcutaneous anechoic abscess cavities.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets were normal: CD3+ 85.04%, CD4+ 45.01%, CD8+ 39.90%, CD4+/CD8+ ratio 1.13, NK cells 7.97%, and CD19+ 5.93%. Chest CT and brain CT were normal (excluding pulmonary or CNS dissemination). Prior renal biopsy was negative for Nocardia on Wade-Fite staining. Pus aspirated from five distinct intact subcutaneous abscesses consistently grew Nocardia species, confirmed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Nocardia brasiliensis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated lymphocutaneous/subcutaneous Nocardia brasiliensis infection (>10 abscesses across all extremities and trunk without pulmonary or CNS involvement) in an HIV-negative 63-year-old man receiving low-dose methylprednisolone (8 mg/day) for mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis and steroid-induced diabetes. Confirmed by culture isolation of Nocardia from five independent abscess aspirates and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Treated with surgical incision and drainage, initial empiric meropenem switched per antimicrobial susceptibility testing to combination linezolid and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) while continuing low-dose methylprednisolone. Fever resolved within 1 week, all abscesses healed within 3 weeks, and he was discharged at 4 weeks to complete a 6-month course of oral TMP-SMX with no recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man presented with acute visual loss in the left eye (LE). The patient denied other ocular or systemic symptoms. He was not taking any medications and his medical, social and family history was unremarkable. Visual acuity (VA) was 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and hand movements in the LE. Slit-lamp examination findings of the anterior segment were normal in both eyes (OU) and intra-ocular pressure was 12 mmHg bilaterally. Dilated fundoscopy of the LE revealed a few vitreous cells and a large yellow macular placoid lesion with a curvilinear edge (Figure 1A (Fig. 1)). Fluorescein angiography (FA) showed early hypofluorescence with late staining in the affected area (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) in the LE demonstrated subretinal fluid overlying the macular lesion (Figure 3 (Fig. 3)). No abnormalities were detected in the RE. Screening blood tests, including syphilis serology, were requested and the patient was monitored without treatment.
Three days after the placoid lesion had extended (Figure 1B (Fig. 1)). The patient did not follow our recommendation for serologic work-up and the tests were ordered again. One week after the initial presentation, VA remained stable but the placoid lesion had increased outside the temporal retinal vascular arcades (Figure 1C (Fig. 1)). New multiple yellow lesions and hemorrhages were observed in the retinal superior nasal area. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) revealed persistent leakage of the choriocapillaris and hypofluorescence areas in the early and late phases (Figure 4 (Fig. 4)). The patient continued not to follow our recommendation for the blood tests and they were ordered for the third time. He was informed again about his clinical situation and the importance of the work-up was underlined. 
The patient abandoned the clinic for two weeks and when observed again, VA had improved to 20/20 in the LE and the lesions showed complete spontaneous resolution (Figure 1D (Fig. 1)). RE examination remained normal. Finally, we had access to the serologic tests results that revealed a positive VDRL (1/128) and FTA-ABS. HIV titers were negative. All other tests were normal. The diagnosis of acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis in the LE was made. The patient was referred to the Infectious Disease Department. He had no other syphilitic manifestations and no abnormalities were detected after computed tomography of the cranium and orbits. A lumbar puncture revealed a positive VDRL and CSF-TPHA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The patient accepted to start treatment only 45 days after the initial presentation. During this period no relapse of the ocular lesions occurred and no systemic manifestation was observed. The patient was treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G (four million units given every 4 h for 2 weeks). Three months after treatment, VA was 20/20 and fundoscopy remained normal both eyes. Follow-up serologic testing revealed a decrease of VDRL to 1/32.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man presented with acute painless visual loss in his left eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with sudden decrease in left eye vision to hand movements without other ocular or systemic complaints. Over the first week of observation (while repeatedly declining ordered blood tests), the left macular placoid lesion expanded beyond the temporal vascular arcades before undergoing complete spontaneous clinical and visual resolution by week 3.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable medical, social, and family history; taking no medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute left visual loss; negative for ocular pain, headache, rash, or other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial ophthalmic examination showed visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and hand movements in the left eye (LE), normal bilateral anterior segments, and intraocular pressure of 12 mmHg OU. Left eye dilated fundoscopy revealed mild vitritis (few vitreous cells) and a large yellowish macular placoid lesion with a curvilinear border that expanded over 7 days with superior-nasal yellow lesions and retinal hemorrhages before spontaneously resolving to 20/20 visual acuity and a normal fundus at week 3. Right eye examination was normal throughout.
objective.routine_investigations: Fluorescein angiography (FA) of the left eye showed early hypofluorescence and late macular staining; optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal fluid overlying the macular lesion; indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed persistent choriocapillaris leakage and early/late hypofluorescence. Blood tests eventually obtained at week 3 revealed reactive serum VDRL (titer 1:128) and positive FTA-ABS, negative HIV serology, and otherwise normal routine labs.
objective.advanced_workup: Cranial and orbital CT was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed reactive CSF VDRL and positive CSF-TPHA confirming neurosyphilis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Unilateral left acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis (ASPPC) with asymptomatic neurosyphilis in an HIV-negative 55-year-old man, confirmed by serum VDRL 1:128, positive serum FTA-ABS, and reactive CSF VDRL and CSF-TPHA. Despite spontaneous resolution of the macular placoid lesion and visual acuity recovery to 20/20 at 3 weeks prior to antibiotic therapy, the patient ultimately consented at day 45 to a 14-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G (4 million units every 4 hours), maintaining 20/20 visual acuity bilaterally and a 4-fold decline in serum VDRL titer (to 1:32) at 3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 29-year-old previously healthy immigrant male patient from Kazakhstan was admitted to hospital with new-onset severe hemoptysis, macroscopic hematuria and extensive cutaneous petechiae on lower extremities. He appeared ill and poorly nourished. The patient was oriented and well cooperated, and there was no previous history of hematologic or liver or another disease and recent medication. He presented with unexplained weight loss of 2 months duration along with intermittent fever, night sweats and cough. The physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 100/70 mm/Hg, pulse 100/min, a temperature 37.2 C, extensive cutaneous petechiae on lower extremities, hemorrhagic bulla on tongue and on mucosa of oral cavity, and amphoric souffle on apex of right chest. No organomegaly or lymphadenomegaly or evidence of another disease such as chronic liver disease was detectable. The initial complete blood count revealed a white blood cell 25.1 x 109/l (58% neutrophils, 29% bants, 9% lymphocytes and 4% monocytes), hemoglobin 11.2 gr/dl, hematocrit 36%, MCV 84 fl, reticulocytes 1% and platelet count 7.6 x 109/l. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 110 mm/h. A peripheral smear was remarkable for a paucity of platelets. Coagulation profile [prothrombin time (PT), activated-partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), fibrin degradation products (FDP)] were normal. A bone marrow aspiration demonstrated hypercellularity of all cell lines with normal maturation of myeloid and erythroid precursors. Megakaryocytes were increased in number with normal morphology. On bone marrow aspiration hemophagocytosis was not observed. A chest X-ray (Figure 1) and computed tomography (CT) (Figure 2) demonstrated bilateral patchy infiltrates and walled cavities on left and right upper lobes. Acid-fast bacilli were strongly positive in sputum (Figure 3). Bone marrow aspirate and urine for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Sputum culture yielded mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. The following laboratory studies were normal or negative: biochemical tests (glucose, urea, creatinine, uric acid, sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, phosphorus, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, total protein and albumin), rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-platelet specific antibodies, Coomb's tests, HIV, hepatitis B and C virus, blood culture, bone marrow aspirate culture and abdominopelvic CT. No granuloma or hemophagocytosis was detected on bone marrow biopsy. The patient was started on rifampin 10 mg/kg/d, isoniazid 5 mg/kg/d, ethambutol 25 mg/kg/d, pyrazinamide 40 mg/kg/d, pyridoxine 75 mg/d and intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) 1 g/kg/d given for 2 days. On day 2 of hospitalization and treatment of anti-tuberculous therapy prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d was added. On day 8, platelet counts started to increase and on day 12 of the treatment it reached to 187 x 109/l level. Patient improved on day 10 and he did not have any complaints on day 14; at time of discharge. He received a total of 6 red blood cell (RBC) units throughout hospitalization. During his hospitalization findings of hemolysis or gastrointestinal bleeding and massive bleeding in another site except hematuria and hemoptysis were not established. A complete blood count at discharge demonstrated a WBC 17 x 109/l, Hb 9.6 g/dl, and platelet count 310 x 109/l (Table 1). Corticosteroids were discontinued on day 14 of therapy and the patient was discharged and recurrent thrombocytopenia was not established after withdrawal of corticosteroid therapy. Ninety days after discharge, the patient was well with a platelet count of 300 x 109/l (Table 1) and he had no side effect thought to be secondary to anti-tuberculous drugs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male immigrant from Kazakhstan presented with acute severe hemoptysis, gross hematuria, and extensive lower-extremity petechiae superimposed on a 2-month history of unexplained weight loss, intermittent fever, night sweats, and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to admission, the previously healthy patient experienced unintentional weight loss, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and cough, before acutely developing severe hemoptysis, macroscopic hematuria, oral hemorrhagic bullae, and widespread lower limb petechiae.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy male immigrant from Kazakhstan; no prior history of hematologic, hepatic, or systemic disease, and no recent medication exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for hemoptysis, gross hematuria, mucocutaneous bleeding/petechiae, 2-month weight loss, intermittent fever, night sweats, and cough.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing and poorly nourished, alert and oriented; blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, pulse 100 beats/min, and temperature 37.2 °C. Mucocutaneous examination revealed extensive petechiae over both lower extremities and hemorrhagic bullae on the tongue and oral mucosa. Chest auscultation revealed an amphoric breath sound (amphoric souffle) over the right pulmonary apex; no hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy was present.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC revealed marked leukocytosis with left shift (WBC 25.1 x 10^9/L: 58% neutrophils, 29% bands, 9% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, MCV 84 fL, reticulocytes 1%), and profound thrombocytopenia (platelets 7.6 x 10^9/L) confirmed on peripheral blood smear. ESR was 110 mm/h. Coagulation profile (PT, aPTT, FDP), renal and liver biochemistry, LDH, RF, ANA, anti-platelet antibodies, direct/indirect Coombs tests, and serologies for HIV, HBV, and HCV were all normal or negative. Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear was strongly positive and sputum culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (urine and bone marrow AFB stains/cultures and blood cultures were negative). Chest X-ray showed bilateral patchy infiltrates and bilateral upper-lobe cavitary lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT confirmed bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates and thick-walled cavities in both the right and left upper lobes; abdominopelvic CT was normal. Bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy demonstrated trilineage hypercellularity with increased normal-appearing megakaryocytes and no granulomas, malignancy, or hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Active cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed by strongly positive sputum AFB smear and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex culture) complicated by severe secondary immune thrombocytopenia (platelet nadir 7.6 x 10^9/L causing severe hemoptysis, gross hematuria, and wet purpura) in an HIV-negative 29-year-old man. Treated with quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy (rifampin 10 mg/kg/day, isoniazid 5 mg/kg/day, ethambutol 25 mg/kg/day, and pyrazinamide 40 mg/kg/day plus pyridoxine 75 mg/day), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1 g/kg/day for 2 days), a 12-day course of oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day started on day 2 and stopped on day 14), and 6 units of packed red blood cells. Platelet count rose to 187 x 10^9/L by day 12 and 310 x 10^9/L at day 14 discharge, remaining normal (300 x 10^9/L) without relapse at 90-day follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 64-year-old male was admitted to our department as an emergency. He suffered from general malaise, fever, chills, and a pronounced nuchal and facial swelling on the left side. Since birth, he suffered from left-sided microtia with complete absence of meatus acusticus. His medical history was positive for diabetes mellitus type 2 treated by diet and an arterial hypertension controlled by 160 mg valsartan 160 mg/d.
On examination, we observed a left-sided head-and-neck edema with herpetiform-grouped vesicles around the left ear and on the nose and yellowish crusts and formation of bullae in the perioral region (Figures 1 and 2). Laboratory findings were remarkable for leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 25.7 (normal range: 3.8-11.0), thrombocytopenia of 64 Gpt/L (120-340), lowered hematocrit of 0.245 L/L (0.40-0.54), hemoglobin of 5.1 mmol/L (8.6-12.1), erythrocyte count of 2.5 Tpt/L (4.6-6.2), neutrophilia of 13.8 Gpt/L (1.8-7.6), lymphopenia of 11% (20-45), increased number of large unstained cells with 2 Gpt/L (0-0.40), and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 333 mg/L (<5). HIV tests were negative.
Before submission, antibiotic treatment with sultamicillin was started and continued after submission at a dosage of 3 x 3 g/d intravenously (iv). The facial swelling, however, worsened. Therefore, the patient was referred to our Ear Nose Throat-department for diagnostics. Diagnostic ultrasound and thoracic computerized tomography (CT) were performed to exclude a bacterial or mycotic abscess formation.
With the diagnosis of impetiginized herpes zoster, antibiotic treatment was changed to 3 x 800 mg clindamycin/d plus aciclovir 3 x 500 mg/d. Pain management was realized using metamizole sodium 3 x 30 gtt/d. During the following days, only a minor clinical improvement was seen. In the peripheral blood, 11% blasts were noted. A bone marrow biopsy was suggested, but the patient refused.
The further course was characterized by malodorous oozing, formation of bullae, and increasing edema. On the left chin and left submandibular region, firm infiltrates were noted, and skin biopsies were taken to exclude specific infiltrates of a malignancy. Histopathology, however, was nonspecific, demonstrating only a putrid inflammation. Vesicles showed dissemination suggesting zoster generalisatus (Figures 3 and 4). Accordingly, we increased the dosage of aciclovir to 10 mg/kg (3 x 1000 mg/d) iv. The pain sensations become worse, and pregabalin was started in increasing doses. Certoparin sodium 3000 I.E. anti-Xa/d was injected subcutaneously for thrombosis prophylaxis.
Nevertheless, the situation did not improve. CRP increased to >400 mg/L, leukocytosis of 28.4 Gpt/L developed, and procalcitonin increased to 3.65 ng/mL (normal range: 0-0.5).
Under the suspicion of septicemia, we transferred the patient to the intensive care unit. Central venous access was realized by a subclavian catheter. The patient was treated by 4.5 g piperacillin, 500 mg levofloxacin, 1000 mg acyclovir every 8 hours, and initially 100 mg prednisolone. During the treatment course, he developed doughy stool; therefore, the antibiosis was changed to vancomycin 4 x 500 mg per os. Stool samples for Clostridium difficile remained negative. Clinical improvement was accompanied by reduction of vesiculation and edema.
After patient consent, CT and bone marrow biopsy were performed. Bone marrow analysis disclosed atypical myelopoiesis, reduced atypical erythropoiesis, and micromegakaryocytic megakaryopoiesis with 10% of bone marrow blasts confirming a myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) refractory anemia and blast excess II (RAEB II). Chromosomal analysis and cytodiagnostics revealed a karyotype 46/XY and translocations t(2;12)(p13; q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34). Due to anemia, erythrocyte concentrates were required.
Two weeks after admission, the patient suffered from pain in his right arm. The skin surrounding the subclavian catheter became erythematous. Therefore, the catheter was removed, but microbial cultures of the tip remained negative. Venous duplex sonography disclosed vena subclavia thrombosis and soft tissue hematoma.
In the following days, oozing of the scalp and the ear helix was observed. Microbial swaps identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
We intensified diuresis because of a progressive edema. Hemato-oncologist initiated cytoreductive treatment with azacitidine. Anemia and thrombocytopenia required erythrocyte and thrombocyte concentrates. Herpes zoster persisted. During intravenous infusion of varicella immunoglobulin, the patient developed an anaphylactic shock, which could be managed by intensive care. Six days later, the patient died due to a septic shock.
Written informed consent has been obtained from the patient before his tragic outcome to have the case details and any accompanying images published.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male presented as an emergency with acute left-sided facial and nuchal swelling, grouped periauricular/nasal vesicles, perioral bullae, fever, chills, and generalized malaise.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute left-sided head-and-neck edema accompanied by herpetiform vesicles around the left ear and nose, crusted perioral bullae, high fever, chills, and severe progressive pain that failed to respond to initial intravenous sultamicillin (3 x 3 g/day), clindamycin (3 x 800 mg/day), and standard-dose acyclovir (3 x 500 mg/day), progressing to generalized cutaneous dissemination (zoster generalisatus) and septicemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital left-sided microtia with complete external auditory canal atresia; diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus; arterial hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, malaise, severe left facial/neck swelling and pain, and disseminated vesicular rash; developed right arm pain (subclavian thrombosis) and loose stools during hospitalization. Home medication: valsartan 160 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Marked left-sided head-and-neck edema, congenital left microtia with absent external auditory meatus, grouped herpetiform vesicles around the left ear and nose, yellowish crusts and bullae in the perioral region, firm indurated infiltrates over the left chin and submandibular area, and subsequent generalized vesicular dissemination across the body with malodorous oozing of the scalp and ear helix.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 25.7 Gpt/L, rising to 28.4 Gpt/L; reference 3.8–11.0), neutrophilia (13.8 Gpt/L; reference 1.8–7.6), lymphopenia (11%; reference 20–45%), 11% peripheral blood blasts, large unstained cells 2 Gpt/L, severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 5.1 mmol/L [reference 8.6–12.1], hematocrit 0.245 L/L, RBC 2.5 Tpt/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 64 Gpt/L; reference 120–340), markedly elevated CRP (333 mg/L, rising to >400 mg/L; reference <5), elevated procalcitonin (3.65 ng/mL; reference 0–0.5), and negative HIV testing. Stool C. difficile testing was negative; scalp and ear helix swabs grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Venous duplex ultrasound at week 2 showed right subclavian vein thrombosis and soft-tissue hematoma.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck ultrasound and thoracic CT excluded deep cervical or thoracic abscesses. Chin/submandibular skin biopsy showed nonspecific putrid inflammation without leukemic cutis. Bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetics confirmed myelodysplastic syndrome with refractory anemia and excess blasts II (MDS RAEB-II) with 10% marrow blasts, atypical trilineage dysplasia, and karyotype 46,XY with dual translocations t(2;12)(p13;q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe generalized herpes zoster (zoster generalisatus) complicated by Pseudomonas aeruginosa superinfection, right subclavian vein thrombosis, anaphylactic shock to intravenous varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, and fatal septic shock in an HIV-negative 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS RAEB-II with 10% marrow blasts, 11% peripheral blasts, and t(2;12)(p13;q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34)). Despite escalation to high-dose IV acyclovir (1,000 mg every 8 hours), piperacillin, levofloxacin, oral vancomycin, RBC/platelet transfusions, and cytoreductive therapy with azacitidine, the patient suffered anaphylactic shock during IV varicella immunoglobulin infusion and died 6 days later of refractory septic shock.

raw_case_text:
An 83-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital presenting with nausea, unsteadiness, and difficulties in walking. He had a two-month history of falls and abnormal gait. He had atrial fibrillation and was on acenocumarol (a vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant), and his family was concerned because of the risk of major bleeding after a fall. On physical examination, he had unsteady gait and dysdiadochokinesia. Eye-hand and eye-knee tests were abnormal. Cranial nerves and speech were normal, and the rest of the examination was unremarkable.
Anticoagulant therapy was discontinued due to the risk of a fall and major bleeding.
Routine laboratory data were normal, including kidney and liver panels. Haemoglobin, white blood cell count, and platelets were normal. A CT scan of the brain was performed, which did not show any acute abnormalities.
Over the days that followed, a gradual worsening occurred, with dysarthria, absent gag reflex and dysphagia, poor attention span, generalised hyperreflexia, and vertical nystagmus.
An MRI of the brain showed an asymmetric abnormal signal in both cerebellar peduncles, the cerebellar white matter, and the front area of the medulla (Figure 1). These abnormalities were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no gadolinium enhancement and no diffusion restriction. The right side structures were the most affected. The rest of the brain parenchyma was normal.
We consulted our neurologist to establish a differential diagnosis-based work-up. The abnormalities were not likely to be ischaemic or cancerous. However, inflammatory conditions, infectious diseases, primary central nervous system lymphoma, paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome, and demyelinating diseases should be ruled out.
Serologic tests including toxoplasma, HIV, CMV, and herpes simplex were negative. Immunological tests such as C3 and C4, immunoglobulin levels, and lymphocyte subsets were also normal. Tumour markers CA19.9, CEA, CA125, and PSA were normal. An abdominal ultrasound and a thoracic-abdominal CT scan did not reveal any abnormalities. A lumbar puncture was performed and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a glucose level of 110 mg/dl, proteins 42 mg/dl (normal range: 15-45 mg/dl), and leucocytes 1/mul. No oligoclonal bands were found.
While performing the work-up, two weeks after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated, with worsening of the neurological symptoms. He was lethargic and stuporous, with pauses in breathing. He started on steroid pulse therapy (1 g methylprednisolone daily for 5 days), but with no improvement.
A sample of the CSF was sent to a specialised laboratory in order to assess antineuronal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, and anti-Ri), which were negative. PCR for neurotropic viruses were also performed, and the JC virus PCR was positive in the CSF. The finding of the JC virus was reported the same day the patient passed away, three weeks after admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old male presented with nausea, unsteadiness, and gait difficulty superimposed on a 2-month history of recurrent falls and abnormal gait.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to hospital admission, the patient experienced recurrent falls and progressive gait instability, culminating in acute nausea, unsteadiness, and difficulty walking. Over the days and weeks following admission, he progressively deteriorated with dysarthria, dysphagia, absent gag reflex, poor attention, vertical nystagmus, lethargy, stupor, and apneic spells.
subjective.past_medical_history: Atrial fibrillation maintained on acenocoumarol oral anticoagulation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, gait instability, falls, and subsequent inpatient dysarthria and dysphagia. Home medication: acenocoumarol (discontinued on admission due to fall/bleeding risk).

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological examination showed an unsteady ataxic gait, dysdiadochokinesia, and abnormal finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin coordination with intact cranial nerves and speech. Over the subsequent 2 weeks, examination evolved to show dysarthria, absent gag reflex, dysphagia, impaired attention, generalized hyperreflexia, vertical nystagmus, and progressive stupor with respiratory pauses.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, renal, and hepatic panels were normal. Serologies for Toxoplasma, HIV, CMV, and HSV were negative. Serum C3, C4, quantitative immunoglobulins, and tumor markers (CA19-9, CEA, CA125, PSA) were normal. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets were normal. Initial head CT and thoracoabdominal CT were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated asymmetric T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense lesions without gadolinium enhancement or diffusion restriction involving both cerebellar peduncles (right greater than left), cerebellar white matter, and the anterior medulla. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed glucose 110 mg/dL, protein 42 mg/dL (normal 15–45 mg/dL), 1 leukocyte/µL, absent oligoclonal bands, negative paraneoplastic antineuronal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-Ri), and positive CSF JC virus PCR.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Posterior fossa / brainstem-cerebellar progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in an HIV-negative, apparently immunocompetent 83-year-old male (confirmed by positive CSF JC virus PCR and characteristic non-enhancing T2-hyperintense/T1-hypointense cerebellar peduncle and medullary white matter lesions on MRI, with normal lymphocyte subsets and negative HIV, autoimmune, and paraneoplastic panels). A 5-day pulse of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily) failed to halt his rapid bulbar and neurological decline, and the patient died 3 weeks after admission on the same day the positive CSF JC virus PCR result was reported.

raw_case_text:
Herein, we report on a 67-year-old Caucasian originating from Portugal admitted to the hospital for fever of unknown origin and asthenia. His medical history was relevant for hypertension, insulin-dependent type two diabetes, and vitiligo and was on aspirin cardio, lisinopril, torasemid, omeprazole, and insulin therapy. On clinical examination, we noticed anasarca with pleural effusion, ascites, and edema of the lower limbs. Laboratory tests revealed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 100 g/l, MCV 75 fl) with thrombocytopenia (73 G/l), marked elevation of C-reactive protein (204 mg/l), renal insufficiency (creatinine 463 micromol/l), and cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase 300 U/l, gamma-GT 56 U/l), with normal transaminases. Urinalysis showed severe proteinuria (5.29 g/l) and glomerular microhematuria. Immunological evaluation revealed normal IgG, IgM, IgA, and complement (C3, C4) levels, anti-nuclear antibodies (1/640 speckled), anti-SSA, anti-actine, and anti-parietal cell antibodies were positive. The infectious work-up was negative (HIV, hepatitis B/C, CMV, TB spot, and blood culture) except for EBV that was slightly positive by PCR (3,560 copies/ml). A thoraco-abdominal CT scan detected multiple mediastinal, axillary and retroperitoneal adenopathies, pleural and pericardial effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites. There was no sign of peripheral hemolysis (absence of schsitocytes). Finally, a cytokine profile showed elevation of IL-6, VEGF, soluble IL-2 receptor, and TNF-alpha, whereas IL-8 was normal.
The etiology remained unclear and the patient underwent several supplementary investigations. An axillary lymph node was surgically removed and showed atreic secondary lymphoid follicles with hyalinized/vascular GCs. Interfollicular areas showed a marked vascular proliferation and contained a small number of CD138-positive plasma cells (Figures 1A-D). Immunohistochemistry for HHV-8 with latency-associated nuclear antigen-1 was negative. The histopathological findings were consistent with the newly defined diagnostic criteria for iMCD. The blood smear and the flow cytometry in the blood were normal without evidence for lymphoproliferative disease. A bone marrow trephine biopsy revealed megakaryocytic hyperplasia and mild reticulin myelofibrosis without abnormal lymphocytic infiltration (Figures 1E,F).
Renal biopsy showed (1) thickening of the peripheral basement membrane and the intern lamina rara, (2) mesangial proliferation without glomerular deposition of immunoglobulin, and (3) a band-like pattern of interstitial fibrosis associated with lymphohistiocytic inflammatory cell infiltrates. Malignancies were also actively searched for. Colon biopsies showed a collagenous colitis rich in eosinophils (Figure 2A). Gastric biopsies revealed chronic inflammation and glandular atrophia with intestinal metaplasia of the fundus suggestive of an atrophic gastritis (Figure 2B). Prostatic biopsies showed mild chronic inflammation without neoplasia (Figure 2C). Liver biopsy showed mild sinusoidal distension, unspecific portal and lobular inflammation, and rare epithelioid granulomas without necrosis (Figures 2D,E). Finally, the patient underwent a bronchial biopsy showing unspecific chronic inflammation without granuloma, which was not suspicious for sarcoidosis (Figure 2F).
Together, these clinicopathological findings are compatible with a diagnosis of iMCD and TAFRO syndrome.
The best management of iMCD disease remains poorly defined with only one randomized clinical trial published in 2014 on siltuximab compared to best supportive care. Thus, this case required multidisciplinary discussion and consensus in 2011 when the diagnosed was made and judgment was based on available data with tocilizumab and rituximab for the treatment of HHV-8-associated MCD. Thus, treatment was initiated with high dose methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) transitioned to prednisone 1 mg/kg for several weeks, one single infusion of tocilizumab (8 mg/kg), and 1 week later rituximab 375 mg/m2 (total 4 weekly doses) (Figure 3A). The rational to use methylprednisolone and tocilizumab was to rapidly stop IL-6-mediated inflammation as induction regimen, whereas rituximab was used as maintenance treatment. We observed resolution of the inflammatory syndrome and slow clinical improvement over the course of 3 weeks, thrombocyte values normalized (>100 G/l) after 5 weeks and cholestasis parameters several months later. Corticosteroids were rapidly weaned off because of poor control of the diabetes, and the patient was hemodialyzed for end-stage renal disease. In the following 5 years, the patient relapsed twice, each time about 1 year after rituximab was discontinued (Figure 3A). The first relapse was successfully treated with rituximab alone and the second with methylprednisolone/tocilizumab (2 doses)/rituximab (4 weekly doses 375 mg/m2). Five years after the diagnosis was made (before the second relapse), the PET-CT showed reduction of the lymphadenopathies (Figures 3B,C). Auto-antibodies disappeared over the years and hypogammaglobulinemia developed, probably due to repeated rituximab treatments. Follow-up bone marrow biopsies were not performed in this case.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old Caucasian male from Portugal presented with fever of unknown origin, profound asthenia, and generalized anasarca.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted with persistent unexplained fevers, severe fatigue, and progressive generalized fluid overload manifesting as bilateral lower extremity edema, ascites, and pleural effusions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, and vitiligo.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prolonged fever, asthenia, and generalized edema/anasarca. Home medications: aspirin, lisinopril, torasemide, omeprazole, and insulin.

objective.physical_examination: Generalized anasarca characterized by bilateral lower extremity edema, ascites, and pleural effusions.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 100 g/L, MCV 75 fL) without schistocytes, thrombocytopenia (platelets 73 G/L), markedly elevated CRP (204 mg/L), severe renal insufficiency (creatinine 463 µmol/L), anicteric cholestasis (ALP 300 U/L, GGT 56 U/L) with normal transaminases, nephrotic-range proteinuria (5.29 g/L), and glomerular microhematuria. Serum IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and C4 were normal; ANA (1:640 speckled), anti-SSA, anti-actin, and anti-parietal cell antibodies were positive. HIV, HBV, HCV, CMV, TB-Spot, and blood cultures were negative; plasma EBV PCR was weakly positive (3,560 copies/mL). Serum cytokine profiling showed elevated IL-6, VEGF, soluble IL-2 receptor, and TNF-alpha with normal IL-8.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry were normal. Thoraco-abdominal CT revealed multiple mediastinal, axillary, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies, hepatosplenomegaly, pleural and pericardial effusions, and ascites. Surgical axillary lymph node biopsy showed atretic hyalinized/vascular germinal centers, marked interfollicular vascular proliferation, scattered CD138+ plasma cells, and negative HHV-8 LANA-1 immunostaining. Bone marrow trephine biopsy showed megakaryocytic hyperplasia and mild reticulin myelofibrosis without lymphoma. Renal biopsy demonstrated thrombotic microangiopathy-like basement membrane/lamina rara interna thickening, mesangial proliferation without immune deposits, and band-like interstitial fibrosis. Colon, gastric, prostate, liver, and bronchial biopsies excluded malignancy and sarcoidosis (showing eosinophil-rich collagenous colitis, atrophic gastritis, and rare non-necrotizing hepatic granulomas).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HHV-8-negative, HIV-negative idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD) with TAFRO syndrome (thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin myelofibrosis, renal insufficiency, and organomegaly), confirmed by axillary lymph node histopathology, bone marrow trephine biopsy, renal biopsy, and elevated serum IL-6 and VEGF levels. Induction therapy with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days, then oral prednisone taper), a single infusion of tocilizumab (8 mg/kg), and 4 weekly infusions of rituximab (375 mg/m2) alongside hemodialysis resolved the systemic inflammatory syndrome within 3 weeks and normalized platelets (>100 G/L) at 5 weeks. Two subsequent disease relapses over 5 years of follow-up (occurring ~1 year after rituximab cessation) were successfully re-induced with rituximab monotherapy and methylprednisolone/tocilizumab/rituximab, respectively.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old male with no past medical history presented with an occipital headache for 10 days. It was associated with fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence and difficulty walking. He denied focal weakness, paresthesia, neck stiffness, visual changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, urinary and bowel incontinence. The patient was in a monogamous heterosexual relationship. He endorsed a history of social drinking but denied smoking or drug abuse. Medication history was unremarkable.
The patient was afebrile with a heart rate of 88 bpm, RR 21/min, and BP 136/97 mmHg. Physical exam was unremarkable except for pallor and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Labs were significant for hypotonic hyponatremia and normal complete blood count (CBC). Computed tomography (CT) scan head without contrast showed ex vacuo dilatation of the left lateral ventricle (Figure 1).
Lumbar puncture was done and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis unveiled cryptococcal meningitis. Multifocal nodularities involving bilateral basal ganglia consistent with cryptococcomas, were present on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), along with leptomeningeal enhancement and chronic lacunar infarcts. Induction chemotherapy was started with amphotericin and flucytosine.
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis reported diffuse mediastinal, retroperitoneal, inguinal lymphadenopathy with splenomegaly. Immunodeficiency workup revealed a CD4 count of 208 muL-1. HIV testing, serum protein electrophoresis, serum light chains and quantitative immunoglobulins were non-diagnostic. CD4 lymphopenia was attributed to acute infection and the patient was sent to a nursing home for two weeks of IV amphotericin therapy. However, he had persistently low absolute CD4 count ranging between 161 and 213 muL-1 on outpatient follow-up.
Three serial lymph node biopsies for etiological workup of CD4 lymphopenia were nonconclusive, revealing a normal analytic cytometric immunophenotypic analysis. A bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotypic and cytogenetic studies (including karyotype, BCR/ABL1, JAK2 V617F, exon 12 mutations, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) for platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGRF) alpha, beta, and fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1)) was normal. IgH gene rearrangement studies showed a weak peak on B cell framework III on repeat assays, not strong enough to be termed as monoclonal. T cell receptor (TCR) gamma gene arrangement did not point towards a definite diagnosis. Moreover, a review of the sample by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) also proved to be inconclusive. The patient was hence labeled as a case of idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia.
After management of acute meningitis, he was discharged on fluconazole and augmentin therapy. The patient had a stable CD4 count without features of any immunodeficiency-related illness on the subsequent outpatient visits but was lost to follow up after three months of initial presentation. Attempts to contact the patient were unsuccessful, however, emergency contact (friend) revealed that he returned to India and was hospitalized for rapidly progressive dyspnea and confusion. He later died of multiorgan failure after 15 days of MICU stay.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 10-day history of occipital headache, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence, and gait difficulty.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 days preceding presentation, the patient developed a progressive occipital headache accompanied by fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, dysarthria, somnolence, and difficulty walking.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history; taking no medications. Monogamous heterosexual relationship; social alcohol use; denied tobacco or illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for occipital headache, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence, and gait unsteadiness; negative for focal limb weakness, paresthesias, neck stiffness, visual changes, chest pain, dyspnea, or bowel/bladder incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: afebrile, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, and blood pressure 136/97 mmHg. Physical examination was unremarkable except for cutaneous pallor and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed hypotonic hyponatremia and a normal CBC. HIV testing, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, and quantitative immunoglobulins were all negative or normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission absolute CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 208 cells/µL, remaining persistently low (161–213 cells/µL) on serial outpatient testing.
