subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for glossodynia, dysgeusia, painful left oral commissure lesion, odynophagia, and weight loss; negative for skin rash. Home medications: lamivudine, tenofovir, and efavirenz; recent ineffective fluconazole and itraconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Intraoral examination revealed shallow, painful, round-to-oval depapillated erosions over a whitish, non-wipeable hyperkeratotic plaque on the posterior dorsal tongue ('plaques en prairie fauchee' / mowed-meadow tongue plaques), plus a painful fibrin-covered split papule at the left oral commissure ('fausse perleche'). There was no cervical lymphadenopathy or cutaneous rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Plasma HIV-1 viral load was undetectable, and routine laboratory panels were unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 995 cells/mm3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis re-infection presenting exclusively with oral mucosal plaques ('plaques en prairie fauchee') and a left commissural split papule ('fausse perleche'; oral candidiasis excluded by antifungal failure and serology), established via seroconversion to a high-titer serum VDRL (1:128) and reactive FTA-ABS IgG and IgM. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks, achieving rapid and complete clinical resolution of all oral and commissural lesions after the first injection.

raw_case_text: A 37-year-old Caucasian male, HIV-infected (CDC A2) in 2012 and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with tenofovir/emtricitabine and efavirenz, was seen in December 2016 for a follow-up visit in our Infectious Disease department. At that time, the patient's CD4 count was 505/microL and the viral load was <20 copies/mL. A physical examination evidenced an enlarged left inguinal lymph node, hepatosplenomegaly, and a barely discernible macular, pink rash on the trunk not involving the palms and soles, coexisting with maculo-papular lesions localized on the proximal volar aspect of both forearms (Figure 1(a) and (b)). Well-demarked purplish, opaque, rough, vertically ridged plaque-like lesions were also present on the proximal portions of some fingernails of both hands. The involved nails were friable. There was no discernible involvement of the periungual skin (Figure 1(c) and (d)). The patient reported the onset of these manifestations about 2 months prior. During the visit, the patient also reported that he had engaged in unprotected sex in July 2016. Laboratory tests evidenced erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ERS) of 26 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CPR) of 3.5 mg/dL (normal value [NV] < 0.5), gamma-globulins of 22%, hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL, hematocrit of 35%, gamma-glutamyltransferase of 102 IU/mL (NV 7-49 IU/mL), and alkaline phosphatase of 334 IU/mL (NV 80-320 IU/mL). Hepatitis B, C, and A serology resulted negative. Syphilis serology, which had been negative in 2012, resulted reactive. Specifically, Rapid Reagin Test (RPR) and Treponema Pallidum Particle Agglutination Assay (TPPA) were positive, with titers of 1:32 and 1:5120, respectively. The patient was reactive to fluorescent treponemal antibodies and positive to anti-treponema IgM antibody. Intramuscular (IM) injection of benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million units, was administered once a week for 3 weeks. A month later, the rash was no longer evident, while the fingernail lesions were reduced in size. At that time, RPR titer was 1:16 and anti-treponema IgM antibody was negative. Five months from the end of therapy, the fingernails were free of disease, with the exception of a linear scar on the left little fingernail (Figure 2(a) and (b)), and all the abnormal blood test, including the liver enzymes, resulted normal. Six months after the end of therapy, RPR resulted reactive (titer 1:2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old HIV-positive Caucasian male presented with a 2-month history of rough, purplish, friable proximal fingernail plaques and a faint macular/maculopapular rash on his trunk and forearms.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Seen in December 2016 for routine HIV follow-up, the patient reported a 2-month history of fingernail plate changes on both hands and a subtle rash on his trunk and volar forearms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection (CDC stage A2) in 2012 (baseline syphilis serology negative in 2012), well-controlled on tenofovir/emtricitabine and efavirenz. Reported engaging in unprotected sexual intercourse in July 2016 (5 months prior to presentation).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-month fingernail dystrophy and truncal/forearm rash; negative for periungual paronychia or palmoplantar skin lesions. Home medications: tenofovir/emtricitabine and efavirenz.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed an enlarged left inguinal lymph node, hepatosplenomegaly, a faint pink macular rash on the trunk (sparing the palms and soles), maculopapular lesions on the proximal volar aspect of both forearms, and well-demarcated purplish, opaque, rough, vertically ridged friable plaque-like lesions on the proximal nail plates of several fingernails on both hands without periungual skin inflammation.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed ESR 26 mm/h, elevated CRP 3.5 mg/dL (normal <0.5), hypergammaglobulinemia (gamma-globulins 22%), hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, hematocrit 35%, elevated GGT 102 IU/mL (normal 7-49), and elevated alkaline phosphatase 334 IU/mL (normal 80-320). Plasma HIV viral load was <20 copies/mL, and HAV, HBV, and HCV serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 505 cells/uL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis presenting with syphilitic onychia (nail plate dystrophy), roseolar/maculopapular rash, and mild cholestatic hepatitis in an HIV-positive patient, established via reactive serum RPR (titer 1:32), high-titer TPPA (1:5,120), reactive FTA-ABS, and positive anti-Treponema pallidum IgM. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 weeks. At 1 month, the rash cleared, nail lesions shrank, RPR declined to 1:16, and anti-treponemal IgM became negative; by 5-6 months, the fingernails and liver enzymes normalized completely and the RPR titer declined 16-fold to 1:2.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old secundigravida Caucasian woman at 19+5 weeks of gestation was referred to our Fetal Medicine Centre to perform a level II ultrasound scan because of positive serology for syphilis in the first trimester. No maternal clinical manifestations of disease was found on examination. She had had a history of a feverish erythematosus maculopapular rush localized to trunk, limbs, palms, and soles two years before. The diagnosis of syphilis was performed only during antenatal screening in the first trimester by a positive venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) and a treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) title of 1:2560. The HIV status of the woman was negative. Antibiotic therapy was started immediately with benzathine penicillin G 7.2 million units total, administered as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals according to the stage of syphilis, in line with CDC guidelines. At the end of the treatment the serology tests were stable with VDRL positive, a TPHA title of 1:2560.
The serology for syphilis also resulted positive in her husband (VDRL positive with TPHA title of 1:320) who was treated with a recommended regimen.
The scan performed at 19+5 weeks of gestation in our centre revealed no abnormalities, the amniotic fluid was found regular, and fetal growth parameters were normal.
At 23+5 weeks of gestation a follow-up scan was performed and a massive hydrocephalus (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)), severe hydrothorax, ascites, and hepatomegaly were found. The measurement of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) was performed and an increased peak systolic velocity for gestational age was found. Careful counseling with the couple was performed after the ultrasound finding of the fetal anomaly. Maternal blood tests for cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, parvovirus, toxoplasma, and herpes virus types 1 and 2 were found negative while syphilis serologic tests were confirmed positive with RPR title 1:4 and TPHA title 1:640. Fetal karyotype was normal. Further counseling was made and the woman decided to pursue the termination of pregnancy. Fetal autopsy showed a cutaneous erythematous papular disseminated rash, widespread edema (stronger in the limbs), ascites, hydrothorax, internal obstructed hydrocephalus, ischemic-haemorrhagic brain injury with disseminated lesions, productive pachymeningitis with dystrophic calcification, hepatomegaly, acute hepatic and splenic hematopoiesis, productive bilateral peripyelitis, pronounced glomerulus-poiesis, and involution of the thymus. The research of Treponema Pallidum with coloring of Warthin-Starry identified images compatible with the morphological appearance of the germ. The diagnostic conclusion deposed for congenital syphilis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old secundigravida Caucasian woman was referred at 19+5 weeks' gestation for fetal medicine surveillance following first-trimester diagnosis and penicillin treatment of maternal syphilis, subsequently developing severe fetal hydrops and hydrocephalus at 23+5 weeks' gestation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed on first-trimester antenatal screening with latent syphilis (positive VDRL, TPHA 1:2,560), the mother immediately completed 3 weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units (total 7.2 million units). Level II fetal ultrasound at 19+5 weeks was normal, but follow-up ultrasound at 23+5 weeks revealed massive fetal hydrocephalus, severe hydrothorax, ascites, hepatomegaly, and elevated MCA peak systolic velocity.
subjective.past_medical_history: 29-year-old G2; history of an untreated febrile erythematous maculopapular rash involving her trunk, limbs, palms, and soles 2 years prior to pregnancy. Her husband also tested positive for syphilis (VDRL positive, TPHA 1:320) and was treated.
subjective.review_of_systems: Maternally asymptomatic during pregnancy.

objective.physical_examination: Maternal physical examination was normal without active mucocutaneous lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Maternal HIV, CMV, Coxsackievirus, parvovirus B19, Toxoplasma, and HSV-1/2 serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Level II obstetric ultrasound at 23+5 weeks' gestation demonstrated massive fetal internal hydrocephalus, severe hydrothorax, ascites, hepatomegaly, and elevated fetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (fetal anemia). Fetal karyotype was normal. Fetal autopsy following pregnancy termination revealed a disseminated papular erythematous rash, generalized hydrops/limb edema, ascites, hydrothorax, obstructive internal hydrocephalus, disseminated ischemic-hemorrhagic cerebral lesions, productive pachymeningitis with dystrophic calcifications, hepatomegaly, extramedullary hepatosplenic hematopoiesis, bilateral peripyelitis, and thymic involution.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed severe fetal congenital syphilis with non-immune hydrops fetalis, obstructive hydrocephalus, and productive pachymeningitis despite first-trimester maternal benzathine penicillin G therapy, established via maternal VDRL/RPR (1:4) and TPHA (1:2,560 -> 1:640) positivity and fetal autopsy Warthin-Starry silver staining demonstrating Treponema pallidum spirochetes. Following multidisciplinary counseling at 23+5 weeks' gestation, the couple elected termination of pregnancy.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man with a history of extensive alcohol and tobacco use presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging, 5-cm ulcerative, and painful midline tongue lesion extending to the floor of mouth resulting in an anterior tongue cleft. This lesion was associated with unintentional weight loss, left otalgia, and submandibular swelling. Bilateral nontender palpable lymphadenopathy in levels I, II, and III were present.
Prior biopsies by an otolaryngologist in private practice did not demonstrate carcinoma but were otherwise inconclusive with reactive inflammatory changes. However, a positron emission tomography scan revealed hypermetabolic lesions of the anterior tongue as well as lymph nodes bilaterally in levels I, II, and III suggestive of malignancy (Figure 1). The assessment was a likely T3/4N2cM0 tongue squamous cell carcinoma. He underwent a panendoscopy with biopsies and a physical examination under anesthesia for surgical planning. Biopsy results again did not yield carcinoma but showed granulomatous inflammation without organisms present.
A multidisciplinary tumor board recommended a rheumatologic workup and an excisional lymph node biopsy. Lymph node biopsy results demonstrated noncaseating granulomatous inflammation with no malignancy (Figure 2), while laboratory results demonstrated markedly elevated ACE (angiotensin converting enzyme) levels. These findings suggested an atypical case of sarcoidosis, and the patient was referred for pulmonary consultation. The patient had developed scattered erythematous macules involving the extremities, palms, soles, and trunk. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated T pallidum immunoglobulin G antibodies present with a reflex RPR (rapid plasma reagin) titer of 1:512. The lymph node biopsy sample was then analyzed with immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealing spirochetes (Figure 3). The patient was diagnosed with tertiary syphilis and started on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 30 days because of a severe penicillin allergy. After receiving treatment, the patient came back to our clinic with his tongue lesion healing well but with a persistent anterior tongue cleft (Figure 4). The patient has not obliged with further laboratory evaluations to recheck a RPR titer after antibiotic therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful 5-cm ulcerative midline anterior tongue mass causing an anterior tongue cleft, accompanied by unintentional weight loss, left otalgia, and submandibular swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 2 months, the patient developed a painful, deeply ulcerated 5-cm midline anterior tongue lesion extending to the floor of the mouth with referred left ear pain, bilateral neck swelling, and weight loss, initially suspected to be stage T3/4N2cM0 oral squamous cell carcinoma. While undergoing workup for noncaseating granulomas found on tongue and lymph node biopsies, he subsequently developed a scattered erythematous macular rash over his trunk, extremities, palms, and soles.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of heavy alcohol and tobacco use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful 5-cm ulcerated tongue mass, left otalgia, submandibular swelling, unintentional weight loss, and subsequent truncal/palmoplantar macular rash. Severe penicillin allergy.

objective.physical_examination: Oral and head/neck examination revealed a 5-cm ulcerative midline anterior tongue mass extending to the floor of the mouth and creating an anterior tongue cleft, accompanied by bilateral nontender palpable cervical lymphadenopathy in levels I, II, and III. Subsequent dermatological examination showed scattered erythematous macules over the trunk, extremities, palms, and soles.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level was markedly elevated.
objective.advanced_workup: 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated an intensely hypermetabolic anterior tongue mass and hypermetabolic bilateral level I-III cervical lymphadenopathy mimicking locally advanced carcinoma. Repeat panendoscopy tongue biopsies and excisional cervical lymph node biopsy ruled out malignancy and demonstrated noncaseating granulomatous inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed syphilitic lingual gumma / granulomatous glossitis and cervical lymphadenitis (tertiary/secondary overlapping syphilis initially mimicking T4N2cM0 tongue squamous cell carcinoma and sarcoidosis), established via positive serum Treponema pallidum IgG, high-titer serum RPR (1:512), and positive Treponema pallidum immunohistochemistry (IHC) demonstrating spirochetes within the excised cervical lymph node. Due to severe penicillin allergy, he was treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 30 days, resulting in complete healing of the tongue ulceration with a residual anterior tongue cleft.

raw_case_text: A 54-year-old gentleman with a history of well-controlled HIV established on Truvada and raltegravir, seizures, migraines, and previously treated syphilis presented to Croydon University Hospital with a 4-week history of progressive left leg weakness, bowel and bladder change, and a 1-week history of dysesthesia (Table 2). He denied any infective symptoms, weight loss, and personal or family history of tuberculosis (TB). He had no recent travel and reported no new sexual partners. Clinical examination revealed a normal cardiorespiratory examination. Neurologically, the patient had brisk reflexes in all limbs with reduced power (MRC 0/5) in the left leg combined with sensory dissociation starting from T5 in keeping with Brown-Sequard syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine undertaken at this time identified two peripherally enhancing cavitating lesions at T4-T5 with associated meningeal thickening and cord oedema. These images were felt indicative of CNS TB. Following this, anti-TB medication was started, and the patient was transferred to St. George's Hospital for further care. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis undertaken revealed highly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and white cell count (7 x 109/L). CSF cryptococcal antigen (CRAG), TB molecular testing (GeneXpert), microscopy and culture, and viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were all negative. Serial sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB), peripheral blood cultures, and Q-interferon tests were negative. At this point, syphilis serological testing was undertaken; this suggested highly active acute infection (serum EIA positive and rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (1 in 64)). CSF serology showed positive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) 10240 and RPR 1 in 2 suggesting active disease. This raised the possibility of neurosyphilis with spinal syphilitic gumma. Due to no conclusive TB diagnosis, concurrent neurosyphilis treatment was initiated by way of 14-day high-dose benzylpenicillin therapy commencing on day 11 of presentation. Repeat MRI of the spine on days 12 and 22 of admission revealed incremental improvement in both spinal cord oedema and the size of the T4-T5 lesions (Figure 1). Following this, positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was performed on day 41 which showed no significant areas of increased uptake outside of the spine for potential biopsy. This improvement in the spinal disease was associated with progressive and marked improvements in his neurology, and by day 55, the patient could walk several lengths of parallel bars from being previously bedbound.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old HIV-positive man presented with a 4-week history of progressive left lower-extremity weakness and bowel and bladder dysfunction, accompanied by a 1-week history of dysesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 weeks, the patient developed progressive left leg paralysis and neurogenic bowel/bladder changes, followed 1 week prior to presentation by truncal/limb dysesthesia below T5. Initial spinal MRI suggested CNS tuberculosis and empiric anti-TB therapy was started prior to transfer, until syphilis serology and CSF testing confirmed spinal syphilitic gumma.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of well-controlled HIV infection on Truvada (tenofovir/emtricitabine) and raltegravir, epilepsy/seizures, migraines, and previously treated syphilis. Denied personal/family history of tuberculosis, recent travel, or new sexual partners.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive left leg weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and T5 sensory dysesthesia; negative for fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Home medications: Truvada and raltegravir.

objective.physical_examination: Cardiorespiratory examination was normal. Neurological examination demonstrated a classic T5 Brown-Sequard hemicord syndrome: severe left lower-limb paralysis (MRC power 0/5), generalized brisk deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, and dissociated sensory loss below the T5 dermatome.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial sputum acid-fast bacilli smears, peripheral blood cultures, and QuantiFERON-TB testing were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine MRI demonstrated two peripherally enhancing cavitating intramedullary lesions at T4-T5 with adjacent meningeal thickening and spinal cord edema. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and pleocytosis (WBC 7 x 10^9/L [7 cells/uL]), with negative CSF cryptococcal antigen, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, AFB smear/culture, and viral PCRs. Day 41 whole-body FDG PET/CT showed no extraspinal hypermetabolic lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed T4-T5 intramedullary spinal syphilitic gummas presenting with Brown-Sequard syndrome in an HIV-positive patient (spinal tuberculoma excluded via negative GeneXpert, AFB cultures, and QuantiFERON), established via positive serum treponemal EIA, serum RPR titer of 1:64, positive CSF TPPA (titer 1:10,240), and reactive CSF RPR (titer 1:2). Commenced on hospital day 11 on a 14-day course of high-dose intravenous benzylpenicillin. Repeat spinal MRIs on days 12 and 22 showed progressive regression of the T4-T5 cavitary gummas and cord edema, and by hospital day 55 he had progressed from complete paraplegia/bedbound status to walking in parallel bars.

raw_case_text: A 38-year-old mentally ill antenatal motherwas referred to the sexually transmitted diseases department for screening at 34 weeks of gestation. History could not be elicitedand there were no clinical features of syphilis. Her rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was reactive in 1:2 dilution. The confirmatory treponema pallidum hemagglutination (TPHA) test was also positive. Lumbar puncture was done, and her cerebrospinal fluid examination was normal. She was diagnosed as latent syphilis of unknown duration and was treated with three doses of injection benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU after test dose at weekly intervals. She delivered a male baby 1 month after the last dose of injection penicillin, and the baby was referred to our department at birth. The baby was well without any clinical or radiological evidence of syphilis. However, RPR was reactive in 1:64 dilution, and TPHA was positive. Maternal RPR at the time of delivery was nonreactive. The child was diagnosed as a case of congenital syphilis and admitted in the neonatal intensive care unit. The baby was treated with injection aqueous crystalline penicillin 50,000 units/kg twice daily for 7 days followed by thrice daily for 3 more days after the test dose as per scenario 1 of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines (serum quantitative nontreponemal serologic titer is fourfold higher than the mother's titer). The mother and the child are on follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A term male newborn delivered to a 38-year-old mother treated at 34 weeks' gestation for latent syphilis was referred at birth for congenital syphilis evaluation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant's mother, a 38-year-old woman with mental illness, had been diagnosed at 34 weeks' gestation with latent syphilis of unknown duration (maternal RPR 1:2, TPHA positive, CSF normal) and treated with 3 weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units, delivering the male infant 1 month after her last injection. Although clinically and radiographically asymptomatic at birth, the newborn was found to have a high serum RPR titer of 1:64.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to a 38-year-old mentally ill mother treated with 3 weekly doses of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU starting at 34 weeks' gestation (maternal RPR seroreverted from 1:2 at 34 weeks to non-reactive at delivery).
subjective.review_of_systems: Clinically well newborn with no overt symptoms at birth.

objective.physical_examination: Newborn physical examination was completely normal with no clinical stigmata of congenital syphilis.
objective.routine_investigations: Newborn radiological skeletal survey was normal. Maternal RPR at delivery was non-reactive.
objective.advanced_workup: Maternal prenatal lumbar puncture CSF examination at 34 weeks' gestation was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed asymptomatic congenital syphilis (CDC Scenario 1: infant quantitative nontreponemal titer >=4-fold higher than maternal titer at delivery), established via a neonatal serum RPR titer of 1:64 and positive neonatal TPHA compared with a non-reactive maternal RPR at delivery. Admitted to the NICU and treated with intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 units/kg twice daily for 7 days followed by three times daily for 3 days (total 10 days) after a negative test dose.

raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old heterosexual male was admitted to the Respiratory and Critical Care Department for a three-day history of left pleuritic chest pain and mild cough. He denied fever, weight loss, dyspnea, or nervous system symptoms. He had a medical history of 10-year chronic hepatitis B.
Physical examination revealed normal body temperature, normal breath sound, lack of mucosal or genitourinary lesion, and presence of erythematous papular rash over the palms and soles. The laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 8370/mL. The procalcitonin level of 0.336 ng/mL (normal range, <0.5) was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was increased to 69 mm/h. The serological tests of hepatitis C antibody and HIV antibody were negative, while the hepatitis B surface antigen was positive. The TP passive particle agglutination assay (TPPA) was positive, and the toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST) revealed titer of 1:64. The TPPA kit was purchased from FUJIREBIO INC. (Tokyo, Japan), and the TRUST kit was obtained from Shanghai Rongsheng-Biotech (Shanghai, China). Based on the history of sex with partners, erythematous papular rash over the palms and soles, and positive serological tests, secondary syphilis was considered in this patient after consultation with a dermatologist.
Chest computed tomography (CT) showed left lower lobe pneumonia, mild left pleural effusion, and mediastinal adenopathy (Figures 1 and 2). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples were collected from the patient and sent to our microbiological laboratory for smear and culture and to Guangzhou Sagene Biotech Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China) for mNGS. The smear and culture were negative. The mNGS analysis of the BALF identified 56 sequence reads uniquely corresponding to the T. pallidum genome, with 0.37% coverage (Figure 3). The details of mNGS sequencing and analysis in the Guangzhou Sagene Biotech Co., Ltd were provided in Supplementary Materials. Combining with clinical manifestations and laboratory data, the diagnosis of secondary syphilis with pulmonary involvement was supported. Benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units 3 doses, 1 dose per week x 3 weeks) was administered intramuscularly. After one month, the CT scan showed that pleural effusion disappeared and pneumonia was resolved (Figure 4). The TRUST titer decreased to 1:16.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old heterosexual male presented with a 3-day history of left pleuritic chest pain and mild cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to the respiratory department with 3 days of left-sided pleuritic chest pain and a mild cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: 10-year history of chronic hepatitis B virus infection; heterosexual male with a history of sexual contact with multiple partners.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left pleuritic chest pain, mild cough, and a palmoplantar rash; negative for fever, weight loss, dyspnea, or neurological symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature and pulmonary auscultation were normal. Cutaneous examination revealed an erythematous papular rash over the bilateral palms and soles, with no oral or anogenital mucosal lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count was normal at 8,370/uL, procalcitonin was normal at 0.336 ng/mL (normal <0.5), and ESR was elevated at 69 mm/h. HBsAg was positive, while anti-HCV and anti-HIV antibodies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated left lower lobe pneumonia/consolidation, a mild left pleural effusion, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) routine smears and cultures were negative, whereas metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of the BALF identified 56 sequence reads uniquely mapping to the Treponema pallidum genome (0.37% coverage).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis with pulmonary involvement (syphilitic pneumonia and pleuritis), established via palmoplantar papular syphilides, positive serum TPPA, reactive serum TRUST (titer 1:64), and direct detection of Treponema pallidum genomic sequences in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid by mNGS. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 weeks; at 1-month follow-up, repeat chest CT showed complete resolution of the left lower lobe pneumonia and pleural effusion, and the serum TRUST titer declined fourfold to 1:16.

raw_case_text: A premature baby boy was born at 34 weeks 1/7 days of pregnancy to a G2P2, 29-year-old mother. The infant had Apgar scale scores of 10, 10, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 min, respectively. The birth weight was 2,200 g. The pregnant woman went to the hospital for prenatal care at 16 weeks 1/7 days of pregnancy, and serological tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis by chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA) were negative. The oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) results were as follows: fasting: 5.8 mmol/L, 1 h after meal: 11.7 mmol/L, and 2 h after meal: 11.8 mmol/L. A diagnosis of gestational diabetes was made, and diet control was recommended. At 24 weeks of gestation, the woman developed a generalized body maculopapular rash that was non-itchy. She went to the dermatology department of the local hospital, and the dermatologist confirmed that the HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening results were negative at 3 months of pregnancy. The maculopapular rash was considered to be related to pregnancy, and it subsided without treatment. The pregnant woman went to the hospital for prenatal care at 32 weeks 4/7 days of pregnancy, and the treponemal serological test (CLIA) was positive. The toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST) titer was 1:16. Subsequently, her husband was screened for syphilis. The treponemal serological test (CLIA) was positive, and the TRUST titer was 1:32. The woman reported that she had unprotected sexual behaviors with her husband during pregnancy. Both individuals were treated with 2.4 million U of benzathine penicillin by intramuscular injection every 7 days for a total of three cycles.

subjective.chief_complaint: A preterm male neonate (born at 34+1 weeks' gestation, birth weight 2,200 g) was evaluated at birth following third-trimester diagnosis and treatment of maternal secondary/latent syphilis acquired during pregnancy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant's 29-year-old mother (G2P2) had negative first-trimester (16+1 weeks) prenatal screening for syphilis (CLIA), HIV, HBV, and HCV, and was diagnosed with diet-controlled gestational diabetes. At 24 weeks' gestation, she developed a self-resolving generalized non-pruritic maculopapular rash that was misattributed to pregnancy based on her negative 16-week screen. Repeat prenatal screening at 32+4 weeks' gestation revealed maternal syphilis seroconversion (CLIA positive, TRUST 1:16; husband also tested CLIA positive, TRUST 1:32), and both parents were treated with 3 weekly intramuscular injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units prior to preterm delivery at 34+1 weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: Preterm male infant born at 34+1 weeks' gestation (Apgar scores 10, 10, and 10) to a 29-year-old G2P2 mother with gestational diabetes (OGTT: fasting 5.8, 1-h 11.7, 2-h 11.8 mmol/L) who acquired gestational secondary syphilis (rash at 24 weeks, TRUST 1:16 at 32+4 weeks) via unprotected marital intercourse during pregnancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Maternal history positive for a generalized non-pruritic maculopapular rash at 24 weeks' gestation.

objective.physical_examination: The preterm male neonate weighed 2,200 g at birth with Apgar scores of 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes.
objective.routine_investigations: Maternal 16+1 week HBV, HCV, HIV, and syphilis CLIA screens were negative; maternal 24-week OGTT confirmed gestational diabetes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed gestational maternal syphilis seroconversion (secondary syphilis rash at 24 weeks' gestation, diagnosed at 32+4 weeks via positive maternal treponemal CLIA and serum TRUST titer of 1:16, with paternal CLIA positive and TRUST 1:32) resulting in preterm delivery at 34+1 weeks' gestation. Both the mother and her husband were treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 cycles.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department of our hospital with a 4-week history of fever, loss of appetite, and myalgia, followed by the onset of skin lesions.
The lesions first began on the trunk and gradually involved the face and the extremities. She also gave a history of weight loss over the past 6 months. She is married with two children, but the husband has been estranged for the past 1 year.
The patient did not give a history of any genital lesion in the past.
The physical examination revealed that the patient was afebrile, conscious, and well-oriented to time, place, and person. She was severely underweight with a BMI of 16.33 (weight -36 kg and height -1.49 m).
There was no pallor/icterus/cyanosis; a few enlarged lymph nodes were seen in the bilateral inguinal region; peripheral edema was present over the bilateral lower limbs extending up to the knee.
The cutaneous examination revealed multiple nodules over the face, the trunk, and the upper and lower limbs. The nodules were covered with thick, yellowish, rupioid-like crusts, and some of them were ulcerated. There was mutilation of the nasal tip, and scarring was present wherever the necrotic crusts were present [Figure 1a-c].
On examination of the oral mucosa, thrush was seen on the tongue and over the buccal mucosa. The genital mucosa appeared normal. There were lesions over the eyelids; however, the ophthalmological examination revealed no significant abnormality.
The neurological, gastrointestinal tract, musculoskeletal, and cardiovascular examinations were all within the normal limits.
From the cutaneous presentation, a differential diagnosis of pemphigus vegetans, pyoderma gangrenosum, lupus vulgaris, deep fungal infection, rupioid psoriasis, and secondary syphilis was thought of.
The patient was admitted and investigated further.
The serum investigations revealed a positive Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) (TITER-1:4) and a positive Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay status. After further enquiry, the patient revealed that she had been diagnosed as HIV positive in the past 6 months, had been started on antiretroviral treatment, but had not continued taking the treatment.
A CD4 cell count was 90 cells/mm3. The serology for hepatitis B and C was negative. A complete blood count revealed pancytopenia with a total white blood cell count of 21,000 and hemoglobin -7.7 gm%, and the liver function test revealed a serum albumin of 2.2 gm% with a total protein level of 6.6. The Mantoux test was negative.
A histopathological examination of the skin revealed pustule formation, i.e. neutrophil collection in the stratum corneum, ulceration, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, inflammatory cells consisting of plasma cells, and histiocytes was seen in the dermis [Figure 2a-c].
Stains for fungal elements were negative. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain was negative. No granulomas or clefting were seen.
Considering the VDRL positivity, HIV positivity, and histopathology revealing plasma cells, a diagnosis of MS was made.
The patient was treated with 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin in a total of three series with an interval of 1 week between the series. The patient showed a significant improvement after each dose [Figures 3-5]. Owing to the low CD4 counts - cotrimoxazole (800/160) and fluconazole (100 mg) prophylaxis was also started. Antiretroviral therapy was started after the completion of the course of benzathine penicillin in view of preventing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome). The lesions healed completely with scarring.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old female presented with a 4-week history of fever, anorexia, and myalgia followed by widespread ulcerated crusted nodular skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 4 weeks of fever, loss of appetite, and myalgia, followed by the eruption of nodular skin lesions that began on the trunk and progressively spread to her face and upper and lower extremities, accompanied by significant weight loss over the preceding 6 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: Married with two children, estranged from her husband for the past 1 year. Upon further inquiry after admission, she disclosed having been diagnosed with HIV infection 6 months earlier and initiated on antiretroviral therapy (ART), which she subsequently discontinued. Denied any history of prior genital lesions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, anorexia, myalgia, 6-month weight loss, and widespread crusted skin nodules. Discontinued home ART.

objective.physical_examination: The patient was afebrile, conscious, and oriented, but severely underweight (weight 36 kg, height 1.49 m, BMI 16.33 kg/m2) without pallor, icterus, or cyanosis. Examination revealed bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy and bilateral pitting lower-limb edema extending to the knees. Cutaneous examination showed widespread nodules over the face, eyelids, trunk, and extremities covered by thick, yellowish rupioid-like necrotic crusts with underlying ulceration, scarring, and mutilation of the nasal tip. Oral mucosa showed candidal thrush on the tongue and buccal mucosa; genital mucosa, ophthalmic exam, and cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and neurological exams were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL and leukocytosis with total WBC count 21,000/mm3 (reported alongside pancytopenia/anemia). Liver function tests revealed hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.2 g/dL) with total protein 6.6 g/dL. Hepatitis B and C serologies and Mantoux tuberculin skin test were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4 T-lymphocyte count was severely depressed at 90 cells/mm3. Skin biopsy histopathology demonstrated stratum corneum pustule formation (neutrophilic collections), epidermal ulceration, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and a dense dermal inflammatory infiltrate composed of plasma cells and histiocytes; fungal (PAS/GMS) and Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stains were negative, with no granulomas or acantholytic clefting.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed malignant syphilis (lues maligna) co-infected with advanced HIV (CD4 90 cells/mm3) and oral candidiasis, established via reactive serum VDRL/RPR (titer 1:4), positive TPHA, and characteristic plasma-cell-rich dermal histopathology (ruling out pemphigus vegetans, pyoderma gangrenosum, lupus vulgaris, deep mycosis, and rupioid psoriasis). Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 doses, plus cotrimoxazole (800/160 mg) and fluconazole (100 mg) prophylaxis, followed by re-initiation of antiretroviral therapy after completing penicillin to minimize IRIS risk. The cutaneous lesions healed completely with residual scarring.

raw_case_text: A 15-year-old female, born in Rio de Janeiro reported the appearance of discreetly pruritic lesions on the face and left palmar region 3 months ago with no other associated symptoms. She reported having had unprotected sex in the last 3 months. Physical examination revealed two well-defined, rounded, non-scaly, brownish plaques with slightly elevated erythematous edges: one located superior to the right oral angle and the other lateral to the right nasal ala. Multiple whitish confluent plaques were observed in the ventral region of the tongue. In the left palmar region, two circular erythematous macules with peripheral whitish scaly collarettes were observed. Dermatological findings included elegant syphilides on the face (Figure 1), mucous plaques on the tongue (Figure 2), and syphilitic roseola with a Biett collarette in the palmar region (Figure 3). The clinical diagnosis was secondary syphilis, confirmed using quantitative VDRL (1/32) and rapid treponemal test (FTA-ABS) reagents. We administered 2,400,000 IU intramuscular single dose of benzathine penicillin that led to resolution of the lesions and treatment of sexual contacts. Secondary syphilis manifests as various types of rashes on the skin and mucous membranes. In afro-descent patients, the lesion on the face can present as elegant syphilide. It occurs infrequently around the nose and mouth, has an annular or circinate configuration, and is a characteristic finding during the secondary phase of the disease that requires further investigation for diagnostic confirmation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old female from Rio de Janeiro presented with a 3-month history of mildly pruritic skin lesions on her face and left palm.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed the appearance of mildly pruritic lesions on her face and left palmar region 3 months prior to presentation, without any systemic or constitutional symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Reported unprotected sexual intercourse within the preceding 3 months.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mildly pruritic facial and left palmar lesions and oral tongue plaques; negative for systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed two well-defined, rounded, non-scaly brownish annular plaques with slightly elevated erythematous borders ('elegant syphilides') on the face—one superior to the right oral commissure and one lateral to the right nasal ala. Intraoral examination showed multiple whitish confluent mucous plaques on the ventral tongue. Examination of the left palm showed two circular erythematous macules surrounded by peripheral whitish scaly collarettes (Biett collarettes).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis presenting with facial elegant syphilides, lingual mucous patches, and palmar syphilitic roseola with Biett collarettes, verified by reactive quantitative serum VDRL (titer 1:32) and positive FTA-ABS rapid treponemal test. Treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G 2,400,000 IU along with partner treatment, resulting in complete resolution of the mucocutaneous lesions.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old male was referred to our clinic with a 3-month history of an ulcerated, nodular-like lesion in the middle of his lower lip. The lesion, approximately 3 cm in diameter, exhibited a rounded shape and a surface covered by a layer of hemorrhagic and purulent fibrin (Figure 1A). Despite its resemblance to a malignant neoplasm, the lesion seemed to arise from conjunctive tissue and caused moderate pain. Palpation revealed no induration of the surrounding tissue, and the nodular area exhibited slight fibrous characteristics. Cervical palpation indicated numerous small lymph nodes in the submental and submandibular chains.
Upon further inquiry, the patient disclosed additional clinical manifestations, reporting lesions on his back skin surface. Examination revealed extensive erythematous papules and plaque lesions covering almost the entire back (Figure 2A). The patient denied any genital lesions. Notably, he was a smoker, a moderate alcohol consumer, and regularly used illicit drugs, including crack. He had no other reported medical conditions and was not using systemic or topical medications.
These comprehensive clinical findings raised suspicions of syphilis, particularly owing to the multiple lymphadenopathies and skin lesions, despite the patient's denial of engaging in sexual behaviors that increased the risk of sexually transmitted diseases. Syphilis serology results confirmed the diagnosis (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory: 1/32; specific antibody anti-Treponema pallidum: 20.29), whereas HIV and hepatitis C tests returned negative results. Subsequently, the patient was referred to a sexually transmitted disease center for treatment and contact tracing. The prescribed treatment involved two doses of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units each), administered two weeks apart. Substantial improvement in the lesions was observed three weeks after the last injection (Figures 1B and 2B), with follow-up scheduled every three months to monitor the decline in titer.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of a moderately painful, ulcerated nodular lesion on the midline of his lower lip and a widespread rash over his back.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred for evaluation of a 3-cm ulcerated nodular lesion on his lower lip that had persisted for 3 months, accompanied by extensive erythematous papules and plaques across his back.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic medical conditions. Social history was notable for cigarette smoking, moderate alcohol consumption, and regular illicit drug use including crack cocaine; he denied high-risk sexual behaviors.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for a painful lower-lip ulcerated nodule and asymptomatic erythematous plaques on his back; denied genital lesions. Taking no systemic or topical medications.

objective.physical_examination: Oral examination revealed an approximately 3-cm rounded, ulcerated, nodular-like lesion in the midline of the lower lip covered by hemorrhagic and purulent fibrin, with slightly fibrous consistency and no surrounding induration. Cervical palpation demonstrated multiple small palpable lymph nodes in the submental and submandibular chains. Cutaneous examination showed extensive erythematous papules and plaques covering nearly the entire back, with no genital lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Serological testing for HIV and hepatitis C virus was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis presenting with an oral lower-lip chancre/mucocutaneous lesion and disseminated dorsal papulosquamous syphilides, verified by a reactive serum VDRL (titer 1:32) and positive anti-Treponema pallidum specific antibody (20.29). Treated at an STD center with two intramuscular injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units administered 2 weeks apart, resulting in marked regression of both the lip and back lesions 3 weeks after the second injection.

raw_case_text:
Informed consent was obtained from the patient. The case presentation involves a 38-year-old bisexual male with a medical history of splenomegaly secondary to viral hepatitis. He presented to the infectious diseases department with non-itchy maculopapular skin lesions and fever. He is a non-smoker and occasionally consumes alcohol. Clinical examination revealed maculopapular lesions on the upper and lower limbs, trunk, back, and both feet soles. Purpuric lesions were also noted on the lower 1/3 of both legs, suggesting a diagnosis of KS. No neurological symptoms were recorded. The rapid HIV test was positive. Biological investigations showed WBCs = 5500/mL, lymphocytes = 1200/mL, Hb = 14.1, and platelets = 133.000/mL. Serological examinations for syphilis (VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) and ECLIA (ElectroChemiluminescence ImmunoAssay) positive), HIV, and CMV (Cytomegalovirus) (IgM and IgG positive) were positive, while they were negative for hepatitis B, C, and toxoplasmosis. The patient was immunized for hepatitis A (IgM and IgG positive). The diagnosis of HIV was confirmed by a positive serological examination with a viral load of 251.000/mL and a CD4 count of 182/mm3. Secondary syphilis was also confirmed by serological tests. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) was ruled out following negative results of the intradermal tuberculin test and the sputum smear test. Indeed, no specific lesions of TB were displayed by the chest X-ray. The patient was treated with Extencilline  2.4 MUI/week for 3 weeks and started on Atripla  (ART). Histological examination of a skin biopsy from the leg lesions showed a regular epidermis bordering the sample. The dermis exhibited tumoral proliferation of spindle cells without a defined fasciculate architecture and monomorphic nuclei. These tumor proliferations were dotted with vascular slit-like spaces lined directly by spindle cells. Mitoses were rare. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed the expression of anti-HHV-8 antibodies, confirming the diagnosis of KS (WHO clinical stage 4) (Figure 1 (a) and (b)). Abdominopelvic examination revealed hepato-hilar adenomegaly, common femoral and bilateral inguinal adenomegaly with minor centimetric axis. Chest X-ray and computed tomography scan displayed multiple bilateral solid nodules and micronodules at the lung bases (Figure 2).
Oral examination in the department of dental medicine revealed maculopapular lesions in the mouth involving the hard and soft palate mucosa (Figure 3(a)). White lesions were also observed on the cheek and tongue mucosa, suggesting HIV-related leukoplakia. In addition, a painful ulcer (1 cm in diameter) induced by cutting edges of the decayed left mandibular first molar was present. The patient also had several decayed and restored teeth, gingivitis, and spontaneous bleeding. An oral examination was completed with a panoramic radiography. Before undergoing chemotherapy, the cutting edges of the decayed first molar were softened and the third left mandibular molar was extracted. The ulcer completely resolved after 1 week. Unfortunately, the patient did not return for further dental treatments. Chemotherapy (Vinblastine  10 mg) for KS was administered once a week for 10 months (nine sessions) along with ART treatment for HIV. The outcome was favorable, with complete resolution of skin and oral mucosa lesions (Figure 3(b)). Eight months later, lung and abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed complete resolution of the lung solid nodules and micronodules, as well as regression of the size of adenopathies. The patient's viral load significantly decreased after ART treatment and reached an undetectable level (<38 copies/ml), along with an increase in the CD4 count, indicating good adherence to treatment. VDRL testing was negative after 1 year. After this favorable outcome, the patient was ready to complete dental treatments. He is still monitored by the infectious diseases department.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old bisexual male presented with fever and non-pruritic maculopapular and purpuric skin lesions on his trunk, extremities, soles, and oral mucosa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the infectious diseases department with fever and widespread non-itchy maculopapular lesions over his trunk, back, upper and lower limbs, and soles, alongside purpuric lesions on the lower third of both legs and oral mucosal lesions including a painful 1-cm traumatic ulcer on the left buccal/lingual mucosa.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bisexual male with a medical history of splenomegaly secondary to viral hepatitis. Non-smoker; occasional alcohol consumer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, disseminated non-pruritic rash, oral mucosal lesions, painful left oral ulcer, and gingival bleeding; negative for neurological symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed diffuse maculopapular lesions on the upper and lower limbs, trunk, back, and bilateral plantar soles, as well as violaceous/purpuric plaques on the lower third of both legs. Abdominopelvic and nodal examination noted hepato-hilar, common femoral, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Intraoral examination showed maculopapular lesions on the hard and soft palate mucosa, white leukoplakic lesions on the buccal and lingual mucosa, a painful 1-cm ulcer adjacent to the sharp edges of a decayed left mandibular first molar, multiple carious teeth, and gingivitis with spontaneous bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed WBC 5,500/uL, lymphocytes 1,200/uL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelets 133,000/uL. Rapid and confirmatory HIV serology was positive with an HIV-1 viral load of 251,000 copies/mL. Serologies were positive for CMV (IgM and IgG) and hepatitis A (IgM and IgG), and negative for HBV, HCV, and toxoplasmosis. Tuberculin skin test and sputum acid-fast bacilli smears were negative. Panoramic dental radiograph was obtained.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 182 cells/mm3. Chest X-ray and chest CT scan showed multiple bilateral solid nodules and micronodules at the lung bases without tuberculous cavitation. Skin biopsy of the lower leg lesion demonstrated dermal proliferation of monomorphic spindle cells forming vascular slit-like spaces with positive anti-HHV-8 immunohistochemistry, confirming AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma (WHO stage 4).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis co-existing with newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (CD4 182/mm3) and mucocutaneous/pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma (tuberculosis ruled out), established via positive serum VDRL and positive syphilis ECLIA alongside HHV-8-positive skin biopsy. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (Extencilline) 2.4 million IU weekly for 3 weeks, antiretroviral therapy (Atripla), dental smoothing/extraction of the decayed left mandibular molars, and 9 sessions of weekly intravenous vinblastine (10 mg) chemotherapy over 10 months. At 8-to-12-month follow-up, skin, oral, and pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma lesions completely resolved, HIV viral load became undetectable (<38 copies/mL), and repeat serum VDRL became negative at 1 year.

raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old male, diagnosed with human retroviral disease and initiated on antiretroviral treatment (ART) for 3 months, presented with passage of frank blood per rectum of 2 months and a cough with expectoration of 3 weeks. He had also developed multiple oral and genital ulcers over the past 2 weeks. His CD4 count was 134 cells/mm3 at admission.
On examination, he had a BMI of 17.2 kg/m2. Pulse oximetry saturation of 88% confirmed hypoxia. There was generalized lymphadenopathy, multiple snail track ulcers in the oral cavity, and a solitary painless penile ulcer. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. The patient had undergone a colonoscopy previously which detected an ulcero-proliferative lesion in the anal canal suspicious of malignancy. Laboratory investigations revealed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, and negligible viral load with an elevated D-Dimer. Microbiological examination of the sputum was negative for bacteria and acid-fast bacilli. Persistent hypoxia prompted us to do a computed tomography chest with pulmonary angiogram that showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism. However, it revealed bilateral parenchymal nodules (peri-lymphatic) with central and peri-broncho vascular ground glass opacities, bilateral mild pleural effusion, and interlobular septal with fissural thickening, suggestive of lymphangitis carcinomatosis [Figure 1]. This clinical presentation compelled us to initiate treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Nonetheless, he failed to respond to the treatment and hypoxia persisted. A Treponema pallidum Hemagglutination test was done as a part of workup for the penile ulcer, which turned positive. He was diagnosed to have secondary syphilis and was started on benzathine penicillin for the same. At this point, a differential diagnosis of primary anorectal malignancy with lymphangitis carcinomatosis vs. pulmonary syphilis was considered. Meanwhile, the patient continued to have bleeding per rectum and therefore underwent a repeat colonoscopy which confirmed the persistence of an ulcer-proliferative lesion and a biopsy was taken. The patient's clinical condition rapidly deteriorated with worsening hypoxia and he succumbed to massive hemoptysis on the third day of his illness. The biopsy report revealed a spindle cell proliferation in the lamina propria with the spindle cells showing mild atypia, suggesting KS [Figures 2 and 3]. This was further confirmed by a positive CD34 staining of the biopsy specimen which subsequently confirmed the diagnosis of KS [Figure 4].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 2-month history of frank hematochezia, a 3-week history of productive cough, and a 2-week history of multiple oral and genital ulcers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 2 months of bright red blood per rectum (previously evaluated by an outside colonoscopy showing an ulceroproliferative anal canal lesion suspicious for malignancy), followed by 3 weeks of cough with expectoration and 2 weeks of multiple oral and penile ulcers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection 3 months prior to admission and initiated on antiretroviral therapy (ART).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for hematochezia, productive cough, dyspnea/hypoxia, oral ulcers, and a painless penile ulcer. Home medications: antiretroviral therapy for 3 months.

objective.physical_examination: BMI was 17.2 kg/m2 and room-air pulse oximetry saturation was 88% (hypoxic). Physical examination revealed generalized lymphadenopathy, multiple oral mucosal 'snail-track' ulcers, and a solitary painless penile ulcer, with an otherwise unremarkable systemic examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory studies showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated D-dimer, and a negligible HIV viral load. Sputum Gram stain, bacterial culture, and acid-fast bacilli smears were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4 count was 134 cells/mm3. CT pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism but demonstrated bilateral perilymphatic parenchymal nodules, central and peribronchovascular ground-glass opacities, mild bilateral pleural effusions, and interlobular septal and fissural thickening resembling lymphangitis carcinomatosis. Repeat colonoscopy with biopsy of the persistent ulceroproliferative anal canal lesion revealed lamina propria proliferation of mildly atypical spindle cells positive for CD34 on immunohistochemistry, confirming Kaposi sarcoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis co-existing with advanced AIDS-associated anorectal and pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma (initially mimicking Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and lymphangitis carcinomatosis/pulmonary syphilis), established via positive serum TPHA alongside oral snail-track ulcers and penile chancre, and CD34-positive anorectal Kaposi sarcoma histopathology. Treated empirically for PJP and initiated on intramuscular benzathine penicillin for secondary syphilis, but his hypoxia rapidly worsened and he died of massive hemoptysis on hospital day 3.

raw_case_text:
The clinical case concerns a four-month-old infant, brought in by an infectious disease specialist for audiological evaluation, as she had not undergone Neonatal Hearing Screening. The baby was born by normal delivery at 39 weeks and two days, weighing 3.475 kg, with a head circumference of 34.5 cm, a length of 51.5 cm, an Apgar score of 9' in the first five minutes. He presented hyperbilirubinemia and underwent phototherapy for three days, VDRL with a titration of 1:32 and a cerebrospinal fluid test with 64 cells, considered altered, since the standard is up to 25 cells. Thus, the baby was diagnosed and treated for neurosyphilis. The mother reported that syphilis was diagnosed at the first prenatal visit, with a VDRL of 1:64; mother and partner were treated with Benzetacil for three weeks. After treatment, maternal VDRL dropped, with a level of 1:32, but remained the same at delivery. Therefore, the mother's and infant's ownership was the same at birth, and the infant had alterations in the cerebrospinal fluid test. No X-rays of the long bones and eye sockets were taken at birth. The eye and heart tests were normal. These data were collected by interviewing the mother before starting the audiological evaluations, and some information was recorded in the child's and pregnant woman's booklet. The infant's first pediatric follow-up appointment at the Pediatrics Unit was only at four months old, and she had a VDRL of 1:16, a test requested by the UBS nurse (SIC).
As for hearing tests, the following procedures were carried out at four months of age, prior to the fNIRS test.
Otoscopy with the Riester E-Scope 3.7V LED Otoscope, there was no accumulation of cerumen or foreign bodies that prevented the audiological procedures from being carried out;
Tympanometry with 1,000Hz probe: on the Interacoustic AT235 equipment, tympanometry was performed automatically by inserting a pressure variation in the external acoustic meatus and observing the presence of a positive peak at 15 daPA and 32 daPA, with a volume of 0.47 and 0.42 cc and compliance of 0.85 and 0.62 cc, respectively, in the right and left ears;
Transient Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (TEOAE): TEOAEs were collected using the IHS SmartTrOAE module with a 10D otoacoustic emissions (OAE) probe. A 75 micros non-linear click was used, at 80 dB SPL at a 21.1/sec rate and automatic gain control. 1,024 sweeps were presented, in an analysis window of 2.5 to 20 ms, recorded in two buffers. A/B for reproducibility check. A signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) >= 6 dB from 1.0 to 4.0 kHz was considered to be present in each frequency band. The result obtained in the infant was the presence of TEOAEs in both ears in the 1.5 to 4.0 Hz frequency bands, with absence in the 1.0 kHz band bilaterally;
Brainstem Auditory Evoked Potential (BAEP): was carried out on the IHS SmartEP module with insert headphones. The click was displayed at a speed of 27.7/sec. Two rarefied polarity measurements of 2,048 sweeps at 80 dBnHL were carried out, using a 30-3,000 Hz filter and a 24 ms analysis window at 80 dBnHL to observe the presence, latency and amplitude of waves I, III and V and interpeaks I-III, III-V and I-V.
Following the two promediations, the repeatability of the two recordings was visually examined. Throughout the two premeditations, the repeatability of the two recordings was visually examined. At 30 dBnHL, the V wave was observed bilaterally, with reproducibility from two sequential measurements which, when added together, can be seen on Figure 1. 
In addition to the audiological assessment, the infant's development was evaluated using the Bayley-III Scale, in the receptive and expressive language, cognition, large and fine motor sub-scales (Chart 1). During the application, the child was accompanied by the mother and remained calm and cooperative. Table 1 shows that the scaled score on the Bayley-III Scale was below expectations in the areas of expressive language and fine motor skills, while performance on the other subscales was within the average range, although performance on the cognitive and receptive language scales was closer to the below-average range.
It was carried out using the NIRStar application for collecting data on the NIRx Medical Tech (760 to 850 nm, 7.81Hz). Natural syllables /ba/ and /da/ recorded by a native Portuguese speaker were presented. The stimuli recordings were provided by Prof. Dr. Pedro de Lemos Menezes, from LATEC-UNCISAL. Each syllable lasted for 300 ms, with an initial rate of 48 kHz.The stimuli were organized and presented using Psychopy, an open-source software written in Python for research in neuroscience.The /ba/ and /da/ audios were edited in the Audacity program (Audacity  Cross-Platform Sound Editor), a open-source tool for digital audio editing, in order to adjust the sampling rate to 44.1 kHz and adapt it to Psychopy's sampling rate.This software enables synchronization between the present stimuli and the concurrent acquisition of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data, thereby facilitating precise temporal alignment between the two modalities.Figure 2 shows the experimental stimuli design, in which 10 blocks were run for 53 minutes.
THus, for the current moment, the baby was laid on her mother's lap, in natural sleep. The fNIRS cap was put on, consisting of 16 optodes (8 sources and 8 detectors) forming 20 channels (10 per hemisphere) separated by 3 cm (Figure 3A). All were positioned in the temporal lobe (Figure 3B), with the region of interest (ROI) being anterior, middle and posterior. Before starting the stimuli presentation, EAR-Tone ER 3C insert earphones (10 ohms) were plugged into each external acoustic meatus (Figure 3A).
It was only possible to execute the procedure in full at 40 dBHL, as the patient was uncomfortable at all the above intensities.At this intensity of 40 dBHL, the entire 10-block recording was processed.
The MNE and MNE-NIRS toolboxes for data analysis and visualization were use for data processing, using Spyder IDE, an environment for Python programming in a scientific context..
The methodological procedure for analysis followed an orderly sequence of steps. Thus, the libraries were installed to ensure the process functionality. Next, a dataframe was created for data storage, followed by the import of the raw fNIRS data. A pre-analysis and filtering phase was carried out, starting with verifying the optode position using graphical representations, as well as identifying and renaming the triggers related to the stimuli. The stimuli duration was defined for subsequent analysis using the Generalized Linear Model (GLM), and the raw signal was converted into optical density. The data quality was then assessed by quantifying the coupling quality between the optodes and the scalp per channel (SCI - Scalp coupling index). Channels with good quality were quantified with SCI greater than 0.521. Temporal Derivative Distribution Repair (TDDR) was used to correct artifacts (baseline shift and spikes). The optical density conversion to hemoglobin concentrations was carried out by implementing the modified Beer-Lambert law. Subsequently, filters were applied: from 0.05 to 0.5 Hz, with a high bandwidth of 0.2 and a low bandwidth of 0.02 to restrict the frequency range. The event of interest was extracted and rejection criteria were applied to remove low-quality epochs, after checking which epochs were excluded for each stimulus. Scatter plots were generated to check the coherence of the answers between the types of stimuli and the concentrations of HbO and HbR.
The subsequent stage involved implementing the Generalized Linear Model (GLM) to measure the hemodynamic response. The matrix design was created by modeling expected hemodynamic responses based on the Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) model. Response regions of interest (ROI's) were defined (anterior, middle and posterior), and GLM analyses were fitted for all channels (1 to 20) and ROI's. After this procedure, the metric results per channel, ROI's and condition were exported to a .xlsx file for statistical analysis. As this study consists of a clinical case, it was possible to describe in Tables 2 and 3 the theta value (estimated coefficient of the GLM model) of HbO for the conditions (/ba/ and /da/), the regions of interest (ROI) and the channels recorded.
Table 2 shows that the theta value for both the /ba/ and /da/ stimuli was higher in the anterior ROI of the left hemisphere (HE) and in the anterior and medial ROI of the right hemisphere (HD). In relation to the (CH) channels, higher theta values can be seen in CH2, CH3, CH4 (anterior region of the HE) and CH13, CH12 and CH14 (anterior region of the HD) (Figure 3B, Table 3) of both stimuli. In both ROI and channel analysis, there was no difference in the HbO theta value of the clinical case presented as a function of the stimuli used (Figure 4A-F).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-month-old female infant treated neonatally for congenital neurosyphilis was referred for comprehensive audiological and neurodevelopmental evaluation after missing newborn hearing screening.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born at 39 weeks and 2 days via vaginal delivery (birth weight 3.475 kg, length 51.5 cm, head circumference 34.5 cm, 5-minute Apgar 9), the infant had neonatal hyperbilirubinemia treated with 3 days of phototherapy, a birth serum VDRL titer of 1:32, and CSF pleocytosis (64 cells/mm3), for which she was diagnosed and treated in the neonatal period for congenital neurosyphilis. She had her first outpatient pediatric follow-up at 4 months of age (with a repeat VDRL of 1:16) and was referred for audiological, developmental, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) assessment.
subjective.past_medical_history: Maternal syphilis was diagnosed at the first prenatal visit (maternal VDRL 1:64); both mother and partner were treated with benzathine penicillin (Benzetacil) for 3 weeks, with maternal VDRL declining to 1:32 and remaining 1:32 at delivery. Neonatal ocular and cardiac screens were normal (long-bone X-rays were not performed at birth).
subjective.review_of_systems: Calm and cooperative infant; no acute systemic or otologic discharge symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Otoscopy at 4 months of age showed patent bilateral external auditory canals without cerumen impaction or foreign bodies. Bayley-III developmental assessment demonstrated below-average scaled scores in expressive language and fine motor skills, with cognitive, receptive language, and gross motor scores within the average range.
objective.routine_investigations: Neonatal serum VDRL at birth was 1:32 (matching maternal VDRL 1:32), declining to 1:16 at 4 months of age.
objective.advanced_workup: Neonatal CSF analysis showed pleocytosis of 64 cells/mm3 (reference <=25 cells/mm3). Audiological workup at 4 months: 1,000-Hz tympanometry showed normal bilateral middle ear function (peaks at 15 and 32 daPa, compliance 0.85 and 0.62 cc); Transient Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (TEOAEs) were present bilaterally from 1.5 to 4.0 kHz but absent bilaterally at 1.0 kHz; Brainstem Auditory Evoked Potentials (BAEP) showed normal wave I, III, and V latencies/interpeaks at 80 dBnHL and reproducible bilateral wave V thresholds down to 30 dBnHL. Cortical fNIRS recording at 40 dBHL using /ba/ and /da/ speech syllables showed preserved bilateral temporal cortical hemodynamic activation (strongest HbO theta values in left anterior CH2-4 and right anterior/medial CH12-14 regions of interest).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed neonatally treated congenital neurosyphilis (birth VDRL 1:32 and CSF 64 cells/mm3; 4-month follow-up VDRL 1:16) with intact peripheral auditory brainstem thresholds (BAEP wave V at 30 dBnHL) and preserved bilateral temporal cortical speech processing on fNIRS, alongside mild early expressive language and fine motor developmental delay on Bayley-III requiring continued pediatric and audiological surveillance.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male presented with asymptomatic, grayish-white, moist, oozy papules over the umbilicus for 1 month [Figure 1a]. Further, cutaneous examination revealed multiple similar moist, erythematous to grayish-white papules and plaques over the left axilla, perianal region [Figure 1b], and scrotum. Bilateral palms and soles showed hyperpigmented plaques with peripheral collarette of scales. The patient gave a positive history of unprotected sexual contact with multiple partners. The exposure was both penetrative as well as receptive involving heterosexuals and homosexuals with the last contact being 1 month back.
Based on the history and clinical findings, a diagnosis of secondary syphilis was made. Rapid plasma reagin test - 1:64 titer and T. pallidum hemagglutination assay - 1.564 tests were performed and were found to be highly positive. While the moist lesions were suggestive of condyloma lata, the extensive lesions as well as the involvement of rare sites such as the umbilicus and axilla were suspicious, and an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was done which was also found to be positive.
The patient was treated with a deep intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin 2.4 million IU (1.2 million IU in each gluteal region) after the test dose. A few hours after the injection, the patient developed a temperature of 106 F with joint pain, suggestive of a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction which responded well to a paracetamol infusion. There was marked improvement of lesions 2 weeks postinjection [Figure 1c and d]. The patient was referred to the antiretroviral (ART) center for further management.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of asymptomatic grayish-white moist papules and plaques over his umbilicus, left axilla, scrotum, and perianal region, alongside scaly palmoplantar plaques.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed asymptomatic, moist, oozy grayish-white papules in his umbilicus 1 month prior to presentation, accompanied by similar plaques in the left axilla, scrotum, and perianal area and scaly lesions on his palms and soles.
subjective.past_medical_history: Reported unprotected penetrative and receptive heterosexual and homosexual intercourse with multiple partners, with the most recent sexual contact 1 month prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for asymptomatic umbilical, axillary, scrotal, perianal, and palmoplantar skin lesions.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple moist, erythematous to grayish-white oozy papules and plaques (condylomata lata) involving the umbilicus, left axilla, perianal region, and scrotum, as well as hyperpigmented plaques with peripheral collarettes of scale (Biett collarettes) on the bilateral palms and soles.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum HIV ELISA screening test was positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis with multifocal intertriginous condylomata lata (umbilical, axillary, perianal, and scrotal) and newly diagnosed HIV co-infection, established via a reactive serum RPR (titer 1:64) and positive TPHA (1.564). Treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million IU (1.2 million IU in each buttock). Several hours post-injection, he developed a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever of 106 F and arthralgia) that resolved with intravenous paracetamol; skin lesions showed marked regression at 2-week follow-up and he was referred to the ART center.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old man with systemic arterial hypertension and a history of cigarette smoking from ages 15 to 19 years (approximately one pack per day, ~4 pack-years) was under outpatient follow-up for low-risk prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 6, ISUP 1). During routine preoperative assessment for urological surgery, he reported mild exertional dyspnea consistent with New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional Class II, prompting further cardiovascular evaluation.
A comprehensive social and infectious risk assessment revealed no history of high-risk sexual practices, illicit drug use, or prior sexually transmitted infections. He reported a monogamous relationship for more than two decades and no family history of syphilis or congenital infection. These details guided interpretation of the serologic findings, supporting late latent or tertiary syphilis rather than recent exposure.
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) angiography demonstrated a giant aneurysm primarily involving the aortic arch, measuring 114 x 94 x 93 mm, with a longitudinal extension of 79 mm. Additional dilatations were observed in the midascending aorta (49 x 48 mm), distal aortic arch (31 x 28 mm), and proximal descending thoracic aorta (26 x 25 mm) (Figures 1 and 2). The aneurysm morphology and maximal diameter indicated a high risk of rupture, leading to urgent referral for surgical management.
Serologic evaluation confirmed active syphilitic infection, with VDRL 1:32, TPHA positive, and negative HIV screening. The hepatitis panel revealed HBsAg negative, anti-HBc IgM negative, protective anti-HBs titers, and anti-HCV negative, excluding viral hepatitis-related vasculopathy. The patient completed a full course of benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million units intramuscularly once weekly for three consecutive weeks, consistent with the CDC and WHO recommendations for late latent/tertiary syphilis.
The procedure was performed via median sternotomy. The ascending aorta and entire aortic arch were replaced using a 28 mm x 30 cm Dacron graft (Figure 3). Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) was instituted at a core temperature of 20 C, with a total circulatory arrest time of 35 min. Selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) was delivered via cannulation of the brachiocephalic trunk throughout the arrest period. The supraaortic trunks were reimplanted en bloc into the graft using the island technique. Cardiopulmonary bypass time was 2 h and 23 min, and aortic crossclamp time was 1 h and 55 min.
The postoperative course was complicated by a left pleural effusion requiring therapeutic thoracentesis and by transient delirium with upper limb myoclonus. Neurological evaluation and imaging revealed no structural abnormalities, and symptoms resolved fully with supportive care.
Histopathologic examination demonstrated advanced atherosclerotic changes with dystrophic calcification, along with inflammatory infiltrates affecting the vasa vasorum, consistent with syphilitic aortitis. This mixed pattern suggests coexistence of chronic infectious aortitis with degenerative aortic disease.
At two-month follow-up, the patient exhibited complete clinical recovery, with improvement in anemia, resolution of chest discomfort, and full restoration of functional capacity. VDRL titers decreased from 1:32 to 1:8, indicating appropriate serologic response. Continued outpatient surveillance with periodic imaging was planned.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old man presented during routine preoperative urological evaluation with mild exertional dyspnea (NYHA functional Class II).
