raw_case_text:
Patient 2 was a 15-year-old Peruvian boy seen in September 2001 with a 1-year history of headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive deterioration in visual function. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan performed in April 2001 showed several large, irregular enhancing mass lesions involving the left occipital and parietal lobes (Figure 2). He had come to the United States in September for further evaluation. On neurologic examination, the patient had a right homonymous hemianopsia, optic nerve atrophy, and major visual impairment (left eye:20/100; right eye:20/200). Repeat MRI showed several irregular areas of enhancement in the left parietooccipital area associated with marked brain edema, left-to-right shift, and mass effect (Figure 2).
The patient was taken to surgery, where a firm avascular mass was found beneath a 0.5-cm layer of softer gliotic cortical tissue. Frozen sections showed lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with granuloma formation. Specimens for cultures and histopathologic examination were obtained. Bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Final histopathologic examination showed numerous granulomas with multinucleated giant cells but no organisms (Figure 1).
Serologic test results for Brucella, T. gondii, and Taenia soleum were negative. On postoperative day 8, mycobacteria cultures (BacT/ALERT MP; Organon Teknika Corp., Durham, NC) showed growth of a gram-negative coccobaccillus, later confirmed as Brucella spp. Treatment with rifampin, doxycycline, and intravenous gentamicin was begun. After 1 week, the gentamicin was discontinued per current recommendations, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was started. Follow-up imaging 7 months later demonstrated resolution of the enhancing areas and edema, with residual areas of brain atrophy (Figure 2). The patient's vision improved, but some visual acuity deficits persisted. Anti-brucella therapy continued for 1 year.
The patient lived in a small town 7 hours from Lima and had not traveled outside of the country before coming to the United States. His diet included regular consumption of queso fresco and occasional ceviche but no other raw meats. He reported no direct contact with marine mammals and seldom visited the Peruvian coast.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old Peruvian boy presented with a 1-year history of headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive visual loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 15-year-old boy from rural Peru developed chronic headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive visual deterioration over 1 year. An April 2001 brain MRI in Peru showed multiple large irregular enhancing masses in the left occipital and parietal lobes, prompting travel to the United States in September 2001 for neurosurgical evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Lived in a small town 7 hours from Lima, Peru; regularly consumed unpasteurized cheese (queso fresco) and occasional ceviche, with no marine mammal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic headache, nausea, vomiting, and severe visual loss.

objective.physical_examination: Right homonymous hemianopsia, bilateral optic nerve atrophy, and marked visual acuity impairment (left eye 20/100, right eye 20/200).
objective.routine_investigations: Serologic tests for Brucella, Toxoplasma gondii, and Taenia solium were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat brain MRI in September 2001 demonstrated multiple large irregular contrast-enhancing mass lesions in the left parieto-occipital lobe with severe perilesional vasogenic edema, mass effect, and left-to-right midline shift. Craniotomy revealed a firm avascular subcortical mass beneath 0.5 cm of gliotic cortex; histopathology showed numerous non-caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and negative bacterial, fungal, and AFB stains.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Despite negative serum Brucella serology, mycobacterial liquid culture (BacT/ALERT MP) of the resected brain mass grew Gram-negative coccobacilli on postoperative day 8 confirmed as Brucella spp., establishing a diagnosis of left parieto-occipital cerebral brucelloma. Treated with surgical resection followed by oral rifampin, oral doxycycline, and 1 week of IV gentamicin transitioned to oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a total of 1 year. Follow-up brain MRI at 7 months showed complete resolution of enhancing masses and edema with residual focal encephalomalacia/atrophy and partial improvement in visual acuity.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old Sistani (a certain ethnicity resided in Sistan Province of Iran) shepherd admitted to the infectious disease ward due to 2 weeks intermittent low-grade fever (38oC), severe pain in left sternoclavicular joint (SCJ), progressive dyspnea, and gradual loss of consciousness. A fluctuant, soft and tender abscess (4 x 4 cm2) was found in his right SCJ area.
A thick wall hypoechoic mass was reported in ultrasonography. Bone appearance was normal in his chest X-ray (CXR) and computed topography scan (CTS). Brucella seroagglutination tests, Wright, and 2ME were requested with regards to his occupational state.
Partial sternotomy and necrotic debridement were done by a thorax surgeon and repaired by the surrounding muscles and soft tissues. Significant laboratory data were as followings: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) = 65 mm/first hour, white blood cells (WBC) = 6800 (63% poly morpho nuclear), Wright = 1/2560, 2ME = 1/1280 and hemoglobin (Hb) = 9.2 g/dL.
Castaneda media culture of purulent material yielded to brucella melitensis infection. Smear and culture were negative for mycobacteria.
Cap. Doxycycline (100 mg/BID/Po), and Amp. Streptomycin (1 g/day, IM) were prescribed for 2 weeks and continued with Doxycycline (100 mg/BID) and Tab. Rifampin (600 mg/day) for 6 weeks. Complete recovery with no complication was reported after 6-month follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male shepherd from Iran presented with a 2-week history of intermittent low-grade fever (38 C), severe left sternoclavicular joint pain, progressive dyspnea, and gradual obtundation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 23-year-old Sistani shepherd was admitted with 2 weeks of intermittent low-grade fever (38 C), severe sternoclavicular pain, progressive shortness of breath, and declining consciousness, accompanied by an anterior chest wall abscess.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupational history as a shepherd in Sistan Province, Iran.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever, severe sternoclavicular pain, chest wall swelling, progressive dyspnea, and altered mental status.

objective.physical_examination: Fever (38 C), progressive dyspnea, depressed level of consciousness, and a 4 x 4 cm fluctuant, soft, tender abscess over the sternoclavicular joint region.
objective.routine_investigations: ESR 65 mm/1st hour, WBC 6,800/mm3 (63% polymorphonuclear cells), hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL. Ultrasonography showed a thick-walled hypoechoic sternoclavicular mass; chest X-ray showed normal osseous appearance.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT showed normal bone appearance. Intraoperative partial sternotomy and necrotic tissue debridement with muscle/soft-tissue flap reconstruction; mycobacterial smear and culture of purulent material were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum Wright agglutination titer was 1:2,560, 2-mercaptoethanol (2ME) titer was 1:1,280, and Castaneda medium culture of evacuated sternoclavicular pus isolated Brucella melitensis, confirming sternoclavicular joint brucellosis with abscess formation. Managed with surgical partial sternotomy and debridement followed by oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) plus intramuscular streptomycin (1 g/day) for 2 weeks, and then oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) plus oral rifampin (600 mg/day) for 6 weeks, achieving complete recovery without complications at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: In early November 2001, a 57-year-old female laboratory worker (laboratory worker 1) began experiencing nonspecific symptoms of malaise, vomiting, headache, lower leg cramping, anorexia, and fever. One week after onset of symptoms, she was evaluated for severe headaches at a local emergency room, where cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood cultures were collected. The CSF culture was negative. From the blood culture, small, gram-positive bacilli were isolated and characterized as coryneform bacilli, which are usually interpreted as contaminants of unknown clinical importance. Despite multiple hospital admissions, the laboratory worker continued to have symptoms, but her condition remained undiagnosed. Approximately 5 weeks after symptom onset, colleagues from the hospital microbiology laboratory where she was employed (laboratory 1) drew her blood for culture again. After 5 days of incubation, gram-variable coccobacilli, later identified as Brucella spp., were isolated. Subculturing and biochemical tests were conducted in a class II biosafety cabinet. The Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) was reactive (1:640) at the NYSDOH laboratory, Wadsworth Center. Laboratory worker 1 was initially treated with doxycycline and gentamicin, followed by doxycycline and rifampin, for 6 weeks of outpatient therapy. The isolate was later identified as B. melitensis by the Wadsworth Center and confirmed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The patient has not relapsed 18 months after completing treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old female microbiology laboratory worker presented in early November 2001 with a 5-week history of persistent fever, severe headache, malaise, vomiting, anorexia, and lower leg cramping.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In early November 2001, a 57-year-old female clinical microbiology technician (laboratory worker 1) developed malaise, vomiting, severe headache, lower leg cramps, anorexia, and fever. One week after symptom onset, an emergency department LP was negative and a blood culture grew tiny bacilli misidentified as coryneform contaminants. Despite multiple hospitalizations over 5 weeks, her febrile illness persisted until laboratory colleagues repeated her blood cultures.
subjective.past_medical_history: Clinical microbiology laboratory technician who routinely subcultured blood culture bottles and performed catalase tests on an open bench without a biosafety cabinet (later linked to processing a blood culture from a 76-year-old Peruvian-born patient in September 2001). Denied foreign travel, unpasteurized dairy intake, or animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe headache, malaise, vomiting, anorexia, and lower leg cramping.

objective.routine_investigations: Initial emergency department blood culture at week 1 grew small bacilli misclassified as coryneform bacilli.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency department lumbar puncture CSF culture was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Repeat blood cultures drawn 5 weeks after symptom onset grew Gram-variable coccobacilli after 5 days of incubation, identified as Brucella melitensis by the NYSDOH Wadsworth Center and CDC, with a reactive Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) titer of 1:640, confirming laboratory-acquired Brucella melitensis bacteremia. Treated with initial doxycycline and gentamicin followed by a 6-week outpatient course of oral doxycycline and rifampin, with no relapse at 18 months post-treatment.

raw_case_text: The likely source of laboratory worker 1's infection was found after reassessing Gram stains performed in laboratory 1 in August, September, and October 2001. A 76-year-old woman visited the emergency room served by laboratory 1 in early September 2001. The patient had had fever (temperature 38.3oC) for 1 day and headache for 3 weeks. She received one dose of ciprofloxacin for a possible urinary tract infection and was discharged. After 4 days of incubation, a Gram stain of this patient's blood culture specimen showed tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, reported as coryneform bacilli. As part of the investigation for the source of infection for laboratory worker 1, this patient's prepared Gram stain slide was referred to the Wadsworth Center, where small, gram-variable cocci were identified. More than 1 year after being seen in the emergency room, this patient was offered Brucella SAT and a repeat blood culture. She refused Brucella SAT, and her physician did not identify symptoms consistent with brucellosis. Six months after this identification, further experimental analysis by the Wadsworth Center with polymerase chain reaction tests performed on Gram stain material detected B. melitensis DNA (Wadsworth Center, NYSDOH, unpub. data). The patient was again contacted, and Brucella SAT (>1.5 years after her initial blood culture) showed a titer of 1:80 (indeterminate). Repeat blood cultures were negative. Upon interview, the patient denied any visits outside the United States since 1989, when she emigrated from Peru. She also denied consuming any unpasteurized products from the United States or abroad. An additional interview was scheduled, but the patient died unexpectedly.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old Peruvian-born woman presented to the emergency department in early September 2001 with a 3-week history of headache and a 1-day history of fever (38.3 C).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 76-year-old woman presented to an emergency room in early September 2001 with a 1-day fever of 38.3 C and a 3-week history of headache. She was given a single dose of ciprofloxacin for a presumed urinary tract infection and discharged.
subjective.past_medical_history: Emigrated to the United States from Peru in 1989; denied travel outside the United States since 1989 or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-day fever and 3-week headache.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.3 C at the September 2001 emergency room visit.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood culture drawn in September 2001 grew tiny Gram-negative/Gram-variable coccobacilli after 4 days of incubation that were originally misreported as coryneform bacilli; repeat blood cultures >1.5 years later were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Experimental PCR performed by the NYSDOH Wadsworth Center on the archived September 2001 blood culture Gram stain slide detected Brucella melitensis DNA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: PCR amplification of Brucella melitensis DNA from the archived September 2001 blood culture Gram stain slide and a follow-up Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) titer of 1:80 (>1.5 years later) identified this patient as the index source case for the laboratory-acquired Brucella melitensis outbreak in laboratory workers 1 and 2. She had received a single dose of ciprofloxacin at her initial ER visit and later died unexpectedly before further follow-up.

raw_case_text:
We present here the case of a 46-old man, a stockbreeder from the Central Bosnia Canton who was treated for PV endocarditis due to Brucella during 2007. In 1998, he underwent an aortic and mitral mechanical valve replacement surgery due to juvenile rheumatic fever. He was doing well, being work-engaged until 2006, when he started to complain about night sweating, chills, exhaustion, dyspnea, palpitations and chest oppression. At that time he did not measure his body temperature. After more than one year of over repeated hospitalizations at the Department of Internal Medicine of Regional Hospital due to "symptoms of heart failure", he was referred to the Clinic for Infectious Diseases, Clinical Center of Sarajevo University. Upon confirmation of the disease, based on positive blood cultures (B.melitensis) taken during everyday subfebrile temperatures, formerly unrecognized, and on transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) indicative of endocarditis, the patient was transferred to Clinic for Infectious Diseases in Sarajevo.
Upon admission, he had cardiac and extra-cardiac manifestations of endocarditis (systolic-diastolic murmur with absolute arrhythmia, splinter haemorrhages, and laboratory criteria for glomerulonephritis) and symptoms of severe heart failure (class III/IV) according to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) criteria. Standard chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound revealed cardiomegaly, hepatosplenomegaly and stasis in the lungs and liver. Coxiella burnetii coinfection was confirmed by ELISA (enzyme linked immunosorbent assey) test (IgG F2+, IgG F1+, IgA F1+).
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) confirmed the presence of restenosis, multiple mobile vegetations (5-8 mm) attached to mitral and aortic valve (MV, AV) and signs of severe pulmonary hypertension. He did not respond to quadruple antimicrobial and cardiac therapy. A follow-up TEE performed at the end of the third therapeutic week confirmed progression of the disease: "...persistent multiple mobile vegetations at both valves 7-10 mm, left atrial thrombus 7x10 mm...".

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male stockbreeder with mechanical aortic and mitral valves presented with a >1-year history of night sweats, chills, exhaustion, dyspnea, palpitations, chest oppression, and daily subfebrile temperatures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 46-year-old male stockbreeder from Bosnia who had undergone mechanical aortic and mitral valve replacements in 1998 developed night sweats, chills, severe fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, chest oppression, and unrecognized daily low-grade fevers starting in 2006. He was hospitalized repeatedly over more than a year at a regional hospital for presumed heart failure before positive blood cultures and TTE prompted transfer to the Sarajevo University Clinic for Infectious Diseases.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mechanical aortic and mitral valve replacement in 1998 for juvenile rheumatic heart disease; occupational exposure as a livestock breeder.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for night sweats, chills, exhaustion, dyspnea, palpitations, chest oppression, and daily subfebrile temperatures.

objective.physical_examination: Subfebrile temperatures, NYHA class III/IV severe congestive heart failure, systolic-diastolic cardiac murmurs with absolute arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation), and peripheral splinter hemorrhages.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evidence of immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, hepatosplenomegaly, and hepatic congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) was indicative of prosthetic valve endocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed prosthetic valve restenosis, multiple mobile vegetations (5-8 mm) attached to both the mechanical mitral and aortic valves, and severe pulmonary hypertension; repeat TEE after 3 weeks of therapy showed disease progression with 7-10 mm vegetations on both valves and a 7 x 10 mm left atrial thrombus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serial blood cultures isolated Brucella melitensis and Coxiella burnetii ELISA was concurrently positive for phase I and phase II antibodies (IgG F2+, IgG F1+, IgA F1+), confirming dual-pathogen (Brucella melitensis and Coxiella burnetii) mechanical aortic and mitral prosthetic valve endocarditis complicated by NYHA class III/IV heart failure, glomerulonephritis, and left atrial thrombus. Quadruple antimicrobial therapy and medical heart failure management failed to halt vegetation growth on 3-week follow-up TEE.

raw_case_text:
Congenital brucellosis was diagnosed in patients 1 and 2, who were 3-month-old twins (Technical Appendix Table). They were prematurely delivered by cesarean section on July 6, 2012, at the Provincial Maternity and Child Care Center (Guangzhou, China). The boy (patient 1, Apgar score 9-10/1-10 min) had a birthweight of 2.3 kg, and the girl (patient 2, Apgar score 9-10/1-10 min) had a birthweight of 1.8 kg. They received standard care for preterm neonates at the hospital. They were discharged once their weight reached 2.5 kg; this happened for patient 1 at 3 weeks of age and for patient 2 at 4 weeks of age (July 29 and August 3, 2012, respectively).
On October 2, 2012, the boy was examined at the hospital for irregular fever up to 39 C. On October 9, he was readmitted to the hospital with a fever of 38 C and weight of 5.0 kg. Chest radiograph showed signs of increased bronchovascular shadows. Mezlocillin sodium and sulbactam sodium (4:1) and ribavirin were administered, but the patient did not improve. On the same day, the girl had a cough and low-level fever (37-37.5 C) but was not hospitalized. On October 16, B. melitensis was isolated from a blood culture from patient 1, in whom brucellosis with alveobronchiolitis, abnormal hepatic function, and moderate anemia were initially diagnosed when he was 3 months and 10 days of age.
On October 17, the twins were transferred to an infectious disease hospital, where they had extensive physical and laboratory examinations (Table 1). During 57 days of hospitalization, the boy received general and specific therapies for brucellosis. Brucellosis and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency were diagnosed in the girl, and she received appropriate treatment. At the time of discharge (December 12), the twins were well and without fever. They left the hospital for home care, which was supervised by a local general practitioner who provided rifampin and sulfamethoxazole for up to 6 weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-month-old preterm male twin (Patient 1) presented on October 2, 2012, with irregular fevers up to 39 C, while his twin sister (Patient 2) developed cough and low-grade fever (37.0-37.5 C) on October 9, 2012.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three-month-old twins delivered prematurely at 34+2 weeks' gestation by cesarean section on July 6, 2012, due to premature rupture of membranes and maternal phase I chorioamnionitis (discharged at 3 and 4 weeks of age once reaching 2.5 kg) developed febrile illness in early October 2012. The male twin (Patient 1) presented on October 2, 2012, with irregular fevers up to 39 C and was readmitted on October 9 (temperature 38 C, weight 5.0 kg), failing empiric mezlocillin-sulbactam and ribavirin; his twin sister (Patient 2) developed cough and low-grade fever (37-37.5 C) on October 9, and both were transferred to an infectious disease hospital on October 17, 2012.
subjective.past_medical_history: Preterm twins born at 34+2 weeks' gestation via cesarean section (birthweight 2.3 kg for boy, 1.8 kg for girl; Apgar 9-10) to a mother with chorioamnionitis and undiagnosed brucellosis; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency diagnosed in the female twin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Boy (Patient 1): Positive for irregular fever up to 39 C. Girl (Patient 2): Positive for cough and low-grade fever (37-37.5 C).

objective.physical_examination: Patient 1 on October 9 readmission: temperature 38.0 C, weight 5.0 kg. Patient 2: low-grade fever (37.0-37.5 C).
objective.routine_investigations: Patient 1: moderate anemia, abnormal liver function tests, and chest radiograph showing increased bronchovascular markings consistent with alveobronchiolitis. Patient 2: diagnosed with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
objective.advanced_workup: Quantitative PCR and abbreviated AMOS PCR of blood culture isolates identified Brucella melitensis biotype 3; 16-locus multilocus variable-number tandem repeat analysis (MLVA-16: 1-5-3-13-2-3-3-2-6-22-9-6-9-11-4-5) confirmed identical genotypes between both twins and their mother.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Blood cultures from both twins grew Brucella melitensis biotype 3, serum standard tube agglutination titers were 1:400 in both twins (declining to 1:200 on follow-up), and archived cord blood plasma was Rose Bengal positive, confirming congenital Brucella melitensis biotype 3 infection in preterm twins. Following a 57-day hospitalization with targeted anti-Brucella therapy, repeat blood cultures on November 18 and 29 were sterile, and the twins were discharged afebrile on December 12, 2012, to complete up to 6 weeks of outpatient oral rifampin and sulfamethoxazole.

raw_case_text: A 50-year-old male livestock farmer was admitted to Sparta General Hospital with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, night sweats, and shortness of breath. He had been diagnosed with blood culture proven Brucella infection 6 months ago and was treated with a double regimen of 21 days of streptomycin and two months of doxycycline. He had recovered completely and Brucella antibodies titers were negative after two months of treatment. On admission, he was febrile (38.7 C) and physical examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a 2/6 diastolic aortic murmur not reported in his previous medical history. According to CBC he was anemic (Ht 24%) and leukopenic (3.200/muL), ESR was 102 mm/h, and biochemistry revealed a serum creatinine value of 2.1 mg/dL while BUN levels were 92 mg/dL. Wright standard tube agglutination test was positive in a titer of 1 : 1600. Blood cultures were positive for Brucella spp. that was identified later as melitensis. In transthoracic echocardiogram, vegetations were present on a bicuspid aortic valve (Figure 1). A triple antibiotic regimen with 900 mg of rifampicin, 200 mg of doxycycline daily, and streptomycin adjusted for renal failure was initiated. Transesophageal echocardiogram was performed the next day and confirmed the presence of active vegetations but also revealed severe aortic regurgitation and rupture of the noncoronary leaflet. He was referred for cardiothoracic consultation and a valve replacement surgery was decided. During hospitalization, fever, malaise, and renal failure had gradually resolved, but he developed decompensated heart failure requiring loop diuretics and oxygen supplementation. On the 21st day of treatment, streptomycin has been replaced with cotrimoxazole and three days later valve replacement was performed. The patient recovered without any surgical complications, continued antibiotic treatment for 6 months, and is currently well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male livestock farmer with a history of brucellosis 6 months earlier presented with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, night sweats, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old male livestock farmer who had been treated 6 months earlier for blood-culture-positive brucellosis (with 21 days of streptomycin and 2 months of doxycycline, achieving negative titers) presented with 4 days of high fever, malaise, night sweats, and dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Livestock farmer; blood-culture-proven brucellosis 6 months prior (treated with 21 days of streptomycin and 2 months of doxycycline); previously unrecognized bicuspid aortic valve.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, night sweats, and dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.7 C; cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a new grade 2/6 diastolic aortic murmur; subsequently developed decompensated congestive heart failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Anemia (hematocrit 24%), leukopenia (WBC 3,200/uL), ESR 102 mm/h, serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, and BUN 92 mg/dL. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed vegetations on a bicuspid aortic valve.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed active vegetations on the bicuspid aortic valve complicated by rupture of the noncoronary leaflet and severe aortic regurgitation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum Wright standard tube agglutination titer was 1:1,600 and blood cultures isolated Brucella melitensis, confirming relapsed Brucella melitensis endocarditis of a bicuspid aortic valve with leaflet rupture and acute renal failure. Initiated on triple antibiotic therapy with oral rifampicin (900 mg/day), oral doxycycline (200 mg/day), and renally adjusted intramuscular streptomycin (switched on day 21 to cotrimoxazole), alongside loop diuretics and oxygen for heart failure, followed on hospital day 24 by surgical aortic valve replacement. The patient had an uneventful surgical recovery, completed 6 months of antimicrobial therapy, and remained clinically well.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old boy, medically free, with history of unpasteurized milk ingestion, living in Shaqra (a village 200 km far from Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia), presented to our emergency department with fever, vomiting, and malaise for 2 weeks followed by 5-day history of left hypochondrial pain. He lost 9 kgs in the preceding two months. He had no history of trauma or surgery. He was admitted to a peripheral hospital where he received a course of antibiotics with no improvement. On clinical examination, he looked ill, in pain with a temperature of 38.4 degree Celsius; pulse rate of 116 beats per minutes; blood pressure 111/68 mmHg; and respiratory rate of 21 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination revealed moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium, no organomegaly on palpation and normal bowel sounds.
 Laboratory investigation showed white blood cell count 4.12 x 109/L; hemoglobin 11.80 g/dL; platelet count 364 x 109/L; ESR 61 mm/H; CRP 66.5 mg/L; amylase 509 U/L; lipase 471 U/L; alanine transaminase 45 U/I; aspartate transaminase 32 U/I; alkaline phosphatase 162 U/I; gamma GT 86 U/I; total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL; albumin 39 g/L; creatinine 0.5 mg/dL; urea 3.2 mmol/L; and lactate dehydrogenase, 303 U/I. Chest X-ray was normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Abdominal X-ray showed no evidence of intestinal obstruction. Computed tomography of abdomen showed multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis and patent splenic veins with no thrombosis (Figure 1). Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation. Brucella serology using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was positive for IgM. Transesophageal echocardiography was negative. Lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin antibodies were negative. Proteins C and S were negative. JAK2 mutation was negative.
 Treatment of brucellosis with rifampicin 600 mg daily (for 6 weeks), doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (for 6 weeks), and gentamycin 300 mg daily (for 7 days) was given to him.
On the 8th day of admission, fever and abdominal pain resolved. High amylase and lipase were normalized and the patient was discharged home in good condition. After 3-month follow-up in outpatient clinic, the patient remained well with significant improvement of splenic infarcts on computed tomography (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old Saudi boy presented with a 2-week history of fever, vomiting, and malaise followed by 5 days of left hypochondrial abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A previously healthy 17-year-old boy from Shaqra, Saudi Arabia, developed fever, vomiting, and malaise 2 weeks prior to presentation along with a 9-kg weight loss over the preceding 2 months, followed 5 days before admission by acute left upper quadrant (hypochondrial) abdominal pain. A prior course of antibiotics at a peripheral hospital failed to improve his symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Medically free with no prior trauma or surgery; lived in rural Saudi Arabia (Shaqra) with a history of unpasteurized milk ingestion.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, vomiting, malaise, 5-day left upper quadrant abdominal pain, and 9-kg weight loss over 2 months.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing and in pain; temperature 38.4 C, pulse 116 beats/min, blood pressure 111/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min. Moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium without palpable hepatosplenomegaly and with normal bowel sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 4.12 x 10^9/L, Hb 11.80 g/dL, platelets 364 x 10^9/L, ESR 61 mm/h, CRP 66.5 mg/L. Markedly elevated pancreatic enzymes: serum amylase 509 U/L and lipase 471 U/L. ALT 45 U/L, AST 32 U/L, ALP 162 U/L, GGT 86 U/L, total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, albumin 39 g/L, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, urea 3.2 mmol/L, LDH 303 U/L. Normal chest and abdominal X-rays; ECG showed sinus tachycardia.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT demonstrated borderline splenomegaly and multiple irregular peripheral wedge-shaped hypodense splenic lesions diagnostic of splenic infarctions, with a normal pancreas and patent splenic vessels without thrombosis. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was negative for endocarditis. Thrombophilia workup (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, protein C, protein S, and JAK2 mutation) was completely negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation and serum anti-Brucella IgM ELISA was positive, confirming acute brucellosis complicated by multiple splenic infarctions and biochemical hyperamylasemia/hyperlipasemia. Treated with oral rifampicin (600 mg daily for 6 weeks), oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 6 weeks), and IV gentamicin (300 mg daily for 7 days). Fever, abdominal pain, and elevated amylase/lipase resolved by hospital day 8, and 3-month follow-up abdominal CT confirmed marked regression of the splenic infarcts.

raw_case_text: Twenty-six-year-old male patient referred from general hospital and admitted to our center with a history of Brucella aortic valve endocarditis, accompanied by hypotension and chest pain. Chest radiography showed moderately enlarged cardiac silhouette and mediastinum. Results of laboratory tests made on admission were as follow: White blood cell count, 19000/mm-3 with 91% neutrophils; platelet count, 89000/mm-3 ; hemoglobin, 8 g/dl; c-reactive protein, 54 mg/dl; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 80 mm/h; blood urea nitrogen (BUN), 40 mg/dL; creatine (Cr), 2.9 mg/dL; and urinalysis revealed no any hematuria and 24-hour urinalysis (U.A) revealed proteinuria). Antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA ), anti-double stranded DNA, rheumatic factor (RF), anticardiolopin antibody, lupus anticoagulant were all negative. Serum agglutination tests were positive (titer>1:1500), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay tests for anti-Brucella IgG and IgM antibodies were strongly positive (133 U/ml and 31.7 U/ml; 30 U/ml and 20 U/ml, respectively). In addition, Brucella melitensis was isolated from 2 of 3 consecutive blood cultures. No significant alterations were observed in the electrocardiogram. TEE revealed normal aortic diameter at the mid-ascending aorta, severe aortic regurgitation, aortic ring abscess in noncoronary sinus, large vegetation in noncoronary sinus leaflet with preserved ventricular function and moderate pericardial effusion (Figure 1A and  1B). Aortic wall fistula from ring abscess to pericardium temporary was blocked by intra fistula vegetation. Intraoperative finding revealed large vegetation and perifistula hematoma in aortic wall. The fistula tract starting from aortic ring (Figures 2 and 3) and extended to aortic wall as intramural tract in a distance of 15 mm above the ring and ending to external aortic wall as a crater of fistula (Figure 4). We think that initial bleeding from fistula tract to pericardium was blocked by vegetation that confirmed intra operatively. The patient then underwent conventional surgical treatment with extracorporeal circulation (ECC), and replacement of aortic valve with prosthetic valve (carbomedic, sorin group, 23 mm size) and resection of aortic wall containing fistula site and its replacement with fresh pericardial patch (Figure 5). Patient treated with ceftriaxone 2 g and gentamicin 3 mg/kg prior to culture report. Therapy with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with gentamicin 3 mg/kg intravenus in 2 divided doses with oral rifampin 600 mg once daily for 6 weeks was started after confirmation of Brucella endocarditis. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged in the 15th postoperative day.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male was referred with Brucella aortic valve endocarditis accompanied by acute chest pain and hypotension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old man diagnosed with Brucella aortic valve endocarditis at a general hospital was transferred to our cardiac center due to hemodynamic instability with hypotension and chest pain.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chest pain, fever, and hypotension.

objective.physical_examination: Hypotensive with chest pain.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 19,000/mm3 (91% neutrophils), platelets 89,000/mm3, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, CRP 54 mg/dL, ESR 80 mm/h, BUN 40 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.9 mg/dL; urinalysis showed no hematuria, while 24-hour urine collection showed proteinuria. Chest X-ray showed moderate cardiomegaly and widened mediastinum; ECG was unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, RF, anticardiolipin antibody, and lupus anticoagulant were all negative. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and intraoperative exploration revealed severe aortic regurgitation, a large vegetation on the noncoronary cusp, a noncoronary sinus aortic ring abscess, a moderate pericardial effusion, and a 15-mm intramural aorto-pericardial fistula tract extending from the aortic ring to the external ascending aortic wall (temporarily plugged by an intrafistula vegetation and perifistula hematoma) with preserved ventricular function.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum agglutination test was positive at >1:1,500, anti-Brucella ELISA IgG (133 U/mL; UNL 30) and IgM (31.7 U/mL; UNL 20) were strongly positive, and 2 of 3 blood cultures isolated Brucella melitensis, confirming Brucella melitensis aortic valve endocarditis complicated by an aortic ring abscess and aorto-pericardial fistula. Following initial empiric ceftriaxone (2 g) and gentamicin (3 mg/kg), the patient underwent surgical aortic valve replacement (23 mm Carbomedics mechanical prosthesis) and resection of the fistulous aortic wall with fresh autologous pericardial patch reconstruction under cardiopulmonary bypass, alongside a 6-week regimen of oral doxycycline (100 mg BID), IV gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses), and oral rifampin (600 mg QD), achieving an uneventful recovery and discharge on postoperative day 15.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old female presented to our hospital with chief complaints of progressive fatigue, fever, myalgia, and shortness of breath for last 3 weeks. There was no significant past illness. There was no history of significant weight loss, cough, orthopnea, pain abdomen. On physical examination, she was febrile, pale, and icteric. The spleen was palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. Her pulse rate was 102/minute with a blood pressure of 106/70 mmHg.
A complete blood count (CBC) revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin:5.8 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume (MCV):92 fl) with a platelet count of 148 x 103/microL and white blood cell count (WBC) of 3.37 x 103/microL. A peripheral blood smear showed few spherocytes, nucleated red blood cells. Biochemistry showed indirect hyperbilirubinemia with high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH:1540 IU/L). On further investigations, corrected reticulocyte count was 5.4%. A direct Coombs test was strongly positive (4+). Based on initial investigations, we made an initial diagnosis of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Viral markers (HIV, HBs Ag, anti-HCV) were negative. Serology for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and mycoplasma was also negative. Antinuclear antibodies were absent. Our patient remained febrile during hospitalisation, which was not explained by hemolytic anemia; on further evaluation, there was a recent history of consumption of unpasteurized milk. Since Brucella is one of the common zoonotic diseases in western India, we suspected brucellosis. The serology for brucellosis was positive in high titre (standard agglutination test:1:640). The diagnosis was confirmed with positive blood culture for Brucella melitensis. We made a final diagnosis of acute brucellosis with Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia. The patient was prescribed a combination of oral doxycycline (100 mg twice a day) with rifampicin (600 mg once a day). She was also prescribed corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day). 1 week after starting steroids, the patient showed significant clinical improvement with a hemoglobin count of 9 gm/dl and serum LDH of 988 IU/L. The patient was discharged, and steroid was gradually tapered with doxycycline, and rifampicin was advised for further 5 weeks. After 6 weeks, corticosteroid was tapered successfully. The patient was symptomatically better with a hemoglobin count of 13 gm/dl (Figure 1). She was doing well with complete remission of hemolytic anemia at 3-month follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old female from western India presented with a 3-week history of progressive fatigue, fever, myalgia, and exertional shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 18-year-old previously healthy female presented with 3 weeks of progressive fatigue, persistent fever, myalgia, and dyspnea accompanied by pallor and jaundice.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history; recent history of consuming unpasteurized milk in western India.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive fatigue, fever, myalgia, dyspnea, pallor, and jaundice; negative for weight loss, cough, orthopnea, or abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, pale, and icteric; pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 106/70 mmHg; splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Severe normocytic anemia (Hb 5.8 g/dL, MCV 92 fL), leukopenia (WBC 3.37 x 10^3/uL), platelets 148 x 10^3/uL, corrected reticulocyte count 5.4%; peripheral blood smear showed spherocytes and nucleated RBCs. Indirect hyperbilirubinemia and markedly elevated LDH (1,540 IU/L). Strongly positive direct Coombs test (4+). Negative HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, EBV, and Mycoplasma serologies.
objective.advanced_workup: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: High-titer serum Brucella standard tube agglutination test (1:640) and blood culture isolating Brucella melitensis, alongside a 4+ direct Coombs test and spherocytic hemolysis, confirmed acute Brucella melitensis bacteremia complicated by severe Coombs-positive autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Treated with oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) and oral rifampicin (600 mg QD) for 6 weeks combined with oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day tapered over 6 weeks). Hemoglobin rose to 9 g/dL (LDH 988 IU/L) after 1 week and normalized to 13 g/dL at 6 weeks, with complete remission maintained at 3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old woman underwent bilateral total knee arthroplasty for treatment of severe degenerative joint disease 10 years prior to her current presentation. She presented to our hospital with progressively worsening pain and swelling of both prosthetic knee joints for six weeks. She also reported a history of indolent fever, night sweats, and malaise started one week prior to joint symptoms. She was recently diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis of the left femoral vein for which she is on rivaroxaban. She reported consumption of possibly unpasteurized milk four weeks prior to her illness.
Examination revealed a lethargic, febrile woman with bilateral swollen, warm, and tender knee joints with moderate effusions. Rest of examination was normal. Initial investigations showed a hypochromic microcytic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 9.4 g/dl, a normal total white cell count (5600 cells/mm3), and elevated inflammatory biomarkers with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 109 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 101 mg/dL. Single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) of both knees is shown in Figure 1.
Diagnostic aspiration of both knee joints was performed. Analysis of the synovial fluid revealed 8200 white cells/muL with predominance of lymphomononuclear cells. Lateral flow alpha-defensin (Synovasure AD test) was performed intraoperatively on fluids from both knee joints and was negative twice. Meanwhile, a blood culture that was sent on admission grew Brucella melitensis after 6 days of incubation. Subsequently, culture of the synovial fluid (from both joints) grew Brucella melitensis on day 8 of incubation. A diagnosis of bacteraemic brucellosis with brucellar bilateral prosthetic knee joint infection was established, targeted antimicrobial therapy was commenced with combination of intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily (for one week) in addition to oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily (both given for 24 weeks), and a rescue revision arthroplasty was planned contingent on the outcome of antimicrobial therapy. In view of the chronicity of symptoms and associated bacteraemia, the patient underwent a transthoracic echo which showed no vegetations. Subsequent follow-up sterility blood cultures were negative. By end of first week of antimicrobial therapy, the patient was able to walk unassisted, and at 3 months, she had complete resolution of symptoms with normalization of inflammatory biomarkers; hence, a revision surgery was not performed. The patient remained symptom-free three years later with no evidence of disease recurrence or relapse.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old woman with bilateral total knee arthroplasties placed 10 years earlier presented with a 6-week history of progressively worsening bilateral knee pain and swelling preceded by 1 week of indolent fever, night sweats, and malaise.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 57-year-old woman who had undergone bilateral total knee arthroplasty (TKA) 10 years earlier developed indolent fever, night sweats, and malaise 7 weeks prior to presentation, followed 1 week later by 6 weeks of progressively worsening pain and swelling of both prosthetic knee joints.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bilateral total knee arthroplasty 10 years prior for severe osteoarthritis; recent left femoral deep vein thrombosis treated with oral rivaroxaban; consumed possibly unpasteurized milk 4 weeks prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bilateral knee pain and swelling, indolent fever, night sweats, and malaise.

objective.physical_examination: Lethargic and febrile; bilateral prosthetic knee joints were swollen, warm, and tender with moderate joint effusions; remainder of physical examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hypochromic microcytic anemia (Hb 9.4 g/dL), normal WBC count (5,600/mm3), ESR 109 mm/h, and CRP 101 mg/dL. Bilateral knee arthrocentesis yielded synovial fluid with WBC 8,200/uL (lymphomononuclear predominance) and twice-negative intraoperative lateral-flow alpha-defensin (Synovasure AD) tests. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no valvular vegetations.
objective.advanced_workup: SPECT/CT of both knees demonstrated increased periprosthetic uptake.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Admission blood culture grew Brucella melitensis on day 6 of incubation and synovial fluid cultures from both prosthetic knees grew Brucella melitensis on day 8, confirming bacteremic brucellosis with bilateral Brucella melitensis prosthetic knee joint infection (despite false-negative synovial alpha-defensin tests). Treated conservatively without prosthesis revision using IV gentamicin (5 mg/kg QD for 1 week) combined with oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) and oral rifampicin (600 mg QD) for 24 weeks. She ambulated unassisted by week 1, achieved complete symptom resolution and biomarker normalization by 3 months (obviating revision arthroplasty), and remained relapse-free at 3-year follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 52-year-old male, with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus, presented to our emergency department (ED) with a history of central, dull chest pain radiating to the back. He complained of intermittent high-grade fever, chills, rigors, sweating, unintentional weight loss, and dysphagia for three months. History was positive for raw milk ingestion and animal contact. Vitals revealed a temperature of 39.1 C; physical exam was unremarkable. Admission laboratory data showed white blood cells 10 (10e9/L), hemoglobin (16.1 mg/dl), platelet count 350 (10e9/L), C-reactive protein 28.5 (mg/dl), and normal electrolytes and coagulation profile. Thoracic CT angiogram demonstrated a saccular aneurysm arising from the descending aorta, distal to origin of the left subclavian artery, with perianeurysmal hematoma compressing the carina, main bronchi, and esophagus (Figure 1). Two sets of blood cultures were positive for Brucella melitensis. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms ruled out IE. Brucella mycotic aneurysm was diagnosed; appropriate intravenous and oral antibiotics (rifampin and doxycycline) were initiated. During hospitalization, the patient developed massive hematemesis necessitating transfusion of six units packed red blood cells. Angiography exhibited an aortoesophageal fistula (Figure 2), and urgent endovascular repair of the aneurysm was done (Figure 3). Subsequent angiography demonstrated satisfactory stent position with no endovascular leak. The patient received intravenous gentamicin for sixteen days along with rifampin and doxycycline. Upon discharge, rifampin and doxycycline were continued in an oral form for a total of six months. He returned to ED with recurrent hematemesis. CT and conventional angiography revealed no endovascular leak. The patient was discharged home. He again revisited with massive hematemesis with a hemoglobin drop, but no endovascular leak was found on imaging. Blood transfusions were given. Vascular surgeons decided to re-stent, as the thoracic surgeon deemed patient unsuitable for invasive surgical intervention for the aortoesophageal fistula. Esophageal stenting was done (Figure 4), but the patient could not tolerate oral intake, requiring stent removal. The following day the patient became unstable, arrested, and died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old diabetic male presented with a 3-month history of central dull chest pain radiating to the back, dysphagia, intermittent high-grade fever, chills, rigors, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 52-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with 3 months of central dull chest pain radiating to the back, progressive dysphagia, intermittent high fevers, chills, rigors, sweating, and weight loss; during hospitalization, he developed recurrent massive hematemesis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus; positive epidemiological history of raw milk ingestion and direct animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for central chest pain radiating to the back, dysphagia, intermittent high fever, chills, rigors, sweating, weight loss, and subsequent massive hematemesis.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 39.1 C; baseline physical examination was otherwise unremarkable; subsequently developed hemodynamic instability from recurrent massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (hematemesis).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 10 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL (subsequently dropping sharply during massive hematemesis requiring 6 units PRBCs), platelets 350 x 10^9/L, CRP 28.5 mg/dL, normal serum electrolytes and coagulation profile. Transthoracic echocardiogram was negative for infective endocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) ruled out valvular endocarditis. Thoracic CT angiography (CTA) demonstrated a saccular mycotic aneurysm of the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery origin, with a large perianeurysmal hematoma compressing the carina, mainstem bronchi, and esophagus. Conventional catheter aortography confirmed an aortoesophageal fistula.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Two sets of peripheral blood cultures isolated Brucella melitensis, confirming a descending thoracic aortic Brucella melitensis mycotic saccular aneurysm complicated by compressive dysphagia and a fatal aortoesophageal fistula. Treated with IV gentamicin (for 16 days) plus IV/oral rifampin and doxycycline (planned for 6 months) and urgent thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR stent-grafting) after massive hematemesis. Despite repeat endovascular aortic re-stenting and attempted esophageal stenting (which was removed due to oral intolerance), he suffered recurrent massive hematemesis, hemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest, and died.

raw_case_text: A 50-year-old man, with diagnosed alcoholic cirrhosis for the past decade, abstaining from alcohol since then, with no history of any cirrhotic complications, under no supportive treatment apart for regular follow-up, was admitted for protracted fever of two months' duration, accompanied by low backache, mild diarrhea, and abdominal distention. He had a history of splenectomy and was a shepherd. Significant ascites, accompanied by moderate pleural fluid effusion, was noted on clinical examination and subsequent imaging, the latter also demonstrating abdominal lymphadenopathy with partial central necrosis. Laboratory tests, compared to his latest follow-up, demonstrated only an increase in CRP and total and direct bilirubin. Blood cultures were positive for B. melitensis, a finding further confirmed by Rose Bengal plate agglutination, Wright seroagglutination test, and ELISA serology (Serion ELISA IgG/IgM/IgA antibodies to Brucella melitensis). The patient was treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, rifampicin 600 mg daily, and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily. Defervescence was achieved on day 5, accompanied though by progressive worsening of liver biochemistry indices and mild prolongation of international normalized ratio (INR) to levels of 1.34 (nv 0.8-1.2). Rifampicin dose was halved, and diuretics were added to treat ascites. Despite improvement/stabilization of other biochemical indices in later days, serum bilirubin continued to increase, reaching a plateau of total 7.2 mg/dl/direct 4.2 mg/dl and the patient was discharged, continuing treatment and follow-up as an outpatient on day 16. On day 41, the patient was readmitted with hepatic encephalopathy and jaundice. Hepatic biochemistry was steady, but total bilirubin was 16.7 mg/dl (direct bilirubin 13.6 mg/dl) and INR was 1.44. Ascites was minimal and subsequent workup excluded any underlying causes of encephalopathy. Antibiotics were discontinued as potential inducers of severe hepatotoxicity, and the patient was referred to a transplantation center due to the gradual worsening of liver function indices. He underwent liver transplantation which unfortunately had an adverse postoperative outcome.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male shepherd with compensated alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 2-month history of protracted fever, low backache, mild diarrhea, and abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old male shepherd with a 10-year history of compensated, abstinent alcoholic cirrhosis presented with 2 months of protracted fever, low back pain, mild diarrhea, and new-onset ascites.
subjective.past_medical_history: Compensated alcoholic cirrhosis for 10 years (abstinent, no prior decompensation), prior splenectomy, and occupational exposure as a shepherd.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-month fever, low back pain, mild diarrhea, and abdominal distension; later developed progressive jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with marked ascites and moderate pleural effusion; readmitted on day 41 with deep jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed elevated CRP and elevated total and direct bilirubin. During triple anti-Brucella therapy, total/direct bilirubin rose to 7.2/4.2 mg/dL with INR 1.34 (normal: 0.8-1.2) by day 16, and progressed by day 41 to total bilirubin 16.7 mg/dL (direct 13.6 mg/dL) and INR 1.44.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracoabdominal imaging demonstrated significant ascites, moderate pleural effusion, and abdominal lymphadenopathy with partial central necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Blood cultures growing Brucella melitensis, positive Rose Bengal plate agglutination, Wright seroagglutination, and Serion anti-Brucella IgG/IgM/IgA ELISA confirmed acute Brucella melitensis bacteremia in a shepherd with alcoholic cirrhosis. Treated with oral doxycycline (100 mg BID), oral rifampicin (600 mg QD, later halved), and oral ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID), which achieved defervescence on day 5 but precipitated severe drug-induced cholestatic liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy by day 41 (total bilirubin 16.7 mg/dL, INR 1.44), leading to orthotopic liver transplantation with a fatal postoperative outcome.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old male with a long history of alcohol abuse was transferred to our department with a novel diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis. He had been admitted to another hospital with delirium tremens and rhabdomyolysis. A diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis was made following evaluation. During that hospitalization, mild fever was observed, which was considered as a consequence of aspiration and treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate. During hospitalization to our department for further evaluation of cirrhosis (which demonstrated extensive ascites, splenomegaly, prolongation of international normalized ratio (INR), hypoalbuminemia, and mild lower esophageal varices), low-grade fever persisted. Medical history revealed a recent, 50 days ago, trip to Spain and consumption of nonpasteurized dairy products (sheep's products).
Blood cultures were positive for B. melitensis, confirmed by Rose Bengal plate agglutination, Wright seroagglutination test, and ELISA serology (Serion ELISA IgG/IgM/IgA antibodies to Brucella melitensis). The patient was treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily, but on day 4, he exhibited rapid worsening of liver function and laboratory indices of diffuse intravascular coagulation (DIC). Discontinuation of doxycycline and subsequently ciprofloxacin, along with supportive treatment, did not reverse the rapid evolution of the syndrome towards hepatic encephalopathy, spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage, and death on day 33.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male with newly diagnosed decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presented with persistent low-grade fever following hospitalization for delirium tremens and rhabdomyolysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 46-year-old man with chronic alcohol abuse who was recently hospitalized at an outside facility for delirium tremens, rhabdomyolysis, and newly diagnosed alcoholic cirrhosis (where low-grade fever was empirically treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate for presumed aspiration) was transferred with persistent low-grade fever and extensive ascites.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic alcohol abuse with newly diagnosed decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis (ascites, splenomegaly, mild lower esophageal varices); recent travel to Spain 50 days prior with consumption of unpasteurized sheep dairy products.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent low-grade fever and abdominal distension.

objective.physical_examination: Low-grade fever, extensive ascites, and splenomegaly; progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and fatal spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline prolonged INR and hypoalbuminemia; developed rapid hepatic decompensation and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) on day 4 of anti-Brucella therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Upper GI endoscopy/evaluation demonstrated mild lower esophageal varices, splenomegaly, and extensive ascites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Blood cultures isolating Brucella melitensis, positive Rose Bengal plate test, Wright seroagglutination, and Serion anti-Brucella IgG/IgM/IgA ELISA confirmed acute Brucella melitensis bacteremia in decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis. Initiation of oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) and ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID) was complicated on day 4 by fulminant hepatic failure and DIC; despite immediate antibiotic withdrawal and supportive care, he progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and fatal spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage on hospital day 33.

raw_case_text: The patient is a 37-year-old Chinese male. In April 2014, he was diagnosed with brucellosis due to fever and fatigue, and his symptoms disappeared after anti-brucellosis medications for three months. In October 2014, the patient developed left hip pain, worsened by weight-bearing, and was admitted to the orthopedics department of our hospital in December 2014 due to the deterioration of symptoms. He is a sheep herdsman without any history of trauma, alcoholism, or hormone use. Physical examination revealed that the active and passive motion of the left hip was somewhat restricted due to pain. X-ray demonstrated that the left femoral head exhibited a strip-like low-density area but no evidence of stenosis (Figure 1A and B). CT scan revealed cavity necrosis in the left femoral head (Figure 1C). MRI revealed necrosis of the left femoral head, and effusion in the left joint cavity (Figure 1D and E). Blood test showed WBC 6.85 x 109/L with neutrophils accounted for 61.8%, CRP 3.5 mg/L, ESR 2.00 mm/h. SAT was positive at a titer of 1:320, and all tests for tuberculosis and rheumatoid arthritis were negative. Having been diagnosed with brucellar hip arthritis complicated by osteonecrosis of the left femoral head, the patient underwent puncture and irrigation of the left hip joint and core decompression and bone grafting. B. melitensis was detected in hip joint effusion and osteonecrosis of femoral head by real-time PCR. HE staining of a core biopsy of the left femoral head revealed amorphous necrotic material (Figure 2A); Giemsa staining can demonstrate scattered positive Brucella (Figure 2B). Triple anti-infective therapy was administered after the operation: rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals), doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals), and levofloxacin (0.2g ivgtt bid; Yangtze River Pharmaceuticals). Upon discharge from the hospital two weeks after the operation, his left hip pain was substantially relieved, and the antibiotic regimen was adjusted to rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals) and doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals) for six months. In follow-up, the symptoms of left hip pain and movement limitation disappeared almost half a year later, and there was no obvious abnormality in the blood test or hip X-ray (Figure 1F). In the telephone follow-up in April 2022, the patient's recovery proceeded well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old Chinese male sheep herdsman with a history of brucellosis 8 months earlier presented in December 2014 with a 2-month history of progressive weight-bearing left hip pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old male sheep herdsman who had been treated for febrile brucellosis for 3 months in April 2014 developed progressive left hip pain aggravated by weight-bearing in October 2014, leading to orthopedic admission in December 2014.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic brucellosis diagnosed in April 2014 and treated for 3 months; occupational exposure as a sheep herdsman. Denied trauma, alcoholism, or corticosteroid use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive weight-bearing left hip pain and restricted hip mobility; negative for recurrent fever.

objective.physical_examination: Painful restriction of both active and passive range of motion of the left hip joint.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 6.85 x 10^9/L (61.8% neutrophils), CRP 3.5 mg/L, ESR 2.00 mm/h; negative tests for tuberculosis and rheumatoid arthritis. Left hip X-ray showed a strip-like radiolucent/low-density area in the left femoral head without joint space narrowing.
objective.advanced_workup: Left hip CT demonstrated cavitary osteonecrosis of the left femoral head; left hip MRI confirmed avascular necrosis of the left femoral head with a left hip joint effusion. Histopathology (H&E) of the left femoral head core biopsy showed amorphous necrotic bone, Giemsa staining demonstrated scattered intracellular Brucella organisms, and real-time PCR of both the hip joint effusion and necrotic femoral head core tissue identified Brucella melitensis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Positive serum agglutination test (SAT titer 1:320), Giemsa staining, and real-time PCR of the left hip joint aspirate and femoral head core biopsy identifying Brucella melitensis confirmed brucellar left hip arthritis complicated by osteonecrosis of the left femoral head. Treated with left hip joint puncture and irrigation, femoral head core decompression and bone grafting, and 2 weeks of inpatient triple therapy with oral rifampicin (0.6 g QD), oral doxycycline (0.1 g BID), and IV levofloxacin (0.2 g BID), followed by 6 months of outpatient oral rifampicin and doxycycline. Left hip pain and motion restriction resolved completely by 6 months, with sustained recovery at April 2022 follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 4-year-old male presented to our attention referring left submandibular swelling accompanied by odynophagia and left flexion of the head, in absence of rhinitis or nasal obstruction. The patient was taken to the emergency room where blood chemistry tests were performed showing an increased level of WBC, CRP, and fibrinogen and normal levels of ALT, AST, and LDH. The SARS-COV-2 nasal swab test resulted negative. The neck ultrasound revealed multiple increased size lymph nodes in left II, III, and IV areas, with well recognizable hilum and no colliquation areas. The clinical examination highlighted a laterocervical mesoadenia and inspection of the oral cavity showed tonsils asymmetry (left > right), lateral oropharynx wall swelling and nasopharynx purulent discharge.
CT scan was performed in the clinical suspicion of parapharyngeal abscess, showing nasopharyngeal airspace asymmetry and multiple oval lymphadenopathies along the laterocervical stations bilaterally. Having evaluated both the clinical and radiological evidence, the multidisciplinary team decided to avoid surgery and proceed with IV antibiotic therapy.
In view of an echographic increase in the lymphadenopathies size after medical therapy, a neck MRI was performed under sedation, confirming the persistence of obliteration on the left deep parapharyngeal and carotid spaces with left retropharyngeal lymphadenopathies (Figure 1).
The hospital's diagnostic protocol for pediatric lymphadenopathies was therefore applied, performing multiple tests to identify possible pathogens (blood culture, nasal secretion culture, intradermal Mantoux reaction, and serologies for EBV), which gave negative results.
Serology for Bartonella henselae resulted weakly positive (1 : 256) and the patient therefore perform an abdominal US that was within limits. Pharyngeal swab resulted positive for Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes (GABHS).
During the patient's hospital stay, gradual reduction of the left cervical lymphadenopathies was documented, with symptoms abate and improvement of inflammatory indexes, except for persistence of a mild platelets level increase and the patient was then discharged at home with clarithromycin therapy.
After 4 months from the hospital discharge, the patient experienced a laterocervical swelling relapse, with left cervicalgia, stiff neck, trismus, and fever. At the same time, pain and swelling of the hands appeared, with polymorphous rush at the level of phalanx, foot-plant and lumbar region, and unilateral lameness in the absence of osteoarticular swellings. These symptoms then regressed spontaneously after some days. The SARS-COV-2 nasal swab test resulted negative, blood chemistry tests showed an increase in WBC, CRP, platelets, and fibrinogen, while blood cultures and throat swab cultures gave negative results. Concomitantly, a new antibiotic IV therapy was started and continued for 15 days. PCR and serology for Bartonella, Brucella, Borrelia, Toxoplasma, CMV, and Francisella were performed, all resulting negative. The neck US and MRI showed numerical and dimensional increase of the previously known laterocervical lymph nodes, with evidence of colliquation areas and retropharyngeal space asymmetry. No septic or meningeal signs were found at the clinical examination and the MRI did not highlight meningeal pathology, so it was not deemed necessary to assay cerebrospinal fluid.
Fibrolaryngoscopy revealed adenoid hypertrophy and a minimal asymmetry of the pharyngeal region without macroscopic swelling, with maintained airways patency.
Contextually, the patient experienced strawberry tongue (Figure 2), conjunctival hyperemia and heart murmur. For this reason, cardiological evaluation and echocardiogram were performed, documenting coronary arteries dilation, wider at the level of the common trunk and the proximal right coronary artery (Z score 4.7 and 3.7, respectively).
Suspecting a potential KD diagnosis, the patient started the administration of intravenous immunoglobulins and acetylsalicylic acid at an anti-inflammatory dose.
This therapy led to a prompt clinical and radiological response as follows: gradual improvement of the symptoms and the thermal curve, reduction in the caliber of the coronary arteries (Z score of 3.1 for the common trunk, 2.3 for the right coronary artery), reduction in the lymphadenopathies dimension at MRI (Figure 3), improvement of platelets level, and reduction of the CRP.
The patient continued IV antibiotic therapy for a total of 14 days and was then discharged in good clinical conditions on the 20th day after the admission. Three months later the cardiologic control showed no cardiological sequelae and cardioaspirin therapy was stopped.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old male presented with left submandibular swelling, odynophagia, and left flexion of the head, followed 4 months later by recurrent laterocervical swelling, left cervicalgia, stiff neck, trismus, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 4-year-old male initially presented to the emergency department with left submandibular swelling accompanied by odynophagia and left head flexion. After initial hospitalization and treatment with intravenous antibiotics and discharge on oral clarithromycin, he experienced a relapse 4 months later characterized by recurrent laterocervical swelling, left cervicalgia, neck stiffness, trismus, and fever. Concurrently, he developed transient pain and swelling of the hands, a polymorphous rash over the phalanges, soles, and lumbar region, and unilateral lameness without osteoarticular swelling, which regressed spontaneously after several days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior hospitalization 4 months earlier for left laterocervical and retropharyngeal lymphadenitis treated with intravenous antibiotics and oral clarithromycin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for odynophagia, fever, neck pain, trismus, transient hand pain/swelling, polymorphous rash on phalanges/soles/lumbar area, and unilateral lameness; negative for rhinitis, nasal obstruction, or osteoarticular swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: laterocervical mesoadenia, tonsillar asymmetry (left > right), lateral oropharyngeal wall swelling, and nasopharyngeal purulent discharge. Relapse presentation (4 months later): laterocervical swelling, stiff neck, trismus, fever, strawberry tongue, conjunctival hyperemia, and cardiac murmur; no septic or meningeal signs and no osteoarticular swelling.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial presentation: elevated WBC, CRP, and fibrinogen; normal ALT, AST, and LDH; negative SARS-CoV-2 nasal swab; neck ultrasound showing multiple enlarged lymph nodes in left levels II, III, and IV with preserved hilum and no colliquation; normal abdominal ultrasound; persistent mild thrombocytosis at discharge. Relapse presentation: negative SARS-CoV-2 nasal swab; elevated WBC, CRP, platelets, and fibrinogen; neck ultrasound showing increased number and size of laterocervical lymph nodes with colliquation; echocardiogram showing coronary artery dilation at the common trunk (Z score 4.7) and proximal right coronary artery (Z score 3.7), which improved after therapy to Z scores of 3.1 and 2.3, respectively.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial neck CT showed nasopharyngeal airspace asymmetry and bilateral oval laterocervical lymphadenopathies. Initial neck MRI under sedation confirmed obliteration of the left deep parapharyngeal and carotid spaces with left retropharyngeal lymphadenopathies. At relapse, neck MRI showed numerical and dimensional increase of laterocervical lymph nodes with colliquation and retropharyngeal space asymmetry without meningeal pathology. Fibrolaryngoscopy revealed adenoid hypertrophy and minimal pharyngeal asymmetry with patent airways.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Initial workup showed negative blood culture, nasal secretion culture, Mantoux test, and EBV serology, weakly positive Bartonella henselae serology (1:256), and positive pharyngeal swab for Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes (GABHS). At relapse, blood and throat cultures as well as PCR and serology for Bartonella, Brucella, Borrelia, Toxoplasma, CMV, and Francisella were all negative. Final clinical diagnosis was Kawasaki disease (KD) presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy and coronary artery dilation (with brucellosis and other infectious lymphadenopathies ruled out). Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), anti-inflammatory dose acetylsalicylic acid, and a 14-day course of IV antibiotics resulted in prompt clinical defervescence, reduction of coronary artery Z scores and lymphadenopathy on MRI, and normalization of CRP and platelets. Discharged on hospital day 20; 3-month cardiology follow-up showed no sequelae and aspirin was discontinued.

raw_case_text:
A three-year-old male patient was admitted with complaints of pain and swelling in both ankles and wrists and rash with fever for more than 6 weeks. In addition to these clinical findings, he was referred to our hospital for the evaluation of increased acute phase reactants and examination of splenomegaly and abdominal distension. In the physical examination, the patient had fever and significant swelling especially in the right knee.
The patient was the second child of consanguineous parents. There was a third-degree cousin marriage without any other parental comorbidities. The other two children of the family were doing well and did not have any health problems.
A preliminary diagnosis of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) was considered because of complaints of fever, splenomegaly, rash, and arthritis lasting more than 10 days. Laboratory findings revealed an increase in acute phase reactants as C-reactive protein (CRP): 13.4 mg/dl (normal: 0-0.5), ferritin: 143.5 ng/ml (normal: 7-140), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 26 mm/h (normal: <15 mm/h), and serum amyloid A (SAA): 209 mg/l (normal: <6.4). Hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG : 3810 mg/dl, IgA : 165 mg/dl, and IgM : 161 mg/dl) and positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) (1/160 cytoplasmic) were detected. Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody (Anti-DsDNA) was negative. His antistreptolysin O titer (ASO), rheumatoid factor (RF), and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were all negative. PPD (purified protein derivative) intradermal test for tuberculosis examination resulted as anergic. Brucellosis and toxoplasmosis laboratory tests were both negative. Ophthalmologic examination for uveitis was found to be normal.
No pathological findings were detected in the chest X-ray. Since the patient had splenomegaly, bone marrow aspiration was performed for possible malignancies and macrophage activation syndrome. In the bone marrow examination, no signs of hemophagocytosis, atypical cells, and blasts were found while a few hypersegmented neutrophils were observed. Treatment of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) was started.
Arthritis, fever, and rash began to recover after two weeks of treatment. However, moniliasis was observed on the oral mucous membranes and tongue in the oropharyngeal examination. Additionally, nail dystrophy and onychomycosis in the right thumb were observed. Nail dystrophy was secondary to onychomycosis and occurred after 4-5 months after onychomycosis. The lymphocyte subset analysis by flow cytometry and T/B cell proliferation tests resulted normal. However, without genetic analysis, we could not exclude innate immune system deficiency, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment (in a dose of 0.5 gm/kg, once in four weeks) was started as it was used both in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and in innate immune deficiencies.
Then, genetic examination could be performed to exclude primary immunodeficiency in this case with chronic onychomycosis. STAT-1 GOF mutation was considered due to moniliasis, onychomycosis, arthritis, hypergammaglobulinemia, and consanguineous marriage. In targeted next-generation sequencing (TNGS), A homozygous mutation in the AIRE gene SAND domain (c.769C > T, p.Arg257Ter) was detected (Figure 1). Then, the patient was diagnosed with APECED syndrome. The parents were heterozygous for the same mutation.
After a short while, he had cough and fatigue and was hospitalized with the diagnosis of pneumonia. In the lung examination, diffuse crepitant rales were present, more prominent on the left. Acute phase reactants were found to be high. Community-acquired pneumonia was considered, with no sequelae. Coronavirus 229E/NL6 was detected in the respiratory virus panel. IVIG treatment was given to prevent chronic infections and for immunomodulation purposes, as it is a Th17-mediated disorder, and T cell assistance was not sufficient.
Dental caries developed in the follow-up of our patient. No other clinical problems were encountered in the next two years with IVIG treatment and fluconazole and trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole prophylactic treatment. He also recovered from arthritis very well without any other medication. At the age of five, hypoparathyroidism developed with low calcium, high phosphorus, low parathormone, and high 25OHD vitamin levels. He is still on treatment with calcium lactate, calcitriol, trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole prophylaxis, and IVIG, and he is doing well.
