A 70-year-old Chinese man with bilateral Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, bilateral pseudophakic and right eye complicated with posterior capsule rent and drop cortical matter about two years ago. The best corrected right eye visual acuity was 6/12 postoperatively. 
His right eye vision dropped to 6/36 at 3 months postoperatively. He was noted to develop cornea decompensation and diagnosed as pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. The cornea was hazy with epithelial bedewing, descemet striae and coin-shaped pigmented KP on cornea endothelium (Figure 2a (Fig. 2)).
Right eye descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK) was done. He developed steroid induced glaucoma and underwent right eye trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 0.02%. About one week after that, right eye visual acuity worsened to 4/60 due to early graft rejection. Intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily was instituted for three days alongwith topical dexaminim hourly followed by oral prednisolone with tapering dose. However right eye visual acuity further worsened to 1/60. Right eye re-DSAEK was done for graft failure. The second cycle of intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily was given. Aqueous sampling done was positive for CMV. HSV and VZV PCR from the aqueous sample were negative. Serum CMV IgM and IgG were not taken. He was started on oral valganciclovir 900 mg bidaily for two weeks and 900 mg daily for six months. Visual acuity improved to 2/60 after two weeks of treatment and KP reduced (Figure 2b (Fig. 2)). Repeated AC tap will be done in six months time and re-PK considered.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 70-year-old Chinese man with bilateral Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy and pseudophakia presented with progressive right-eye vision loss (dropping from 6/12 to 6/36, 4/60, and 1/60) and recurrent corneal graft failure following Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two years after complicated right-eye cataract surgery (posterior capsule rent and dropped nuclear cortex, post-op BCVA 6/12), the patient's right-eye vision declined to 6/36 at 3 months due to pseudophakic bullous keratopathy with coin-shaped pigmented keratic precipitates (KPs). He underwent right-eye DSAEK complicated by steroid-induced glaucoma requiring trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 0.02%. One week post-trabeculectomy, vision dropped to 4/60 from presumed early graft rejection (unresponsive to 3 days of IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/day, hourly topical dexamethasone, and oral prednisolone taper), worsening further to 1/60 and requiring repeat DSAEK and a second pulse of IV methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) before diagnostic aqueous humor tap.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bilateral Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy, bilateral pseudophakia (right eye complicated 2 years prior by posterior capsule rupture and dropped cortical matter), right pseudophakic bullous keratopathy status post DSAEK and repeat DSAEK, and right steroid-induced glaucoma status post trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 0.02%.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive right-eye visual acuity loss (6/12 to 1/60). Medications: pulse IV methylprednisolone, oral prednisolone taper, and topical dexamethasone.

objective.physical_examination: Right eye ophthalmic exam: BCVA 6/12 initially, declining to 6/36 at 3 months, 4/60 post-trabeculectomy, and 1/60 prior to re-DSAEK (improving to 2/60 after 2 weeks of valganciclovir). Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed corneal stromal haze, epithelial bedewing, Descemet's striae, and coin-shaped pigmented keratic precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum CMV IgM and IgG were not obtained.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic anterior chamber aqueous humor paracentesis PCR was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of right-eye cytomegalovirus (CMV) corneal endotheliitis causing pseudophakic bullous keratopathy and recurrent DSAEK graft failure, confirmed by characteristic coin-shaped pigmented endothelial keratic precipitates and positive aqueous humor CMV PCR (with HSV and VZV excluded by negative aqueous PCR). Treated with oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily induction for 2 weeks followed by 900 mg once daily maintenance for 6 months), resulting in reduction of keratic precipitates and visual acuity improvement from 1/60 to 2/60 at 2 weeks, with repeat anterior chamber tap and penetrating keratoplasty planned at 6 months.

raw_case_text: A 2-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital with purpura, bloody stools, and thrombocytopenia. His medical history included a recurrent skin rash, which first presented at birth. On admission, he was generally well, but had purpura and hepatosplenomegaly (liver: 2 cm below the right costal margin and spleen: 5 cm below the left costal margin). His platelet (PLT) count was 10 x 109 L-1, his hemoglobin level was 7.6 g/dL, and his leukocyte count was 15.9 x 109 L-1. His mean platelet volume (MPV) was 9.9 fL (normal range: 8.9-12.6 fL). Although a bone marrow examination revealed normal cellularity without any malignant cells, it did not reveal hypermegakaryocytes. Subsequently, an infectious laboratory workup was performed. An HCMV infection was confirmed because positivity for the specific antibody against HCMV immunoglobulin M and HCMV antigenemia (23 of 48,000 cells were positive) were detected. There was no laboratory evidence of a maternal cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection during pregnancy. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with ITP secondary to a CMV infection acquired after birth. An ophthalmic examination and audiogram produced normal findings. He received an intravenous infusion of immunoglobulins (IVIG: 1 g/kg/day) as a first-line therapy. Although the patient's PLT count temporarily rose (118 x 109 L-1) following the IVIG therapy, it gradually decreased to 10 x 109 L-1 within a week. Treatment with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) failed to improve the patient's PLT count, and repeated PLT transfusions were required. The intravenous administration of ganciclovir (10 mg/kg/day) was initiated for the CMV infection. Although no CMV antigenemia was present after 1 month, CMV antigenemia was seen again after the cessation of ganciclovir. Based on the patient's clinical course and the refractoriness of his condition to therapies targeting ITP and CMV antigenemia, WAS was strongly suspected. Flow cytometric (FCM) analysis revealed that the level of WAS protein (WASP) expression on the CD3-, CD19-, and CD56-positive cells from the patient was only 20% of that seen in the control (his father). Through direct DNA sequencing, we identified a novel missense mutation in exon 3 of the patient's WASP gene (c. 343 C > T, p. H115T; Figure 1). This mutation has not been described previously. The patient was diagnosed with WAS at 3 months after the onset of his condition. Subsequently, he underwent a cord blood transplant from an unrelated donor after receiving a conditioning regimen consisting of busulfan and cyclophosphamide. Ganciclovir was continued during the hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) until CMV antigenemia was no longer detected (Day 180). At present, the patient is 9 years old and well. His PLT count is within the normal range, and 100% donor engraftment was achieved.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old boy presented with purpura, bloody stools, and severe thrombocytopenia on a background of a recurrent skin rash present since birth.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having experienced a recurrent eczematous skin rash since birth, the infant was admitted at 2 months of age with cutaneous purpura, hematochezia, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe thrombocytopenia (10 x 10^9/L) that proved refractory to IVIG, oral prednisolone, and ganciclovir therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent skin rash since birth; no maternal history or laboratory evidence of gestational CMV infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cutaneous purpura, bloody stools, and recurrent skin rash since birth.

objective.physical_examination: Generally well-appearing infant with cutaneous purpura and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin). Ophthalmic examination and audiogram were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC: severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 10 x 10^9/L (transiently rising to 118 x 10^9/L after IVIG before relapsing to 10 x 10^9/L within 1 week), mean platelet volume (MPV) 9.9 fL (normal 8.9-12.6 fL), hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, and WBC 15.9 x 10^9/L. Serology was positive for human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) IgM, and peripheral blood HCMV pp65 antigenemia was positive (23 positive cells per 48,000 WBCs; cleared after 1 month of IV ganciclovir, recurred upon stopping ganciclovir, and cleared permanently by day +180 post-HSCT).
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow examination showed normal cellularity without malignancy or hypermegakaryocytosis. Flow cytometric analysis of CD3+, CD19+, and CD56+ lymphocytes demonstrated severely reduced Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) expression at 20% of normal control (paternal) levels. Direct DNA sequencing of the WAS gene identified a novel hemizygous missense mutation in exon 3: c.343C>T (p.H115Y / reported as p.H115T).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS; confirmed at 3 months after onset by 80% reduction in lymphocyte WASP expression on flow cytometry and a novel WAS exon 3 missense mutation c.343C>T) presenting initially at 2 months of age with postnatally acquired cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection and refractory severe thrombocytopenia/bloody stools (confirmed by positive HCMV IgM and HCMV antigenemia of 23/48,000 cells). Thrombocytopenia failed IVIG (1 g/kg/day) and prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day), and CMV antigenemia relapsed after initial 1-month IV ganciclovir (10 mg/kg/day). Curative unrelated umbilical cord blood transplantation (conditioned with busulfan and cyclophosphamide) with continuous peri-transplant IV ganciclovir through day +180 achieved permanent clearance of CMV antigenemia, 100% donor chimerism, normal platelet counts, and healthy survival at 9 years of age.

raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old boy a known case of relapsed AML has been admitted with impression of febrile neutropenia after the last course of chemotherapy on 16 April 2016. He received the FLAI regimen including fludarabine, cytarabine, and idarubicin (FLAI). After full sepsis workup, meropenem was started and cotrimoxazole (TMP/SMX) was continued with prophylaxis dosage (200 mg/12 hours by oral route). He received voriconazole as a fungal prophylaxis because of the previous history of proven pulmonary aspergillosis. Total white blood cell count was 200/mm3 (without countable neutrophils), hemoglobin was 10 g/dl, and platelet was 6000/mm3. First blood culture was positive for viridans streptococcus (by BACTEC system, time to detection: 9 hours) which was sensitive to vancomycin. Because high-grade fever continued after 48 hours of treatment and according to blood culture results, systemic vancomycin was added to antibacterial medications. The patient developed acute visual loss on 6th day of admission despite the appropriate type and dose of antibiotics. The neurological exam was normal. Retinal detachment and cancer associated retinopathy have been suggested as differential diagnoses in the first general ophthalmologist examination. The therapeutic dose of liposomal amphotericin B has been replaced with voriconazole.
Because high-grade fever was not resolved in 8th day of therapy (24 April), the blood sample was sent for a new culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR; for aspergillosis, mucormycosis, candida, CMV, and tuberculosis), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELIZA; for toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus antibody assay). A new chest X-ray has also been requested which revealed no new findings.
According to the results, toxoplasmosis IgM level was negative (0.1 IU/ml) and IgG level was at a borderline level (9.8 IU/ml). CMV blood PCR was reported to be 950  copy/mL. Anti-CMV antibody (IgG) was positive. Repeated blood PCR was negative for other fungal or viral pathogens.
Due to poor patient condition, spiral chest CT scan was requested on 10th day of admission with normal result. Rifampin has been added to the treatment regimen due to deteriorating patient's condition to achieve additive anti-Gram-positive synergistic effect. As the new blood culture results again revealed viridans streptococcus, which is susceptible to linezolid, linezolid has thus been replaced with vancomycin because of persistent bacteremia on 12th day of admission.
Lumbar puncture was performed on 29 April with total cells of 50/mm3 (white blood cells, 40/mm3 (polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 40%); red blood cells, 10/mm3), glucose of 50 mg/dl, protein of 48 mg/dl, and lactate dehydrogenase of 40 IU/L. Cytology report of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was positive for blasts, and PCR was negative for all viral and fungal suspicious agents.
Along with the patient's general condition, the patient complained of deteriorated visual function in the right eye. Therefore, a second ophthalmologist consult with a vitreoretinal specialist has been performed on 16th day of admission. The consultant ophthalmologist reported fluffy lesions with diffuse retinal hemorrhage and patchy focal necrosis (brush fire pattern) in the right eye and normal left eye (Figure 1). Thus, with first impression of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, vitreous aspiration was performed under anesthesia, and the sample was sent to the laboratory for PCR analysis. DNA was extracted from 100 microL ocular fluid by using High Pure Viral Nucleic Acid Kit (Roche Diagnostic GmbH, Germany) according to the instruction manual. Cytomegalovirus viral load was determined using a genesig quantitative real-time PCR kit (Primer Design Ltd. TM, Advanced Kit, United Kingdom) according to the manufacturer's instruction. The target sequence (glycoprotein B) has previously been shown to be a good genetic marker for CMV in other real-time PCR-based studies. This quantitative PCR assay was sensitive enough to detect 10 copies of CMV genomic DNA. Real-time PCR was performed using an ABI Step One Plus System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA) with standard reagents (TaqMan Gene Expression Master Mix, Applied Biosystems, UK), which showed positive results for CMV (5000 copy/ml). Upon confirmation, the patient received 2 intravitreal injections of ganciclovir 1 week apart with adjunctive systemic antiviral therapy with ganciclovir 5 mg/kg twice daily on 24th day of admission for 2 weeks as induction. In addition, our plan was to continue for about 4 weeks.
On 34th day after admission, a new blood sample was requested for CMV PCR, which was shown 1150 copy/ml of CMV DNA in plasma without significant change in baseline CMV viral load.
Because of severe retinal necrosis and hole formation at some retinal areas, barrier argon laser photocoagulation was suggested and performed by the responsible ophthalmologist. The final blood culture became negative, but finally he was died due to refractoriness of leukemia and poor response to chemotherapy 8 weeks after admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old boy with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia presented with febrile neutropenia after salvage FLAI chemotherapy and subsequently developed acute visual loss in his right eye on hospital day 6.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted on April 16, 2016, with profound febrile neutropenia following salvage FLAI chemotherapy (fludarabine, cytarabine, idarubicin) while on prophylactic oral cotrimoxazole and voriconazole (for prior proven pulmonary aspergillosis), the patient had persistent high-grade fever and viridans streptococcal bacteremia despite meropenem and vancomycin. On hospital day 6, he developed acute right-eye visual loss that progressively worsened by day 16.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) status post salvage FLAI chemotherapy; prior history of proven pulmonary aspergillosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent high-grade fever and progressive right-eye visual loss (starting hospital day 6). Medications at admission: prophylactic voriconazole and cotrimoxazole (200 mg PO q12h).

objective.physical_examination: Persistent high-grade fever; normal neurological examination. Day 16 vitreoretinal specialist dilated fundoscopic examination of the right eye revealed fluffy white retinal lesions with diffuse retinal hemorrhage, patchy focal retinal necrosis in a 'brush-fire' pattern, and retinal hole formation; the left eye was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC: WBC 200/mm3 (ANC 0/mm3), hemoglobin 10 g/dL, and severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 6,000/mm3. Serial blood cultures (admission and day 8) grew vancomycin- and linezolid-susceptible viridans group Streptococcus (cleared after switching to linezolid and rifampin). Day 8 serologies: Toxoplasma IgM negative (0.1 IU/mL), Toxoplasma IgG borderline (9.8 IU/mL), and anti-CMV IgG positive. Day 8 chest X-ray was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 8 quantitative blood CMV PCR was positive at 950 copies/mL (1,150 copies/mL on day 34); blood PCRs for Aspergillus, Mucorales, Candida, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Day 10 spiral chest CT was normal. Day 13 (April 29) lumbar puncture showed CSF total cells 50/mm3 (WBC 40/mm3 with 40% PMNs, RBC 10/mm3), glucose 50 mg/dL, protein 48 mg/dL, LDH 40 IU/L, positive CSF cytology for leukemic blasts, and negative CSF viral and fungal PCRs. Diagnostic right-eye vitreous humor aspiration under anesthesia (day 16) tested by quantitative real-time PCR targeting the CMV glycoprotein B gene confirmed CMV retinitis with a vitreous viral load of 5,000 copies/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of unilateral right-eye cytomegalovirus (CMV) necrotizing retinitis in a profoundly neutropenic child with relapsed AML and CNS leukemic involvement, confirmed by classic 'brush-fire' hemorrhagic necrotizing retinitis on fundoscopy, vitreous fluid quantitative real-time PCR viral load of 5,000 copies/mL, and plasma CMV PCR of 950-1,150 copies/mL (concurrent with viridans streptococcal bacteremia). Treated with two weekly intravitreal ganciclovir injections, systemic intravenous ganciclovir induction (5 mg/kg twice daily started on hospital day 24 for 2 weeks), and barrier argon laser photocoagulation for retinal necrosis/holes, alongside meropenem, vancomycin switched to linezolid plus rifampin, and liposomal amphotericin B. Although bacteremia cleared, the patient died 8 weeks after admission due to chemotherapy-refractory leukemia.

raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old man, with a past medical history significant for acute myeloid leukemia, underwent induction with cytarabine and idarubicin followed by consolidation with three cycles of high-dose cytarabine. After one year of achieving remission, he was found to have relapsed leukemia during workup for anemia. He was admitted to the hospital for salvage chemotherapy with cytarabine and mitoxantrone. Ten days after salvage chemotherapy, he developed a neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and elevated total bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound showed no signs of biliary obstruction. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed pericecal inflammatory stranding without pneumatosis concerning cecal typhlitis as well as an "apple-core mass" of the ascending colon near the hepatic flexure concerning colon cancer (Figure 1).
Colonoscopy was deferred because he was critically ill with neutropenic enterocolitis. Despite initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics consisting of vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, his clinical condition deteriorated. He was transferred to the medical intensive care unit with acute respiratory failure requiring assisted ventilation for several days. Blood cultures revealed Granulicatella adjacens and transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an aortic valve vegetation consistent with endocarditis requiring 6 weeks treatment with intravenous vancomycin. Additionally, he was noted to have hyperbilirubinemia secondary to hepatic veno-occlusive disease for which he completed a course of defibrotide with eventual normalization of liver enzymes. The patient improved clinically, and subsequent bone marrow biopsy obtained 7 weeks after induction chemotherapy showed no evidence of leukemia. After six weeks of inpatient treatment and subsequent clinical improvement, a colonoscopy was performed to rule out colon cancer given the suspicious apple-core lesion noted on the CT at the hepatic flexure. It revealed diffuse friable changes of the colonic wall extending from the cecum to the hepatic flexure and the transverse colon (Figure 2). Biopsies of the ascending colon, cecum, hepatic flexure, and transverse colon were taken. He was discharged to acute rehabilitation due to deconditioning and a 55 pound weight loss after 7 weeks of inpatient hospitalization.
Final pathology from the cecal biopsy specimens showed chronic active colitis with cryptitis, ulceration, and architectural distortion (Figure 3). CMV immunohistochemical staining was positive for CMV type inclusions compatible with CMV colitis (Figure 4). The biopsies were negative for dysplasia and malignancy. The ascending colon, hepatic flexure mass, and transverse colon mass were negative for CMV inclusions on immunohistochemical stains but showed features consistent with chronic active colitis with cryptitis and architectural distortion.
Our patient remained asymptomatic, without recurrence of diarrhea, fever, or abdominal pain.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old man with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia developed neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hyperbilirubinemia 10 days after salvage cytarabine and mitoxantrone chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having relapsed 1 year after initial AML remission (previously treated with cytarabine + idarubicin induction and 3 cycles of high-dose cytarabine consolidation), the patient received inpatient salvage chemotherapy with cytarabine and mitoxantrone. Ten days post-chemotherapy, he developed febrile neutropenia, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hyperbilirubinemia, and subsequently deteriorated on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam with acute respiratory failure requiring ICU transfer and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) status post prior cytarabine/idarubicin induction, 3 cycles of high-dose cytarabine consolidation, and current salvage cytarabine/mitoxantrone chemotherapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, jaundice/hyperbilirubinemia, acute respiratory failure, and a 55-pound hospital weight loss with deconditioning.

objective.physical_examination: Critically ill with neutropenic enterocolitis and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, followed by severe deconditioning and a 55-pound weight loss over a 7-week hospitalization.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated total bilirubin and liver enzymes (secondary to hepatic veno-occlusive disease, normalized after defibrotide). Blood cultures grew Granulicatella adjacens. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction; transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed an aortic valve vegetation consistent with infective endocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominopelvic CT on day 10 post-chemotherapy demonstrated pericecal inflammatory fat stranding without pneumatosis (concerning for cecal typhlitis) and an 'apple-core' mass in the ascending colon near the hepatic flexure concerning for colon carcinoma. Bone marrow biopsy at week 7 confirmed complete leukemia remission. Colonoscopy performed after 6 weeks of inpatient recovery revealed diffuse friable colonic mucosa extending from the cecum to the hepatic flexure and transverse colon; histopathological examination of the cecal biopsy demonstrated chronic active colitis with cryptitis, ulceration, architectural distortion, and positive CMV immunohistochemical staining for CMV inclusion bodies (while biopsies of the ascending colon, hepatic flexure mass, and transverse colon showed chronic active colitis negative for malignancy, dysplasia, and CMV inclusions).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cecal cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis presenting as neutropenic typhlitis and an ascending colon inflammatory pseudotumor ('apple-core' lesion mimicking colon adenocarcinoma) following salvage AML chemotherapy, confirmed by positive CMV immunohistochemical staining and chronic active ulcerative colitis on cecal biopsy (with colonic malignancy ruled out), complicated by Granulicatella adjacens aortic valve endocarditis and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD). Treated with a 6-week course of intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, defibrotide for hepatic VOD, and ICU supportive care, achieving complete AML bone marrow remission and resolution of diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain without antiviral therapy requirement at rehabilitation discharge.

raw_case_text: A 41-year-old man, a native from Rio de Janeiro and an HIV and HCV carrier, without criteria for the treatment for HCV (detectable viral load, without cirrhosis and with normal transaminase levels), who had abandoned ART, had attended the Gaffree and Guinle University Hospital's immunology clinic complaining about continuous epigastric burning pain without irradiation and with diffuse abdominal pain that was mild and continuous, which had started approximately two months prior to admission. He also complained about intense hematochezia that had started three weeks before, with intense flow and with "pure blood" appearance without clots. He presented with daily hyperthermia since the abdominal symptoms had started with intermittent high fever and an over 10% body weight loss in the same period. The physical examination revealed oral candidiasis, bleached mucous membranes, and cachexia. At the admission time, the HIV viral load was recorded at 905,569 copies per ml, and the TCD4 lymphocyte count was 144 cells/dL. Prophylactic sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim 400/80 mg 2 IV ampoules once daily and fluconazole 200 mg IV once daily for treatment of the oral candidiasis were prescribed. The patient's condition evolved without major occurrences or complaints, presented with high fever, above 38 C almost every day. Blood counts revealed thrombocytopenia, neutrophilia, lymphopenia, anemia, microcytosis, and anisocytosis (Table 1). The medical team requested upper digestive endoscopy (Figure 1) and colonoscopy (Figure 2), which verified the presence of ulcer with irregular and raised edges, fibrinonecrotic base, measuring approximately 3 cm in the middle third of the esophagus and 30 cm from the incisors and the mild antrum gastritis, and swollen, irregular, and fibrinous ulcers in the ileocecal valve, descending colon, and all other segments. The lesions were similar to those found in the esophagus, which could suggest the same etiology. It was suggested by the internal medicine team that the diagnosis could be a coinfection (tuberculosis, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus disease). The diagnosis of tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus coinfection of the gastrointestinal tract was confirmed by the histopathological report (Ziehl-Neelsen staining of acid-fast bacilli, CMV intracytoplasmic inclusions in Giemsa staining, and immunohistochemical study with positive labeling for CMV in cells with clear halos), and some time later, culture with the growth of M. tuberculosis (Figure 3). Treatment was started with an RIPE scheme (rifampicin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + ethambutol) 4 tablets daily and ganciclovir 350 mg IV for 21 days with a weight gain of 4 kg and clinical and laboratory improvement. He was discharged from the hospital with ART lamivudine, tenofovir, and efavirenz (TDF + 3TC + EFV) one tablet per day and was referred to a clinical follow-up for tuberculosis and HIV/HCV coinfection monitoring. At the end of the treatment for tuberculosis and 6 months after ART was restarted, the patient's viral load was <40 copies/dL and the CD4+ T-cell count was 356 cells/dL, asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male with untreated HIV and HCV co-infection presented with a 2-month history of continuous burning epigastric pain, mild diffuse abdominal pain, daily high fevers, >10% weight loss, and a 3-week history of profuse bright-red hematochezia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having previously abandoned antiretroviral therapy (ART), the patient developed continuous non-radiating burning epigastric pain, mild diffuse abdominal pain, daily intermittent high fevers (>38 °C), and >10% body weight loss starting 2 months prior to admission, complicated over the preceding 3 weeks by intense, clot-free bright-red hematochezia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection (off ART due to non-adherence) and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) carrier without cirrhosis and with normal baseline transaminases. Native of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2 months of continuous burning epigastric pain, diffuse abdominal pain, daily high fevers (>38 °C), >10% weight loss, and 3 weeks of profuse hematochezia. No active home medications at admission.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic, pale/bleached mucous membranes, oral candidiasis, and daily high fevers >38 °C.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed anemia with microcytosis and anisocytosis, thrombocytopenia, neutrophilia, and lymphopenia; normal baseline transaminases.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission plasma HIV viral load was 905,569 copies/mL and CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 144 cells/uL (reported as 144 cells/dL in text). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (EGD) revealed a 3-cm ulcer with irregular raised edges and a fibrinonecrotic base in the middle third of the esophagus (30 cm from the incisors) plus mild antral gastritis; colonoscopy revealed similar swollen, irregular, fibrinous ulcers involving the ileocecal valve, descending colon, and remaining colonic segments. Esophageal and colonic mucosal biopsies confirmed gastrointestinal Mycobacterium tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus (CMV) co-infection via positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli, subsequent culture growth of M. tuberculosis, Giemsa staining showing intracytoplasmic CMV inclusions, and positive anti-CMV immunohistochemistry in enlarged cells with clear perinuclear halos.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of synchronous esophageal and pan-colonic Mycobacterium tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus (CMV) ulcerative co-infection in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 144 cells/uL, HIV viral load 905,569 copies/mL) and oral candidiasis, confirmed by endoscopic biopsy Ziehl-Neelsen AFB staining, M. tuberculosis tissue culture, Giemsa intracytoplasmic CMV inclusions, and positive CMV immunohistochemistry. Treated with intravenous ganciclovir (350 mg daily for 21 days), oral RIPE anti-tuberculous therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, 4 tablets daily), IV fluconazole (200 mg daily), prophylactic IV trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and re-initiation of ART at discharge (tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz). The patient gained 4 kg during hospitalization and at 6-month follow-up was asymptomatic with an undetectable HIV viral load (<40 copies/mL) and a CD4+ count of 356 cells/uL.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old South East Asian female with background of recurrent abortions (not investigated before) presented to the emergency department with 4 days history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with abdominal distention, nausea and recurrent vomiting. She denied any cough, phlegm production, hemoptysis, joint pain, skin rash, oral ulcers and palpitations. There was no significant history of similar episodes in the past. She denied use of alcohol and was not on any home medication.
On admission, the patient was conscious, alert and oriented. She appeared in mild distress, with respiratory rate of 25 and temperature of 39 C. The examination was remarkable for mild epigastric tenderness and abdominal distention, few bi-basilar lung crackles and normal heart sounds.
Initial labs showed hemoglobin (Hb) of 13 g/dL, platelets of 71 x103 microL and WBC of 14 x 103. Her lipase was >3300 U\L and amylase of 960 U\L. Further investigations showed aPTT of 67.8 s, D-dimer of 2.96 mg/L FEU, alanine transaminase of 14 U\L, aspartate transaminase of 16 U\L, alkaline phosphatase of 48 U\L, total bilirubin of 14 micromol\L, lactic acid of 0.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin of 0.8 ng/mL, LDH of 794 U/L and CRP of 323 mg/L. CT abdomen with contrast showed ill-defined hypodensities in the tail of the pancreas with irregular outlines and fluid in the peripancreatic space (Figure 5). Echocardiography showed normal ejection fraction of 50% with no structural or valve abnormality. The patient was initially treated as case of acute pancreatitis and received IV fluid resuscitation and analgesics.
However, a few days after admission, her condition deteriorated with persistent abdominal pains, continuing fever spikes and worsening dyspnea with desaturation. CXR showed increased left lower zone and retro-cardiac density suggestive of collapse, with left-sided pleural effusion (Figure 6). Repeated echocardiography showed global hypokinesia with drop in her ejection fraction (20%-25%) but no vegetation. Her labs were significant for rise in alanine transaminase to 196 U\L, aspartate transaminase of 194 U\L, alkaline phosphatase of 148 U\L and total bilirubin of 64.5 micromol\L with direct component of 40 micromol\L; for that she required management in the ICU.
Septic workup showed negative pan cultures, but her viral panel for acute hepatitis came back positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) with a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of 5863 copies. She received Ganciclovir for 2 weeks with little clinical improvement upon clearance of CMV viremia. Her abdominal symptoms also showed minimal resolution in contrast to the biochemical improvement in acute pancreatitis. Repeated imaging of the abdomen showed peri-pancreatic inflammation, with heterogeneous enhancement in the right posterior hepatic segments and segmental portal vein thrombosis (Figure 7).
Giving her high aPTT and low platelets with a history of recurrent abortions, there was no clear cause of acute pancreatitis and multi-organ involvement; autoimmune study was sent to rule out CAPS. The results were antinuclear antibody positive (1:160), with speckled pattern; anti-dsDNA (11, equivocal); C3 of 93 mg/dL; C4 of 16 mg/dL; antinuclear cytoplasmic antibody (negative); anticardiolipin IgM Ab: (negative); anticardiolipin IgG Ab: (positive, 20 mg/dL) and anti B2 glycoprotein IgM (positive, 30 mg\dL).
She was started on aspirin and heparin infusion. After discussion with the rheumatology team, we decided to start her on HCQ (200 mg/once daily). Several days later, her condition improved with dramatic relief of her abdominal pain and no more difficulty in breathing or spikes of fever.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old Southeast Asian female presented with a 4-day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, abdominal distension, nausea, and recurrent vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: With an uninvestigated history of recurrent spontaneous abortions, the patient presented to the emergency department after 4 days of right upper quadrant and epigastric pain, abdominal distension, nausea, and recurrent vomiting. Several days after admission for acute pancreatitis, she deteriorated with persistent abdominal pain, spiking fevers, worsening dyspnea, hypoxemia, acute systolic heart failure (LVEF 20-25%), cholestatic hepatitis, and segmental portal vein thrombosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of recurrent spontaneous abortions (previously uninvestigated); no prior similar episodes. Social history: denied alcohol use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 4 days of RUQ/epigastric pain, abdominal distension, nausea, recurrent vomiting, fever (39 °C), and subsequent worsening dyspnea. Pertinent negatives: no cough, sputum, hemoptysis, arthralgia, skin rash, oral ulcers, or palpitations. No home medications.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, alert, and oriented in mild distress; temperature 39 °C, respiratory rate 25/min; mild epigastric tenderness and abdominal distension; few bibasilar lung crackles; normal heart sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: hemoglobin 13 g/dL, thrombocytopenia with platelets 71 x 10^3/uL, WBC 14 x 10^3/uL, lipase >3,300 U/L, amylase 960 U/L, prolonged aPTT 67.8 s, D-dimer 2.96 mg/L FEU, ALT 14 U/L (rising to 196 U/L), AST 16 U/L (rising to 194 U/L), ALP 48 U/L (rising to 148 U/L), total bilirubin 14 umol/L (rising to 64.5 umol/L with direct bilirubin 40 umol/L), lactic acid 0.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 0.8 ng/mL, LDH 794 U/L, and CRP 323 mg/L. Pan-cultures were negative. Autoimmune/antiphospholipid panel: ANA positive (1:160 speckled), anti-dsDNA equivocal (11), C3 93 mg/dL, C4 16 mg/dL, ANCA negative, anticardiolipin IgM negative, anticardiolipin IgG positive (20 mg/dL), and anti-beta2-glycoprotein IgM positive (30 mg/dL). Admission TTE showed normal LVEF (50%) without valvular lesions; repeat TTE during ICU deterioration showed global hypokinesia with LVEF drop to 20-25% and no vegetations; chest X-ray showed left lower zone/retrocardiac collapse-consolidation and left pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed ill-defined hypodensities in the pancreatic tail with irregular outlines and peripancreatic fluid. Viral hepatitis panel and quantitative PCR confirmed active cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia at 5,863 copies/mL. Repeat abdominal CT after 2 weeks of ganciclovir showed persistent peripancreatic inflammation, heterogeneous right posterior hepatic perfusion, and segmental portal vein thrombosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) / antiphospholipid syndrome (confirmed by history of recurrent abortions, prolonged aPTT 67.8 s, thrombocytopenia, positive anticardiolipin IgG [20 mg/dL], positive anti-beta2-glycoprotein IgM [30 mg/dL], ANA 1:160, acute pancreatitis, myocardial dysfunction [EF 20-25%], and segmental portal vein thrombosis) triggered by or co-occurring with acute cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (confirmed by CMV PCR of 5,863 copies/mL). While a 2-week course of ganciclovir cleared CMV viremia with biochemical improvement in pancreatitis, persistent multi-organ and thrombotic symptoms resolved dramatically within days of initiating therapeutic intravenous heparin, aspirin, and oral hydroxychloroquine (200 mg once daily).

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old HIV-1-infected male farmer presented with a five-day history of right hypochondriac abdominal pain associated with decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, and two days of yellowish discolouration of sclera, with no history of fever, diarrhoea, blurring of vision, and odynophagia or dysphagia.
He presented to us for the first time in September 2016, when he was diagnosed with pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonitis (PJP) on transbronchial lung biopsy and successfully treated with co-trimoxazole and prednisolone. This biopsy did not reveal CMV inclusion bodies. His CD4 count was 109/muL and HIV-1 viral load was 4.89 log copies/ml.
He was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection in 2000 and was treated by another physician, for which he was initiated on zidovudine (ZDV)/lamivudine (3TC)/nevirapine (NVP) and switched to tenofovir disproxil fumarate (TDF)/3TC/atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) in 2011 due to virological failure. After control of PJP, we switched his HAART to raltegravir (RAL)/darunavir (DRV)/r based on the genotypic resistance report. Within 4 weeks of initiating HAART, he presented with the above mentioned symptoms.
Physical examination was unremarkable except for icterus and tender hepatomegaly. Fundoscopy did not reveal CMV retinitis. He had normocytic normochromic anaemia (Hb: 10.7 g/dl), normal total leucocyte, and differential counts. Liver enzymes were total bilirubin: 9.2 mg/dl (reference value: 0-1 mg/dl), aspartate transaminase (AST): 109 U/L [15-37 U/L], alanine transaminase (ALT): 41 U/L (14-59 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 906 U/L (46-116 U/L). Tests for hepatitis B and hepatitis C were negative.
Hepatomegaly (liver span-18 cm) with grade I-II intrahepatic biliary dilatation with focal parenchymal lesion was seen on abdominal ultrasound. The common bile duct (CBD) was dilated, measuring 14 mm suggestive of possible obstruction at the level of ampulla with no definitive mass or obstructive lesion.
An endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography (ERCP) was performed, which revealed oedematous papilla with stenosis. Cholangiogram showed a dilated CBD with prepapillary CBD stricture. All these features were suggestive of AIDS cholangiopathy (Figure 1(a)).
Wide papillotomy was performed, and a 7 Fr CBD stent was placed for biliary drainage. Bile aspirate was negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora, and Mycobacterium. Brush cytology of the stricture revealed inflammatory cells, pigment-laden macrophages, and several red blood cells with no acid-fast organisms.
Histopathological examination of ampullary biopsy showed focal ulcerations with superficial mucosal necrosis and acute and chronic inflammation in the mucosa and lamina propria. Cells of submucosal Brunner's glands showed nucleomegaly with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic CMV inclusions (Figure 1(b)).
After intervention, the patient had immediate symptomatic relief and did not receive any anti-CMV treatment. Liver enzymes normalised 2 weeks later.
After 6 months, CD4 improved to 363 cells/muL with HIV viral load of 423 copies/ml. Repeat ERCP revealed normal cholangiogram with no residual stricture in lower CBD, with normal papilla (Figure 2(a)). Previously placed stent had migrated out. Cells from ampullary biopsies did not reveal intranuclear/cytoplasmic CMV inclusions (Figure 2(b)).
A repeat viral load after 8 months was <50 copies/ml. ART was switched to dolutegravir (DTG)/DRV/r.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old HIV-1-infected male farmer presented with a 5-day history of right hypochondriac abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting, and 2 days of scleral icterus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV-1 in 2000 (previously treated with ZDV/3TC/NVP and switched in 2011 to TDF/3TC/ATV/r for virological failure), the patient had presented in September 2016 with biopsy-proven Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (CD4 109/uL, HIV-1 viral load 4.89 log copies/mL; lung biopsy negative for CMV inclusions), which was treated with co-trimoxazole and prednisolone followed by resistance-guided HAART switch to raltegravir plus darunavir/ritonavir (RAL/DRV/r). Within 4 weeks of starting RAL/DRV/r, he developed 5 days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting, and 2 days of scleral jaundice.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection (diagnosed in 2000) status post recent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (September 2016). Occupation: farmer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 5 days of right hypochondriac pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and 2 days of jaundice. Pertinent negatives: no fever, diarrhea, visual blurring, odynophagia, or dysphagia. Home medications: raltegravir, darunavir/ritonavir, and co-trimoxazole.

objective.physical_examination: Scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm); fundoscopic examination showed no CMV retinitis; remainder of physical exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL), normal WBC and differential counts, total bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL (ref 0-1 mg/dL), AST 109 U/L (ref 15-37 U/L), ALT 41 U/L (ref 14-59 U/L), and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 906 U/L (ref 46-116 U/L); hepatitis B and C tests negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly (18 cm), grade I-II intrahepatic biliary dilatation, a focal parenchymal lesion, and a dilated common bile duct (CBD, 14 mm) to the level of the ampulla without a discrete mass.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4 count was 109 cells/uL and HIV-1 viral load was 4.89 log copies/mL (improving at 6 months to CD4 363 cells/uL and HIV viral load 423 copies/mL, and <50 copies/mL at 8 months). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) demonstrated an edematous, stenotic major papilla and a 14-mm dilated CBD with a prepapillary distal CBD stricture consistent with AIDS cholangiopathy (wide endoscopic papillotomy and 7 Fr CBD stent placement performed). Bile aspirate and stricture brush cytology were negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia, Cyclospora, and acid-fast mycobacteria. Ampullary mucosal biopsy revealed focal ulceration, superficial mucosal necrosis, mixed inflammation, and submucosal Brunner's gland cells exhibiting nucleomegaly with characteristic eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic cytomegalovirus (CMV) inclusions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV)-associated AIDS cholangiopathy (papillary stenosis and prepapillary CBD stricture) unmasked as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) 4 weeks after starting raltegravir/darunavir/ritonavir, confirmed by characteristic eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic CMV inclusions in submucosal Brunner's glands on ampullary biopsy (with Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia, Cyclospora, and mycobacteria excluded). Treated with ERCP wide endoscopic papillotomy, 7 Fr biliary stenting, and continued HAART without systemic anti-CMV therapy, resulting in immediate symptom relief, normalization of liver enzymes within 2 weeks, and complete resolution of the CBD stricture and histological disappearance of CMV inclusions on 6-month repeat ERCP and ampullary biopsy.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old woman was referred to our hospital after having high fever and systemic joint pain for 10 days. She was admitted to our hospital for further examination and treatment. She had a past medical history of diabetes mellitus, herpes zoster, and lichen planus; her family history was unremarkable. On admission, her body temperature was 38.3 C, her blood pressure was 119/90 mmHg, her pulse rate was 110 beats/min, and the oxygen saturation in the room air was 97%. Erythematous papule appeared on the anterior chest and bilateral forearm. She had no pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal pain. Her total white blood cell count was 9,200/microL (neutrophils 87%, lymphocytes 7%, and atypical lymphocytes 2%), CD4+ T cell was 44.3%, CD8+ T cell was 34.5%, hemoglobin was 15.3 g/dL, and platelet count was 123,000/microL. Her laboratory test results were as follows (Table 1): C-reactive protein level, 6.83 mg/dL; aspartate transaminase, 96 U/L; alanine transaminase, 130 U/L; alkaline phosphatase, 489 U/L; gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, 349 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase, 315 U/L; total bilirubin, 1.2 mg/dL; HbA1c, 8.7%; immunoglobulin G, 1574 mg/dL; immunoglobulin A, 186 mg/dL; immunoglobulin M, 144 mg/dL. The results of the serological tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. The result of renal function test was normal. Urinalysis showed negative occult blood and urinary protein. The blood cultures showed no growth. Because the patient continued to have high fever, we performed an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan, which revealed splenomegaly and a geographic low attenuation area in the dorsal and upper external side of the spleen (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)); this finding was consistent with splenic infarction.
We considered the splenic infarction to be in a hypercoagulable state. Her coagulopathy tests showed the following results: prothrombin time, 14.9 sec (normal, 10.6-14.9 sec); activated partial thromboplastin time, 33.9 sec (normal, 23.3-38.2 sec); d-dimer, 6.4 microg/mL; lupus anticoagulant, 1.05 (normal values <1.2, with dilute Russell's viper venom method); anticardiolipin antibody IgG, <8.0 U/mL; and anticardiolipin-beta2-glycoprotein I complex antibody, <1.2 U/mL. There were no abnormal coagulopathy results.
Because of atypical lymphocytosis and elevated transaminase, infectious mononucleosis was considered the cause of her sustained fever. The serological test for EBV antiviral capsid antigen IgM was negative at 0.1 (normal level, <0.5), antiviral capsid antigen IgG was positive at 7.5 (normal level, <0.5), and antibody to EBV nuclear antigen was positive at 4.6 (normal level, <0.5). These results suggest past infection for EBV. The serological test for CMV IgM was positive at 4.60 (normal level, <0.8), CMV IgG was slightly positive at 2.5 (normal level, <2.0), and parvovirus B19 IgM was also slightly positive at 0.99 (normal level, <0.8). The CMV antigen pp65 (antigenemia method of C10C11) was detectable at a level of 33 positive cells per 150,000 cells and 25 positive cells per 150,000 cells, which confirmed her diagnosis of acute CMV infection. The results of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) antigen/antibody and human T-cell leukemia virus type-1 (HTLV-1) antibody were negative. Although the patient was originally treated with conservative therapy, her fever persisted; therefore, she was subsequently treated with intravenous ganciclovir. The day after beginning the treatment with ganciclovir, her fever, joint pain, and erythematous papule improved (Figure 2). After 13 days of ganciclovir therapy, the CMV antigen pp65 was decreased at a level of 1 positive cells per 150,000 cells and she was discharged. Two weeks after the first serological tests of the virus antibodies, a follow-up serological test was performed. CMV IgM was positive at 4.80, CMV IgG was elevated to 11.7, and parvovirus B19 IgM was elevated to 2.38. Acute parvovirus infection was confirmed by the increasing level of parvovirus B19 IgM antibody. Seven weeks after discharge, we performed an additional abdominal CT scan. The splenic infarction area was decreased without atrophy, and splenomegaly was improved (Figures 1(c) and 1(d)).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of persistent high fever and systemic polyarthralgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred and admitted after experiencing 10 days of sustained high fever and generalized joint pain, accompanied on admission by erythematous papules on her anterior chest and bilateral forearms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.7%), prior herpes zoster, and lichen planus. Unremarkable family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 10 days of high fever, systemic joint pain, and anterior chest/forearm erythematous papules. Pertinent negatives: no pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.3 °C, blood pressure 119/90 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air; erythematous papular rash on the anterior chest and bilateral forearms; no pharyngitis, peripheral lymphadenopathy, or abdominal tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 9,200/uL (87% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes, 2% atypical lymphocytes; CD4+ T cells 44.3%, CD8+ T cells 34.5%), hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, mild thrombocytopenia with platelets 123,000/uL, CRP 6.83 mg/dL, AST 96 U/L, ALT 130 U/L, ALP 489 U/L, GGT 349 U/L, LDH 315 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.7%, IgG 1,574 mg/dL, IgA 186 mg/dL, IgM 144 mg/dL, normal renal function, and negative urinalysis and blood cultures. Coagulation/thrombophilia panel: PT 14.9 s (normal 10.6-14.9 s), aPTT 33.9 s (normal 23.3-38.2 s), elevated D-dimer 6.4 ug/mL, normal lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT 1.05, normal <1.2), anticardiolipin IgG <8.0 U/mL, and anti-cardiolipin-beta2-GPI complex <1.2 U/mL. Viral serologies: HBV, HCV, HIV-1 Ag/Ab, and HTLV-1 negative; EBV VCA-IgM negative (0.1), VCA-IgG positive (7.5), and EBNA positive (4.6) indicating past EBV infection; CMV IgM positive at 4.60 (normal <0.8; 4.80 at 2 weeks), CMV IgG weakly positive at 2.5 (normal <2.0; rising to 11.7 at 2 weeks), and parvovirus B19 IgM weakly positive at 0.99 (normal <0.8; rising to 2.38 at 2 weeks).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed splenomegaly and a wedge-shaped geographic low-attenuation splenic infarction in the dorsal/superior-lateral spleen (which decreased in size without atrophy alongside improved splenomegaly on 7-week post-discharge follow-up CT). Peripheral blood CMV pp65 antigenemia (C10/C11 method) was positive at 33 and 25 positive cells per 150,000 WBCs (decreasing to 1 positive cell per 150,000 WBCs after 13 days of IV ganciclovir).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of acute primary cytomegalovirus (CMV) and human parvovirus B19 co-infection complicated by atraumatic splenic infarction in a non-anticoagulated diabetic woman, confirmed by positive CMV pp65 antigenemia (33 and 25 positive cells/150,000 WBCs), CMV IgM positivity (4.60 to 4.80) with CMV IgG seroconversion (2.5 to 11.7), and rising parvovirus B19 IgM titers (0.99 to 2.38), with antiphospholipid antibodies excluded. After persistent fever on initial conservative management, treatment with intravenous ganciclovir for 13 days produced rapid improvement in fever, polyarthralgia, and rash within 24 hours, reduction of CMV pp65 antigenemia to 1/150,000 cells at discharge, and regression of the splenic infarction on 7-week follow-up CT.

raw_case_text:
We report a 60-year-old, CMV seropositive female patient with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Cytogenetics revealed trisomy 8 in 3 out of 10 metaphases. Verification of mutations in ASXL1, EZH2 and NPM1 led to high risk classification according to European LeukemiaNet ELN guidelines. Administering induction and consolidation chemotherapy (cytarabine 1.000 mg/m2, bid, on day 1, 3, 5 and 7, idarubicin 12 mg/m2, qd, on days 1-3) resulted in achieving complete remission. After conditioning therapy with treosulfan (day -6 to -4 at doses of 14 g/m2, qd), fludarabine (day -6 to -2 at doses of 30 mg/m2, qd) and anti-thymocyte globulin (Grafalon ; neovii Biotech, days -4 to -2 at a dose of 20 mg/kg body weight (bwt)) the patient received 6.06 x 106 CD34+ peripheral blood stem cells/kg bwt from a 24-year-old, unrelated, male, human leukocyte antigen allele mismatched 9/10, EBV seropositive, CMV seronegative donor. Prophylaxis of Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) consisted of cyclosporine (CsA), starting on day -1, combined with methotrexate (MTX). CsA was maintained at therapeutic plasma levels. Acyclovir was administered as antiviral prophylaxis.
Loads of CMV were routinely monitored once a week by PCR technique using whole-blood (for detailed information about viral copy numbers see figure 1). CMV reactivation with 7 x 104 copies/ml was detected on day +43. Despite a change in antiviral medication to GCV at a dosage of 5 mg/kg bwt, bid, viral load kept on increasing up to 4.8 x 105 copies/ml after ten days of initiation of treatment. The viral load finally decreased underuse of FOS at a dosage of 90 mg/kg bwt bid and early but slow reduction of immunosuppressive therapy. Additionally, we administered 1 ml/kg bwt CMV Immunoglobulins (Cytotect  CP Biotest) on day +48. The CMV-treatment schedule is given in figure 1.
Due to delayed engraftment, several bone marrow aspirates were obtained, revealing increasing chimerism from 89% on day +30, 94% on day +54 up to 100% since day +82. As a result of minimal residual disease (MRD) of AML, we quickly reduced CsA. This resulted in decreasing leukemia associated molecular markers. However, CMV copy numbers raised from 1.5-3.5 x 103 copies/ml up to 3.9 x 105 copies/ml (please refer to figure 1, day 88 et seq.) and EBV reactivation (up to 0.83-1.65 x 105) despite sustained administration of FOS. Except for nephrotoxicity, no clinical side effects of FOS occurred. EBV reactivation was effectively treated with the monoclonal CD20 antibody rituximab throughout four weeks, at a dosage of 375 mg/m2 per week (Figure 1). 
At the same time, CMV copy number increased despite the continuation of treatment with FOS. Therefore, we attempted to exclude the existence of viral mutations by DNA sequencing following nested PCR amplification. With modifications, amplification and sequencing of UL56 were performed as described previously. The method allows identification of the UL56 coding region from amino acids 1 to 620. Albeit clinically expected, verifying the viral kinase UL97 and the viral polymerase UL54 as wild-type, no mutation conveying resistance was demonstrable. A retrospective analysis revealed no mutation in the viral terminase region UL56, too. As a consequence, administration of CsA was terminated at day +118.
Based on delayed engraftment, drug-associated myelotoxicity and nephrotoxicity, and prolonged hospitalization, we initiated LMV at a dose of 480 mg qd. The patient was discharged from stationary treatment, and LMV resulted in an increase first, and within a treatment period of five weeks in an impressive decrease of CMV copy numbers (from 90.000 at LMV initiation up to 1.000.000 to 8.200 per milliliter) as already reported for other cases. Due to the occurrence of herpes stomatitis, acyclovir was administered, adapted to renal function. Simultaneously, the patient developed a maculopapular rash on day +155 affecting the lower arms and the abdominal skin. Subsequently, a skin biopsy was performed, and suspected acute GvHD confirmed by histology.
Consequently, prednisolone 25 mg qd was started at day +165 in the absence of any signs of gastrointestinal or liver involvement of GvHD and tapered without recurrence of acute GvHD afterward. However, under the intensified immunosuppression the viral load increased up to 410.000 copies per milliliter despite the continuation of LMV treatment. Upon genotyping, mutation C325Y (cytosine at amino acid position 325 was substituted by tyrosine) was detected within UL56 which is supposed to confer high-level resistance to LMV. 
Consequently, administration of LMV was stopped, and FOS application, adapted to renal function, 3.000 mg bid commenced once again in combination with administration of CMV-hyperimmune globulin. This change in antiviral treatment resulted in a decrease of viral loads. On day +292, the patient is alive in complete remission of AML without signs of GvHD or clinical signs of active CMV infection, still receiving FOS without any side effects. Of note, during the whole course of treatment, CMV was below 1 x 103 copies/ml only until day +42, between day +63 and +67 as well as day +75 and +84 after HSCT.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old CMV-seropositive female with high-risk acute myeloid leukemia underwent 9/10 HLA-mismatched unrelated-donor allogeneic stem cell transplantation (D-/R+) and developed multi-relapsing CMV reactivation, EBV reactivation, acute skin GVHD, and UL56 C325Y-mutant letermovir resistance.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In first complete remission of ELN high-risk AML (trisomy 8, ASXL1, EZH2, and NPM1 mutations) after cytarabine/idarubicin chemotherapy, the patient underwent 9/10 HLA-mismatched unrelated-donor allogeneic PBSC transplantation (6.06 x 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg from a 24-year-old male EBV+/CMV- donor; recipient CMV+) following treosulfan, fludarabine, and ATG (Grafalon) conditioning with cyclosporine A, methotrexate, and acyclovir prophylaxis. She experienced delayed engraftment/MRD requiring cyclosporine reduction (terminated day +118), recurrent whole-blood CMV reactivation starting on day +43, EBV reactivation around day +88, herpes stomatitis, and biopsy-proven acute maculopapular skin GVHD on day +155 (treated with prednisolone 25 mg/day from day +165).
subjective.past_medical_history: High-risk acute myeloid leukemia (trisomy 8, ASXL1, EZH2, NPM1 mutated) in first complete remission status post 9/10 HLA-mismatched unrelated-donor allogeneic PBSC transplantation (CMV serostatus D-/R+, EBV D+).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for herpes stomatitis and day +155 maculopapular rash on the forearms and abdomen; negative for gastrointestinal or hepatic GVHD symptoms; developed foscarnet-related nephrotoxicity.

objective.physical_examination: Herpes stomatitis and maculopapular skin rash on the lower arms and abdomen on day +155.
objective.routine_investigations: Foscarnet-associated nephrotoxicity and antiviral myelotoxicity.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial bone marrow aspirates showed donor chimerism rising from 89% (day +30) and 94% (day +54) to 100% from day +82 onward with declining AML MRD markers. Weekly whole-blood quantitative CMV PCR documented complex viral dynamics: initial reactivation on day +43 at 7 x 10^4 copies/mL rising on ganciclovir to 4.8 x 10^5 copies/mL (day +53), declining on foscarnet to 1.5-3.5 x 10^3 copies/mL before surging on day +88 to 3.9 x 10^5 copies/mL alongside EBV reactivation (0.83-1.65 x 10^5 copies/mL); initial nested PCR sequencing confirmed wild-type UL97, UL54, and UL56. On letermovir (started at 90,000 copies/mL), CMV load transiently rose to 1,000,000 copies/mL before falling to 8,200 copies/mL over 5 weeks, but rebounded to 410,000 copies/mL after starting prednisolone on day +165; repeat UL56 sequencing (amino acids 1-620) identified an emergent UL56 C325Y mutation conferring high-level letermovir resistance. Day +155 skin biopsy confirmed acute cutaneous GVHD.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of refractory/relapsing cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation in a high-risk D-/R+ allogeneic HSCT recipient complicated by emergent UL56 C325Y terminase mutation conferring high-level resistance to letermovir during steroid therapy for acute skin GVHD, plus concurrent EBV reactivation. Initial clinical ganciclovir non-response (day +43 to +53) and day +88 relapse (wild-type UL97/UL54/UL56) were managed with IV foscarnet (90 mg/kg BID), CMV hyperimmune globulin (Cytotect 1 mL/kg on day +48), and cyclosporine withdrawal (day +118), while EBV reactivation cleared with 4 weekly doses of rituximab (375 mg/m2). Off-label letermovir (480 mg daily) suppressed CMV DNA to 8,200 copies/mL over 5 weeks until prednisolone (25 mg/day on day +165 for skin GVHD) triggered viral rebound (410,000 copies/mL) and selection of the UL56 C325Y mutation; letermovir was stopped and renal-adjusted IV foscarnet (3,000 mg BID) plus CMV hyperimmune globulin controlled viral loads, keeping the patient alive in complete AML remission without GVHD or symptomatic CMV disease at day +292.

raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old male with hypertension and atrial fibrillation was admitted to the University of Rochester Medical Center with fever, chest pain, and dyspnea. A CT Chest angiogram revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no embolic disease. He was admitted to the general medicine service and was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. His fevers persisted for the first three days. On hospital day 6 his antimicrobial therapy was broadened to vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and azithromycin due to worsening hypoxia and was continued for 10 days. He was found to be HIV positive with a RNA level greater than 500,000 copies/ml and a CD4 count of 15. On hospital day 9 he required intubation for worsening hypoxia. He underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with pneumocystis jiroveci identified on PCR testing and microscopy and CMV was identified on viral cell culture. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and glucocorticoid therapy was empirically started and he completed 21 days of therapy.
On hospital day 23 he was extubated. Due to increasing lethargy he was reintubated on hospital day 27 for airway protection. After intubation he developed intermittent fevers for 25 days with altered mental status. Vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were restarted. An initial work up for encephalopathy was performed with normal ammonia (18 mumol/L), normal CT head with and without contrast, and negative evaluation for infection including blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool cultures. An electroencephalogram was performed and showed moderate encephalopathy without epileptiform abnormalities. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 33 after HIV genotype testing returned. There was concern for drug fever from dexmedetomidine and piperacillin-tazobactam and both drugs were discontinued on hospital day 32 and 37. After no improvement in fevers a MRI of the head with and without contrast was performed on hospital day 37 and showed acute infarcts in the bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia. Neurology felt it was embolic phenomena from atrial fibrillation. He also developed persistent, nonbloody loose stools with negative bacterial and parasite stool studies so serum CMV PCR was checked on hospital day 43 showing 2,623,108 IU/mL. With new nuchal rigidity on exam and right lower extremity weakness a lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 44 after another head CT was normal. Spinal fluid analysis was consistent with encephalitis and CSF PCR for CMV DNA was positive (Table 1). After serum CMV PCR positivity returned ganciclovir was started on hospital day 47. MRI imaging of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine showed extensive linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the lower spinal cord, conus medullaris, and roots of the cauda equine with thickening of the roots concerning for radiculomyelitis (Figure 1). At this point his mental status remained poor with quadriparesis and flaccid paraplegia. He underwent tracheostomy on hospital day 50.
Serum CMV DNA PCR and HIV RNA PCR were checked weekly to monitor treatment efficacy, and both decreased significantly on treatment (Table 2). No further lumbar punctures were performed. He received 30 days of IV ganciclovir 469mg twice daily before decreasing to IV ganciclovir 469mg daily after two consecutive weeks of undetectable serum CMV DNA PCR, hospital day 76. He received IV ganciclovir daily for 85 days total, before switching to oral valganciclovir 900mg daily. The serum HIV RNA PCR continued to decline and was 49 copies/mL on hospital day 128 (96 days after initiation of HAART therapy). He remained on mechanical ventilation and was able to move his upper extremities with assistance and could answer simple questions. He never regained function in his lower extremities. After minimal improvement he opted to stop mechanical ventilation and passed away on hospital day 147.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presented with fever, chest pain, and dyspnea, and subsequently developed prolonged encephalopathy, persistent fevers, loose stools, nuchal rigidity, and flaccid paraplegia/quadriparesis during hospitalization.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted for fever, chest pain, and dyspnea unresponsive to empiric community-acquired pneumonia antibiotics (ceftriaxone/doxycycline, then vancomycin/piperacillin-tazobactam/azithromycin), the patient was newly diagnosed with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 15 cells/uL, HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL), intubated on hospital day 9 for hypoxic respiratory failure, and treated for 21 days with TMP-SMX and corticosteroids for BAL-confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (with BAL viral culture also growing CMV). Extubated on day 23, he was re-intubated on day 27 for progressive lethargy, had 25 days of persistent fevers and encephalopathy despite starting HAART (elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) on day 33, and developed nonbloody loose stools, nuchal rigidity, right lower extremity weakness, and subsequent flaccid paraplegia and quadriparesis by days 43-47.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: fever, chest pain, and dyspnea. Subsequent ICU course (days 27-47): lethargy, altered mental status, persistent fever, nonbloody loose diarrhea, neck stiffness, and progressive four-limb weakness/flaccid paraplegia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intubation (day 9). Day 27-47 exam: persistent fever, poor mental status/encephalopathy, new nuchal rigidity, and right lower extremity weakness progressing to flaccid paraplegia and quadriparesis (tracheostomy performed on day 50).
objective.routine_investigations: Normal serum ammonia (18 umol/L); negative blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool bacterial/parasitic cultures. EEG showed moderate diffuse encephalopathy without epileptiform activity.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline HIV-1 RNA was >500,000 copies/mL (declining to 49 copies/mL on day 128) and CD4 count was 15 cells/uL. Admission chest CT angiogram showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without PE. Day 9 bronchoscopy with BAL was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (by PCR and microscopy) and cytomegalovirus (CMV, by viral cell culture). Head CTs were normal; day 37 brain MRI showed acute cardioembolic infarcts in the bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia. Day 43 quantitative serum CMV DNA PCR was 2,623,108 IU/mL. Day 44 lumbar puncture CSF analysis confirmed encephalitis with positive CSF CMV DNA PCR. Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine MRI demonstrated extensive linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the lower spinal cord, conus medullaris, and cauda equina nerve roots with nerve root thickening consistent with CMV polyradiculomyelitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis and lumbosacral polyradiculomyelitis (confirmed on days 43-47 by serum CMV DNA viral load of 2,623,108 IU/mL, positive CSF CMV DNA PCR, and conus medullaris/cauda equina leptomeningeal enhancement and nerve root thickening on spine MRI, following untreated day 9 BAL CMV culture positivity during PJP corticosteroid therapy) in a patient with newly diagnosed AIDS (CD4 15 cells/uL) and cardioembolic thalamic/basal ganglia strokes. Treated with intravenous ganciclovir starting on hospital day 47 (469 mg twice daily for 30 days until 2 consecutive weekly negative serum CMV PCRs by day 76, then 469 mg once daily completing 85 total days of IV ganciclovir before transitioning to oral valganciclovir 900 mg daily) alongside HAART. Although serum CMV DNA became undetectable, HIV RNA fell to 49 copies/mL, and mental status and assisted upper-extremity movement partially improved, his lower-extremity paraplegia and ventilator dependence persisted; he elected to withdraw mechanical ventilation and died on hospital day 147.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old male with multiple myeloma on his eighth cycle of chemotherapy with bortezomib, lenalidomide (recently decreased to 10 mg po daily from 25 mg po daily), and dexamethasone presented with a two-week history of worsening blurriness and floaters in his right eye. An outside provider noted panuveitis and retinal whitening on examination. Anterior chamber paracentesis was negative for CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and Toxoplasmosis. Oral valacyclovir and topical steroids and cycloplegics were started for presumed acute retinal necrosis, and the patient was referred to our institution for further diagnostic work-up and management. Of note, recent serum laboratory values revealed a normal white blood cell count (9.41 k/microL; range 4.5-11 k/microL) and neutrophilic profile (71.0%; range 39-69%) with negative CMV antigen and aerobic blood culture; lambda light chain immunoglobulins were significantly elevated (67.29 mg/L, range 5.7-26.3 mg/L) and alpha-2 globulin proteins were abnormally high on serum electrophoresis (0.93 g/dL, range 0.58-0.84 g/dL) as expected given his disease.
Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/60 in the right eye, 20/20 in the left. Pupils and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit lamp examination of the right eye revealed mild anterior chamber flare without cell, mild cataract, and 3+ cell in the anterior vitreous. Dilated funduscopic examination revealed vitreous haze, diffuse vascular sheathing, and a poorly-defined area of inferotemporal retinal whitening without associated hemorrhage (Figure 1). The left eye was normal. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right eye showed no significant abnormalities aside from overlying hyperreflective vitreous debris (Figure 2). Fluorescein angiography demonstrated irregular vascular filling and blockage from vitreous debris (Figure 3).
Given the previous negative anterior chamber tap, worsening clinical exam, and high suspicion for infectious retinitis, the decision was made to proceed with a diagnostic vitrectomy. Diluted and undiluted vitreous biopsy were obtained via a 23-gauge pars plana vitrectomy. Intraoperatively, extensive retinal whitening and granular necrosis were observed along with diffuse vascular sheathing and perivascular inflammatory aggregates (Figure 4). Endolaser was placed 360 degrees prophylactically. The vitreous biopsy was sent for gram stain, cytology (to rule out malignant infiltration), fungal culture, Toxoplasmosis, AFB, VZV, EBV, CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, and RPR testing.
On postoperative day 2, the vitreous PCR returned positive for CMV; all other tests were negative. The patient was switched from oral valacyclovir to valganciclovir 900 mg po twice daily. By postoperative day 3, the patient's visual acuity declined to 20/200 and there was an increase in anterior chamber cell. Hence, intravitreal foscarnet (2.4 mg/0.1 cc) was injected. At the postoperative week 1 visit, visual acuity had not improved, but the area of retinitis appeared less active (Figure 5). Repeat intravitreal foscarnet was given. Improvement continued over the first month with complete resolution of the patient's uveitis, vasculitis, and retinitis. By postoperative month 2, BCVA had improved to 20/63 without evidence of active disease. Five months after the vitreous biopsy, the patient remained without signs of intraocular infection with BCVA 20/50, mostly limited by cataract. Following cataract extraction one year later, his visual acuity was 20/25 with stable fundus findings (Figure 6).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male with multiple myeloma presented with a 2-week history of worsening blurred vision and floaters in his right eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Receiving his eighth cycle of bortezomib, lenalidomide (recently reduced from 25 mg to 10 mg PO daily), and dexamethasone for lambda light-chain multiple myeloma, the patient developed 2 weeks of progressive right-eye blurriness and floaters. An outside ophthalmologist noted right panuveitis and retinal whitening, found a negative anterior chamber paracentesis PCR panel (negative for CMV, HSV-1/2, VZV, and Toxoplasma), started oral valacyclovir, topical steroids, and cycloplegics for presumed acute retinal necrosis, and referred him to our institution.
subjective.past_medical_history: Lambda light-chain multiple myeloma on cycle 8 of bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone chemotherapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2 weeks of worsening right-eye blurred vision and floaters. Home medications: bortezomib, lenalidomide 10 mg daily, dexamethasone, oral valacyclovir, topical corticosteroids, and topical cycloplegics.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic exam: best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) 20/60 OD (declining transiently to 20/200 on post-vitrectomy day 3 before recovering to 20/63 at month 2, 20/50 at month 5, and 20/25 after cataract extraction at 1 year) and 20/20 OS; normal pupils and IOPs OU; left eye normal. Right eye slit-lamp exam showed mild anterior chamber flare without cells, mild cataract, and 3+ anterior vitreous cells; dilated fundoscopy OD revealed vitreous haze, diffuse retinal vascular sheathing, and a poorly defined inferotemporal area of retinal whitening without retinal hemorrhage.
objective.routine_investigations: Recent labs: WBC 9.41 K/uL (ref 4.5-11 K/uL), neutrophils 71.0% (ref 39-69%), negative serum CMV antigenemia, negative aerobic blood cultures, elevated serum free lambda light chains (67.29 mg/L, ref 5.7-26.3 mg/L), and elevated alpha-2 globulins on SPEP (0.93 g/dL, ref 0.58-0.84 g/dL).
objective.advanced_workup: Outside anterior chamber aqueous paracentesis was negative for CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and Toxoplasma. Right-eye spectral-domain OCT showed hyperreflective overlying vitreous debris; fluorescein angiography showed irregular retinal vascular filling and blockage from vitreous debris. Diagnostic 23-gauge pars plana vitrectomy (with prophylactic 360-degree endolaser retinopexy) demonstrated extensive intraoperative granular retinal whitening/necrosis, diffuse vascular sheathing, and perivascular inflammatory aggregates; vitreous biopsy PCR returned positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) on postoperative day 2 and negative for HSV-1/2, VZV, EBV, Toxoplasma, AFB, fungal/bacterial cultures, RPR, and malignant cytology.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of unilateral right-eye cytomegalovirus (CMV) panuveitis and necrotizing retinitis in a non-neutropenic multiple myeloma patient on bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone, confirmed by diagnostic 23-gauge pars plana vitrectomy fluid CMV PCR positivity despite a prior false-negative anterior chamber paracentesis and negative serum CMV antigenemia. Switched from oral valacyclovir to oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) and treated with two weekly intravitreal foscarnet injections (2.4 mg/0.1 mL), achieving complete resolution of uveitis, retinal vasculitis, and retinitis within 1 month and final BCVA of 20/25 following cataract extraction 1 year later.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old female with the second relapse of B-ALL received chimeric antigen T-cell (CART) salvage therapy, followed by co-transplantation of haploidentical stem cells and unrelated cord blood in September 2021. The patient had a previous disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis infection during the first relapse in July 2020. However, she recovered well after treatment with anti-tuberculosis drugs, including isoniazid (10 mg/kg/day), rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day), and levofloxacin (10 mg/kg/day) from July 2020 to April 2021, and continued to receive oral isoniazid prophylaxis until 3 days prior to HSCT. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed no residual tuberculosis lesions and interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) release assays was negative prior to transplantation. Furthermore, there was no evidence of fungal infection during chemotherapy or prior to HSCT.
The patient received a myeloablative conditioning regimen consisting of cyclophosphamide, busulfan, fludarabine, and thiotepa without total body irradiation.
