Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. He had thrush under his tongue and on the palate. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Heart rate was regular with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops by auscultation. There were no palpable thrills. He had equal chest rise bilaterally. Breath sounds were diminished throughout, with rales and dullness to percussion in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Sensory and motor examination was grossly intact.
Laboratory data revealed white blood count 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL, sodium 131 mmol/L potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, carbon dioxide 17 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 155 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, bicarbonate 19.1 mmol/L, and pO2 74.5 mmHg on 3 L nasal cannula. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities (Figure 1). He was found to be HIV positive with CD4 count of <5 cells/cc and viral load of 1,180,000 copies. Bronchoalveolar lavage was preformed; Grocott's methenamine silver stain of the washings demonstrated Pneumocystis jiroveci (Figure 2). He received antibiotics and steroids with gradual improvement.
On hospital day 14, he became confused and acutely developed nystagmus with both a horizontal and prominent vertical component. He was also found to have ataxia with finger to nose testing and difficulty sitting up without support. Considering his immunosuppressed state, infectious and neoplastic etiologies were the primary diagnostic considerations. Lumbar puncture revealed clear CSF, normal opening pressure, and normal cell counts. Polymerase chain reactions for Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and John Cunningham (JC) virus were negative. Nontreponemal serological screening for syphilis (VDRL), toxoplasmosis antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative. CT of the head did not show any intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or other acute findings. MRI of the brain revealed a slight increase in T2 signal within the medial aspect of thalamus bilaterally (Figure 3). After excluding infection and neoplasm, the clinical diagnosis of Wernicke's encephalopathy was made. Intravenous thiamine was administered resulting in resolution of symptoms, which confirmed the diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnea and productive cough, accompanied by decreased appetite and a 50-pound weight loss over 5 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy, the patient developed progressive shortness of breath, productive cough over 4 months, and anorexia with a 50-pound weight loss over 5 months. Following admission, diagnosis of AIDS and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and gradual respiratory improvement on antibiotics and corticosteroids, he acutely developed confusion, horizontal and prominent vertical nystagmus, finger-to-nose dysmetria, and truncal ataxia on hospital day 14.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known prior medical or surgical history. Social history: factory janitor, former US Army soldier stationed in Hawaii for 4 years (visited a female commercial sex worker several times while in Hawaii), currently in a long-term heterosexual relationship; quit smoking tobacco 2 months prior due to dyspnea, rare alcohol use, no illicit drug use. Family history unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 4 months of progressive dyspnea and productive cough, 5 months of anorexia and 50-pound weight loss, oral thrush, and hospital day 14 acute confusion, oscillopsia/nystagmus, and gait/truncal ataxia. No home medications.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: temperature 99.9 °F, blood pressure 128/83 mmHg, heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 92% on room air; awake, alert, in moderate respiratory distress; intact extraocular movements without nystagmus or icterus; sublingual and palatal oral thrush; no lymphadenopathy; regular tachycardia without murmurs; diminished breath sounds throughout with bibasilar rales and dullness to percussion; intact baseline neurological exam. Hospital day 14 neurological exam: acute confusion, horizontal and prominent vertical nystagmus, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and severe truncal ataxia (unable to sit unsupported).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, CO2 17 mmol/L, BUN 155 mg/dL, serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL; ABG on 3 L nasal cannula: pH 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, bicarbonate 19.1 mmol/L, pO2 74.5 mmHg. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities. HIV test positive.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was <5 cells/mm3 and plasma HIV viral load was 1,180,000 copies/mL. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated Pneumocystis jirovecii. Day 14 lumbar puncture showed clear CSF with normal opening pressure and normal cell counts; CSF PCRs for EBV, HSV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and JC virus were negative, and VDRL, Toxoplasma antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative. Head CT was negative for mass or hemorrhage; brain MRI revealed symmetric mild T2 hyperintensity in the bilateral medial thalami.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with newly identified advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 <5 cells/mm3, HIV viral load 1,180,000 copies/mL), Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed on BAL GMS stain), severe renal failure, and non-alcoholic Wernicke's encephalopathy on hospital day 14 (confirmed by classic triad of confusion, horizontal/vertical nystagmus, and ataxia, bilateral medial thalamic T2 hyperintensity on brain MRI, exclusion of CNS opportunistic infections including CMV, EBV, HSV, JCV, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, and neurosyphilis on CSF analysis, and rapid clinical resolution following parenteral thiamine). Treated with antibiotics and corticosteroids for PJP and intravenous thiamine for Wernicke's encephalopathy with complete resolution of neurological symptoms.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old man had fever, headache, general malaise, and bilateral swelling of the parotid glands. Three days after symptom onset, he was admitted to our hospital because of impaired consciousness. On admission, the patient was drowsy. Neurologic examinations revealed nuchal stiffness, but muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Plantar responses were flexor. The pupils were equal and normally reactive to light. No cerebellar symptoms were present. Laboratory examinations revealed mild thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia. Serum antibodies against herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, Epstein-Barr, and mumps viruses, cytomegalovirus, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were not elevated. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed pleocytosis (70/mul, predominantly lymphocytes) with a markedly increased protein level (526 mg/dl). Herpes simplex virus DNA was not detected in CSF. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the brain revealed an abnormal signal in the left medial temporal lobe (Fig. 1). There were no epileptiform discharges on the electroencephalogram. Several days later, the patient became comatose and received artificial ventilation because of respiratory failure with hypercapnia. His consciousness gradually improved after intravenous administration of aciclovir, cytarabine, and methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days). One month after symptom onset, he became alert, and repeated CSF examinations revealed no leukocytes, with a normal protein level (56 mg/dl). However, paralysis of the arms and legs developed, and the deep tendon reflexes were diminished. Sensory examinations demonstrated diminished pain sensation in the distal part of the legs and diminished vibration sense in the arms and legs. It was difficult to precisely determine the time of the onset of muscle weakness and sensory disturbance because the patient was sedated with midazolam and receiving ventilatory support. Nerve conduction studies revealed demyelinating sensory and motor polyneuropathy (Table 1). The serum contained no anti-ganglioside antibodies. The blood pressure was 143/97 mmHg in the supine position and 73/49 mmHg on 70-degree passive head-up tilt; the heart rate was 82 bpm and 86 bpm, respectively, suggesting orthostatic hypotension (OH). He also had urinary retention and constipation. The R-R interval variation at rest was decreased. On 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) myocardial scintigraphy, the MIBG washout rate was slightly decreased (42.2%), indicating mild cardiac sympathetic involvement. Intraocular instillation of a 1.25% epinephrine solution provoked hypersensitive mydriasis, suggesting postganglionic autonomic failure.
The results of these clinical, laboratory, electro-physiologic, and imaging studies indicated somatic motor and sensory demyelinating neuropathy accompanied by sympathetic and parasympathetic dysfunction, findings consistent with AASMN. The patient was given IVIg at a dose of 0.4 g/kg body weight/day for 5 days. Motor and sensory symptoms resolved markedly and promptly within 2 months (Fig. 2). Deep tendon reflexes in the arms and legs continued to be weak. Repeated nerve conduction studies revealed slight improvements in motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities in the upper and lower extremities. OH, urinary disturbance, and constipation resolved gradually over the course of the next 2 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of fever, headache, general malaise, and bilateral parotid gland swelling followed by impaired consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days after developing fever, headache, general malaise, and bilateral parotid swelling, the patient was admitted with drowsiness. Several days into hospitalization, he progressed to coma and hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Upon regaining alertness 1 month after symptom onset following acyclovir, cytarabine, and pulse methylprednisolone therapy, he was found to have four-limb paralysis, sensory loss, orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, and constipation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: fever, headache, general malaise, bilateral parotid gland swelling, and drowsiness. At 1 month: quadriparesis, distal leg hypoalgesia, four-limb decreased vibration sense, orthostatic dizziness/hypotension, urinary retention, and constipation.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: drowsy, nuchal stiffness, normal muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes (DTRs), flexor plantar responses, equal reactive pupils, and no cerebellar signs. At 1 month after onset: alert, paralysis of arms and legs, diminished DTRs in all four limbs, diminished pain sensation in distal legs, diminished vibration sense in arms and legs, severe orthostatic hypotension on 70-degree passive head-up tilt (BP dropping from 143/97 mmHg supine [HR 82 bpm] to 73/49 mmHg tilted [HR 86 bpm]), urinary retention, constipation, and hypersensitive mydriasis upon 1.25% epinephrine ocular instillation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: mild thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia; serum antibodies against HSV, VZV, EBV, mumps virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and HIV were not elevated; serum anti-ganglioside antibodies negative. EEG showed no epileptiform discharges; ECG showed decreased R-R interval variation at rest.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (70/uL) and markedly elevated CSF protein (526 mg/dL) with negative CSF HSV DNA (repeat CSF at 1 month: 0 leukocytes, protein 56 mg/dL). Brain MRI showed an abnormal signal in the left medial temporal lobe. Nerve conduction studies at 1 month demonstrated demyelinating sensory and motor polyneuropathy. Cardiac 123I-MIBG myocardial scintigraphy showed a mildly decreased washout rate (42.2%) consistent with cardiac sympathetic involvement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with meningoencephalitis followed by acute autonomic and sensory-motor neuropathy (AASMN; confirmed by demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy on nerve conduction studies, severe orthostatic hypotension on tilt-table testing, postganglionic pupillary supersensitivity to 1.25% epinephrine, abnormal 123I-MIBG cardiac scintigraphy, and exclusion of HSV, VZV, EBV, mumps, CMV, HIV, and anti-ganglioside antibodies). Meningoencephalitis and coma resolved after mechanical ventilation, IV acyclovir, cytarabine, and pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days). Subsequent AASMN was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days), resulting in marked recovery of motor, sensory, orthostatic, urinary, and gastrointestinal autonomic symptoms within 2 months.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old primigravida started with pain and mild heaviness in the both lower limbs distally associated with occasional pins and needles sensation in 35th week of pregnancy. Her symptoms were progressive. Over the next 10 days, the patient noticed knee buckling with frequent falls and difficulty in sitting and standing from supine position. At the end of 36th week, an emergency LSCS (lower segment caesarian section) was performed for decreased fetal heart rate. LSCS was uneventful and a healthy baby was born. Second post-partum day, the patient was discharged. On third post-partum day, the patient complained of weakness all the four limbs (in addition to persisting symptoms), more in lower limbs and was not able to maintain the erect posture. In this state, the patient was brought to our accident and emergency department. A detailed history was taken which revealed initiation of symptoms during third trimester of pregnancy without any preceding illness. Subsequent clinical examination revealed sinus tachycardia, fluctuating hypertension, power of 4/5 in upper limbs, 3/5 in lower limbs, hypotonia, areflexia (lower limbs), flexor plantar response, and mild involvement of all the modalities of sensation. A working diagnosis of GBS was made and all other investigations including nerve conduction studies, arterial blood gases, electrolytes, and later cerebrospinal fluid analysis were planned.
Arterial blood gas analysis showed pO2=89 mmHg, saturation = 94.6%, pCO2=42 mmHg, and pH = 7.39. Serum potassium was 4.1 meq/L, sodium 136 meq/L and bicarbonate 25 meq/L. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia and routine blood chemistry was normal. Serological tests for campylobacter jejuni, EBV, cytomegalovirus, and mycoplasma pneumonae were negative. Electrophysiological studies revealed decreased amplitude of compound action potentials in median and common peronial nerves with decreased conduction velocity and abnormal F waves. After 7 days, lumbar puncture was performed and cerebrospinal fluid chemistry revealed raised protein of 7.8 g/L and normal cell count, confirming the diagnosis. The patient received treatment in the form of physiotherapy and close observation of symptoms and signs to which she rapidly responded with respect to power and sense of well-being over next 72 h, without the intervention of immunomodulating drugs. Sinus tachycardia and episodic hypertension was treated with atenolol. The patient was discharged after 2 weeks of hospital stay with power of 5/5 in upper limbs, 4+/5 in right lower limb, and 4/5 in left lower limb with persisting areflexia in lower limbs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old primigravida presented on postpartum day 3 with progressive four-limb weakness (worse in the lower extremities) and inability to stand upright.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At 35 weeks of gestation, without any preceding infectious illness, the patient developed progressive distal lower-limb pain, mild heaviness, paresthesias ('pins and needles'), knee buckling, frequent falls, and difficulty rising from a supine or seated position. She underwent an emergency lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) at the end of week 36 for fetal bradycardia (delivering a healthy infant) and was discharged on postpartum day 2, but returned to the emergency department on postpartum day 3 with quadriparesis and inability to maintain an erect posture.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent primigravid pregnancy delivered at 36 weeks' gestation via emergency cesarean section for fetal distress; no preceding infectious illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for distal lower extremity pain, heaviness, paresthesias, progressive lower-then-upper limb weakness, falls, and inability to stand.

objective.physical_examination: Sinus tachycardia, fluctuating hypertension, hypotonia, muscle power 4/5 in bilateral upper limbs and 3/5 in bilateral lower limbs, lower-limb areflexia, flexor plantar responses, and mild pan-modal sensory impairment.
objective.routine_investigations: ABG: pH 7.39, pO2 89 mmHg, pCO2 42 mmHg, SpO2 94.6%. Electrolytes and routine biochemistry normal (potassium 4.1 mEq/L, sodium 136 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L). ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Serological tests for Campylobacter jejuni, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Nerve conduction studies demonstrated reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes, slowed conduction velocities, and abnormal F-waves in the median and common peroneal nerves. Lumbar puncture performed 7 days after presentation showed albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated CSF protein (7.8 g/L) and a normal CSF cell count.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of pregnancy/postpartum-associated Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) with autonomic dysfunction (confirmed by ascending areflexic quadriparesis, demyelinating/axonal features with abnormal F-waves on nerve conduction studies, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation [protein 7.8 g/L, normal cells]; C. jejuni, CMV, EBV, and M. pneumoniae ruled out). Managed conservatively with close monitoring, physiotherapy, and oral atenolol for autonomic sinus tachycardia and episodic hypertension, achieving rapid spontaneous motor improvement within 72 hours (without IVIG or plasmapheresis) and hospital discharge at 2 weeks with 5/5 upper limb strength and 4+/5 right / 4/5 left lower limb strength.

raw_case_text:
Ms. A, a 25-year-old married lady presented in the hospital's Walk-in clinic with the symptoms of suspiciousness and hearing voices. The symptoms had been present for about 5 years. She was very irritable and was unable to sleep. She also suffered few episodes suggestive of dissociative spells in which she would call herself "Goddess Kali." There was also occasional history of disinhibition in the form of taking of her clothes in front of her family members.
Detailed evaluation revealed delusions of persecution and second person auditory hallucination. There were no features suggestive of a mood disturbance or organicity. She was diagnosed as having unspecified non-organic psychosis on International Classification of Diseases, tenth edition. Olanzapine was started and gradually increased to 15 mg/day. The psychotic symptoms were controlled over a period of 2 months with olanzapine. After 1 month of treatment with olanzapine, the patient became pregnant (this was her first pregnancy) and sought consultation for safety of medications during the 2nd month of gestation. Considering the severity of the symptoms in the past and duration of illness, on mutual discussions, it was decided to continue olanzapine. She was referred to the obstetrics service of the hospital to keep a close watch for any untoward event. She followed-up there regularly as advised by the obstetrician. A discussion with the consulting obstetrician and review of records revealed no major untoward event during pregnancy. Careful history revealed absence of fever, rashes or other skin lesions. Antibody titers for herpes simplex, varicella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma and rubella were conducted and found to be normal. Fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels performed at the time of first consultation and repeated in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters were found to be in the normal range. On follow-up, the fetus was detected to have microcephaly on ultrasonography. No other major anomalies were detectable.
Ms. A delivered a female baby weighing 3.4 kg with microcephaly and congenital anopthalmos (bilateral) at full term. The head circumference was 30.5 cm at birth, which falls below the third percentile. The baby was seen at department of pediatrics, genetics and ophthalmology. B scan ultrasound revealed absence of ocular tissue. No additional causative factors could be elicited despite the above mentioned specialist referrals. However, detailed imaging and genetic investigations could not be done due to cost limitations. She was not on any other medication known to cause teratogenicity during the period. There was no history of any substance use or family history of congenital anomalies. Patient had adequate nutrition and rest during her pregnancy. There was no history of trauma or exposure to radiation either. The history was corroborated by the patient's mother as well as husband Although this adverse event scored only three on the the Naranjo et al. adverse drug reaction probability scale, the lower scores were due to non-applicability of some questions to this situation. For instance, the issue of improvement on discontinuation of drug or administration of antagonist obviously does not apply to this case. Similarly, re-administration and replication of the adverse effect also cannot be done in this case for ethical reasons.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old married woman with a 5-year history of unspecified non-organic psychosis conceived while taking oral olanzapine (15 mg/day) and delivered a full-term female neonate with microcephaly and bilateral congenital anophthalmos.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially presenting with 5 years of persecutory delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, irritability, insomnia, dissociative spells, and behavioral disinhibition, the patient achieved psychiatric remission over 2 months on oral olanzapine titrated to 15 mg/day. She conceived after 1 month of treatment, continued olanzapine (15 mg/day) throughout her first pregnancy following risk-benefit counseling, had an otherwise uncomplicated gestation with prenatal ultrasound detecting isolated fetal microcephaly, and delivered a full-term 3.4 kg female infant with microcephaly and bilateral congenital anophthalmos.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unspecified non-organic psychosis (ICD-10) treated with olanzapine 15 mg/day; primigravida. Social and family history: no substance use, radiation exposure, trauma, or family history of congenital anomalies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial psychiatric symptoms controlled on olanzapine; negative for gestational fever, rash, or skin lesions during pregnancy. Medication: olanzapine 15 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Full-term female newborn physical exam: birth weight 3.4 kg, head circumference 30.5 cm (<3rd percentile, microcephaly), and bilateral congenital absence of the eyes (anophthalmos).
objective.routine_investigations: Maternal TORCH antibody titers for herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Toxoplasma gondii, and rubella were normal/negative; maternal fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd trimesters were normal. Prenatal obstetric ultrasound showed fetal microcephaly without other major anomalies; neonatal ocular B-scan ultrasound confirmed complete bilateral absence of ocular tissue.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with neonatal congenital bilateral anophthalmos and microcephaly potentially associated with in utero first- through third-trimester exposure to olanzapine (15 mg/day; Naranjo score 3), after excluding maternal gestational diabetes, teratogenic co-medications, substance abuse, and congenital TORCH infections (including CMV, HSV, VZV, Toxoplasma, and rubella). Evaluated by pediatrics, genetics, and ophthalmology.

raw_case_text: An 83-year-old man presented to our hospital with acute onset of dyspnea and hypoxia. The patient had been diagnosed with CLL 14 months prior to the event, with asymptomatic lymphocytosis of 15.5 x 109/L, evidence of CD5, CD23, and CD38-positive, CD10-negative B-cell leukemia on flow cytometry, hemoglobin of 133 g/L, and platelet count of 132 x 109/L. After 8 months of watchful waiting he experienced progressive adenopathy and thrombocytopenia, which constituted indications for therapy. The patient received single-agent oral chlorambucil at the dose of 0.6 mg/kg every 14 days for 6 months. There were no significant toxicities during therapy, which resulted in a partial remission of CLL and resolution of adenopathy and cytopenias. Six weeks after the last dose of chlorambucil, the patient noted rapidly escalating dyspnea on exertion and then resting shortness of breath. There was minimal nonproductive cough and no fever, hemoptysis, or chest pain. The patient had a history of 60 pack-year tobacco use but had quit smoking over 5 years ago and had no known underlying lung disease. His medical history was significant for diabetes mellitus, hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, glaucoma, and gout. Ambulatory medications included metformin, doxazosin, and latanoprost. On admission the patient was tachypneic and hypoxic with a resting pulse oximetry of 85% on 2 liters of oxygen but without fever, rales, or wheezing on examination. The neutrophil count was normal (5.3 x 109/L, reference range 2.0-10.0 x 109/L) as were serum brain natriuretic peptide (44 pg/mL, reference range <100 pg/mL), lactate dehydrogenase (116 units/L, reference range: 98-192 units/L), urine Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila antigen tests, and cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM serologies. A 2D echocardiogram revealed normal systolic and diastolic function without any significant valvular dysfunction or pericardial effusion. A computerized tomography (CT) angiogram of the chest on admission ruled out a pulmonary embolism but demonstrated bilateral basal interlobular septal thickening compatible with interstitial pneumonitis. A staging CT scan performed 1 year earlier did not show any evidence of interstitial pneumonitis (Figure 1). No infectious cause was found for the patient's symptoms and there was no improvement with azithromycin. The patient declined a diagnostic open lung biopsy, and a clinical diagnosis of drug-induced interstitial pneumonitis was made. He was treated empirically with prednisone 1 mg/kg and albuterol inhalers which led to a rapid resolution of his dyspnea and hypoxia. Prednisone was tapered off over 2 months. Pulmonary function tests performed after discontinuation of steroids revealed the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) of 73%, vital capacity of 2.63 L (74% predicted), total lung capacity of 5.23 L (121% predicted), and diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide, hemoglobin corrected, of 19.29 mL/min/mmHg (96% predicted), interpreted as consistent with normal aging process. Although the patient's respiratory function returned to baseline, a repeat high-resolution CT scan 3 months later showed persistent subpleural fibrosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with acute-onset, rapidly escalating dyspnea and hypoxia 6 weeks after completing a 6-month course of oral chlorambucil.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 14 months prior with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and treated after 8 months of watchful waiting with single-agent oral chlorambucil (0.6 mg/kg every 14 days for 6 months, achieving partial remission), the patient developed rapidly progressive exertional and then resting dyspnea with minimal nonproductive cough 6 weeks after his final chlorambucil dose.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CD5+, CD23+, CD38+, CD10- B-cell CLL) status post 6 months of chlorambucil; diabetes mellitus, hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, glaucoma, and gout; no known underlying lung disease. Social history: former smoker (60 pack-years, quit >5 years prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for rapidly escalating exertional and resting dyspnea and minimal nonproductive cough. Pertinent negatives: no fever, hemoptysis, or chest pain. Home medications: metformin, doxazosin, and latanoprost.

objective.physical_examination: Tachypneic and hypoxic with resting SpO2 85% on 2 L/min supplemental oxygen; afebrile, with clear lung auscultation without rales or wheezing.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline CLL diagnosis labs (14 months prior): lymphocytes 15.5 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 132 x 10^9/L. Admission labs: absolute neutrophil count 5.3 x 10^9/L (ref 2.0-10.0 x 10^9/L), BNP 44 pg/mL (ref <100 pg/mL), LDH 116 U/L (ref 98-192 U/L), negative urine Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila antigens, and negative cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG and IgM serologies. 2D transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal biventricular systolic/diastolic function without valvular disease or pericardial effusion. Follow-up PFTs after steroid taper: FEV1/FVC 73%, VC 2.63 L (74% predicted), TLC 5.23 L (121% predicted), hemoglobin-corrected DLCO 19.29 mL/min/mmHg (96% predicted).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT angiogram ruled out pulmonary embolism and demonstrated new bilateral basal interlobular septal thickening compatible with interstitial pneumonitis (absent on staging chest CT 1 year prior). Follow-up HRCT at 3 months showed persistent subpleural fibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Clinical diagnosis of chlorambucil-induced interstitial pneumonitis in a patient with CLL, confirmed by characteristic bilateral basal interlobular septal thickening on chest CT, exclusion of heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and infectious etiologies (negative CMV IgG/IgM, S. pneumoniae and L. pneumophila urinary antigens, and lack of response to empiric azithromycin; open lung biopsy declined), and rapid resolution of dyspnea and hypoxia upon initiating oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day tapered over 2 months) and albuterol inhalers. Respiratory function returned to normal age-adjusted baseline on post-treatment PFTs.

raw_case_text: We present the case of an 18-month-old female patient with PB following pneumonia. At 2 months of age, the patient was hospitalized due to pneumonia. At 6 months of age, she underwent a palliative bidirectional Glenn procedure (Fontan-type) due to CHD (double-inlet and double-outlet ventricle with common atrioventricular canal). The perioperative period was uneventful. Echocardiography at 12 and 18 months of age showed proper heart function (ejection fraction, 67%). At 18 months of age, she was again hospitalized due to pneumonia that remained unresolved after three courses of antibiotics in the home setting. Infiltration and atelectasis of the left upper lobe had been clinically suspected (because of dullness and diminished breath sounds over that region) and was confirmed by a chest X-ray. Blood pressure was normal. However, SpO2 was approximately 50% (having previously been at 70-80%). In addition, hypogammaglobulinemia was detected. In the differential diagnosis, we excluded atopy, cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency disorders, viral infections (with cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and pneumotropic viruses), and fungal infections (Aspergillus sp. and Candida sp.). Within a few days, her coughs were more productive and there was expectoration of small mucoid casts. Despite antibiotic treatment, gamma-globulin replacement therapy, oxygen therapy, and intensive chest physiotherapy, as well as the use of nebulized bronchodilators and mucolytics, there was no clinical improvement. On post-admission day 17, fiberoptic bronchoscopy (FB) revealed complete obliteration of the left bronchus. Application of suction allowed to remove bronchial casts, followed by bronchial lavage of that region (Figure 1). Cultures of the bronchial lavage fluid were negative for fungi and bacteria. Microscopic analysis of the material collected revealed type-1 bronchial casts. After the bronchoscopy, the inflammation of the left lobes was resolved. Treatment with azithromycin, systemic and inhaled steroids, () and enalapril maleate was initiated, as was the use of nebulized 3% NaCl solution plus a bronchodilator. One week after treatment initiation, a control FB revealed only small fragments of casts, which were removed easily and completely. On post-admission day 33, the patient was discharged.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-month-old girl with a history of bidirectional Glenn palliation for complex congenital heart disease presented with persistent pneumonia unresponsive to three outpatient antibiotic courses, worsening cyanosis, and productive cough with expectoration of mucoid bronchial casts.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having undergone an uneventful palliative bidirectional Glenn procedure at 6 months of age for double-inlet/double-outlet ventricle with common atrioventricular canal, the patient was hospitalized at 18 months of age for left upper lobe pneumonia and atelectasis that failed three home antibiotic courses, accompanied by a drop in oxygen saturation from her 70-80% baseline to ~50% and subsequent expectoration of small mucoid bronchial casts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Complex congenital heart disease (double-inlet and double-outlet ventricle with common atrioventricular canal) status post palliative bidirectional Glenn procedure at 6 months of age (LVEF 67% on 12- and 18-month echocardiograms); prior hospitalization for pneumonia at 2 months of age.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent productive cough, expectoration of small mucoid casts, and worsening hypoxemia/cyanosis.

objective.physical_examination: Normal blood pressure, severe hypoxemia with SpO2 ~50% (baseline 70-80%), and dullness to percussion with diminished breath sounds over the left upper lung lobe.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray confirmed left upper lobe infiltration and atelectasis. Echocardiography showed preserved ventricular function (EF 67%). Hypogammaglobulinemia was detected; diagnostic workup excluded atopy, cystic fibrosis, primary immunodeficiency disorders, viral infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], Epstein-Barr virus [EBV], and pneumotropic viruses), and fungal infections (Aspergillus spp. and Candida spp.).
objective.advanced_workup: On hospital day 17, fiberoptic bronchoscopy (FB) revealed complete obliteration of the left mainstem bronchus by extensive branching mucoid casts; suction extraction and bronchial lavage removed the casts, with negative bacterial and fungal lavage cultures and microscopic histopathology confirming acellular/inflammatory type-1 plastic bronchitis casts (repeat FB 1 week later removed only small residual cast fragments).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of type-1 plastic bronchitis (PB) following pneumonia in a child with bidirectional Glenn circulation, confirmed by bronchoscopic extraction and microscopic identification of type-1 bronchial casts (with CMV, EBV, pneumotropic viruses, Aspergillus, Candida, cystic fibrosis, and atopy ruled out). Following failure of initial antibiotics, IVIG replacement, oxygen, chest physiotherapy, and nebulized bronchodilators/mucolytics, bronchoscopic cast removal on day 17 (and repeat clearance 1 week later) combined with azithromycin, systemic and inhaled corticosteroids, sildenafil, enalapril maleate, and nebulized 3% hypertonic saline plus bronchodilators resolved the left lung atelectasis/inflammation, and the patient was discharged on hospital day 33.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male with a history of pre-B cell ALL presented to our hospital with a 2- to 3-day history of shortness of breath with exertion. He endorsed a decreasing exercise tolerance and increased lower extremity edema over the previous 2 weeks. He denied chest pain, heart palpitations, neck pain, jaw pain, lightheadedness, dizziness, or sick contacts.
His oncologic history extends back 2 months; at this time he was diagnosed with pre-B cell ALL after a routine lab work showed an abnormal complete blood count with 30,000 white blood cells and 29% blasts. He was initiated on HyperCVAD chemotherapy (consisting of cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, dexamethasone, high-dose methotrexate), which was discontinued prior to the end of the first cycle, secondary to acute kidney injury. Based on cytogenetic studies showing the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, he was started on nilotinib, a second-generation TKI, as an adjunct to chemotherapy. A bone marrow biopsy 1 week prior to presentation following the first cycle of HyperCVAD and 6 weeks of nilotinib therapy showed a mildly hypercellular bone marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis. Pathology, flow cytometry and chromosome studies showed no evidence of leukemia in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.
Upon initial evaluation, he was found to have a regular pulse of 84, a blood pressure of 132/80, a respiratory rate of 20 and nonlabored breathing at rest. His SaO2 was 100% in room air. His initial exam was significant for clear oropharynx and nares, gray tympanic membranes bilaterally and clear lungs with good air movement. His cardiac exam was notable for muffled S1 and S2 with an S3 at the left lower sternal border and apex, a nondisplaced point of maximum impulse, a jugular venous distension of 17 cm H2O with sustained hepatojugular reflexes, and a pitting edema extending up to the mid-lower-legs bilaterally. He demonstrated the presence of pulsus paradoxus with a decrease in systolic blood pressure by 15 mm Hg with inspiration. There was no friction rub. His EKG was notable for a new finding of low voltage with electrical alternans (fig. 1, fig. 2). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 2.2-cm pericardial effusion during systole with a 2.7-cm effusion during diastole with an early diastolic tamponade physiology (fig. 3). His prior echocardiograms had shown a normal right and left ventricular function without any wall motion abnormalities or evidence of effusion.
He underwent pericardiocentesis with the removal of 450 ml of serosanginous fluid and catheter placement with a subsequent normalization of his EKG (fig. 4). He experienced an additional 100 ml of drainage over the next 24 h and prior to the removal of the catheter. The effusion was bloody with 2,257 white blood cells, 40 polymorphs and 60% mononuclear cells. Cytopathology and flow cytometry revealed no evidence of leukemia. The plasma and pericardial fluid were negative for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus B19, enterovirus, and adenovirus via polymerase chain reaction. The pericardial fluid was negative for cryptococcal antigen. Plasma beta-D-glucan, galactomannan, antinuclear antibodies, rapid plasma reagin, histoplasma, and HIV tests were all negative. A nasopharyngeal aspirate respiratory viral panel was negative. Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures resulted in no growth from the pericardial fluid.
As the evaluation of the effusion ruled out likely alternative etiologies, it was attributed to the patient's TKI, nilotinib. This medication was transitioned to bosutinib and he underwent a repeat transthoracic echocardiogram 1 month after discharge, noting the presence of only a trace of pericardial effusion. At that time, his symptoms of dyspnea on exertion had resolved and he showed no evidence of jugular-venous distention, pulsus paradoxus, hepatojugular reflux, or lower extremity edema.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male with Philadelphia chromosome-positive pre-B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with a 2- to 3-day history of exertional dyspnea and 2 weeks of decreasing exercise tolerance and bilateral lower-extremity edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 2 months prior with Philadelphia chromosome-positive pre-B cell ALL (initial WBC 30,000/uL with 29% blasts), the patient received one partial cycle of HyperCVAD (stopped early due to acute kidney injury) and 6 weeks of adjunct oral nilotinib, achieving complete bone marrow and cytogenetic remission 1 week prior to presentation. Over the preceding 2 weeks, he developed declining exercise tolerance and worsening lower-extremity pitting edema, culminating in 2-3 days of shortness of breath on exertion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Philadelphia chromosome-positive pre-B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (diagnosed 2 months prior, in complete hematologic and cytogenetic remission) status post partial cycle 1 HyperCVAD complicated by acute kidney injury and 6 weeks of nilotinib therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-3 days of exertional dyspnea and 2 weeks of decreased exercise tolerance and bilateral leg edema. Pertinent negatives: no chest pain, palpitations, neck or jaw pain, lightheadedness, dizziness, or sick contacts. Medication: nilotinib.

objective.physical_examination: Heart rate 84 bpm (regular), blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min (nonlabored at rest), SpO2 100% on room air; pulsus paradoxus of 15 mmHg on inspiration; jugular venous distension (JVD) of 17 cm H2O with sustained hepatojugular reflux; muffled S1 and S2 heart sounds with an S3 gallop at the left lower sternal border and apex, nondisplaced PMI, and no pericardial friction rub; clear lungs and oropharynx; bilateral pitting edema extending to the mid-lower legs.
objective.routine_investigations: ECG showed new low-voltage QRS complexes with electrical alternans (normalized after pericardiocentesis). Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 2.2 cm in systole and 2.7 cm in diastole with early diastolic cardiac tamponade physiology (prior baseline TTEs were normal). Plasma beta-D-glucan, galactomannan, ANA, RPR, Histoplasma, HIV, and nasopharyngeal respiratory viral panel were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow biopsy 1 week prior showed mildly hypercellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and no evidence of leukemia by pathology, flow cytometry, or cytogenetics. Pericardiocentesis drained 450 mL of bloody/serosanguinous fluid (plus 100 mL over the next 24h) containing 2,257 WBCs (40% PMNs, 60% mononuclear cells); pericardial fluid cytopathology and flow cytometry were negative for leukemia, bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial cultures showed no growth, cryptococcal antigen was negative, and both plasma and pericardial fluid PCRs were negative for EBV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), parvovirus B19, enterovirus, and adenovirus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with nilotinib-induced large hemorrhagic pericardial effusion with early cardiac tamponade physiology in a patient with Ph+ pre-B ALL in complete remission, confirmed after comprehensive exclusion of leukemic pericardial infiltration, autoimmune serositis, and viral/bacterial/fungal pericarditis (negative plasma and pericardial fluid PCRs for CMV, EBV, parvovirus B19, enterovirus, and adenovirus). Treated with therapeutic pericardiocentesis (550 mL total drainage) and substitution of nilotinib with bosutinib; at 1-month follow-up, exertional dyspnea and physical signs of tamponade had completely resolved with only a trace residual effusion on repeat TTE.

raw_case_text: A 58-year-old male had a history of end-stage renal failure with 3 kidney transplantations (1979, 1981 and 2008). He had previous chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever and cytomegalovirus infection. The last renal transplantation was associated with acute rejection requiring a combination of anti-thymoglobulin, plasma exchanges, rituximab, mycophenolate mofetil 1g/d, tacrolimus 4.5mg/d and prednisone 10 mg/d. In 2004 Leishmania PCR in blood was positive (Fig 1B). L-AmB treatment initially induced clinical cure. Relapse occurred in August 2009 when plasma exchanges and corticosteroids boluses were administered for the graft rejection. Fever, anemia (Hb = 9.1g/dL) and leukopenia (leukocytes = 1600/mm3) were observed, along with 431 Leishmania per ml of blood (assessed by quantitative PCR). L-AmB (induction total dose, 40 mg/Kg) provided improvement and reduced parasitemia to 6.9 Leishmania/ml. A second recurrence with fever and a rise in parasitemia to 29.6 Leishmania/ml occurred in January 2010 during monthly maintenance administration of 3 mg/kg of L-AmB. High-dose L-AmB was reintroduced followed by miltefosine for 4 months. Parasitemia decreased but remained positive (0.4 Leishmania/ml) and number of CD4 lymphocytes increased from 87 to 147/mm3. A third recurrence was reported in July 2010 with fever, 29.8 Leishmania/ml and positive Leishmania culture from venous blood. L-AmB was reintroduced, followed by maintenance infusions for 4 months, 3 mg/Kg every 3 weeks plus downgrading of immunosuppressive therapies. As symptoms persisted, infusions were performed once-weekly and then twice-weekly. Parasitemia decreased from 88 to 0.6 Leishmania/ml but a fourth recurrence occurred in April-June 2011 with fever, leukopenia (leukocytes = 1200/mm3, CD4 lymphocytes = 186/mm3), anemia (Hb = 9.1g/dL) and parasitemia at 40 Leishmania/ml. Patient refused to increase the L-AmB dose, it continued at 3 mg/Kg twice-weekly. Transplant nephrectomy was performed in November 2011 and chronic dialysis reinstituted. In February 2012, fever, splenomegaly, anemia (Hb = 8.6g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count = 50,000/mm3) were observed with 12,870 Leishmania/ml and 60,440 Leishmania/ml of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Thereafter, meglumine antimoniate adapted to renal clearance was administered daily for 28 days, then 1-3 times/week for maintenance. Liver function remained normal. ECG showed a T-wave inversion but troponin remained normal. Fever and sweats resolved, spleen size decreased from 21 to 17 cm, and blood counts normalized in 4 weeks, number of CD4 lymphocytes = 833/mm3 in June 2012,. Leishmania blood PCR and cultures became negative within a month and remained negative over eight monthly evaluations until death in January 2013 due to hypovolemic shock following a dental extraction.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male three-time kidney transplant recipient presented with four relapsing episodes of visceral leishmaniasis characterized by recurrent fevers, sweats, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia between 2009 and 2012.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following a third kidney transplant in 2008 complicated by acute rejection (treated with ATG, plasmapheresis, rituximab, MMF 1 g/day, tacrolimus 4.5 mg/day, and prednisone 10 mg/day), the patient—who had previously been cured of visceral leishmaniasis in 2004 with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB)—experienced four successive relapses of visceral leishmaniasis (August 2009, January 2010, July 2010, and April-June 2011) despite high-dose and maintenance L-AmB, 4 months of miltefosine, immunosuppression reduction, and transplant nephrectomy with return to hemodialysis in November 2011. In February 2012, he presented with a severe fifth episode marked by fever, night sweats, massive splenomegaly, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease status post three kidney transplantations (1979, 1981, and 2008; transplant nephrectomy in November 2011 and return to chronic hemodialysis); acute graft rejection in 2008-2009; visceral leishmaniasis first diagnosed in 2004; prior history of chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fevers, night sweats, and left upper quadrant fullness/splenomegaly across relapses (2009-2012). Immunosuppressive medications (prior to Nov 2011 nephrectomy): mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone.

objective.physical_examination: Recurrent fevers and splenomegaly (measuring 21 cm in February 2012, decreasing to 17 cm after meglumine antimoniate therapy).
objective.routine_investigations: August 2009 relapse: Hb 9.1 g/dL, WBC 1,600/mm3. April-June 2011 relapse: WBC 1,200/mm3, Hb 9.1 g/dL. February 2012 relapse: Hb 8.6 g/dL, platelets 50,000/mm3. During February 2012 meglumine antimoniate treatment: liver function tests remained normal, and ECG showed T-wave inversion with normal serum troponin.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts were 87/mm3 (rising to 147/mm3 in 2010), 186/mm3 (April 2011), and 833/mm3 (June 2012). Quantitative blood Leishmania PCR documented serial relapses: 431 Leishmania/mL (Aug 2009, reduced to 6.9/mL after 40 mg/kg L-AmB), 29.6/mL (Jan 2010, reduced to 0.4/mL after L-AmB + miltefosine), 29.8/mL with positive venous blood Leishmania culture (July 2010), 40/mL (April-June 2011), and a peak in February 2012 of 12,870 Leishmania/mL in blood and 60,440 Leishmania/mL in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with chronic, multi-relapsing visceral and pulmonary leishmaniasis refractory to liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) and miltefosine in a heavily immunosuppressed three-time renal transplant recipient with a remote history of CMV, HBV, Q fever, and Legionella infections (confirmed by serial quantitative blood Leishmania PCRs peaking at 12,870/mL, positive blood culture, and BAL Leishmania PCR of 60,440/mL). Following transplant nephrectomy (Nov 2011) and severe relapse in February 2012, treatment with renal-adjusted meglumine antimoniate (daily for 28 days followed by 1-3x/week maintenance) achieved complete clinical resolution, splenic regression (21 to 17 cm), normalization of blood counts, CD4 recovery to 833/mm3, and persistently negative Leishmania blood PCR and cultures for 8 months until the patient died in January 2013 from hypovolemic shock after a dental extraction.

raw_case_text:
Case  2. The second patient is a 60-year-old male with history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, who was referred to our clinic by his cardiologist for evaluation of diffuse lymphadenopathy. One week prior to presenting to his cardiologist, he reported having acute viral illness, consisting of acute diarrhea and nausea. His symptoms improved after four to five days, but then he developed new cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, difficulty swallowing, decreased appetite, and an eight-pound weight loss over two weeks. Initial workup was negative for Epstein Bar Virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection. Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid levels were elevated. Review of his peripheral blood smear was notable for large, atypical lymphocytes. Subsequent flow cytometry analysis of the peripheral blood was significant for a CD5+ monoclonal B-cell population with lambda light chain restriction. CT of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed diffuse lymphadenopathy (Figure 2(a)). The bone marrow core biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow (95%) (Figure 2): 50% of the cells were large lymphoid cells positive for CD5, CD20, and dimly BCL 6 positive. These same cells were also found in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis.
He was diagnosed with stage IV nongerminal center DLBCL with leptomeningeal involvement and was started on standard rituximab, cyclophosphamide, Adriamycin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) with IT-MTX. His first cycle of R-CHOP was complicated by pancytopenia and neutropenic fever which was successfully treated with broad spectrum antibiotics. Upon completion of his second IT-MTX treatment, no monoclonal B-cells were seen in his CSF by flow cytometry and cytology. After 3 cycles of R-CHOP and five doses of IT-MTX, the patient subsequently developed a right cranial nerve (CN) III palsy and right eyelid lag despite significant response in the lymphadenopathy. Given clinical evidence of leptomeningeal disease, we decided to continue R-CHOP but added high dose intravenous MTX every three weeks, given one week after R-CHOP. High dose MTX was added because of known central nervous system (CNS) penetration and activity. We also added IT-cytarabine along with IT-MTX alternating between cycles.
Despite receiving two more doses of R-CHOP, two doses of IT-MTX and Ara-C, and three doses of high dose intravenous MTX, he developed progressive lymphadenopathy and additional neurologic deficits (right CN VI palsy and right arm weakness in addition to his right CN III palsy and right eye lid lag). Restaging PET/CT confirmed progression of his diffuse lymphadenopathy with no malignant foci in the brain or spine. Despite progression of disease, his performance status remained intact with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 1. The patient was then treated with salvage chemotherapy using R-DHAP (rituximab, dexamethasone, high dose Ara-C, and cisplatin) and IT-depot liposomal cytarabine. He developed acute kidney injury, likely from cisplatin, and new hoarseness due to involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Further treatment with R-DHAP salvage chemotherapy was stopped due to continued, progressive disease (Figure 3(b)). Despite disease progression on cisplatin-based salvage chemotherapy, the patient's performance status was still excellent and the patient expressed willingness to pursue alternative therapy. Reanalysis of the bone marrow specimen revealed that approximately 10-15% of the lymphoma cells expressed CD30 by immunohistochemistry (Figure 2). We then decided to combine BV (1.8 mg/kg given on day 1) with topotecan (1 mg/m2 given on days 1-6) on a 21-day schedule. Topotecan was chosen for its ability to penetrate the CNS and the dose and schedule were adopted from the TTR (taxol, topotecan, and rituximab) regimen. Upon completion of cycle 1 of this regimen, he developed Grade 2 vertigo. A magnetic resonance imaging scan (MRI) of his brain did not show a CNS lesion. The patient otherwise continued to have good functional status and treatment was continued. A staging PET/CT performed after completion of the 2nd cycle of TTR showed significant improvement in adenopathy (Figure 3(c)), but he developed Grade 2 diarrhea, Grade 3 neutropenia, Grade 3 anemia, Grade 2 thrombocytopenia, and Grade 2 vertigo, with a subsequent decrease in his ECOG performance status from 1 to 2. He otherwise had no new neurological deficits. Repeated CSF analysis showed no malignant lymphocytes. He received the third dose of BV and topotecan and was evaluated for stem cell harvest for possible ASCT. Unfortunately, the patient developed episodic syncope, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis, thought to be due to autonomic dysfunction, and his performance status declined drastically. Although brain and spinal MRI did not reveal any focal abnormalities and CSF analysis was negative, clinical progression of the leptomeningeal disease could not be ruled out. He was empirically treated for adrenal insufficiency with a trial of fludrocortisone which was ineffective. At this point, he declined further treatment and was transitioned to best supportive care with home hospice. Two months after discontinuing therapy, he died at home.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of progressive cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, decreased appetite, and an 8-pound weight loss following a 4- to 5-day acute diarrheal illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week before seeing his cardiologist, the patient experienced 4-5 days of acute nausea and diarrhea, followed over the next 2 weeks by diffuse cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, anorexia, and an 8-pound weight loss. Following diagnosis of stage IV CD5+ non-germinal center diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with leptomeningeal involvement, his course progressed through R-CHOP + intrathecal/high-dose IV methotrexate + IT cytarabine (complicated by right CN III palsy, right CN VI palsy, and right arm weakness), salvage R-DHAP + IT liposomal cytarabine (complicated by cisplatin AKI and right recurrent laryngeal nerve vocal cord palsy/hoarseness), and 3 cycles of brentuximab vedotin + topotecan, culminating in autonomic dysfunction (episodic syncope, lightheadedness, diaphoresis) and performance status decline.
subjective.past_medical_history: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: preceding nausea/diarrhea, cervical/axillary swelling, dysphagia, anorexia, and 8-lb weight loss. Subsequent course: neutropenic fever, right ptosis/eyelid lag and diplopia (CN III and CN VI palsies), right arm weakness, hoarseness, treatment-related grade 2 vertigo and diarrhea, and terminal episodic syncope, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam: diffuse cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; baseline ECOG performance status 1. Subsequent neurological deficits during chemotherapy progression: right cranial nerve III palsy with right eyelid lag, right cranial nerve VI palsy, right upper extremity weakness, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, and terminal orthostatic/autonomic syncope and diaphoresis (ECOG 2+).
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: elevated serum LDH and uric acid; peripheral blood smear showed large atypical lymphocytes; infectious workup was negative for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and HIV. Subsequent cycle 1 R-CHOP complicated by pancytopenia and neutropenic fever; R-DHAP complicated by cisplatin-induced AKI; cycle 2 brentuximab vedotin + topotecan complicated by grade 3 neutropenia, grade 3 anemia, and grade 2 thrombocytopenia.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood flow cytometry identified a CD5+ monoclonal B-cell population with lambda light-chain restriction. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis (and subsequent restaging PET/CTs) showed diffuse lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow core biopsy revealed 95% hypercellularity with 50% large lymphoid cells positive for CD5, CD20, dim BCL6, and 10-15% CD30 expression on IHC. Baseline lumbar puncture CSF cytology/flow cytometry confirmed leptomeningeal involvement by the same monoclonal B-cells (cleared after 2 doses of IT-MTX and negative on repeat CSF analyses, with negative brain/spinal MRI).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of stage IV CD5-positive, partially CD30-positive (10-15%) non-germinal center diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with leptomeningeal CNS involvement (confirmed by peripheral blood/CSF flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy; EBV, CMV, and HIV excluded). Treated sequentially with R-CHOP + IT-MTX/IT-Ara-C + high-dose IV MTX, salvage R-DHAP + IT liposomal cytarabine, and 3 cycles of brentuximab vedotin (1.8 mg/kg day 1) plus topotecan (1 mg/m2 days 1-6 q21d, which transiently reduced systemic adenopathy on PET/CT). Due to progressive clinical leptomeningeal/autonomic neuropathy (syncope, cranial neuropathies) unresponsive to empiric fludrocortisone, the patient transitioned to home hospice and died 2 months later.

raw_case_text:
A 28 year old, healthy Thai male, employed in Israel as an agricultural worker, presented to the emergency room with complaints of nausea, vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain starting 3 days earlier. Past medical history was unremarkable and without mention of recent illness. On presentation, the patient was well oriented in no severe distress, physical examination was notable for epigastric tenderness with guarding. Heart rate was 116 beats/minute, blood pressure 94/59 mm/Hg and a temperature of 37.4 C. The patient was admitted to the surgical department for evaluation. A chest and abdomen CT revealed marked liver enlargement with fatty change, and minimal amounts of pleural and pericardial fluid. No surgical etiology was recognized and due to laboratory findings of renal failure (Creatinine 3.88 mg/dl BUN 119.7 mg/dl), the patient was transferred to the medical department.
Shortly after arrival, the patient's condition deteriorated rapidly to a state of agitation and shock and he was transferred to the intensive care unit. On arrival blood pressure measured 79/45 mm/Hg, pulse 170 beats/minute with episodes of SVT. In addition, the patient developed dyspnea, with a respiratory rate of 48 breaths/minute and anuria. Core temperature measured 33.1 C. Examination revealed marked peripheral cyanosis, distended jugular veins with cool extremities. Air entry to both lungs was reduced and palpation of the abdomen was noted for tenderness and an enlarged liver. Laboratory analysis showed lactic acidosis (pH 7.22, lactate 129 mg/dl), renal failure (creatinine 2.11 mg/dl), and rhabdomyolysis (CPK 3,205 IU/l). Liver function tests and coagulation indices were also disturbed ( total bilirubin 2.74, direct bilirubin 1.03 mg/dl, AST 1169 IU/l, ALT 890 IU/l, LDH 1743 IU/l, INR 1.7, factor V level 18%,). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was within normal limits. Factor V levels continued to decline to a nadir of 5%. The above laboratory results, in combination with encephalopathy, indicated fulminant hepatic failure accompanied by multi-system organ failure.
The patient failed a trial of positive pressure ventilation and was subsequently intubated and ventilated mechanically. A Swan-Ganz catheter was inserted and fluid resuscitation started, steroids and vasopressors were given. Echocardiography was used to rule out pericardial tamponade; normal ventricular and valvular function was demonstrated. Continuous hemodiafiltration was started and switched to standard hemodialysis a week later. A tracheotomy was later performed due to the need for prolonged ventilation. Blood, urine, sputum and peritoneal fluid aspirate were cultured and gram and Ziell-Nielsen stained. Empiric antibiotic therapy was then started. Culture results were negative. Serologic testing for acute or chronic infection with viral hepatitis types A, B and C, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, Cytomegalovirus returned negative. Further serologic testing for Ricketsia conorii, Coxiella burnetii were also negative. A thick film smear for blood-borne parasites and stool collection for ova and parasites were negative. Due to a high osmolar gap, levels of methanol, ethylene glycol and acetyl salicylic acid were checked and no traces were found.
A health bureau inspector was sent to the residence of the patient and found a stock of canned food the patient consumed almost exclusively for a period of months. Specimens were examined at the ministry of health. AFB1 was found at a level of 19.6 ppb (allowed level < 5 ppb). The patient's condition gradually improved on supportive treatment. Vasopressors were stopped and dialysis discontinued after blood pressure, renal function and CPK values returned to normal. Liver function tests improved markedly. After 21 days of mechanical ventilation the patient was weaned and the tracheotomy closed on the 36th day. The patient was returned to the medical department for observation and physiotherapy. No apparent sequels were observed other than mild residual hypertension. The patient was discharged on day 45.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old previously healthy Thai male agricultural worker presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy without recent illness, the patient presented after 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. Shortly after transfer from the surgical to the medical ward for acute renal failure, he rapidly deteriorated into agitation, supraventricular tachycardia, severe hypothermia (33.1 °C), tachypnea, anuria, and profound circulatory shock requiring ICU transfer, mechanical ventilation, and hemodiafiltration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Social and dietary history: Thai national employed as an agricultural worker in Israel; subsisted almost exclusively for several months on a personal stock of canned food later found to be heavily contaminated with aflatoxin B1.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain, followed by acute agitation, dyspnea, and anuria.

objective.physical_examination: On ED presentation: alert and oriented, heart rate 116 bpm, blood pressure 94/59 mmHg, temperature 37.4 °C, epigastric tenderness with abdominal guarding. At rapid ICU deterioration: agitated and encephalopathic, blood pressure 79/45 mmHg, heart rate 170 bpm (with episodes of SVT), respiratory rate 48 breaths/min, core temperature 33.1 °C, anuria, marked peripheral cyanosis, cool extremities, distended jugular veins, reduced bilateral air entry, and abdominal tenderness with hepatomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: creatinine 3.88 mg/dL, BUN 119.7 mg/dL. ICU labs: severe lactic acidosis (pH 7.22, lactate 129 mg/dL), high osmolar gap (negative methanol, ethylene glycol, and salicylates), creatinine 2.11 mg/dL, rhabdomyolysis (CPK 3,205 IU/L), total bilirubin 2.74 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.03 mg/dL, AST 1,169 IU/L, ALT 890 IU/L, LDH 1,743 IU/L, INR 1.7, factor V level 18% (declining to a nadir of 5%), and normal ESR. Blood, urine, sputum, and peritoneal fluid Gram/Ziehl-Neelsen stains and cultures were negative; thick blood smear and stool ova/parasites negative; serologies for HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV, EBV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Rickettsia conorii, and Coxiella burnetii were all negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal ventricular and valvular function without tamponade.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest and abdominal CT revealed marked hepatomegaly with diffuse fatty infiltration and minimal pleural and pericardial effusions. Ministry of Health toxicology analysis of the canned food stock from the patient's residence detected aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) at 19.6 ppb (maximum permitted level <5 ppb).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with acute aflatoxicosis (confirmed by detection of aflatoxin B1 at 19.6 ppb in the patient's staple canned food supply) causing fulminant hepatic failure, severe lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and multisystem organ failure (with viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, HIV, rickettsial infections, bacterial sepsis, and toxic alcohols ruled out). Managed in the ICU with invasive mechanical ventilation (tracheostomy performed, weaned at day 21, decannulated day 36), Swan-Ganz-guided fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, corticosteroids, empiric antibiotics, and continuous hemodiafiltration transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis. Hepatic, renal, and hemodynamic parameters normalized completely, and the patient was discharged on hospital day 45 with only mild residual hypertension.

raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old man presented with an eight-day history of a blurry patch of vision in the right eye. He could not identify any precipitants, had no significant medical history and did not take any regular medication. His best corrected visual acuity was 6/4 unaided in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes and anterior segments appeared quiet. On dilated fundoscopy, a filling defect was apparent in a branch of the inferotemporal retinal artery of the right eye approximately 1-2 disc diameters away from the optic disc, associated with pale areas resembling cotton wool spots. The diagnosis of branch retinal artery occlusion was made. These findings were also visualised with optical coherence tomography - Figure 1. One week later, the patient's symptoms of blurriness had subjectively improved, and the pale areas previously described had reduced in size. Screening for cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, human immunodeficiency virus, vasculitis and thrombophilia were all negative. Routine blood tests were insignificant with a total cholesterol of 4.6 mmol/L, triglycerides of 1.9 mmol/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 2 urea and normal renal and liver function. 
Referral to cardiology was made to investigate for possible cardiac causes of embolism, and the patient was empirically started on aspirin. General cardiological assessments were unremarkable with a blood pressure of 135/83 mmHg, heart rate of 81 beats per minute, normal heart sounds with no murmurs or added sound and no carotid bruits were detected. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head, magnetic resonance angiogram of the head and neck vessels (specifically looking for carotid artery dissection), and carotid doppler scans were all normal. A 72-hour Holter monitoring test showed sinus rhythm throughout, and conventional transthoracic echocardiography was insignificant. However, a transthoracic echocardiographic bubble contrast study, which showed no evidence of bubbles transiting at rest, did show a large right to left shunt at the atrial level within one beat of release of valsalva manoeuvre - Figure 2. This was strongly suggestive of a large patent foramen ovale. No other potential causes for the retinal artery embolus were identified at any point. 
In view of the potential consequences of future emboli causing further occlusions of the retinal or cerebral circulations, percutaneous closure of the patent foramen ovale was undertaken, alongside six months of low-dose aspirin and lifelong clopidogrel therapy. This patient has had no further episodes and at 12 months since the episode he is asymptomatic with normal visual acuity (6/6 unaided in each eye).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old man presented with an 8-day history of a painless blurry patch in the visual field of his right eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy without identifiable precipitants, the patient noticed a localized blurry patch of vision in his right eye 8 days prior to presentation, which began to subjectively improve 1 week after initial ophthalmic evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for a localized blurry patch in the right visual field. No regular home medications.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic exam: unaided best-corrected visual acuity 6/4 OU (6/6 OU at 12-month follow-up), normal intraocular pressures OU, quiet anterior segments OU; dilated fundoscopy OD revealed a filling defect in a branch of the inferotemporal retinal artery 1-2 disc diameters from the optic disc with adjacent pale cotton-wool-like retinal ischemia (reduced in size 1 week later). Cardiovascular exam: blood pressure 135/83 mmHg, heart rate 81 bpm, normal heart sounds without murmurs or carotid bruits.
objective.routine_investigations: Total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.9 mmol/L, ESR 2 mm/h, and normal renal and liver function tests; infectious, vasculitic, and thrombophilia screens—including cytomegalovirus (CMV), Toxoplasma gondii, HIV, vasculitis autoantibodies, and thrombophilia panel—were all negative. 72-hour Holter monitor showed normal sinus rhythm; carotid Doppler ultrasound and conventional TTE were normal. Transthoracic echocardiographic agitated saline bubble contrast study demonstrated a large right-to-left atrial shunt within one cardiac cycle of Valsalva release, diagnostic of a large patent foramen ovale (PFO).
objective.advanced_workup: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) confirmed right inferotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion and inner retinal ischemia. Brain MRI and head/neck MR angiography were normal (ruling out carotid artery dissection).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with right inferotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) secondary to paradoxical embolism across a large patent foramen ovale (PFO; confirmed by dilated fundoscopy, OCT, and bubble-contrast echocardiography with Valsalva maneuver; infectious retinitis/vasculitis including CMV, Toxoplasma, and HIV, systemic vasculitis, carotid dissection, and thrombophilia ruled out). Treated with percutaneous transcatheter PFO closure, 6 months of low-dose aspirin, and lifelong clopidogrel, remaining asymptomatic with 6/6 unaided visual acuity OU at 12-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with complaints of increasing lethargy and fatigue over the course of several weeks, along with a one-day history of shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations. Past medical history was significant for HIV, anemia, and septoplasty. She was intubated on admission for airway protection due to concern for impending respiratory failure. On exam she was found to be febrile with Tmax of 39.9C, heart rate of 122 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 91/57 mmHg, saturating at 97% on 35% FiO2. Complete blood count revealed white blood cells of 3 x 103 cells/mL with 73% segs and 15% bands, hemoglobin of 4.5 g/dL, hematocrit of 17.7%, and platelets of 4,000 cells/mL. Ferritin was significantly elevated at 19,406 ng/mL and triglycerides were 412 mg/dL. HIV viral load was 1,842,730 copies/mL and CD4 count was 4 cells/mL. Physical exam revealed hepatosplenomegaly which was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound. The patient was diagnosed with HLH based on meeting the required five of eight criteria set forth in HLH-2004 guidelines (fever > 38.5C, splenomegaly, bicytopenia with hemoglobin < 9 g/dL and platelets < 100,000 cells/mL, triglycerides > 265 mg/dL, and ferritin > 500 ng/mL). The other three criteria (NK cell activity, CD25 level, and pathological evidence of hemophagocytosis) were not evaluated due to unavailability of labs and thrombocytopenia precluding bone marrow biopsy.
The patient was placed on empirical antibiotics (levofloxacin and vancomycin) for sepsis while investigation for infectious source was conducted. She was also started on methylprednisolone for respiratory failure at admission, which was continued for three days. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Sputum culture grew normal flora. Tests were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid fast bacilli, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, cryptococcus, histoplasmosis, syphilis, and influenza A. The only positive finding was antibody for influenza B, which was attributed to a mild upper respiratory infection that had resolved on its own with supportive measures two weeks prior to admission.
Despite aggressive transfusions, significant anemia and thrombocytopenia persisted. At this point, the most likely trigger of the HLH was determined to be an uncontrolled HIV infection. Given the patient's clinical instability and unresponsiveness to supportive treatment, ART was empirically initiated with tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir. Within one week of initiation of ART, the patient improved clinically and was able to be extubated, and her laboratory parameters began to normalize (Figure 1). By the time the patient was discharged three weeks after ART initiation, hemoglobin had risen to 10.5 g/dL and platelets to 169,000 cells/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old Caucasian female with HIV presented to the emergency department with several weeks of progressive lethargy and fatigue and a 1-day history of shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: With a known history of untreated/uncontrolled HIV and anemia and a self-resolved mild upper respiratory illness 2 weeks prior, the patient developed progressive lethargy and fatigue over several weeks followed by 1 day of acute dyspnea, hematemesis, and palpitations, requiring emergency endotracheal intubation upon arrival for impending respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection (off antiretroviral therapy), anemia, and prior septoplasty; mild self-limited upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for several weeks of progressive lethargy and fatigue, and 1 day of dyspnea, hematemesis, and palpitations.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (Tmax 39.9 °C), heart rate 122 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 91/57 mmHg, SpO2 97% on 35% FiO2 (intubated); hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal palpation.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 3.0 x 10^3 cells/mL (73% segmented neutrophils, 15% bands), severe anemia with hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL and hematocrit 17.7%, severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 4,000 cells/mL, markedly elevated serum ferritin 19,406 ng/mL, and elevated fasting triglycerides 412 mg/dL. Blood and urine cultures negative; sputum culture grew normal flora; infectious workup was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid-fast bacilli, cytomegalovirus (CMV), parvovirus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, syphilis, and Influenza A, and positive only for Influenza B antibody. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 4 cells/mL and plasma HIV viral load was 1,842,730 copies/mL (bone marrow biopsy deferred due to severe thrombocytopenia of 4,000/mL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; fulfilling 5/8 HLH-2004 criteria: fever >38.5 °C, splenomegaly, severe bicytopenia [Hb 4.5 g/dL, platelets 4,000/mL], triglycerides 412 mg/dL, and ferritin 19,406 ng/mL) triggered by uncontrolled advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 4 cells/mL, HIV viral load 1,842,730 copies/mL; opportunistic infections including CMV, EBV, parvovirus, PJP, AFB, Cryptococcus, and Histoplasma excluded). After persistent cytopenias and clinical instability despite transfusions, empiric levofloxacin/vancomycin, and a 3-day course of methylprednisolone, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir) produced rapid clinical improvement and extubation within 1 week and hospital discharge at 3 weeks with hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL and platelets 169,000 cells/mL.

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old male with past medical history of orthoptic liver transplant secondary to NASH cirrhosis 4 years earlier and chronic kidney disease, presented with vague abdominal pain, weight loss, and fatigue. Mycophenolate and tacrolimus provided immunosuppression. Upon admission liver function tests (AST, ALT, and ALP), CBC, and tacrolimus level were all within normal limits. Additionally, the patient had an unremarkable RUQ ultrasound. He had some raised s. creatinine (1.58) compared to baseline of 1.28 due to poor oral intake. Patient was afebrile and vitals were stable, with no evidence of infection or sepsis. Hydration brought the creatinine down to baseline. A CT scan showed nonspecific bowel edema (Figure 1). Stool heme/WBC and culture, fungal culture, gram stain, AFB quantiferon, AFB culture, Yersinia, and urine culture were sent. LFTs and coagulation were still normal. Stool WBC was negative. Patient was still afebrile, without bandemia.
Colonoscopy showed an area at the distal ileum which was inflamed, granular, and necrotic, biopsy of which was consistent with nonspecific/ischemic ileitis. Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole) were started empirically due to ischemic changes in pathology.
