Tests were carried out by a microdilution method described previously and adapted from the reference method for molds recommended by the National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards, with RPMI 1640 medium buffered to pH 7.0 with 0.165 M morpholinepropanesulfonic acid, an inoculum of 9.1 x 105 CFU/mL, an incubation temperature of 30 C, a second-day reading (48 h), and an additive drug-dilution procedure. MICs and minimum fungicidal concentrations (MFC) were as follows: amphotericin B 1 and >16 mug/mL, flucytosine 64 and >64 microg/mL, itraconazole 0.25 and 0.25 microg/mL, voriconazole 0.25 and 0.5 microg/mL, and UR-9825 0.06 and 0.5 microg/mL, respectively. Results demonstrated good activity of the four-azole derivatives tested. UR-9825, a novel triazole not yet licensed, showed the lowest MIC. MFCs of amphotericin B and flucytosine were very high, indicating the ineffectiveness of these drugs. These data correlate with our clinical results since a total dose of 1 g of amphotericin B was unable to reduce the brain abscesses, while the patient responded well to itraconazole at daily doses of 400 mg.
This case report is important because such clinical isolates of Neosartorya spp. that produce white colonies and do not become green, like colonies of A. fumigatus, are often discarded as contaminants. Therefore, the real incidence of aspergillosis caused by Neosartorya species could be underreported. Many Neosartorya species, other than N. fischeri or N. pseudofischeri, are thermotolerant and can grow at temperatures above 37 C, showing their inherent ability to invade the brain.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old Brazilian woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive memory loss, confusion, involuntary right upper arm movements, and a short-stepped gait with balance loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following a fall 1 year prior to admission on May 5, 1999, the patient developed progressive memory loss, confusion, involuntary right upper arm movements, and a short-stepped, unbalanced gait initially misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease in March 1999 (unresponsive to antiparkinsonian therapy). An outpatient brain CT on April 30, 1999 revealed multiple bilateral hemispheric lesions, prompting hospital referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: History in 1996 of productive cough with hemoptysis, night sweats, and intermittent fever evaluated by bronchoscopy (showing nonspecific vascular congestion and focal intra-alveolar edema without identified pathogen).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for memory loss, confusion, involuntary right arm movements, gait instability, and chronic ill appearance.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically ill-appearing, mildly pale, disoriented, and confused woman able to follow simple commands. Lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds and rales in the lower thirds bilaterally. Neurological exam showed slow, repetitive upper arm movements with reduced strength, short-stepped gait with impaired balance, and normal deep tendon reflexes.
objective.routine_investigations: Thoracentesis of the left pleural effusion (80 mL clear yellow fluid) showed pH 7.5, 19,870 leukocytes/mL, and 970 erythrocytes/mL, with negative bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures. During a subsequent readmission in August 1999, urine/blood workup confirmed Escherichia coli urinary sepsis.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT and post-drainage brain MRI demonstrated multifocal supratentorial and subtentorial brain abscesses (frontal, parietal, and occipital). Chest X-ray and thoracic CT showed small bilateral pleural effusions and a left pulmonary cavitary lesion. Surgical aspiration of frontal, parietal, and occipital brain abscesses on two occasions yielded thick yellowish fluid containing septate hyphae on direct microscopy (negative for neoplastic cells, bacteria, and mycobacteria) and grew a thermotolerant white-to-greenish mold identified by ascospore scanning electron microscopy and phenotypic comparison (CBS 109356 / IHEM 18438) as Neosartorya hiratsukae (Aspergillus section Fumigati). Antifungal susceptibility testing (MIC / MFC in ug/mL) showed resistance to amphotericin B (1 / >16) and flucytosine (64 / >64) and susceptibility to itraconazole (0.25 / 0.25), voriconazole (0.25 / 0.5), and UR-9825 (0.06 / 0.5).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal cerebral abscesses (with a likely primary left pulmonary cavitary lesion) caused by Neosartorya hiratsukae (sexual state of Aspergillus), confirmed by direct microscopy showing septate hyphae in aspirated brain pus, repeated culture isolation from two neurosurgical drainages, and definitive morphological/SEM ascospore identification. After failing 21 days of antibacterial therapy (ceftriaxone, oxacillin, metronidazole) and 1 g cumulative dose of amphotericin B (complicated by refractory hypokalemia and abscess enlargement), repeat neurosurgical drainage and oral itraconazole (400 mg/day) led to neurological improvement and radiographic abscess shrinkage on follow-up brain MRI; however, the patient later died in a nursing hospital in November 1999 from multiple organ failure.

raw_case_text:
A 78-year-old white caucasian lady presented to her local hospital with rapid loss of vision in her right eye over 12 hours. She had been suffering from non-specific joint pains for several months for which she had been receiving acupuncture. Ten days prior to her admission a rheumatologist had diagnosed polymyalgia rheumatica based on her symptomatology and scalp tenderness, but she had not been started on steroid treatment. She had had an anterior resection for adenocarcinoma of the bowel in 2001 and a computed tomography scan six months previously showed no evidence of tumour recurrence. There was a past medical history of melanoma (resected from her right foot) in 1983, and a transient ischaemic attack but had no history of diabetes, ocular trauma or sinusitis. There had been no recent hospital admissions or medical procedures.
Initial examination revealed a reduction in her visual acuity on the right to hand movements only, there was also tenderness over the right temporal artery. The left eye vision was normal. The right fundus seen with a direct ophthalmoscope showed an elevated, yellow, sub retinal macular lesion with associated retinal haemorrhages and cotton wool spots. There was no evidence of uveitis. The physical examination was otherwise normal. At this time her erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 58 mm/hr, her C reactive protein 1 mg/L, total white cell count of 11.9 x 109/L. Giant cell arteritis was suspected to be the cause of her pain and she was commenced on 80 mg of prednisolone daily. After five days the pain worsened and became more localised to the right eye and she developed panuveitis with 1 mm hypopyon in the anterior chamber. She was transferred to our institute for further management. An ultrasound B scan of the eye showed retinal elevation at the macula, choroidal thickening and subretinal fluid suggesting the diagnosis of endogenous endophthalmitis. A vitreous biopsy was performed which showed the macular lesion to orginate from a subretinal mass accompanied by an area of macular retinitis with intense inflammatory exudate in the posterior vitreous. Intravitreal ceftazidime and vancomycin were administered. The Gram stain of the vitreous biopsy showed moderate numbers of neutrophils, branching septate hyphae and no bacteria (Figure 1). Bacterial cultures were negative but culture on Sabouraud's agar revealed a mould identified as Aspergillus fumigatus on the basis of typical colonial and microscopic morphology. The organism was susceptible to voriconazole (MIC 0.25 mug/ml) using the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute MS27-A2 method. She was commenced on oral voriconazole 400 mg twice a day for 24 hours as a loading dose. The following day she complained of visual hallucinations at night, a well-known side effect of the drug and the agent was discontinued for a day. She subsequently tolerated maintenance treatment at a dose of 200 mg 12 hourly to complete a two-week course. Systemic steroids were tapered and discontinued over two weeks. Six days after commencing voriconazole she underwent a second vitreous biopsy with intravitreal injection of 5 mcg of amphotericin B. Gram stain and culture of this sample were negative. Voriconazole levels were measured in serum and vitreous aspirate, both eight hours after her last 200 mg dose, by means of a bioassay. Both the assay of the serum and the vitreous revealed a concentration of 0.69 mug/ml.
An extensive search for a source of her infection (blood cultures, echocardiogram, computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain) was negative. The uveitis improved substantially during the first week of treatment, but there was no improvement in her visual acuity due to the macular involvement. On review two months later the uveitis had settled, but there was persistent pain and low intraocular pressure (4 mmHg) in the right eye indicating the onset of phthisis bulbi. She was blind in the right eye. Therefore enucleation of the right eye was suggested and the patient consented to the procedure. Histological examination of the enucleated eye showed non-specific chronic fibrosing vitritis with no fungal elements seen using special stains.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old Caucasian woman presented with rapid loss of vision in her right eye over 12 hours, accompanied by scalp tenderness and non-specific joint pains.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had experienced non-specific arthralgias for several months treated with acupuncture and was clinically diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica 10 days prior to admission based on joint pains and scalp tenderness. She then presented to her local hospital with rapid visual loss in the right eye over 12 hours and right temporal artery tenderness. Suspecting giant cell arteritis, high-dose oral prednisolone (80 mg/day) was started, but 5 days later her right eye pain worsened and she developed panuveitis with a 1-mm hypopyon, prompting transfer to our institute.
subjective.past_medical_history: Colonic adenocarcinoma treated with anterior resection in 2001 (no recurrence on CT 6 months prior); right foot melanoma resected in 1983; prior transient ischemic attack; recent clinical diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica (10 days prior); recent acupuncture therapy. No history of diabetes, ocular trauma, sinusitis, or recent hospitalization.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for rapid right eye vision loss, severe right ocular pain, scalp tenderness, and chronic arthralgias; negative for visual hallucinations until after initial voriconazole loading dose.

objective.physical_examination: Initial right eye visual acuity was hand movements only (left eye normal), with right temporal artery tenderness. Initial direct ophthalmoscopy of the right eye showed an elevated yellow subretinal macular lesion with retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots without uveitis; 5 days after starting prednisolone 80 mg/day, exam revealed severe right panuveitis with a 1-mm hypopyon. At 2 months, the right eye had no light perception and hypotony (IOP 4 mmHg, early phthisis bulbi).
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed ESR 58 mm/hr, CRP 1 mg/L, and WBC 11.9 x 10^9/L. Extensive systemic workup including blood cultures and echocardiogram was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Ocular B-scan ultrasound demonstrated macular retinal elevation, choroidal thickening, and subretinal fluid. Vitreous biopsy revealed a subretinal macular mass with macular retinitis and dense posterior vitreous exudate; Gram stain showed moderate neutrophils and branching septate fungal hyphae without bacteria, and Sabouraud agar culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus susceptible to voriconazole (MIC 0.25 ug/mL). Repeat vitreous tap after 6 days of voriconazole was sterile, with simultaneous serum and vitreous voriconazole concentrations both measuring 0.69 ug/mL. Systemic staging with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and brain MRI was negative. Histopathology of the subsequently enucleated right eye showed chronic fibrosing vitritis with complete fungal clearance.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Endogenous Aspergillus fumigatus macular chorioretinitis and endophthalmitis of the right eye initially masquerading as giant cell arteritis (potentially seeded via acupuncture and exacerbated by high-dose prednisolone), confirmed by vitreous biopsy microscopy and culture growing voriconazole-susceptible A. fumigatus. Treated by tapering and stopping systemic corticosteroids, administering intravitreal amphotericin B (5 ug), and completing a 2-week course of oral voriconazole (400 mg bid loading, then 200 mg bid maintenance after a 1-day pause for transient visual hallucinations), which sterilized the eye and resolved the uveitis; due to macular destruction, blindness, persistent pain, and phthisis bulbi (IOP 4 mmHg), right eye enucleation was performed at 2 months.

raw_case_text:
A 66 years old African American man presented to the hospital with 1 week history of progressive shortness of breath and bilateral calf pain. He complained of occasional productive cough but denied any chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, palpitation, or dyspnea. He had a history of peripheral vascular disease and prostate cancer Gleason's score 6(3+3) about 8 years ago for which he had prostatectomy and subsequent penile implant for erectile dysfunction. He had an extensive smoking history but no alcohol or street drug abuse. Furthermore, he had a prior 8-year history of incarceration and a family history of lung cancer.
Due to his chest symptoms, he had a chest x-ray followed by Computerized Tomography (CT) scan of the chest which showed a left upper lung mass (4.5 x 5.5 x 5 cm) with mediastinal and right hilar adenopathy [Fig.1]. No pleural or pericardial effusion was noted. CT of the head and bone scan revealed no metastasis.
A CT guided fine needle aspiration cytology of the left lung mass showed inflammatory necrotic background with several large aggregates of fungi. On Gomori Methanamine Silver (GMS) stain, the hyphae had uniform diameter, septation and branching at 45 degree, morphologically compatible with aspergillus species [Fig. 2]. A special stain for Acid Fast Bacilli (AFB) was negative, and no tumor cells were identified. Based on these findings, he was commenced on liposomal Amphotericin B for 2 weeks followed by Voriconazole to complete a 6 week course of antifungal therapy for pulmonary aspergillosis. His hemoglobin was 7.7 g/dl, white blood cell count 7.7 k/mm3, and absolute neutrophil, monocyte and lymphocyte count of 4.6 k/mm3, 0.6 k/mm3 and 3.2 k/mm3 respectively. Serum creatinine was 1.4 mg/dl and blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dl. HIV and Hepatitis C serology were negative. He improved and was discharged on voriconazole. However, he presented again after about 8 weeks with new onset hemoptysis and night sweats. He subsequently had bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) which returned negative for mycobacterium, fungus, legionella and cytomegalovirus on culture. Direct Fluorescent Antibody of BAL fluid was negative for Parainfluenza 1, Adenovirus, Herpes Simplex I&II, Respiratory Syncytial Virus, Varicella Zoster Influenza A&B and Adenovirus. BAL fluid was negative for malignant cells and Pneumocystis carinii.
Pulmonary function test showed an obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC ratio 58% of reference). He subsequently had a thoracotomy with a left upper lobectomy revealing biphasic malignant tumor (carcinosarcoma).
A left upper lobectomy (20 x 15.5 x 5.5 cm) was done. Sectioning revealed a large tan-white circumscribed partly hemorrhagic mass with central necrotic cavity. The mass was abutting the pleural surface and measured 8.5 x 6.5 x 5.5 cm of which intra-operative frozen section was diagnosed as poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Interestingly, final surgical pathology examination revealed a poorly differentiated biphasic malignant neoplasm with epithelial and spindle cell components and necrosis [Fig. 3]. The carcinomatous component showed predominantly squamous cell differentiation with foci of aborted glandular structures. The sarcomatous component displayed interlacing short fascicles of malignant spindle cells with areas of marked cellular pleomorphism and bizarre giant tumor cells. Numerous atypical mitoses and large areas of geographic necrosis were evident. Morphologically, the differential included poorly differentiated lung carcinoma with "sarcomatoid" growth pattern, primary pulmonary carcinosarcoma and biphasic poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma. The tumor involved the pleural surface and the surgical bronchial margin. An extensive panel of immunostains was performed for further classification and more precise diagnosis. The epithelial carcinomatous tumor cells showed strong immunoreactivity with pankeratin AE1/AE3 (Fig. 4) and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) (Fig. 5) and focally for P63; while vimentin stain was strongly positive in the spindle cell component but not in the carcinomatous component [Fig. 6]. Patchy foci of spindle tumor cells were reactive for calponin and smooth muscle actin. All other markers including desmin, cKit (CD117), S100 protein, CD 34, HMB45, bcl2, and CD99 were negative essentially excluding synovial sarcoma. Also, Fluorescence In-situ Hybridization (FISH) analysis did not detect t(X;18) translocations of the SYT/18q11.2 region that are characteristic of synovial sarcoma.
Within the resection specimen areas of infarction and coagulative necrosis were identified, some of them bordering viable tumor (Fig. 7). In one such area, fungal hyphae morphologically consistent with aspergillus species were seen and confirmed by GMS fungal stain (Fig. 8). Furthermore, shadow outlines of destructed blood vessels were noted in the infarcted areas.
Additionally, intraoperatively obtained pleural fluid showed many malignant cells arranged in sheets and single cell pattern. The tumor cells were round to spindle and highly pleomorphic. Immunostains for CK 5/6, CK 7, CK 20, TTF-1, CD 15 and CD 30 were all negative in the tumor cells.
Unfortunately, our patient had a complicated postoperative course in the intensive care unit. He developed pneumonia with Acinetobacter and was difficult to wean him from the ventilator. He finally succumbed to cardiac arrest.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old African American man presented with a 1-week history of progressive shortness of breath, bilateral calf pain, and occasional productive cough, followed 8 weeks later by new-onset hemoptysis and night sweats.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 1 week of progressive shortness of breath, bilateral calf pain, and occasional productive cough, and was found to have a cavitary left upper lobe mass with Aspergillus hyphae on CT-guided FNA; he improved and was discharged on a 6-week course of liposomal amphotericin B (2 weeks) followed by oral voriconazole. Approximately 8 weeks later, he re-presented with new-onset hemoptysis and night sweats, prompting re-evaluation and left upper lobectomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Peripheral vascular disease; Gleason 6 (3+3) prostate adenocarcinoma status post radical prostatectomy 8 years prior and penile prosthesis implantation for erectile dysfunction. Heavy smoking history (no alcohol or illicit drug use); prior 8-year incarceration; family history of lung cancer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially positive for progressive shortness of breath, bilateral calf pain, and occasional productive cough (negative for chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, or palpitations); on readmission 8 weeks later, positive for hemoptysis and night sweats.

objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed anemia with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, WBC 7.7 x 10^3/mm3 (ANC 4.6 x 10^3/mm3, monocytes 0.6 x 10^3/mm3, lymphocytes 3.2 x 10^3/mm3), serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, and negative HIV and Hepatitis C serologies. Pulmonary function testing on readmission showed an obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC ratio 58% of reference).
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest X-ray and chest CT showed a 4.5 x 5.5 x 5 cm left upper lobe mass with mediastinal and right hilar lymphadenopathy without pleural/pericardial effusion; head CT and bone scan were negative for metastases. Initial CT-guided FNA cytology of the left upper lobe mass showed an inflammatory necrotic background with large fungal aggregates of uniform septate hyphae branching at 45 degrees on GMS stain compatible with Aspergillus species (AFB stain and malignant cytology negative). Upon readmission 8 weeks later, bronchoscopy with BAL was negative for fungi, mycobacteria, Legionella, respiratory viruses, Pneumocystis, and malignant cells. Left upper lobectomy resected an 8.5 x 6.5 x 5.5 cm centrally necrotic, cavitary mass abutting the pleura: final surgical pathology, immunohistochemistry (epithelial component AE1/AE3+, EMA+, focal p63+; spindle component vimentin+, focal calponin/SMA+; negative SYT/18q11.2 translocation on FISH), and intraoperative pleural fluid cytology established primary pulmonary carcinosarcoma coexisting with GMS-positive Aspergillus hyphae in areas of vascular invasion and coagulative necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary pulmonary carcinosarcoma of the left upper lobe masked by secondary cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, confirmed initially by CT-guided FNA showing 45-degree branching septate Aspergillus hyphae on GMS stain and definitively diagnosed on left upper lobectomy pathology, immunohistochemistry, and FISH after hemoptysis recurred despite a 6-week course of liposomal amphotericin B and voriconazole. Following left upper lobectomy, the patient's ICU course was complicated by ventilator-associated Acinetobacter pneumonia, failure to wean from mechanical ventilation, and fatal cardiac arrest.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male of Chinese ethnicity received allogeneic filgastrim-mobilised peripheral blood HSCT from his HLA 6/6 matched sister using reduced-intensity conditioning regimen. He was in his first complete remission from underlying B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia that had been diagnosed 6 months earlier. The course of transplantation was complicated by steroid-refractory grade III acute GVHD of the liver that began 7 months post-transplantation, requiring intensive immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone followed by subsequent addition of other immunosuppressive agents including tacrolimus, mycopheolate mofetil and sirolimus for steroid-sparing purposes. He continued to receive dapsone and acyclovir prophylaxis, but was not on any antifungal prophylaxis.
In December 2007, at 9 months post-transplantation, he presented with acute-onset dry cough and shortness of breath following close contact with a client who had an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). The initial chest X-ray was unremarkable with no evidence of pneumonia. His symptoms worsened over the ensuing few days, culminating one week later in acute respiratory failure requiring hospitalization and non-invasive mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU). The patient was afebrile, with bilateral respiratory rhonchi on chest auscultation. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, renal and liver function. A chest x-ray (Figure 1) showed patchy bilateral lower zone and right upper zone air-space changes.
High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the thorax (Figure 2) showed bilateral extensive, circumscribed areas of ground-glass opacification throughout both lung fields associated with a fine reticular pattern in keeping with pneumonitis. There were no nodules or pleural-based lesions to suggest a concomitant invasive fungal infection. Empirical antimicrobial therapy with intravenous levofloxacin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was prescribed for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and possible pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonitis. Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) was added as the possibility of influenza-associated pneumonia was entertained.
All microscopy and cultures of clinical samples were negative for aerobic bacteria, acid-fast bacilli or fungi. Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (PCR) performed on nasopharyngeal specimens were positive for RSV, although viral culture from the same swab was negative. Serial serum galactomannan screening and quantitative real-time PCR for cytomegalovirus DNA from peripheral blood were all negative. Diagnostic bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was not performed at this point owing to the concern of worsening hypoxemia.
The patient's overall condition improved gradually over one week, with reduced oxygen requirement and dyspnea. However, a repeat HRCT thorax (Figure 3) 4 weeks later showed new cavitary lesions. Nonetheless, a conservative approach of close clinical monitoring and radiological follow-up was adopted as the serial serum galactomannan tests remained negative and the patient's overall clinical condition continued to improve. He was discharged one week following the second HRCT.
However, he was re-admitted 10 days later with acute onset right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea and diaphoresis. Chest x-ray (Figure 4A) and CT thorax (Figure 4B) showed enlarged thick-walled cavitary lesions in both lungs, with a moderate-sized right pneumothorax. Following chest tube insertion, he was transferred to the ICU for invasive mechanical ventilation. Thoracotomy with right upper lobectomy was subsequently performed. The histology was consistent with IPA, while lung tissue cultures grew Aspergillus fumigatus. He was prescribed voriconazole, which was continued for 6 months. Serial CT thorax showed gradual regression of the left pulmonary cavitary lesion and complete resolution of the ground grass changes. His respiratory symptoms improved despite receiving continued immunosuppressive therapy for his ongoing extensive chronic GVHD.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old Chinese male 9 months post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant presented with acute-onset dry cough and shortness of breath progressing to acute respiratory failure, followed 5 weeks later by acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Nine months after an HLA-matched sibling allogeneic HSCT for B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (complicated by steroid-refractory grade III hepatic GVHD treated with prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and sirolimus without antifungal prophylaxis), the patient developed acute dry cough and dyspnea after close contact with an individual with an upper respiratory tract infection (December 2007). Within 1 week, he progressed to hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring ICU non-invasive ventilation for RSV pneumonitis. Although he clinically improved over 1 week and was discharged despite new asymptomatic cavitary lung lesions on 4-week follow-up HRCT, he was readmitted 10 days post-discharge with acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis due to a secondary right pneumothorax.
subjective.past_medical_history: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia in first complete remission status post reduced-intensity allogeneic peripheral blood HSCT from an HLA 6/6-matched sister 9 months prior; steroid-refractory grade III acute/extensive chronic hepatic GVHD on prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and sirolimus; receiving dapsone and acyclovir prophylaxis (no mould-active prophylaxis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive initially for acute dry cough and progressive dyspnea (afebrile), and on readmission for acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis.

objective.physical_examination: During initial ICU admission, the patient was afebrile in acute respiratory failure with bilateral rhonchi on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, renal function, and liver function tests were normal. Initial chest X-ray was normal on day 1 but progressed at 1 week to patchy bilateral lower-zone and right upper-zone airspace opacities. Nasopharyngeal RT-PCR was positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Routine bacterial, AFB, and fungal smears/cultures and blood CMV quantitative PCR were negative. On readmission 5 weeks later, chest X-ray showed enlarged bilateral cavitary lesions and a moderate right pneumothorax.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum galactomannan assays remained persistently negative throughout both admissions. Initial thoracic HRCT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities with a fine reticular pattern consistent with viral pneumonitis without nodules. Repeat HRCT 4 weeks later revealed new cavitary lung lesions, and readmission CT thorax 10 days post-discharge demonstrated enlarged thick-walled bilateral cavitary lesions complicated by a moderate right pneumothorax. Following chest tube drainage and right thoracotomy with right upper lobectomy, lung histopathology confirmed invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) and lung tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven cavitary invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) complicated by secondary right pneumothorax following severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonitis in a heavily immunosuppressed allogeneic HSCT recipient with chronic GVHD, confirmed by right upper lobectomy histopathology and lung tissue culture growing A. fumigatus despite persistently negative serial serum galactomannan assays. Treated with tube thoracostomy, invasive mechanical ventilation, right upper lobectomy, and a 6-month course of voriconazole, resulting in gradual regression of the contralateral left cavitary lesion, complete resolution of ground-glass opacities, and sustained respiratory recovery despite ongoing immunosuppression for chronic GVHD.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 71-year-old female with a history of adult-onset diabetes mellitus, hypertension, rectal cancer and end-stage renal disease who had a successful deceased donor renal transplant 18 months prior to presentation. Her immunosuppression included belatacept, administered as part of an institutional review board (IRB) approved study. She presented acutely with complaints of breathing difficulties and substernal chest pain that was initially pleuritic in nature, but had become constant. She was also noted to have new onset of word-finding difficulty with inappropriate word substitution approximately 7 days prior to evaluation. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.
Her clinical examination was significant for the aphasia and a substernal mass, which was firm, and tender to palpation. She had no other focal neurologic or physical findings. The routine chest roentgenograph demonstrated a mediastinal mass with a left lower lobe process. A subsequent computerized tomography (CT) scan confirmed only a mediastinal mass that was adherent to the pericardium and extended anteriorly [Figure 1].
Following admission for further workup, she rapidly developed right retro-orbital pain with ipsilateral decreased vision. On re-examination, she had a predominantly expressive aphasia, a mild right pronator drift, and some slight right nasolabial fold flattening. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed corneal erosion for which she received topical ophthalmologic polymyxin B. Head imaging with CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a deep-seated left frontal lesion [Figure 2a-d]. The lesion was heterogeneously contrast enhancing after intravenous gadolinium administration, measured 25 x 18 x 10 mm and showed associated perifocal edema, resulting in a mild midline shift. She was started on dexamethasone for the edema and levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis.
Routine blood work included compete blood count and differential, electrolytes and chemistries, all of which were within normal limits. Her baseline creatinine was 0.8 mg/dl. Infectious causes were considered. Blood cultures for bacteria and fungus were obtained (but showed no growth), serum toxoplasma IgG and IgM, cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan and beta-d-glucan antigen tests were negative; urinary histoplasma antigen was also negative. Sampling of her CSF was not performed because of concerns of increased intracranial pressure. Given her history of a distant squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, the presence of an erosive mediastinal mass and being a relatively recent solid organ transplant recipient, metastatic or recurrent malignancy as well as post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease were of concern and it was felt that a biopsy was needed of both foci. The patient first underwent a CT-guided transthoracic lung biopsy followed 2 days later by a stereotactic brain biopsy. Both yielded specimen demonstrating septated, branching hyphae with culture data that confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus. Nucleic acid testing for mycobacteria, toxoplasma, and Epstein Barr Virus from the brain biopsy specimen was negative.
Antifungal therapy was initiated and included high-dose oral voriconazole (6 mg/kg twice daily) and parenteral liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day). Because of an acute rise in serum creatinine from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/dl the liposomal amphotericin was discontinued, and caspofungin (75 mg parenteral load, then 50 mg daily) was initiated. Her immunosuppression was changed from belatacept to mycophenolate mofetil 250 mg twice daily. The patient remained neurologically stable with resolution of her expressive aphasia within 4 weeks of initiation of dexamethasone and antifungal therapy. Repeat MRI of her CNS lesion was grossly unchanged at 6 weeks after initiation of antifungal therapy and by 12 weeks, the lesion regressed on MRI imaging with a concomitant decrease in edema [Figure 3]. Intravenous caspofungin was discontinued at this point, and she was continued on oral voriconazole, with trough levels in the 3-4 microg/ml range. Further chest imaging demonstrated improvement of disease with complete resolution by 6 months. However, repeat MRI of her head at 7 months demonstrated an increase in size of the lesion [Figure 4], now measuring 17 x 24 mm, with increased perilesional vasogenic edema despite medication compliance. The patient was not obviously aphasic; however, her family noted subtle word finding difficulties over the preceding 2 weeks. Because of the prior radiographic and clinical changes documenting improvement, concerns for secondary or superinfection were raised, as were CNS post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), or the possibility of voriconazole-resistant Aspergillus infection. She underwent a second stereotactic brain biopsy and intraoperative stains were negative for organisms or leukocytes. Pathology did not reveal a neoplasm but did identify gliosis. Specific fungal stains and fungal cultures were negative, and the only recovered organism was penicillin susceptible Proprionobacter acnes. This could have been culture contamination but was treated as a possible pathogen with 6 weeks of parenteral penicillin, 12 million units/day.
Although clinically her aphasia had again resolved, follow up MRI of the brain failed to demonstrate improvement in the size of the lesion and showed developing areas of necrosis and edema. For this reason the patient was taken to the operating room for an image-guided, left-sided, fronto-temporal microscopic resection and duraplasty. The abscess appeared densely encapsulated at the time of surgery, but establishment of a perilesional dissection plane was complicated because of an intense inflammatory reaction of surrounding glia and its vessels, which created dense tissue adherence. Pathology demonstrated in toto excision of an encapsulated abscess with septated hyphae in the periphery of the abscess and culture confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus, with susceptibility to voriconazole. She had an unremarkable post-operative course.
Now 2 years from the excision, she remains symptom free with only mild, persistent flattening of the nasolabial fold. She has no radiographic evidence of recurrence either in her CNS [Figure 5] or chest. Her renal function remains good with a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dl, on mycophenolate mofetil alone for immunosuppression, and voriconazole and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old female renal transplant recipient presented with acute breathing difficulties, constant substernal chest pain, and a 7-day history of word-finding difficulty.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eighteen months after a deceased-donor renal transplant maintained on belatacept immunosuppression, the patient presented with acute dyspnea, substernal chest pain (initially pleuritic, becoming constant), and 1 week of expressive dysphasia with inappropriate word substitution. Shortly after admission, she developed acute right retro-orbital pain and ipsilateral decreased vision.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease status post deceased-donor renal transplant 18 months prior (on belatacept protocol); adult-onset diabetes mellitus; hypertension; history of rectal/anal squamous cell carcinoma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea, substernal chest pain, word-finding difficulty/expressive aphasia, right retro-orbital pain, and decreased right vision; negative for fever, chills, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam revealed expressive aphasia and a firm, tender substernal mass. Following in-hospital progression, exam showed predominantly expressive aphasia, mild right pronator drift, slight right nasolabial fold flattening, and a right corneal erosion.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC with differential, serum electrolytes, and chemistries were normal, with a baseline serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. Bacterial and fungal blood cultures, serum Toxoplasma IgG/IgM, serum cryptococcal antigen, and urinary Histoplasma antigen were negative. Chest radiograph showed a mediastinal mass with a left lower lobe process.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum galactomannan and 1,3-beta-D-glucan assays were negative. Chest CT confirmed an anterior mediastinal/pulmonary mass adherent to the pericardium. Head CT and brain MRI revealed a 25 x 18 x 10 mm heterogeneously ring-enhancing deep left frontal mass with perilesional vasogenic edema and mild midline shift. Both CT-guided transthoracic lung/mediastinal biopsy and stereotactic left frontal brain biopsy (performed 2 days apart) demonstrated branching septate hyphae on histopathology and grew Aspergillus fumigatus on culture (brain biopsy PCRs for mycobacteria, Toxoplasma, and EBV were negative). At 7 months, despite chest resolution and therapeutic voriconazole troughs (3-4 ug/mL), brain MRI showed enlargement of the left frontal lesion (17 x 24 mm) with edema and necrosis; after a repeat stereotactic biopsy showed gliosis and Propionibacterium acnes, left frontotemporal craniotomy with en bloc microsurgical resection of the densely encapsulated abscess and duraplasty revealed viable septate hyphae in the abscess periphery and grew voriconazole-susceptible Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven disseminated invasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) presenting as an anterior mediastinal/pulmonary mass and a left frontal cerebral abscess in a renal transplant recipient receiving belatacept, confirmed by both transthoracic and stereotactic brain biopsies and cultures despite negative serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan. Managed by switching immunosuppression from belatacept to mycophenolate mofetil (250 mg bid), dexamethasone and levetiracetam, initial combination antifungal therapy with high-dose oral voriconazole (6 mg/kg bid, maintained at troughs of 3-4 ug/mL) and IV caspofungin for 12 weeks (after liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day caused acute creatinine elevation from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/dL), a 6-week course of IV penicillin G (12 million units/day), and definitive microsurgical en bloc excision of the encapsulated left frontal brain abscess at 7 months. At 2-year follow-up, she remained recurrence-free in both the CNS and chest with preserved allograft function (creatinine 1.2 mg/dL).

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old woman with progressive hepatic region discomfort was referred to a hematological department in May 2006. Her previous medical history was significant for chronic aplastic anemia and she was treated with stanozolol and intermittent gamma-globulin infusion. Full blood and bone marrow examination on a regular time schedule showed significant remission.
On admission, the patient had a body temperature of 36.5  C, pulse of 75 beats per minute, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Her abdomen was soft to palpation. Full blood test showed leukocyte count of 3.0 x 109/L, hemoglobin 110 g/L and platelet 23 x 109/L. Immunological studies, including quantitative immunoglobulins analysis, CD4/CD8 T lymphocyte ratio, and delayed hypersensitivity skin tests, were all normal. No predisposing disease associated with immunosuppression, such as diabetes mellitus, was found. Her human immunodeficiency virus status was negative, indicating the patient was in a non-immunocompromised condition. Abdominal ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple heterogeneous solid nodules in the right lobe of the liver (Figure 1). No abdominal lymphadenopathy or effusions were visible.
Malignant ailments and metastatic diseases were initially suspected, but serum tumor marker screening (including CEA, CA-125, CA-199, PSA, AFP, etc.) was within normal limits. Her aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 80 U/L (normal range <40 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 65 U/L (normal range <40 U/L). Other laboratory investigations, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), galactomannan antigenemia (GM) test, and autologous antibody, performed twice a week, were not specific. Complete liver disease studies, including hepatitis virology, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus serology, urinary copper, serum ceruloplasmine failed to lead a significant result.
Two weeks after admission, ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration was performed. On histopathological examination, abundant fungal hyphae were observed in the background of necrosis and chronic inflammation (Figure 2). A. fumigatus was subsequently isolated and cultured from the biopsy aspirate. Bacterial and acid-fast smears and cultures were negative. Pulmonary aspergillosis with liver dissemination was suspected, but the patient denied relevant infectious and occupational exposure history. A comprehensive whole body evaluation, including chest and paranasal sinus computed tomography (CT), did not indicated aspergillosis lesions. Regular GM tests continued to be negative. On the basis of these findings, we concluded the diagnosis of liver aspergilloma.
The patient was prescribed caspofungin acetate (Cancidas , Merck Sharp & Dohme Pty. Ltd., Australia) according to the minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) tests. An antifungal regimen was started with caspofungin acetate 70 mg on day 1 and 50 mg daily from day 2 to day 10. Serum liver enzymes were monitored to interrupt potential adverse effects. The patient received one course of caspofungin acetate first-line therapy every month and responded well in the clinical symptoms. Two months after the initial diagnosis, repeated MRI images showed a significant reduction in the sizes and number of the liver nodules (Figure 3). Our patient underwent caspofungin acetate therapy for six months and was discharged. During our last time follow-up in May 2012, she was stable without signs of progression or recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old woman with chronic aplastic anemia in remission presented with progressive right upper quadrant hepatic discomfort.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In May 2006, the patient was referred to the hematology department for progressive discomfort in the hepatic region without fever or constitutional symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic aplastic anemia in hematological remission maintained on stanozolol and intermittent gamma-globulin infusions; no history of diabetes mellitus, HIV, or occupational fungal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive hepatic region discomfort; afebrile and negative for respiratory or sinonasal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: temperature 36.5 C, pulse 75 bpm, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. Abdomen was soft to palpation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC showed WBC 3.0 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 110 g/L, and platelets 23 x 10^9/L. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated with AST 80 U/L (normal <40 U/L) and ALT 65 U/L (normal <40 U/L). Quantitative immunoglobulins, CD4/CD8 T-cell ratio, delayed-type hypersensitivity skin tests, HIV serology, viral hepatitis panel, CMV and EBV serologies, urinary copper, serum ceruloplasmin, ESR, CRP, autoantibodies, and serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA19-9, PSA, AFP) were all normal or negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed multiple heterogeneous solid nodules in the right hepatic lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal MRI confirmed multiple heterogeneous solid nodules in the right lobe of the liver without abdominal lymphadenopathy or ascites. Twice-weekly serial serum galactomannan antigenemia (GM) assays were persistently negative, and chest and paranasal sinus CT scans showed no extrahepatic fungal lesions. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the liver lesions 2 weeks after admission demonstrated abundant fungal hyphae in a background of necrosis and chronic inflammation on histopathology, and aspirate culture isolated Aspergillus fumigatus (bacterial and AFB smears/cultures were negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary isolated hepatic aspergilloma (multiple right-lobe liver nodules caused by Aspergillus fumigatus) in a patient with remitted aplastic anemia, definitively confirmed by ultrasound-guided liver biopsy histopathology and fungal culture growing A. fumigatus (with hepatic malignancy and extrahepatic dissemination ruled out). Treated with MIC-guided intravenous caspofungin acetate (70 mg loading on day 1, then 50 mg daily on days 2-10, repeated monthly for 6 months), resulting in symptomatic resolution, marked reduction in liver nodule size and number on 2-month follow-up MRI, and sustained recurrence-free stability through 6-year follow-up in May 2012.

raw_case_text: A 73-year-old woman with past medical history of hypertension and rheumatoid arthritis stage 4 under regular anti-hypertension medication and long-term corticosteroid therapy, presented to us in August 2010 with the chief complaint of decline of visual acuity of her right eye and right periorbital pain for 2 months. At the beginning of the clinical course, she had brain computed tomography (CT) scan and orbit magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) done in June 2010, which disclosed a small enhancing lesion, about 1.2 cm x 1.1 cm x 1 cm in size, near the right side orbital apex and adjacent right side superior orbital fissure with mild encasement of the right optic nerve, and this lesion showed mild extension to the adjacent right side posterior ethmoid sinus [Figure 1 a, b]. She had pulse steroid therapy in ophthalmology service, but it was ineffective. On admission, her neurological examination showed that she had right eye blindness, right ptosis, right ophthmaloplegia, and tingle in the territory of ophthalmic branch of right trigeminal nerve. Repeated MRI of orbit after admission in August 2010 showed the progression of the lesion which enlarged up to 1.5 cm x 1.3 cm x 1.2 cm [Figure 2 a, b]. She underwent endoscopic endonasal transethmoid approach with the removal of the lesion on 19 August 2010 under general anesthesia. After the surgery, she recovered well and her right periorbital pain was much released. However, 5 days after surgery, she experienced a severe headache followed by loss of consciousness. After endotracheal tube intubation and resuscitation, brain CT was checked which showed diffuse high-density acute SAH in the basal cistern, pre-pontine cistern, ambient cistern, quadrigeminal cistern, cerebellomedullary cistern, and right sylvian fissure, with acute hydrocephalus [Figure 3a]. Emergent external ventricular drainage was done followed by performing CT angiography which showed several bleb-like wide base aneurysms over right supraclinoid internal carotid artery (ICA), and one aneurysm, about 4 mm in size and located at the medial side of the right supraclinoid internal carotid artery, showed extravasation of contrast medium. The dome of the ruptured aneurysm projected medially and superiorly [Figure 3b]. On the same day, the histology examination reported that the lesion was composed of many fungal septate hyphae demonstrated on both HE stain and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain [Figure 4a, b]. Fungal infection was diagnosed and the culture turned out to be Aspergillus fumigatus. Her intracranial aneurysms were probably fungal aneurysms, which are one of the sequels of central nervous system (CNS) fungal infection. Unfortunately, after the event, she remained in deep coma and finally she expired due to central failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old woman on long-term corticosteroids for rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 2-month history of progressive right-sided visual loss and right periorbital pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In June 2010, the patient developed right periorbital pain and declining right visual acuity. Initial brain CT and orbital MRI revealed a 1.2 x 1.1 x 1.0 cm enhancing right orbital apex lesion extending into the superior orbital fissure and right posterior ethmoid sinus; she received pulse corticosteroid therapy in an ophthalmology clinic without improvement, and her vision deteriorated to complete right eye blindness with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia by the time of admission in August 2010.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage 4 rheumatoid arthritis on long-term corticosteroid therapy; hypertension on regular antihypertensive medication.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right eye blindness, right periorbital pain, right ptosis, diplopia/ophthalmoplegia, and right V1 trigeminal paresthesia; 5 days postoperatively developed sudden severe headache and coma.

objective.physical_examination: Admission neurological and ophthalmic examination revealed complete blindness of the right eye, right upper eyelid ptosis, total right ophthalmoplegia, and tingling paresthesia in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the right trigeminal nerve. Five days postoperatively, she developed deep coma.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial orbital MRI (June 2010) showed a 1.2 x 1.1 x 1.0 cm enhancing mass at the right orbital apex and superior orbital fissure mildly encasing the right optic nerve and extending to the right posterior ethmoid sinus; repeat orbital MRI on admission (August 2010) showed enlargement to 1.5 x 1.3 x 1.2 cm. She underwent endoscopic endonasal transethmoid resection on August 19, 2010; histopathology (H&E and PAS stains) revealed abundant septate fungal hyphae and tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus. Five days postoperatively, emergent head CT for sudden headache and coma demonstrated diffuse acute subarachnoid hemorrhage across the basal, prepontine, ambient, quadrigeminal, and cerebellomedullary cisterns and right Sylvian fissure with acute hydrocephalus, and CT angiography revealed multiple bleb-like wide-based mycotic aneurysms of the right supraclinoid internal carotid artery (ICA), including a ruptured 4-mm medial supraclinoid ICA aneurysm with active contrast extravasation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Right orbital apex and posterior ethmoid invasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) complicated by fatal rupture of right supraclinoid internal carotid artery mycotic aneurysms causing diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage and acute hydrocephalus, confirmed by endoscopic biopsy histopathology (H&E and PAS stains), fungal culture growing A. fumigatus, and cerebral CT angiography. Despite initial pain relief after endoscopic endonasal transethmoid resection and emergent external ventricular drainage following aneurysmal rupture on postoperative day 5, the patient remained in a deep coma and died of central brain failure.

raw_case_text:
A 78-year-old woman was diagnosed 4 months before admission with a right frontal GBM with extension to the basal ganglia and temporal lobe. The patient underwent a frontal craniotomy and partial resection of the lesion, followed by hypofractionated radiation therapy (16 fractions of 250 cGy) with concomitant daily TMZ (75 mg/m2). During the concurrent phase, she developed grade 1 lymphopenia and grade 2 nausea, but the treatment was otherwise well tolerated. Two days after completing chemoradiation, the patient was admitted for dyspnea and asymmetrical lower extremity edema. At admission, she denied cough, sputum, hemoptysis or thoracic pain. She reported no fever, chills, sweats or weight loss. Neurologic symptoms were stable since her last assessment. She had a history of hypertension and controlled type 2 diabetes. Medications included omeprazole, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide, sitagliptin and prophylactic sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. She was also taking dexamethasone 4 mg/day on a tapering scale.
Upon physical examination, she had normal vital signs, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. She had asymmetric edema of the lower limbs and, on auscultation, fine respiratory crackles bilaterally. Electrolytes, liver enzymes and renal function were normal. Blood counts were: hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, platelets 67,000/mm3 and leukocytes 7,030/mm3, with an absolute lymphocyte count of 800/mm3. A venous duplex-scan of the lower extremities showed an extensive deep vein thrombosis involving the left common femoral vein. An angiotomography of the thorax diagnosed an acute pulmonary embolism and also revealed scattered lobulated nodules with areas of cavitation, measuring up to 2.7 cm, located predominately in the upper lobes, some with a surrounding ground-glass halo. There was no pleural effusion. Areas of peribronchial infiltrates and centrilobular nodules were also present (fig. 1). Serum galactomannan levels, determined using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, were elevated (optical density index = 6.7, optical density index >=0.5 is considered a positive result). Blood samples obtained for culture and Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma antigen assays were negative.
A CT-guided pulmonary biopsy was then performed. Histochemical analysis (Gomori's silver stain) showed septate hyphal elements with acute-angle branching (fig. 2), and culture of the pulmonary tissue was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. The patient was promptly started on antifungal therapy with voriconazole and was discharged to complete the treatment as an outpatient. Chemotherapy with TMZ was resumed after 4 weeks of antifungal therapy. A control CT scan done approximately 30 days after admission revealed a reduction of the nodular lesions and ground-glass component previously identified (fig. 3).
Written informed consent for publication of the clinical details and/or clinical images was obtained from the guardian/relative of the patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old woman with glioblastoma multiforme presented 2 days after completing concurrent chemoradiation with acute dyspnea and asymmetrical lower extremity edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to admission, the patient underwent partial resection of a right frontal glioblastoma multiforme followed by hypofractionated radiotherapy (16 fractions of 250 cGy) with concurrent daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2) and tapering dexamethasone (4 mg/day), complicated by grade 1 lymphopenia. Two days after completing chemoradiation, she presented with acute dyspnea and asymmetrical left lower limb swelling without fever or cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right frontal glioblastoma multiforme (extending to the basal ganglia and temporal lobe) diagnosed 4 months prior, status post partial craniotomy resection and concurrent temozolomide/radiotherapy; hypertension; controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute dyspnea and asymmetrical lower limb edema; negative for cough, sputum, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, or neurological deterioration. Home medications: dexamethasone 4 mg/day, TMP-SMX prophylaxis, omeprazole, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide, and sitagliptin.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal with respiratory rate 18 breaths/min and room-air SpO2 95%. Physical exam showed asymmetrical lower extremity edema (left > right), bilateral fine inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation, and stable neurological exam.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, thrombocytopenia (platelets 67,000/mm3), WBC 7,030/mm3 with lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 800/mm3), and normal electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function. Blood cultures and serum Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma antigen assays were negative. Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound confirmed extensive deep vein thrombosis of the left common femoral vein.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT angiography confirmed an acute pulmonary embolism and simultaneously revealed scattered lobulated, cavitary pulmonary nodules up to 2.7 cm predominantly in the upper lobes—some with a surrounding ground-glass halo sign—along with peribronchial infiltrates and centrilobular nodules without pleural effusion. Serum galactomannan ELISA was strongly positive (optical density index 6.7; cutoff >=0.5). CT-guided lung biopsy histopathology (Gomori methenamine silver stain) demonstrated septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, and lung tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven cavitary invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) coexisting with left common femoral deep vein thrombosis and acute pulmonary embolism in a patient with glioblastoma multiforme following concurrent temozolomide chemoradiation and dexamethasone therapy, confirmed by positive serum galactomannan (ODI 6.7), CT halo and cavitary nodules, and CT-guided lung biopsy GMS histopathology and culture. Treated with oral voriconazole, achieving marked reduction of pulmonary nodules and ground-glass halos on 30-day follow-up chest CT and enabling safe resumption of adjuvant temozolomide chemotherapy after 4 weeks of antifungal therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old male presented to our hospital with progressive dyspnea, productive cough, and hemoptysis of 2 weeks duration. Three days prior to admission his history was significant for massive hemoptysis, averaging 200-500 mL of gross blood daily. However, there was no evidence of chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, recent travel, or contact with the sick, nor was there any other bleeding noted. His past medical history was significant for asthma and 30 years of smoking. He was also treated for active pulmonary tuberculosis 7 years ago. He had one similar episode of hemoptysis 1 year prior to this admission, but declined full work-up and failed to follow up after discharge.
Upon presentation, his vital signs were within normal limits, with a respiratory rate of 20 cycles/minute and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. The lungs were clear to both percussion and auscultation, except for a decreased breath sound at the left upper lobe apex. Other findings on physical examination were within normal limits. Laboratory results were as follows: hemoglobin, 11.2 g/dL; hematocrit, 33.1 g/dL; white blood cell count, 5.7 x 109/L; and a normal differential count. Basic metabolic profile, liver chemistry, and coagulation parameters were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph revealed hyperinflation, bilateral nodularity, pleural thickening with fibrocystic changes in the left apex and a possible cavitary lesion. Further work-up with a chest computed tomogram (Figure 1) revealed irregular speculated density, representing a cavitary lesion filled with mycetoma (fungal ball), numerous nodules scattered throughout both lungs and extensive bullous disease, especially at the left upper lobe. Sputum staining for acid-fast organisms was negative, but Haemophilus parainfluenzae was grown on culture media. Left upper lung biopsy revealed CPAM type 1 with aspergilloma (Figures 2 and 3). The Periodic acid-Schiff and Grocott's methenamine silver stains showed tightly packed septate hyphae. He was started on itraconazole and ceftriaxone. Due to persistent massive hemoptysis, he was referred for bronchial artery angiography and embolization. The bronchial arteriogram showed neovascularity supplying the inflammatory changes within both apices of the lungs, which were successfully embolized. Subsequently, he had some improvement of the cough and hemoptysis; however, 2 days after the embolization, massive hemoptysis recurred, which necessitated emergency surgical intervention. He had a left upper lobectomy. Intraoperatively, he developed diffuse oozing from the dissected surfaces, leading to hemodynamic instability and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. Every effort to resuscitate him including massive transfusion of blood products was futile. He died from hemorrhagic shock secondary to left lobectomy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, productive cough, and hemoptysis escalating to massive hemoptysis (200-500 mL/day) over the 3 days prior to admission.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive dyspnea, productive cough, and hemoptysis 2 weeks prior to admission, which worsened over the last 3 days to massive gross hemoptysis averaging 200-500 mL/day. He had experienced a similar episode of hemoptysis 1 year earlier but had declined full evaluation and lost to follow-up.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bronchial asthma; active pulmonary tuberculosis treated 7 years prior; 30-year smoking history; prior uninvestigated episode of hemoptysis 1 year ago.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive dyspnea, productive cough, and massive hemoptysis (200-500 mL/day); negative for chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, recent travel, sick contacts, or other bleeding sites.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals were normal with respiratory rate 20 breaths/min and room-air SpO2 96%. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds at the left upper lobe apex with clear lung fields elsewhere; remaining physical exam was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 33.1%), WBC 5.7 x 10^9/L with normal differential, and normal basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, and baseline coagulation profile. Sputum AFB smear was negative, while sputum bacterial culture grew Haemophilus parainfluenzae. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation, bilateral nodularity, left apical pleural thickening with fibrocystic changes, and a suspected left apical cavitary lesion.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated an irregular spiculated left upper lobe cavitary lesion containing an intracavitary mycetoma (fungal ball), extensive left upper lobe bullous disease, and scattered bilateral pulmonary nodules. Left upper lung biopsy histopathology (H&E, PAS, and Grocott methenamine silver stains) revealed congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) type 1 colonized by a fungal ball of tightly packed septate Aspergillus hyphae. Selective bronchial arteriography showed hypervascularity supplying bilateral apical inflammatory lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left upper lobe aspergilloma (mycetoma) arising within a congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) type 1 and post-tubercular bullous lung disease, complicated by life-threatening massive hemoptysis and confirmed by chest CT and lung biopsy PAS/GMS histopathology. Treated initially with oral itraconazole, ceftriaxone (for Haemophilus parainfluenzae), and bilateral apical bronchial artery embolization; however, massive hemoptysis recurred 2 days post-embolization, and during emergency left upper lobectomy the patient developed uncontrollable diffuse pleural/raw-surface oozing, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and fatal hemorrhagic shock.

raw_case_text: A 65-year-old male patient, with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, presented to us with painless, progressive diminished vision in both eyes over 4 months (asymmetrical involvement; right eye defect more than left eye). On examination, right eye had only perception of light and left eye had vision of counting fingers up to 2 feet. Fundus showed features of optic atrophy. His neurological examination was unremarkable. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. He was negative for  HIV, HBsAg and HCV done by ELISA as a routine presurgical investigation. His chest X-ray was unremarkable. Mantoux was negative. Sputum AFB (done in the postoperative period after the tissue cultures showed growth of tuberculosis) was negative. Sputum for acid fast bacilli was negative. He had an FBS = 176 mg/dl, PPBS = 231mg/dl, and Hb1Ac = 8.2%. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with orbit showed a lesion, which was heterogeneously hypointense on T1W and hyperintense on T2W, located in the orbit, encircling the optic nerve and was extending through the optic foramen into the cranial cavity. On gadolinium contrast T1W imaging, the lesion was brilliantly enhancing and was extending onto the planum sphenoidale [Figure 1]. Mild enhancement was also noted in the right orbit. The paranasal sinuses were normal. A working diagnosis of orbital meningioma was made. A left supraorbital craniotomy and deroofing of the orbit was followed by subtotal excision of the lesion. The tumor was grayish, mildly vascular, firm, nonsuckable and was encircling the left optic nerve and was extending into the optic canal. The frozen section examination was suggestive of granulomatous pathology and hence the specimen was subjected to microbiological examination as per our departmental protocol for suspected infections (aerobic, tubercular and fungal staining, and cultures). Histopathological examination showed multi-septate hyphae suggestive of fungus. On day 5, growth of Aspergillus flavus was noted on fungal culture. The patient was started on antifungal drugs immediately (Inj. Voriconazole 400 mg on day 1 followed by 200 mg daily for 14 days, followed by oral Voriconazole 200 mg, twice daily for 4 weeks, to be reviewed with repeat imaging). On day 28, all three cultures tubes for tuberculosis [BACTEC 460 Tb system (Becton Dickinson, USA) using the 12 B vials] were positive. He was started on antitubercular drugs as per his body weight (Isoniazid 300 mg once a day, Rifampicin 600 mg once a day, Pyrazinamide 750 mg twice daily, Ethambutol 800 mg once a day, and Benadone 20 mg once a day). He was discharged on 14th postoperative day with no change in his visual status. He, however, had a cerebrovascular accident and succumbed to it on 38th postoperative day.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 4-month history of painless, progressive bilateral visual loss affecting the right eye more than the left.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 months, the patient experienced insidious, painless, asymmetric decline in visual acuity in both eyes (right worse than left) without headache or meningeal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painless progressive bilateral vision loss; negative for headache, ocular pain, or meningeal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination showed visual acuity reduced to light perception in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 feet in the left eye, with bilateral optic atrophy on fundoscopy. Neurological examination was otherwise unremarkable with no signs of meningeal irritation.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative blood tests showed fasting blood sugar 176 mg/dL, postprandial blood sugar 231 mg/dL, and HbA1c 8.2%. ELISA screening for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV was negative. Chest X-ray, Mantoux tuberculin skin test, and postoperative sputum AFB smears were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and orbital MRI demonstrated a T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense, brilliantly gadolinium-enhancing orbital mass encircling the left optic nerve and extending through the optic canal onto the planum sphenoidale, with mild right orbital enhancement and normal paranasal sinuses (initially suspected to be an orbital meningioma). Following left supraorbital craniotomy, orbital deroofing, and subtotal excision of the firm, grayish, mildly vascular mass, frozen section and histopathology revealed granulomatous inflammation with multiseptate fungal hyphae. Fungal culture of the excised orbital tissue grew Aspergillus flavus on day 5, and all three BACTEC 460 TB liquid culture vials grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis on day 28.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary orbital apex and intracranial optic nerve granuloma caused by dual co-infection with Aspergillus flavus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis mimicking an orbital/planum sphenoidale meningioma in a poorly controlled diabetic patient, definitively confirmed by surgical biopsy histopathology, fungal culture growing A. flavus (day 5), and BACTEC mycobacterial culture growing M. tuberculosis (day 28). Treated with subtotal surgical decompression via left supraorbital craniotomy, intravenous voriconazole (400 mg day 1, then 200 mg daily for 14 days) followed by oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily), and four-drug anti-tubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, plus pyridoxine) initiated on day 28; he was discharged on postoperative day 14 with unchanged vision but died of a cerebrovascular accident on postoperative day 38.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old Caucasian female received in November 2011 the diagnosis of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML), M4 subtype according to French-American-British (FAB) classification, with intermediate cytogenetic risk. Initially treated without benefit with induction chemotherapy, the patient received salvage chemotherapy with high-dose cytarabine combined with idarubicin and cyclosporin A, obtaining complete disease remission, followed by consolidation chemotherapy with high-dose cytarabine. In June 2012 the patient underwent a first allogeneic HSCT from a 8/10 HLA-matched unrelated donor (MUD) upon busulfan/cyclophosphamide conditioning regimen and in vivo T cell depletion by thymoglobulin. Fluconazole antifungal prophylaxis was administered.
In September 2012 the patient relapsed and received a fludarabine-based salvage therapy without benefit. Since the diagnosis of AML, the patient had experienced several infectious episodes: a catheter-related sepsis from Staphylococcus hominis and an episode of diarrhoea caused by Clostridium difficile after induction therapy, and, after the first allogeneic HSCT, a sepsis by Escherichia coli. No history of fungal infections was reported. In November 2012 the patient was referred to our Institute for a second allogeneic transplant.
The patient presented acute onset of fever and dry cough with sepsis at the hospital admission in November 2012. Blood analyses demonstrated pancytopenia, including grade IV neutropenia (secondary to the disease relapse), and high level of serum c-reactive protein. According to our institutional guidelines for febrile neutropenia, the patient was tested for standard blood, urine and sputum culture and galactomannan antigen test on blood, which all resulted negative. Chest X-ray was normal. A wide-spectrum empirical antibiotic therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin was therefore initiated.
The initial management of the infection requires formulating a probable diagnosis, obtaining cultures, performing imaging studies to confirm the source of infection, and finally initiating appropriate and timely empirical antimicrobial therapy. High-risk patients require early hospitalization to receive broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy; in this setting the use of an antipseudomonal b-lactam agent, such as piperacillin-tazobactam, is recommended. Concomitantly to the other microbiologic analyses, SeptiFast was performed and resulted positive for Aspergillus fumigatus (Figure 1); the positive result was available after only 4 hours from patient's admission, and importantly was confirmed in three consecutive samples of patient's peripheral blood.
Fluconazole antifungal therapy was promptly changed on the basis of this evidence, and the patient received voriconazole, a triazole antifungal agent that has fungicidal activity against Aspergillus.
Large studies have demonstrated the superiority of voriconazole to improve response rate and survival in highly immunosuppressed patients developing invasive aspergillosis (IA) after allogeneic HSCT. The following day a computerized tomography (CT) scan of the chest (Figure 2) was performed, evidencing an extensive lobar pneumonia, highly suggestive for fungal infection.
A bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was also performed and cytology resulted positive for septate hyphae suggestive for Aspergillus (Figure 3) classifying a diagnosis of probable IFI, while all other microbiological tests performed on BAL were negative. Importantly serial galactomannan antigen tests on blood resulted all negative.
Clinical symptoms rapidly improved upon the start of voriconazole therapy, with resolution of sepsis and rapid response of the fever. A CT scan (Figure 4) performed 10 days after starting voriconazole showed a marked reduction of the lobar pneumonia and ground-glass opacities.
SeptiFast-guided early initiation of antifungal therapy prompted rapid resolution of the sepsis, enabling the patient to sustain a second allogeneic HSCT from a haploidentical donor in December 2012. The conditioning regimen consisted of treosulfan, fludarabine and melphalan followed by T cell-replete peripheral blood stem cells. Post-grafting immunosuppression consisted of high-dose post-transplant cyclophosphamide followed by oral administration of mycophenolate mofetil and sirolimus.
Of notice, the evidence of fungal infection was fundamental to guide the choice of the transplant protocol towards a conditioning devoid of anti-thymocyte globulins to favour rapid immune reconstitution and reduce the risk of fungal infection reoccurrence. In the aplastic phase and during the post transplant course the patient maintained a secondary prophylaxis with voriconazole; therapeutic drug monitoring allows a safe and effective administration of voriconazole along with sirolimus. Episodes of sepsis from Pseudomonas aeruginosa were reported after transplant, but all solved with targeted antibiotic therapy.
The targeted secondary antifungal prophylaxis and the rapid immune reconstitution (Figure 5) avoided any other fungal infection, despite the occurrence of cutaneous acute graft versus host disease (GvHD) initially, and a severe overlap chronic GvHD (involving skin, liver, mouth, eyes and lung) which required profound immunosuppression afterwards.
At the last follow up (1 year after transplant) the patient is still in complete remission of the haematological disease, without any sign of fungal infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old Caucasian female with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia presented on admission for a second allogeneic stem cell transplant with acute-onset fever, dry cough, and sepsis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with AML FAB M4 in November 2011, the patient underwent salvage chemotherapy and an 8/10 HLA-matched unrelated donor allogeneic HSCT in June 2012 (on fluconazole prophylaxis), relapsed in September 2012, and was refractory to fludarabine-based salvage therapy. Upon admission in November 2012 for a second (haploidentical) HSCT, she presented with acute fever, dry cough, grade IV neutropenia, and clinical sepsis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (FAB M4, intermediate cytogenetic risk) status post first 8/10 matched unrelated donor allogeneic HSCT (June 2012); prior infectious history of catheter-related Staphylococcus hominis bacteremia, Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, and post-HSCT Escherichia coli sepsis; on fluconazole prophylaxis with no prior history of fungal infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute fever, dry cough, and sepsis.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with acute fever and signs of clinical sepsis.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed severe pancytopenia with grade IV neutropenia and elevated serum CRP. Standard bacterial and fungal blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative, and admission chest X-ray was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum galactomannan antigen assays were persistently negative. However, peripheral blood multiplex real-time PCR (LightCycler SeptiFast) returned positive for Aspergillus fumigatus within 4 hours of admission and was confirmed on three consecutive peripheral blood samples. Chest CT the following day demonstrated extensive lobar pneumonia with ground-glass opacities, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cytology revealed branching septate hyphae consistent with Aspergillus (with negative BAL bacterial/viral/fungal cultures).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Probable invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) with fungemia/DNAemia in a patient with relapsed AML and grade IV neutropenia, rapidly diagnosed within 4 hours of admission by three consecutive positive peripheral blood SeptiFast PCR assays, lobar pneumonia on chest CT, and septate hyphae on BAL cytology despite negative blood cultures and negative serial serum galactomannan. Promptly switched from fluconazole to voriconazole alongside empirical piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin, achieving rapid defervescence, resolution of sepsis, and marked CT regression within 10 days. This enabled successful haploidentical HSCT in December 2012 (using ATG-free conditioning with treosulfan, fludarabine, melphalan, and post-transplant cyclophosphamide/MMF/sirolimus plus TDM-guided secondary voriconazole prophylaxis), with complete leukemia remission and no fungal recurrence at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old Nigerian boy with a diagnosis of SCA disease and recurrent episodes of vaso-occlusive crisis was referred to our centre as candidate to related allogeneic BMT. According to our internal protocol aimed at evaluating the possible lung damage of SCA patients before the transplant, computed tomography (CT) scan of the lung and spirometry were performed.
