In August 2013, she developed 3 months of productive cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and weight loss with a new intensely FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and hilar lymphadenopathy. After repeated non-diagnostic biopsies and VATS wedge resection, she was treated with two courses of oral prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day in late 2013 and 1 mg/kg/day plus macrolide in March 2014) for presumed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, during which the mass invaded the mediastinum and she developed right upper arm paresis and sensory loss, enlarging cerebral abscesses, hydrocephalus with somnolence, and multiple ill-defined skin lesions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right-sided breast cancer treated with mastectomy in 2006 (no adjuvant therapy); 30-mm stable right lower lobe lung nodule (2006-2011); lifetime non-smoker; iatrogenic corticosteroid exposure (prednisone 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day) for presumed organizing pneumonia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for productive cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss, subsequent right upper arm weakness and sensory loss, somnolence, and multiple skin lesions; negative for fever or night sweats.

objective.physical_examination: Developed progressive muscle weakness and sensory loss of the right upper arm in March 2014, followed in May 2014 by multiple ill-defined cutaneous lesions and progressive somnolence from hydrocephalus.
objective.routine_investigations: Immunological workup was normal, including normal total IgG, IgG subclasses, IgA, IgM, and complement levels, and negative ANA and ANCA.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial 18F-FDG PET-CT scans (August 2013 to May 2014) showed an enlarging FDG-avid right lower lobe mass invading the mediastinum, station 4R lymph nodes, right pulmonary artery, and left superior pulmonary vein. Initial bronchoscopies, CT-guided biopsy, EBUS-TBNA, VATS wedge resection, and mediastinoscopy showed only fibrosis and chronic histiocytic inflammation without malignancy; sporadic Aspergillus-like hyphae on bronchial aspirate cytology in January 2014 were initially dismissed as colonization. Brain MRI (March and May 2014) revealed multiple diffusion-restricting cortical, watershed, corpus callosum, left thalamic, and centrum semiovale abscesses with marked perilesional edema and hydrocephalus. In May 2014, both stereotactic cerebral biopsy and skin lesion biopsy demonstrated marked inflammation and dichotomously branching septate fungal hyphae without malignancy, and skin biopsy wound fluid culture grew Aspergillus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven disseminated invasive aspergillosis involving the lung, mediastinum, brain, and skin in a previously immunocompetent woman whose dissemination was promoted by empirical corticosteroid therapy for misdiagnosed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, definitively confirmed by cerebral and skin biopsy histopathology (dichotomously branching septate hyphae) and skin wound culture growing Aspergillus. Treated with serum- and CSF-TDM-guided voriconazole and five neurosurgical CSF drainage procedures culminating in ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, achieving marked cerebral MRI and chest CT regression at 6 months, hospital discharge at 7 months (December 2014), and near-complete neurological recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 77-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension presented with visual loss in the left eye. Ophthalmic examination revealed best-corrected decimal VA (BCVA) of 1.0 and 0.3. Light reflex of the left eye was weakened with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundus examination showed optic disc swelling of the left eye (Fig. 1a). Goldmann perimetry (GP) revealed lower altitudinal hemianopia in the left eye (Fig. 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on fat-suppressed T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) and short-T1 inversion recovery (STIR) showed no optic nerve or paranasal sinus abnormalities without gadolinium (Gd) enhancement due to renal dysfunction (Fig. 2a, b). Thus, the previous ophthalmologist suspected her as having anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and administered mini-pulse steroid therapy and 500 mg methylprednisolone to relieve the disc swelling. After mini-pulse therapy, which was not followed by the administration of oral prednisolone, BCVA in the left eye increased to 0.8 within 3 days. However, 2 days later, VA in the left eye abruptly decreased to 0.1, and although additional mini-pulse therapy was performed, BCVA in the left eye further decreased to no light perception within a month. Two months later, BCVA in the right eye also decreased to 0.5, the right optic disc began to swell, and swelling of the left optic disc persisted and became more severe (Fig. 1c, d). Fluorescein angiography exhibited marked hyperfluorescence of the optic disc with filling defect in the choroidal circulation in the left eye and slight hyperfluorescence of the optic disc in the right eye (Fig. 1e, f). Finally, she was referred to our hospital for further treatment.
Our initial examination showed that BCVA was 0.3 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. GP in the right eye showed irregular visual defect in both the superior and inferior visual field (Fig. 1g). There was no pain with eye movement, and there were no abnormal signs on general neurological examination. Laboratory data showed increased creatinine (1.24 mg/dL) and decreased estimated glomerular filtration rate (32.6 mL/min/1.73 m2), indicating renal dysfunction, and slightly increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL2-R, 670 U/mL). Other routine blood and metabolic laboratory studies were unremarkable, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were not elevated. Antibodies for anti-aquaporin 4 and anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were also negative. No abnormalities were seen on chest X-ray. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no elevation of CSF pressure, no significant infectious changes, and no tumor cells (initial pressure 10 mm Hg, colorless and transparent, cells < 1/microL, proteins 47 mg/dL, glucose 71 mg/dL, sIL2-R < 50 U/mL, myelin basic protein < 31.3 ng/mL, and positive oligoclonal IgG bands). Cytologic examination of CSF was performed 3 times throughout the course, but no tumor or atypical cells were detected.
MRI of the brain and orbits revealed no obvious optic nerve swelling without any apparent parenchymal hyperintensity on STIR images (Fig. 2c). There were no other findings of nasal sinusitis or space-occupying lesion. Echocardiography of the temporal artery showed negative signs of giant-cell arteritis. Bilateral arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and invasive optic neuropathy were suspected because of the lack of significant findings on MRI and the occurrence of bilateral disc swelling. Because oral prednisolone was not given following mini-pulse therapy at the first hospital, we again initiated intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1,000 mg/day for 3 days), followed by prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg of body weight. BCVA of the right eye improved to 0.7 after two courses of steroid pulse therapy, but the left eye had not improved on hospital day 15. However, BCVA of the right eye suddenly decreased to 0.2 following the third course of steroid pulse therapy. We rechecked CSF for further examination including cytology, but no abnormalities were seen (colorless and transparent cells < 1/microL, proteins 49 mg/dL, glucose 65 mg/dL, and sIL2-R < 50 U/mL). We initiated anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy consisting of warfarin 2 mg and clopidogrel sulfate 75 mg taken orally. On hospital day 34, VA in the right eye further decreased to hand motions, and the patient's body temperature elevated to 38  with depressed consciousness. On the same day, repeat MRI showed suspected midbrain infarction (Fig. 2d-f), and CSF findings indicated cerebral meningitis (cells 303/muL, proteins 63 mg/dL, glucose 89 mg/dL, and negative cryptococcal antigen). Arterial and venous blood and CSF culture demonstrated no bacterial or fungal growth. Despite transfusions, antibiotic therapy, and anticoagulant therapy, the patient died on hospital day 40. After we obtained informed consent from her family, the autopsy was conducted. The autopsy findings revealed a primary cause of death of subarachnoid hemorrhage. No apparent paranasal sinus inflammatory changes were observed. Histological examination showed a significant amount of Aspergillus hyphae, inflammatory cells, and fibrous formation mainly localized in the dura mater, whereas cellular infiltration into the parenchyma of the optic nerve was less observed (Fig. 3a-d). Fungal ball formation was observed surrounding the mesencephalic aqueduct with massive invasion of A. hyphae and further destroyed the wall of the cerebral artery, suggesting a primary cause of midbrain and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 77-year-old diabetic female presented with progressive bilateral visual loss and optic disc swelling beginning in the left eye and involving the right eye 2 months later.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented to an outside ophthalmologist with left eye visual loss (BCVA 0.3), left optic disc swelling, and inferior altitudinal hemianopia without orbital/sinus MRI abnormalities; she was treated for presumed anterior ischemic optic neuropathy with IV methylprednisolone mini-pulses (500 mg), transiently improving to 0.8 before deteriorating to no light perception (NLP) within 1 month. Two months later, right eye vision declined to 0.5 (and 0.3 on referral) with new right optic disc swelling. At our hospital, two courses of high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day for 3 days) transiently improved right BCVA to 0.7, but vision dropped to 0.2 after the third pulse and to hand motions on hospital day 34 accompanied by fever (38 C) and depressed consciousness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and chronic renal dysfunction.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sequential bilateral visual loss (left NLP, right hand motions) and on hospital day 34 fever (38 C) and depressed consciousness; negative for pain with eye movement or baseline headache.

objective.physical_examination: Initial referral exam showed BCVA 0.3 in the right eye and NLP in the left eye, left relative afferent pupillary defect, bilateral optic disc edema (severe on the left, mild-to-moderate on the right), no pain on extraocular movement, and normal general neurological exam. On hospital day 34, she developed fever (38 C), depressed consciousness, and right visual decline to hand motions.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed renal impairment (creatinine 1.24 mg/dL, eGFR 32.6 mL/min/1.73 m2), mildly elevated serum sIL-2R (670 U/mL), normal ESR and CRP, and negative anti-AQP4 and anti-MOG antibodies. Chest X-ray and temporal artery ultrasound were normal. Fluorescein angiography showed marked left optic disc hyperfluorescence with choroidal filling defect and mild right optic disc hyperfluorescence. Initial and day 15 CSF analyses were acellular (<1 cell/uL, protein 47-49 mg/dL, glucose 65-71 mg/dL, sIL-2R <50 U/mL, positive oligoclonal bands, negative cytology x3); on day 34, CSF showed meningitis (303 cells/uL, protein 63 mg/dL, glucose 89 mg/dL, negative cryptococcal antigen, and negative blood/CSF bacterial and fungal cultures).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial non-contrast fat-suppressed T2/STIR brain and orbital MRIs (gadolinium withheld due to renal dysfunction) showed no obvious optic nerve hyperintensity or paranasal sinusitis until hospital day 34, when repeat brain MRI revealed an acute midbrain infarction. Postmortem autopsy following death on hospital day 40 revealed fatal subarachnoid hemorrhage, no macroscopic paranasal sinusitis, extensive dural infiltration by Aspergillus hyphae with fibrosis and inflammation encasing the optic nerves, and a fungal ball of Aspergillus hyphae surrounding the mesencephalic aqueduct with direct fungal invasion and destruction of the cerebral arterial wall causing midbrain infarction and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal occult dural-based invasive central nervous system aspergillosis presenting as sequential bilateral steroid-responsive/relapsing compressive/ischemic optic neuropathy (masquerading as anterior ischemic optic neuropathy) and culminating in mesencephalic fungal arteritis, midbrain infarction, and fatal subarachnoid hemorrhage, definitively diagnosed at autopsy by histopathology demonstrating dural and cerebral arterial wall invasion by Aspergillus hyphae despite normal sinus imaging and sterile premortem CSF cultures. Repeated high-dose corticosteroid pulses without antifungal coverage contributed to fungal progression and fatal vascular rupture on hospital day 40.

raw_case_text:
The 40-year-old male patient presented initially with multiple petechiae and ecchymosis on his legs, which had appeared during his summer holidays. Emergency blood count revealed pancytopenia and bone marrow biopsy proved aplasia; vSAA was diagnosed with neutrophils under 0.1/nL, platelets under 20/nL and reticulocytes 2 per mille. Immunosuppressive therapy with antithymocyte globulin (ATGAM ; Pfizer, days 1-4; 40 mg/kg, 3,400 mg daily) and cyclosporine A was initiated but did not improve the blood count. Subsequently, repeated admissions to hospital were necessary due to febrile neutropenia. Additionally, he developed pretibial erysipelas after a mosquito bite on day -66 before SCT. Despite the initiation of broad spectrum anti-infective therapy, his clinical condition deteriorated with increasing inflammation scores and fever. SM was detected in blood cultures and in drained pus gained from the pretibial ulcers (Fig. 1). In addition, computed tomography and microbiological workup of bronchoalveolar lavage revealed invasive aspergillus flavus and SM pneumonia. Based on resistogram (sensitivity towards ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and tigecycline; despite inpatient intolerance towards trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole), the anti-infective medication was modified, but therapy proved difficult, prolonged and required repeated modification of the antibiotic regime. The wounds (6 x 4 and 2 x 2 cm) had to be surgically revised repeatedly (in detail: incision and drainage on day -54; debridement of extensors tendon sheath and of muscles, negative wound pressure therapy on day -40; debridement and renewing of negative wound pressure therapy on days -33 and -28, finally debridement of muscles and resection of extensor hallucis longus muscles' tendon on day -23 before SCT) and were initially treated with bandages changed daily and then with negative wound pressure therapy (for illustration see Fig. 1). Due to necrosis and initially exposed wound conditions, extensor hallucis longus muscles' tendon had to be resected and extensor tibialis anterior muscles' tendon atrophied resulting in a drop foot, which was treated with a peroneus orthesis. Over the following weeks and despite intensive wound management, no signs of wound healing occurred and amputation was discussed. In addition, the patient developed septic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 32%) with symptomatic congestive heart failure. Since his complex invasive infections (necrotizing deep skin ulcers, aspergillus pneumonia) were all caused by vSAA, the patient underwent a salvage allogeneic HSCT in October 2016, 6 months after diagnosis. The conditioning regimen consisted of cyclophosphamide (day -6 to -3 at doses of 300 mg/m2, qd), fludarabine (day -6 to -3 at doses of 30 mg/m2, qd), antithymocyte globulin (Thymoglobulin ; Genzyme, day -4 to -3; 3.75 mg/kg bodyweight [bwt], qd) and total body irradiation with 2 Gy on day 0. He received 1.01 x 106 CD34+ bone marrow stem cells/kg bwt from an unrelated, male, human leukocyte antigen allele matched 10/10 donor. Prophylaxis of Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) consisted of tacrolimus, starting on day -5, combined with methotrexate given at doses of 10 mg/m2 on day +1 and 8 mg/m2 on day +3 and +6. Engraftment of granulocytes and leukocytes occurred both on day +22 and of thrombocytes on day +33. G-CSF was administered daily from day +2 to day +17 to avoid prolonged neutropenia in the setting of very severe infectious complications. The anti-infective medication consisted of aciclovir, moxifloxacin, atovaquone, isavuconazol and amphotericin B.
Concerning the pretibial wounds, extensive surgical debridement was continued and of two 20 cm gentamycin mini chains were placed into the deep ulcers combined with debridement and renewing of negative pressure wound therapy on days +40 and +47. On day +54 after allogeneic SCT, autologous full-thickness meshed skin graft transplantation from his lower leg was performed in the absence of signs of acute GvHD (for results see Fig. 2).
Antifungal medication was continued for 1 year leaving post inflammatory residue in sectional images. Cardiomyopathy recovered and left ventricular ejection fraction improved up to 46%. On day +650 the patient is alive and doing well in complete remission of vSAA. The use of the orthesis and intensive physiotherapeutic therapy resulted in nearly unaffected mobility (almost unremarkable drop foot, compensation by discreet hyperflexion in hip joint while walking, only lateral toes can be lifted, active plantar flexion only up to 30 degrees and dorsiflexion to up 10 degrees, nearly no active inversion and reduced eversion; muscle strength 4/5).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented initially with lower extremity petechiae and ecchymoses due to very severe aplastic anemia, subsequently developing refractory febrile neutropenia, deep necrotizing pretibial ulcers after a mosquito bite, pneumonia, and symptomatic heart failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with very severe aplastic anemia (vSAA) after presenting with leg petechiae and ecchymoses during summer holidays, the patient failed immunosuppressive therapy with horse ATG (40 mg/kg/day x 4 days) and cyclosporine A. On day -66 prior to salvage allogeneic HSCT, a mosquito bite on his shin progressed into two deep necrotizing pretibial ulcers (6 x 4 cm and 2 x 2 cm) with Stenotrophomonas maltophilia bacteremia, invasive Aspergillus flavus and S. maltophilia pneumonia, and septic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32%).
subjective.past_medical_history: Very severe aplastic anemia (vSAA) refractory to antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine A; inpatient intolerance to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for initial leg petechiae/ecchymoses, recurrent febrile neutropenia, painful necrotic pretibial ulcers with foot drop, dyspnea/cough from pneumonia, and congestive heart failure symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial petechiae and ecchymoses on the legs; subsequently developed two deep necrotizing pretibial ulcers (6 x 4 cm and 2 x 2 cm) with exposed necrotic extensor tendons and muscle requiring resection of the extensor hallucis longus tendon and atrophy of the tibialis anterior tendon, resulting in a drop foot (compensated with a peroneal orthosis; final muscle strength 4/5). Signs of symptomatic congestive heart failure were also present pre-SCT.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline CBC and bone marrow biopsy confirmed vSAA (ANC <0.1/nL, platelets <20/nL, reticulocytes 0.2%). Blood cultures and pretibial wound pus cultures isolated Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (susceptible to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, TMP/SMX, and tigecycline). Echocardiography showed septic cardiomyopathy with LVEF 32% (recovering to 46% post-SCT).
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) microbiological workup confirmed dual invasive pulmonary infection with Aspergillus flavus and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Very severe aplastic anemia (vSAA) complicated by invasive pulmonary Aspergillus flavus pneumonia, concurrent Stenotrophomonas maltophilia pneumonia, bacteremia, and deep necrotizing pretibial ecthyma/myonecrosis, and septic cardiomyopathy, confirmed by blood, wound, and BAL cultures and thoracic CT. Treated with salvage 10/10 HLA-matched unrelated donor allogeneic bone marrow transplantation (conditioned with cyclophosphamide, fludarabine, Thymoglobulin, and 2 Gy TBI; G-CSF days +2 to +17; neutrophil engraftment on day +22), 1 year of systemic antifungal therapy (isavuconazole and amphotericin B) plus targeted antibacterials (moxifloxacin/ciprofloxacin/tigecycline), repeated surgical wound debridements with local gentamicin chains and negative-pressure wound therapy, and autologous full-thickness meshed skin grafting on day +54. At day +650, the patient was alive in complete hematologic remission with healed leg grafts, near-normal mobility using a peroneal orthosis, and recovered cardiac function (LVEF 46%).

raw_case_text:
We report a 27 year old man, 10 pack-years smoker, with a one-month history of dry cough, shortness of breath and general status's deterioration. A lung X ray showed bilateral alveolar opacities (Figure 1). Blood gases analysis in ambient air showed a pO2 of 57 mmHg, a pCO2 of 38.6 mmHg, a HCO3- of 29.2 mmHg. Because of the considerable deterioration in his respiratory condition and the need for high oxygen flow, he was referred to intensive care unit (ICU) with the diagnosis of an acute respiratory failure (ARF). Chest computed tomography (CT) showed diffuse ground-glass opacities (Figure 2A, Figure 2B) and mediastinal lymphadenopathies. All microbiological infectious investigations, especially tuberculosis, were negative. He had hypergammaglobulinemia of 21.9 g/l. Other immunological tests were otherwise negative. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed finding a hyperkinetic left ventricle, a small dilation of right ventricle with PAPs 48 mmHg and an intrapulmonary shunt revealed by contrast test. The bronchial endoscopy showed an inflammatory bronchial tree and the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) concluded to lymphocytic alveolitis with a ratio CD4 (helper T cells) over CD8 (suppressor T cells) (CD4/CD8) of 0.5. The bronchial biopsies showed inflammatory bronchial mucosa without any specificities. Despite the absence of Koch's bacillus in sputum analysis, we decided to begin a trial anti-tuberculosis treatment because of the severity of lung involvement added to high endemicity of tuberculosis in our country. Two weeks later, the patient presented an allergic skin reaction. As no recovery's signs were noted, we decided to stop the treatment. Corticosteroids were initiated considering idiopathic diffuse infiltrating pneumonitis. Unfortunately, the patient did not show any improvement and the chest scan performed after 27 days of treatment showed worsening interstitial infiltrates and fibrosis.
Clinically, he required high flow oxygen (14 l/mn) alternating with non invasive ventilation sessions. Histological examination of the open lung's biopsy then performed showed diffuse lung parenchyma damage. It was altered by a mutilating fibrosis that was widening the alveolar septa. This fibrosis contained an abundant inflammatory infiltrate made of lymphocytes, plasmocytes and fewer neutrophils and eosinophils. Epithelioid and giant cell granulomas were also observed without either caseous or fibrinoid necrosis. This mutilating fibrosis induced an enlargement of some alveoli resulting in the formation of a honeycomb aspect. Fibroblastic foci were also noticed. Some alveoli contained hyaline membranes that were sometimes incorporated in the septa. There were no mineral particles observed with polarized light (Figure 3). Regarding these features, the diagnosis of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) associated to lesions of sarcoidosis or berylliosis with aspects suggestive of an acute exacerbation was retained. Since sarcoidosis was not very likely according to CD4/CD8 ratio in BAL, we investigated risk factors for chronic beryllium disease, particularly occupation's patient history. He was working as glassblower in an artistic glass factory since six months. Further to our request, occupational department's experts inspected the workplace and confirmed beryllium existence in compounds of colored glass. After confirmation of CBD, steroids were maintained and oxygen requirement slowly decreased. The patient was finally discharged at home after 55 days steroid treatment with long term oxygen therapy (2 l/minute). Pulmonary function tests at discharge showed a severe restrictive impairement. Steroid doses were slowly decreased and stopped after 10 months. A pre-transplant assessment was also made. One year after discharge, the patient felt somewhat better and pulmonary function tests showed a slight improvement. The CT scan performed found a partial regression of lung consolidations and ground glass opacities, but increase of distortion signs, cavities appearance of which one filled by aspergilloma. He received oral voriconazole 200 mg per day during 3 months. After a two-year period from the date of CBD diagnosis, the patient was again admitted in ICU for ARF. An enhanced CT scan performed showed further deterioration of pulmonary parenchyma (Figure 2C, Figure 2D) and pulmonary embolism with fatal issue.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male artistic glassblower presented with a 1-month history of dry cough, progressive shortness of breath, and general deterioration culminating in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Employed for 6 months as a glassblower in an artistic colored-glass factory, the patient presented with 1 month of dry cough, dyspnea, and constitutional decline requiring ICU admission and high-flow oxygen/non-invasive ventilation for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. After failing a 2-week empirical anti-tuberculosis trial (stopped due to allergic rash) and initial 27-day corticosteroid therapy, an open lung biopsy and workplace inspection established chronic beryllium disease. One year after discharge on a 10-month steroid taper and home oxygen, follow-up chest CT revealed cavitary lung distortion containing an intracavitary aspergilloma.
subjective.past_medical_history: 10 pack-year tobacco smoker; occupational beryllium exposure for 6 months as an artistic glassblower working with colored glass compounds.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, severe progressive dyspnea, and general physical deterioration; developed an allergic skin rash to empirical anti-TB drugs.

objective.physical_examination: Admitted in severe hypoxemic acute respiratory failure requiring high-flow oxygen (up to 14 L/min) alternating with non-invasive ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission room-air ABG showed severe hypoxemia (PaO2 57 mmHg, PaCO2 38.6 mmHg, HCO3 29.2 mmol/L). Labs showed polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (21.9 g/L) with negative autoimmune and microbiological panels (including negative sputum AFB). Chest X-ray showed bilateral alveolar opacities. TTE showed a hyperkinetic left ventricle, mild right ventricular dilation with systolic PAP 48 mmHg, and an intrapulmonary shunt on bubble contrast. Discharge PFTs showed a severe restrictive ventilatory defect.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, progressing at day 27 to worsening interstitial infiltrates and fibrosis. Bronchoscopy showed diffuse bronchial inflammation, and BAL revealed lymphocytic alveolitis with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.5. Open lung biopsy demonstrated mutilating interstitial fibrosis with architectural honeycombing, fibroblastic foci, hyaline membranes, abundant lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and non-caseating epithelioid and giant-cell granulomas; occupational hygiene inspection confirmed beryllium in the factory's colored glass compounds. At 1-year follow-up, repeat chest CT showed partial regression of ground-glass opacities but progressive fibrotic architectural distortion and newly formed cavities, one of which contained an intracavitary fungus ball (aspergilloma). At 2 years, contrast-enhanced chest CT during terminal ICU readmission showed severe parenchymal progression and acute pulmonary embolism.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Chronic beryllium disease (berylliosis) presenting with acute respiratory failure and fibrotic UIP/granulomatous lung disease in an artistic glassblower, complicated 1 year later by a secondary cavitary pulmonary aspergilloma (confirmed on 1-year follow-up chest CT) following prolonged corticosteroid therapy. The chronic beryllium disease was managed with a 10-month oral corticosteroid taper and long-term home oxygen (2 L/min), and the secondary cavitary aspergilloma was treated with oral voriconazole 200 mg daily for 3 months; 2 years after initial diagnosis, the patient died in the ICU from progressive respiratory failure and acute pulmonary embolism.

raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old female patient presented to the department of oral pathology and microbiology with a chief complaint of difficulty in eating for the past 1 week. The patient also gave a history of pain in the upper right back tooth region for 8 months, following which extraction was performed due to the presence of periodontally compromised 16 and 17, after which the symptoms were temporarily relieved. On intraoral examination, a well-defined lesion approximately 2.5 cm x 1.5 cm in size with everted and slightly indurated margins was present on the edentulous alveolar ridge with respect to missing 16 and 17, which was extending to the vestibule. There were no symptoms of nasal regurgitation, but the patient presented with a nasal twang.
The patient was diabetic and was under medication for the past 8 months after extraction was done. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were slightly enlarged and mobile. Orthopantomogram showed irregular alveolar bone loss. Water's view depicted slight haziness in the right maxillary sinus and bone loss in the involved area. The patient complained of discomfort in the same region for the past 7 days and also submitted a piece of tissue which had been dislodged from the upper left back tooth region while eating. The tissue was immediately preserved, subjected to decalcification, processed and then histopathologically examined.
The decalcified sections of the hard tissue bit received showed abundant bony trabeculae with empty osteocytic lacunae, absence of osteoblastic rimming and prominent resting and reversal lines. Numerous fungal hyphae and spores of varying morphology were seen in the marrow spaces. Some fungal hyphae were broad, aseptate and ribbon shaped, showing branching at obtuse angles representing Mucorales species, whereas others were thin and septate, showing branching at acute angles representing Aspergillus species [Figure 1]. Fungal spores of varying sizes were observed, exhibiting budding at some places along with fruiting bodies of Aspergillus [Figure 1]. These were easily identified as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus.
Numerous actinomycotic colonies were also noted along with other bacterial colonies, including both bacilli and cocci arranged in clusters as well as individually in close association with peripheral bony trabeculae [Figure 1]. Focal areas showed chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate comprising lymphocytes. A few small blood vessels, extravasated RBCs, areas of necrosis and vegetable matter were observed. Grocott's methenamine silver staining showed septate Aspergillus hyphae, aseptate Mucorales hyphae and fungal spores along with actinomycotic colonies [Figures 2-5]. The final diagnosis was given as chronic osteomyelitis associated with a combination of mucormycosis, aspergillosis and actinomycosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old diabetic female presented with a 1-week history of difficulty eating, right maxillary discomfort, nasal speech, and spontaneous dislodgement of a necrotic bone fragment from the posterior maxilla while eating.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eight months prior to presentation, the patient underwent extraction of periodontally compromised upper right molars (teeth 16 and 17) after experiencing 8 months of localized dental pain, and was started on oral antidiabetic medication. One week prior to presentation, she developed difficulty eating, right posterior maxillary discomfort, a nasal twang without nasal regurgitation, and brought in a piece of necrotic bone tissue that had spontaneously dislodged from her posterior maxilla while eating.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus on oral medication for the past 8 months; dental extraction of upper right first and second molars (16 and 17) 8 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for difficulty eating (1 week), right maxillary discomfort, nasal speech (twang), and spontaneous oral bone sequestration; negative for nasal regurgitation.

objective.physical_examination: Extraoral exam revealed slightly enlarged, mobile bilateral submandibular lymph nodes. Intraoral exam showed a well-defined 2.5 x 1.5 cm ulcerated lesion with everted, slightly indurated margins on the edentulous right maxillary alveolar ridge (missing teeth 16 and 17) extending into the buccal vestibule, accompanied by a nasal twang.
objective.routine_investigations: Orthopantomogram (OPG) demonstrated irregular maxillary alveolar bone loss, and Waters' sinus radiograph showed haziness of the right maxillary sinus with adjacent alveolar bone destruction.
objective.advanced_workup: Histopathological examination of the decalcified exfoliated maxillary bone sequestrum (H&E and Grocott methenamine silver [GMS] stains) revealed necrotic bony trabeculae with empty osteocytic lacunae, absent osteoblastic rimming, prominent reversal lines, and marrow spaces packed with three distinct groups of organisms: (1) thin septate fungal hyphae branching at acute angles with fungal spores and characteristic Aspergillus fruiting bodies (conidial heads) identified morphologically as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus; (2) broad, ribbon-like aseptate hyphae branching at obtuse/right angles characteristic of Mucorales; and (3) numerous basophilic filamentous actinomycotic colonies alongside mixed coccal and bacillary bacterial clusters.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Chronic maxillary osteomyelitis caused by a rare triple polymicrobial co-infection with aspergillosis (Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus), mucormycosis (Mucorales), and actinomycosis in a 76-year-old diabetic patient following dental extraction, definitively confirmed by H&E and Grocott methenamine silver histopathology of the exfoliated maxillary bone sequestrum.

raw_case_text:
An 82-year-old male was diagnosed with bronchial asthma at 10 years of age and treated with inhalants and he did not receive treatment for asthma since the age of 30 because of the resolution of bronchial asthma. He was followed at our hospital for idiopathic interstitial pneumonia by annual regular chest X-ray and computed tomography (CT) scans for 4 years. The patient's interstitial pneumonia, with minimal change in radiological findings was stable over the years, he complained no symptoms. He did not indicate exposure to fungus. Chest X-ray and CT scan obtained in December 2017 revealed high-attenuation mucus plug in right intermediate bronchial trunk, right pleural effusion (Fig. 1a), and infiltration in the right lung field (Fig. 1b). 
We also found unilateral bronchiectasis in the right upper lobe.
Additionally, a slight fibrotic change along the pleural line reflecting interstitial pneumonia was observed. CT of paranasal sinuses obtained to investigate nasal congestion for 3 years, revealed high-attenuation mucus plug in the left ethmoid sinuses (Fig. 2). Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field. No wheezing and rhonchi were observed on auscultation. 
Blood tests showed a total leucocyte count of 9300/mm3 with 8% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count, 744/mm3) and elevated C-reactive protein. Radioimmunosorbent test revealed elevated IgE levels (1460 IU/ml), and the radioimmunosorbent test for specific IgE antibodies against Aspergillus, Penicillium and Candida were positive. Serum precipitins to Aspergillus were also positive. We confirmed local urticaria and lash 15 min after subcutaneous injection of A. fumigatus antigen and this was positive of immediate cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction. He had a history of right nephrectomy because of renal cancer and did not experience recurrence.
Pulmonary function test showed the following: forced vital capacity (FVC), 1.86 L (55.4% of predicted value); forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), 1.60 L (64.3% of predicted value); and FEV1/FVC, 86.0%. Bronchoscopy for definite diagnosis confirmed bronze-colored, hard mucus plug in the right intermediate bronchial trunk (Fig. 3a), and pathological examination of multiple biopsy specimens stained by hematoxylin-eosin revealed allergic mucin with layers of mucus, eosinophils, and eosinophil-predominant mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate and Charcot-Leyden crystals (Fig. 4a). Grocott's stain revealed fungal hyphae with a 45  branch angle within the allergic mucin (Fig. 4b). We performed open biopsy of the ethmoid sinuses and found similar mucus plug there, which revealed similar pathological findings in the right intermediate bronchial trunk (Fig. 3b), including fungal hyphae with a 45  branch angle within allergic mucin (Fig. 4c). Mucus plug cultures were positive for A. fumigatus. The patient met of the diagnostic criteria for ABPA by Rosenberg and Patterson as well as those for AFRS, and thus he was diagnosed with SAM syndrome.  
The patient was treated with 0.5 mg/kg prednisolone daily for 1 month, which was reduced to 0.35 mg/kg prednisolone daily. His total IgE levels fell to 206 IU/ml after 3 months. CT of the lung and paranasal sinuses showed apparent amelioration (Fig. 5a-c), and nasal congestion was resolved after 3 months steroid therapy. Now, there has been about 1 year and 4 months after the diagnosis, the patient is currently receiving oral steroid therapy (0.1 mg/kg) and remains in good condition with no deteriorations.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 82-year-old male with a 3-year history of chronic nasal congestion and a remote history of childhood asthma presented with asymptomatic right lung infiltrates, right pleural effusion, and central bronchial mucus plugging on annual surveillance chest imaging.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Followed annually by chest X-ray and CT for 4 years for stable, asymptomatic idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, the patient was found in December 2017 to have a new high-attenuation mucus plug in the right truncus intermedius, right upper lobe bronchiectasis, right lung infiltrates, and a right pleural effusion, alongside a 3-year history of chronic nasal congestion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Childhood bronchial asthma diagnosed at age 10 and in complete medication-free remission since age 30; stable idiopathic interstitial pneumonia followed for 4 years; prior right radical nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma without recurrence; no known fungal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic nasal congestion for 3 years; negative for cough, wheezing, or dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field without wheezing or rhonchi.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed WBC 9,300/mm3 with mild eosinophilia (8% eosinophils, absolute eosinophil count 744/mm3), elevated CRP, and markedly elevated total serum IgE of 1,460 IU/mL (declining to 206 IU/mL after 3 months of prednisolone). RAST specific IgE antibodies were positive for Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Candida; serum precipitating antibodies to Aspergillus were positive; and subcutaneous skin testing with Aspergillus fumigatus antigen elicited an immediate wheal-and-flare reaction at 15 minutes. Spirometry showed FVC 1.86 L (55.4% predicted), FEV1 1.60 L (64.3% predicted), and FEV1/FVC 86.0%.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (December 2017) demonstrated a high-attenuation mucus plug obstructing the right truncus intermedius, right upper lobe bronchiectasis, right parenchymal infiltration, right pleural effusion, and mild subpleural interstitial fibrosis. Paranasal sinus CT revealed a high-attenuation mucus plug in the left ethmoid sinus. Bronchoscopy confirmed a hard, bronze-colored mucus plug in the right truncus intermedius, and open left ethmoid sinus biopsy retrieved an identical mucus plug; histopathology (H&E and Grocott stains) of both the bronchial and ethmoid sinus specimens demonstrated laminated allergic mucin packed with eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and 45-degree branching septate fungal hyphae, and cultures of the mucus plugs grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Sinobronchial allergic mycosis (SAM) syndrome—comprising concurrent allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA, fulfilling Rosenberg-Patterson criteria) and left ethmoidal allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS)—caused by Aspergillus fumigatus in an 82-year-old man after a 52-year remission of childhood asthma, confirmed by high-attenuation sinobronchial mucus plugs on CT, peripheral eosinophilia, elevated total IgE (1,460 IU/mL), positive A. fumigatus skin test, specific IgE, and precipitins, and identical Grocott-positive 45-degree branching hyphae and A. fumigatus culture growth from both bronchial and ethmoid sinus allergic mucin. Treated with oral prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day for 1 month, tapered to 0.35 mg/kg/day and maintained at 0.1 mg/kg/day), achieving resolution of nasal congestion, reduction of total IgE to 206 IU/mL, and radiographic clearing of lung and sinus lesions at 3 and 16 months.

raw_case_text:
A 75-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and sequelae of ischemic stroke and mild right hemiplegia accidentally fell into a creek (depth of water about 0.3 m) on 2nd Dec 2016. He was found with his face submerged in the water. After being rescued, he was first brought to a local hospital that was not ours, near Kurume City, Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan. On arrival at that hospital, his Glasgow Coma Scale was E3V3M6, body temperature was 33.4 C, heart rate was 88 beats/min, blood pressure was 120/60 mmHg, respiratory rate was 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 92% on supplemental oxygen at a flow rate of 10 L/min. He had no obvious injury but showed bilateral coarse crackles and hypothermia. Rewarming using a warming blanket and antibiotic therapy (ampicillin and sulbactam) were started. Even after starting non-invasive ventilation, the patient's oxygenation steadily deteriorated to oxygen saturation levels at 80% on 100% oxygen. He was intubated and mechanically ventilated, and transferred to the emergency department of our tertiary hospital in Kurume City on the same day.
On arrival at our hospital, he was sedated with propofol. His body temperature was 36.4 C, heart rate was 104 beats/min, blood pressure was 123/84 mmHg, respiratory rate was 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation level was 91% on supplemental oxygen at a flow rate of 10 L/min. The physical examination was unremarkable except for bilaterally diminished breath sounds. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.34, a PaCO2 of 42 mmHg, a PaO2 of 199 mmHg, and an HCO3 of 21.9 mmol/L under 100% oxygen.
Laboratory investigations on day 1 (2nd Dec) showed a white blood cell count of 2980/muL (normal range 3500-9000/muL) with 63.5% neutrophils (normal range 40-73%), a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL (normal range 13-17 g/dL), a platelet level of 159,000/muL (normal range 140,000-340,000/muL), a C-reactive protein level of 0.6 mg/dL (normal range 0-0.2 mg/dL), and a highly increased procalcitonin level of 59.37 ng/mL (normal range <0.05 ng/mL). Ultrasonographic examination of the heart on the same day showed a normal ejection fraction with no valvular disease. Chest radiography and computed tomography (CT) of the lung showed diffuse infiltrates bilaterally with no pleural effusion (Figure 1).
The diagnosis was acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) caused by aspiration pneumonitis as a result of non-fatal drowning and septic shock. He was treated with isotonic crystalloids, an intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotic (meropenem 1.0 g every 12 hrs), vasopressors, and protective ventilation. Methylprednisolone 80 mg daily was started on day 3 for ARDS (Figure 2A). A beta-D-glucan assay (beta-glucan test; FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corporation, Japan) on day 4 found it to be elevated at 37.6 pg/mL (normal range <11.0 pg/mL); serum galactomannan was not measured. The vasopressors could be stopped on day 5 but the hypoxia did not improve (Figure 2B). On day 6, the tracheal aspirate culture was found positive for Aeromonas hydrophila but the blood culture was negative. The patient was switched to piperacillin/tazobactam at a dosage of 4.5 g every 6 hrs based on the susceptibility test. The hypoxia continued to worsen and the patient died on day 7.
CT scans obtained at autopsy did not reveal any focal lesion in the brain; however, both lungs were completely infiltrated with effusion (Figure 3), were severely congested, and each weighed over 1000 g (Figure 4A). An embolus was detected in the right pulmonary artery (Figure 5A) but not in either femoral vein. Microscopic analysis with Grocott staining revealed diffuse filamentous fungi throughout the lungs within necrotizing tissue and intravascular lesions (Figure 4B), as well as in the heart, stomach, and thyroid gland. The pulmonary embolus also contained filamentous fungi (Figure 5B), which might have been responsible for the patient's acute deterioration. We cultured biopsies from both lungs taken from the histological preparations and the fungi were identified as Aspergillus fumigatus. Therefore, we diagnosed this case as invasive aspergillosis complicated by pulmonary embolism.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old Japanese man was brought to the emergency department with hypothermia, altered consciousness, and rapidly progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure after falling face-down into a shallow creek.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On December 2, 2016, the patient accidentally fell into a 0.3-m-deep creek and was found with his face submerged. Upon rescue and arrival at a local hospital, he was hypothermic (33.4 C) and hypoxic (SpO2 92% on 10 L/min O2), rapidly deteriorating to SpO2 80% on 100% non-invasive ventilation, requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and same-day transfer to our tertiary hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension and prior ischemic stroke with residual mild right hemiplegia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for freshwater aspiration/near-drowning, hypothermia, stupor, and severe hypoxemia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial local hospital exam: GCS E3V3M6, temperature 33.4 C, heart rate 88 bpm, BP 120/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, SpO2 92% on 10 L/min O2, and bilateral coarse pulmonary crackles without external trauma. On arrival at our hospital (sedated on propofol and intubated): temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 104 bpm, BP 123/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, SpO2 91% on 10 L/min O2, and bilaterally diminished breath sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ABG on FiO2 1.0 showed pH 7.34, PaCO2 42 mmHg, PaO2 199 mmHg, and HCO3 21.9 mmol/L. Day 1 labs showed leukopenia (WBC 2,980/uL; 63.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, platelets 159,000/uL, CRP 0.6 mg/dL, and markedly elevated procalcitonin of 59.37 ng/mL (normal <0.05 ng/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Chest X-ray and chest CT showed diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates without pleural effusion. Day 6 tracheal aspirate culture grew Aeromonas hydrophila (blood cultures negative).
objective.advanced_workup: On hospital day 4 (1 day after starting methylprednisolone 80 mg/day for ARDS), serum beta-D-glucan was elevated at 37.6 pg/mL (normal <11.0 pg/mL; serum galactomannan was not measured). Following death on hospital day 7, postmortem CT and autopsy revealed severely congested lungs weighing >1,000 g each and a right pulmonary artery embolus (without femoral DVT); Grocott methenamine silver histopathology demonstrated diffuse necrotizing and angioinvasive filamentous fungal hyphae throughout both lungs, the right pulmonary artery embolus, myocardium, stomach, and thyroid gland, and postmortem bilateral lung biopsy cultures isolated Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fulminant disseminated angioinvasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) and Aeromonas hydrophila pneumonia complicated by a fungal right pulmonary artery embolism and fatal ARDS following freshwater near-drowning and short-term methylprednisolone therapy, definitively confirmed at autopsy by Grocott histopathology (showing angioinvasive hyphae in the lungs, right pulmonary artery thrombus, heart, stomach, and thyroid) and bilateral lung tissue cultures growing A. fumigatus. Despite mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, meropenem switched to piperacillin/tazobactam (4.5 g q6h), and methylprednisolone (80 mg/day), refractory hypoxemia persisted and the patient died on hospital day 7.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 10-year-old boy with confirmed CGD as an underlying disease at 11 months of age based on hematological and immunological tests (nitroblue-tetrazolium=0). He had several admissions to the Children Medical Center of Tehran, Iran. The patient had a previous history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia for which he was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and long-term prophylaxis, including itraconazole (5 mg/kg/day), along with co-trimoxazole (5 mg/kg/day) and IFN gamma (1.5 mcg/kg). At the age of nine years, the patient was hospitalized for several clinical signs and symptoms, such as knee pain, night sweets, lethargy, coryza, and progressive weakness. 
A plain X-ray imaging showed a soft tissue density destructive lesion in T4-T5 vertebral bodies with adjacent prevertebral soft tissue mass involving the central spinal column. There was also evidence of an expansile lytic lesion involving the right fifth rib, laminectomy of L4-L5 with pedicular screw, along with post-operative changes (Figure 1). Laboratory findings included ESR of 75 mm/h, CRP of 69, white blood cell count of 6000/mm3, monocyte of 37.4%, hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dl, and thrombocyte of 383000/mm3. The results of histopathology and fungal culture obtained from surgical debridement samples revealed the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus species (Figure 2).
In addition, a microscopic examination showed abundant hull cells and the conidial head pattern of A. nidulans (Figure 2). The specific primer pair 5'-GGT AAC CAA ATC GGT GCT GCT TTC-3' and 5'-ACCCTC AGT GTA GTG ACC CTT GGC-3' was used to amplify beta-tubulin genes and confirm the isolate as A. nidulans [19]. Then, the nucleotide sequence was deposited in GenBank under the accession number MK749954. At this time, the treatment was continued with amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) which was subsequently changed to voriconazole (9 mg/kg/day). Finally, caspofungin (50 microg/m2) was also added to the therapy, and the patient was discharged from the hospital. However, after a few months, this case was readmitted because of severe headache, blurred vision, and brain abscess, while receiving voriconazole therapy (200 mg/day). 
Treatment was continued with amphotericin B, caspofungin, voriconazole, and interferon-gamma. Due to the lack of antifungal response and deterioration of the symptoms, he underwent the insertion of a right parietal ventriculoperitoneal shunt. An urgent computed tomography scan of the brain did not depict any damage. However, it revealed the dilation of the left ventricle and dilation of the occipital horn of the right ventricle, along with extensive vasogenic edema in the right temporoparietal lobe (Figure 1). 
In spite of performing aggressive surgery and different treatments, the child passed away within one year. Postmortem antifungal susceptibility profile of the isolate was examined against itraconazole (Sigma-Aldrich Quimica, Madrid, Spain), amphotericin B (Sigma-Aldrich Quimica, Madrid, Spain), and voriconazole (Pfizer SA, Madrid, Spain) using EUCAST method [20]. The in vitro minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of the mentioned antifungals were obtained as 1, > 16, and 0.25 mg/L, respectively. Furthermore, the minimum effective concentration for caspofungin (Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ) was estimated at 1 mg/L. This species was found to show resistance to amphotericin B (MIC>2 mg/L).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy with chronic granulomatous disease presented with knee pain, night sweats, lethargy, coryza, and progressive weakness, followed several months later by severe headache and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease at 11 months of age (NBT = 0) and maintained on long-term itraconazole, co-trimoxazole, and interferon-gamma prophylaxis for recurrent pneumonias, the patient was hospitalized at age 9 with knee pain, night sweats, lethargy, coryza, and progressive weakness due to destructive T4-T5 vertebral and right 5th rib osteomyelitis caused by Aspergillus nidulans. Despite surgical debridement and combination voriconazole plus caspofungin, he was readmitted a few months later (at age 10) with severe headache and blurred vision due to a cerebral abscess and hydrocephalus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) confirmed at 11 months of age by nitroblue tetrazolium test (NBT = 0); history of recurrent pneumonias and prior L4-L5 laminectomy with pedicle screw fixation; long-term prophylaxis with itraconazole (5 mg/kg/day), co-trimoxazole (5 mg/kg/day), and subcutaneous interferon-gamma (1.5 ug/kg).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission (age 9): knee pain, night sweats, lethargy, coryza, and progressive weakness. Readmission (age 10): severe headache and blurred vision.

objective.physical_examination: Presented at age 9 with lethargy and progressive weakness, and at age 10 with neurological deterioration and visual blurring requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs at age 9 showed ESR 75 mm/h, CRP 69 mg/L, WBC 6,000/mm3 with monocytosis (37.4% monocytes), anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL), and platelets 383,000/mm3. Spine and chest radiographs showed a destructive lesion of the T4-T5 vertebral bodies with a prevertebral soft-tissue mass, an expansile lytic lesion of the right 5th rib, and prior L4-L5 laminectomy/pedicle screw hardware.
objective.advanced_workup: Histopathology and fungal culture of surgical spinal/costal debridement specimens demonstrated invasive aspergillosis with abundant Hulle cells and conidial heads characteristic of Aspergillus nidulans, confirmed by beta-tubulin gene PCR sequencing (GenBank accession MK749954). EUCAST antifungal susceptibility testing showed intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B (MIC >16 mg/L), itraconazole MIC 1 mg/L, voriconazole MIC 0.25 mg/L, and caspofungin MEC 1 mg/L. On readmission for severe headache and blurred vision, cranial imaging demonstrated a brain abscess with extensive right temporoparietal vasogenic edema and dilation of the left lateral ventricle and right occipital horn.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal disseminated invasive aspergillosis caused by amphotericin B-resistant Aspergillus nidulans presenting with T4-T5 vertebral osteomyelitis, right 5th rib osteomyelitis, and subsequent right temporoparietal brain abscess and hydrocephalus in a child with chronic granulomatous disease (breaking through itraconazole and IFN-gamma prophylaxis), confirmed by surgical biopsy histopathology, culture showing Hulle cells, beta-tubulin sequencing (MK749954), and EUCAST susceptibility testing. Despite spinal surgical debridement, right parietal ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, and combination therapy with voriconazole (9 mg/kg/day IV, then 200 mg/day orally), caspofungin (50 ug/m2), amphotericin B deoxycholate, and interferon-gamma, the child died within 1 year.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old male farmer consulted with a chief complaint of blurred vision in the left eye. The history started about 2 months prior when mud was flung onto his left eye while farming. He washed his eye with tap water and carried on. About 2 weeks later, he noted development of redness, blurred vision, mild pain, and a small white opacity on the left eye. He consulted with a private physician who assessed him to have an eye infection, and he was started on topical terramycin ointment. Despite treatment, there was persistence of eye redness and enlargement of the whitish opacity. The patient sought a second opinion with another physician, who prescribed him a regimen consisting of tobramycin-dexamethasone drops, again with no improvement in the patient's symptoms. The patient eventually noted loss of useful vision in his left eye. The persistence of symptoms prompted consult.
On presentation, the visual acuity of the left eye was hand movement with poor light projection. There was good color perception. A reverse relative afferent pupillary defect was not noted. On slit lamp examination, there was a very thick yellow plaque consisting of a rounded mass projecting above the entire corneal surface, similar to a mound, measuring 9x9.5 mm with a depth of 2 mm at its thickest point located centrally (Figure 1 (Fig. 1)). Despite the large plaque, there seemed to be no signs of prolapse of intraocular contents. There was associated scleritis. The ocular ultrasound showed only few vitreous cellularities. The right was grossly unremarkable with a visual acuity of 20/20.
The plaque did not stain with fluorescein, lissamine green, and rose bengal dyes. Careful scraping of the mass revealed it to be semi-solid, albeit very friable in consistency. There was no bleeding on scraping. Giemsa stain of the corneal scraping showed numerous hyphal elements (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). Culture of the plaque later revealed to be positive for Aspergillus sp.
The patient was admitted and initiated on topical natamycin drops, and topical moxifloxacin drops were added as prophylaxis for any superimposed bacterial infection. Topical atropine drops were also started for relief of ciliary pain. The patient was started on oral itraconazole as well.
A therapeutic keratoplasty with a tectonic corneal graft was performed under retrobulbar anesthesia. The recipient bed was sized by measuring the fungal plaque and adding a 2 mm border. The corneal graft was sized to a 12 mm diameter, necessitating manual cutting using corneal scissors. After the host cornea was excised, it was revealed that the fungus had invaded the anterior chamber, and the iris had become necrotic. A 360-degree iridectomy was performed. Lens extraction and anterior vitrectomy were done. After reforming the anterior chamber with an ophthalmic viscoelastic device, the tectonic corneal graft was placed and sutured with 16 interrupted nylon 10-0 sutures (Figure 3 (Fig. 3)). The surgery was uncomplicated.
The patient was maintained on a regimen of topical natamyin, topical moxifloxacin, and topical atropine drops for the first 2 weeks after surgery. He also completed a 2-week course of oral itraconazole. The postoperative course was relatively unremarkable with decreasing signs of inflammation and no recurrence of infection. At the 2nd week postoperatively, topical prednisolone drops were added. The patient's vision improved to counting fingers at 6 inches. He was advised that a second procedure consisting of an optical penetrating keratoplasty and secondary intraocular lens implantation as well as possible interventions for secondary glaucoma would be needed in the future.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male farmer presented with a 2-month history of progressive blurred vision, redness, mild pain, and an enlarging central white-yellow corneal mass in his left eye after mud trauma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to consultation, mud splashed into the patient's left eye while farming, which he rinsed with tap water. Two weeks later, he developed left eye redness, mild pain, blurred vision, and a small white corneal opacity that progressively enlarged into a thick yellow mound with loss of useful vision despite sequential treatment with topical oxytetracycline (Terramycin) ointment and topical tobramycin-dexamethasone drops.
subjective.past_medical_history: Agricultural mud ocular trauma 2 months prior; subsequent topical corticosteroid-antibiotic exposure (tobramycin-dexamethasone drops).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left eye redness, mild pain, enlarging central corneal plaque, and severe visual loss.

objective.physical_examination: Left eye visual acuity was hand movements with poor light projection (intact color perception, no reverse RAPD); right eye was normal with 20/20 vision. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed associated scleritis and a massive, rounded, mound-like yellow central corneal plaque measuring 9 x 9.5 mm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness projecting above the entire corneal surface without globe perforation (negative staining with fluorescein, lissamine green, and rose bengal). Intraoperatively during excision of the host cornea, fungal invasion into the anterior chamber with total iris necrosis was identified.
objective.routine_investigations: B-scan ocular ultrasonography of the left eye showed only mild anterior vitreous cellularity.
objective.advanced_workup: Superficial corneal scraping of the friable, semi-solid plaque demonstrated numerous fungal hyphal elements on Giemsa staining, and fungal culture of the corneal plaque isolated Aspergillus species.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe post-traumatic Aspergillus keratitis (9 x 9.5 x 2 mm corneal fungal plaque) complicated by scleritis, anterior chamber fungal invasion, and total iris necrosis following agricultural mud injury and topical corticosteroid use, confirmed by Giemsa staining of corneal scrapings and fungal culture growing Aspergillus sp. Treated with a 12-mm tectonic penetrating keratoplasty, 360-degree iridectomy, cataractous lens extraction, and anterior vitrectomy, combined with a 2-week course of oral itraconazole and topical natamycin, moxifloxacin, and atropine drops (with topical prednisolone added at week 2 postoperatively), achieving eradication of infection and visual improvement to counting fingers at 6 inches while awaiting secondary optical keratoplasty and IOL implantation.

raw_case_text:
A 60-year-old female patient, resident of Moradabad, India, was referred to the Otorhinolaryngology Department of the Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital and PGIMER, New Delhi, India, with complaints of insidious onset of swelling for 7 days, which had progressed gradually leading to nasal blockade. The patient also complained of swelling followed by loss of vision in the left eye for 7-10 days. There was no history of any purulent nasal discharge nor bleeding. There was no previous history of photophobia, diplopia, squint nor vision abnormality in the left eye. No facial weakness nor impaired facial expression was present. There was no family history of any similar clinical condition. The patient was a known diabetic for the previous 5 years and also gave history of hypertension for the previous 10 years, and was taking on and off treatment for both conditions (Table 1).
The general physical examination of the patient was normal, with no obvious external deformity except localized swelling on the left side eye and nose. The blood pressure of the patient was noted as 140/70 mmHg. On local examination, a blackish crust was observed in the left nasal cavity when examined by anterior rhinoscopy. On ocular examination, perception of light was absent in the left eye, and chemosis, proptosis and ptosis were present (Table 1). Laboratory investigation revealed: 11.2 g/dl haemoglobin, 12 100 cells mm-3 total leukocyte count and 177 mg/dl random blood sugar, with the rest of the biochemical parameters within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CEMRI) showed altered heterogeneously enhanced oedema involving the left periorbital soft tissue, including the left eyelid, with left proptosis and sinusitis (Fig. 1, Table 2).
Based on the above findings, a provisional clinical diagnosis of fungal sinusitis was made and the patient was started on 1 mg kg-1 day-1 intravenous amphotericin B. After a few days of treatment, the patient was subjected to endoscopic debridement of the nasal crest under general anaesthesia. A clinical specimen obtained during this procedure was sent for both microbiological and histopathological examination. In the microbiology laboratory, 10 % KOH mount analysis was performed, which initially showed branched septate hyphae of 3-6 microm in diameter with characteristic dichotomous branching, along with a few broad non-septate hyphae (Fig. 2). Cultures were plated on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with and without antibiotics at 25 and 37  C. After 1 week of incubation on SDA without antibiotic at 25  C, a velvety greenish growth was observed. After 3-4 days of further incubation, a scanty white cottony growth was also observed. A lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) mount of this mixed growth showed both septate hyphae with phialides, and broad non-septate hyphae with sporangium and rhizoids (Fig. 3). The mixture of this fungal growth was subcultured on separate SDA slants to isolate individual fungal colonies. After 3 days of incubation at 25  C, greenish velvety growth appeared in one slant. The other slant showed cottony white dense growth after 8-10 days of incubation (at 25  C) (Fig. 4). On LPCB examination of the greenish velvety colonies, branched septate hyphae with conidiophores arising from them were seen. The conidiophores terminated in vesicles, where biseriate phialides covered all around a whole vesicle, suggestive of Aspergillus flavus. The LPCB mount of the cottony white colony showed broad (7-10 microm) non-septate, ribbon-like, hyaline hyphae of varied sizes, bearing unbranched sporangiophores. Nodular rhizoids were visualized at the base of these sporangiophores. Sporangia were round, dark brown, with a flattened base, up to 175 microm in diameter and contained many spores suggestive of Rhizopus sp. Histopathological examination showed mixed inflammatory infiltrate with necrotic debris. It also showed both acute angle branching septate hyphae with spores and ribbon-like aseptate broad hyphae (Fig. 5).
Based on the KOH mount report suggestive of septate along with aseptate hyphae, oral voriconazole at a dose of 200 mg twice daily was added to ongoing parenteral amphotericin B treatment. The patient started responding well to the treatment and there was a gradual decrease in the swelling over the left eye. After 2.5 months of treatment another MRI was carried out, which showed a significant decrease in the soft tissue problems. Fluid noted in the sphenoid sinus was labelled as likely postoperative collection (Fig. 6). Treatment continued for another 15 days, after which the patient was discharged with 200 mg oral voriconazole twice daily for 15 days, with advice for further follow-up every fortnight in the Otorhinolaryngology Outpatient Department. The patient attended for 3 months, and showed complete recovery of the facial and nasal swelling and sinusitis (Table 3). The fungal isolates of Rhizopus species and A. flavus were sent to the Vallabhbhai Patel Chest Institute and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Delhi, India, for molecular confirmation. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight (MALDI -TOF) MS confirmed the fungi as Rhizopus arrhizus and A. flavus.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old diabetic and hypertensive Indian female presented with a 7- to 10-day history of progressive left nasal blockade, left periorbital and nasal swelling, and complete loss of vision in the left eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 7-10 days prior to referral, the patient developed insidious swelling of the left side of her nose and left orbit resulting in nasal obstruction, followed rapidly by complete visual loss in the left eye without purulent nasal discharge or epistaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus for 5 years and hypertension for 10 years with irregular medication adherence; no family history of similar illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left nasal obstruction, left facial/periorbital swelling, and complete left eye blindness; negative for nasal discharge, epistaxis, photophobia, prior diplopia, or facial nerve weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 140/70 mmHg; localized left periorbital and nasal swelling. Anterior rhinoscopy revealed a blackish necrotic crust in the left nasal cavity. Ocular exam of the left eye showed absent light perception, conjunctival chemosis, proptosis, and ptosis.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, leukocytosis (WBC 12,100/mm3), random blood glucose 177 mg/dL, and otherwise normal serum biochemistry.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced orbital and sinus MRI demonstrated heterogeneously enhancing edema of the left periorbital soft tissues and eyelid, left proptosis, and paranasal sinusitis (markedly regressing on 2.5-month follow-up MRI). Endoscopic nasal debridement specimens examined by 10% KOH mount, histopathology, Sabouraud dextrose agar subcultures (at 25 C and 37 C), lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) microscopy, and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry confirmed dual rhino-orbital fungal co-infection with Aspergillus flavus (3-6 um dichotomously branching septate hyphae with biseriate phialides covering the entire vesicle) and Rhizopus arrhizus (7-10 um broad aseptate ribbon-like hyphae with unbranched sporangiophores, nodular rhizoids, and 175-um dark brown round sporangia).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute invasive rhino-orbital fungal sinusitis caused by dual co-infection with Aspergillus flavus and Rhizopus arrhizus in a poorly controlled diabetic patient, definitively confirmed by 10% KOH microscopy, histopathology, Sabouraud agar differential subcultures, LPCB morphology, and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Treated with endoscopic surgical nasal debridement combined with 3 months of dual systemic antifungal therapy using intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day) and oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily, continued for 15 days post-discharge), achieving complete resolution of sinonasal and periorbital infection at 3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
CT scan and MR images of a 32-year-old nondiabetic female who presented with complaints of headache for the past 4 months and double vision of 3 months' duration are shown in [Figures 1 and 2]. Headache was generalized, holocranial, mild to moderate, non-progressive and was not associated with features of raised intracranial pressure or with febrile episodes. Diplopia was binocular, which worsens in either lateral gaze, more severe on looking right side. She also admitted to having been suffering from secondary amenorrhea for the past 5 years. No significant neurological deficits elicited on examination except bilateral sixth nerve palsy. Her routine blood investigations and pituitary with thyroid hormone profiles were completely normal.
As shown in [Figure 1a], the lesion on CT scan appears to be an isodense pathology with expansile nature, grossly involving the clivus, and extending into posterior sphenoid cavity as well as into sella. On bone window [Figure 1b], it is appearing to be an osteolytic lesion completely destroying whole length of clivus extending from basiocciput to basisphenoid, invading dorsum sella to sellar floor.
The soft-tissue component of the lesion is better delineated on MRI, as shown in [Figure 2a-f]. Isointense well-defined lesion on T1-W MR images sagittal cuts [Figure 2a] seem to fill posterior part of the sphenoid cavity, whole of the sella, and almost reaching up to the tuberculum sella. Lesion is hypointense on T2-W images [Figure 2b] suggestive of high fibrous component of the lesion. Bilateral internal carotid arteries were seen to be encased by the lesion [Figure 2c]. These features were spot-on match with a radiological diagnosis of clival chordoma. Clival chordomas also appear as an extra-axial destructive lesion that primarily involves the bone and have a well-defined appearance with clearly delineated margins. On plain CT scan, chordomas may also have either osteolytic, osteosclerotic, or a mix of these features. On MR images, these lesions may have an extraosseous component compressing over the neurovascular structures, that is, basilar artery and obliteration of prepontine cistern. On T1-weighted images, it is known to be iso- to hypointense on appearance. On T2-W images, it gives variable signals depending on the proportion of the lesion's fibrous factor, that is, more hypointense with an increasing fibrous component. On contrast-enhanced CT scan, as well as on gadolinium-enhanced MRI, it shows brilliant enhancement. All these features are also noted in current case, as shown in [Figure 2d-f].
With a working diagnosis of clival chordoma, the patient underwent transnasal transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of the tumor under general anesthesia. The lesion was grayish-pink in color, moderately vascular, completely destroying the clival region, and locally infiltrating and extending up to sphenoid sinus. It was firm in consistency and not easily suckable. To our surprise, peroperative squash analysis of tissue sent for frozen section revealed fungal infection. Exploring into the surgical field, being more enthusiastic after frozen, did not show any traces of greenish-yellow or black tinge, commonly seen in fungal lesions. In postoperative period, the patient was started on voriconazole injections, empirically. She recovered from anesthesia smoothly with no new deficits and responded well to voriconazole treatment. Aspergillus flavus growth was seen after aerobic incubation of tissue sample for four weeks, as seen in [Figure 3]. After microbiological confirmation, antifungal was converted to oral therapy for another 6 weeks and she was regularly followed up in the outpatient department. At 3 months after surgery, the patient was completely asymptomatic and interval MR images after 6 months of surgery, discloses complete resolution of the disease.
We account that fungal infection at the skull base is extremely rare, but there is every possibility under the sun that neurosurgeon may encounter with this saprophyte to have caused bilateral sixth nerve palsy in his/her patient with disease masquerading as a clival chordoma on imaging. Therefore, fungal infections are important among the various differentials, leading to skull base lesions even for nondiabetic or immunocompetent patients.
Patient's consent not required as patients identity is not disclosed or compromised.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old nondiabetic, immunocompetent female presented with a 4-month history of mild-to-moderate generalized headache and a 3-month history of binocular horizontal diplopia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 months, the patient experienced non-progressive holocranial headaches without fever or signs of raised intracranial pressure, followed 1 month later by binocular horizontal diplopia worse on lateral gaze (especially to the right).
subjective.past_medical_history: Secondary amenorrhea for the past 5 years; nondiabetic and immunocompetent.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized headache (4 months), binocular horizontal diplopia (3 months), and secondary amenorrhea (5 years); negative for fever, vomiting, or focal limb weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination was normal except for isolated bilateral abducens (CN VI) nerve palsy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests, thyroid function tests, and complete pituitary hormone profile were within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Cranial CT (plain and bone window) demonstrated an expansile isodense osteolytic mass completely destroying the entire length of the clivus from the basiocciput to the basisphenoid, invading the dorsum sellae, sellar floor, and posterior sphenoid sinus. Brain MRI showed a well-defined T1-isointense, T2-hypointense, brilliantly gadolinium-enhancing mass filling the posterior sphenoid sinus and sella up to the tuberculum sellae and encasing the bilateral internal carotid arteries, radiologically mimicking a clival chordoma. During endoscopic transnasal transsphenoidal resection of the firm, grayish-pink, moderately vascular clival mass, intraoperative frozen-section squash cytology unexpectedly revealed fungal hyphae, and 4-week aerobic fungal culture of the excised tissue isolated Aspergillus flavus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary destructive clival and sphenoid-sellar skull-base aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus flavus masquerading clinically and radiologically as a clival chordoma with bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsy in a young immunocompetent, nondiabetic woman, confirmed by intraoperative squash cytology and tissue fungal culture growing A. flavus. Treated with endoscopic transnasal transsphenoidal resection followed by intravenous voriconazole transitioned to a 6-week course of oral voriconazole, achieving complete resolution of headache and diplopia at 3 months and complete radiographic disease resolution on 6-month follow-up MRI.

raw_case_text:
In November of 2014, a 73-year-old female with acute myeloid leukemia presented to Peking University Third Hospital (Beijing, China) with progressive nose swelling and ulceration after a severe cold. The lesions had begun two months earlier as infiltrated erythema, then rapidly increased in size and ulcerated. The patient was initially diagnosed with skin and subcutaneous infection in the nose and face (rhinofacial) and treatment with antibiotics was ineffective. Next, the lesion was diagnosed as a malignant ulcer and chemotherapy was administered, but the necrotic ulcer became progressively enlarged. Subsequent clinical diagnosis of rhinofacial mucormycosis was made and the patient was treated with AMB (initial dose 5 mg/day, increased by 5 mg daily), but the ulcer still progressed. Two months after onset of the malignant ulcer, the patient was transferred to Peking University Third Hospital.
The patient had a 1-year history of acute myeloid leukemia and had received one cycle of DA chemotherapy (daunorubicin and cytarabine), two cycles of MA chemotherapy (mitoxantrone and cytarabine), one cycle of CAG chemotherapy (cytarabine, aclarubicin, and recombinant human granulocyte-colony stimulating factor), and one cycle of AA chemotherapy (aclarubicin and cytarabine). She denied any history of preceding injury or insect bite at the site of infection.
