QuantiFERON was negative for tuberculosis. Serologies for aspergillus, blastomycosis, coccidioides, cryptococcus, histoplasma, HIV, and toxoplasma were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for acid-fast bacilli, fungal organisms, and pneumocystis.
Immunologic evaluation was negative for ANCA, proteinase 3, and myeloperoxidase antibodies. This excluded granulomatosis with polyangiitis as a differential diagnosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for cytology.
Punch biopsy of one of the skin lesions demonstrated poorly circumscribed granulomas surrounding blood vessels and skin appendages, mild lymphocytic infiltration with no features to suggest cutaneous lymphoma, and no evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Stains for fungal and acid-fast bacilli were negative.
Left upper and lower lobe wedge biopsies of the nodules were taken through video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) as the diagnosis was still unclear. The biopsies revealed EBV-positive DLBCL with features of LG grade 3 (Figure 2). The features that favor LG over DLBCL include a background that consisted predominantly of inflammatory cells with a minority of large B-cells and vascular invasion. In addition, lung involvement and EBV positivity are not exclusive to LG, but are almost always present in LG. Flow cytometry did not detect the large B-cells which are sometimes too fragile to survive flow cytometric processing, but did detect rare, small monoclonal B-cells with a CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) phenotype. The flow cytometric findings are compatible with the morphology as no significant CLL/SLL population could be identified with CD5 and CD23 immunostaining (Figure 3). In this case, the source of rare CLL cells is likely peripheral blood, either physiologically through the inflammatory response or contamination during resection. Features of secondary organizing pneumonia were also present.
The patient underwent PET-CT 4 weeks following the initial chest CT (Figure 4). This showed significant progression and confluence of bilateral peribronchovascular lung opacities. The lung opacities had diffuse FDG uptake with a maximum SUV of 22.3. The PET/CT also demonstrated intense uptake in the cutaneous lesions of the lower extremities.
Bone marrow biopsy was consistent with hypercellular marrow with 20-30% marrow involvement by CLL/SLL cells. The patient was started on R-CHOP chemotherapy with Neupogen support. IVIG was also given for hypogammaglobulinemia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male with chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with mild productive cough, progressive dyspnea, high fever, and violaceous lower extremity skin papules.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented as an outpatient with mild productive cough and dyspnea and was found on chest CT to have innumerable new bilateral peribronchovascular pulmonary nodules with ground-glass halos. Despite outpatient antibiotics and corticosteroids, he experienced progressive clinical decline over several weeks and was admitted with exertional hypoxia, fever up to 102.4 F, and new erythematous-to-violaceous papules on both lower extremities.
subjective.past_medical_history: Longstanding chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mild productive cough, progressive dyspnea, fever up to 102.4 F, and bilateral lower extremity erythematous/violaceous skin papules.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals showed fever up to 102.4 F, mild tachycardia (low 100s bpm), and exertional hypoxia; pulmonary auscultation was unremarkable, and skin exam revealed erythematous-to-violaceous papules on both lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL), normal BMP, hypogammaglobulinemia (low serum IgG), negative blood and sputum cultures, negative QuantiFERON-TB, and negative ANCA, PR3, and MPO antibodies. Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with 20%-30% CLL/SLL involvement.
objective.advanced_workup: Serologies for Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, HIV, and Toxoplasma were all negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was negative for AFB, fungi, Pneumocystis, and malignant cytology. Chest CT showed innumerable bilateral ill-defined peribronchovascular solid nodules with peripheral ground-glass halos, which progressed on 4-week follow-up PET-CT to confluent intensely FDG-avid pulmonary masses (SUVmax 22.3) alongside FDG-avid lower extremity skin lesions. Punch biopsy of a leg lesion showed perivascular/periadnexal granulomatous inflammation (AFB/fungal stains negative). VATS wedge biopsies of the left upper and lower lobes established EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with grade 3 lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LG) features and secondary organizing pneumonia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with grade 3 lymphomatoid granulomatosis features (Richter transformation) presenting with bilateral halo-sign pulmonary nodules and granulomatous skin papules in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia; angioinvasive pulmonary aspergillosis, endemic mycoses, tuberculosis, and ANCA-associated vasculitis were ruled out by negative fungal serologies, negative BAL microbiology, negative ANCA, and VATS lung biopsy histopathology. Treated with R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy, filgrastim (Neupogen) support, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for hypogammaglobulinemia.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old female presented with complaints of generalized abdominal distension, weight loss, swelling of legs, and muscle weakness extant for several weeks. Her past medical history was significant for a well-controlled HIV infection of 6 years on highly active anti-retroviral therapy, hypertension, ESRD secondary to HIV-associated nephropathy, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. She was a non-smoker and had no history of alcohol or drug abuse. Her initial renal biopsy revealed collapsing focal glomerular sclerosis, microcystic dilation of renal tubules, lymphocytic interstitial infiltrates, and interstitial fibrosis. She received chronic cycler-assisted peritoneal dialysis (PD) for 5 years and was well controlled clinically regarding uremic and volume status with no abnormalities regarding color, viscosity, or volume of exchanges. Subsequently, she was transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis (HD) due to personal preferences. A few weeks after the transition to intermittent HD, ascites of unclear etiology developed, ultimately requiring repeated large-volume paracentesis with ~ 5 - 7 L ascitic fluid removals every other week. 
There were no associated symptoms of coughing, palpitations, or shortness of breath. She was chronically anuric. Vital signs showed blood pressure of 160/80 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats/min (regular), respiratory rate 16/min and temperature 36.9  C. Oxygen saturation was 98% on ambient room air. Her physical examination was remarkable for moderate ascites and edema of the lower extremities. Otherwise neurological, respiratory, and cardiovascular examinations were normal without organomegaly and without clinical stigmata or symptoms of chronic liver disease or heart failure. 
Laboratory investigations showed normocytic, normochromic anemia with a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL and uncorrected serum calcium of 8.6 mg/dL. Other labs were as follows: CD4 T-cell count: 600/mm3, HIV viral load: 986 copies/mL (reference: < 40 copies/mL), serum creatinine: 10.3 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase: 13 U/L (normal range: 5 - 34 U/L), alanine aminotransferase: 17 U/L (5 - 45 U/L), bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL, prothrombin time INR: 1.01, serum albumin: 2.3 mg/dL, serum amylase: 105 IU/L (27 - 130 U/L), serum lipase: 40 IU/L (8 - 78 U/L). Her tumor antigens (Ag) were within reference range for cancer antigen (CA) 15-3 and CA19-9. CA 125 levels were repeatedly elevated (197 - 416 U/mL (normal: < 34.9 U/mL)), but no further follow-up was obtained. Analysis of the ascites fluid showed an albumin level of 1.5 g/dL and protein of 3.5 g/dL. The serum-to-ascites albumin gradient was < 1.1 excluding portal hypertension as a cause of ascites. The culture of peritoneal fluid was negative for acid-fast bacilli. There were no fungi seen by calcofluor white stain. Histoplasma Ag and Aspergillus Ag were negative. The pancreas was reported normal on computed tomography. Her beta-2 microglobulin was elevated to 47.30 mg/L (normal: 0.80 - 2.3). Serum protein electrophoresis showed hypoalbuminemia and decreased total protein, with minimal monoclonal M-component only (IgG-kappa 0.30 g/dL in the gamma zone). Immunofixation electrophoresis showed polyclonal immunoglobulins (Ig) with polyclonal light chains. kappa and lambda light chains were increased to 66.86 mg/dL (normal: 0.33 - 1.94) and 18.55 mg/dL (normal: 0.57 - 2.63), respectively, yielding a ratio of 3.6 (normal: 0.26 - 1.65) (Table 1). Ascitic fluid analysis showed a marked increase in plasma cells with an abnormal kappa : lambda ratio, i.e., > 5 : 1. 
Liver biopsy was essentially normal, hence an omental biopsy was performed which on immunohistochemistry showed similar findings as the ascitic fluid with predominant kappa and faint lambda staining (Figure 1). Multiple myeloma work-ups with skeletal surveys revealed no focal osseous lesions, apart from the osseous changes of hyperparathyroidism. Accordingly, the diagnosis of omental EMP with malignant ascites was established. Omental resection and radiation were offered to the patient, but she refused further intervention. Two years of follow-up, she remained stable without any further complication, apart from requiring regular paracenteses.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old HIV-positive female on hemodialysis presented with several weeks of generalized abdominal distension, weight loss, bilateral leg swelling, and muscle weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After 5 years of stable cycler-assisted peritoneal dialysis for HIV-associated nephropathy, the patient transitioned by personal preference to intermittent hemodialysis. Within a few weeks of switching to hemodialysis, she developed progressive refractory ascites requiring large-volume paracenteses (5-7 L every 2 weeks), accompanied by weight loss, lower extremity edema, and muscle weakness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled HIV infection for 6 years on HAART; end-stage renal disease secondary to biopsy-proven HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis), on peritoneal dialysis for 5 years before recently transitioning to intermittent hemodialysis; hypertension; secondary hyperparathyroidism; lifetime non-smoker with no alcohol or illicit drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized abdominal distension, weight loss, bilateral leg swelling, muscle weakness, and chronic baseline anuria; negative for cough, palpitations, or dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: blood pressure 160/80 mmHg, heart rate 74 bpm (regular), respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.9 C, and room-air SpO2 98%. Physical exam was notable for moderate-to-massive ascites and bilateral lower extremity edema without hepatosplenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, heart failure signs, or neurological deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL), CD4 count 600/mm3, HIV viral load 986 copies/mL, creatinine 10.3 mg/dL, calcium 8.6 mg/dL, AST 13 U/L, ALT 17 U/L, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, INR 1.01, hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dL), normal amylase (105 IU/L) and lipase (40 IU/L), normal CA 15-3 and CA19-9, elevated CA-125 (197-416 U/mL), markedly elevated beta-2 microglobulin (47.30 mg/L; normal 0.80-2.3), small IgG-kappa M-spike on SPEP (0.30 g/dL), and elevated serum free kappa (66.86 mg/dL) and lambda (18.55 mg/dL) light chains (kappa:lambda ratio 3.6). Skeletal survey showed only secondary hyperparathyroidism without lytic myeloma lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Paracentesis revealed exudative ascites (ascitic protein 3.5 g/dL, albumin 1.5 g/dL, SAAG <1.1 g/dL) with negative AFB culture, negative calcofluor white fungal stain, and negative Histoplasma and Aspergillus antigen assays, but marked clonal plasmacytosis with a kappa:lambda ratio >5:1. Abdominal CT showed a normal pancreas, liver biopsy was normal, and laparoscopic omental biopsy with immunohistochemistry confirmed a kappa-light-chain-restricted extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary omental IgG-kappa extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) presenting as refractory low-SAAG malignant plasmacytic ascites following transition from peritoneal dialysis to hemodialysis in a patient with well-controlled HIV; tuberculous and fungal peritonitis (including Aspergillus and Histoplasma peritonitis) and portal hypertension were excluded by SAAG <1.1 g/dL, normal liver biopsy, negative peritoneal fluid calcofluor white stain, AFB culture, and Aspergillus/Histoplasma antigens, and omental biopsy immunohistochemistry. The patient declined omental resection and radiotherapy and remained clinically stable on maintenance hemodialysis and periodic therapeutic paracenteses over 2 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 13-year-old boy underwent pericardial fenestration and thoracic duct ligation for pericardial and pleural effusion at 3 years of age and was diagnosed with GLA after a pleural biopsy. The patient experienced no pleural effusion before his 11th birthday. The patient had a history of cerebrospinal fluid leakage due to a skull fracture at 7 years of age. The patient was referred to our department immediately following pleural effusion when he was 11 years old. A hematological examination showed high values for D-dimer (22.2 mug/mL) and P-FDP (50.9 mug/mL). A radiograph showed pleural effusion in the right lung (Figure 1). Thoracentesis revealed chylothorax mixed with blood components. Magnetic resonance imaging showed additional lesions on the lymph ducts on both sides of the inner auditory channels; computed tomography (CT) showed diffuse osteolytic changes on both sides of the femoral neck and thoracic vertebra.  Figure 2 shows the patient's clinical course. Although the patient abstained from eating and parenteral nutrition was provided in addition to octreotide testing and pulse steroid therapy, pleural effusion worsened and became bilateral. Two or more liters were drained on days when there was a large amount of pleural effusion. We were unable to locate the site of the leakage even though we conducted a lymphogram to treat the pleural effusion and identify the leakage site. Sirolimus administration was initiated at 0.88 mg/m2/day, which proved to be an insufficient dosage. However, when the dosage was increased to 1.3 mg/m2/day after 1 month, the patient experienced an onset of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) after 1 week. At that time, a blood examination showed platelet (1.4 x 104/muL), P-FDP (590 mug/mL), fibrinogen (114 mg/dL), prothrombin time rate (1.35), antithrombin (129%), and no liver dysfunction. The urine and blood cultures were negative. Viral serology was negative for cytomegalovirus, and aspergillus antigen was negative. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody were normal levels. The CT scan showed no sign of pneumonia or pyothorax. We diagnosed him with DIC using DIC score. Although we temporarily paused the administration of sirolimus, the patient experienced an additional onset of DIC 10 days after we resumed administration. Thus, he underwent thoracoscopic removal of the hematoma (Figure 3). The trough level of sirolimus during administration was 3.4-8.9 ng/mL, which does not represent abnormal elevation. Although an additional pause in the administration of sirolimus did not reduce the amount of pleural fluid, there were no additional onsets of DIC. Subsequently, there was a significant decrease in pleural fluid once Eppikajyutsuto was administered at 0.2 g/kg/day. We were able to proceed with tube thoracostomy removal 40 days after the initiation of oral administration. There was no re-accumulation of pleural fluids in the 18 months following the initiation of oral administration.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old boy with generalized lymphatic anomaly presented with recurrent massive chylous and hemorrhagic pleural effusions complicated by recurrent disseminated intravascular coagulation after starting sirolimus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed at age 3 with generalized lymphatic anomaly (GLA) requiring pericardial fenestration and thoracic duct ligation, the patient remained effusion-free until age 11, when he presented with a large right-then-bilateral chylous/hemorrhagic pleural effusion (>2 L/day drainage) refractory to fasting, TPN, octreotide, pulse corticosteroids, and lymphangiography. One week after escalating oral sirolimus from 0.88 to 1.3 mg/m2/day (and again 10 days after rechallenge), he developed acute disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and intrathoracic hematoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Generalized lymphatic anomaly (GLA) diagnosed by pleural biopsy at age 3 (status post pericardial fenestration and thoracic duct ligation); skull fracture with CSF leak at age 7.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea/pleural effusion and hemorrhagic coagulopathy (DIC).

objective.physical_examination: Signs of massive right-sided and subsequent bilateral pleural effusions requiring chest tube drainage (>2 L/day).
objective.routine_investigations: Initial referral labs at age 11 showed elevated D-dimer (22.2 ug/mL) and plasma FDP (50.9 ug/mL). Thoracentesis yielded bloody chylothorax. During sirolimus-triggered DIC (at therapeutic sirolimus troughs of 3.4-8.9 ng/mL), labs showed severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 1.4 x 10^4/uL), markedly elevated P-FDP (590 ug/mL), hypofibrinogenemia (114 mg/dL), PT ratio 1.35, antithrombin 129%, and normal liver function tests. Blood and urine cultures, CMV serology, rheumatoid factor, and ANA were all negative/normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum Aspergillus antigen was negative, and chest CT showed no pneumonia or empyema. MRI demonstrated bilateral internal auditory canal lymphatic lesions, and CT showed diffuse osteolytic lesions in the bilateral femoral necks and thoracic vertebrae consistent with GLA. Following recurrent DIC and intrathoracic clotting, thoracoscopic evacuation of the pleural hematoma was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Generalized lymphatic anomaly (GLA) complicated by refractory bilateral hemorrhagic chylothorax and sirolimus-triggered consumptive coagulopathy/disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); infectious triggers of DIC including invasive aspergillosis, CMV, and bacterial sepsis were excluded by negative Aspergillus antigen, negative CMV serology, negative cultures, and chest CT. Managed with thoracoscopic hematoma removal, discontinuation of sirolimus, and initiation of the oral Japanese Kampo herbal medicine Eppikajyutsuto (0.2 g/kg/day), which dramatically reduced pleural fluid output, permitted chest tube removal after 40 days, and maintained complete remission of pleural effusions over 18 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old female with past medical history of tobacco dependence presented for low-grade fever and sudden onset of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain with associated nausea and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) completed in the emergency department revealed an intraluminal polypoid filling defect arising from the isthmus of the aorta projecting into the proximal descending aorta and findings consistent with infarctions of the spleen and right kidney (Figures 1(a)-1(c)). Given the fever, there was a concern for sepsis so she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Heparin has also initiated cardioembolic phenomena of unclear etiology; however, it was later discontinued to prevent hemorrhagic transformation of the existing infarcts. The patient was admitted for further evaluation.
A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no findings to suggest valvular or cardiac source of embolus (Figure 2). An agitated saline bubble contrast study was performed with no evidence of intracardiac shunting (Figure 3). A transesophageal echocardiogram was then completed and revealed a large echogenic mobile mass attached to the wall of the descending thoracic aorta (Figures 4(a) and 4(b)). Bilateral lower extremity arterial Dopplers were obtained and revealed severe popliteal-tibial arterial disease in the left lower extremity (Figure 5).
Work-up for other organic causes was extensive. Infectious work-up was negative and included testing for bacterial infection, fungal infection, HIV, Bartonella henselae antibody, Coxiella burnetii antibodies, Leptospira antibodies, syphilis, aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and histoplasma antigen. Hypercoagulability work-up was also unremarkable and included DRVVT screening for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies (x2), homocysteine levels, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria screening, Protein C and S activity, antithrombin mutations, and factor V Leiden and prothrombin genotyping. Autoimmune work-up was also unyielding and included testing for antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antidouble-stranded DNA antibody, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide, Sjogren antibody, myeloperoxidase antibodies, proteinase 3 autoantibodies, complement levels, Smith antibody, and RNP antibody. Given that there are no acute threat to limb or organ ischemia, the largely negative work-up, and no straight-forward mechanism to remove the aortic thrombus, we decided to manage the patient medically with close outpatient follow-up. She was started on heparin while inpatient which was transitioned to apixaban 5 mg twice a day and 81 mg of aspirin daily. This was done primarily because of the patient's preference to avoid frequent INR checks. A board-certified hematologist agreed with the use of apixaban with monthly outpatient follow-up to ensure patient compliance and clinical improvement. Patient was also counseled regarding smoking cessation. Catheter-based or surgical thromboembolectomy would have been considered if the patient would have developed acute limb ischemia or threatened organ.
At one month, the patient was seen in the clinic and denied symptoms of chest, back, or abdominal pain. She denied significant pain at rest or with exertion and did not exhibit any nonhealing wounds in either of her lower extremities. She noted being able to walk roughly one-quarter of a mile without symptoms prior to resting. She reported adherence with her daily aspirin and twice-daily Eliquis. At this time, arterial computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis was repeated which revealed complete resolution of the filling defect involving the aortic isthmus and proximal descending aorta. There was no CT evidence to suggest vacuities. The spleen exhibited a lobulated superior margin with volume loss and the right kidney demonstrated a lobulated appearance of the right lower pole compatible with scarring from the previous infarct (Figure 6). The patient was instructed to continue with her antithrombotic regimen and follow-up in one month.
At this time, the patient no longer expressed having any symptoms of LE pain, swelling, or claudication. She reported being able to resume her daily activities with no limitations. Findings of the CTA were discussed with the patient at her two-month follow-up, and she was encouraged to continue with activity as tolerated. At this time, given the resolution of the mass after anticoagulation, it was felt that it was most likely an aortic thrombus. With regards the duration of therapy, we felt that this was likely unprovoked, and given it was arterial, we decided to continue anticoagulation for at least 12 more months pending further hematologic evaluation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old female smoker presented with low-grade fever and sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department with acute severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever, and was found on CT to have a mobile descending thoracic aortic mural mass complicated by embolic splenic and right renal infarctions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Tobacco dependence; severe left popliteal-tibial peripheral arterial disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive on admission for low-grade fever, severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; negative at 1- and 2-month follow-ups for chest, back, abdominal, or lower extremity claudication pain.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (low-grade) with right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness on admission; no acute limb threat or nonhealing lower extremity wounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Transthoracic echocardiogram with agitated saline bubble study was normal without valvular vegetation or intracardiac shunt. Bilateral lower extremity arterial Doppler ultrasound showed severe left popliteal-tibial arterial occlusive disease. Extensive infectious (bacterial/fungal blood cultures, HIV, Bartonella henselae, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, syphilis, Histoplasma antigen), hypercoagulable (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, homocysteine, PNH flow, Protein C/S, antithrombin, Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene), and autoimmune (ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, RF, CCP, SSA/SSB, MPO, PR3, complement, anti-Sm, anti-RNP) workups were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen was negative. Emergency department abdominal/thoracic CT and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated a large echogenic mobile polypoid filling defect attached to the aortic isthmus projecting into the proximal descending thoracic aorta, accompanied by wedge-shaped embolic infarctions of the spleen and right lower renal pole. Repeat CT angiography at 1 month confirmed complete dissolution of the aortic thrombus with expected chronic splenic and right renal cortical infarct scarring.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Unprovoked mobile mural thrombus of the aortic isthmus and proximal descending thoracic aorta complicated by acute embolic splenic and right renal infarctions in a 46-year-old smoker; mycotic aortic thrombus/endarteritis (including Aspergillus, Histoplasma, Coxiella, and Bartonella) as well as inherited thrombophilia and autoimmune vasculitis were ruled out by negative infectious, hypercoagulable, and autoimmune workups and complete thrombus resolution on anticoagulation. Managed medically with inpatient intravenous unfractionated heparin transitioned to oral apixaban (5 mg twice daily for at least 12 months) plus aspirin (81 mg daily) and smoking cessation counseling, achieving complete radiographic resolution of the aortic thrombus and full symptom-free recovery at 1- and 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 81-year-old female presented with increasing cough and a chest x-ray revealed a right lower lung mass. Subsequent work-up with CT scans, PET scan, and needle core-biopsy yielded a diagnosis of a clinical stage T1cN0M0 adenocarcinoma of the lung. Her past medical history was pertinent in that she had chronic atrial fibrillation for which she had undergone cardiac ablation and placement of a permanent pacemaker. Pulmonary function studies revealed an FEV1 of 0.97 liters which was 56% of predicted. Her medications included allopurinol 300mg daily, atenolol 50mg daily, diltiazem extended release 180mg daily, furosemide 40mg daily, rivaroxaban 15mg daily and, amiodarone 200mg twice daily. The patient had been on amiodarone for at least three years and after first-line therapy for atrial fibrillation had been ineffective.
After presentation at a multi-disciplinary lung cancer conference, it was decided that she was not a surgical candidate. Therefore, she was treated with a total of 50Gy in 5 fractions of SBRT using two co-planar arcs (Figure 1). The Dose-Volume Histogram (DVH) for the treatment plan showed total lung minus target dose within accepted guidelines (Figure 2).
One month later, she presented with mild dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. She denied fevers, chills, hemoptysis, weight loss, or chest pain. Her physical examination did reveal coarse rales in the right lung field. A chest x-ray at that time revealed a new right upper lung infiltrate at the treated site (Figure 3). Her laboratory work was unremarkable with no elevation of the white blood cell count. A diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis was made and she was placed on prednisone 20 milligrams b.i.d.
Unfortunately, she presented 5 days later to the emergency room with increasing dyspnea and nonproductive cough. A chest x-ray now revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (Figure 4). There had been marked worsening of the infiltrates in the right lung. The patient's respiratory status declined and she required intubation and mechanical ventilation
A nuclear medicine ventilation/perfusion scan revealed a low probability for pulmonary emboli. A CT scan of the chest revealed diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in all lobes of both lungs (Figure 5).
Urine tests for Streptococcus Pneumonia antigen, Histoplasma antibody, Blastomycosis antibody, and Legionella antigen were negative. Serum tests for Cryptococcal antigen, Histoplasma antibody, Coccidioides antibody, Blastomycosis antibody, and Aspergillus antibody were negative. Blood cultures and urine cultures were negative. A respiratory viral panel was negative.
She was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone. Empiric intravenous antibiotic and antifungal therapy was started with doxycycline, meropenem, vancomycin, and caspofungin. Her rivaroxaban was discontinued in preparation for fiber-optic bronchoscopy once the risk of bleeding during the procedure had subsided. Her amiodarone was not discontinued.
In spite of maximal support, she succumbed to her disease within 72 hours after her initial presentation with the suspected radiation induced changes and prior to evaluation with bronchoscopy.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 81-year-old female on chronic amiodarone therapy presented 1 month after stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for stage I right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma with mild dyspnea and a nonproductive cough that rapidly progressed over 5 days to fatal hypoxemic respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Deemed medically inoperable for a clinical stage T1cN0M0 right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma (baseline FEV1 0.97 L, 56% predicted), the patient underwent SBRT (50 Gy in 5 fractions) while taking chronic amiodarone (200 mg twice daily for >3 years). One month post-SBRT, she presented with mild dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and a localized right lung infiltrate treated with oral prednisone (20 mg twice daily) for radiation pneumonitis. Five days later, she returned to the emergency department with rapidly worsening dyspnea and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates requiring mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage T1cN0M0 right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma treated with SBRT (50 Gy in 5 fractions) 1 month prior; chronic atrial fibrillation status post cardiac ablation and permanent pacemaker placement; COPD/reduced pulmonary reserve (FEV1 0.97 L, 56% predicted). Home medications: amiodarone 200 mg twice daily (for >3 years), rivaroxaban 15 mg daily, atenolol 50 mg daily, diltiazem ER 180 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and allopurinol 300 mg daily.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive dyspnea and nonproductive cough; negative for fever, chills, hemoptysis, chest pain, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Coarse rales over the right lung field at initial 1-month post-SBRT visit, rapidly progressing 5 days later to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count and routine laboratory panels were normal. Blood and urine cultures, respiratory viral panel, urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigens, urinary Histoplasma and Blastomyces antibodies, and serum cryptococcal antigen, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces, and Aspergillus antibodies were all negative. Chest X-ray initially showed a focal right infiltrate at the irradiated site, progressing within 5 days to diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Nuclear medicine V/Q scan showed low probability for pulmonary embolism.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates involving all lobes of both lungs.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal fulminant bilateral radiation pneumonitis potentiated by concurrent chronic amiodarone therapy (200 mg twice daily) occurring 1 month after lung SBRT (50 Gy in 5 fractions); opportunistic fungal pneumonia (including pulmonary aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, and cryptococcosis) as well as bacterial and viral pneumonia were ruled out by negative serum Aspergillus and endemic fungal antibodies, negative urinary antigens, and negative blood/urine/viral tests. Despite high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobials (doxycycline, meropenem, vancomycin, and caspofungin), and mechanical ventilation, the patient died within 72 hours of hospital admission.

raw_case_text:
The patient's medical history included recurrent acute otitis media and seasonal allergic rhinitis (AR), both beginning when he was 5 years-old. He was diagnosed with bronchial asthma (BA) when he was 6 years old, when AR became continuous and severe. He lived with his parents and younger brother, all of whom exhibited BA and pollinosis. There were no pets or smokers in his house.
On physical examination, the patient appeared to be well. His weight was 21.9 kg (- 1.0 SD) and his height was 126.6 cm (- 0.2 SD). His vital signs were as follows: pulse rate, 81 beats per minute; respiratory rate, 20 breaths per minute; temperature, 37.0  C; and oxygen saturation, 99% while breathing ambient air. Examination of the chest revealed prolonged expirations, sibilant rhonchi, and coarse crackles on the right side. Spirometry showed a forced vital capacity of 92%, a 1-s forced expiratory volume of 64%, and poor reversibility upon inhalation of a beta stimulant.
Hematological and serum biochemical examinations revealed a white blood cell count of 8600/muL, with a differential profile of 23% eosinophils, and a serum total IgE level of 151 IU/mL. ImmunoCAP tests for IgEs produced in response to Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, Aspergillus, Candida, Alternaria, Cladosporium, and other common allergens were all negative.
Eosinophilia, bilateral nasal polyps, and pansinusitis were observed via computed tomography (Fig. 1), and the diagnosis was severe refractory BA associated with ECRS. The patient received oral prednisolone (PSL, 10 mg/day), which alleviated both the BA and nasal symptoms. However, during tapering of the steroid, the symptoms soon recurred, and nasal-opening surgery (endoscopic sinus surgery) was performed half a year later. After surgery, the BA was controlled during PSL dose reduction, but 4 months after surgery, the nasal polyps recurred and an eosinophilic infiltrate was found in the extracted nasal polyps (Fig. 2). Therefore, PSL at 10 mg/day was continued.

subjective.chief_complaint: A school-aged boy presented with severe corticosteroid-dependent bronchial asthma and chronic pansinusitis with recurrent bilateral nasal polyposis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed recurrent acute otitis media and seasonal allergic rhinitis at age 5, which progressed at age 6 to continuous severe allergic rhinitis and refractory bronchial asthma. Although oral prednisolone (10 mg/day) controlled his asthma and nasal symptoms, symptoms rapidly relapsed upon steroid tapering, and bilateral nasal polyps recurred 4 months after endoscopic sinus surgery.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent acute otitis media and allergic rhinitis since age 5; bronchial asthma since age 6. Family history positive for bronchial asthma and pollinosis in his parents and younger brother; no household pets or tobacco smoke exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic nasal obstruction/polyposis, wheezing, and cough.

objective.physical_examination: Well-appearing child; weight 21.9 kg (-1.0 SD), height 126.6 cm (-0.2 SD), pulse 81 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 37.0 C, and room-air SpO2 99%. Chest auscultation revealed prolonged expiration, sibilant rhonchi, and right-sided coarse crackles.
objective.routine_investigations: Spirometry demonstrated airflow obstruction with FVC 92% predicted, FEV1 64% predicted, and poor bronchodilator reversibility. Blood tests showed WBC 8,600/uL with marked peripheral eosinophilia (23% eosinophils) and serum total IgE of 151 IU/mL. ImmunoCAP allergen-specific IgE testing was negative for Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, Aspergillus, Candida, Alternaria, Cladosporium, and other common inhalant allergens.
objective.advanced_workup: Paranasal sinus CT demonstrated bilateral nasal polyps and pansinusitis. Histopathological examination of nasal polyps resected during endoscopic sinus surgery confirmed dense mucosal eosinophilic infiltration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pediatric severe refractory bronchial asthma associated with eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis (ECRS) and recurrent eosinophilic nasal polyposis, confirmed by peripheral eosinophilia (23%), sinus CT showing bilateral polyposis and pansinusitis, and polyp histopathology demonstrating dense eosinophilic infiltration; allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis/aspergillosis and IgE-mediated fungal sensitization were excluded by negative ImmunoCAP specific IgE to Aspergillus, Candida, Alternaria, and Cladosporium. Managed with endoscopic sinus surgery and maintenance low-dose oral prednisolone (10 mg/day) after polyp recurrence 4 months postoperatively.

raw_case_text:
A 16-year old boy underwent laparoscopic surgery for varicocele. His past medical history was uneventful, except for febrile seizures during early childhood. He had no allergies, history of recurrent pneumonia or other chronic respiratory diseases. Likewise, his family history was unremarkable. Smoking habits were asked but not disclosed. Complete blood cells count, liver and kidney function tests and first level coagulation studies (platelets count, prothrombin time test, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen) were all normal before the general anesthesia. According to the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) risk classification1, he was a healthy patient (ASA 1).
Prior to the operation, the patient was given general anesthesia consisting of propofol (2 mg/kg) and rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg), with remifentanil (0.25 mcg/kg/min) for intubation. General anesthesia was maintained with 2% sevoflurane and remifentanil (0.25-0.125 mcg/kg/min). Sugammadex (2 mg/Kg) was administered before extubation (TOF ratio > 0.9). Both surgery and extubation were conducted without any complications and the patient had no obvious signs of upper airway obstruction, neither cough nor laryngospasm.
Thirty minutes after waking up, he manifested hemoptysis, dyspnea, and ARF. He was alert, tachypnoeic, and normothermic. His Glasgow Coma Scale was 15, and his initial vital signs were: pulse 80 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation averaging 73% on room air. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed: pH 7.37; pCO2 39.6 mmHg (5.27 kPa); pO2 39.5 mmHg (5.26 kPa); oxyhemoglobin (oxyHb) 73.7%; and HCO3- 23.1 mEq/L. Otorhinolaryngoiatric evaluation with nasal and laryngeal fibro-endoscopy unveiled no evidence of previous bleeding from the upper respiratory tract. Respiratory auscultation revealed diffuse rhonchi, with no other remarkable signs. His initial chest x-ray (Figure 1) showed infiltrative opacification pattern mainly seen in the mid zones with apical sparing suggestive for impaired pulmonary microcirculation, raising the suspect of DAH. To further investigate our hypothesis, a chest CT scan (Figure 2) was performed, which revealed multiple dense opacities with blurred, confluent margins due to diffuse alveolar involvement in the pulmonary lobes.
Given the evidence of hypoxemic respiratory failure and the suspect of DAH, the patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit, where he was subjected to immediate bronchoalveolar lavage, revealing the presence of abundant blood, but after the bronchoalveolar lavage with 0.9% sodium chloride solution, the bronchial mucosa appeared without signs of pathological lesions. More specifically, three lavage of 50 mLs each were done and afterwards 35, 35, and 50 mLs of BAL fluid were retrieved. Direct microscopic examination showed leucocytes, macrophages and bronchial epithelial cells. Further confirmation arrived from cytologic analysis of his bronchoalveolar lavage secretions which described the presence of blood, 85% of alveolar macrophages and 15% of granulocytes. Hemosiderin was not assessed because hemoptysis started 4 h before and the endoscopic appearance of the bleeding itself appeared to be very recent, undergoing from <48 h. The patient was given fraction inspired oxygen (FiO2) (40%; 12 L/min) by means of a Venturi mask for ARF, intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g per day as antibiotic prophylaxis and intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g per day for anti-inflammatory action for 5 days, while waiting for the results of microbial studies and autoimmune diseases screening.
Initial blood tests performed at Day 1 revealed: hemoglobin levels 13.5 g/dl (135 g/L); leukocytosis 14.540 mm-3 (14.54 109/L), of which 83.7% were neutrophils, and normal platelet count (221 x 109 /L). Renal function, liver function, electrolytes, coagulation studies (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen) were all normal. Von Willebrand factor deficiency was also ruled out on the basis of Von Willebrand factor antigen and Ristocetin cofactor activities which resulted within normal range (Von Willebrand factor antigen was 90%, with a normal reference range between 57 and 147%; Ristocetin cofactor was 120% with a normal reference range of 51-147% considering our patient's specific age group). Urinalysis was unremarkable, and direct microscopic exam did not reveal any dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs). The diagnostic work-up, which included serological exams and blood and sputum cultures for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Aspergillus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nocardia spp., Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Pneumocystis Jirovecii, Herpesviruses, and the complete respiratory viral panel, ruled out any pulmonary infections. An extensive rheumatological serologic evaluation including CRP, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, ANA, and ENA panel came back negative as well. Lastly, the echocardiography was completely normal, excluding any congenital or acquired cardiomyopathy as well as pulmonary hypertension.
Questioned on smoking habits, the boy revealed to be a frequent cannabis smoker since few years. He admitted to have smoked about 1-2 joints per day in the last month before surgery and to have used a marijuana smoking device known as "water bong" at least once. Moreover, he denied having used any other type of street drugs. We therefore performed a toxicological urine test that resulted positive for cannabinoids. Cocaine was not tested since the patient's parents declined their consent.
The patient's general conditions rapidly improved after 24 h: he was no longer dyspneic, and oxygen supplementation was stopped on day 2 of hospitalization after a second chest radiograph (Figure 3) revealed the resolution of DAH. He was discharged after 6 days with tapering prednisone. Although he was recommended an ambulatory follow-up, his parents declined.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male developed acute hemoptysis, dyspnea, and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure 30 minutes after uneventful extubation from laparoscopic varicocelectomy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An otherwise healthy ASA I adolescent underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic varicocelectomy under propofol, rocuronium, sevoflurane, and remifentanil anesthesia reversed with sugammadex (2 mg/kg, TOF >0.9) without cough or laryngospasm at extubation. Thirty minutes post-extubation, he developed acute frank hemoptysis, tachypnea, and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (room-air SpO2 73%). Upon further questioning in the ICU, he disclosed smoking 1-2 cannabis joints daily over the preceding month and using a water bong.
subjective.past_medical_history: Childhood febrile seizures; otherwise healthy (ASA I) with no allergies, chronic respiratory disease, or bleeding family history. Social history significant for habitual daily cannabis smoking (1-2 joints/day) and water-bong use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute postoperative hemoptysis and dyspnea; negative for prior respiratory symptoms or bleeding diathesis.

objective.physical_examination: Thirty minutes post-extubation: alert (GCS 15), tachypneic, normothermic, pulse 80 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, and room-air SpO2 73%. Nasal and laryngeal fiberoptic endoscopy showed no upper airway bleeding source; chest auscultation revealed diffuse rhonchi.
objective.routine_investigations: Post-extubation room-air ABG showed severe hypoxemic respiratory failure: pH 7.37, PaCO2 39.6 mmHg, PaO2 39.5 mmHg, oxyhemoglobin 73.7%, and HCO3 23.1 mEq/L. Preoperative and Day 1 labs showed hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, WBC 14,540/mm3 (83.7% neutrophils), platelets 221 x 10^9/L, normal renal/liver function and electrolytes, normal PT/aPTT/fibrinogen, normal vWF antigen (90%) and ristocetin cofactor activity (120%), normal urinalysis without dysmorphic RBCs, normal echocardiography, and positive urine cannabinoid screen. Extensive infectious workup (blood/sputum cultures and serologies for S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Legionella, Aspergillus, M. tuberculosis, Nocardia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Pneumocystis jirovecii, herpesviruses, and respiratory viruses) and autoimmune workup (CRP, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, ANA, ENA) were all negative. Chest X-ray showed mid-zone alveolar infiltrates with apical sparing, which resolved completely by hospital day 2.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated multiple confluent bilateral alveolar ground-glass and dense opacities consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Immediate ICU bronchoscopy with three 50-mL saline bronchoalveolar lavages returned grossly bloody fluid with normal underlying bronchial mucosa; BAL cytology showed abundant red blood cells, 85% alveolar macrophages, and 15% granulocytes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute postoperative diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) associated with habitual cannabis and water-bong smoking following general anesthesia for laparoscopic varicocelectomy, confirmed by chest CT and grossly hemorrhagic bronchoalveolar lavage fluid after excluding upper airway bleeding, negative-pressure laryngospasm, coagulopathy/von Willebrand disease, autoimmune capillaritis (negative ANCA/ANA), and pulmonary infections including aspergillosis. Treated with Venturi mask oxygen (FiO2 40%), intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days followed by an oral prednisone taper), and prophylactic IV ceftriaxone (2 g/day), achieving complete clinical and radiographic resolution within 48 hours and discharge on hospital day 6.

raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old female with a distant 15 pack year smoking history presented to the pulmonary clinic for evaluation of a 4 cm right upper lobe mass found on a CT thorax. She had a dry cough with occasional fatigue and night sweats that began about a year earlier. She denied recent travel, weight loss, hemoptysis, epistaxis, wheezing, joint pain, hematuria, peripheral edema, orthopnea, easy bruising or alopecia. Her vitals and physical exam were within normal limits on room air.
She had been treated as an outpatient for presumed community acquired pneumonia when her symptoms first began. Follow up chest X-ray showed a persistent opacity in the right upper lobe and a CT scan showed a large, spiculated 4 cm right upper lobe mass (Figure 1). It was hypermetabolic with an SUV of 19 on PET CT (Figure 2). Her pulmonary function tests revealed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity without obstruction or restriction. Her FEV1/FVC ratio was 71%. FVC was 90% of predicted at 2.94 L. FEV1 was 83% of predicted at 2.08 L. Her TLC was 94% of predicted at 4.77 L and vital capacity was 90% of predicted at 2.94 L. Her DLCO was 54% of predicted at 12.8.
She underwent a bronchoscopy and EBUS guided needle aspiration of the mass. Pathology revealed a population of CD10 positive lymphocytes suggestive of follicular lymphoma.
A CT guided biopsy was performed to obtain additional tissue for histological and genetic testing. It surprisingly turned out to be negative for lymphoma but instead showed necrotizing pneumonia. There were areas of necrosis with surrounding fibrosis. Neoplastic cells were not identified (Figures 3 and 4). AFB cultures and fungal cultures were negative. Quantiferon, aspergillus galactomannan, histoplasma, blastomyces and coccidioides antibodies were also negative. ANCA serology including MPO (<9 u/mL) and PR3 (<3.5 u/mL) testing was negative. Rheumatoid factor, C3 and C4 were also negative. Her ANA speckled pattern was 250. Her urinalysis had 3+ protein with a normal protein/creatinine ratio. There were no casts. Her BMP and CBC were within normal limits without eosinophilia.
The patient's cough persisted despite conservative treatment with intranasal steroids, cough suppression, and antihistamines. ENT evaluation with nasopharyngolaryngoscopy (NPL) did not reveal upper airway inflammation or ulceration. A repeat CT scan of the thorax showed that the mass was enlarging.
A video assisted thoracoscopy (VAT) with right upper lobectomy was performed. It revealed a right upper lung mass with multiple adhesions to the pleura. The pathology revealed necrotizing granulomas with eosinophils and giant cells. There were no malignant cells, active vasculitis, or organisms found.
The favored diagnosis was granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old female former smoker presented with a 1-year history of dry cough, occasional fatigue, and night sweats and an enlarging 4-cm spiculated right upper lobe lung mass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a dry cough, occasional fatigue, and night sweats 1 year prior to presentation and was initially treated as an outpatient for community-acquired pneumonia. Follow-up chest imaging revealed a persistent, enlarging 4-cm spiculated, hypermetabolic (SUV 19) right upper lobe mass that failed to improve with intranasal corticosteroids, antitussives, and antihistamines.
subjective.past_medical_history: Distant 15 pack-year smoking history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic dry cough, occasional fatigue, and night sweats (1 year); negative for weight loss, hemoptysis, epistaxis, wheezing, arthralgias, hematuria, edema, orthopnea, bruising, alopecia, or recent travel.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs and physical examination were normal on room air; ENT nasopharyngolaryngoscopy showed no upper airway inflammation or mucosal ulceration.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC and BMP were normal without peripheral eosinophilia; urinalysis showed 3+ protein with a normal protein-to-creatinine ratio and no cellular casts. Autoimmune workup showed speckled ANA 1:250 and negative MPO-ANCA (<9 U/mL), PR3-ANCA (<3.5 U/mL), rheumatoid factor, and C3/C4. Pulmonary function tests showed normal spirometry and lung volumes (FEV1/FVC 71%, FVC 2.94 L [90% predicted], FEV1 2.08 L [83%], TLC 4.77 L [94%]) with moderately reduced diffusing capacity (DLCO 12.8 [54% predicted]).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT and PET-CT demonstrated an enlarging 4-cm spiculated right upper lobe mass with intense FDG avidity (SUV 19). QuantiFERON-TB, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides antibodies, and tissue AFB and fungal cultures were all negative. Initial EBUS-TBNA showed CD10+ lymphocytes raising suspicion for follicular lymphoma, whereas CT-guided core biopsy showed only fibrotic necrotizing inflammation without neoplasia. Definitive video-assisted thoracoscopic (VATS) right upper lobectomy demonstrated pleural adhesions and necrotizing granulomas with eosinophils and multinucleated giant cells without malignancy or infectious organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Localized, ANCA-negative pulmonary granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) presenting as a 4-cm hypermetabolic (SUV 19) right upper lobe mass mimicking primary lung malignancy or fungal pneumonia; pulmonary aspergillosis, endemic mycoses, tuberculosis, and follicular lymphoma were excluded by negative Aspergillus galactomannan, fungal/AFB cultures, and VATS right upper lobectomy histopathology confirming necrotizing granulomas with eosinophils and giant cells.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old female patient visited the ear nose and throat department of the local hospital, complaining mainly of headache and dysosmia. She was diagnosed with unilateral paranasal sinusitis by CT and underwent conservative treatment, but she did not show much improvement. Since the MRI reading indicated a nasal tumor, she was referred to our hospital. There was no record of paranasal sinusitis or allergic rhinitis in her medical history. At the initial diagnosis, we confirmed the presence of a substance suggesting allergic mucin of colloidal mucus and a polyp-like lesion in the left paranasal cavity. CT images showed soft-tissue contrast filled in the left maxillary sinus, the left frontal sinus, the left ethmoid sinus, and both sphenoid sinuses, along with bone thinning at the lamina papyracea and the base of the skull (Figures 5(a)-5(c)). MRI showed isosignals in T1-weighted images of the paranasal sinus mucosa and the nasal mucosa, high signals in T2-weighted images of the paranasal sinus and the nasal mucosa, and no signals to low signals at the substance suspected to be allergic mucin (Figures 5(d) and 5(e)).
Hematological findings at the initial diagnosis included 3.5% eosinophil (213.5/muL) and 550 IU/ml nonspecific IgE; as for the allergen-specific IgE, there was 3.1 pg/ml beta-D glucan, and fungi was class 2+, Candida was class 2+, and Aspergillus was class 0. The results of a biopsy conducted on the left nasal polyp at the initial diagnosis showed only inflammatory cell infiltration or partial adhesion of filamentous fungus; we did not confirm evident malignancy.
According to these results, we eliminated the possibility of a malignant tumor and suspected AFS. We therefore performed endoscopic sinus surgery. We removed the polyps at the left nasal/paranasal cavity and cleared the pathway to each of the paranasal sinuses; for the colloidal mucus evident in the nasal/paranasal cavity, we performed a thorough irrigation using the hydrodebrider.
We examined the resected tissue samples to confirm the presence of inflammatory cell infiltration of eosinophil and neutrophil, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and altered mycelia; we also confirmed the presence of calcium oxalate crystals using a polarizing microscope. We performed short-term follow-up treatments of steroid administration and nasal irrigation; as a maintenance therapy, we continued nasal corticosteroid spray and montelukast administration. Subjective symptoms such as headache or dysosmia subsided, and CT images and visual inspection of the nasal cavity have not shown evidence of disease recurrence in the three years since the surgery (Figures 5(f) and 5(g)).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old immunocompetent female presented with chronic headache and dysosmia refractory to conservative sinusitis treatment.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially diagnosed with unilateral paranasal sinusitis by CT at a local ENT clinic, the patient failed conservative therapy and was referred to our hospital after an outside MRI raised suspicion for a sinonasal tumor.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history of paranasal sinusitis or allergic rhinitis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic headache and dysosmia (olfactory dysfunction).

objective.physical_examination: Anterior rhinoscopy/endoscopy revealed a polypoid lesion and thick colloidal allergic mucin in the left nasal and paranasal cavity.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed 3.5% eosinophils (213.5/uL), elevated total non-specific IgE of 550 IU/mL, plasma beta-D-glucan of 3.1 pg/mL (negative), and allergen-specific IgE positive (class 2+) for fungi and Candida and negative (class 0) for Aspergillus.
objective.advanced_workup: Sinus CT demonstrated soft-tissue opacification filling the left maxillary, left frontal, left ethmoid, and bilateral sphenoid sinuses with pressure-induced bony thinning of the left lamina papyracea and skull base. Paranasal sinus MRI showed T1-isointense, T2-hyperintense inflamed sinonasal mucosa surrounding central signal voids/hypointensity corresponding to inspissated allergic mucin. Following endoscopic sinus surgery, polypectomy, and hydrodebrider sinus irrigation, histopathological and polarized-light microscopic examination of the resected mucin and tissue confirmed eosinophilic and neutrophilic infiltration, Charcot-Leyden crystals, degenerated filamentous fungal mycelia, and birefringent calcium oxalate crystals without malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left-sided allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) with skull base and lamina papyracea bone remodeling, confirmed by characteristic CT/MRI central allergic mucin signal voids, elevated total IgE (550 IU/mL) with class 2+ fungal/Candida specific IgE (class 0 Aspergillus IgE), and surgical pathology demonstrating allergic mucin, Charcot-Leyden crystals, filamentous fungal hyphae, and calcium oxalate crystals. Treated with functional endoscopic sinus surgery, hydrodebrider irrigation, a short postoperative oral corticosteroid taper, and maintenance intranasal corticosteroid spray plus oral montelukast, achieving complete resolution of headache and dysosmia with no recurrence over 3 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 93-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to the Internal Medicine Consultation due to cervical adenopathies with 3 months duration. With respect to past medical history, 4 years earlier she had been diagnosed with cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face and submitted to surgical excision. The patient denied having fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss or night sweats; furthermore, there were no respiratory symptoms. She denied having a previous history of tuberculosis (TB) and recent contact with people with known or suspected TB. There was no epidemiological context or contact with animals. On physical examination, an enlarged, mobile and painful right cervical lymph node was evident; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
Cervico-thoraco-abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a right cervical mass (Fig. 1) with multiple adenopathies and some fibrotic lesions in the upper right lobe; there were no other adenopathies nor evidence of neoplastic disease. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the cervical node was performed and yielded a noncaseous granulomatous process. There was no evidence of Reed-Sternberg cells or neoplastic cells; Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative, as well as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assessment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT) and culture. The patient was kept under close surveillance. In the meantime, an IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy was diagnosed; renal function and calcium metabolism were normal, there was no anaemia or elevated urinary free light chains and beta-2 microglobulin was normal. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B cell population. In addition, serology tests for syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus were negative, and QuantiFERON testing was positive. Two months later, the adenopathies had grown and there was cutaneous fistulization with suppurative lymphadenitis (Figs. 2A and 2B).
Microbiologic examination of a suppuration swab was positive for Staphylococcus aureus and the patient was treated with cefuroxime, displaying only slight improvement. An excisional biopsy was programmed and histological examination revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration.
PCR assessment of the samples was negative for MT, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum and Leishmania infantum. Considering the presence of persistent cervical lymphadenopathy with caseous granulomas, a positive QuantiFERON test, and the exclusion of other potential causes, the hypothesis of cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis was strongly suspected, even without a positive PCR test for MT. The patient started presumptive treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Afterwards, diagnostic confirmation was obtained by isolation of MT in one of the lymph node cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing did not demonstrate resistances. The patient presented a favourable clinical outcome with gradual reduction in the size of the adenopathies and there were no side effects attributable to the antituberculous drugs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 93-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of a painful, enlarging right cervical lymph node that subsequently progressed to cutaneous fistulization and purulent drainage.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Referred to internal medicine for a 3-month history of painful right cervical lymphadenopathy without constitutional or respiratory symptoms, the patient initially had a non-caseating granulomatous fine-needle aspiration biopsy with negative AFB stain/PCR. Two months later, the cervical lymph nodes enlarged further and fistulized through the skin with purulent suppuration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face surgically excised 4 years prior; newly identified incidental IgG-lambda monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS); no prior history of tuberculosis, TB contacts, or animal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful right cervical swelling and subsequent cutaneous suppuration; negative for fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam showed an enlarged, mobile, tender right cervical lymph node with an otherwise unremarkable systemic exam; 2 months later, exam showed nodal enlargement with cutaneous fistulization and purulent discharge (scrofula).
objective.routine_investigations: Labs revealed an IgG-lambda monoclonal gammopathy with normal hemoglobin, normal renal function and serum calcium, normal urinary free light chains and beta-2 microglobulin, and polyclonal peripheral blood B-cell immunophenotyping. Serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis were negative, while QuantiFERON-TB testing was positive. Swab culture of the cutaneous fistula drainage grew Staphylococcus aureus (partially improved with cefuroxime).
objective.advanced_workup: Cervico-thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT showed a right cervical necrotic nodal mass with multiple adjacent cervical lymphadenopathies and right upper lobe fibrotic pulmonary scars without distant neoplasia. Initial FNA showed non-caseating granulomas (negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain, MTB PCR, and culture). Subsequent excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrated granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration; although tissue PCR was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, MAC, Nocardia, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum, and Leishmania infantum, mycobacterial culture of the excised lymph node isolated pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula) complicated by secondary Staphylococcus aureus fistula superinfection in a 93-year-old woman; fungal lymphadenitis (including Aspergillus fumigatus), nocardiosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and metastatic malignancy were ruled out by excisional biopsy histopathology and negative multiplex PCRs, and tuberculosis was confirmed by positive QuantiFERON-TB, caseating granulomas on excisional biopsy, and lymph node culture growing pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Treated with standard four-drug antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol), achieving progressive nodal regression without drug-related adverse effects.

raw_case_text:
In July 2015, a 24-year-old woman was referred to our Department of Internal Medicine for a high fever (39 C) lasting 3 days, fatigue, myalgias, chills, and vomiting. She had been followed since 2008 for primary ITP, initially treated with oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), which achieved complete remission. Because of occasional severe relapses (two between 2009 and 2012, with gynecological bleeding), she was subsequently treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg) with good responses. In January 2012, at age 21, she suffered a severe relapse, again justifying the use of IVIg and corticosteroids. At that time, she had detectable autoimmunity with an antinuclear antibody titer of 1 : 250 (anti-SSA specificity but without any sign suggestive of lupus) and platelet-directed anti-glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antibodies. In June 2012 (baseline), a new IVIg cycle was administered, followed by RTX (375 mg/m2 once-a-week for 4 consecutive weeks). A complete platelet response was obtained within 6 weeks and, at the last follow-up (March 2015), her blood platelet level was normal (321 x 109/L) without treatment. Before RTX infusion (June 2012), her blood total gamma-globulin level >3 months before IVIg infusion had been normal (8.9 g/L) but she was lymphopenic (total lymphocytes: 0.513 x 109/L), while her peripheral blood lymphocyte count had been normal at ITP diagnosis (1.199 x 109/L). The previously available phenotype profiles of her peripheral circulating lymphocytes are reported in Table 1. No infection occurred during the 3 years following the last RTX administration and she remained clinically well at biannual consultations in our department.
At admission, in July 2015, at age 24, her temperature was 39.2 C and she complained of lower abdominal pain, vomiting but without diarrhea; her physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP: 114 mg/L, normal range (NR): <5 mg/L), hepatic cytolysis (aspartate aminotransferase: 144 U/L, NR: 7-40 U/L; alanine aminotransferase: 265 U/L, NR: 5-50 U/L) and cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase: 389 IU/L, NR: 40-130 U/L; gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase: 698 U/L, NR: 5-38 U/L). The hemogram revealed agranulocytosis and thrombocytopenia (leukocytes: 4.9 x 109/L; neutrophils: 0.02 x 109/L; hemoglobin: 14.5 g/dL; platelets: 46 x 109/L). Bone-marrow aspirate showed normal density, several megakaryocytes but hypoplastic granulopoiesis in blocked maturation, without blasts. Computed-tomography (CT) scans of the thorax and abdomen were normal. Once urine and blood samples had been collected, empirical ceftazidime and gentamicin were begun, and achieved apyrexia within 48 h. After 46 h, blood cultures came back positive for Campylobacter jejuni, and the identical strain isolated from the patient's feces; amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (1 g 3 times a day for 2 weeks) was prescribed. Seven days postadmission, CRP, neutrophil and platelet levels returned to normal (3 mg/L, 6.61 x 109/L and 521 x 109/L, respectively); blood cultures were negative; and liver function was improved.
Laboratory evaluation for immunodeficiency yielded: negative serology for human immunodeficiency viruses-1 and -2, very low serum Ig levels (Table 1) and no circulating B cells. Flow-cytometry quantification of T-cell subsets found expansion of circulating CD4+ T lymphocytes expressing surface DR, suggesting their activation; low natural killer cells and CD8+ T-lymphocyte levels. Urine immunofixation electrophoresis was negative. Ig-replacement therapy was started but not pursued by the patient.
Ten months later (May 2016, age 25) she was hospitalized for a 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. CRP, lactate dehydrogenase and beta2-microglobulin levels were 40 mg/L, 340 U/L (NR 5-240 U/L) and 3.53 mg/L (NR 1.2-2.5 mg/L), respectively. As shown in Table 1, hypogammaglobulinemia, CD19+ B lymphopenia and low peripheral CD8+ T-cell count persisted but without T activation, as assessed by HLADR-positivity. CT scans visualized bilateral diffuse infiltrates, ground-glass opacities and large nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis revealed Pneumocystis jiroveci cysts with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (4,000 copies/mL); high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids were prescribed. Searches for other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, Cryptococcus and Aspergillus species, were negative. At that time, her bone-marrow biopsy was normal.
Despite appropriate antibiotics and clinical improvement, thoracic CT scans revealed worsened dense infiltrates (Figure 1(a)), pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly and nodular lesions of both kidneys (Figure 1(b)). A new bronchoscopy with biopsies found CD20+ large lymphomatous cell infiltration (Figure 2) in bronchi. Those large atypical lymphoid tumor cells were CD10-BCL-6- and MUM1+BCL-2+, with an 80% Ki-67-proliferation index on immunolabeling. EBV, as assessed by in situ hybridization with an EBV-encoded small RNA probe, was diffusely positive in about 80% of tumor cells (Figure 2). The FISH assay for MYC gene rearrangement (MYC FISH DNA Probe, Split Signal, (Y5410), Dako, Locus 8q24) was negative. EBV-positive DLBCL with a nongerminal center phenotype was diagnosed without bone-marrow infiltration. Circulating EBV-DNA was positive (2,430,000 IU/mL). DLBCL treatment consisted of RTX, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone. Even with EB viremia becoming negative, she developed fever, cytopenias, liver damage and neurological manifestations, as a consequence of her prominent bone-marrow hemophagocytosis. Unfortunately, she died of multiorgan failure at age 25.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old woman with primary immune thrombocytopenia treated with rituximab 3 years earlier presented with a 3-day history of high fever (39.2 C), chills, myalgias, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain, followed 10 months later by a 15-day history of low-grade fever, weight loss, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having achieved a 3-year complete remission of primary ITP after four weekly rituximab infusions (375 mg/m2) in June 2012, the patient presented in July 2015 (age 24) with 3 days of high fever, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain due to Campylobacter jejuni bacteremia/enteritis in the setting of agranulocytosis, complete B-cell aplasia, and severe hypogammaglobulinemia (declining long-term IVIg). Ten months later (May 2016, age 25), she was readmitted with 15 days of fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and progressive dyspnea; despite treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, she developed worsening pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral renal nodules.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) diagnosed in 2008 (positive anti-GPIIb/IIIa and ANA 1:250 with anti-SSA specificity), treated with corticosteroids, repeated IVIg courses, and rituximab (4 weekly doses of 375 mg/m2 in June 2012) with baseline pre-rituximab lymphopenia (0.513 x 10^9/L).
subjective.review_of_systems: July 2015 admission: high fever, chills, fatigue, myalgias, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain without diarrhea. May 2016 admission: 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and progressive dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: July 2015 admission: temperature 39.2 C with normal physical examination. May 2016 admission: developed hepatosplenomegaly, pleural effusions, and subsequent neurological manifestations during hemophagocytic syndrome.
objective.routine_investigations: July 2015 labs showed CRP 114 mg/L (<5), AST 144 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, ALP 389 IU/L, GGT 698 U/L, WBC 4.9 x 10^9/L with agranulocytosis (ANC 0.02 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 46 x 10^9/L, bone marrow granulocytic maturation block, positive blood and stool cultures for Campylobacter jejuni, negative HIV-1/2 serology, profound pan-hypogammaglobulinemia, absent circulating CD19+ B cells, low NK and CD8+ T cells, and expanded HLA-DR+ CD4+ T cells. May 2016 labs showed CRP 40 mg/L, LDH 340 U/L, beta-2 microglobulin 3.53 mg/L, persistent hypogammaglobulinemia and B-cell aplasia, high plasma EBV-DNA viral load (2,430,000 IU/mL), and subsequent prominent bone marrow hemophagocytosis.
objective.advanced_workup: May 2016 thoracic CT initially showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and large nodules; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) detected Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and DNA (4,000 copies/mL) while testing negative for Aspergillus species, Cryptococcus, CMV, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and atypical mycobacteria. Follow-up thoracic and abdominal CT scans showed worsening dense pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral renal cortical nodules. Repeat bronchoscopy with endobronchial biopsy established non-germinal-center EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (CD20+, CD10-, BCL-6-, MUM1+, BCL-2+, Ki-67 80%, EBER-ISH positive in ~80% of tumor cells, MYC FISH negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Prolonged post-rituximab B-cell aplasia and severe hypogammaglobulinemia complicated sequentially by Campylobacter jejuni septicemia with agranulocytosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (with Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, CMV, and mycobacterial co-infections excluded on BAL), and fatal non-germinal-center EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Campylobacter sepsis resolved with ceftazidime/gentamicin and amoxicillin-clavulanate, and PJP responded to high-dose TMP-SMX and corticosteroids; however, despite R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy clearing plasma EBV-DNA, the patient died of hemophagocytosis-induced multiorgan failure at age 25.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old male with no significant medical history presented with shortness of breath and flu-like symptoms including generalized weakness, fatigue, chills, diaphoresis, fever, and cough. The patient denied any recent sick contacts, travel history, history of shortness of breath, or history of lung disease. The patient reported only smoking conventional marijuana for 20 plus years, smoking 2 to 3 times per day, and had approximately a 4-6-month history of vape pen usage, with and without flavor additives. The cannabis vape pens were purchased in bulk from an informal source. The patient reported a less than 1-year history of conventional cigarette use and quit over 20 years ago. He denied the use of chewing tobacco, electronic cigarettes containing nicotine, or any other nicotine-containing products during this time.
On arrival, the patient was afebrile with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation was 96% on ambient air, blood pressure was 126/82 mmHg, and heart rate was 96 beats per minute. Over the next 4 hours, the patient rapidly deteriorated into acute hypoxic respiratory failure with hypoxia down to 86% while on 2 liters nasal cannula. The patient was increased to 13 liters high-flow nasal cannula, started on empiric antibiotics, and intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg which corrected the hypoxia with sustained oxygen saturation of 94%.
Physical exam was remarkable for diaphoresis, tachypnea, labored breathing with accessory muscle use, and diffuse inspiratory crackles. An arterial blood gas showed a pH of 7.51 [7.35-7.45], pCO2 38 [35-45 mmHg], pO2 84 [80-100 mmHg], and HCO3 of 30.3 mmol/L [22-26 mmol/L]. Lab work showed a venous lactic acidosis at 2.3 mmol/L [0.9-1.7 mmol/L], white blood cell count of 14.8 x 103/mul [4.4 - 10.5 x 103/mul], and a normal sedimentation rate. Chest X-ray noted diffuse, bilateral pulmonary consolidation sparing the apices, and bases with bronchopulmonary cuffing (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed extensive bilateral airspace disease with increased reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and ground glass opacities but noted sparing of apical spaces bilaterally (Figure 2).
Further lab work including blood and sputum cultures, HIV, urine Histoplasma, Legionella, Pneumococcal antigens, and respiratory viral panel were all negative. Serologies:coccidiomycosis, histoplasmosis, and pneumocystis:were also negative. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsies were performed and a sample from the right lower lobe was significant for intra-alveolar inflammation including foamy macrophages and activated type II pneumocytes (Figure 3). These findings were consistent with organizing pneumonia. A histopathology examination on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sample stained with Oil red O showed numerous lipid-laden macrophages and intra-alveolar macrophages containing blackish-brown pigment (Figure 4). This was consistent with a diagnosis of lipoid pneumonia. Additional testing was negative for AFB stain, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex antigen, and aspergillus antigen. During the hospital course, the patient improved over a six-day regimen of bronchodilators, steroids, and empiric antibiotics with supportive care of oxygen supplementation. He was discharged on the same regimen for 14 days with follow-up with pulmonology and repeat CT imaging in six weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, diaphoresis, cough, and generalized weakness after 4 to 6 months of using informal-source cannabis vape pens.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: With no baseline pulmonary disease, the patient presented with acute dyspnea, cough, fever, chills, diaphoresis, and fatigue following 4-6 months of vaping cannabis cartridges (with and without flavor additives) purchased in bulk from an informal source. Within 4 hours of emergency department arrival, his oxygen saturation dropped from 96% on ambient air to 86% on 2 L/min nasal cannula, requiring escalation to 13 L/min high-flow nasal cannula.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history; 20+ year history of smoking conventional marijuana (2-3 times/day) and a 4-6 month history of using informal-market cannabis vape pens; quit conventional cigarettes >20 years ago (<1 year use) and denied nicotine e-cigarette use, recent travel, or sick contacts.
