24-year-old male patient had pungent-stinging chest pain with shortness of breath. His history revealed that he had many cats and dogs as pets in his house. His cardiovascular system examination revealed "decreased" heart sounds. Heart beats were coming from deep inside and barely heard. There were also barely heard respiratory sounds in his right lung and middle and basal segments. Other system examinations were normal. Vital signs were stable. There was no pathological finding in his electrocardiography. Teleradiography revealed enlarged mediastinum, closed right sinus, displacement of apex more superiorly and to the left side. When we looked more carefully, we noticed that extraspur at apex was not a solid mass. Instead, it was a kind of a radiolucent tissue (Figure 1). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed cystic structure with mobile-scolex inside. Diameter of cyst was 2.5 x 2.4 cm at the anterolateral section of left ventricle. Fibrinous pericardial effusion was also noticed within pericardial sac (Figure 2).
 Thorough examination of thoracoabdominal computerized tomography revealed 4.5 x 5 cm cystic mass inside heart apex, together with 2.5 cm pericardial effusion (Figure 3). There were no other cysts in lungs or liver. Final diagnosis was myocardial hydatid cyst. Treatment would be surgical so we decided our operative strategy. We performed median sternotomy and aortobicaval cannulation. During the operation, antegrade blood cardioplegic solution was administered. Systemic and topical cooling (with isotonic) was also performed. Approximately, 600 cc inflammatory and fibrinous pericardial effusion was aspirated. 1200 cc serous effusion was aspirated from right hemithorax. The cystic mass appeared to be limited between left anterior descending (LAD) artery and diagonal 2 arteries. It was not extending into cardiac cavities. It was also adherent or sticking to pericardium (Figure 4). For pathological examination and culture-antibiogram, the ingredients and content of cystical mass was aspirated with an injector. 7 cc purulent effusion was taken into injector. Then, we injected 8 cc hypertonic saline solution into cyst. We cautiously used green sterile covers with holes throughout the operation in order to prevent contamination. We used gauze-pads with povidone-iodine all around the operative site.
 We opened the cystic mass with oblique incision. We observed germinative membrane and 15 small-to-large daughter vesicles which were having different colors and shapes. We excised the cyst from myocardium together with its sticky capsule. Myocardial cavity was washed thoroughly with hypertonic saline solution. Then, we used teflon patch (felt) and sutured myocardial cavity using pledged-U-sutures. We protected the shape and appearance (geometry) of ventricle. Laboratory results revealed no reproduction at culture-antibiogram. Pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of hydatid cyst both macroscopically and microscopically. Germinative membrane, cuticular membrane, and eosinophilic inflammation were detected (Figure 5). Preoperatively started (10 mg/kg/day) albendazol treatment was continued for 4 weeks even after the operation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presented with pungent, stinging chest pain and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for evaluation of stinging chest pain accompanied by dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Kept multiple cats and dogs as household pets.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for stinging chest pain and shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were stable. Cardiovascular auscultation revealed distant, muffled heart sounds, and respiratory auscultation revealed markedly diminished breath sounds over the right middle and basal lung fields. Other systemic examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: ECG was normal. Chest teleradiography showed an enlarged mediastinum, blunted right costophrenic sinus, and superior/leftward displacement of the cardiac apex with a radiolucent apical contour. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a 2.5 x 2.4 cm cystic structure containing a mobile scolex in the anterolateral left ventricular wall along with a fibrinous pericardial effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracoabdominal CT demonstrated a 4.5 x 5 cm cystic mass within the left ventricular cardiac apex and a 2.5-cm pericardial effusion, without pulmonary or hepatic cysts. Median sternotomy under cardiopulmonary bypass evacuated 600 mL of fibrinous pericardial effusion, 1,200 mL of right pleural serous effusion, and an apical intramyocardial cyst located between the LAD and second diagonal coronary arteries containing 7 mL of purulent fluid, a germinative membrane, and 15 daughter vesicles (bacterial culture was sterile; histopathology confirmed germinative membrane, cuticular membrane, and eosinophilic inflammation).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary isolated left ventricular apical myocardial hydatid cyst complicated by fibrinous pericardial effusion and right pleural effusion, confirmed by TTE visualization of a mobile scolex and postoperative histopathology showing germinative and cuticular membranes. Under cardiopulmonary bypass, the cyst was aspirated, injected with 8 mL hypertonic saline, excised with its pericystic capsule, and reconstructed using felt-pledgeted U-sutures, accompanied by preoperative and 4-week postoperative oral albendazole (10 mg/kg/day).

raw_case_text:
A 22-year-old female, farmer by occupation, presented with complaints of chest pain and progressive weakness of left lower limb that had persisted for 3 months. There was no history of fever, weight loss, or trauma. The general physical examination was unremarkable. Respiratory system examination revealed dullness on percussion and tenderness in left infraclavicular, suprascapular, and interscapular regions. The routine laboratory investigations were normal.
Radiographs of chest, performed in posterior-anterior (PA) and lateral projections, demonstrated well-defined homogenous soft tissue opacity in the posterior mediastinum. There was erosion of the 4th rib posteriorly, scalloping of superior margin of 5th rib, and widened fourth intercostal space [Figure 1a and b]. Contrast enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the thorax revealed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic mass in the left paravertebral space, extending into the spinal canal by causing erosion of the adjoining pedicle and lamina of fourth thoracic vertebra. There was erosion of the overlying 4th rib with scalloping of the 5th rib and widened intervening intercostal space [Figures 2 and 3].
Based on the imaging findings, the possible differential diagnosis included neurogenic tumors, aggressive malignant masses like round cell tumors (Ewing's sarcoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumors, and others), lymphoma, or metastasis. Since the mass was predominantly cystic with multiloculated appearance and considering the occupation of the patient, hydatid cyst was also considered a possible differential diagnosis.
The serological test with enzyme linked immunosorbant assay (ELISA) was positive for echinococcosis, thus suggesting hydatid cyst as a possible etiology. The patient was operated and the cystic mass along with the involved 4th rib were completely excised. The diagnosis was confirmed macroscopically preoperatively and by histopathological studies postoperatively. Postoperative recovery was uneventful and the patient was discharged and put on adjuvant chemotherapy with mebendazole for 2 years. The patient was monitored with routine follow-ups for 5 years with no evidence of recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old female farmer presented with a 3-month history of chest pain and progressive left lower limb weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed persistent chest pain and progressively worsening weakness of her left lower extremity over 3 months without fever, weight loss, or trauma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Worked as a farmer; no history of trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chest pain and progressive left lower limb weakness; negative for fever or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: General physical examination was unremarkable; chest examination revealed dullness to percussion and local tenderness over the left infraclavicular, suprascapular, and interscapular regions.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were normal. Echinococcus IgG ELISA serology was positive. PA and lateral chest radiographs demonstrated a well-defined homogeneous posterior mediastinal opacity with posterior erosion of the left 4th rib, superior margin scalloping of the 5th rib, and widening of the 4th intercostal space.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed a well-defined multiloculated cystic mass in the left paravertebral posterior mediastinum eroding the left 4th rib, scalloping the 5th rib, and extending through the eroded T4 pedicle and lamina into the spinal canal. Complete surgical excision of the cystic mass and involved 4th rib with macroscopic and histopathological evaluation confirmed a hydatid cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary posterior mediastinal paravertebral hydatid cyst with rib erosion and T4 intraspinal extradural extension, confirmed by positive Echinococcus ELISA and postoperative histopathology (ruling out neurogenic tumor, Ewing sarcoma/PNET, lymphoma, and metastasis). Following complete surgical excision of the cyst and involved 4th rib, the patient received adjuvant oral mebendazole for 2 years and remained recurrence-free over 5 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 20 kg, 7-year-old girl with history of recurrent hemoptysis was scheduled for thoracoscopic excision of a pulmonary hydatid cyst. Chest X-ray revealed a 4 cm homogenous opacity in lower lobe of left lung. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography chest revealed 3-4 cm well-defined hypodense lesion in lower lobe of left lung. ELISA test for a hydatid cyst was positive. All other relevant investigations were within normal limits. The patient had taken multiple courses of albendazole for the same.
Single lung ventilation with 3.5 mm ID Uninvent tube (for 6-8 years) was planned. A 20 G venous access was taken in the dorsum of left hand. Electrokardiograph, noninvasive blood pressure, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2), and capnography monitoring was initiated.
The patient was administered fentanyl 40 mcg and hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously (IV). Pheniramine maleate 34.125 mg was given intramuscularly. After preoxygenation for 3 min, anesthesia was induced with propofol 40 mg and vecuronium 2 mg IV. The trachea was intubated with the 3.5 mm ID Univent tube and lung ventilation was confirmed. The bronchial blocker was guided into the left bronchus under fiberoptic guidance for isolating the two lungs. The patient was positioned in the right lateral position. Tube position and lung isolation were reconfirmed clinically by auscultation and fiberoptically. Anesthesia was maintained with an oxygen-nitrous oxide inhalation mixture (1:1) with isoflurane <=1% and supplemental IV doses of fentanyl and vecuronium.
While creating pneumothorax there was sudden fall of SpO2 from 98% to 56% with bradycardia (heart rate dropped from 110 to 46/min) and bloody discharges appeared in the Univent tube. Airway pressures increased from 18 cm to 35 cm. Pneumothorax was released, atropine 0.4 mg IV was given, 100% oxygen administered and tube suction done. SpO2 improved to 98-99% and heart rate increased to 130/min. Patient's blood pressure remained stable. Anaphylaxis and contra-lateral pneumothorax was ruled out clinically. On chest auscultation, there was decreased air entry on the right side and air entry was present on the left side.
Anticipating a displaced bronchial blocker patient's position was made supine and flexible fiberscopy was done which showed fluid with membranes along with a displaced bronchial blocker in the trachea. Suctioning was done through the flexible fiberscope suction channel but membranes could not be removed. The Univent tube was withdrawn and rigid bronchoscopy was performed with 4.5 mm pediatric ventilating bronchoscope. About 20-25 ml of fluid with flakes of membrane was removed by forceps, bronchoalveolar lavage, and suction [Figures 1 and 2]. After bronchoscopy, trachea was reintubated with a 6 mm ID uncuffed endotracheal tube.
Patient$s vital parameters remained stable. At the end of procedure, the patient was shifted to ICU for elective ventilation. Postoperative chest X-ray was normal. The trachea was extubated the next day and the patient was discharged home on the 7th postoperative day. Histopathological examination of membranes was of suggestive of a hydatid cyst.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old girl weighing 20 kg with a history of recurrent hemoptysis presented for scheduled thoracoscopic excision of a left lower lobe pulmonary cyst.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child had a history of recurrent hemoptysis and had received multiple courses of oral albendazole after imaging and serology identified a left lower lobe pulmonary hydatid cyst, and was admitted for elective thoracoscopic excision.
subjective.past_medical_history: Multiple prior courses of oral albendazole for a known left lower lobe pulmonary hydatid cyst.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent hemoptysis. Prior medication: oral albendazole.

objective.physical_examination: Weight 20 kg; baseline vital signs were stable (SpO2 98%, heart rate 110/min). During intraoperative induction of left pneumothorax in the right lateral decubitus position, she developed acute desaturation (SpO2 dropping from 98% to 56%), bradycardia (46/min), elevated peak airway pressure (35 cm H2O), bloody endotracheal tube discharge, and absent right-sided breath sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative routine labs were normal, Echinococcus ELISA was positive, and chest X-ray showed a 4-cm homogeneous opacity in the left lower lung lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative chest CECT demonstrated a 3-4 cm well-defined hypodense cystic lesion in the left lower lobe. Intraoperative flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy and urgent rigid bronchoscopy (4.5-mm pediatric bronchoscope) revealed intratracheal rupture/spillage of hydatid fluid and laminated membrane flakes with displacement of the 3.5-mm Univent bronchial blocker into the trachea, occluding the right main bronchus; 20-25 mL of fluid and pearly membranes were evacuated via forceps, bronchoalveolar lavage, and suction, and histopathology of the retrieved membranes confirmed a hydatid cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Left lower lobe pulmonary hydatid cyst complicated by intraoperative endobronchial rupture and contralateral right mainstem bronchus occlusion by laminated membranes and a displaced Univent bronchial blocker during one-lung ventilation, confirmed by positive ELISA and histopathology of bronchoscopically extracted membranes. Following urgent rigid bronchoscopic extraction of the membranes, reintubation with a 6-mm uncuffed endotracheal tube, and overnight ICU ventilation, the child was extubated on postoperative day 1 with a normal chest X-ray and discharged on postoperative day 7.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old female patient presented with complaints of fever, breathlessness, dull-aching, continuous pain, and dragging sensation on the left side of the abdomen since 3 months. Also, there was history of loss of weight and appetite. Past history was insignificant. On examination, abdomen was slightly distended with a palpable mass reaching up to the umbilicus, 6-7 cm from the left costal margin. The mass was tender, firm, irregular and fingers could not be insinuated below the ribs. A systemic examination was normal. Routine investigations revealed leucocytosis (Total leukocyte count=12,000/mm3) with eosinophilia (7%, absolute eosinophil count=840/mm3) and raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (35 mm in first hour). An X-ray study of both abdomen and chest was found to be normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed enlarged spleen with multiple cystic areas, together measuring 18x15x11 cm. [Figure 1]. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed a large mass measuring 17.5x15x10 cm, containing air fluid levels and heterogeneous contents with predominant low-density areas, elevating left dome of the diaphragm [Figure 2]. Other abdominal organs were found to be normal. Therefore, the clinical diagnosis of the cystic lesion of spleen was made.
Left subcostal exploratory laparotomy was performed revealing huge cystic mass occupying lower pole of spleen. Splenectomy was performed and sent for HPE. Tab. Mebendazole 200 mg/kg/day was started on fifth post operative day and continued after surgery for three months.
Grossly, the splenectomy specimen measured 17x14x10 cm. The posterior aspect showed a cystic cavity having a white and smooth cyst wall, filled with multiple, variable-sized daughter cysts in a flower-shaped arrangement [Figure 3]. The hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained slides showed a cyst wall comprising of three layers [Figure 4]. The cystic contents consisted of mixture of multiple infolded membranes, fragmented hooklets, and debris which were part of hydatid sand. Multiple scolices of Echinococcus granulosus were also seen [Figure 5]. Definitive diagnosis of a hydatid cyst was, hence, made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old female presented with a 3-month history of fever, breathlessness, continuous dull left abdominal pain, a left upper quadrant dragging sensation, anorexia, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced continuous dull aching pain and a dragging sensation on the left side of the abdomen accompanied by fever, breathlessness, loss of appetite, and weight loss for 3 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, dyspnea, left abdominal pain/dragging sensation, anorexia, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Abdomen was slightly distended with a tender, firm, irregular mass extending 6-7 cm below the left costal margin to the umbilicus (fingers could not be insinuated beneath the left costal margin); systemic examination was otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed leukocytosis (TLC 12,000/mm3), eosinophilia (7%; absolute eosinophil count 840/mm3), and elevated ESR (35 mm in the 1st hour). Chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed massive splenomegaly containing multiple cystic areas measuring 18 x 15 x 11 cm overall.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT demonstrated a 17.5 x 15 x 10 cm heterogeneous cystic splenic mass containing air-fluid levels and low-density areas elevating the left hemidiaphragm, with normal remaining abdominal viscera. Following left subcostal laparotomy and total splenectomy, gross pathology (17 x 14 x 10 cm specimen) showed a smooth white posterior cyst cavity filled with flower-arranged daughter cysts, and H&E microscopy confirmed a three-layered cyst wall, hydatid sand, fragmented hooklets, and multiple Echinococcus granulosus scolices.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary giant infected splenic hydatid cyst (17.5 x 15 x 10 cm), definitively confirmed by histopathological identification of a three-layered cyst wall, fragmented hooklets, and Echinococcus granulosus scolices. The patient underwent open total splenectomy and completed a 3-month postoperative course of oral mebendazole (started on postoperative day 5).

raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old woman was admitted suffering from constant mild pain in the right hypochondrium reflecting to the epigastrium; and often accompanied by nausea during the previous 6 months. There was no history of fever or jaundice. The physical examination didn't show abnormal abdominal signs except tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Routine blood tests proved unremarkable. Plain abdominal X-rays was normal. The ultrasound examination showed that her gallbladder was deformed with a localised thickening of its wall (Figure 1). There was no image of gallstone.
To eliminate gallbladder neoplasm; a CT abdominal scan was performed showing inflammatory gallbladder wall which is free of suspect lesions (Figure 2). Against this diagnosis difficulty; it has been decided to practice a magnetic resonance abdominal imaging. This examination showed many daughter cysts in the lumen of the gallbladder (Figure 3-A, B); while hepatic parenchyma proved absolutely normal (Figure 3-C)
Antiechinococcal antibodies were not found in serum. The diagnosis of primary hydatid cyst of gallbladder was supported and surgery has been decided. The patient underwent right subcostal laparotomy. Intraoperatively it has been found a cyst of the body of the gallbladder which is inflammatory and deformed. No other cysts were found in the liver and peritoneal cavity. A cholecystectomy was performed. It permitted a total removal of the cyst without rupture. A preoperative cholangiography searching daughter cysts in the common bile duct proved unremarkable (Figure 4). The patient's postoperative course was uneventful and she was discharged in the fourth postoperative day. The histopathology confirmed the presence of hydatid cyst of the gallbladder (Figure 5). At six month follow up, the patient has had no recurrence of hydatid disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of constant mild right hypochondriac pain radiating to the epigastrium accompanied by nausea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced constant mild right upper quadrant pain radiating to the epigastrium and frequently associated with nausea over the preceding 6 months, without fever or jaundice.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right hypochondriac/epigastric pain and nausea; negative for fever or jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination showed right upper quadrant tenderness without other abnormal findings.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests, serum anti-echinococcal antibody serology, and plain abdominal radiographs were normal/negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a deformed gallbladder with localized wall thickening and no gallstones.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT showed an inflammatory thickened gallbladder wall without focal hepatic lesions. Abdominal MRI demonstrated numerous daughter cysts filling the gallbladder lumen with completely normal hepatic parenchyma. Right subcostal laparotomy with intact cholecystectomy and unremarkable intraoperative cholangiography (showing no common bile duct daughter cysts) was performed, and histopathology confirmed a primary hydatid cyst of the gallbladder.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary isolated hydatid cyst of the gallbladder, confirmed by MRI visualization of intraluminal daughter cysts and postoperative histopathology despite negative serum anti-echinococcal antibodies (ruling out gallbladder carcinoma). The patient underwent open cholecystectomy without rupture, was discharged on postoperative day 4, and had no recurrence at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A fifteen year old girl referred to our institute for complaints of colicky pain in right lumbar region and dysuria with passage of small pale ruptured-grape like structures in urine for the last 6 months. Her general physical examinations and routine investigations were in normal limits. Ultrasonography of abdomen was suggestive of multiloculated cystic lesion, with typical spoke-wheel appearance, in the mid pole of right kidney and ELISA test was positive for echinococcus antibodies. CT scan obtained which revealed 11.5 cm X 11.0 cm multiseptated cystic lesion in mid and lower pole of right kidney and upper ureter with typical "cyst within the cyst" appearance (Fig. 1), without any contrast excretion from right kidney. With four weeks of albendazole therapy, surgical exploration done by flank extraperitoneal approach and right nephroureterectomy done as almost entire kidney was converted into a bag of cysts with multiple cysts filled up in the upper ureter as well (Fig. 2). Postoperatively, patient was put on albendazole (10 mg/kg daily) for eight weeks. Histopathological examination was consistent with hydatid disease. Follow-up ultrasound abdomen at 6 months showed no recurrence.
Renal hydatid cysts primarily develop when the larvae, which are not filtered in the liver, pass through the pulmonary circulation and travel to the kidney.[1] Presenting symptoms depend on the kind of cyst. Closed cyst that contains all 3 layers, pericyst, ectocyst, and endocyst, usually remain asymptomatic unless large enough to stretch renal capsule. Once the pericyst is lost, exposed cyst expands rapidly and presents as chronic dull flank pain. In communicating cysts, all the three layers of the cyst rupture with direct communication into the collecting system, causing hydatiduria and acute colic or obstruction but it is seen in only 10-20% of renal hydatidosis and is usually microscopic in nature.[1, 2]
There is no pathognomonic serological test for hydatid disease. Sonography is a sensitive method for the detection of membranes, septa, and hydatid sand within the cyst. Gharbi et al classified them into five types.[3] Present case, as having multiseptated daughter cysts, is a Type III cyst. Contrary to this, the most common variety reported in different paediatric series are Type I cysts, that have appearance of simple renal cysts but with double-contoured thick wall and hydatid sand as "falling snowflakes" [2, 3]. The CT scan has a higher accuracy and sensitivity to demonstrate the cyst wall and the daughter cysts.
Medical management with oral albendazole alone, is mostly unreliable and radiological intervention in the form of Percutaneous Aspiration Injection Re-aspiration followed by Percutaneous drainage (PAIR-PD) has limited success in only 70% of cases of unilocular cysts with vested fear of spillage and anaphylactic shock.[1, 4] Surgery remains the mainstay of treatment and a variety of surgical procedures are tailored to suit individual cases. Kidney sparing surgery i.e. marsupialization, closed total cystectomy, partial pericystectomy, or capitonnage with or without omentoplasty are possible in most (75%) cases.[1, 5] In other 25% cases, where the kidney is almost destroyed, nephrectomy is the only option.[1,2] In recent years, laparoscopic approach has also been used, but, the major problem with large renal hydatid cysts is the spillage of contents during dissection and the extent of the incision for the delivery of specimen.[1] Pre and postoperative one-month courses of albendazole should be considered in order to sterilize the cyst and to decrease the tension in the cyst wall that reduces the risk of spillage during surgery.[2] Though treatment is mostly surgical, it must be individualized.
Source of Support: Nil
Conflict of Interest: None declared

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of colicky right lumbar pain, dysuria, and passage of pale ruptured-grape-like structures in her urine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced recurrent colicky right flank pain, dysuria, and gross hydatiduria (passage of small pale grape-like structures in the urine) for 6 months prior to referral.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for colicky right lumbar pain, dysuria, and gross hydatiduria.

objective.physical_examination: General and systemic physical examinations were within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were normal. Serum Echinococcus antibody ELISA was positive. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a multiloculated cystic lesion with a typical spoke-wheel appearance (Gharbi type III) in the mid-pole of the right kidney.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT demonstrated an 11.5 x 11.0 cm multiseptated cystic lesion in the mid and lower poles of the right kidney and upper ureter with a classic cyst-within-cyst appearance and absent contrast excretion from the right kidney. Extraperitoneal flank exploration and right nephroureterectomy revealed the entire right kidney converted into a bag of cysts with multiple daughter cysts filling the upper ureter; histopathology confirmed renal hydatid disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary right renal and ureteric cystic echinococcosis (Gharbi type III) presenting with gross hydatiduria and a non-functioning right kidney, confirmed by positive Echinococcus ELISA and histopathological examination of the right nephroureterectomy specimen. The patient received 4 weeks of preoperative oral albendazole, underwent right nephroureterectomy, and completed 8 weeks of postoperative albendazole (10 mg/kg/day), with no recurrence on 6-month follow-up abdominal ultrasound.

raw_case_text:
We present a case of a 42-year-old man already operated 10 years ago for CE of the liver and 3 years ago for mediastinal and primary spinal disease involvement.
He comes to our attention in 2010 after access to our emergency department for progressive paraparesis since 1 week with inability to walk, level of anesthesia below D2 associated with worsening and marked sphincter disorders, and pain associated with cervical-dorsal refractory to analgesic therapy.
Computed tomography (CT) (Figure 1) demonstrated cystic tissue localized to the mediastinum and the paravertebral muscles with the erosion of the second rib and the vertebral bodies of D1 and D2.
Cervicodorsal spine MRI with intravenous injection of gadolinium (Figure 2) showed multiple and heterogeneous lesions located in the intraspinal extradural space at D1-D2 level, with severe spinal cord compression and involvement of the transverse processes, spinous processes, the left laminae, the second rib, the mediastinum on the right side, and cervical paraspinal muscles from C4 to D2. The patient was subsequently treated with an anthelmintic drug (Albendazole) and steroid therapy for the neurologic deficit. The patient underwent a first surgical approach by right sided paramedian longitudinal incision from C4 to D2 with the removal of the hydatid cyst (2 x 5 cm) located within the paraspinal muscle (Figure 3(a)); the second surgical approach was performed in the same surgical procedure to remove numerous smaller hydatid cysts (Figure 3(b)) with a median posterior approach, performing decompressive laminectomy and spinal stabilization from C6 to D4 with Universal Clamp Spinal Fixation System-Zimmer (Figure 4).
MRI performed after surgery showed the persistence of a small cyst located in the body of D2. It was decided with the thoracic surgeon to remove the small residual cyst during surgery for the removal of mediastinal cysts, with an anterior approach; however, the patient refused the thoracic surgery.
Three years later (in 2013) after he voluntary stopped medical treatment, the patient develops a rapid worsening of spinal deficits with motor deficit predominantly on the right side with progressive paraparesis, neuralgiform distal pain, marked sphincter disorders, and lack of peripherical sensitivity.
CT (Figure 5) and MRI with intravenous injection of gadolinium (Figure 6) showed a recurrence of multiple intraspinal extradural cystic lesions, with the spinal cord compression involving the body of D2 and minimally the body of D1. The patient will undergo a second surgical procedure of decompression of the spinal cord, removing the recurred cysts and maintaining the spinal stabilization system. The patient recovered successfully and was able to walk autonomously on the fifth day after surgery. Later the patient began treatment with anthelmintic drug (Albendazole), with stability of the pathology until today.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old man with prior hepatic, mediastinal, and spinal echinococcosis presented with a 1-week history of progressive paraparesis, inability to walk, sensory loss below T2, sphincter dysfunction, and refractory cervicodorsal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department in 2010 with 1 week of rapidly progressive paraparesis resulting in inability to ambulate, a T2 sensory anesthesia level, severe bladder/bowel sphincter dysfunction, and analgesic-refractory cervicodorsal pain. After surgical decompression and voluntary discontinuation of albendazole, he re-presented 3 years later (2013) with recurrent right-predominant paraparesis, distal neuropathic pain, sphincter dysfunction, and sensory loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Operated 10 years earlier for hepatic cystic echinococcosis and 3 years earlier for mediastinal and primary spinal hydatid disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for paraparesis, gait inability, T2 sensory level, sphincter disorders, and severe cervicodorsal/radicular pain.

objective.physical_examination: Severe paraparesis with inability to walk, sensory anesthesia level below D2 (T2), and sphincter dysfunction.
objective.advanced_workup: In 2010, cervicothoracic CT and gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed cystic lesions in the right mediastinum and C4-T2 paravertebral muscles with erosion of the 2nd rib and T1-T2 vertebral bodies, multiple intraspinal extradural cysts at T1-T2 causing severe spinal cord compression, and involvement of the transverse/spinous processes and left laminae. Combined right paramedian (excising a 2 x 5 cm paraspinal hydatid cyst) and posterior midline decompressive laminectomy (excising multiple extradural cysts with C6-T4 Universal Clamp stabilization) left a small residual T2 vertebral body cyst after the patient declined anterior thoracic surgery. In 2013, repeat CT and contrast MRI demonstrated recurrent intraspinal extradural hydatid cysts at T1-T2 compressing the spinal cord.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Recurrent cervicothoracic intraspinal extradural, vertebral (T1-T2), paraspinal, and mediastinal cystic echinococcosis causing recurrent spinal cord compression. In 2010, the patient underwent two-stage paraspinal cystectomy, C6-T4 decompressive laminectomy with posterior instrumentation, corticosteroids, and oral albendazole; following relapse in 2013 after self-discontinuing albendazole, he underwent repeat posterior spinal cord decompression while maintaining the spinal fixation system, regained independent ambulation by postoperative day 5, and remained stable on long-term albendazole.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 20-year-old female from north of Iran without any previous history of lung or liver disease presented with complaints of right upper quadrant and right side chest pain, cough and a low grade fever for the past one month. Her coughing and pain were persistent.
Upon physical examination, her vital signs were normal. However, her oxygen saturation rate reduced to 96% in room air. Chest and abdominal examinations were normal. Laboratory investigations showed eosinophilia (15%) and anti cestod antibody was positive. Chest X ray showed a well-defined, smoothly outlined, oval shaped soft tissue and opaque in density in each lung. These findings were indicative of bilateral hydatid cysts of the lungs. An ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed two large well-defined cysts with homogenous walls in right lobe of the liver. It was septated and daughter cyst was identified within each cyst. The ultrasonography of other parts of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. A computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen showed three large, bilateral and well circumscribed loculated cysts in the lungs (Figure 1) and two cysts in the liver (Figure 2).
Due to the symptoms caused by these cysts, the cysts were decided to be treated surgically. The patient underwent separated bilateral antero-lateral thoracotomies and phrenotomy under general anesthesia with double lumen and tracheal tube in the supine position. First, we operated the left side pulmonary cyst. Intraoperatively, cysts were found to be hydatid cysts, they were first aspirated and then evacuated. Laminated membrane and bronchial opening were closed with capitonnage. The pleural cavities were thoroughly irrigated with hypertonic saline. A chest tube was placed and the chest was closed primarily. Two cysts in the right side were evacuated similar to those in the left side. The two liver cysts were evacuated with pherenotomy. Two Foley catheters were placed in the cavity of liver cysts after evacuation. To reduce recurrence in the postoperative period, Albendazole was given for 3 months. Her postoperative recovery was smooth with no evidence of sepsis, pneumonia or bronchiectasis that. These complications sometimes occur after conservative parenchyma saving lung procedures. At one-year follow-up, the patient showed complete resolution of all symptoms and well expanded lungs with no residual cysts visible on the chest X-ray (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old female from northern Iran presented with a 1-month history of persistent right upper quadrant abdominal pain, right-sided chest pain, cough, and low-grade fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The previously healthy patient experienced persistent cough, right-sided chest pain, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and low-grade fever over the preceding month.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy without prior lung or liver disease; resided in northern Iran.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right chest pain, right upper quadrant pain, persistent cough, and low-grade fever.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal except for mildly reduced oxygen saturation of 96% on room air; chest and abdominal examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed eosinophilia (15%) and a positive anti-cestode antibody test. Chest X-ray demonstrated well-defined, smoothly outlined oval opacities in both lungs. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed two large well-defined septated cysts containing daughter cysts in the right hepatic lobe, with normal remaining abdominal and pelvic organs.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracoabdominal CT demonstrated three large, well-circumscribed loculated cysts across both lungs (one left, two right) and two large cysts in the right lobe of the liver. Single-stage sequential bilateral anterolateral thoracotomies and right phrenotomy evacuated one left pulmonary hydatid cyst, two right pulmonary hydatid cysts (with bronchial closure, capitonnage, and hypertonic saline pleural irrigation), and two right hepatic hydatid cysts (drained with Foley catheters).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Synchronous bilateral pulmonary (three cysts) and right hepatic (two cysts) cystic echinococcosis, confirmed by positive anti-cestode serology, daughter cysts on ultrasound/CT, and intraoperative extraction of laminated membranes. The patient underwent single-stage bilateral anterolateral thoracotomies and right phrenotomy with cyst evacuation and capitonnage, followed by 3 months of postoperative oral albendazole; at 1-year follow-up, she was completely asymptomatic with fully expanded lungs and no residual cysts on chest X-ray.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old Bulgarian woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of acute onset epigastric pain which had migrated to the lower abdomen. She reported mild, intermittent, dull epigastric pain for the preceding year. There was no history of trauma or any past medical history of note. At presentation, she was haemodynamically stable with a pulse rate of 69 bpm and blood pressure of 108/36 mmHg. There was no respiratory compromise and O2 saturation was 98% on room air. Her temperature was 36.9 C. Palpation of the abdomen elicited significant epigastric and suprapubic tenderness with guarding and percussion tenderness. A faint erythematous rash was noted over her face and arms. Thirty minutes later she became shocked, tachypnoeic, and hypothermic at 35.2 C. The rash was more extensive, appeared urticarial and she had developed periorbital oedema. Her condition was stabilised with aggressive fluid resuscitation and intravenous steroids (Hydrocortisone 200 mg) and antihistamines (Chlorpheniramine 20 mg).
Initial blood investigations were normal apart from a haemoglobin of 16.1 g/dL (12-16), glucose of 11.7 mmol/L (3-7), and lactate of 2.73 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Liver and renal function tests were normal and there was no leucocytosis or eosinophilia. Venous blood gas demonstrated a pH of 7.287 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate of 22.6 mEq/L (22-29), and base excess of -1.6 (-2 to 2) with normal pO2 and pCO2. Urine dipstick and beta-HCG were negative. Contrast CT of her abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, well-defined area of low density occupying almost the entire left lobe of the liver with serpiginous enhancing strands within. Significant free fluid was noted throughout the abdomen and pelvis (see Figure 1). The appearances were highly suggestive of a ruptured hepatic hydatid cyst.
The decision was made to perform a diagnostic laparoscopy with a view to proceeding to laparotomy if required. Laparoscopy revealed a large ruptured cystic mass within the left lateral lobe of the liver, almost completely replacing the hepatic parenchyma (see Figure 2). There were also features of cholecystitis noted. Large amounts of free fluid were noted in all four quadrants. Removal of the cyst was achieved by way of an open left partial hepatectomy and the peritoneal cavity was washed out with hypertonic saline with a drain left in the subhepatic space. A cholecystectomy was also performed. Post-operatively she was managed in ITU and was commenced on Albendazole and Tazocin (Piperacillin/Tazobactam) with ongoing therapy for anaphylaxis. Praziquantel was also commenced but the patient subsequently became bradycardic to 30 bpm (although remained haemodynamically stable). No other cause was identified and resolved after discontinuation of Praziquantel. She was discharged 9 days post-operatively on reducing dose oral steroids and 3 cycles of Albendazole (4 weeks on, 2 weeks off). At follow-up, she remained well.
Histology of the resected tissue confirmed the presence of a hyalinised, PAS-positive pseudocapsule (Brodie's capsule) with numerous scolices present, thus confirming the diagnosis of a hydatid cyst (see Figure 3). Histology of the gall bladder showed mild cholecystitis. No protoscolices or hooklets were seen in the drain fluid. Echinococcal serology (Hydatid ELISA) was positive.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old Bulgarian woman presented with a 2-hour history of acute severe epigastric pain migrating to the lower abdomen, followed within 30 minutes by anaphylactic shock.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed sudden-onset severe epigastric pain that migrated to the lower abdomen 2 hours prior to emergency presentation, on a 1-year background of mild intermittent dull epigastric pain without trauma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; originated from Bulgaria; no history of trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute epigastric/lower abdominal pain, chronic intermittent epigastric pain, and acute urticarial rash.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: pulse 69 bpm, blood pressure 108/36 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 C. Abdominal exam showed marked epigastric and suprapubic tenderness with guarding and percussion tenderness, and a faint erythematous rash on her face and arms. Within 30 minutes, she developed anaphylactic shock with tachypnea, hypothermia (35.2 C), generalized urticaria, and periorbital edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL (12-16), glucose 11.7 mmol/L (3-7), lactate 2.73 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), venous pH 7.287 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 22.6 mEq/L (22-29), base excess -1.6 (-2 to 2), normal WBC and eosinophil counts, normal liver and renal function tests, and negative urine dipstick and beta-hCG. Postoperative Hydatid IgG ELISA serology was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT demonstrated a large, well-defined low-density cystic lesion occupying nearly the entire left hepatic lobe with internal serpiginous enhancing strands (detached membranes) and abundant four-quadrant free intraperitoneal fluid. Diagnostic laparoscopy converted to open left partial hepatectomy and cholecystectomy confirmed a ruptured left lateral lobe hepatic hydatid cyst; histopathology identified a hyalinized PAS-positive pseudocapsule (Brodie's capsule) containing numerous scolices and mild cholecystitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture of a left lobe hepatic hydatid cyst presenting with acute abdomen and anaphylactic shock, confirmed by positive Hydatid ELISA and histopathological demonstration of a PAS-positive pseudocapsule and numerous scolices. After resuscitation with IV fluids, hydrocortisone 200 mg, and chlorpheniramine 20 mg, she underwent open left partial hepatectomy, cholecystectomy, and hypertonic saline peritoneal washout, followed by ICU management with piperacillin/tazobactam and oral albendazole (3 cycles of 4 weeks on, 2 weeks off; praziquantel was discontinued due to sinus bradycardia to 30 bpm), achieving full recovery at discharge on postoperative day 9.

raw_case_text:
A fifty-year-old male with no special note of past or social history presented with high-grade fever and right hypochondrial pain of two week duration. The patient was jaundiced, febrile and had a tender hepatomegaly just below right costal. Investigations showed a deranged liver function test (LFT) with a total bilirubin of 258,40mg/dl, AST(420 U/L), ALT(415 U/L), G.G.T(328 UI/L) and raised serum alkaline phosphatase(1181 U/L). Hydatid serology was positive. CT scan revealed intraparenchymic hydatid cyst type IV(4th and 5th segments) that opened totally into common bile duct (Figure 1, Figure 2).
The cyst was seen to communicate inferiorly with common hepatic duct in the region of ductal confluence with extension of the hydatid membranes into common hepatic duct (CHD) and proximal CBD withupstream dilatation of the right and left hepatic ducts and intra-hepatic biliary radicles with ruptured membranes present, the right intrahepatic duct was seen communicating with cyst cavity. CBD was dilated with internal debris seen inside and Gallbladder was distended showing irregular linear intensities inside. Atretic hydatid liver cyst containing infected bile with ruptured membranes into common bile duct through probably right hepatic duct (Figure 3). Patient under went right subcostal laparotomy was performed, cholecystectomy and choledochotomy with evacuation of cystic content and debris via CBD with irrigation with 0.9% NaCl solution, T-tube drainage of CBD and under hepatic drainage by Salem tube. The postoperative period was unremarkable and patient was discharged on day 7, Salem's tube was removed on day 6thand the T-tube was removed after a control cholangiography was done on day 16th postoperatively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of high-grade fever, jaundice, and right hypochondriac pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute high-grade fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice over the 2 weeks preceding hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and social history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, jaundice, and right hypochondriac pain.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile and jaundiced male with tender hepatomegaly palpable just below the right costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests were markedly deranged: total bilirubin 258.40 mg/dL [umol/L], AST 420 U/L, ALT 415 U/L, GGT 328 UI/L, and ALP 1,181 U/L. Hydatid serology was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT/MRI revealed a Gharbi type IV intraparenchymal hepatic hydatid cyst in segments IV and V communicating inferiorly with the right hepatic duct and common hepatic duct at the biliary confluence, with ruptured hydatid membranes and debris filling the dilated common bile duct, intrahepatic biliary radicles, and distended gallbladder. Right subcostal laparotomy with cholecystectomy, choledochotomy, evacuation of intrabiliary hydatid membranes and debris, 0.9% NaCl irrigation, T-tube CBD drainage, and subhepatic Salem tube drainage confirmed the diagnosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Infected hepatic hydatid cyst (segments IV-V) with frank intrabiliary rupture into the right and common hepatic ducts causing acute obstructive suppurative cholangitis, confirmed by positive hydatid serology, CT/MRCP imaging, and choledochotomy extraction of hydatid membranes. Following open cholecystectomy, choledochotomy membrane evacuation, and T-tube drainage, the patient was discharged on postoperative day 7 and had his T-tube removed on postoperative day 16 after a normal control cholangiogram.

raw_case_text: A nine-year old boy was admitted to our referral hospital in August 2013 with a history of trauma caused by a fall two days before admission. He had chest pain, and mild respiratory distress and four years with non productive cough. He was sent to our center due to suspicious diagnosis of ruptured giant pulmonary hydatid cysts confirmed by 5 ml hydatid fluid thoracentesis. Chest roentgenogram, demonstrated a mass density of right hemithorax supposed to be massive pleural effusion with mediastinal shifting to the left (Fig. 1). On admission, the patient status included the mild respiratory distress (i.e., RR=29, PR=80, T=37. 5), and normal vital signs on physical examinations. Respiratory sounds were not audible over the right side lung. Serologic hemagglutination test (ELISA) for Echinococcosis was also positive. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest confirmed the right side pulmonary giant mediastinal cyst with mediastinal shift to the left and an absent shadow of collapsed right lung (Fig. 2). He was scheduled for perfoming the thoracotomy. After right-thoracotomy, a giant hydatid cyst with dimensions of 30*22*20cm was found extending from the right diaphragm toward the apex of the lung. There was not any pneumothorax, or pleural effusion at the time of operation owing to severe adhesions of the right pulmonary hydatid cyst to the extensive surface of the chest wall. After lyses of the adhesions, the chest cavity, all around the cyst was covered with spongy hypertonic normal saline. Then, the cyst was removed without contamination, the pericyst was opened and the laminated membrane was extracted from the right lower lobe (RLL). No pulmonary parenchyma remained in the RLL, and right lower lobectomy was successfully performed. The remaining lobes of the lung were expanded completely. Two chest tubes were inserted into the hemithorax cavity, and then the chest was closed. The patient discharged the hospital on the fifth day without any complications. After six months, the controlled chest X-ray was normal (Fig. 3). He was in good condition during the six months follow up period while medically treated by Albendazole 800 mg/day. Moreover, pathologic examinations have confirmed the existence of a pulmonary hydatid cyst (Fig. 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy presented with chest pain and mild respiratory distress 2 days after a fall, on a 4-year background of chronic nonproductive cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child had a 4-year history of chronic dry cough and developed acute chest pain and mild respiratory distress 2 days after falling. Prior to referral, an outside thoracentesis aspirated 5 mL of hydatid fluid from the right hemithorax.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of a fall 2 days prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute post-traumatic chest pain, mild dyspnea, and 4 years of chronic dry cough.

objective.physical_examination: Mild respiratory distress with respiratory rate 29 breaths/min, pulse 80 bpm, temperature 37.5 C, and completely absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax.
objective.routine_investigations: Serologic hemagglutination/ELISA test for echinococcosis was positive. Chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the right hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift to the left.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated a giant cystic lesion occupying the entire right hemithorax with leftward mediastinal shift and complete collapse of the right lung. Right thoracotomy revealed a giant 30 x 22 x 20 cm pulmonary hydatid cyst extending from the right hemidiaphragm to the lung apex with dense pleural adhesions and complete parenchymal destruction of the right lower lobe; laminated membranes were extracted, right lower lobectomy was performed, and histopathological examination confirmed a pulmonary hydatid cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Giant right lower lobe pulmonary hydatid cyst (30 x 22 x 20 cm) mimicking a massive pleural effusion with complete right lower lobe destruction, confirmed by positive Echinococcus serology, intraoperative extraction of laminated membranes, and histopathology. The patient underwent right thoracotomy, cyst evacuation with hypertonic saline protection, and right lower lobectomy, was discharged on postoperative day 5, and completed 6 months of oral albendazole (800 mg/day) with a normal chest X-ray at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
This 8-year-old boy presented with complaints of progressively worsening headaches along with vomiting and intermittent fever since 20 days. There were no significant findings on general physical and neurological examination. The patient's routine laboratory investigations were normal. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was performed which showed multiple intracranial cysts predominantly in the right frontal region with significant mass effect [Figure 1]. The patient's chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, and eosinophil counts were normal. The patient was started on dexamethasone, leviteracetem, and albendazole and scheduled for surgery.
A frontoparietal craniotomy was performed. There was significant dural tension, and a c-shaped durotomy was done which revealed a huge hydatid cyst extending toward the lateral ventricle [Figure 2a]. A soft rubber catheter was inserted between the brain parenchyma and the cyst capsule (Dowling's technique); a cleavage plane was established using warm hypertonic saline and the cyst was delivered unruptured [Figure 2d]. Numerous daughter cysts were then identified which were carefully delivered unruptured using the same technique [Figure 2b and c]. We were able to remove all of the 19 cysts without rupturing the cyst capsule this way. An endoscope was used after removing all the cysts to make sure that none of the daughter cysts was left behind. The cavity was copiously irrigated with hypertonic saline and hydrogen peroxide. Histopathological examination confirmed hydatid cyst and no bacterial agent was isolated.
The patient continued taking albendazole (200 mg, BID), dexamethasone, cefazolin, and levetiracetam postoperatively and had an uneventful postoperative course. The patient was seen in clinic on 3 months postoperative visit and his complaints of headache and vomiting had completely resolved. His neurological examination was completely normal and considering financial constraints a follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan was thus not performed.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy presented with a 20-day history of progressively worsening headaches, vomiting, and intermittent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child developed progressively worsening headaches accompanied by vomiting and intermittent fever over the 20 days prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive headache, vomiting, and intermittent fever.

objective.physical_examination: General physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests, peripheral eosinophil count, chest X-ray, and abdominal ultrasound were all normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI demonstrated multiple intracranial cysts predominantly in the right frontal lobe extending toward the lateral ventricle with marked mass effect. Right frontoparietal craniotomy and C-shaped durotomy delivered one giant mother cyst and 18 daughter cysts (19 cysts total) completely unruptured using Dowling's hydrodissection technique with warm hypertonic saline, followed by neuroendoscopic inspection and hypertonic saline/hydrogen peroxide irrigation; histopathology confirmed cerebral hydatid cysts with negative bacterial cultures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary multiple right frontal cerebral hydatid cysts (19 cysts total), confirmed by intraoperative unruptured delivery via Dowling's technique and histopathological examination. The patient was treated perioperatively with oral albendazole (200 mg twice daily), dexamethasone, levetiracetam, and cefazolin, and at 3-month outpatient follow-up he was completely asymptomatic with a normal neurological examination.

raw_case_text: Twenty-one-year-old adult female with rural background presented in the OPD with chief complaints of headache since 3 years and difficulty in walking since 6 months. Physical examination was unremarkable. A neurologic examination revealed bilateral papilledema. The hematological investigation was within normal limits. No abnormality was found in X-ray chest, echocardiography, ultrasonography (USG) abdomen, and pelvis. Computed tomography (CT) scan of brain revealed mild asymmetrical dilatation of left ventricle with normal size right lateral, third and fourth ventricles without periventricular edematous changes suggesting possibility of outlet obstruction of lateral ventricle [Figure 1a]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed evidence of altered signal intensity complex cystic lesion measuring, approximately 4 cm x 3 cm x 3 cm, noted in left lateral ventricle near foramen of Munro leading to widening of left lateral ventricle with mild midline shift toward right side. Few small daughter cysts noted within the cyst. No significant postcontrast enhancement noted within the lesion [Figure 1b]. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed acetate peak. No evidence of any other lesions in ventricles and brain parenchyma noted. There was no family history of hydatid infection. The patient underwent left frontal craniotomy. Intraoperative USG of the cystic mass showed a hypoechoic cystic lesion in the left lateral ventricle with another small cystic lesion within this hypoechoic lesion [Figure 2a]. The left lateral ventricular wall including the choroid plexus was exposed. The cystic mass was removed successfully by gentle irrigation of the cleavage plane between the cyst wall and the brain interface with saline [Figure 2b]. After cyst removal, the ventricle was irrigated several times with 3% hypertonic saline. The histopathologic findings were consistent with hydatid cyst [Figure 3a and b]. The postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged 10 days after surgery. The patient was continued on anthelmintic albendazole 10 mg/kg 3 times daily for 3 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old woman from a rural area presented with a 3-year history of headache and a 6-month history of difficulty walking.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced chronic headaches for 3 years and developed progressive gait difficulty 6 months prior to outpatient presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in a rural background; no family history of hydatid disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic headache and gait difficulty.

objective.physical_examination: General physical examination was unremarkable; neurological examination revealed bilateral papilledema.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological investigations, chest X-ray, echocardiography, and abdominopelvic ultrasonography were all normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT showed asymmetrical dilatation of the left lateral ventricle suggesting foramen of Monro obstruction. Brain MRI and MR spectroscopy (MRS) demonstrated a 4 x 3 x 3 cm complex non-enhancing cystic lesion containing a few small daughter cysts within the left lateral ventricle near the foramen of Monro, causing left ventricular dilatation, mild rightward midline shift, and an MRS acetate peak. Left frontal craniotomy with intraoperative ultrasound guidance and saline cleavage hydrodissection excised the intraventricular cyst intact followed by 3% hypertonic saline ventricular irrigation; histopathology confirmed a hydatid cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary solitary intraventricular hydatid cyst of the left lateral ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus, confirmed by MRI/MRS (daughter cysts and acetate peak), intraoperative ultrasound, and postoperative histopathology. Following intact microsurgical removal via left frontal craniotomy, the patient had an uneventful recovery, was discharged on postoperative day 10, and completed a 3-month course of oral albendazole (10 mg/kg three times daily).

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old married female from countryside with poor socio-economic background reported to our department with a complaint of mild pain and pressure sensation on right side of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) area on mastication and opening and closing of jaws since 2-3 years. The associated pain was dull, localized, and aggravated on talking and taking food. She was unemployed and managed all domestic chores at home.
On examination, there was no gross facial asymmetry, deviation of jaw toward left side on opening and closing was appreciated with acceptable mouth opening. Clinical examination revealed a painless, soft mass in the right TMJ area with egg shell cracking and no evidence of a sound condylar unit. TMJ movements were diminished on right side. Intraorally, occlusion was good with healthy gingiva. The general health of the patient was normal with no cervical lymphadenopathy.
An orthopantomogram of the region revealed an ill-defined osteolytic lesion involving the ramus condyle unit of the right side of size 3 cm x 1.5 cm. Computerized tomographic scan showed a well encapsulated fluid filled cystic lesion of size 4.9 cm x 3.8 cm with osteolysis and thinning out of the condylar unit encroaching the infratemporal region and abutting the pterygoid plates on right side [Figures 1-3]. USG liver and plain posteroanterior view chest radiograph were normal with only a slight increase in eosinophil count. Surgical procedure under general anesthesia was planned. The region was approached via an extended Risdon's approach extending and curving near the lower ear lode. Dissecting sub platysmally, pterygomassetric sling was incised. The cyst was judiciously dissected out of the surrounding tissues in toto. The intraoperative and postoperative course were uneventful.
The gross macroscopic specimen revealed two cystic cavities. The outer was tough reddish-brown and the inner was thin, slimy and fragile [Figure 4]. In histopathology, scanner view, x10 view and x 40 view showing daughter cysts with scolex and germinal layers [Figures 5-7]. The patient was followed up for 2 year with no recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2-to-3-year history of mild pain and pressure sensation over the right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) aggravated by mastication and jaw movement.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced dull, localized pain and a pressure sensation in the right TMJ region for 2-3 years, worsened by talking, eating, and opening or closing her jaw.
subjective.past_medical_history: Married homemaker from a rural countryside area of low socioeconomic status.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right TMJ pain and pressure on mastication.

objective.physical_examination: Deviation of the mandible to the left on mouth opening and closing with acceptable interincisal opening, diminished right TMJ excursion, and a painless soft mass in the right TMJ region exhibiting eggshell cracking on palpation with loss of a palpable intact condylar unit. Intraoral occlusion and gingiva were normal, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Peripheral blood count showed mild eosinophilia; PA chest radiograph and liver ultrasonography were normal. Orthopantomogram (OPG) revealed an ill-defined 3 x 1.5 cm osteolytic lesion involving the right mandibular ramus-condyle unit.
objective.advanced_workup: Maxillofacial CT demonstrated a well-encapsulated 4.9 x 3.8 cm fluid-filled cystic lesion causing osteolysis and cortical thinning of the right mandibular condylar unit, encroaching into the infratemporal fossa and abutting the right pterygoid plates. Complete en bloc surgical excision via an extended Risdon subplatysmal approach revealed a tough reddish-brown outer pericyst and a thin slimy inner endocyst; histopathology identified daughter cysts with scolices and germinal layers.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary intraosseous/infratemporal hydatid cyst of the right mandibular condyle and temporomandibular joint (4.9 x 3.8 cm), definitively confirmed by histopathological visualization of daughter cysts, scolices, and germinal layers. Following intact surgical excision via an extended Risdon approach, the patient had an uneventful recovery with no recurrence over 2 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 50 year old Moroccan female patient of rural origin presented in Avicenna hospital Rabat-Morocco with history of pain and swelling of the medial aspect of the right leg for two years. The patient had been operated, in another hospital, three years earlier for echinococcosis of the subcutaneous tissue of the right leg with no adjuvant treatment. No history of trauma, fever and weight loss was reported. A painful mass (Figure 1) next the previous incision was palpated on the medial side of the right leg; it was 5x7cm in diameter and there was no erythema and no sign of neurovascular compression, recurrence of hydatid disease was suspected. X-ray of the right leg showed an increased density of soft tissue in the medial aspect of the tibia (Figure 2). MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) revealed the presence of a subcutaneous collection in proximity to the medial surface of the tibia at the junction of his upper and middle third adherent to the periosteum with a thick and scalloped wall, enhanced after gadolinium injection and fluid filled measuring 52x28x72 mm and a second deep collection at the tibialis posterior muscle measuring 21x9x38 mm sitting in front of the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries (Figure 3). Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasonography did not reveal any abnormality. Complete blood count and electrolytes was normal, ELISA (Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) test for echinococcosis was positive. The diagnosis of recurrent hydatidosis has been retained. A three stages Therapeutic protocol was carried out in: Preoperative Albendazole chemotherapy for one month was performed followed by a complete surgical excision of subcutaneous cyst with two-centimeter margin of medial gastrocnemius and intraoperative drainage of the tibialis posterior muscle cyst with hydrogen peroxide irrigation of its pouch as it was adherent to the posterior tibial artery (Figure 4 A;B). Pathological examination of the cyst confirmed the diagnosis. Adjuvant Albendazole chemotherapy was prescribed postoperatively for one year. At two years follow up, no sign of local or distant recurrence was noted and the patient sill under medical surveillance each six months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old rural Moroccan woman presented with a 2-year history of pain and swelling on the medial aspect of her right leg at the site of a prior hydatid cyst excision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive pain and swelling over the medial aspect of her right leg for 2 years, adjacent to the surgical scar from a subcutaneous hydatid cyst resection performed 3 years earlier without adjuvant anthelmintic therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Operated 3 years earlier at an outside hospital for a subcutaneous hydatid cyst of the right leg without adjuvant medical therapy; rural Moroccan resident; no history of trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right leg pain and swelling; negative for fever or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: A painful 5 x 7 cm mass was palpated on the medial aspect of the right leg adjacent to the prior surgical incision, without overlying erythema or neurovascular deficit.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and serum electrolytes were normal, and Echinococcus IgG ELISA was positive. Plain radiograph of the right leg showed increased soft-tissue density along the medial tibia without bone erosion. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasonography were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Right leg MRI demonstrated two fluid-filled cystic collections with thick, scalloped, gadolinium-enhancing walls: a 52 x 28 x 72 mm subcutaneous collection adherent to the medial tibial periosteum at the upper-middle third junction, and a deep 21 x 9 x 38 mm collection within the tibialis posterior muscle anterior to the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries. Histopathology of the excised surgical specimen confirmed recurrent hydatidosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Recurrent subcutaneous and deep intramuscular (tibialis posterior) hydatidosis of the right leg, confirmed by positive Echinococcus ELISA, MRI, and postoperative histopathology. A three-stage therapeutic protocol was implemented: 1 month of preoperative oral albendazole, wide surgical excision of the subcutaneous cyst (with a 2-cm medial gastrocnemius margin) plus intraoperative drainage and hydrogen peroxide pouch irrigation of the deep tibialis posterior cyst adherent to the posterior tibial artery, and 1 year of postoperative adjuvant albendazole, achieving 2-year recurrence-free survival.

raw_case_text: A 58-year-old male from North-East China who was an immigrant worker for 4 years, presented with a cystic mass of the liver that was incidentally detected on abdominal ultrasound. Blood liver battery showed no abnormal findings and stool helminth was negative. Serologic markers for hepatitis A, B, and C virus were all negative and blood levels of tumor markers including alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 were within normal limits. Computed tomography (Fig. 1A, coronal view) and magnetic resonance imaging (Fig. 1B, axial view) of the liver revealed an approximately 9 cm-sized non-enhancing exophytic cyst with several daughter cysts, a radiologic finding typical of cystic echinococcosis of the liver, on the left lobe lateral segment of the liver. Surgical resection was performed for complete removal. Grossly, the mass showed a 9.5 x 9.5 x 8.5 cm-sized yellowish unilocular cyst containing several variable-sized cysts (Fig. 2A). Microscopically, a brood of capsules containing degenerated protoscolices of Echinococcus granulosus (arrows) were scattered on the laminated cystic walls (Fig. 2B). After uncomplicated postoperative recovery, the patient was discharged with albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, with encouragement to consume fatrich meal diet. Hepatic echinococcosis, also called hydatid disease of the liver, is a representative zoonosis that contributes to major health public problem in several countries. It usually occurs as a result of infection by larval stage of species E. granulosus, genus Echinococcus, via the ingestion of food and water fecally contaminated with eggs from the definitive hosts such as dogs and wolves, indicating that humans are an accidental intermediate host of the infection. Surgical resection followed by antihelminthic prophylaxis with albendazole remains the standard of care rather than percutaneous-based therapeutic approach.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male immigrant worker from Northeast China presented with an asymptomatic cystic liver mass incidentally discovered on abdominal ultrasound.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred after a routine abdominal ultrasound detected an incidental cystic mass in the left lobe of the liver.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immigrant worker from an endemic area in Northeast China for 4 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Asymptomatic; negative for abdominal pain or constitutional symptoms.

objective.routine_investigations: Liver function panel, viral hepatitis serologies (HAV, HBV, HCV), stool helminth examination, and serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) were all normal/negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a cystic mass in the left hepatic lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT and liver MRI demonstrated an approximately 9-cm non-enhancing exophytic cyst containing multiple internal daughter cysts in the left lateral segment of the liver. Complete surgical resection yielded a 9.5 x 9.5 x 8.5 cm yellowish cyst containing variable-sized daughter cysts; microscopy confirmed laminated cystic walls lined by brood capsules containing degenerated protoscolices of Echinococcus granulosus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Hepatic cystic echinococcosis (Echinococcus granulosus) of the left lateral hepatic segment, confirmed by characteristic daughter cysts on CT/MRI and histopathological visualization of laminated cyst walls, brood capsules, and degenerated protoscolices. Following complete surgical resection, the patient had an uncomplicated recovery and was discharged on oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily with fat-rich meals for 4 weeks.

raw_case_text: A 44-years-old man was seen in the clinic for recurrent (R) flank pain of 2-year duration. Ultrasound and subsequent CT scan performed 2 years ago showed a (R) suprarenal mass. He denied a history of hypertension, palpitations, or syncopal attacks. Serum cortisol, ACTH, metanephrine, and normetanephrine were normal at 201 nmol/L, 2.8 pmol/L (NR 1.6-13.90), 29 ng/L (NR < 90), and 92.0 ng/L (NR < 129), sequentially. Similarly, aldosterone and renin levels were normal with aldosterone/renin ratio of 3.6. Serum testosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate were also normal, at 5.94 nmol/L and 3.61 mumol/L successively. He was labeled as a nonfunctioning (R) adrenal mass. He later admitted to a strong history of childhood contact with animals including dogs. His elder brother was operated for multiple hydatid cysts in the abdomen. There were no urinary or other systemic symptoms. General examination including the blood pressure was normal apart from mild tenderness in the (R) renal angle. CT scan abdomen in July 2015 showed a large well-defined oval shaped heavily calcified cystic mass at the right adrenal gland, measuring 8.5 x 6.6 cm on transverse and AP diameter, respectively (Figures 1 and 2). MRI confirmed the CT finding. The mass depicts low T1 and heterogeneous high T2 signal intensity with internal stripes in T2 resembling water lily sign but showed no enhancement. It is surrounded with thin rim of dark T2 signal likely representing calcification (Figures 3 and 4). There was a mass effect on the upper pole of the right kidney and in some areas it appears inseparable from segment VI of the liver. The radiological features were consistent with hydatid cyst. IHA for hydatid was negative at 1 : 80. He was started on albendazole (400 mg twice daily) and praziquantel 600 mg weekly, for four weeks prior to surgery. In view of the persistent loin pain and the large cysts (>=5 cm diameter), he underwent (R) adrenalectomy through a right subcostal incision without spillage of the cyst content. The patient tolerated the procedure well with uneventful postoperative course. Macroscopic appearance showed well circumscribed cystic lesion measuring 10 x 8 x 4.5 cm (Figure 5) with focal multiloculated appearance. Histopathology revealed dense fibrous capsule with three layers showing a middle layer with characteristic lamination pattern and focal calcification. The cyst content is a lightly dense proteinaceous, with a jelly-like matrix material (Figures 6, 7, and 8). No scolices or hooks were seen and no associated granulomas or neoplasia. The histological features were consistent with hydatid cyst. He was finally discharged on albendazole 400 mg BD for another four weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of recurrent right flank pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was evaluated for recurrent right flank pain of 2 years' duration after an initial ultrasound and CT scan 2 years earlier had identified a right suprarenal mass.
subjective.past_medical_history: Strong history of childhood contact with animals including dogs; family history was positive for an elder brother who underwent surgery for multiple abdominal hydatid cysts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent right flank pain; negative for hypertension, palpitations, syncope, urinary symptoms, or systemic complaints.

objective.physical_examination: General examination and blood pressure were normal; abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right renal angle.
objective.routine_investigations: Endocrine workup confirmed a nonfunctioning adrenal mass: serum cortisol 201 nmol/L, ACTH 2.8 pmol/L (normal 1.6-13.90), metanephrine 29 ng/L (normal <90), normetanephrine 92.0 ng/L (normal <129), aldosterone/renin ratio 3.6, testosterone 5.94 nmol/L, and DHEAS 3.61 umol/L. Echinococcus indirect hemagglutination (IHA) serology was negative at 1:80.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT (July 2015) and MRI demonstrated a well-defined 8.5 x 6.6 cm oval, heavily calcified cystic mass in the right adrenal gland compressing the upper pole of the right kidney and abutting hepatic segment VI, showing low T1 signal, heterogeneous high T2 signal with internal detached membrane stripes (water-lily sign), a dark T2 calcified rim, and no contrast enhancement. Following right adrenalectomy via a right subcostal incision, pathology of the 10 x 8 x 4.5 cm multiloculated cyst revealed a dense three-layered fibrous capsule with a characteristic acellular laminated middle layer, focal calcification, and proteinaceous jelly-like matrix without viable scolices or hooklets.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary isolated right adrenal hydatid cyst (10 x 8 x 4.5 cm), confirmed by MRI water-lily sign and histopathological demonstration of a three-layered cyst wall with a characteristic acellular laminated layer despite negative IHA serology (1:80).
