subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old woman with systemic erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis presented with occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath prior to her fifth scheduled dose of belimumab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In July 2022, the patient was diagnosed with SLE, lupus nephritis, and polyserositis (initial SLEDAI score 20) after presenting with facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distention, cough, and white phlegm. She was treated with glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone, prednisone), cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), hydroxychloroquine sulfate, and four infusions of intravenous belimumab (480 mg starting July 22, 2022, through September 29, 2022), achieving clinical improvement that allowed tapering of glucocorticoids and MMF. In October 2022, she developed herpes zoster virus infection. Prior to her fifth scheduled belimumab infusion on November 1, 2022, she reported occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath without noticeable cough or expectoration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus nephritis, and polyserositis (diagnosed July 2022); herpes zoster infection (October 2022); reported history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath at the November 2022 presentation; negative for noticeable cough or sputum expectoration. Prior July 2022 onset included facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distention, cough, and white phlegm.

objective.routine_investigations: November 2022 laboratory workup: White blood cell count and C-reactive protein (CRP) normal; HIV antibody negative; anti-IFN-gamma autoantibody negative; serum galactomannan, cryptococcal capsular antigen, tuberculosis antibody, Candida IgG antibody, and Candida antigen tests all negative; quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay normal. Immunoglobulins: IgG 5.44 g/L (reference range: 8–18 g/L), IgA 1.16 g/L (reference range: 0.9–4.5 g/L), and IgM 0.64 g/L (reference range: 0.84–1.32 g/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (November 1, 2022): Patchy, nodular, and flocculent ground-glass density shadows across all lung lobes, accompanied by nodules and cavities in the dorsal segment of the left lower lobe. Fungal biomarker: Serum beta-D-glucan negative. Lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 332/μL (reference range: 180–324/μL), CD8+ T-lymphocyte count 646/μL (reference range: 1,185–1,901/μL), and absolute NK cell count 16/μL (reference range: 200–587/μL). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) detected Pneumocystis jirovecii (178,940 sequence reads) and Talaromyces marneffei (7,480 sequence reads); BALF PCR was positive for P. jirovecii, and BALF fungal culture grew Talaromyces marneffei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Co-infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) and pulmonary Talaromyces marneffei infection in an immunosuppressed patient with SLE and lupus nephritis receiving belimumab, glucocorticoids, and mycophenolate mofetil, confirmed by BALF mNGS (178,940 P. jirovecii reads and 7,480 T. marneffei reads), positive BALF P. jirovecii PCR, and positive BALF culture for T. marneffei. Plan and clinical course: The fifth dose of belimumab was discontinued. Voriconazole (0.6 g/day on day 1, then 0.4 g/day from day 2) was initiated for T. marneffei. Due to her reported history of G6PD deficiency, PJP was treated with clarithromycin (1.8 g/day) during the first week and subsequently switched to sulfamethoxazole once repeat G6PD testing returned normal. Maintenance SLE therapy was continued with prednisone 5 mg/day, MMF 0.75 g/day, and hydroxychloroquine sulfate 0.2 g/day. Repeat chest CT after 1 month of therapy demonstrated significant improvement of pneumonia, and she remained stable under outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old Chinese woman presented to our hospital because of progressive onset of fever, sore throat, maculopapular skin rash, and bilateral knee joint pain for 3 days. Blood results are shown in Table 1. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone was prescribed but there was no improvement. Three sets of blood cultures yielded negative results. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax and abdomen did not reveal any significant changes at that time (Figure 1A). Adult Still's disease was suspected and a high dose corticosteroid was commenced (Figure 2). Initially, the patient responded to the corticosteroid and so did the C-reactive protein and serum ferritin levels. However, the fever and other symptoms relapsed when the dose of corticosteroid was reduced and therefore the dose was increased again. Three weeks after disease onset, cyclosporine A was given for a total of 38 days. Eight weeks after disease onset, one dose of tocilizumab was prescribed.
Eight weeks after the commencement of the corticosteroid (the total amount of corticosteroid received was equivalent to 5,193 mg of prednisone), she developed severe and progressive shortness of breath, which rapidly evolved into type I respiratory failure (Figure 2). Blood results are shown in Table 1. A CT scan of the thorax revealed right pleural effusion and bilateral infiltrates and cavitation (Figure 1B). A blood culture, pleurocentesis, and bronchoscopic examination were performed. The pleural fluid and bronchoalveolar lavage samples were sent for bacterial and fungal culture. The bronchoalveolar lavage sample was also sent for NGS analysis. Empirical intravenous meropenem, vancomycin, and micafungin were started.
After 3 days of incubation, the aerobic bottles of two sets of blood cultures were positive for a Gram-positive rod which was also modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain positive (Figure 2). The same bacterium was also recovered from the pleural fluid as well as four bronchoalveolar lavage samples collected over a period of 6 days. MALDI-TOF MS by the direct transfer method using the MALDI-TOF MS spectrometer (Bruker Daltonik) and the spectrum analyzed with IVD MALDI Biotyper 2.3 and reference library DB-9607 (Bruker Daltonik) did not show any confident identity. 16S rDNA gene targeted NGS (tNGS) of the isolate using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies' MinION device with protocols described revealed that the 16S rDNA gene sequence of the isolate (HKU-SZH_220830) was identical to those of N. kroppenstedtii (GenBank accession numbers NR133794.1, DQ157924.2, and MN567716.1), indicating that the isolate was a strain of N. kroppenstedtii. In addition, tNGS analysis of a bronchoalveolar lavage sample was also positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Epstein-Barr virus, and Candida albicans sequence reads. Meropenem and vancomycin were stopped and intravenous imipenem-cilastatin, amikacin, and cotrimoxazole were started. Unfortunately, despite intensive care and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, the patient continued to deteriorate and succumbed 18 days after the development of shortness of breath.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old Chinese woman initially presented with a 3-day history of progressive fever, sore throat, maculopapular skin rash, and bilateral knee arthralgia, and subsequently developed severe progressive shortness of breath 8 weeks after initiating high-dose immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 3 days of fever, sore throat, maculopapular rash, and bilateral knee pain refractory to empirical intravenous ceftriaxone, with negative blood cultures and an unremarkable baseline thoracoabdominal CT. Suspected of having adult-onset Still's disease, she was treated with high-dose corticosteroids (total cumulative dose equivalent to 5,193 mg of prednisone over 8 weeks), cyclosporine A (given for 38 days starting at week 3 after symptom relapse during steroid taper), and a single dose of tocilizumab at week 8. Eight weeks after starting corticosteroids, she developed severe, rapidly progressive shortness of breath that evolved into type I respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Suspected adult-onset Still's disease treated over the preceding 8 weeks with high-dose corticosteroids (cumulative 5,193 mg prednisone equivalent), cyclosporine A (38 days), and tocilizumab (1 dose).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for fever, sore throat, maculopapular rash, and bilateral knee joint pain; week 8 presentation positive for severe progressive shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: At week 8 deterioration: Severe respiratory distress with acute type I respiratory failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: Three sets of blood cultures negative; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum ferritin that transiently improved with corticosteroids; baseline CT of thorax and abdomen unremarkable. At week 8 deterioration: Repeat aerobic blood cultures (2 sets after 3 days of incubation) and pleural fluid cultures grew a Gram-positive rod that stained positive on modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT at week 8: Right pleural effusion with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and cavitation. Bronchoscopy with serial bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and pleurocentesis: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen-positive Gram-positive rods were isolated from pleural fluid and four BAL samples collected over 6 days; while MALDI-TOF MS (Bruker Biotyper 2.3) yielded no confident identification, 16S rDNA targeted NGS (tNGS) via Oxford Nanopore MinION identified the isolate (HKU-SZH_220830) as Nocardia kroppenstedtii (100% identity to GenBank NR133794.1, DQ157924.2, MN567716.1). In addition, tNGS of BAL fluid was positive for sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and Candida albicans.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Nocardia kroppenstedtii bacteremia, pleuritis, and cavitary pneumonia co-infected with Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Epstein-Barr virus, and Candida albicans (confirmed by blood/pleural/BAL cultures and Oxford Nanopore 16S rDNA tNGS of the isolate and BAL fluid) following intensive immunosuppression for suspected adult-onset Still's disease. Plan and clinical course: Empirical intravenous meropenem, vancomycin, and micafungin were initiated upon respiratory deterioration, then switched after tNGS identification to intravenous imipenem-cilastatin, amikacin, and cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMX), alongside ICU mechanical ventilation and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Despite intensive care and ECMO support, the patient progressively deteriorated and died 18 days after the onset of dyspnea.

raw_case_text:
On August 8, 2022 (day 1), a 46-year-old female was admitted to our hospital with a 2-day history of cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. She had been seen at the local hospital, where chest CT showed flocculent faint shadow in both lungs and she was prescribed with moxifloxacin (MXF), but the symptoms were not relieved. Previously, she had a history of chronic renal failure and had undergone allogeneic renal transplantation in April 2022. After renal transplantation, she orally took methylprednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus for a long time to combat rejection. She had a history of sulfonamides allergy, which manifested as localized skin urticarial.
On admission, blood gas analysis suggested an oxygenation index of 361 (normal 400-500) (Figure 1), blood routine tests showed white blood cell count was 7.25x109 /L (normal 3.5-9.5) and neutrophil percentage 88.70% (normal 40-75), biochemical tests showed procalcitonin (PCT) (0.06 ng/mL, normal <0.05), C-reactive protein (CRP) (5.33 mg/L, normal 0-7.44), and GM test (0.11, normal <0.5) were within reference intervals and an increase in level of G test (193.89 pg/mL, normal <60). Conventional microbiological tests were negative, including Cytomegalovirus (CMV) PCR, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) PCR, T-SPOT, respiratory virus antigen, sputum anti-acid staining, and sputum fungal and bacterial cultures. Creatinine was elevated (119 umol/L, normal 45-84). T-lymphocyte subsets results showed the decreased level of lymphocyte count (364.05 /muL, normal 800-4000), CD4+ T-cell count (125.58 /muL, normal 410-1590), and CD8+ T-cell count (126.78 /muL, normal 190-1140). Chest CT showed thickened vascular bronchial bundles and multiple cord-like faint shadow in both lungs (Figure 2a-c). To maintain adequate oxygenation, the nasal cannula was administered with low-flow oxygen (2 L/min). Piperacillin tazobactam (TZP, 4.5 g iv q8h) and CAS (70 mg iv qd first dose, 50 mg iv qd maintenance) were given. Oral immunosuppressants were stopped, and methylprednisolone (40 mg iv qd) was given to replace anti-rejection.
On day 3, the fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed a smooth surface of bronchial mucosa in each lobe segment of both lungs, no erosion and bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) was harvested for metagenomics next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Results were returned on day 4, which revealed P. jiroveci (261569 sequence reads) (Figure 3a). For the sake of sulfonamide allergies, sulfonamide desensitization therapy (Table 1) was given on day 5, followed by TMP-SMX (1.44 g po q6h) against PJP, and the rest of the anti-infection regimen remained unchanged. On the following day (day 6), oxygenation index was 130 and the patient's shortness of breath aggravated with obvious signs of respiratory distress and hypoxemia (SaO2 <90%) requiring high flow nasal cannula at 6 L/min. Then, the patient was adjusted to non-invasive ventilator-assisted ventilation. Methylprednisolone (40 mg iv q12h) was adjusted for the suppression of pulmonary inflammatory exudation. On day 9, bedside chest X-ray illustrated bilateral lung texture increased and blurred, and scattered patchy shadows in the left middle and lower lobe plus right lower lobe (Figure 4a). However, respiratory distress worsened again and the oxygenation index dropped on day 13. She was intubated and connected to an invasive ventilator to assist breathing. On day 16, oral TMP-SMX reached 12 days but patient showed no improvement of respiratory function. Bedside chest X-ray illustrated bilateral lung exudate shadow without change (Figure 4b), so TMP-SMX was changed into intravenous therapy (1.92 g iv q8h). On day 18, oxygenation index was 213. A repeat bedside chest radiograph showed a lighter exudative shadow than before (Figure 4c). For economic reasons, TMP-SMX was changed into oral therapy (1.44 g po q6h). On Day 22, oxygenation index was 313. The ventilator was withdrawn with adequate assessment, and the high-flow transnasal humidified oxygen therapy was continued, and methylprednisolone (40 mg iv qd) was adjusted. 
On day 26, body temperature climbed into 38.5 C and she still presented with cough with sputum and felled distress of breath after activity. On day 28, multiple patchy and stripy high-density shadows were seen in both lungs by chest CT (Figure 5a, c and e). Meanwhile, the peak temperature did not decrease, and PCT was higher than before. Thus, on day 29, a second fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed foamy secretions in both bronchi, especially in the right bronchus. BALF was collected for mNGS and culture. On day 30, BALF mNGS results reported Enterobacter cloacae complex (157651) (Figure 6a), Klebsiella michiganensis (47538), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (65650) (Figure 6b), Enterococcus faecium (11112), Enterococcus faecalis (3531), Citrobacter floridis (3179), P. jiroveci (27) (Figure 3b), where E. cloacae complex and P. aeruginosa carried carbapenem drug resistance genes, including blaIMP (4), blaKPC (187), blaNDM (141), blaSHV (168), blaTEM (289), and blaVIM (30). Considering the secondary infection of multi-drug resistant bacteria, the anti-infection regimen was adjusted to meropenem (MEM, 1 g iv q8h), polymyxin B [PMB, nebulized (0.25 miu q12h) plus intravenous (first doses: 1.25 miu, maintenance dose: 0.75 miu q12h)], CAS (50 mg iv qd), linezolid (LNZ, 0.6 g po q12h), and TMP-SMX (0.96 g po qd).
On day 33, BALF bacterial culture results showed E. cloacae (Table 2), only sensitive to amikacin (AMK) and colistin, and P. aeruginosa (Table 3), only sensitive to colistin and aztreonam (AZT). Sputum bacterial culture results reported Klebsiella oxytoca. On day 41, sputum culture showed K. oxytoca and P. aeruginosa, and LNZ was discontinued.  
On day 50, a repeat chest CT showed that multiple patchy shadows and stripe shadows in both lungs were obviously absorbed (Figure 5b, d and f). On day 52, the patient's cough and shortness of breath were relieved. The patient was discharged after discontinuation of MEM, PMB (nebulized + intravenous), and CAS. The patient was followed up for 2 months without any further discomfort such as cough, shortness of breath, and fever.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old female renal transplant recipient presented with a 2-day history of cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea 2 days prior to admission on August 8, 2022. She had initially visited a local hospital where a chest CT showed bilateral flocculent faint shadows, and she was prescribed moxifloxacin without relief. Four months earlier (April 2022), she had undergone allogeneic renal transplantation for chronic renal failure and was maintained on long-term oral methylprednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic renal failure status post allogeneic renal transplantation in April 2022; long-term post-transplant immunosuppression with oral methylprednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. History of sulfonamide allergy manifesting as localized skin urticaria.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Maintained on low-flow nasal cannula oxygen (2 L/min). On hospital day 6, developed obvious signs of respiratory distress and hypoxemia (SaO2 <90%). On hospital day 26, developed fever up to 38.5 °C, productive cough, and exertional breathlessness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission arterial blood gas: Oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2) 361 mmHg (normal: 400–500 mmHg). Complete blood count: WBC 7.25 x 10^9/L (normal: 3.5–9.5 x 10^9/L), neutrophil percentage 88.70% (normal: 40%–75%). Biochemistry and inflammatory markers: Serum creatinine 119 μmol/L (normal: 45–84 μmol/L), procalcitonin (PCT) 0.06 ng/mL (normal: <0.05 ng/mL), C-reactive protein (CRP) 5.33 mg/L (normal: 0–7.44 mg/L). Conventional microbiology: Negative serum/blood CMV PCR, EBV PCR, T-SPOT, respiratory virus antigen panel, sputum acid-fast staining, and sputum bacterial/fungal cultures. Subsequent serial chest X-rays (days 9, 16, 18): Bilateral increased/blurred lung markings and patchy exudative shadows that improved by day 18 after IV TMP-SMX.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission fungal and immunological biomarkers: Elevated serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G test) at 193.89 pg/mL (normal: <60 pg/mL); normal serum galactomannan (GM test 0.11, normal: <0.5). T-lymphocyte subsets: Decreased total lymphocyte count 364.05/μL (normal: 800–4,000/μL), CD4+ T-cell count 125.58/μL (normal: 410–1,590/μL), and CD8+ T-cell count 126.78/μL (normal: 190–1,140/μL). Admission chest CT: Thickened bronchovascular bundles and multiple bilateral cord-like faint shadows (local hospital CT showed bilateral flocculent faint shadows). Day 3 fiberoptic bronchoscopy and BALF mNGS (returned day 4): Smooth bronchial mucosa; BALF mNGS detected Pneumocystis jirovecii (261,569 sequence reads). Day 28–33 secondary deterioration workup: Chest CT (day 28) showed new bilateral patchy and stripy high-density shadows; repeat bronchoscopy (day 29) showed bilateral foamy bronchial secretions; repeat BALF mNGS (day 30) detected Enterobacter cloacae complex (157,651 reads), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (65,650 reads), Klebsiella michiganensis (47,538 reads), Enterococcus faecium (11,112 reads), Enterococcus faecalis (3,531 reads), Citrobacter freundii/floridis (3,179 reads), and reduced P. jirovecii (27 reads), along with carbapenem resistance genes blaIMP (4), blaKPC (187), blaNDM (141), blaSHV (168), blaTEM (289), and blaVIM (30). BALF cultures (day 33) grew MDR E. cloacae (sensitive only to amikacin and colistin) and MDR P. aeruginosa (sensitive only to colistin and aztreonam); sputum cultures grew Klebsiella oxytoca and P. aeruginosa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by 261,569 P. jirovecii reads on BALF mNGS, elevated G test 193.89 pg/mL, and CD4+ count 125.58/μL) in a renal transplant recipient with sulfonamide allergy, complicated by secondary hospital-acquired multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial pneumonia (carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter cloacae complex and Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Plan and clinical course: Oral immunosuppressants were held on admission and replaced with IV methylprednisolone (40 mg qd), low-flow oxygen, piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g IV q8h), and caspofungin (70 mg loading, 50 mg IV qd). Following BALF mNGS confirmation of PJP, rapid sulfonamide desensitization was performed on day 5 and oral TMP-SMX (1.44 g PO q6h) was started. Due to progressive hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 130 on day 6; intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation on day 13) and lack of radiographic resolution after 12 days of oral TMP-SMX, therapy was switched on day 16 to intravenous TMP-SMX (1.92 g IV q8h) with methylprednisolone 40 mg IV q12h, improving the oxygenation index to 213 by day 18 and 313 by day 22 (permitting extubation to HFNC and step-down to oral TMP-SMX). When fever (38.5 °C) and infiltrates recurred on days 26–28 from MDR E. cloacae and P. aeruginosa co-infection, treatment was adjusted to meropenem (1 g IV q8h), intravenous plus nebulized polymyxin B, caspofungin (50 mg IV qd), linezolid (0.6 g PO q12h, stopped day 41), and prophylactic-dose oral TMP-SMX (0.96 g PO qd). Repeat chest CT on day 50 showed marked absorption of bilateral lesions; she was discharged on day 52 and remained asymptomatic at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 29 years-old man was hospitalized in May 2023, presenting with a 3 days history of fever and dyspnea. The patient had previously been diagnosed with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) 9 years ago and had been on a long-term use of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). He denied any related family history. On 6 November 2021, the patient was admitted to the hepatology department presenting symptoms of jaundice and lower limb edema. After admission, the patient was diagnosed with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) and underwent liver transplantation surgery after 1 year. The patient adhered to the prescribed regimen of tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil after liver transplantation to prevent transplant rejection. The physical examination of the patient revealed a temperature of 38.4 C, a heart rate of 84 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, an oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 99%, a blood pressure of 120/82 mmHg, and lung auscultation revealed diminished sounds with a few moist crackles heard. Other physical examinations were negative. Blood tests indicated a white blood cell count of 3.75 x 109/L, a neutrophilic granulocyte percentage (NE%) of 77.6%, a procalcitonin (PCT) of 21.8 ng/mL, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 22 mg/L. The results of 1-3-beta-D-glucan and G-lipopolysaccharide tests were negative, and the absolute counts of helper T lymphocytes and killer T lymphocytes were 220/muL and 261/muL. Upon admission, a chest computed tomography (CT) scan indicated minimal bilateral pulmonary exudates. According to the aforementioned findings, the preliminary diagnosis indicated that the patient had community-acquired pneumonia. Empiric therapy with cefuroxime was initiated upon admission for prophylactic purposes. Nevertheless, the patient's pyrexia remained refractory, and there was an escalation of bilateral moist rales on the third day. Therefore, for further insights into the etiology, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples were obtained through fiberoptic bronchoscopy, which revealed yellow foam-like exudates in the lungs that were positive for Gomori methenamine silver staining and displayed a small quantity of pneumocystis jirovecii encapsulation. Thus, the patient was diagnosed with PJP. The immunosuppressive agent and cefuroxime were discontinued, and caspofungin was introduced in conjunction with sulfamethoxazole (SMZ) for anti-infective purposes. Additionally, 40 mg of methylprednisolone was administered to mitigate the inflammatory response. After treatment, the patient continued to experience recurrent hyperpyrexia and dyspnea, accompanied by deterioration in vital signs. The patient's temperature was recorded at 39.4 C, heart rate was 101 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was 32 breaths per minute. Then, despite the utilization of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) with an oxygenation flow rate of 50 L/min and FiO2 of 70%, as well as non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) with an IPAP of 18 cmH2O, an EPAP of 8 cmH2O, a frequency of 20 breaths/min, and FiO2 of 90% on alternate occasions, the pO2/FiO2 (P/F) ratio of arterial blood gas (ABG) was 100 mmHg. The P/F value satisfied the diagnostic criteria for severe ARDS. The patient experienced an exacerbation of dyspnea, and a reexamination of chest CT revealed an aggravation of lesions in both lungs (Figure 1). On the 15th day, the patient was admitted to the ICU under consideration of PJP and severe ARDS as diagnoses. He was still under hyperpyrexia and dyspnea physical examination and laboratory data showed a deterioration of general conditions: temperature: 39.3 C, heart rate: 102 beats/min, respiratory rate: 34 breaths/min, SpO2: 88% under high-flow nasal cannula oxygen (HFNC: oxygen flow rate of 40 L/min, FiO2 of 60%, and blood pressure: 115/74 mmHg). Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe hypoxemia: pH: 7.41, PaO2: 51.3 mmHg, PaCO2: 29.7 mmHg, and P/F 86 mmHg. The patient was expected to require mechanical ventilation for an extended period, which significantly increased the risk of mechanical complications. Meanwhile, given the patient's desire for autonomy to manage his own behavior during dyspnea, without resorting to endotracheal intubation, coupled with the urgent need for oxygenation, the early employment of awake VV-ECMO represented the optimal course of action. With the patient's consent, the VV-ECMO was connected to him. A 15F cannula inserted through the right internal jugular vein and a 23F catheter through the right femoral vein were placed for VV-ECMO under local anesthesia. ECMO parameters (blood flow velocity: 4.5 to 5.0 L/min, gas flow rate: 4 L/min, FiO2: 100%) were continued to be given with HFNC (Oxygen flow rate: 60 L/min, FiO2: 50%). On the basis of SMZ treatment, meropenem (1 g q8h) combined with vancomycin (1 g q12h) was given for antimicrobial therapy, dexmedetomidine (from 0.3 mug/kg/h to 0.5 mug/kg/h) was used for shallow sedation, and remifentanil (from 0.03 mug/kg/min to 0.05 mug/kg/min) for analgesia with the purpose to smooth the dyspnea. We maintained the RASS score from -1 to 0 of shallow sedation and controlled the spontaneous breathing rate at 8-15 breaths/min for lung protection. To prevent the formation of blood clots, we employed continuous infusion of heparin and frequently monitored the patient's activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) with the aim of maintaining a target APTT value between 60 and 80 s. Additionally, we administered enteral nutrition through a nasogastric tube to ensure a daily caloric intake of 2,100 kcal for the patient. On the 17th day, respiratory physiotherapy was initiated, which included daily use of the Portex Acapella Breathing Trainer was made at 6250 Shier Ring and sitting at the bedside with the intention of exercising respiratory muscles, preventing ICU-acquired weakness, and promoting pulmonary recruitment. On the 21st day, the manifestation of respiratory distress exhibited complete alleviation, the body temperature gradually regressed to the normal range, and the parameters obtained from blood gas analysis (Figure 2) as well as the radiological interpretation of the thoracic X-ray (Figure 3) depicted a gradual enhancement. According to Figure 4, the counts of NE, CRP, PCT, and IL-6 exhibited a gradual decrease over time, implying a potential amelioration or resolution of the infection. We partially adhered to the guidelines recommended by ELSO for weaning off VV-ECMO. We initiated a weaning trial at a PaO2 condition of 131 mmHg on supplemental O2 with an oxygenation flow rate of 40 L/min and FiO2 of 45% on HFNC while the fraction of delivered oxygen (FDO2) of VV-ECMO was 21%. Subsequently, we gradually reduced the sweep gas flow rate by 1 L/min from 5.0 L/min to our goal of 1 L/min over 4 h. Since the patient was able to tolerate the low sweep gas flow rate of VV-ECMO, we turned off the sweep gas for 4 h. Then, the arterial blood gas results obtained during the off-sweep gas trial demonstrated a PaO2 of 125 mmHg and pH of 7.41 without any excessive work of breathing based on the patient's condition. Following an 8 h spontaneous breathing test mentioned above, the patient's P/F was 277 mmHg, leading to the withdrawal of ECMO support. The patient was finally discharged from the ICU, and the LOS in ICU was only for 7 days without any adverse and unanticipated complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male orthotopic liver transplant recipient presented in May 2023 with a 3-day history of fever and dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever and dyspnea 3 days prior to hospital admission in May 2023. He had undergone orthotopic liver transplantation roughly 6 months earlier (late 2022, 1 year after a November 2021 admission for acute-on-chronic liver failure) and was maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil to prevent graft rejection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) diagnosed 9 years prior (treated long-term with ursodeoxycholic acid); acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) diagnosed in November 2021 (presenting with jaundice and lower limb edema) treated with liver transplantation 1 year later; maintained on post-transplant tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. Denied relevant family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and dyspnea for 3 days. Home medications included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and ursodeoxycholic acid.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 120/82 mmHg, and SpO2 99%. Chest auscultation: Diminished breath sounds with a few moist crackles (which escalated to bilateral moist rales by hospital day 3). Remainder of physical exam negative. Subsequent ICU admission vitals (day 15): Temperature 39.3 °C, heart rate 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 34 breaths/min, BP 115/74 mmHg, and SpO2 88% on HFNC (flow 40 L/min, FiO2 60%).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests: WBC 3.75 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 77.6%, procalcitonin (PCT) 21.8 ng/mL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 22 mg/L; G-lipopolysaccharide test negative. Day 15 arterial blood gas (on HFNC 40 L/min, FiO2 60%): pH 7.41, PaO2 51.3 mmHg, PaCO2 29.7 mmHg, and PaO2/FiO2 ratio 86 mmHg (down from 100 mmHg on alternating HFNC/NIPPV).
objective.advanced_workup: Admission immunological and fungal workup: Serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan negative; absolute helper T-lymphocyte (CD4+) count 220/μL and killer T-lymphocyte (CD8+) count 261/μL. Admission chest CT: Minimal bilateral pulmonary exudates (repeat chest CT prior to day 15 showed marked bilateral progression). Day 3 fiberoptic bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis: Yellow foam-like exudates in the airways; Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining was positive, demonstrating encapsulated Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) complicated by severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS; PaO2/FiO2 86 mmHg) in a liver transplant recipient, definitively confirmed by positive Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric cefuroxime for presumed community-acquired pneumonia was stopped on day 3 after BALF GMS confirmation of PJP; tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil were held, and targeted therapy was initiated with sulfamethoxazole (SMZ), caspofungin, and methylprednisolone (40 mg). Due to refractory hyperpyrexia (39.3–39.4 °C), severe dyspnea, and worsening hypoxemia (P/F 86 mmHg) refractory to alternating HFNC and NIPPV—and in accordance with the patient's wish to avoid endotracheal intubation—awake veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO; 15F right internal jugular and 23F right femoral cannulae, blood flow 4.5–5.0 L/min, sweep gas 4 L/min) combined with HFNC was initiated upon ICU admission on day 15. Adjunctive ICU management included broad-spectrum coverage with meropenem (1 g q8h) and vancomycin (1 g q12h), shallow sedation/analgesia with dexmedetomidine and remifentanil (targeting RASS -1 to 0 and spontaneous respiratory rate 8–15 breaths/min), heparin anticoagulation (target APTT 60–80 s), nasogastric enteral nutrition (2,100 kcal/day), and daily bedside respiratory physiotherapy (Portex Acapella trainer) starting day 17. By day 21, fever and respiratory distress resolved with improving inflammatory markers (NE, CRP, PCT, IL-6) and chest radiographs; after passing an 8-hour off-sweep spontaneous breathing trial (PaO2 125 mmHg, P/F 277 mmHg), VV-ECMO was decannulated and he was discharged from the ICU after a 7-day ICU stay without complications.

raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old man was admitted to the hospital due to a fever lasting for 5 days. He had a medical history of hypertension, psoriasis, urticaria, and had recently been treated with carbamazepine for nerve spasm two weeks ago. Five days before his hospitalization, the patient presented with high fever (39 C), accompanied by chills, abdominal pain, bilateral upper limb muscle pain, and enlargement of retro-occipital lymph nodes. One day before his admission, the patient experienced trunk pain, facial edema, and diffuse erythema on the extremities and trunk. A detailed timeline of diagnosis and treatment is provided in Figure 1.
Upon admission, laboratory tests revealed that the white blood count (WBC) was 9.03x10^9/L (reference interval 3.5-9.5x10^9/L), eosinophils (EOS) were 1.01x10^9/L (reference interval 0.02-0.52x10^9/L), alanine transferase (ALT) was 251 IU/L (reference interval 9-50 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 144 IU/L (reference interval 15-40 IU/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 366 IU/L (reference interval 100-240 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasonic examination revealed enhanced hepatic parenchymal echo and changes in the cholecystectomy. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal results. Ultrasonography of the lymph nodes revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck, axillary, and inguinal regions. CMV IgG/M, EBV IgG/M, epidemic hemorrhagic fever antibody, anti-nuclear antibody, and nine respiratory virus antibodies were negative.
After admission, the patient developed oliguria (<400mL/24h) and showed elevated serum creatinine levels, liver enzymes, and cardiac troponin I. The patient was diagnosed with DRESS syndrome based on diagnostic criteria (Table 1). Methylprednisolone (80mg, qd) and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (5g, qd) were prescribed, resulting in significant relief of skin rash and edema. However, the patient's symptoms worsened after IVIG was discontinued. Laboratory indicators such as eosinophils and transaminases fluctuated throughout the course of treatment (Figure 2), and cyclosporine (50mg, bid) was prescribed. Subsequently, serum creatinine and aminotransferase levels decreased, indicating effective treatment (Figure 2). 
However, 63 days after admission, the patient developed fever (38.5 C) accompanied by chills and dyspnea. Laboratory examination revealed an increase in hypersensitive C-reactive protein levels (Figure 2). Blood gas analysis (conducted in room air) indicated a pH of 7.495, pCO2 of 35.5 mmHg, and pO2 of 55 mmHg. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed diffuse interstitial infiltrations with ground-glass shadow in both lungs, suggestive of a PJ infection (Figure 3). Empirical therapy with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (4 tablets, q8h) was initiated.
66 days after admission, the patient was transferred to the respiratory intensive care unit for further treatment. Etiological results revealed a large number of PJ cysts in the sputum. Targeted therapy with TMP-SMX (4 tablets, q8h) was prescribed. In light of persistent fever and inadequate improvement in oxygenation, the administration of TMP-SMX was adjusted to primaquine (30mg, qd) in conjunction with clindamycin (600mg, q8h). However, due to the development of methemoglobinemia likely caused by primaquine's side effects, primaquine and clindamycin were discontinued, and TMP-SMX (4 tablets, q8h) was resumed. No PJ cysts were detected in subsequent sputum tests.
Given the patient extended treatment with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine, a positive (1,3)-beta-D-glucan and galactomannan test was observed. The presence of spores and mycelium in the sputum suggested possible candida or aspergillus infections, prompting antifungal treatments with caspofungin (50mg, qd) and voriconazole (200mg, qth). Tests for HHV-6, CMV, EBV, and other respiratory viruses were negative. Blood cultures detected Staphylococcus epidermidis, which was considered a contaminant microorganism. Empirical therapy with meropenem (1g, bid) and fosfomycin (4g, q8h) was initiated to prevent bacterial infections.
Following the patient transferred to the intensive care unit, there was an escalation in the medications administered. The patient developed an intensified skin rash marked by redness and desquamation. Blood tests revealed a surge in lgE levels to 4208 kU/L, indicative of a recurrent or persistent of DRESS syndrome. Chest CT exhibited multiple exudations in both lungs, suggestive of interstitial pneumonia (Figure 3). Blood gas analysis indicated decreased oxygenation. Beyond potential infections, the manifestations also raised concerns of immune-related lung damage. In response, high doses of methylprednisolone (500mg, 2 days) were administered. Regrettably, the patient's oxygenation progressively declined, blood gas analyses reflected a worsening condition. Unfortunately, the patient passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old man initially presented with a 5-day history of high fever (39 °C), myalgias, lymphadenopathy, facial edema, and diffuse erythema two weeks after starting carbamazepine, and later developed acute fever (38.5 °C), chills, and dyspnea on hospital day 63 after prolonged immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to admission, the patient was started on carbamazepine for nerve spasms. Five days before admission, he developed high fever (39 °C), chills, abdominal pain, bilateral upper limb myalgias, and retro-occipital lymphadenopathy, followed 1 day before admission by trunk pain, facial edema, and diffuse erythema across the trunk and extremities. Following admission, he developed oliguria (<400 mL/24 h) and acute kidney, liver, and myocardial injury, leading to a diagnosis of carbamazepine-induced DRESS syndrome. He was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (80 mg qd), IVIG (5 g qd), and oral cyclosporine (50 mg bid), with improvement in rash, renal function, and transaminases. However, on hospital day 63 of immunosuppressive treatment, he acutely developed recurrent fever (38.5 °C), chills, and dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, psoriasis, urticaria, nerve spasm treated with carbamazepine 2 weeks prior to admission, and prior cholecystectomy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Admission review positive for high fever (39 °C), chills, abdominal pain, bilateral upper limb muscle pain, trunk pain, facial edema, diffuse erythematous rash, and oliguria; hospital day 63 review positive for recurrent fever (38.5 °C), chills, and dyspnea. Drug allergy/hypersensitivity to carbamazepine (DRESS syndrome) and later primaquine-induced methemoglobinemia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: Febrile (39 °C), facial edema, diffuse erythema on the trunk and extremities, and enlarged retro-occipital, bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. Hospital day 63–66 deterioration: Fever 38.5 °C, chills, dyspnea, and subsequent recurrent intensified skin redness and desquamation in the ICU.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs: WBC 9.03 x 10^9/L (reference: 3.5–9.5 x 10^9/L), eosinophils 1.01 x 10^9/L (reference: 0.02–0.52 x 10^9/L), ALT 251 IU/L (reference: 9–50 IU/L), AST 144 IU/L (reference: 15–40 IU/L), LDH 366 IU/L (reference: 100–240 IU/L), with subsequent elevations in serum creatinine and cardiac troponin I; negative CMV IgG/IgM, EBV IgG/IgM, epidemic hemorrhagic fever antibody, ANA, and 9-respiratory-virus panel. Admission imaging: Normal ECG; abdominal ultrasound showed enhanced hepatic parenchymal echogenicity and post-cholecystectomy changes; lymph node ultrasound showed multiple enlarged bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes. Day 63 deterioration labs: Elevated hypersensitive C-reactive protein (hs-CRP); room-air arterial blood gas showed pH 7.495, pCO2 35.5 mmHg, and pO2 55 mmHg. Subsequent ICU labs: Positive sputum fungal smears (spores and mycelium), blood culture positive for contaminant Staphylococcus epidermidis, negative HHV-6/CMV/EBV PCRs, and markedly elevated serum IgE at 4,208 kU/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 63 chest CT: Diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrations with ground-glass shadows (later ICU chest CT showed multiple bilateral exudations). Day 66 sputum examination: Large number of Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJ) cysts identified in sputum. Fungal biomarkers in ICU: Positive serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan and galactomannan tests.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by abundant P. jirovecii cysts in sputum and diffuse ground-glass interstitial infiltrates on chest CT) and suspected secondary pulmonary candidiasis/aspergillosis, occurring as opportunistic complications of prolonged methylprednisolone and cyclosporine therapy for carbamazepine-induced DRESS syndrome. Plan and clinical course: DRESS syndrome was initially controlled with methylprednisolone (80 mg qd), IVIG (5 g qd), and cyclosporine (50 mg bid). When hypoxemic respiratory failure (room-air PaO2 55 mmHg) and diffuse GGOs developed on day 63, empirical oral TMP-SMX (4 tablets q8h) was initiated and continued upon ICU transfer on day 66 after sputum confirmed P. jirovecii cysts. Due to persistent fever and poor oxygenation, therapy was briefly switched to primaquine (30 mg qd) plus clindamycin (600 mg q8h), which was discontinued due to primaquine-induced methemoglobinemia; resumed TMP-SMX (4 tablets q8h) successfully cleared P. jirovecii cysts from repeat sputum samples. Co-existing fungal and bacterial risks were treated with caspofungin (50 mg qd), voriconazole (200 mg q12h), meropenem (1 g bid), and fosfomycin (4 g q8h), while recurrent DRESS flare (generalized desquamative rash, IgE 4,208 kU/L) and immune-mediated lung injury were treated with pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg/day for 2 days). Despite aggressive ICU management, oxygenation progressively declined and the patient died.

raw_case_text:
The patient, a 52-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital due to persistent afternoon fever and fatigue lasting over a month. Her body temperature exhibited fluctuations ranging from 37.1-38.2 during the afternoon and night, accompanied by a cough and a small amount of phlegm. She was admitted to lower-level hospital for treatment. Patient clinical conditions deteriorated, in absence of a clear diagnosis and she was transferred to our hospital. After hospitalization, the whole set before blood transfusion(-), aspartate aminotransferase: 80IU/L (<35IU/L), lactate dehydroase:947IU/L (110-220IU/L), alpha-fetoprotein:7.02ng/ml(<7ng/ml), CA15-3: 27.49U/ml(<24U/ml), serum CA-125: 19.18U/ml (<24U/ml), serum CA19-9: 7.86U/ml(<30U/ml), enolase: 45.38ng/ml(<20.4g/ml), C-reactive protein: 20.80mg/L(<5mg/L), interleukin-6: 47.99pg/ml(0-7pg/ml).Procalcitonin:0.09ng/ml(<0.046ng/ml), pH:7.45, PCO2: 29.5mmHg; PO2: 63mmHg; SO2:93%. Mycoplasma pneumonia antibody: titer 1:40 positive (+), titer 1:80 positive (+), titer 1:160 positive (+), titer 1:320 retained (+/-), Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibody (agglutination) positive (+), CD4 cell subpopulation 50.85%, cryptococcal antigen titer detection: Negative, immunoglobulin GAM(IgG, IgA, IgM), rheumatoid factor (RF), complement C3, C4, B factor: complement C3 0.7690g/L, complement C4 0.1360g/L, VTE score: 1; Sputum and pharyngeal bacteria culture did not show obvious abnormalities. Chest CT showed multiple nodules in both lungs, mainly in the upper lobes of both lungs, which were suspected to be inflammatory nodules. Both lungs had mild inflammation with thickened interlobular septa, which were alleged to be mild pulmonary oedema ( Figure 1A ). A contrast-enhanced CT of the whole abdomen showed multiple mild enhancement nodules and patchy shadows in the renal cortex, which were supposed to be caused by infection. A slightly hypodense nodule with a long diameter of 1.1cm was found in the right upper posterior lobe of the liver, which was mildly enhanced and suspected of inflammation ( Figure 1B ).
Based on the patient's clinical symptoms, imaging and laboratory results, clinicians first consider infectious lesions. Moxifloxacin was used as an anti-infective therapy after discussion with patients and their families; however, it did not produce satisfactory results. Combined with the follow-up examination results: The results of the antihistone antibody and anti-mitochondrial antibody tests were inconclusive, while the anti-dSDNA and antinuclear antibody assays showed suspicious (+-) results for both; thyroid function: Triiodothyronine was 0.91nmol/L, free triiodothyronine was 1.84pmol/L, thyroxine was 40.30nmol/L, and free thyroxine was 5.67pmol/L. ANCA antibody profile (6 items) showed no significant abnormality. Considering the blood-derived infection, the clinician adjusted the antibiotics to Piperacillin/+minocycline/doxycycline for anti-infective treatment, but the patient still had a recurrent fever. Combined with the detection of Staphylococcus aureus, pneumocystis carinii and human herpes virus type 5(HHV-5) in the patient's alveolar perfusion fluid next-generation sequencing(NGS), the antibiotics were adjusted to meropenem+vancomycin, and the patient did not have fever after treatment with compound sulfamethoxazole against pneumocystis. Consider patients with pneumocystis pneumonia, and give meprednisolone anti-inflammatory therapy. No bacterial growth was found in subsequent blood culture, identification and anaerobic culture. However, the patient still had intermittent low fever and was found to be positive for novel coronavirus COVID-19 during late hospitalization. The attending doctor recommended that the patient undergo a PET-CT examination to identify the cause of the fever further, but the patient refused due to his financial situation and radiation.
Additional ultrasonography indicated no abnormal growth of lymph nodes in the neck, supraclavicular region, axilla, abdominal cavity and retroperitoneum. Routine ultrasound examination showed a 1.4x1.1cm hypoechoic nodule under the upper capsule of the right posterior lobe of the liver, with clear boundaries, regular shape and no blood flow signal ( Figure 1C, D ). The patient's liver nodules did not disappear under the treatment of anti-inflammatory drugs. Considering that clarifying the nature of the liver may be a diagnostic breakthrough for the patient, contrast-enhanced ultrasound is recommended to describe the nature and evaluate the path of percutaneous liver puncture to obtain a pathological diagnosis, and the patient's consent is obtained.
To achieve the best diagnostic display results, the ultrasound machine was adjusted according to the doctor's habits. A 1.5 ml ultrasound contrast agent SonoVue (Bracco, Milan, Italy) suspension and 5 ml saline were injected successively along the left cubital vein to achieve the purpose of angiography and flushing the tube. The target lesion and liver parenchyma were observed continuously for 5 minutes after the injection. According to the guidelines, the arterial, portal, and delayed phases were defined as 10 to 30 seconds, 30 to 120 seconds, and 121 to 360 seconds after injection, respectively. All results were recorded on the ultrasound system. In the arterial phase, the solid component of the nodule rapidly becomes uniformly hyper-enhanced, and the scope becomes larger after enhancement ( Figure 2A ). Then, the enhancement washout begins in the late arterial phase ( Figure 2B ). The portal and parenchymal phases showed slightly less enhancement ( Figure 2C, D ). No unenhanced region was found in the three stages of the lesion. Unlike the inflammation suggested by enhanced CT diagnosis, CEUS is similar to the "fast in and fast out" enhancement model of hepatic malignant tumors. A biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy is difficult because of the high location and small size of the tumor. So, the selection of laparoscopic biopsy under general anaesthesia was made to determine the nature and possible origin of the nodules. Intraoperative freezing indicated a potential tumor, leading to the performance of laparoscopic resection on the right hepatic mass. Most postoperative paraffin sections revealed neoplasms originating from the lymphopoietic system. An immunohistochemical study showed that the tumor cells were positive for CD20, CD79a, CD10, Bcl-6, Bcl-2, c-Myc and MUM1 ( Figure 3 ). The positive rate of Ki-67(MIB-1) is about 70%. IgH and IgK gene rearrangement tests were positive, and other results were negative. These findings, together with the morphology, support a diagnosis of NHL, and the subtype was diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that favors a non-germinal center B-cell origin. Combined with ultrasonography and CT examination results, no other lesions were suggested, and primary hepatic lymphoma was considered. Subsequently, the patient was referred to the hematology department for chemotherapy with the DA-EPOCH regimen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old female presented with persistent afternoon and evening fever (37.1–38.2 °C), fatigue, and cough with scant phlegm lasting over 1 month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced daily afternoon and nighttime low-grade fevers (37.1–38.2 °C), fatigue, and a cough productive of a small amount of phlegm for more than 1 month. She was initially hospitalized at a lower-level hospital where her clinical condition deteriorated without a definitive diagnosis, prompting transfer to our hospital.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent afternoon/night fever, fatigue, cough, and scant sputum.

objective.physical_examination: Afternoon/nighttime temperature fluctuations between 37.1 °C and 38.2 °C; VTE risk score 1.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission arterial blood gas: pH 7.45, pCO2 29.5 mmHg, pO2 63 mmHg, SO2 93%. Biochemistry, inflammatory markers, and tumor markers: AST 80 IU/L (<35 IU/L), LDH 947 IU/L (110–220 IU/L), C-reactive protein (CRP) 20.80 mg/L (<5 mg/L), interleukin-6 (IL-6) 47.99 pg/mL (0–7 pg/mL), procalcitonin (PCT) 0.09 ng/mL (<0.046 ng/mL), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 7.02 ng/mL (<7 ng/mL), CA15-3 27.49 U/mL (<24 U/mL), CA-125 19.18 U/mL (<24 U/mL), CA19-9 7.86 U/mL (<30 U/mL), neuron-specific enolase (NSE) 45.38 ng/mL (<20.4 ng/mL). Serology and immunology: Pre-transfusion infectious panel negative; Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibody positive at titers 1:40 (+), 1:80 (+), 1:160 (+), and 1:320 (+/-) with positive agglutination; cryptococcal antigen negative; IgG/IgA/IgM and RF normal; complement C3 0.7690 g/L and C4 0.1360 g/L; ANA and anti-dsDNA borderline (+/-); antihistone and anti-mitochondrial antibodies inconclusive; ANCA (6-item) negative; thyroid panel showed T3 0.91 nmol/L, FT3 1.84 pmol/L, T4 40.30 nmol/L, FT4 5.67 pmol/L. Microbiology: Sputum, pharyngeal, and blood cultures (aerobic/anaerobic) negative; positive SARS-CoV-2 test later in hospitalization. Ultrasound: No cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, abdominal, or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy; routine liver ultrasound showed a well-defined, avascular 1.4 x 1.1 cm hypoechoic nodule under the upper capsule of the right posterior liver lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ cell subpopulation 50.85%. Chest and whole-abdomen contrast-enhanced CT: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules (predominantly upper lobes) with mild interlobular septal thickening; multiple mildly enhancing nodules and patchy shadows in the renal cortex; a 1.1 cm mildly enhancing hypodense nodule in the right upper posterior liver lobe. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Detected Pneumocystis carinii (P. jirovecii), Staphylococcus aureus, and human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5/CMV). Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) of the liver lesion (SonoVue 1.5 mL): Rapid uniform arterial-phase hyperenhancement with late arterial/portal/parenchymal washout ('fast-in and fast-out' malignant pattern). Laparoscopic right hepatic mass resection pathology and immunohistochemistry: Non-Hodgkin diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL, non-germinal center B-cell subtype), positive for CD20, CD79a, CD10, Bcl-6, Bcl-2, c-Myc, and MUM1, with Ki-67 ~70% and positive IgH and IgK gene rearrangements.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (non-GCB subtype; confirmed by CEUS and laparoscopic liver biopsy/resection pathology and immunohistochemistry) complicated by opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), Staphylococcus aureus, and HHV-5 (CMV) co-infection (confirmed by BALF mNGS) as well as nosocomial COVID-19 infection. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric moxifloxacin and subsequent piperacillin plus minocycline/doxycycline failed to resolve the fever. Following BALF mNGS identification of P. jirovecii and S. aureus, treatment was adjusted to compound sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), meropenem, vancomycin, and methylprednisolone, which resolved the high fevers. Because the 1.4 x 1.1 cm right hepatic nodule persisted and demonstrated malignant washout on CEUS, laparoscopic biopsy and resection were performed, establishing primary hepatic DLBCL, and the patient was referred to hematology for DA-EPOCH chemotherapy.

raw_case_text:
The investigations arose from the proband, a 48-year-old female of Asian origin who was previously well other than a history of schizophrenia, presenting to the hospital with 6 months of persistent cough and worsening breathlessness. Chest imaging revealed diffuse ground glass opacities. The patient rapidly deteriorated and required intubation for severe type I respiratory failure requiring veno-venous extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation assistance. The clinical course of the patient is as described in  Supplementary Figure S1A . Bronchoalveolar lavage examination revealed Pneumocystis jirovecii on microscopy. Treatment with trimethoprim-cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMX) and adjunctive corticosteroids was promptly initiated. Despite repeat negative HIV tests, the patient had an absolute CD4+ count of 25 cells/microl. Over 6 weeks, she progressively improved before discharge 3 months later. As her CD4+ counts had remained consistently low, the patient was prescribed long-term TMP-SMX as a secondary prophylaxis and remained stable.
Given that the atypicality of the clinical course was suggestive of underlying immunodeficiency, whole exome sequencing was performed. The sequencing revealed two heterozygous rare variants of TRAP1 on chromosome 16p13 (GRCh37): one at g.3739109 C>G (exon 3) resulting in amino acid switch from Glutamate-to-Glutamine at protein position 93 (E93Q) ( Figure 1A ) and another at g.3740885 C>T (exon 2) resulting in alanine-to-threonine switch at position 64 (A64T) ( Figure 1A ). Both E93Q and A64T SNPs lie in the N-terminal ATP-binding domain (NTD) of TRAP1 and were predicted to be deleterious in-silico ( Figure 1B ;  Supplementary Table S1 ).
Western blot and qRT-PCR analysis of the patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) revealed diminished TRAP1 expression and transcript ( Figure 1C ,  Supplementary Figure S1B ). TRAP1 had previously been shown to protect against apoptosis. In line with those data, we observed increased cleaved, active caspase-3 and caspase-7 in the patient's cells, which may be associated with an overall decline in TRAP1 expression ( Figure 1C ). Caspase-3 mediates apoptosis by activating Cyclophilin D (CypD), an isomerase that regulates the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. This pore allows the release of pro-apoptotic factors from the mitochondria into the cytoplasm, initiating mitochondria-mediated apoptosis. Indeed, CypD was accentuated ( Figure 1C ), in line with caspase-3 augmentation in the patient's cells.
As caspase 3 can co-activate caspase-1, the downstream mediator of inflammasome activation that leads to interleukin-1 beta (IL-1beta) secretion, we stained for cleaved caspase 1 and IL-1beta. We observed increased caspase-1 cleavage and mature IL-1beta in the patient's cells treated with TLR1/2 or TLR4 ligands, suggesting that the mutant TRAP1s exacerbate inflammasome activation ( Figures 1C, E ,  Supplementary Figure S1C ). However, the aggravated apoptosis exerted a limited inhibitory effect on the NFkappaB complex through NFkappaB2, NFkappaB1, and RelB ( Figure 1D ).
When plasmids containing WT or mutant TRAP1 (E93Q, A64T, or the double E93Q/A64T mutant) were transfected into A549 cells, any mutant, whether single or double, was expressed lower compared to the WT protein itself. The mutants re-capitulated the immunotypic phenotype as was observed in the patient: enhanced cleaved caspase-3, caspase-7, and CypD. Of note, enhanced caspase activity was more evident in E93Q over A64T in line with in-silico prediction, and an additive effect was observed with co-expressed E93Q-A64T double mutant ( Figure 1E ). As was observed in patient cells, mutant TRAP1 reduced NFkappaB signaling, with the most prominent inhibitory effect on NFkappaB1, RelB and p65 activity observed in double E93Q/A64T mutant.
As the presentation with PjP suggested that the effects of mutant TRAP1 was exacerbated during PjP infection, we infected TRAP1-transfected A549 human lung cells with P. jiroveci. Compared against WT-TRAP1, cells expressing the A64T or E93Q variant displayed reduced viability to P. jiroveci infection. In particular, dual E93Q/A64T-transfected cells exhibited highest cell loss (>80%) ( Figure 1F ).
The increased apoptotic markers found in patient PBMCs in the presence of idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia suggest that CD4+ T cells are especially sensitive to TRAP1 dysfunction. To confirm this hypothesis, patient cells were treated with staurosporine to induce apoptosis. At rest and 6 hours after staurosporine treatment, the patient's PBMC gated on CD4+ cells showed elevated annexin-V-positive, propodium iodide(PI)-negative cells in the apoptotic stage compared to healthy controls. Following staurosporine, the patient's annexin-V-positive, PI-positive cells marking cell death significantly doubled ( Figure 1G ). Collectively, our results suggest that the patient's CD4+ lymphopenia was a result of increased apoptosis.
As TRAP1 regulates mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and suppresses ROS production, we next evaluated the effect of TRAP1 mutation on ROS production. Total ROS production, as measured by 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein, was incrementally elevated in mutant-TRAP1 cells relative to WT ( Figure 2A ; top panel). Specifically, when stained with mito-SOX which probed specifically for mito-ROS, the frequency and median fluorescence intensity of E93Q- and A64T-transfected cells increased relative to WT ( Figure 2A ; bottom panel). Notably, dual-E93Q/A64T cells had 6-fold increased mito-ROS ( Figure 2A ; bottom panel). Similarly, the patient's PBMC demonstrated markedly increased total and mito-ROS ( Figure 2B ).
As previous studies have shown the involvement of TRAP1 in regulating OXPHOS and glycolysis, Seahorse Mito Stress and glycolytic rate assays were performed on A549 cells transfected with the respective TRAP1 variants. Compared to cells transfected with WT-TRAP1 or empty vector, the double E93Q/A64T mutant expressing cells had the most markedly reduced mitochondrial respiration over the single mutants, as measured by the Mito-Stress assay ( Figure 2C ). To determine if the OXPHOS defects were due to electron transport chain (ETC) defects, we ran a BN-PAGE to look at the ETC complexes. There were no differences, suggesting that TRAP1 altered the efficiencies of ETC complexes rather than their assembly ( Supplementary Figure S2 ). Similar to the observed decrease in mitochondrial respiration, the double mutant displayed a guarded reduction in the ability to increase glycolysis when the electron transport chain was blocked ( Figure 2D ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old Asian female presented with a 6-month history of persistent cough and progressively worsening breathlessness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been previously physically well, experienced 6 months of persistent cough and progressive dyspnea prior to hospital presentation, where she rapidly deteriorated into severe type I respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of schizophrenia; otherwise previously healthy with no known history of immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic cough and progressive breathlessness for 6 months.

objective.physical_examination: Rapid respiratory deterioration into severe type I respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
objective.routine_investigations: Serial HIV testing: Repeatedly negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest imaging: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) microscopy: Directly identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms. Lymphocyte subsets: Profound idiopathic CD4+ T-cell lymphocytopenia with an absolute CD4+ count of 25 cells/μL. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and functional immunogenetics: Identified compound/double rare heterozygous missense variants in the N-terminal ATP-binding domain of TRAP1 on chromosome 16p13 (GRCh37): g.3739109C>G (exon 3, p.Glu93Gln / E93Q) and g.3740885C>T (exon 2, p.Ala64Thr / A64T). PBMC and A549 functional assays demonstrated diminished TRAP1 protein/mRNA expression, increased cleaved caspase-3, caspase-7, and Cyclophilin D (CypD), heightened caspase-1/IL-1beta inflammasome activation, reduced NF-kappaB signaling, 6-fold increased mitochondrial ROS (mito-SOX), impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic reserve on Seahorse assays, and accelerated CD4+ T-cell apoptosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Life-threatening Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by BAL microscopy) requiring VV-ECMO, secondary to idiopathic CD4+ T-cell lymphocytopenia (CD4+ count 25 cells/μL) driven by deleterious digenic/compound heterozygous TRAP1 variants (p.E93Q and p.A64T) causing mitochondrial dysfunction, excess mitochondrial ROS, and accelerated CD4+ T-cell apoptosis. Plan and clinical course: Managed with endotracheal intubation, VV-ECMO support, intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), and adjunctive corticosteroids. She progressively improved over 6 weeks, was discharged after 3 months, and remained clinically stable on long-term secondary TMP-SMX prophylaxis due to persistently low CD4+ counts.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old Colombian male patient with HIV/AIDS diagnosis, characterized by a CD4 cell count of 28 cells/mm3 and a plasma HIV RNA level of 566.357 copies/mL, started antiretroviral therapy (ART) with zidovudine combined with lamivudine and efavirenz. Thirty days after the HIV/AIDS diagnosis and the start of the therapy (day 0), the patient complained of asthenia, fatigue, odynophagia, headache, dizziness, nausea, inappetence, diarrhea, and cough with expectoration of white sputum. These symptoms had persisted for the previous 15 days. No alteration of vital signs was registered. Physical examination revealed cachexia, pale conjunctiva, ulcerative lesions of the oral mucosa, and painful hepatomegaly without jaundice. No other physical abnormalities were identified. Laboratory tests were requested, and the results thus obtained are shown in Table 1.
Blood cultures for fungi, mycobacteria, and anaerobic and aerobic bacteria were drawn. H. capsulatum urine antigen, serum Aspergillus galactomannan, and Cryptococcus spp. antigen were requested. A stool wet mount microscopic examination, modified Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain for fecal smears, and stool culture were carried out. Parasites and Cryptosporidium spp. were not observed, nor were enteropathogenic bacteria isolated. The patient had oral ulcers clinically compatible with herpetic stomatitis. He was not receiving TMP-SMX for PJP prophylaxis. Therefore, treatment with intravenous (IV) acyclovir 500 mg every eight hours was initiated for seven days. Additionally, PJP prophylaxis was started with IV TMP-SMX 160/800 mg daily.
On day 1, a local allergic reaction appeared, prompting the replacement of PJP TMP-SMX prophylaxis with oral dapsone 50 mg/dose and pyrimethamine 25 mg/dose weekly. Additionally, calcium folinate therapy was added. At this time, the patient underwent a colonoscopy and a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the head, which revealed no abnormalities. However, chest contrast-enhanced CT showed a ground-glass and micronodular miliary pattern (Figure 1), suggesting both PJP and either histoplasmosis or milliary tuberculosis. Therefore, a ZN stain was requested on a clinical sample obtained via bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). On day 2, PJP prophylaxis was discontinued due to chest contrast-enhanced CT findings. Treatment with IV clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours and oral primaquine 30 mg/day therapy was then started. Additionally, because of the high suspicion of histoplasmosis, IV amphotericin deoxycholate B 50 mg/day was administered. Due to low hemoglobin levels (8.0 g/dL), zidovudine/lamivudine was withdrawn, and emtricitabine/tenofovir 200 mg/300mg plus efavirenz 600 mg/day was started. Blood chemistry revealed a high level of liver enzymes x3 times the upper limit of normal (alanine aminotransferase 153 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 108 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase x5 (ALP 688 U/L), raising suspicion of hepatic infiltration (Table 2). Consequently, a laparoscopic liver biopsy was performed, and the samples were sent for histological assessment, Gram staining, direct potassium hydroxide examination, ZN stain, and modified Kinyoun stain for Nocardia spp. Cultures for aerobic bacteria, fungi, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were also performed. Additionally, the molecular genetic test GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Ultra) was used for M. tuberculosis DNA detection.
On day 3, the HIV viral load was quantified, and clinical samples for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and cryptococcal capsular antigen detection were obtained. On day 4, sputum ZN staining was performed, and no acid-fast bacilli were observed. With this result and considering clinical improvement, treatment for tuberculosis was not recommended, and suspicion of histoplasmosis increased. On day 5, the results of the aerobic bacteria culture on the liver tissue were negative. On day 6, the Platelia  Aspergillus assay (Bio-Rad, Marnes-la-Coquette, France) was performed for Aspergillus galactomannan serum detection, according to the manufacturer's instructions. The result of the test was 3.27 (cutoff index >0.5 is reported as positive).
On day 8, the HIV viral load was measured and showed a significant decrease to 74 copies/mL, compared to the initial value of 566,357 copies/mL. Hepatitis B surface antigen was measured at 0.51 cutoff index (COI; reference range: 0-0.89 COI), and the immunoglobulin M antibody to hepatitis B core was at 0.08 COI (reference range: 0-0.99 COI). The hepatitis B DNA PCR test result was less than 117 international units (IU)/mL (reference range: 0-117 IU/mL). The antibody test for hepatitis C showed 0.05 COI (reference range: 0-0.89 COI). Based on these results, hepatitis B and C infections were ruled out. Additionally, the cryptococcal antigen test yielded negative results. The level of creatinine increased to 1.34 mg/dL, which was assumed to be due to amphotericin B nephrotoxicity. On day 11, the patient presented acute kidney injury (creatinine: 1.6 mg/dL). Consequently, amphotericin B was infused over 24 hours, and renal function improved by day 14. On day 15, BAL was obtained via fiberoptic bronchoscopy to detect M. tuberculosis, fungi, or bacteria.
On day 16, microbiological results of staining for bacteria and molecular tests for M. tuberculosis in BAL and liver tissue were negative, but Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining revealed cyst-like (ascii) structures of P. jirovecii in the BAL sample (Figure 2). This finding was confirmed by PCR. Furthermore, cystic-like structures (ascii) of P. jirovecii were observed in liver tissue stained with GMS (Figure 3). Additionally, Histoplasma urine antigen (IMMY, Norman, OK, USA) was detected.
On day 17, the patient showed significant improvement in clinical and laboratory outcomes, leading to his discharge home. For outpatient treatment, amphotericin B therapy was replaced by oral itraconazole 200 mg every 12 hours until the CD4 cell count exceeds 200/mL. Additionally, clindamycin 600 mg orally every eight hours and primaquine 30 mg/day orally were prescribed for another five days. Furthermore, primary prophylaxis against PJP was prescribed with TMP-SMX 160/800 mg orally three times a week, along with loratadine 10 mg orally daily to mitigate mild allergies.
On day 42, the H. capsulatum infection was confirmed through fungal isolation from blood cultures (Figures 4, 5). The identification of H. capsulatum was further confirmed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time of flight mass spectrometry. The patient recovered from his infection; however, follow-up was discontinued after he moved to a different medical center for social security reasons.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old Colombian male with newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS presented 30 days after starting antiretroviral therapy with a 15-day history of asthenia, fatigue, odynophagia, headache, dizziness, nausea, anorexia, diarrhea, and productive cough with white sputum.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Thirty days prior to presentation, the patient was diagnosed with advanced HIV/AIDS (baseline CD4 count 28 cells/mm3, HIV RNA viral load 566,357 copies/mL) and initiated on antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz) without PJP prophylaxis. Fifteen days after starting ART, he developed progressive asthenia, fatigue, painful swallowing, headache, dizziness, nausea, loss of appetite, diarrhea, and cough with white sputum expectoration lasting 15 days up to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS diagnosed 30 days prior to admission (baseline CD4 28 cells/mm3, HIV viral load 566,357 copies/mL).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for asthenia, fatigue, odynophagia, oral ulcers, headache, dizziness, nausea, inappetence, diarrhea, and cough with white sputum. Developed a localized allergic reaction to IV TMP-SMX on hospital day 1. Home medications included zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs within normal limits on admission. General and systemic examination: Cachexia, pale conjunctivae, ulcerative lesions of the oral mucosa compatible with herpetic stomatitis, and tender hepatomegaly without jaundice; remainder of exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission and hospital laboratory tests: Severe anemia (hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL), elevated transaminases at 3x ULN (ALT 153 U/L, AST 108 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase at 5x ULN (ALP 688 U/L); serum creatinine rose to 1.34 mg/dL on day 8 and 1.6 mg/dL on day 11 during amphotericin B therapy before recovering by day 14. Virological and serological panel (day 8): HIV RNA viral load decreased to 74 copies/mL (from 566,357 copies/mL); HBsAg 0.51 COI (negative), anti-HBc IgM 0.08 COI (negative), HBV DNA <117 IU/mL, anti-HCV 0.05 COI (negative); serum Cryptococcus antigen negative. Stool studies: Wet mount, modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain, and stool cultures negative for parasites, Cryptosporidium spp., and enteropathogenic bacteria. Sputum ZN stain (day 4): Negative for acid-fast bacilli.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count: 28 cells/mm3. Endoscopy and neuroimaging (day 1): Colonoscopy and contrast-enhanced head CT normal. Contrast-enhanced chest CT (day 1): Diffuse ground-glass opacities with a micronodular miliary pattern. Fungal biomarkers and cultures: Serum Aspergillus galactomannan index positive at 3.27 (cutoff >0.5 on day 6, reflecting cross-reactivity with Histoplasma); positive urinary Histoplasma capsulatum antigen (IMMY, day 16); blood fungal cultures grew Histoplasma capsulatum on day 42 (confirmed by MALDI-TOF MS). Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL, day 15) and laparoscopic liver biopsy: Negative bacterial cultures, ZN/modified Kinyoun stains, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra in both BAL and liver tissue; Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining and PCR confirmed cyst-like ascus structures of Pneumocystis jirovecii in both BAL fluid and liver biopsy tissue (extrapulmonary hepatic pneumocystosis).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Pneumocystis jirovecii infection (pulmonary PJP and hepatic pneumocystosis confirmed by GMS staining and PCR on BAL fluid and laparoscopic liver biopsy) co-existing with disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection (confirmed by positive urinary Histoplasma antigen, cross-reactive serum galactomannan 3.27, and blood culture isolation confirmed by MALDI-TOF MS) and oral herpetic stomatitis in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 28 cells/mm3). Plan and clinical course: Treated initially with IV acyclovir (500 mg q8h for 7 days) for herpetic stomatitis and switched from zidovudine/lamivudine to emtricitabine/tenofovir (200/300 mg) plus efavirenz (600 mg/day) due to anemia (Hb 8.0 g/dL). After a day 1 allergic reaction to prophylactic IV TMP-SMX (briefly substituted with dapsone/pyrimethamine/folinate) and chest CT demonstration of miliary/GGO infiltrates, therapeutic anti-Pneumocystis therapy was initiated on day 2 with IV clindamycin (600 mg q8h) plus oral primaquine (30 mg/day), alongside IV amphotericin B deoxycholate (50 mg/day, infused over 24 h after day 11 for reversible AKI) for histoplasmosis. Following significant clinical and laboratory improvement, he was discharged on day 17 on oral clindamycin (600 mg q8h) and primaquine (30 mg/day) for 5 additional days, secondary PJP prophylaxis with thrice-weekly TMP-SMX (160/800 mg) plus daily loratadine (10 mg), and maintenance oral itraconazole (200 mg q12h).

raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital on May 3, 2022, due to fever and cough for 3 days; respiratory symptoms worsened and dyspnea developed 1 day prior to admission. Fever was present during this period, and body temperature fluctuating between 37.4 C and 38.3 C. Her respiratory symptoms were characterized by dry cough and progressive dyspnea. She was treated with antibiotics in another hospital, but the symptoms did not improve. Therefore, she was transferred to our department.
She was diagnosed with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in November 2021 at an another hospital. She was initiated on oral prednisone at a dose of 2 mg/kg/day, which was gradually tapered. At the time of admission to our hospital, she was receiving prednisone 15 mg twice daily.
On admission, the girl was alert, communicative, tachypneic (RR 50/min) with fine basal rales on chest auscultation; and no special conditions in other important organs and systems.
Laboratory examination: white blood cell count (WBC) 5.85 x 109/L, neutrophil (NE) 4.92 x 109/L, hemoglobin (HGB) 108 g/L, platelets (PLT) 261 x 109/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 25.2 mg/L (reference range 0-3), procalcitonin (PCT) 0.27 ng/ml (reference range 0-0.05), plasma (1,3)-beta- D-glucan test (BDG) 154.2 pg/ml (reference range 0-60), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1495 U/L (reference range 120-246), serum ferritin level 282.6 ng/ml(reference range 4-204). Gram-negative bacteria lipopolysaccharide was negative. Serology assays for HIV, CMV, HCV, and HBV were negative. Liver and renal function, electrolytes, and myocardial enzymes were normal. The serum levels of immunoglobulin M, G, and A were normal. The CD4+ lymphocyte count, B lymphocyte count and NK cell count were normal. Blood gas analysis: PH 7.39,pCO2 26 mmHg,pO2 50 mmHg,Lac 0.7 mmol/L,BE -8 mmol/L,SaO2 88.7%. Chest X-ray indicated diffuse exudative lesion in both lungs (Figure 1).
After admission, she was intubated and mechanically ventilated. Meropenem was used for anti-infective treatment. On the third day after hospitalization, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of blood detected Pneumocystis jirovecii with a specific sequence number of 326 (Figure 2A). mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) also detected Pneumocystis jirovecii with the specific sequence number of 2644 (Figure 2B), and the antibiotics were adjusted to caspofungin combined with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ). 6 days after admission, the blood and BALF bacterial culture was negative. The girl was treated with prone position ventilation, due to pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (pARDS) was considered. Despite above treatments, the child's respiratory condition did not improve. On the 10th day, her body temperature fluctuated between 38 C and 40 C, laboratory examination showed that WBC, NE, HGB and PLT decreased to 0.65 x 109/L, 0.14 x 109/L, 62 g/L, 51 x 109/L, respectively; serum ferritin level was increased progressively at 1351.76 ng/ml; fibrinogen (FIB) was reduced to 1 g/L; triglycerides increased to 3.85 mmol/L; an NK cell activity assay was 2% (reference range >= 4%); solubleinter leukin-2 receptor levels (sCD25) was 2421 U/ml (reference range 223-710) (Figure 3).
