Due to the laboratory testing limitations of our hospital (the hospital's clinical laboratory does not have the corresponding detection kits and technical platforms for these two biomarkers), IL-18 and CD163 were not tested. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed extensive ground-glass opacities (GGO) in both lungs (Figure 4). Bone marrow aspirate showed an extensive hemophagocytosis (Figure 5). So she was diagnosed with HLH, but her parents refused to complete genetic investigations. Given the severity of the pulmonary infection, she was treated with dexamethasone in combination with continuous renal replacement treatment (CRRT) and plasmapheresis instead of chemotherapy. Unfortunately, her pulmonary infection was getting worse (Ventilator parameters: FIO2 100%, PEEP 12cmH2O, VT 6 ml/kg), and she was discharged on day 22, because her parents gave up treatment. We knew that she died on the day of discharge, through telephone follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old girl on oral prednisone for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura presented with a 3-day history of fever and dry cough and a 1-day history of rapidly worsening dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever (fluctuating between 37.4 °C and 38.3 °C) and a dry cough 3 days prior to admission on May 3, 2022, which progressed to severe dyspnea 1 day prior to admission despite empiric antibiotic treatment at an outside hospital. Six months earlier (November 2021), she had been diagnosed with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and started on oral prednisone (initially 2 mg/kg/day, maintained at 15 mg twice daily at the time of admission).
subjective.past_medical_history: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) diagnosed in November 2021, treated with continuous oral prednisone for 6 months.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever (37.4–38.3 °C), dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. Home medication was oral prednisone 15 mg twice daily.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Alert and communicative, marked tachypnea with respiratory rate 50 breaths/min, and fine basilar rales on chest auscultation; remainder of systemic exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission arterial blood gas: pH 7.39, pCO2 26 mmHg, pO2 50 mmHg, lactate 0.7 mmol/L, base excess -8 mmol/L, and SaO2 88.7%. Admission laboratory tests: WBC 5.85 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 4.92 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 108 g/L, platelets 261 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 25.2 mg/L (reference: 0–3 mg/L), procalcitonin (PCT) 0.27 ng/mL (reference: 0–0.05 ng/mL), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1,495 U/L (reference: 120–246 U/L), and serum ferritin 282.6 ng/mL (reference: 4–204 ng/mL). Negative/normal baseline studies: Negative Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide, negative HIV, CMV, HBV, and HCV serologies, negative blood and BALF bacterial cultures (day 6), and normal hepatic/renal function, electrolytes, myocardial enzymes, and serum IgG, IgA, and IgM. Admission chest X-ray: Diffuse bilateral exudative pulmonary lesions. Day 10 HLH progression labs: Pancytopenia with WBC 0.65 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.14 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 62 g/L, and platelets 51 x 10^9/L; serum ferritin surged to 1,351.76 ng/mL; fibrinogen decreased to 1 g/L; triglycerides rose to 3.85 mmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission fungal biomarker and lymphocyte subsets: Elevated plasma (1,3)-beta-D-glucan (BDG) at 154.2 pg/mL (reference: 0–60 pg/mL); normal baseline CD4+ T-cell, B-cell, and NK-cell counts. Day 3 metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Peripheral blood mNGS detected 326 specific sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS detected 2,644 specific sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii. Day 10 secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) workup: Chest CT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs); NK-cell activity decreased to 2% (reference >=4%); soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) elevated to 2,421 U/mL (reference: 223–710 U/mL); bone marrow aspirate demonstrated extensive hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by 2,644 reads on BALF mNGS, 326 reads on blood mNGS, plasma BDG 154.2 pg/mL, and LDH 1,495 U/L) complicated by pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (pARDS) and secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; confirmed by bone marrow hemophagocytosis, pancytopenia, ferritin 1,351.76 ng/mL, hypofibrinogenemia 1 g/L, hypertriglyceridemia 3.85 mmol/L, NK activity 2%, and sCD25 2,421 U/mL) in a 10-year-old girl on chronic corticosteroids for ITP. Plan and clinical course: Immediately intubated for invasive mechanical ventilation (with prone positioning) and started on empiric meropenem, which was switched on day 3 after mNGS confirmation to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) plus caspofungin. When she developed high fevers (38–40 °C) and secondary HLH on day 10, she was treated with intravenous dexamethasone, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), and plasmapheresis. Despite maximal ventilatory support (FiO2 100%, PEEP 12 cmH2O), her respiratory failure worsened; her parents elected to withdraw care on day 22, and she died on the day of discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old Caucasian girl was diagnosed with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (CD), Paris classification L3, L4a, B1, G1, having presented with growth failure and abdominal pain and having undergone endoscopic and magnetic resonance enterography assessment. She failed exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) and was treated with oral prednisone tapered over 3 months with maintenance azathioprine (AZA) (2 mg/kg/day). Treatment resulted in resolution of clinical symptoms and improved biochemical markers. She had recurrence of symptoms after 9 months with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Infective work-up was negative and she was commenced on oral budesonide 9 mg and her AZA dose was increased (2.5 mg/kg/day). Thiopurine metabolites at this stage were normal [6-TGN 278 pmol/8 x 108 (normal range 230-400), 6-MMPN 734 pmol/8 x 108 (normal range <5,700)].
Three months later, she presented with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. On examination, she was hypoxic with SaO2 90% despite 15 l/min high flow oxygen. She had severe lymphopenia (0.0 x 109/l on manual count), elevated white cell count (10.8 x 109/l), raised C-reactive protein (268 mg/l), and lactate dehydrogenase was 763 U/l. Chest X-ray showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates (Figure 1). She required intensive care for bi-level positive airway pressure respiratory support. AZA and budesonide were discontinued and she was commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam, clarithromycin, and oseltamivir to provide empiric coverage against bacteria (including atypical) and influenza, with minimal improvement in symptoms. An induced sputum sample was negative for bacterial and viral pathogens [culture and broad panel polymerase chain reaction (PCR)] but revealed P. jirovecii on silver stain (Figure 2). Intravenous (IV) trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 20 mg/kg TMP/100 mg/kg SMX and methylprednisone 1 mg/kg twice daily were initiated, which resulted in improvement in respiratory status and weaning of respiratory support over 7 days.
Prior to discharge, she was investigated for an underlying primary immunodeficiency. Human immunodeficiency (HIV) testing was negative and immunoglobulin levels were normal. B and T cell panel revealed a low absolute count of CD3, CD4, and CD8 (0.47, 0.36, 0.14 x 109/l respectively) with normal number of B cells (0.43 x 109/l), normal CD4/CD8 ratio (2.43), and a good response to previous diphtheria and tetanus vaccines. She remained lymphopenic during admission, but this slowly improved. Notably, at IBD diagnosis, she had normal lymphocyte levels [lymphocyte count 1.7-2.6 (normal range 0.9-3.5 x 109/l)]; however, after AZA initiation, she had intermittent lymphopenia (0.4-1.2 x 109/l). Thiopurine methyltransferase activity testing was unfortunately unavailable at diagnosis.
She was discharged on oral TMP-SMX for 21 days, having had 3 days of IV therapy. She received 3 days of methylprednisone followed by 5 days of oral prednisone, which was tapered over 2.5 months. AZA was restarted at a reduced dose (1.5 mg/kg/day). Within 2 months, she had normal lymphocyte numbers with a normal absolute CD4 count (0.56 x 109/l) and normal T-cell numbers. She developed an urticarial rash thought to be secondary to TMP-SMX 4 days post discharge and was changed to oral clindamycin and primaquine to complete the 21-day treatment course. She was then started on prophylactic oral dapsone, which was discontinued when she developed arthralgia. She has not subsequently taken PCP prophylaxis.
One year post-PCP admission, she was commenced on adalimumab monotherapy due to ongoing poor growth, abdominal pain, and an elevated fecal calprotectin (>1,800 mug/g). This resulted in resolution of symptoms, catch-up growth, and progression through puberty. She has had no further significant infections in the last 5 years and her lymphocyte count has remained stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old Caucasian girl with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease presented with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea three months after escalating azathioprine and adding oral budesonide.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (Paris L3, L4a, B1, G1) after presenting with growth failure and abdominal pain, the patient had initially been treated with a 3-month oral prednisone taper and maintenance azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day), during which she exhibited intermittent lymphopenia (0.4–1.2 x 10^9/L vs. pre-treatment baseline 1.7–2.6 x 10^9/L). Nine months into therapy, a clinical flare of abdominal pain and diarrhea prompted adding oral budesonide (9 mg daily) and increasing azathioprine to 2.5 mg/kg/day (with normal thiopurine metabolites: 6-TGN 278, 6-MMPN 734). Three months later, she presented with 3 days of fever, dry cough, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (Paris classification L3, L4a, B1, G1) with growth failure; azathioprine-induced intermittent lymphopenia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, dry cough, and severe progressive dyspnea. Subsequent post-discharge drug allergies/adverse reactions included urticarial rash to TMP-SMX and arthralgia to dapsone. Home medications on admission were azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg/day) and oral budesonide (9 mg/day).

objective.physical_examination: Severely hypoxemic on admission with SaO2 90% despite 15 L/min high-flow supplemental oxygen, requiring pediatric ICU admission for bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Profound lymphopenia with absolute manual lymphocyte count 0.0 x 10^9/L (baseline 1.7–2.6 x 10^9/L, normal: 0.9–3.5 x 10^9/L), WBC 10.8 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 268 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 763 U/L. Immunological screening: HIV negative; normal serum immunoglobulin levels; preserved vaccine antibody responses to diphtheria and tetanus. Admission chest X-ray: Bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Induced sputum microbiological analysis: Negative bacterial and viral cultures and broad-panel respiratory PCR, but silver stain directly identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms. Pre-discharge lymphocyte subset phenotyping: Depressed absolute T-cell subsets with CD3+ 0.47 x 10^9/L, CD4+ 0.36 x 10^9/L, and CD8+ 0.14 x 10^9/L (normal CD4/CD8 ratio 2.43 and normal B-cell count 0.43 x 10^9/L; CD4+ count normalized to 0.56 x 10^9/L within 2 months).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by positive silver staining of induced sputum, LDH 763 U/L, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates) secondary to azathioprine- and budesonide-induced profound T-cell lymphopenia (manual lymphocyte count 0.0 x 10^9/L) in a 12-year-old girl with Crohn's disease. Plan and clinical course: Azathioprine and budesonide were stopped, BiPAP support was instituted in the PICU, and after minimal response to empiric piperacillin-tazobactam, clarithromycin, and oseltamivir, targeted intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX 20 mg/kg TMP / 100 mg/kg SMX) plus IV methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days, then oral prednisone tapered over 2.5 months) were initiated, weaning her off respiratory support over 7 days. Four days after discharge on oral TMP-SMX, an urticarial drug rash prompted switching to oral clindamycin plus primaquine to complete the 21-day course (and subsequent prophylactic dapsone was stopped due to arthralgia). One year later, she was transitioned to adalimumab monotherapy with sustained remission, catch-up growth, and stable lymphocyte counts over 5 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 9-month-old boy was admitted to our unit due to dry cough and wheezing for 2 weeks, and tachypnea for 5 days. He is the second child of nonconsanguineous parents with an uneventful birth history. Medical history revealed three prior episodes of lower respiratory tract infections necessitating hospitalization and one instance of methylprednisolone treatment before referral to our hospital.
Physical examination revealed that the Z-score of weight for age and weight for height was 0.60; respiratory rate, 66 bpm; heart rate, 156 bpm, and temperature, 36.6 C. A depression of the suprasternal and supraclavicular fossa with coarse breath sounds without rale were noted in both lungs. The liver and spleen were non-palpable below the costal margin. Laboratory data showed a high white blood cell count, 30.61 x 109 cells/L, with 41.1% neutrophils; hemoglobin, 130 g/L; hypersensitive C-reactive protein, <1 mg/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 8.0 mm/h, and serum lactate dehydrogenase, 323 U/L (normal range, 135.0-215.0 U/L). Additionally, low levels of immunoglobulin A, 0.04 g/L (normal range, 0.10-0.56 g/L) and immunoglobulin G, 0.15 g/L (normal range, 3.60-9.20 g/L), and normal levels of immunoglobulin M, 0.48 g/L (normal range 0.40-1.28 g/L), were found. T cell subsets:CD19+, CD20+, CD4+, CD4+, and CD4+/CD8+-were in their normal ranges. Screening tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis C, mycobacteria, nocardia, Epstein-Barr virus, and fungal pathogens were negative or within normal range. Antinuclear, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-smooth muscle actin, anti-ribonucleoprotein, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, respectively.
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed ground-glass density images in both lungs (Figure 1). On the 7th day of hospitalization, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and lung biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. The bronchoalveolar lavage fluid appeared milky (Figure 2A), while hematoxylin-eosin staining showed extensive macrophage infiltration in the alveolar and bronchial cavities without evidence of fibrosis and hexamine-silver staining for bronchoalveolar lavage fluid revealed the presence of P. jirovecii (Figure 2B). Moreover, large amount of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain-positive and diastase-Periodic acid-Schiff (D-PAS) stain-positive substance was found in the alveolar and bronchial cavities (Figures 3A,B), consistent with pathological characteristics of PAP and non-specific interstitial pneumonia.
Whole exome sequencing was conducted by Huada Inspection Center (Shenzhen, China) to detect gene mutation related to immunodeficiency, alveolar surface-active substance or inherited disorder associated with PAP. A c.511dupA hemizygous mutation in the EX5E region of the CD40 ligand (CD40LG, OMIM 300386) gene, present on Xq26.3 and coding for CD40L protein, was noted. Bioinformatic analysis suggested a frameshift mutation inducing the early termination of the amino acid-encoded protein (p.I171N). Genetic analysis of the patient's parents indicated maternal inheritance of the mutation.
Following the confirmation of P. jirovecii infection, imipenem, sulperazone, and erythromycin were administered intravenously, and sulfamethoxazole was given orally. Meanwhile, sodium bicarbonate tablets were given to alkalize urine and methylprednisolone and human immunoglobulin was used for anti-inflammatory and immune support therapy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was repeated 10 days later, and significant clearing of the lavage fluid was observed. The patient displayed gradual improvement and was eventually discharged on the 48th day of hospitalization.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-month-old boy with a history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and wheezing and a 5-day history of tachypnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant developed a dry cough and wheezing 2 weeks prior to admission, followed by progressive tachypnea for 5 days. Prior to referral, he had experienced three previous hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract infections and had received one course of methylprednisolone.
subjective.past_medical_history: Three prior hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract infections (including one course of methylprednisolone); second child born full-term to non-consanguineous parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, wheezing, and tachypnea.

objective.physical_examination: Anthropometrics and vital signs: Weight-for-age and weight-for-height Z-score 0.60, respiratory rate 66 breaths/min, heart rate 156 beats/min, and temperature 36.6 °C. Chest and abdominal exam: Suprasternal and supraclavicular retractions with bilateral coarse breath sounds without rales; liver and spleen not palpable below the costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Marked leukocytosis with WBC 30.61 x 10^9 cells/L (41.1% neutrophils), hemoglobin 130 g/L, hs-CRP <1 mg/L, ESR 8.0 mm/h, and elevated serum LDH at 323 U/L (normal: 135.0–215.0 U/L). Immunoglobulin profile: Profoundly decreased IgG at 0.15 g/L (normal: 3.60–9.20 g/L) and IgA at 0.04 g/L (normal: 0.10–0.56 g/L) with normal IgM at 0.48 g/L (normal: 0.40–1.28 g/L). Negative infectious and autoimmune screening: Negative HIV, syphilis, HCV, mycobacteria, Nocardia, EBV, and fungal screens; negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-SMA, anti-RNP, and ANCA.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subsets: Normal CD19+, CD20+, CD4+, CD8+, and CD4+/CD8+ T- and B-cell percentages. Chest CT scan: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass density opacities. Hospital day 7 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy: Milky-appearing BAL fluid; hexamine-silver (GMS) staining of BAL fluid identified Pneumocystis jirovecii; lung biopsy H&E, Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), and diastase-PAS (D-PAS) stains demonstrated extensive intra-alveolar and bronchial macrophage infiltration and abundant PAS/D-PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material without fibrosis, diagnostic of secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and parental testing: Identified a maternally inherited hemizygous frameshift mutation in exon 5 of the CD40LG gene (Xq26.3: c.511dupA, p.Ile171Asn / early termination), confirming X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by hexamine-silver staining of milky BAL fluid) complicated by secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP; confirmed by PAS/D-PAS-positive alveolar material on lung biopsy) as the presenting manifestation of X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency caused by a maternally inherited hemizygous CD40LG c.511dupA frameshift mutation). Plan and clinical course: Treated with oral sulfamethoxazole (with oral sodium bicarbonate for urinary alkalinization), intravenous imipenem, cefoperazone-sulbactam (Sulperazone), and erythromycin, systemic methylprednisolone, intravenous human immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement, and repeat therapeutic bronchoalveolar lavage 10 days later (which showed marked clearing of the milky lavage fluid). The infant gradually improved and was discharged on hospital day 48.

raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old previously healthy female visited a local hospital presenting with cough and fever. She had a history of spontaneous abortion twice and underwent induction of labor for a stillborn fetus 2 months before. Subsequently erythema on her face was noticed, accompanied by continuous cough, but no phlegm. Allergic disease was considered, and anti-allergic treatment was given, but her symptoms did not improve. Her condition was then managed with oral prednisolone for 10 days, and the facial erythema and cough disappeared. The patient's clinical course is shown in Figure 1.
On admission, the patient showed no cutaneous and muscular manifestations. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed bilateral ground glass opacities (Figure 2A). Anti-MDA5 antibody was not measured because there was no consideration of CAMD and ILD. After receiving antibiotic therapy for 12 days, the patient's status did not improve and worsened in later stages; the clinical manifestations were shortness of breath and dyspnea. CT of the chest showed bilateral pulmonary patchy infiltrates, and interstitial pneumonia was considered (Figure 2B). Shortly thereafter, the patient presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2: 68 mmHg), and intubation and mechanical ventilation were subsequently performed 3 days after admission. Using next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BLF) sample and cultured isolates from the patients, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Pneumocystis jirovecii were found. Sulfamethoxazole (SMZ) was added for the treatment of pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. The patient' s respiratory status continued to deteriorate, and mediastinal emphysema and subcutaneous emphysema developed 4 days after invasive ventilation.
VV-ECMO via the right internal jugular and right femoral vein cannulation was initiated on ventilator day 4, and she was then referred to the ECMO center. Laboratory investigations revealed that serum anti-Ro-52 was positive via ELISA, and serum ferritin (SF) was significantly higher without elevated serum muscle enzymes. NGS of BLF also showed Pneumocystis jirovecii and Acinetobacter baumannii; thus, antibiotic therapy and SMZ were continued. Considering the COVID-19 epidemic in China, the patient received a nucleic acid test for COVID-19, but the result was negative. CT of the chest showed bilateral pulmonary extensive infiltrates and lobular interstitium thickness, and pulmonary fibrosis was considered (Figure 2C). CT of the head was normal (Figure 3A), and the patient was conscious after withdrawal of the sedative. Although lung protective ventilation, recruitment maneuver and prone position ventilation were implemented, she did not tolerate attempts to wean from ECMO within 28 days of ECMO. She required continuous sedation and analgesia because of patient-ventilator asynchrony.
Therefore, a decision was made to place the patient on the lung transplant waitlist, and she was subsequently transferred to the transplantation center for lung transplant evaluation. Anti-MDA5 antibody was tested by ELISA, and the result was positive. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with CADM and ILD. At 31 days of ECMO, the patient underwent a successful sequential double lung transplant and received tacrolimus as an immunosuppressive regimen after the transplant. Her explant pathology showed extensive consolidation of lung tissue and pulmonary interstitial fibrosis (Figure 4). The patient's respiratory status gradually improved, and CT of the chest showed bilateral pulmonary scattered infiltration (Figure 2D), which was improved compared with previous imageological diagnosis. ECMO was weaned successfully 3 days after transplant, and the patient's oxygenation status did not deteriorate with ventilator support. The patient's state of consciousness deteriorated, and she presented with coma. Head CT showed bilateral parieto-occipital low-density lesions, which were considered to be due to PRES (Figure 3B). Since the condition was considered to be related to immunosuppressive agents, tacrolimus was suspended for 1 day, and the dosage was gradually reduced to 0.5 mg/day, after which the patient's consciousness returned. Unfortunately, the patient developed a disturbance of consciousness once more after hemodynamic instability, which may be related to implant infection; consciousness did not return after active treatment. After 14 days of lung transplant, the patient declined further treatment for financial reasons and was discharged.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old female presented with persistent dry cough, fever, and rapidly progressive dyspnea 2 months after labor induction for a stillborn fetus and recent facial erythema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months after undergoing labor induction for a stillborn fetus, the patient developed facial erythema and a continuous nonproductive cough. Initially misdiagnosed with an allergic condition, she received a 10-day course of oral prednisolone with transient resolution of her facial rash and cough, but subsequently presented to the hospital with recurrent cough, fever, and rapidly progressive hypoxemic dyspnea refractory to 12 days of empiric antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Two prior spontaneous abortions and an induced labor for a stillborn fetus 2 months prior; otherwise previously healthy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recent resolved facial erythema, continuous dry cough, fever, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath; negative for clinical muscle weakness.

objective.physical_examination: No active cutaneous or muscular manifestations on admission; rapidly progressed 3 days after admission to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 68 mmHg) requiring endotracheal intubation, followed 4 days later by ventilator-associated pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema.
objective.routine_investigations: Autoimmune and biochemical workup: Positive serum anti-Ro-52 and anti-MDA5 antibodies by ELISA; markedly elevated serum ferritin with normal serum muscle enzymes; negative SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid test. Head CT scans: Normal prior to transplant; post-transplant coma evaluation showed bilateral parieto-occipital hypodensities diagnostic of tacrolimus-induced posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial chest CT scans: Bilateral ground-glass opacities on admission, progressing to bilateral patchy infiltrates, extensive consolidation, interlobular septal thickening, pneumomediastinum, and diffuse pulmonary fibrosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and cultures: Initial BALF mNGS and cultures identified Pneumocystis jirovecii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; repeat BALF mNGS on VV-ECMO detected persistent Pneumocystis jirovecii and Acinetobacter baumannii. Bilateral explanted lung histopathology (at day 31 of VV-ECMO): Extensive parenchymal consolidation and diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Anti-MDA5 and anti-Ro-52-positive clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM)-associated rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD), complicated by Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed on serial BALF mNGS) and polymicrobial Gram-negative superinfections (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Acinetobacter baumannii), barotrauma (pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema), and ECMO dependence requiring sequential bilateral lung transplantation. Plan and clinical course: Intubated on hospital day 3 and placed on veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) on ventilator day 4 alongside sulfamethoxazole (SMZ) for PCP and targeted broad-spectrum antibiotics. After failing to wean from VV-ECMO over 28 days despite lung-protective and prone ventilation, she underwent sequential bilateral lung transplantation on ECMO day 31 and was successfully weaned off ECMO 3 days post-transplant. Postoperative tacrolimus-induced PRES (bilateral parieto-occipital lesions and coma) transiently reversed with tacrolimus dose reduction (to 0.5 mg/day), but recurrent encephalopathy and hemodynamic instability from suspected graft infection prompted the family to withdraw further treatment for financial reasons on post-transplant day 14.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old woman was admitted to the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University, Hunan, China because of recurrent cough for 6 years and wheezing for 7 months, which aggravated for half a month in May 2021. The patient started to cough sputum early in September 2014, and pulmonary tuberculosis was considered the reason at the local hospital and therefore anti-tuberculosis was given. The symptoms improved significantly until 2015; the patient complained of cough with fever during the anti-tuberculosis therapy and visited our hospital for the first time. Laboratory tests showed an elevated level of leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and serum total IgE (2,500 IU/ml, normal range: <130 IU/ml). The chest CT revealed multiple cavitary lesions in both upper lungs and the dorsal segment of the left lower lung and bronchiectasis of bilateral lobes (Figure 1A). A combined infection of aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus was confirmed by positive culture of both sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Anti-infection with teicoplanin and itraconazole was prescribed, and her symptoms were relieved on therapy. The patient remained stable until 2019; she began coughing intermittently and the symptoms gradually worsened when accompanied with dyspnea and wheezing. She visited our hospital for the second time in December 2020. Blood tests showed a moderately elevated level of eosinophil count (0.97 x 109/L, normal range: 0.02-0.52 x 109/L) and a markedly increased serum total IgE level (>2,500 IU/ml). Total levels of aspergillosis-specific IgE, IgM, and IgG were above normal. A pulmonary function test revealed decreased FVC (2.41 L; expected value: 2.92 L), decreased FEV1 (1.54 L, expected value: 2.53 L), and decreased FEV1/FVC (63.68%, expected value: 84.52%), indicating moderate obstructive pulmonary ventilation dysfunction and positive bronchodilation test (FEV1 increased by 16.8%). The chest CT revealed bilateral multiple bronchiectases, pulmonary bulla, and atelectasis in the right middle lung lobe (Figure 1B). Based on these data, a diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) was made. Oral voriconazole 200 mg two times daily and methylprednisolone 16 mg per day plus inhaler were prescribed but were demonstrated to be insufficient without the improvement of symptoms. Since February 2021, she was given omalizumab 600 mg three times every month; she was readmitted due to the aggravation of cough and wheezing. The patient denied any history of food or drug allergies. Her family history was negative for any inherited genetic diseases.
On physical examination, her body weight was 58 kg on admission. She exhibited facial flushing, a full moony face, buffalo back, and mossy skin changes on the scalp. Moist rales could be heard on bilateral lung fields. Her laboratory findings on admission revealed moderate C-reactive protein level (33.6 mg/l, reference range: 0-6 mg/l) and a normal level of leukocyte count and erythrocyte sedimentation. Serum IgE was above normal (770 IU/ml, reference range: <130 IU/ml); serum -beta-D-glucan test, galactomannan test, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, vasculitis antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Pulmonary CT suggested diffuse multiple ground glass shadows and scattered striae in both lungs and more cystic lesions than previously observed (Figure 1C). Bronchoscopy showed viscous jelly-like secretions in the tracheal lumen. The next-generation sequence (NGS) of BALF indicated Pneumocystis jirovecii (sequence reads 34909), Human Herpes Virus Type 5 (also named CMV, sequence reads 1843), and Human Herpes Virus Type 4 (also named EBV, sequence reads 7). With classic diffuse ground-glass lesions appearing in the chest CT images and high sequence reads of CMV and P. jirovecii in BALF detected by mNGS, we identified that the patient had CMV and P. jirovecii coinfection. The sequence reads of EBV, which is ubiquitous in most of the population, were too few to be identified as pathogenic. SMZ-TMP and ganciclovir were given and symptoms were gradually relieved (Figure 2).
Given that the young patient was predisposed to multiple pathogens, including some opportunistic strains, we carefully reviewed the patient's medical history. Surprisingly, she had multiple skin rashes and pruritus all over the body since childhood. A minor traumatic fracture of the right calf occurred at the age of 12. She underwent cutaneous abscesses requiring incision and drainage at 13 years of age. The patient also had a previous diagnosis of pelvic abscess, tubal occlusion, and primary infertility. The patient had recurrent infections of different strains including opportunistic pathogens in multiple organs, skin rashes, and markedly elevated IgE levels. HIES were suspected, and she scored 45 points on the National Institutes of Health clinical HIES scoring system. Further whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed to screen potential mutations, indicating a heterozygous missense mutation in exon 15 of STAT3 (c.1294G>T, g.62382G>T, p.Val432Leu, NM_139276.2). Consequently, the final diagnosis was made as AD-HIES. Her parents and younger sister are wild-type genotypes. In addition to the standard anti-infection therapy, we prescribed omalizumab 300 mg every 2 weeks and Seretide inhalation. Oral corticosteroids gradually reduced and stopped. During 6 months of follow-up, the patient did not experience recurrent infection. After an initial fluctuation of the level, serum IgE remained stable recently. The patient's symptoms and lung function improved on therapy (Figure 3). The chest CT scan demonstrated improved infiltrates (Figure 1D).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old woman with a 6-year history of recurrent cough and 7 months of wheezing (previously treated with voriconazole, methylprednisolone, and omalizumab for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis) presented in May 2021 with a 2-week acute aggravation of cough and wheezing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed productive cough in September 2014 (initially treated empirically for TB), was diagnosed in 2015 at our hospital with cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus co-infection (serum IgE 2,500 IU/mL; treated with teicoplanin and itraconazole), and in December 2020 was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA; eosinophils 0.97 x 10^9/L, total IgE >2,500 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgM/IgG, moderate reversible airflow obstruction, and bilateral bronchiectasis/bullae). She was treated with oral voriconazole (200 mg BID), oral methylprednisolone (16 mg/day), and—starting February 2021—subcutaneous omalizumab (600 mg three times monthly), before presenting in May 2021 with a 2-week exacerbation of cough and wheezing.
subjective.past_medical_history: Generalized pruritic skin rashes since childhood; minor-trauma right calf fracture at age 12; cutaneous abscesses requiring incision and drainage at age 13; prior pelvic abscess, fallopian tube occlusion, and primary infertility; cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and S. aureus pneumonia (2015); allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA, diagnosed December 2020). Negative family history of genetic diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic recurrent cough (6 years), wheezing (7 months, acutely worse for 2 weeks), childhood pruritic skin rashes, and exogenous Cushingoid changes. Denied food or drug allergies. Home medications were oral methylprednisolone (16 mg/day), oral voriconazole (200 mg BID), inhaled bronchodilator/steroid, and subcutaneous omalizumab (600 mg thrice monthly).

objective.physical_examination: Body weight 58 kg; Cushingoid habitus with facial flushing, full moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad ('buffalo hump'), and mossy scalp skin changes; bilateral moist rales on lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: May 2021 admission laboratory tests: Moderately elevated C-reactive protein (CRP 33.6 mg/L, reference: 0–6 mg/L), normal WBC count and ESR, and elevated serum total IgE at 770 IU/mL (reference <130 IU/mL; previously >2,500 IU/mL in 2015 and Dec 2020 with eosinophils 0.97 x 10^9/L). Negative autoimmune screening: Negative ANA, ANCA, vasculitis antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, ENA panel, and rheumatoid factor. Prior December 2020 pulmonary function tests: Moderate reversible obstructive defect (FVC 2.41 L [expected 2.92 L], FEV1 1.54 L [expected 2.53 L], FEV1/FVC 63.68% [expected 84.52%], bronchodilator FEV1 increase +16.8%).
objective.advanced_workup: May 2021 fungal biomarkers: Negative serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan and negative galactomannan tests. May 2021 chest CT: New diffuse bilateral ground-glass shadows, scattered linear striae, and increased bilateral cystic/bronchiectatic lesions compared to December 2020. Bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Viscous jelly-like secretions in the tracheal lumen; BALF mNGS identified Pneumocystis jirovecii (34,909 sequence reads), human herpesvirus 5 / cytomegalovirus (CMV; 1,843 sequence reads), and background EBV (7 reads). Clinical scoring and whole-exome sequencing (WES): NIH hyper-IgE syndrome clinical score of 45 points; WES identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in exon 15 of STAT3 (NM_139276.2: c.1294G>T, p.Val432Leu; parents and sister wild-type).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES; confirmed by NIH score 45 and a de novo heterozygous STAT3 exon 15 missense mutation c.1294G>T, p.Val432Leu) complicated by allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) and secondary corticosteroid-induced opportunistic co-infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia (confirmed by 34,909 P. jirovecii reads and 1,843 CMV reads on BALF mNGS and diffuse ground-glass opacities on chest CT, despite negative serum beta-D-glucan). Plan and clinical course: Treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-TMP) and intravenous ganciclovir, gradual tapering and discontinuation of systemic oral corticosteroids, maintenance subcutaneous omalizumab (reduced to 300 mg every 2 weeks), and inhaled salmeterol/fluticasone (Seretide). Over 6 months of follow-up, her symptoms, lung function, and chest CT infiltrates improved without recurrent opportunistic infections.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old male was diagnosed with DLBCL (stage IA) after presenting the left leg pain and swelling for 6 months and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan demonstrated abnormalities of the bone marrow cavity of the left tibia suggestive of malignancy. His past medical history included coronary artery disease treated with percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting and atorvastatin, clopidogrel, and beta-blocker therapy. The patient was thus started on R-CHOP chemotherapy, which consisted of rituximab 375 mg/m2 (0.5 g on day 1), cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2 (1.2 g d1), vincristine 1.4 mg/m2 (2 mg d1), doxorubicin liposome (6 mg d1), and prednisone 100 mg (d1-5 q21d).
Overall, each round of R-CHOP treatment went well except for an episode of severe bone marrow suppression after the second chemotherapy cycle, accompanied by bacterial pneumonia, from which the patient recovered with antibiotic therapy. Two weeks after completing the fifth chemotherapy cycle, the patient weighing 64 kg was readmitted to assess the efficacy of the chemotherapy regimen by positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan. On admission, he complained of intermittent mild cough with a small amount of white sputum. The vital signs were normal. There were no palpable lymphadenopathy and auscultation of the lung fields bilaterally demonstrated normal vesicular breath sounds without adventitious sounds. Laboratory results revealed leukocytosis, lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated C-reaction protein level, normal procalcitonin, and normal serum 1-3-beta-D-glucan level (Table 1). The hepatic and renal profiles were within normal limits. Sputum cultures did not isolate any respiratory pathogens and the serum cytomegalo virus (CMV) viral load was undetectable on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. The HIV test was nonreactive during each course. The chest X-ray on admission exhibited patchy shadows in both lung fields (Figure 1).
The patient's PET-CT scan showed that the tumor focus in the lower left tibia had decreased in size and glucose metabolism, suggesting that his lymphoma was in remission. However, multiple patchy and cord-like opacities with increased glucose metabolism were observed in the lungs, indicating pneumonia. Meanwhile, the patient experienced daily fever up to 38.9 C, and had a mild cough with minimal white sputum. He was thus empirically treated with cefoperazone and levofloxacin (Figure 2).
On day 8 of admission, the patient developed dyspnea and hypoxemia, with an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Ganciclovir and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (240 mg/1.2 g q6 h) were administered to cover viruses, bacteria and P. jirovecii (Figure 2). However, the patient's respiratory condition rapidly deteriorated, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) for ventilatory support. He received noninvasive ventilation (NIV), under which the oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2 ratio) was around 100 +- 17, strongly suggesting acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and severe PJP. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) liquid was obtained and sent for bacterial culture and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). BALF-mNGS yielded abundant P. jirovecii DNA. Meanwhile, laboratory tests revealed increased levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (536 U/L) and 1-3-beta-D-glucan (564.6 pg/mL) (Table 1), and complete blood cell counts showed the CD4+ T cell count was 189 cells/microL. In addition, the chest CT showed multiple ground glass opacities (GGOs) in both lungs (Figure 3). Based on the above evidence, the diagnosis of severe PJP in our DLBCL patient was confirmed. The echinocandin, caspofungin (70 mg d1, 50 mg qd) was early added to the standard TMP/SMX (dose increased to 320 mg/1.6 g, q6 h) regimen to eliminate both the cysts and trophic forms of P. jirovecii. Piperacillin + tazobactam, moxifloxacin, and ganciclovir were concurrently administered to cover possible bacterial and viral infections (Figure 2). Systemic methylprednisolone was used to alleviate pneumonia.
On day 11, the patient was intubated and placed on invasive mechanical ventilation due to severe dyspnea. Prone position ventilation was also attempted to improve gas exchange in the lungs. However, repeated chest X-ray findings showed no significant improvement but dilated bowel loops (Figure 4). Since gastrointestinal dysfunction could impair the absorption of oral TMP/SMX and decrease the plasma drug concentration, the patient was switched to intravenous TMP/SMX, supplemented with clindamycin (0.6 g q8 h) (Figure 2).
After treatment with a combination of TMP/SMX, caspofungin, and clindamycin, the oxygenation index was significantly improved, and the levels of LDH and 1-3-beta-D-glucan began to decline (Table 1). With an improvement of the patient's respiratory condition and resorption of pulmonary infiltrates on the repeat chest CT (Figure 5), clindamycin and caspofungin were discontinued after 7 and 10 days of use, respectively, to avoid potential side effects. As the patient's general condition improved, he then was switched to oral TMP/SMX and the dosage was decreased when a mild increase in hepatic transaminases was observed (Table 1). The blood samples were sent to the company (BGI Co., Ltd, Shenzhen) for determination of blood TMP/SMX concentrations sponsored by the pharmaceutical manufacturer, given that intravenous TMP/SMX has only recently become available in mainland China. On day 15, after 3 days of us-ing intravenous TMP/SMX, the trough and peak levels of sulfamethoxazole were, respectively, 152.92 mg/L and 177.98 mg/L, which was reasonable for treating severe PJP, which reportedly requires an effective blood concentration of 150-200 mg/L.
The patient was successfully extubated on day 16 and received high-flow oxygen therapy. After a 10-day ICU stay, he was transferred back to the Oncology Department, where TMP/SMX was prescribed for another 3 weeks. During that period, the patient had no fever or dyspnea, with the ground-glass opacities disappearing on chest X-rays (Figure 6). At follow-up 2 months later, his chest CT revealed no ground-glass opacities, demonstrating a full recovery from PJP and no relapse of pneumonia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male with stage IA diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presented with an intermittent mild cough and scant white sputum two weeks after his fifth cycle of R-CHOP chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been diagnosed with stage IA diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the left tibia (after presenting with 6 months of left leg pain and swelling) and underwent five cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy (rituximab 375 mg/m2 [0.5 g d1], cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2 [1.2 g d1], vincristine 1.4 mg/m2 [2 mg d1], liposomal doxorubicin 6 mg d1, and prednisone 100 mg d1–5 q21d). His course had been complicated after the second cycle by severe myelosuppression and bacterial pneumonia that resolved with antibiotics. Two weeks after completing his fifth cycle, he was readmitted for a restaging PET-CT scan and reported an intermittent mild cough with a small amount of white sputum.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage IA diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the left tibia; coronary artery disease status post percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting; prior episode of chemotherapy-induced severe myelosuppression and bacterial pneumonia after cycle 2 of R-CHOP.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent mild cough with scant white sputum on admission; negative for fever or dyspnea at initial presentation. Home medications included atorvastatin, clopidogrel, and a beta-blocker.

objective.physical_examination: Admission weight 64 kg; vital signs normal on admission; no palpable lymphadenopathy; bilateral lung auscultation showed normal vesicular breath sounds without adventitious sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Leukocytosis, lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), normal procalcitonin, normal hepatic and renal profiles, and normal initial serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan. Microbiological screening: Sputum cultures negative for respiratory pathogens; serum CMV viral load undetectable by PCR; HIV test nonreactive. Admission chest X-ray: Bilateral patchy shadows. On day 8 (upon clinical deterioration): PaO2/FiO2 ratio ~100 ± 17 mmHg on noninvasive ventilation, elevated serum LDH of 536 U/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Restaging PET-CT on admission: Decreased size and glucose metabolism of the left lower tibia lymphoma focus (indicating remission), but multiple bilateral patchy and cord-like pulmonary opacities with increased glucose metabolism suggestive of pneumonia. Day 8 workup during acute hypoxemic deterioration: Chest CT showed multiple bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs); serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan elevated to 564.6 pg/mL; peripheral CD4+ T-cell count 189 cells/μL; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected abundant Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS; PaO2/FiO2 ~100 ± 17) in a patient with DLBCL in remission following R-CHOP immunochemotherapy, definitively confirmed by abundant P. jirovecii DNA on BALF-mNGS, elevated 1,3-beta-D-glucan (564.6 pg/mL), elevated LDH (536 U/L), low CD4+ T-cell count (189 cells/μL), and bilateral GGOs on chest CT. Plan and clinical course: Initially treated empirically with cefoperazone and levofloxacin for daily fevers up to 38.9 °C, then escalated on day 8 (when SpO2 dropped to 90% on room air) to oral TMP/SMX (240 mg/1.2 g q6h), ganciclovir, and ICU noninvasive ventilation. Following BALF-mNGS confirmation, therapy was intensified to high-dose TMP/SMX (320 mg/1.6 g q6h), caspofungin (70 mg day 1, then 50 mg daily), piperacillin-tazobactam, moxifloxacin, ganciclovir, and systemic methylprednisolone. On day 11, he required intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation with prone positioning, and conversion from oral to intravenous TMP/SMX plus IV clindamycin (0.6 g q8h) due to bowel loop dilatation/gastrointestinal dysfunction on CXR (day 15 sulfamethoxazole trough 152.92 mg/L, peak 177.98 mg/L). Oxygenation, LDH, and 1,3-beta-D-glucan subsequently improved; clindamycin and caspofungin were stopped after 7 and 10 days, respectively. He was extubated to high-flow oxygen on day 16, stepped down to reduced-dose oral TMP/SMX (due to mild transaminitis) for 3 additional weeks on the oncology ward, and achieved complete radiographic resolution of GGOs at 2-month follow-up without relapse.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man, nonsmoker, without past medical history especially personal or family history of inherited immunodeficiency disorders or autoimmune diseases, was admitted to the hospital complaining of hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, fever, weight, and appetite loss for 45 days. On examination, the patient was febrile at 38.5 C and hypoxemic (Oxygen saturation on a nasal cannula at 1 L was 91%). The chest X-ray revealed bilateral and extensive alveolar opacities (Figure 1).
Laboratory results indicated the presence of inflammatory syndrome (white blood cell: 11,800/mm3, C-reactive protein: 220 mg/L), hemoglobin: 11.7 g/dL, hepatic cytolysis, and cholestasis. Sputum and blood culture did not yield any organisms. Serology for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative. Pneumococcal antigen urinary testing was negative. The HIV antibody test was negative. Serum rheumatoid factor was positive (64 UI/mL). Antinuclear antibodies, anti-cyclical Citrullinated Peptide antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.
The lymphocyte subpopulations CD4, CD8, and CD4/CD8 were carried out and were normal (1050/mm3, 480/mm3, 2.18%, respectively) .The serum levels of immunoglobulin M, G, and A were within the normal ranges (1.7 g/L, 12 g/L, 2.3 g/L, respectively).
Computed tomography (CT) (Figure 2) revealed multiple diffuse consolidations associated with nodules sometimes displaying necrosis, along with enlarged necrotized bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and pericardial effusion.
The patient was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 1 g x 3 daily for 7 days. On the fifth day, bronchoscopy with bronchial aspiration was performed for cytology, BK testing, and bacteriological examination, and it was normal. The bacteriological study of bronchial fluid has been performed, excluding specific testing for Pneumocystis. Both direct examination and culture were unable to identify any microorganisms. Dyspnea escalated (relying on 5 L per minute with a high-concentration mask and subsequently necessitating noninvasive ventilation due to hypercapnia), while the fever remained. The chest film showed an extension of alveolar opacities (Figure 3). Inflammatory syndrome increased (white blood cell: 16,800/mm3, C-reactive protein: 343 mg/L). Antibiotic therapy switched to imipenem 1 g x 3 daily, vancomycin 1 g x 2 daily for 12 days for both, and levofloxacin 500 mg x 2 daily for 2 days, then 500 mg daily for 10 days.
A second bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and protected distal sampling was conducted due to ongoing fever and the advancement of alveolar opacities. It revealed inflammation throughout the entire bronchial tree mucosa. The protected distal sampling showed a polymorphic pattern. Bronchial biopsy showed an inflammatory mucosa. The bronchial fluid was examined by optic microscopy. It contained inflammatory but not neoplastic cells. A study of bronchial fluid by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) on cellblock revealed a few Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms (Figure 4(a) and 4(b)).
The diagnosis of PCP was established. The patient was, therefore, treated with oral Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim 1600 mg per day in four doses and dexamethasone 40 mg twice per day (which was gradually tapered off) for 3 weeks.
The patient exhibited clinical improvement (afebrile, oxygen saturation: 95% on room air) and biological improvement (white blood cell count: 14,000/mm3, C-reactive protein: 23 mg/L). He was discharged home without complications.
The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic 1 month after discharge from the hospital, and he reported no respiratory complaints. Subsequently, he was lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 42-year-old nonsmoking man presented with a 45-day history of hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, fever, weight loss, and anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had no known medical comorbidities or immunodeficiency risk factors, developed progressive hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, fever, loss of appetite, and weight loss over 45 days prior to hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable; nonsmoker with no personal or family history of inherited immunodeficiency disorders or autoimmune diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, fever, weight loss, and loss of appetite.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile with body temperature 38.5 °C and hypoxemic with SpO2 91% on 1 L/min nasal cannula oxygen.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 11,800/mm3 (later rising to 16,800/mm3), C-reactive protein (CRP) 220 mg/L (later rising to 343 mg/L), hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, and elevated liver transaminases/cholestatic enzymes (hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis). Microbiological screening: Sputum and blood cultures negative; serologies for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydia pneumoniae negative; urinary pneumococcal antigen negative; HIV antibody test negative. Autoimmune and immunoglobulin panel: Positive serum rheumatoid factor (64 IU/mL); negative ANA, anti-CCP, and ANCA; normal serum IgM (1.7 g/L), IgG (12 g/L), and IgA (2.3 g/L). Chest X-ray: Extensive bilateral alveolar opacities (which extended further during initial empirical antibiotic therapy).
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline lymphocyte subsets: Normal CD4 count (1,050/mm3), CD8 count (480/mm3), and CD4/CD8 ratio (2.18). Chest CT: Multiple diffuse consolidations associated with variably necrotic pulmonary nodules, enlarged necrotic bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, and pericardial effusion. First bronchoscopy (day 5): Normal bronchial aspiration cytology, acid-fast (BK) testing, and routine bacteriology (Pneumocystis stain not initially performed). Second bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), protected distal sampling, and bronchial biopsy: Diffuse bronchial mucosal inflammation without neoplastic cells; Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining on the bronchial fluid cellblock identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in an immunocompetent, HIV-negative adult with normal CD4+ T-cell counts (1,050/mm3), confirmed by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining on bronchoalveolar lavage cellblock. Plan and clinical course: The patient initially failed 7 days of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (1 g TID) and 12 days of broad-spectrum escalation to imipenem (1 g TID), vancomycin (1 g BID), and levofloxacin (500 mg BID for 2 days, then 500 mg daily), during which his dyspnea progressed to require a 5 L/min high-concentration mask and noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnia. Following GMS confirmation of P. jirovecii on the second bronchoscopy, he was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (1,600 mg/day divided in four doses) and dexamethasone (40 mg twice daily, gradually tapered) for 3 weeks. He achieved full clinical recovery (afebrile, SpO2 95% on room air) and inflammatory improvement (WBC 14,000/mm3, CRP 23 mg/L), was discharged home without complications, and remained asymptomatic at 1-month outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A woman in her 70s was referred to our hospital because of persistent dyspnea for two days. She had been treated for MF with phototherapy and local radiation to the skin of her left lower leg 13 years ago. Etretinate administration and topical steroidal treatment were continued during the visit. She had never received anticancer or immunosuppressive drugs for MF or other diseases. No other history suspicious of noninfectious lung diseases, including hypersensitive pneumonia or drug-induced lung injury, was observed.
Physical examination revealed 36.9 C body temperature, 85% percutaneous oxygen saturation (SpO2) without supplemental oxygenation, 120/62 mmHg blood pressure, and 62 beats/min heart rate. Laboratory blood tests showed increased levels of C-reactive protein, white blood cell count, and soluble IL-2 receptor and decreased serum albumin levels (Table 1). Cytological analysis of peripheral blood did not reveal any atypical cells.
High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities (GGO) in both lungs (Figure 1A). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 was negative, but the cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigenemia test (C7-HRP) was positive (46/50000). Beta-D glucan (264 pg/mL) and KL-6 (500.4 U/mL) levels were elevated. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis showed lymphocyte predominance (28.3%), and Grocott's stain of BALF revealed the presence of P. jirovecii (Figure 2), and PCR for P. jirovecii using BALF was positive. Although anti-HIV and antihuman T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) antibodies were both negative, the CD4+ T-cell count (281/microL) was moderately low.

subjective.chief_complaint: A woman in her 70s with mycosis fungoides presented with a 2-day history of persistent dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred to our hospital after experiencing persistent shortness of breath for 2 days. She had been diagnosed with mycosis fungoides (MF) 13 years earlier, treated initially with phototherapy and localized radiation to the left lower leg skin, and was maintained strictly on oral etretinate and topical corticosteroids without ever receiving systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy or immunosuppressive agents.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mycosis fungoides (treated 13 years ago with phototherapy and local radiation to the left lower leg; maintained on oral etretinate and topical steroids). No history of systemic anticancer or immunosuppressive drug use, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, or drug-induced lung injury.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent dyspnea for 2 days. Home medications included oral etretinate and topical corticosteroids.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs on admission: Body temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 120/62 mmHg, heart rate 62 beats/min, and percutaneous oxygen saturation (SpO2) 85% on room air.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests: Elevated white blood cell count, C-reactive protein (CRP), and soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R), with decreased serum albumin; peripheral blood cytology showed no atypical cells. Virological testing: SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative; anti-HIV and anti-HTLV-1 antibodies negative; positive CMV antigenemia test (C7-HRP: 46 positive cells per 50,000 leukocytes).
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Diffuse ground-glass opacities (GGO) throughout both lungs. Serologic biomarkers and lymphocyte subsets: Elevated serum beta-D-glucan (264 pg/mL) and KL-6 (500.4 U/mL); moderately decreased peripheral CD4+ T-cell count at 281/μL. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis: Lymphocyte predominance (28.3%); Grocott's methenamine silver stain of BALF directly visualized Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts, and BALF P. jirovecii PCR was positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) with concurrent cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigenemia in an elderly patient with mycosis fungoides and idiopathic/disease-associated CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia (281/μL) despite no systemic chemotherapy or systemic immunosuppressive therapy, definitively confirmed by positive Grocott's staining and positive P. jirovecii PCR on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (supported by bilateral diffuse GGOs on HRCT and serum beta-D-glucan of 264 pg/mL).

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old male had a medical history of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and had undergone multiple rounds of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy, resulting in complete remission three years prior. He was later diagnosed with gastric malignancy and underwent distal gastrectomy, followed by Billroth II anastomosis and jejunojejunostomy. The postoperative pathology indicated poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with some signet ring cell carcinoma. Following the surgery, he was treated with XELOX (oxaliplatin 200 mg IV + capecitabine 1 g twice a day OS) and trastuzumab 400 mg IV for three cycles. Before chemotherapy, his kidney function (creatinine was 57 micromol/L and blood urea nitrogen was 4.73 mmol/L) and urinary test were normal. However, the patient's therapy was interrupted due to increased creatinine at 346 micromol/L and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at 9.58 mmol/L. An abdominal CT scan showed no evidence of urinary tract obstruction. Urine analysis revealed trace proteinuria (1+) and microscopic hematuria (1600/microL); microscopy showed heterogeneous erythrocytes, without gross hematuria, and an elevated urine microalbumin/urine creatinine ratio (53.04 mg/g.crea). A nephrology consultation was requested due to concerns of AKI. However, no further treatment was supplied based on the patient's decision. Two weeks later, the patient developed cough, yellow phlegm with blood in the sputum, intermittent epistaxis, and fever, with a body temperature up to 39  C, accompanied by chills. His blood pressure was 152/84 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed a high white blood cell count (WBC) at 12.03*109/L, low hemoglobin at 60 g/L, a high neutrophil percentage at 95.4%, elevated levels of hypersensitive C-reactive protein (HS-CRP) at 157.14 mg/L, high levels of procalcitonin (PCT) at 7.47 ng/ml and interleukin 6 at 113.10 pg/ml. Creatinine was increased to 537 micromol/L, and BUN was increased to 22.06 mmol/L. PaO2 was 62 mmHg (without oxygen inhalation). Coagulation tests revealed high levels of fibrinogen at 6.04 g/L and D dimer at 950 ng/ml. The antinuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, C3, C4, anti-GBM, and anti-SSA/SSB were negative. However, anti-myeloperoxidase (anti-MPO) antibody was elevated at 152.82 RU/ml, and anti-protease 3 (anti-PR3) antibody was elevated at 98.48 RU/ml. Sputum culture revealed the presence of Klebsiella pneumoniae. Chest CT showed multiple lesions in the lower lobe of the right lung and the upper and lower lobes of the left lung, with diffuse pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage mainly located around the pulmonary hilum and bilateral ground glass opacities (Figure 1A-D). Nasopharynx MRI showed chronic inflammation of the bilateral maxillary sinuses and ethmoid sinuses. A kidney biopsy (4 months after the first chemotherapy) showed capillary loop necrosis, cell crescents, fibrocellular crescents, and fibrous crescents, and immunofluorescence was negative (Figure 2) (Supplementary Data ).
The patient was diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage related to AAV and bacterial pneumonia. He received treatments including blood transfusion, antibacterial therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam, and posterior nasal canal tamponade hemostasis. After infection control, methylprednisolone (0.25 g) for 3 days followed by a 40 mg intravenous drip was administered. Additionally, the patient was given cyclophosphamide (0.6 g/day) intravenously for two days. After 1 week of treatment, chest CT reexamination showed that the pulmonary infiltration lesions in both lungs of the patient had significantly decreased (Figure 1E-H). The anti-MPO decreased to 64.65 RU/ml, the anti-PR3 decreased to 49.38 RU/ml, and the PaO2 increased to 84 mmHg (without oxygen inhalation). The CT scan after 2 weeks showed that most of the lung lesions had been absorbed (Figure 11-L). The patient's symptoms of nasal bleeding and hemoptysis disappeared, and BUN decreased to 19.9 mmol/L, while creatinine decreased to 335 micromol/L. Subsequently, the patient was administered oral prednisone at 40 mg/day, along with sulfamethoxazole to prevent Pneumocystis carinii infection. Prednisone was reduced by 4 mg every 2 weeks. After one month of treatment, the patient experienced fever and coughed up yellow sticky sputum again. The results of the laboratory tests revealed a WBC of 2.45*109/L, hemoglobin level of 83 g/L, neutrophil percentage of 95.1%, HS-CRP level of 244.92 mg/L, and PCT level of 66.99 ng/ml. Sputum culture revealed Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and chest CT showed pulmonary infection in both lungs. The patient was given meropenem and moxifloxacin for anti-infection treatment. The dose of prednisone was reduced to 16 mg/day and was decreased by 4 mg every week. After 6 weeks of treatment, renal function tests showed that the BUN was 20.75 mmol/L, creatinine decreased to 246 micromol/L, anti-MPO was 55.41 RU/ml and anti-PR3 was 30.79 RU/ml. However, the patient's pulmonary infection remained severe, and bronchoalveolar lavage targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) examination revealed a sequence count of 573 for Legionella pneumophila, 2 for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex group, 211 for Yeast-like Pneumocystis jirovecii, and 108 for Klebsiella pneumoniae. Although the tuberculosis culture and acid-fast staining were negative, tuberculosis infection was still considered, and the patient was given ethambutol hydrochloride 0.75 g/day, isoniazid 0.3 g/day, rifampicin 0.45 g/day, and moxifloxacin 0.4 g/day for anti-tuberculosis and anti-Legionella pneumophila treatment. Prednisone was reduced to 8 mg/day, and sulfamethoxazole was given at a dose of 0.96 g twice daily to prevent Pneumocystis carinii infection. However, the patient gave up on treatment and was discharged from the hospital and did not return for follow-up. The patient died at home after 3 months.
Malignant tumors can also lead to vasculitis, but the patient's renal function and urine routine were normal before and after the resection of his malignant tumors, and vasculitis occurred after chemotherapy. Therefore, we believed that the vasculitis was not caused by malignant tumors but by drugs. In most cases of drug-induced AAV, patients exhibit MPO-ANCA, often in combination with antibodies to other neutrophil cytoplasmic proteins such as PR3 and human neutrophil elastase (HNE), as well as anti-nuclear antibodies. If a patient tests positive for both MPO and PR3-ANCA, it suggests that the disease may be drug-induced (Supplementary References). After reviewing the patient's medical history and medication, it is believed that the XELOX plus trastuzumab chemotherapy regimen may have triggered the development of ANCA-related vasculitis. However, it is challenging to pinpoint which specific drug within the regimen caused this reaction. Currently, there are no reports of AAV induced by oxaliplatin or capecitabine. However, multiple reports have indicated that oxaliplatin can cause cutaneous vasculitis and leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Capecitabine-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis has also been reported. There were also reports of vasculitis caused by trastuzumab. However, there have been no reports of AAV causing damage to multiple systems. This is the first report of XELOX plus trastuzumab-induced ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis affecting the lungs, kidneys, and nasal mucosa.
Regrettably, a kidney injury had not been considered until there was a significant increase in the serum creatinine level. Then, a nephrology consultation was sought, resulting in a delay in diagnosis and treatment. This patient had rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and massive pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage, and glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive therapy were used. Therefore, after stopping XELOX plus trastuzumab chemotherapy, glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide were given, the patient's pulmonary hemorrhage and nasal bleeding stopped, and the lung lesions were absorbed. Renal function also improved. Pulmonary infection is one of the most common complications of AAV and one of the main causes of death. High-dose glucocorticoids contribute to the risk of infection. The patient later experienced pulmonary infection again, and tNGS indicated Legionella pneumophila and pulmonary tuberculosis infection. Despite active anti-infection treatment, the steroid dose was rapidly reduced. Ultimately, the patient gave up on treatment and eventually died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old male with gastric adenocarcinoma and prior nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with cough, hemoptysis (yellow blood-streaked sputum), intermittent epistaxis, and high fever up to 39 °C with chills two weeks after interrupting XELOX plus trastuzumab chemotherapy for acute kidney injury.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had achieved complete remission of nasopharyngeal carcinoma 3 years earlier, underwent distal gastrectomy with Billroth II and jejunojejunostomy for poorly differentiated/signet-ring cell gastric adenocarcinoma and received three cycles of adjuvant XELOX (oxaliplatin 200 mg IV + capecitabine 1 g PO bid) plus trastuzumab (400 mg IV). Chemotherapy was halted when his serum creatinine rose from a normal baseline (57 μmol/L, BUN 4.73 mmol/L) to 346 μmol/L (BUN 9.58 mmol/L) with microscopic hematuria (1,600/μL) and proteinuria (1+, urine microalbumin/creatinine ratio 53.04 mg/gCr). He initially declined nephrology intervention, but 2 weeks later he presented with cough, yellow blood-streaked sputum, intermittent epistaxis, chills, and fever up to 39 °C.
subjective.past_medical_history: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma in complete remission for 3 years (status post chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy); poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cell features status post distal gastrectomy (Billroth II and jejunojejunostomy) and 3 cycles of XELOX plus trastuzumab complicated by acute kidney injury.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, yellow blood-streaked sputum (hemoptysis), intermittent epistaxis, high fever (up to 39 °C), and chills.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile up to 39 °C with chills; admission blood pressure 152/84 mmHg; active epistaxis and hemoptysis.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 12.03 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 95.4%), hemoglobin 60 g/L, hs-CRP 157.14 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT) 7.47 ng/mL, IL-6 113.10 pg/mL, serum creatinine 537 μmol/L, BUN 22.06 mmol/L, room-air PaO2 62 mmHg, fibrinogen 6.04 g/L, and D-dimer 950 ng/mL. Autoimmune serology: Negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, anti-GBM, and anti-SSA/SSB with normal C3/C4; dual-positive ANCA with elevated anti-MPO (152.82 RU/mL) and anti-PR3 (98.48 RU/mL). Microbiology: Admission sputum culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae; 1-month relapse sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa (with WBC 2.45 x 10^9/L, Hb 83 g/L, hs-CRP 244.92 mg/L, PCT 66.99 ng/mL); TB culture and AFB staining negative. Nasopharynx MRI: Bilateral chronic maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission chest CT: Multiple lesions in the right lower lobe and left upper and lower lobes with perihilar diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and bilateral ground-glass opacities. Renal biopsy (4 months post-first chemotherapy): Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with capillary loop necrosis and cellular, fibrocellular, and fibrous crescents (negative immunofluorescence). Six-week relapse bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS): Detected Legionella pneumophila (573 sequence reads), yeast-like Pneumocystis jirovecii (211 sequence reads), Klebsiella pneumoniae (108 sequence reads), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (2 sequence reads).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Drug-induced dual-positive (MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA) ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis (AAV) triggered by XELOX plus trastuzumab—manifesting as rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage—subsequently complicated by polymicrobial opportunistic pneumonia involving Legionella pneumophila, Pneumocystis jirovecii (211 reads on BALF tNGS), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (2 reads on BALF tNGS). Plan and clinical course: Initial AAV and K. pneumoniae pneumonia were treated with blood transfusions, posterior nasal packing, piperacillin-tazobactam, IV methylprednisolone (0.25 g/day for 3 days, then 40 mg/day IV, followed by oral prednisone 40 mg/day tapered by 4 mg q2w), IV cyclophosphamide (0.6 g/day for 2 days), and prophylactic oral sulfamethoxazole, resulting in resolution of hemoptysis/epistaxis, absorption of alveolar hemorrhage on 1- and 2-week CTs, improved oxygenation (room-air PaO2 84 mmHg), and decreased creatinine (335 μmol/L) and ANCA titers. One month later, he relapsed with severe febrile pneumonia (P. aeruginosa on sputum culture, followed by BALF tNGS detection of L. pneumophila, P. jirovecii, K. pneumoniae, and MTB complex at week 6). Despite treatment with meropenem, moxifloxacin (0.4 g/day), ethambutol (0.75 g/day), isoniazid (0.3 g/day), rifampicin (0.45 g/day), sulfamethoxazole (0.96 g twice daily), and rapid prednisone taper to 8 mg/day, the patient elected to discontinue therapy, was discharged against medical advice, and died at home 3 months later.

raw_case_text:
An 11-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of proximal muscle weakness and a typical heliotrope rash, and was admitted to our hospital in July, 2022. His CMAS score was 12. Serum CK was elevated (4,718 U/L, reference range: 0-164 U/L). Electromyography indicated myogenic damage. Muscle biopsy showed typical perifascicular atrophy, inflammatory cells primarily distributed around the muscle fascicles, endomysium, and small blood vessels, and extensive positive staining of MHC I on the muscle membrane. MSA analysis confirmed the presence of anti-NXP2 antibody and anti-Ro-52 antibody. Anti-NXP2 antibody IgG level was 115.42 RU/ml, with ANA 1:320 (+). He was diagnosed with definite JDM according to 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria with a total aggregate score 14.9 > 8.7. Considering the critical condition of the patient, he was initiated on IVIG at a dose of 2 g/kg and IVMP at 500 mg/day for three days, followed by oral prednisone at 2 mg/kg/day. A dose of IVCY at 500 mg was also administered.
After treatment, muscle weakness persisted, and the patient gradually developed dysphagia. Two weeks after treatment, he suddenly experienced tonic-clonic seizures and remained in a coma between seizures, indicating status epilepticus. Sedative medications and assisted ventilation via endotracheal intubation were administered, and he was promptly admitted to the PICU. Physical examination revealed significant skin and periorbital edema (Figure 4A). Blood pressure was 126/81 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary physical examination showed no abnormalities. There were no enlarged lymph nodes or hepatosplenomegaly. Positive Babinski sign was observed bilaterally, while other pathological signs were negative. Laboratory examinations revealed elevated levels of AST (269 U/L), ALT (76 U/L), LDH (1,200 U/L), and CK (4,784 U/L). White blood cell count was 17.15 x 109 /L, with 91.4% neutrophils. Hemoglobin level was 137 g/L, and platelet count decreased to 39 x 109 /L. C-reactive protein level was within normal range. Serum ferritin was significantly elevated (>2,000 ng/ml), indicating hyperferritinemia. Triglyceride was 2.56 mmol/L. Serum electrolytes were in the normal range. There were no coagulation disorders. NXP2 antibody titer IgG was higher than initial admission: 139.76 RU/ml. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac function. Chest CT indicated bilateral lung infiltrates and partial consolidation. Cerebral CT showed blurred gray-white matter differentiation, and contrast-enhanced cerebral MRI (Figure 5A) revealed abnormal signals in the left parieto-occipital lobe and thalamus. Cerebral MRA and MRV were negative. EEG showed diffuse background slow waves (2-5 Hz low-to-moderate amplitude slow waves). Spinal fluid studies revealed normal cell counts and glucose level, with a slight increase in protein concentration (64 mg/dl, reference range: 15-45 mg/dl), and no evidence of bacteria or viruses.
After a thorough examination and analysis, considering the significant skin and periorbital edema, muscle weakness, significantly elevated muscle enzymes, and an increasing trend in NXP2 antibody titer IgG, we concluded that the patient was in the active stage of JDM, and seizures were attributed to CNS involvement. Considering the patient's worsening condition despite conventional treatment, we discussed his case and decided to initiate therapeutic PEs. As shown in Figure 6, four PEs were performed, including two sessions of double filtration plasmapheresis. IVMP (1.6 mg/kg/day) and maintenance IVIG (2 g/kg/month) was continued. In addition, pneumocystis jirovecii was detected in the metagenome next-generation sequencing analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid on PICU hospitalization day 6, so antifungal treatments were administered. Despite intensive PE treatment, his condition deteriorated further, and CK levels increased to 16,219 U/L. Two additional courses of IVMP therapy (500 mg/day for three days), over a two-week interval, were administered. Considering that the patient presented with hyperferritinemia and thrombocytopenia, macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) could not be ruled out, despite the absence of fever. Therefore, oral administration of tacrolimus (i.e., FK506) was initiated. Subsequently, a bone marrow examination revealed the presence of macrophages. In addition, tracheostomy was performed because prolonged intubation was needed.
