At this point his mental status remained poor with quadriparesis and flaccid paraplegia. He underwent tracheostomy on hospital day 50.
Serum CMV DNA PCR and HIV RNA PCR were checked weekly to monitor treatment efficacy, and both decreased significantly on treatment (Table 2). No further lumbar punctures were performed. He received 30 days of IV ganciclovir 469mg twice daily before decreasing to IV ganciclovir 469mg daily after two consecutive weeks of undetectable serum CMV DNA PCR, hospital day 76. He received IV ganciclovir daily for 85 days total, before switching to oral valganciclovir 900mg daily. The serum HIV RNA PCR continued to decline and was 49 copies/mL on hospital day 128 (96 days after initiation of HAART therapy). He remained on mechanical ventilation and was able to move his upper extremities with assistance and could answer simple questions. He never regained function in his lower extremities. After minimal improvement he opted to stop mechanical ventilation and passed away on hospital day 147.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male with hypertension and atrial fibrillation presented with fever, chest pain, and dyspnea, and following treatment for HIV-associated Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia developed persistent fevers, loose stools, encephalopathy, nuchal rigidity, and progressive quadriparesis/paraplegia from cytomegalovirus encephalitis and radiculomyelitis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was initially admitted to the general medicine service with fever, chest pain, and dyspnea and failed empiric ceftriaxone/doxycycline (days 1–5) and vancomycin/piperacillin-tazobactam/azithromycin (days 6–15). He was newly diagnosed with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 15 cells/μL, HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL), intubated on hospital day 9 for worsening hypoxia, and diagnosed via BAL with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and CMV co-isolation. He completed 21 days of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and glucocorticoids and was extubated on day 23, but required re-intubation on day 27 for progressive lethargy. Thereafter, he experienced 25 days of persistent intermittent fevers, altered mental status, nonbloody loose stools, nuchal rigidity, and progressive quadriparesis/flaccid paraplegia despite initiating elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide on day 33.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension; atrial fibrillation; newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 15 cells/μL, HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission positive for fever, chest pain, and dyspnea; late hospital course (day 27 onward) positive for lethargy, persistent fever, nonbloody diarrhea, neck stiffness, and progressive four-limb weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Initial course marked by progressive hypoxemia requiring intubation on day 9. Late course (days 27–50): Persistent fevers, severe encephalopathy, nuchal rigidity, right lower extremity weakness progressing to quadriparesis and flaccid paraplegia, requiring re-intubation (day 27) and tracheostomy (day 50).
objective.routine_investigations: Initial HIV workup: HIV-positive with plasma HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL (declining to 49 copies/mL on hospital day 128). Day 27–44 encephalopathy and diarrhea workup: Normal serum ammonia (18 μmol/L); negative blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool bacterial/parasitic cultures; non-contrast/contrast head CTs normal; EEG showed moderate diffuse encephalopathy without epileptiform discharges; day 43 serum CMV DNA PCR markedly elevated at 2,623,108 IU/mL (becoming undetectable by day 76 after IV ganciclovir).
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count: 15 cells/μL. Admission CT chest angiogram: Bilateral ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without pulmonary embolism. Day 9 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by both PCR and microscopy, and positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) by viral cell culture. Day 37 brain MRI: Acute cardioembolic infarcts in the bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia. Day 44 lumbar puncture and spine MRI: CSF profile consistent with encephalitis with positive CSF CMV DNA PCR; contrast-enhanced cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine MRI demonstrated extensive linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the lower spinal cord, conus medullaris, and thickened cauda equina nerve roots diagnostic of CMV radiculomyelitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 15 cells/μL) complicated initially by severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed by BAL microscopy and PCR) and subsequently by severe cytomegalovirus (CMV) meningoencephalitis and lumbosacral radiculomyelitis (confirmed by CSF CMV DNA PCR, serum CMV viral load 2,623,108 IU/mL, and conus medullaris/cauda equina leptomeningeal enhancement on spine MRI) plus cardioembolic cerebral infarcts from atrial fibrillation. Plan and clinical course: Completed a 21-day course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and glucocorticoids for PJP and started HAART (elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) on day 33. Following confirmation of CMV encephalitis/radiculomyelitis, intravenous ganciclovir (469 mg BID for 30 days, then 469 mg daily for 85 total IV days before transitioning to oral valganciclovir 900 mg daily) cleared his serum CMV viremia by day 76 and suppressed HIV RNA to 49 copies/mL by day 128; however, due to persistent ventilator dependence and irreversible paraplegia, the patient elected terminal ventilator withdrawal and died on hospital day 147.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old Japanese man presented to our hospital with a nonproductive cough of two weeks in duration. He did not have fever or dyspnea. He had a history of right hemiparesis, intellectual disability with pica, and symptomatic epilepsy caused by intracerebral hemorrhage, which occurred at two years of age. He had never smoked or consumed alcoholic beverages.
His initial vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 105/55 mm Hg; pulse rate, 70 beats/minute; respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min; SpO2, 93% in room air; body temperature, 36.5 C. There was no lymphadenopathy. Auscultation revealed no chest rales. A cardiovascular examination was normal, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops were detected. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable, and the patient had no rash or petechiae. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse infiltration (Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral airspace consolidation and ground-glass opacity (Figure 2).
The patient's laboratory test values were as follows: hemoglobin, 14.9 g/dl; white blood cell count, 8,850/mm3 with a left shift; platelets, 329,000/mm3; serum aspartate aminotransferase 29 U/L (normal, 0-35 U/l); serum alanine aminotransferase, 31 U/L (normal, 0-35 U/l); serum lactate dehydrogenase, 425 U/L (normal, 119-229 U/l); serum total protein, 5.3 g/dl (normal, 6.5-8 g/dl); serum albumin, 2.1 g/dl (normal, 4-5 g/dl); serum C-reactive protein, 9.18 mg/dl (normal, < 0.2 mg/dl); serum KL-6, 2940 U/ml (normal, < 500 U/ml); serum surfactant protein D, 173.0 ng/ml (normal, < 109.9 ng/mL); and serum surfactant protein A, 115.0 ng/ml (normal, < 43.8 ng/mL). The patient's serum was negative for rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies. The serum levels of immunoglobulin M, G, and A were within the normal ranges. An electrocardiogram revealed normal findings. An examination of the patient's sputum showed no predominant pathogen and no acid-fast organisms were observed on staining. Two sets of blood cultures were prepared at the time of admission; however, they did not yield any organisms.
The patient underwent a fiberoptic bronchoscopic examination that revealed a normal endobronchial system, and combined bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)/transbronchial biopsy (TBLB) was performed. BAL fluid (BALF) was obtained from the right middle lobe. The results of the BALF analysis were as follows: histiocytes, 87%; neutrophils, 6%; lymphocytes, 4%; and eosinophils, 3%. Routine cultures of bronchial the washings were negative. The TBLB sample from the right upper lobe revealed alveolar septal thickening due to chronic inflammation, as well as collagen-type fibrosis.
After these examinations, the patient was diagnosed with acute interstitial pneumonia, and intravenous levofloxacin (500 mg) was administered once daily with corticosteroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone [1000 mg] for three days) followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). On the 5th day after the initiation of therapy, his respiratory condition worsened and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation was started. His interstitial pneumonia was thought to be getting worse, and cyclophosphamide (500 mg/body) was administered intravenously. On the same day, an additional examination revealed the elevation of the serum (1-3) beta-D glucan (BG) level (104.3 pg/ml; normal, <6.0 pg/ml). He was therefore suspected to have fungal infection or PCP, and voriconazole (200 mg, every 12 hours) and sulfamethoxazole trimethoprim (1600 mg and 320 mg, respectively, every 8 hours) were started. An additional HIV antibody test was negative and the serum protein electrophoresis revealed normal findings. Despite the additional antifungal therapy, his respiratory status gradually worsened, and intravenous corticosteroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone [1000 mg] for three days) and cyclophosphamide therapy (500 mg/body) were each administered a second time, on the 8th and 11th days, respectively, without improvement. The patient died due to respiratory failure on the 12th day.
A postmortem pathological examination of the lung tissue demonstrated that the alveolar spaces were filled with foamy amorphous material composed of abundant numbers of cystic forms of Pneumocystis jirovecii and cellular debris, as well as an inflammatory reaction with hyaline membranes (Figure 3). Retrospectively, Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of the BALF and TBLB samples obtained on the day of admission revealed a small amount of the cystic form of Pneumocystis jirovecii (Figure 4). It was therefore thought that PCP had been present on the day of his admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old Japanese man with intellectual disability, right hemiparesis, and epilepsy presented with a 2-week history of nonproductive cough without fever or dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the hospital with a 2-week history of isolated dry cough without fever or shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right hemiparesis, intellectual disability with pica, and symptomatic epilepsy secondary to an intracerebral hemorrhage at 2 years of age. Lifetime nonsmoker and non-drinker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for a 2-week nonproductive cough; negative for fever, dyspnea, rash, or petechiae on presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: Blood pressure 105/55 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 93% on room air, and body temperature 36.5 °C. Physical examination: No palpable lymphadenopathy; clear lung auscultation without rales; normal cardiac, abdominal, skin, and baseline neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL, WBC 8,850/mm3 with left shift, platelets 329,000/mm3, AST 29 U/L (normal: 0–35 U/L), ALT 31 U/L (0–35 U/L), elevated LDH 425 U/L (119–229 U/L), hypoproteinemia 5.3 g/dL (6.5–8.0 g/dL), hypoalbuminemia 2.1 g/dL (4.0–5.0 g/dL), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) 9.18 mg/dL (<0.2 mg/dL). Interstitial lung biomarkers: Markedly elevated serum KL-6 at 2,940 U/mL (<500 U/mL), surfactant protein D (SP-D) 173.0 ng/mL (<109.9 ng/mL), and surfactant protein A (SP-A) 115.0 ng/mL (<43.8 ng/mL). Immunological and microbiological screening: HIV antibody negative; RF and ANA negative; normal serum IgG, IgA, IgM, and serum protein electrophoresis; negative sputum AFB stain and routine culture; two sets of blood cultures negative. Electrocardiogram: Normal. Chest radiograph: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltration.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Bilateral airspace consolidation and diffuse ground-glass opacities. Admission fiberoptic bronchoscopy with right middle lobe bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and right upper lobe transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB): Normal endobronchial tree; BALF differential showed 87% histiocytes, 6% neutrophils, 4% lymphocytes, and 3% eosinophils with negative routine bacterial cultures; initial TBLB H&E reading noted chronic inflammatory alveolar septal thickening and collagen fibrosis. Day 5 fungal biomarker: Elevated serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan at 104.3 pg/mL (normal <6.0 pg/mL). Post-mortem lung autopsy and retrospective Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of admission BALF/TBLB: Autopsy revealed alveolar spaces filled with foamy amorphous exudate containing abundant Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts, cellular debris, and hyaline membranes; retrospective GMS staining of the admission BALF and TBLB confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts had been present on admission.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal HIV-negative Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in a 37-year-old man without traditional pharmacologic immunosuppression, definitively confirmed by post-mortem lung histopathology, retrospective Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of admission BALF and transbronchial lung biopsy specimens, and elevated day 5 serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan (104.3 pg/mL), after being initially misdiagnosed as acute interstitial pneumonia. Plan and clinical course: Initially treated for presumed acute interstitial pneumonia with IV levofloxacin (500 mg daily) and pulse methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). On hospital day 5, respiratory deterioration prompted noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, IV cyclophosphamide (500 mg), and—upon receipt of the elevated beta-D-glucan result—oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (320 mg/1,600 mg q8h) plus voriconazole (200 mg q12h). Despite repeat steroid pulse (day 8) and cyclophosphamide (day 11), the patient died of refractory respiratory failure on hospital day 12.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old man with no relevant medical history presented with complaints of a persistent dry cough, fever, and night sweats in August 2014. He sought urgent medical assistance a couple of times during this period and underwent empirical antibiotic therapy without improvement. A more detailed investigation using chest-computed tomography (CT) revealed thoracic lymphadenopathies; an excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node was compatible with mixed cellularity classical HL (CD20 negative, CD3 negative, CD30 positive, CD15 negative, and PAX5 positive). Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) was performed for staging, which revealed involvement of the supra- and infradiaphragmatic lymph nodes, with no extranodal involvement, consistent with Ann Arbor stage IIIB disease.
The patient underwent polychemotherapy consisting of adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD). After two cycles, an interim PET-CT scan was negative; he underwent a total of six cycles of ABVD treatment; nevertheless, the posttreatment PET-CT scan remained negative.
Unfortunately, five months later, in January 2015, a screening CT scan revealed iliac and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. A new biopsy revealed relapse of his HL. He then underwent second-line therapy with ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide (ICE); however, the disease remained refractory after two cycles. A third-line therapy based on gemcitabine was successful, and hematopoietic stem cells were collected by apheresis in April 2015. A PET-CT scan after two cycles revealed complete response (Deauville score, 2), and the patient was referred to the authors' service for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) as consolidation therapy.
The autologous transplant was performed following a conditioning regimen with carmustine, etoposide, cytarabin and melphalan (BEAM) in May 2016. His transplant course was unremarkable, and neutrophil engraftment occurred 10 days later. A posttransplant PET-CT scan revealed persistent complete response.
Because the disease had relapsed <12 months after the completion of frontline therapy, the patient was started on BV according to the brentuximab vedotin as consolidation therapy after autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma at risk of relapse or progression (AETHERA) study, as posttransplant consolidation in July 2016. He received BV 1.8 mg/kg every three weeks, for a total of 16 doses.
In April 2017, after 10 doses of BV, the patient presented with sneezing, dry cough, and odynophagia, but without dyspnea, thoracic pain, or other associated symptoms. His workup revealed no abnormalities in whole blood count or acute inflammatory markers, and a chest CT scan was normal. Empirical treatment with levofloxacin and oseltamivir for upper respiratory tract infection was started, and he experienced partial improvement of symptoms. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for respiratory viruses was negative; therefore, oseltamivir was discontinued. Two weeks later, the patient returned to the authors' center with fever, chills, dyspnea, and asthenia. His physical examination was remarkable for a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, hypoxemia (arterial oxygen partial pressure 69 mmHg), and crackles on pulmonary auscultation. No adenopathies were observed.
On admission, a repeat workup revealed a hemoglobin level of 10.8 g/dL (108 g/L), leucocytes 4670/mm3 (neutrophils 3540/mm3 and lymphocytes 650/mm3), a platelet count of 105,000/mm3, and a lactate dehydrogenase level of 740 U/L (normal range, 240-480 U/L). A chest CT scan revealed areas of parenchymal consolidation and diffuse ground-glass opacities in both lungs, with predominantly peribronchovascular distribution in the upper and middle fields (Figure 1). He was started on empirical therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g every 6 h), oseltamivir (75 mg twice per day), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (trimethoprim 17 mg/kg/day). A bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed, which was positive for PJ according to toluidine blue staining and to PCR analysis.
Prophylaxis against pneumocystis was initiated in the patient at the time of neutrophilic engraftment after the transplant in June 2016 according to institutional guidelines. However, the patient had stopped it on his own due to gastrointestinal adverse effects for the preceding two months. The last CD4 lymphocyte count available from the patient in March 2017 was 317 cells/mm3.
After a 21-day course of treatment with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, the patient experienced full clinical recovery and was restarted on prophylaxis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old man with relapsed classical Hodgkin's lymphoma receiving post-autologous transplant brentuximab vedotin consolidation presented in April 2017 with fever, chills, dyspnea, and asthenia two weeks after a mild upper respiratory prodrome.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in August 2014 with stage IIIB mixed-cellularity classical Hodgkin's lymphoma, the patient relapsed 5 months after frontline ABVD (January 2015), proved refractory to two cycles of ICE, achieved a complete response (Deauville 2) with third-line gemcitabine, and underwent BEAM-conditioned autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in May 2016. In July 2016, he initiated brentuximab vedotin (BV 1.8 mg/kg q3w) consolidation per the AETHERA protocol. Two months prior to April 2017, he self-discontinued his post-transplant TMP/SMX prophylaxis due to gastrointestinal intolerance. In April 2017, after 10 doses of BV, he initially presented with sneezing, dry cough, and odynophagia with a normal CBC, normal chest CT, and negative respiratory viral PCR (partially improving with empiric levofloxacin). Two weeks later, he returned with acute fever, chills, dyspnea, and asthenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed/refractory stage IIIB mixed-cellularity classical Hodgkin's lymphoma (CD30+, PAX5+, CD15-, CD20-, CD3-) status post 6x ABVD, 2x ICE, gemcitabine salvage, BEAM autologous HSCT (May 2016), and 10 cycles of brentuximab vedotin consolidation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial prodrome positive for sneezing, dry cough, and odynophagia; 2 weeks later positive for fever, chills, dyspnea, and asthenia. Self-discontinued prophylactic TMP/SMX 2 months earlier due to gastrointestinal side effects.

objective.physical_examination: At acute readmission: Tachypneic with respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, crackles on pulmonary auscultation, and no palpable lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission arterial blood gas: Hypoxemia with PaO2 69 mmHg. Complete blood count and biochemistry: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (108 g/L), leukocytes 4,670/mm3 (neutrophils 3,540/mm3, lymphocytes 650/mm3), platelets 105,000/mm3, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 740 U/L (normal: 240–480 U/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Most recent peripheral CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (March 2017) was preserved at 317 cells/mm3. Chest CT scan: Bilateral parenchymal consolidations and diffuse ground-glass opacities in a predominantly peribronchovascular distribution in the upper and middle lung fields (contrasting with a normal chest CT 2 weeks earlier). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by both toluidine blue O staining and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by positive BAL toluidine blue staining and PCR) occurring during brentuximab vedotin post-autologous HSCT consolidation despite a CD4+ T-cell count >300 cells/mm3 (317 cells/mm3) after the patient self-discontinued TMP/SMX prophylaxis. Plan and clinical course: Empirically started on piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q6h), oseltamivir (75 mg BID), and therapeutic trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (17 mg/kg/day of trimethoprim component). He completed a 21-day course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole with full clinical recovery, resumed PJP prophylaxis, and completed all 16 planned consolidation doses of brentuximab vedotin.

raw_case_text: At 12 years of age the patient was admitted with gastroenteritis, generalized intestinal edema and severe nephrotic syndrome progressing to acute renal failure. Quantitative CMV PCR was positive >2 x 106 copies/ml in blood and positive in a renal biopsy (not quantified in tissue). Renal histology showed focal-segmental glomerulosclerosis with extracapillary hypercellularity and mild tubulointerstitial atrophy. Ultrastructural findings showed complete pedicellar effacement characteristic of minimal change nephropathy and no intracellular inclusions or antibody deposits were demonstrated on cytopathology (Figure 1D). Immunofluorescence was faintly positive for C3 and IgG and negative for C1q, IgA, IgM, and fibrin. Exome files were screened for pathogenic podocin mutations that can be associated with nephrotic syndrome, and no pathogenic variants were identified. Interestingly, elevations in CMV titers in blood seemed to precede nephrotic syndrome relapses and correlate with increases in proteinuria (Figure 1F). Due to chronic systemic CMV infection and severe nephrotic syndrome with acute renal failure, she required intermittent critical level care and treatment with systemic steroids. She also received IVIG, broad-spectrum antibiotics, Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, ganciclovir progressing to foscarnet due to proven resistant CMV strains and hyperimmune CMV-specific immunoglobulin (Cytogam ). Despite aggressive anti-viral therapy, it was impossible to fully control the CMV infection or the nephrotic syndrome that fluctuated in accordance with blood CMV titers that remained between 1 x 106 and 4 x 106 copies/ml despite aggressive treatment. Immunosuppressive therapy, first mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) later cyclosporine were initiated. She had an initial response to this treatment achieving reduction of proteinuria. Unfortunately, CMV infection could not be cleared and the nephrotic syndrome finally became unresponsive to treatment. In this clinical context stem cell transplant was not feasible. During this final end stage disease, she developed Pneumocytis jiroveci pneumonia and fungal lung infection (Figure 1E). Bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for Pneumocystis jiroveci, CMV and galactomannan. She progressed to multi-organ failure and died at 13 years of age, 1 year after her initial admission for nephrotic syndrome associated with systemic CMV infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old girl with severe systemic cytomegalovirus-associated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and nephrotic syndrome developed end-stage opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii and fungal pneumonia at 13 years of age following prolonged immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted at 12 years of age with gastroenteritis, generalized intestinal edema, and severe nephrotic syndrome progressing to acute renal failure, the patient was found to have high-level systemic cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (>2 x 10^6 copies/mL in blood and positive in renal biopsy tissue) driving biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with podocyte foot-process effacement. Over the ensuing year, her persistent CMV viremia (1 x 10^6 to 4 x 10^6 copies/mL) proved refractory to ganciclovir, foscarnet (for resistant CMV strains), CMV-specific hyperimmune globulin (CytoGam), and IVIG, while her relapsing nephrotic syndrome was treated with systemic corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and cyclosporine alongside co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. At 13 years of age, during refractory end-stage disease, she developed severe opportunistic pulmonary infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe nephrotic syndrome / focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS; podocin exome screening negative) associated with chronic refractory drug-resistant systemic cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection since age 12.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for gastroenteritis, generalized edema, and oliguria/renal failure; terminal stage at age 13 positive for severe respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Generalized edema and nephrotic syndrome at baseline, progressing to critical illness and multiorgan failure at age 13.
objective.routine_investigations: Virological monitoring: Persistent high-grade plasma CMV DNAemia (initially >2 x 10^6 copies/mL, fluctuating between 1 x 10^6 and 4 x 10^6 copies/mL in parallel with proteinuria relapses).
objective.advanced_workup: Renal biopsy (age 12) and exome screening: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with extracapillary hypercellularity, mild tubulointerstitial atrophy, faint C3/IgG immunofluorescence, complete podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy without viral inclusions, and positive tissue CMV PCR; whole-exome screening negative for pathogenic podocin mutations. Terminal-stage chest imaging and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL, age 13): Severe pulmonary infiltrates; BAL fluid tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Aspergillus galactomannan.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal polymicrobial opportunistic pneumonia with Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (confirmed by positive BAL for P. jirovecii, CMV, and galactomannan) complicating refractory antiviral-resistant systemic CMV infection and steroid/MMF/cyclosporine-treated nephrotic syndrome (FSGS). Plan and clinical course: Despite intensive care, systemic corticosteroids, MMF, cyclosporine, IVIG, CytoGam, ganciclovir, foscarnet, and prior co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, she was ineligible for stem cell transplantation due to uncontrolled CMV and renal failure, progressed to multiorgan failure, and died at 13 years of age.

raw_case_text:
In July 2015, a 24-year-old woman was referred to our Department of Internal Medicine for a high fever (39 C) lasting 3 days, fatigue, myalgias, chills, and vomiting. She had been followed since 2008 for primary ITP, initially treated with oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), which achieved complete remission. Because of occasional severe relapses (two between 2009 and 2012, with gynecological bleeding), she was subsequently treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg) with good responses. In January 2012, at age 21, she suffered a severe relapse, again justifying the use of IVIg and corticosteroids. At that time, she had detectable autoimmunity with an antinuclear antibody titer of 1 : 250 (anti-SSA specificity but without any sign suggestive of lupus) and platelet-directed anti-glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antibodies. In June 2012 (baseline), a new IVIg cycle was administered, followed by RTX (375 mg/m2 once-a-week for 4 consecutive weeks). A complete platelet response was obtained within 6 weeks and, at the last follow-up (March 2015), her blood platelet level was normal (321 x 109/L) without treatment. Before RTX infusion (June 2012), her blood total gamma-globulin level >3 months before IVIg infusion had been normal (8.9 g/L) but she was lymphopenic (total lymphocytes: 0.513 x 109/L), while her peripheral blood lymphocyte count had been normal at ITP diagnosis (1.199 x 109/L). The previously available phenotype profiles of her peripheral circulating lymphocytes are reported in Table 1. No infection occurred during the 3 years following the last RTX administration and she remained clinically well at biannual consultations in our department.
At admission, in July 2015, at age 24, her temperature was 39.2 C and she complained of lower abdominal pain, vomiting but without diarrhea; her physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP: 114 mg/L, normal range (NR): <5 mg/L), hepatic cytolysis (aspartate aminotransferase: 144 U/L, NR: 7-40 U/L; alanine aminotransferase: 265 U/L, NR: 5-50 U/L) and cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase: 389 IU/L, NR: 40-130 U/L; gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase: 698 U/L, NR: 5-38 U/L). The hemogram revealed agranulocytosis and thrombocytopenia (leukocytes: 4.9 x 109/L; neutrophils: 0.02 x 109/L; hemoglobin: 14.5 g/dL; platelets: 46 x 109/L). Bone-marrow aspirate showed normal density, several megakaryocytes but hypoplastic granulopoiesis in blocked maturation, without blasts. Computed-tomography (CT) scans of the thorax and abdomen were normal. Once urine and blood samples had been collected, empirical ceftazidime and gentamicin were begun, and achieved apyrexia within 48 h. After 46 h, blood cultures came back positive for Campylobacter jejuni, and the identical strain isolated from the patient's feces; amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (1 g 3 times a day for 2 weeks) was prescribed. Seven days postadmission, CRP, neutrophil and platelet levels returned to normal (3 mg/L, 6.61 x 109/L and 521 x 109/L, respectively); blood cultures were negative; and liver function was improved.
Laboratory evaluation for immunodeficiency yielded: negative serology for human immunodeficiency viruses-1 and -2, very low serum Ig levels (Table 1) and no circulating B cells. Flow-cytometry quantification of T-cell subsets found expansion of circulating CD4+ T lymphocytes expressing surface DR, suggesting their activation; low natural killer cells and CD8+ T-lymphocyte levels. Urine immunofixation electrophoresis was negative. Ig-replacement therapy was started but not pursued by the patient.
Ten months later (May 2016, age 25) she was hospitalized for a 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. CRP, lactate dehydrogenase and beta2-microglobulin levels were 40 mg/L, 340 U/L (NR 5-240 U/L) and 3.53 mg/L (NR 1.2-2.5 mg/L), respectively. As shown in Table 1, hypogammaglobulinemia, CD19+ B lymphopenia and low peripheral CD8+ T-cell count persisted but without T activation, as assessed by HLADR-positivity. CT scans visualized bilateral diffuse infiltrates, ground-glass opacities and large nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis revealed Pneumocystis jiroveci cysts with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (4,000 copies/mL); high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids were prescribed. Searches for other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, Cryptococcus and Aspergillus species, were negative. At that time, her bone-marrow biopsy was normal.
Despite appropriate antibiotics and clinical improvement, thoracic CT scans revealed worsened dense infiltrates (Figure 1(a)), pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly and nodular lesions of both kidneys (Figure 1(b)). A new bronchoscopy with biopsies found CD20+ large lymphomatous cell infiltration (Figure 2) in bronchi. Those large atypical lymphoid tumor cells were CD10-BCL-6- and MUM1+BCL-2+, with an 80% Ki-67-proliferation index on immunolabeling. EBV, as assessed by in situ hybridization with an EBV-encoded small RNA probe, was diffusely positive in about 80% of tumor cells (Figure 2). The FISH assay for MYC gene rearrangement (MYC FISH DNA Probe, Split Signal, (Y5410), Dako, Locus 8q24) was negative. EBV-positive DLBCL with a nongerminal center phenotype was diagnosed without bone-marrow infiltration. Circulating EBV-DNA was positive (2,430,000 IU/mL). DLBCL treatment consisted of RTX, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone. Even with EB viremia becoming negative, she developed fever, cytopenias, liver damage and neurological manifestations, as a consequence of her prominent bone-marrow hemophagocytosis. Unfortunately, she died of multiorgan failure at age 25.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old woman with persistent rituximab-induced B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinemia (administered 4 years earlier for primary immune thrombocytopenia) presented in May 2016 with a 15-day history of low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and progressive dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in 2008 with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP; ANA 1:250 anti-SSA, anti-GPIIb/IIIa positive), the patient had received oral prednisone, multiple courses of IVIg, and four weekly infusions of rituximab (375 mg/m2) in June 2012, achieving a sustained complete platelet response. Three years post-rituximab (July 2015, age 24), she was hospitalized with high fever (39.2 °C), vomiting, agranulocytosis (neutrophils 0.02 x 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (46 x 10^9/L), and Campylobacter jejuni bacteremia/enteritis (treated with ceftazidime/gentamicin and amoxicillin-clavulanate), at which time profound hypogammaglobulinemia and complete absence of circulating CD19+ B cells were discovered; she declined ongoing Ig replacement. Ten months later (May 2016, age 25), she was hospitalized with a 15-day history of low-grade fever, weight loss, dry cough, and progressive shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) diagnosed in 2008, in sustained remission after 4 weekly doses of rituximab in June 2012; persistent post-rituximab panhypogammaglobulinemia and complete B-cell aplasia; Campylobacter jejuni bacteremia and transient agranulocytosis in July 2015.
subjective.review_of_systems: May 2016 admission positive for a 15-day low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and progressive dyspnea (July 2015 admission positive for high fever, chills, myalgias, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain).

objective.physical_examination: July 2015 admission: Temperature 39.2 °C with otherwise normal physical examination. May 2016 admission: Low-grade fever and progressive dyspnea.
objective.routine_investigations: July 2015 admission labs: CRP 114 mg/L (<5 mg/L), AST 144 U/L (7–40 U/L), ALT 265 U/L (5–50 U/L), ALP 389 IU/L (40–130 U/L), GGT 698 U/L (5–38 U/L), WBC 4.9 x 10^9/L, agranulocytosis with neutrophils 0.02 x 10^9/L, Hb 14.5 g/dL, platelets 46 x 10^9/L; blood and stool cultures positive for Campylobacter jejuni; HIV-1/2 negative. May 2016 admission labs: CRP 40 mg/L, elevated LDH 340 U/L (normal: 5–240 U/L), elevated beta-2 microglobulin 3.53 mg/L (normal: 1.2–2.5 mg/L), and later markedly elevated plasma EBV DNA viral load at 2,430,000 IU/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial lymphocyte phenotyping and immunoglobulins: Profound persistent hypogammaglobulinemia, complete absence of circulating CD19+ B cells, and low CD8+ T-cell and NK-cell counts (4 years post-rituximab). May 2016 chest CT and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, ground-glass opacities, and large pulmonary nodules; BAL fluid microscopy identified Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and BAL quantitative PCR was positive at 4,000 copies/mL (negative for M. tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, CMV, Cryptococcus, and Aspergillus); initial bone marrow biopsy normal. Subsequent CT and repeat bronchoscopy with bronchial biopsy: Worsening dense pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral renal nodules; bronchial mucosal biopsy demonstrated non-germinal center (CD20+, CD10-, BCL-6-, MUM1+, BCL-2+, Ki-67 80%, MYC FISH negative) Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (EBV+ DLBCL; ~80% EBER-positive tumor cells), followed terminally by prominent bone marrow hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Prolonged rituximab-induced B-cell aplasia and severe hypogammaglobulinemia (4 years after ITP treatment) complicated sequentially by Campylobacter jejuni bacteremia/agranulocytosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed by BAL cyst microscopy and PCR of 4,000 copies/mL), and fatal Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (EBV+ DLBCL; confirmed by bronchial biopsy and plasma EBV viral load 2,430,000 IU/mL) with terminal hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Plan and clinical course: Treated in May 2016 with high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids for PJP with initial clinical improvement; upon diagnosis of bronchial/renal EBV+ DLBCL, she received R-CHOP immunochemotherapy, which cleared her EBV viremia but was complicated by severe bone marrow hemophagocytosis (fever, cytopenias, hepatic and neurologic failure), resulting in death from multiorgan failure at age 25.

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man was evaluated in the emergency room (ER) of our institution for persistent diarrhea of 3 weeks duration. He also reported abdominal pain along with lightheadedness. He described the abdominal pain as vague, diffuse, nonradiating, and mild in intensity without any precipitating or relieving factors. He reported up to 10 episodes of watery diarrhea which did not contain any blood. He also complained of fever and dysuria. About 3 weeks before the current presentation, the patient had presented to the ER with dysuria, abdominal pain, and intermittent diarrhea. At that time he was admitted and treated for a urinary tract infection (UTI) with ciprofloxacin and later discharged home. As per patient, his diarrhea had worsened after taking the antibiotics and had presented with the current symptoms. There was no nausea, vomiting, constipation, fever, and early satiety or appetite changes. He had a prior history of HIV/AIDS, had not been adherent to antiretroviral therapy or PCP prophylaxis. He had a high viral load and low CD4 count.
He was a current smoker and admitted smoking 4 or more cigarettes per day but denied using alcohol except on social occasions or illicit drugs. He did not have a family history of liver, stomach, or colon cancer. His medications included acetaminophen and ciprofloxacin.
On examination, he was found to have a temperature of 39.1 C, blood pressure of 108/52 mmHg, a pulse rate of 99 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. The patient was alert, fully oriented, and communicative. The abdomen was scaphoid, nontender, and nondistended with normal bowel sounds. There was no palpable hepatomegaly; however, the spleen was palpable. Shotty cervical and inguinal lymph nodes were palpated. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
Routine laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL, white blood cell count of 3.7 k/uL, serum potassium level of 3.4 mEq/L, and albumin level of 1.7 g/dL. Stool studies including Clostridium difficile cytotoxin, fecal leucocyte stain, and fecal fat were negative. His blood and stool cultures were negative for the growth of Mycobacterium avium complex. A chest X-ray revealed a right lower lobe consolidation and bilateral pleural effusions. The patient was initiated on broad spectrum antibiotics for hospital-acquired infection. A CT of the chest was done as a part of workup revealed moderate right and small left pleural effusions, consolidation in the dependent lung bases, nodular opacities in both lungs, some cavitary in nature, and patchy ground glass opacity in both lungs (Figure 1). Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was negative, ruling out pulmonary tuberculosis. CT abdomen and pelvis done for chronic diarrhea and abdominal pain revealed a hypodense lesion within the cephalad aspect of the spleen, a 6.7 cm splenic mass with adjacent small nodule, multiple hypodense hepatic lesions, measuring up to 12 mm in diameter, and mild ascites in the upper abdomen (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abdomen showed a heterogeneous lesion within the upper pole of the spleen measuring 5.2 x 4.3 cm in size with absent enhancement centrally, with some enhancement along the peripheral aspect of the lesion, suggesting central necrosis (Figure 3). He underwent an ultrasound-guided core biopsy with an 18-gauge (18G) needle. Two core biopsies were obtained for histologic analysis of the splenic mass. The histopathology revealed necrotizing granulomas on hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figures 4 and 5) with Pneumocystis jirovecii infection on Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) stain (Figures 6(a) and 6(b)). A fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy was also done revealing P. jirovecii pneumonia, while bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for malignant cells. His alpha fetoprotein (AFP) level was 3.2 ng/ml. Results of the rest of the laboratory parameters are given in Table 1. The patient was started on sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, and no steroids were given. Antiretroviral therapy was not started at the time of discharge due to concerns over IRS (immune reconstitution syndrome). He continued to follow-up at our hospital as an outpatient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old man with untreated HIV/AIDS presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of persistent watery diarrhea, vague diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and dysuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to current presentation, the patient had been admitted via the emergency room for dysuria, abdominal pain, and intermittent diarrhea, and was discharged on oral ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Following antibiotic treatment, his watery nonbloody diarrhea worsened to up to 10 episodes daily accompanied by mild diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and persistent dysuria. He had a known history of HIV/AIDS with high viral load and low CD4 count and was nonadherent to antiretroviral therapy and PCP prophylaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS with nonadherence to antiretroviral therapy and PCP prophylaxis; urinary tract infection treated 3 weeks prior with ciprofloxacin. Social history: Current smoker (>=4 cigarettes/day), social alcohol use, no illicit drug use; negative family history of GI malignancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for watery nonbloody diarrhea (up to 10 episodes/day), vague diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and dysuria; negative for nausea, vomiting, constipation, early satiety, or appetite changes. Recent medications were ciprofloxacin and acetaminophen.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Temperature 39.1 °C, blood pressure 108/52 mmHg, pulse 99 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Physical exam: Alert, oriented, and communicative; scaphoid, nontender, nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds, palpable splenomegaly, and no hepatomegaly; shotty cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Anemia with hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, leukopenia with WBC 3.7 K/μL, hypokalemia with serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L, severe hypoalbuminemia with albumin 1.7 g/dL, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 3.2 ng/mL. Stool and microbiological studies: Negative Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin, fecal leukocyte stain, and fecal fat; blood and stool cultures negative for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC); sputum smears negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Admission chest X-ray: Right lower lobe consolidation and bilateral pleural effusions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Moderate right and small left pleural effusions, dependent basilar consolidations, bilateral nodular opacities (some cavitary), and bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities. Abdominopelvic CT and abdominal MRI: Multiple hypodense hepatic lesions (up to 12 mm), mild upper abdominal ascites, and a large centrally necrotic upper-pole splenic mass (6.7 cm on CT; 5.2 x 4.3 cm on MRI with peripheral enhancement) plus an adjacent small splenic nodule. Ultrasound-guided 18G core needle biopsy of the splenic mass and fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy: Both splenic core biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated necrotizing granulomas on H&E and abundant Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms on Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining (BAL negative for malignancy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Pneumocystis jirovecii infection presenting with cavitary/nodular Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, hepatosplenic pneumocystosis (necrotizing granulomatous 6.7 cm splenic mass and multiple hepatic lesions), and chronic diarrhea in a nonadherent patient with advanced HIV/AIDS, definitively confirmed by Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining on both ultrasound-guided splenic core biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy. Plan and clinical course: Treated with oral/IV trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole without adjunctive corticosteroids (and with antiretroviral therapy temporarily deferred at discharge to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome), followed by outpatient infectious disease follow-up.

raw_case_text:
We present a 39-year-old heterosexual man with a pertinent past medical history of well-controlled HIV on HAART, including dolutegravir, lamivudine, and abacavir, and atovaquone prophylaxis and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Atovaquone prophylaxis, 750 mg PO every 12 hours, was initiated 5 months prior when the patient was first diagnosed with HIV with CD4 count 81 cells/muL and acute renal failure. The patient first presented to the hospital for evaluation of shortness of breath. During this admission, computerized axial tomography (CT) chest demonstrated interstitial lung disease with ground glass opacities and intrathoracic lymphadenopathy (Figures 1 and 2). The patient underwent bronchoscopy, which was suboptimal due to technical difficulties. Transbronchial biopsies, bronchoalveolar lavage, and cytology were inconclusive. Furthermore, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) cultures were negative. Unfortunately, the patient declined VATS. In addition, the patient had significant peripheral eosinophilia 11.8% (ref.: 0.0-6.0) and occasional urine eosinophils (ref.: negative). At this time, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was not suspected due to normal CD4 count 487 cells/muL with atovaquone prophylaxis and HIV RNA <20 copies/mL. Other diagnosis considerations included iatrogenic-induced subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis. Abacavir was switched to rilpivirine due to suspicion of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and the patient was discharged on 40 milligrams prednisone daily, and atovaquone prophylaxis was continued due to prednisone therapy. Following these treatments, there was both a radiographic and clinic response. The patient received a twenty-four-day course of prednisone. Follow-up CT chest demonstrated persistent, extensive bilateral ground glass opacities and improved mediastinal lymphadenopathy (Figure 3).
The patient presented back to the hospital ten days after discontinuation of prednisone for evaluation of worsening shortness of breath, malaise, and fever. On presentation, the patient was hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), febrile (38.8 C), tachycardic (heart rate low 100 s), and tachypneic (29 breaths per minute). Physical exam was remarkable for increased work of breathing and diffuse bilateral rales.
Repeat CT scan showed substantially worsened diffuse bilateral ground glass and more dense airspace consolidations (Figure 4). A bronchoscopy with right VATS and lung biopsy was performed. Cytology was negative for malignancy, and AFB stain was negative. Grocott's methenamine silver stain of pathology from right upper, middle, and lower lobe resulted positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.
The patient's atovaquone for PCP prophylaxis was discontinued, and renally dosed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg/day (trimethoprim component) IV was initiated. The patient was discharged on 2 tablets of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg tablet) daily for a total course of twenty-one days, in addition to a short course of prednisone. The patient experienced significant relief of shortness of breath following completion of trimethoprim-sulfamethazine course and prednisone taper. PCP prophylaxis was changed to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (80-400 mg) three times a week after dialysis. The patient has not had recurrence of respiratory complaints since completion of treatment for PCP and is expected to complete a 12-month minimum course of trimethoprim-sulfamethazine prophylaxis in September 2019.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old heterosexual man with well-controlled HIV and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with worsening shortness of breath, malaise, and fever 10 days after completing a 24-day course of oral prednisone despite ongoing atovaquone prophylaxis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV and acute renal failure 5 months earlier (initial CD4 count 81 cells/μL), the patient was started on dolutegravir, lamivudine, abacavir, maintenance hemodialysis, and prophylactic oral atovaquone (750 mg PO q12h), achieving immune recovery (CD4 487 cells/μL, HIV RNA <20 copies/mL). He first presented with shortness of breath, ground-glass opacities and intrathoracic lymphadenopathy on chest CT, peripheral eosinophilia (11.8%), and urine eosinophils; after a technically suboptimal bronchoscopy, abacavir was switched to rilpivirine for suspected drug-induced hypersensitivity pneumonitis and he completed a 24-day course of oral prednisone (40 mg daily) while continuing atovaquone prophylaxis. Ten days after stopping prednisone, he re-presented with acute worsening shortness of breath, malaise, and high fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 5 months prior (well controlled with CD4 487 cells/μL and HIV RNA <20 copies/mL on dolutegravir, lamivudine, and rilpivirine); end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis; recent 24-day course of oral prednisone (40 mg/day) for suspected abacavir hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening shortness of breath, malaise, and fever at readmission. Home medications were dolutegravir, lamivudine, rilpivirine, and prophylactic oral atovaquone (750 mg PO q12h).

objective.physical_examination: Readmission vital signs: Hypoxemic with SpO2 88% on room air, febrile at 38.8 °C, tachycardic (heart rate in the low 100s beats/min), and tachypneic (respiratory rate 29 breaths/min). Physical exam: Increased work of breathing and diffuse bilateral rales on lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission labs: Peripheral blood eosinophilia of 11.8% (reference: 0.0%–6.0%), occasional urine eosinophils, HIV RNA <20 copies/mL, and negative AFB cultures.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status at first admission: Recovered CD4+ T-cell count of 487 cells/μL (up from 81 cells/μL at diagnosis 5 months prior). Serial chest CT scans: First admission CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and intrathoracic lymphadenopathy (mediastinal adenopathy improved after prednisone, but GGOs persisted); readmission CT demonstrated substantially worsened diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and dense airspace consolidations. Readmission bronchoscopy and right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) wedge biopsies of the right upper, middle, and lower lobes: Negative for malignancy and AFB; Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of lung biopsy tissue from all three right lung lobes was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Breakthrough Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in a virologically suppressed HIV-positive hemodialysis patient with a normal CD4+ T-cell count (487 cells/μL) receiving oral atovaquone prophylaxis (750 mg BID), unmasked/precipitated by a 24-day course of oral prednisone (40 mg/day) and definitively confirmed by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining on right upper, middle, and lower lobe VATS lung biopsies. Plan and clinical course: Atovaquone was discontinued, and the patient was treated with renally dosed intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5 mg/kg/day TMP component) transitioned at discharge to oral TMP-SMX (two 160/800 mg tablets daily to complete a 21-day course) plus a short oral prednisone taper. His dyspnea resolved completely, and he remained recurrence-free on thrice-weekly post-dialysis TMP-SMX prophylaxis (80/400 mg).

raw_case_text:
At the age of 13 weeks, a girl born at term who had previously been healthy was brought to the emergency unit of a local hospital in respiratory distress (day 0, see Figure 1 for the detailed timeline). The pregnancy had been uneventful; the 6-month maternal HIV screen was negative. The initial clinical evolution was pejorative; the child was placed under mechanical ventilation after orotracheal intubation on day 3. At that time, diffuse alveolo-interstitial lesions were evident on a chest X-ray. Viral PCR revealed a rhinovirus in pulmonary secretions. No other infective agent was noted, but empirical antibiotics were commenced given the gravity of the situation. The condition worsened during a flight between two ICU units, triggering an emergency landing. At arrival in a local, general pediatric ICU, curarization, optimization of ventilation, and prone positioning rapidly improved oxygenation. Such aggressive treatment encouraged the commencement of ventilator weaning on day 17. The favorable clinical course ended on day 20; septic shock developed on ventilation, associated with pneumonia and bacteremia (Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia). The antibiotics were changed to ceftazidime and cotrimoxazole. Given the new bacterial infections, possible immunosuppression was evaluated in terms of immunoglobulin and complement component levels; no abnormality was evident. Despite treatment re-escalation and a priori antimicrobial therapy, her respiratory status worsened, and uncontrolled hypoxemia developed on day 28. No ventricular dysfunction was evident on transthoracic echocardiography, but major confluent bilateral opacities were apparent on a chest X-ray (Figure 2). Refractory ARDS in the absence of multivisceral failure or right ventricular dysfunction was attributed to bacterial pneumonia, justifying the use of VV-ECMO. After cannulation, the patient was transferred to the cardiac pediatric ICU. VV-ECMO afforded efficient gaseous exchange. Pulmonary compliance was very low at ICU arrival (0.45 mL/cm H2O with a tidal volume of 2 mL/kg (i.e., 10 mL); 8 cm H2O of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP); and 22 cm H2O of driving pressure). Antibiotic therapy (cotrimoxazole with 60 mg/kg sulfamethoxazole and 12 mg/kg trimethoprim) and ceftazidime were maintained.
A nurse was accidentally exposed to the child's urine (by pricking herself during collection). In order to decide if a postexposure prophylaxis was indicated, systematic evaluation of viral status of the patient was realized and revealed an HIV-positive serology; the child was found to be HIV-positive on day 31. The viral load as revealed by RT-PCR was extremely high at 6.96 log10 copies/mL. The CD4+ lymphocyte count was very low at 72/mm3. The mother was diagnosed with an HIV infection that had developed late in pregnancy (after the 6-month screen), which had then been congenitally transmitted to the child. We screened for all classic AIDS co-opportunistic infections; all tests were negative except that for Pneumocystis carinii, which was strongly positive on PCR of a tracheal aspirate (8,229 copies/mL). On day 32, the cotrimoxazole dose was changed to 100 mg/kg/day sulfamethoxazole combined with 20 mg/kg/day trimethoprim. Antiretroviral therapy was commenced in association with a corticosteroid (1 mg/kg/day methylprednisolone) to prevent the development of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Such treatment greatly increased the daily fluid intake (the daily cotrimoxazole alone was delivered in 160 mL of solvent) of the 5 kg infant; we thus commenced VV-ECMO ultrafiltration to control the fluid balance.
Compliance slowly improved; computed tomography (Figure 3) revealed persistent pulmonary consolidation but without major fibrosis. More aggressive PEEP combined with sessions of percussive ventilation allowed alveolar lung recruitment. At day 45, the hemodynamic status became aggravated. Erosion of the right atrium caused by cannular malpositioning (amplified by the percussive ventilation) had created hemopericardium causing a cardiac tamponade. This was surgically treated; three interventions were required on the same day to iteratively evacuate hemoperitoneum emanating from a lesion in an abdominal arteriole created during the initial procedure. Despite this episode and a new bacterial pneumonia (caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae ESBL), her respiratory state progressively improved. Ventilator weaning commenced on day 53 with decannulation on day 57 and extubation and ICU discharge on day 61. The patient was transferred a few days later to a dedicated AIDS center without any need for assisted ventilation. The infant's parents kindly gave us written informed consent for publication of this case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 13-week-old full-term female infant presented to the emergency department with acute severe respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born full-term following an uneventful pregnancy with a negative 6-month maternal HIV screen, the infant presented at 13 weeks of age in acute respiratory distress (day 0), requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation on day 3. Initial respiratory PCR detected rhinovirus, and after an emergency in-flight landing during ICU transfer, prone positioning and neuromuscular blockade transiently allowed ventilator weaning by day 17. However, on day 20 she developed septic shock with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia pneumonia/bacteremia, progressing on day 28 to refractory ARDS requiring veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
subjective.past_medical_history: Full-term female infant; negative maternal HIV screening at 6 months of gestation (mother subsequently found to have acquired primary HIV infection late in pregnancy after the 6-month screen, resulting in vertical perinatal transmission).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe respiratory distress and progressive hypoxemia.

objective.physical_examination: Severe acute respiratory distress requiring intubation on day 3 and VV-ECMO cannulation on day 28 (weight 5 kg); profound loss of pulmonary compliance on ICU arrival (0.45 mL/cmH2O with tidal volume 2 mL/kg [10 mL] on PEEP 8 cmH2O and driving pressure 22 cmH2O); complicated on day 45 by cannula-related right atrial erosion causing hemopericardium/cardiac tamponade and surgical hemoperitoneum.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial microbiological and immunological workup: Day 3 respiratory viral PCR positive for rhinovirus; day 20 blood and respiratory cultures positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (and later ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia); normal serum immunoglobulin and complement levels. Day 31 HIV workup (performed after an accidental nurse needlestick/urine exposure): Positive HIV serology with an extremely high plasma HIV RNA viral load of 6.96 log10 copies/mL. Serial chest X-rays and echocardiography: Diffuse alveolo-interstitial infiltrates on day 3 progressing to confluent bilateral white-out opacities on day 28; normal ventricular function on TTE.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 31 lymphocyte subsets: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with an absolute CD4+ count of 72/mm3. Tracheal aspirate opportunistic infection screening (day 31): Strongly positive Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) quantitative PCR at 8,229 copies/mL (all other classic AIDS opportunistic infection screens negative). Follow-up chest CT on VV-ECMO: Persistent pulmonary consolidation without major pulmonary fibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Vertically transmitted perinatal HIV/AIDS (from unrecognized late-gestation maternal seroconversion; infant HIV viral load 6.96 log10 copies/mL, CD4 count 72/mm3) presenting with life-threatening Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed by tracheal aspirate PCR of 8,229 copies/mL) and refractory pediatric ARDS requiring 29 days of veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO), complicated by rhinovirus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and ESBL Klebsiella pneumoniae superinfections. Plan and clinical course: Placed on VV-ECMO on day 28 while receiving ceftazidime and intermediate-dose co-trimoxazole (12/60 mg/kg/day). Upon day 31 discovery of HIV and P. jirovecii, co-trimoxazole was escalated on day 32 to full therapeutic dosing (20 mg/kg/day TMP / 100 mg/kg/day SMX) alongside antiretroviral therapy, methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for IRIS prevention), VV-ECMO ultrafiltration, and high-PEEP percussive ventilation. Despite requiring emergency surgical repair of right atrial cannula erosion/tamponade and hemoperitoneum on day 45, she was successfully decannulated from VV-ECMO on day 57, extubated and discharged from the ICU on day 61, and transferred breathing spontaneously on room air to a specialized pediatric AIDS center.

raw_case_text:
A 22-year-old Chinese male form Zhejiang province initially presented to the local community hospital. He complained of 10 days of intermittent fever with a temperature of up to 38.7 C and 3 days of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. He was given moxifloxacin at the local community hospital. However, he contracted chest thrush after using moxifloxacin, so this treatment was stopped and he was given ambroxol hydrochloride. Due to a history of male sexual partners and weight loss, an HIV test was obtained which returned positive. Then he came to our institution, the infectious disease department of the First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, and hospitalized.
Upon presentation at our institution, he still had fever, dyspnea, fatigue, cough with a small amount of pale sputum, and occasionally pectoralgia and dyspnea during activity. Physical examination found a body temperature of 37.4 C, blood pressure of 113/50 mmHg, a pulse of 115 beats per minute, a respiration rate of 23 breaths per minute, and SpO2 93% using fingertip pulse oximetry. The bilateral lung presented moist rales. The patient did not have a skin rash. The laboratory results were as follows: white blood cell count 7.7 x 109/L, with a neutrophil ratio of 65.7%, hemoglobin 133 g/L, and platelet count 365 x 109/L; C-reactive protein (CRP) 8.5 mg/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 5 mm/h; and procalcitonin 0.08 ng/mL. Blood biochemical index results showed that lactate dehydrogenase content increased to 401 U/L (reference range 150-250 U/L), and -hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase content increased to 326 U/L (reference range 72-182 U/L). The 1,3-beta-D-glucan test (G test) result (251.64 pg/ml) was positive, while galactomannan test (GM test) (0.1 mug/L) and cryptococcus capsular antigen test results were negative. His CD4 count was 16 cells/muL. Arterial blood gas analysis (with O2 3 L/min via nasal catheter) showed pH 7.51; pCO2 27 mmHg; pO2 98 mmHg; HCO3 -21.9 mmol/L; SBE -0.8 mmol/L; lactate 0.8 mmol/L; and O2 saturation 99%. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed extensive ground-glass opacities in the bilateral lung with multiple thin-walled cavity lesions in the left upper lung (Figures 1A,B). The IgG and IgM antibodies of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) were negative. The nucleic acid detection of COVID-19 was negative. Nucleic acid detection of common respiratory pathogens (including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, and influenza A and B) was negative. The IgG antibodies of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and human cytomegalovirus (CMV) were positive, while the IgM antibodies of EBV and CMV were negative. The nucleic acid of CMV in the blood was reported at 1.86 x 104 copies/mL by quantitative PCR. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) was negative based on blood test with T-SPOT.TB as well as acid-fast staining of sputum smear and GeneXpert. The blood, sputum, and urine smear and culture of bacteria and fungi were negative. We also sent the sputum sample to perform Gomori-Grocott methenamine silver nitrate staining (GMS) for Pneumocystis jirovecii detection and obtained a negative result. Given the patient's hypoxia and demonstration of diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT of the chest, a clinical diagnosis of P. jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) was made. Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, TMP 0.24 g /SMX 1.2 g, q8h), intravenous clindamycin (0.6 g, q12h), and methylprednisolone (40 mg daily) were administered, which resulted in the improvement of general conditions and abatement of fever and dyspnea in 3 days.
To verify pathogen-induced pneumonia, the patient underwent a bronchoscopy examination with a collection of BALF specimens on day 5 of admission. The BALF was sent to the laboratory for conventional tests and an NGS test [using the MGISeq 2000 platform (MGI Tec Co. Ltd, Shenzhen, China)]. The BALF Gram stain and acid-fast stain were negative. The G test and GM test of BALF were negative. In addition, a BALF culture of fungal and bacteria showed no organisms. Microbiological tests of BALF were negative for MTB by the smear and GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay. Two days later, the NGS results showed that P. jirovecii (1,000,078 reads) and CMV (4,192 reads) were found in the BALF. The other microorganisms detected by NGS were bacteria and are listed in Table 1, but they were not regarded as responsible for the invasive pulmonary infection. Based on the report, the diagnosis of multi-pathogenic pneumonia due to PCP and CMV was made in this patient, and intravenous ganciclovir (0.25, Q12H) was started.
After 2 weeks of hospitalization, his symptoms disappeared, general conditions returned to normal, and laboratory findings improved. The chest CT scan showed that lesions had been significantly absorbed except for a faint patchy opacity in the lateral segment and thin-walled cavity lesions in the left upper lung (Figures 1C,D). So, the patient began antiretroviral therapy with Truvada (emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate tablets, 500 mg QD) and dolutegravir (50 mg QD). He was discharged to complete 1 week of TMP-SMX and 2 weeks of oral ganciclovir (500 mg, three times daily) at home, and then switch to prophylactic doses of TMP-SMX until CD4 count recovery. At his 2-week follow-up visit, he had no symptoms. At his 2-month follow up, he appeared healthy with no symptoms and a chest CT scan exhibited no abnormal findings except for a faint patchy opacity in the left lateral segment (Figures 1E,F).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old Chinese male with newly diagnosed HIV infection presented with a 10-day history of intermittent fever (up to 38.7 °C) and a 3-day history of progressive dyspnea and dry cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to admission, the patient developed intermittent fever peaking at 38.7 °C, followed 3 days before admission by progressive shortness of breath and dry cough. At a community hospital, he was treated with moxifloxacin (stopped after developing thrush) and ambroxol, and tested positive for HIV in the setting of weight loss and male-to-male sexual contact, prompting referral to our infectious disease department. On admission, he reported persistent fever, fatigue, cough with scant pale sputum, exertional dyspnea, and occasional chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Newly diagnosed HIV infection; recent weight loss. Social/epidemiological history: History of male sexual partners.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever (up to 38.7 °C), progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, cough with scant pale sputum, occasional pectoralgia, weight loss, and recent moxifloxacin-associated thrush; negative for skin rash.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Temperature 37.4 °C, blood pressure 113/50 mmHg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, and fingertip SpO2 93%. Physical exam: Bilateral pulmonary moist rales on auscultation; no skin rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas (on 3 L/min nasal cannula oxygen): pH 7.51, pCO2 27 mmHg, pO2 98 mmHg, HCO3- 21.9 mmol/L, SBE -0.8 mmol/L, lactate 0.8 mmol/L, and O2 saturation 99%. Hematology, biochemistry, and inflammatory markers: WBC 7.7 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 65.7%), hemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 365 x 10^9/L, CRP 8.5 mg/L, ESR 5 mm/h, procalcitonin 0.08 ng/mL, elevated LDH at 401 U/L (reference: 150–250 U/L), and elevated alpha-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (HBDH) at 326 U/L (reference: 72–182 U/L). Virological and microbiological screening: Quantitative blood CMV DNA PCR positive at 1.86 x 10^4 copies/mL (CMV and EBV IgG positive, IgM negative); negative SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid and IgG/IgM; negative respiratory pathogen nucleic acid panel; negative T-SPOT.TB, sputum AFB smear, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF; negative blood, sputum, and urine bacterial/fungal cultures; negative sputum Gomori-Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain for Pneumocystis jirovecii.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological and fungal biomarkers: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with CD4 count of 16 cells/μL; positive serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G test) at 251.64 pg/mL; negative serum galactomannan (0.1 μg/L) and cryptococcal capsular antigen. Admission chest CT scan: Extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities accompanied by multiple thin-walled cystic/cavitary lesions in the left upper lobe. Day 5 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS (MGISeq 2000): Conventional BALF stains, cultures, G/GM tests, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF were negative, whereas BALF mNGS identified 1,000,078 sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii and 4,192 sequence reads of human cytomegalovirus (CMV).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 16 cells/μL) complicated by severe cavitary/ground-glass Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) co-infection, definitively confirmed by BALF metagenomic next-generation sequencing (1,000,078 P. jirovecii reads and 4,192 CMV reads), positive serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (251.64 pg/mL), and blood CMV viral load (1.86 x 10^4 copies/mL) despite negative sputum GMS staining. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP 0.24 g / SMX 1.2 g q8h), IV clindamycin (0.6 g q12h), and IV methylprednisolone (40 mg daily) abated his fever and dyspnea within 3 days, and intravenous ganciclovir (0.25 g q12h) was added on day 7 following BALF mNGS confirmation of CMV co-infection. After 2 weeks of inpatient therapy with marked CT lesion absorption, he initiated antiretroviral therapy with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Truvada 500 mg qd) plus dolutegravir (50 mg qd), was discharged to complete 1 additional week of therapeutic TMP-SMX (followed by secondary TMP-SMX prophylaxis) and 2 weeks of oral ganciclovir (500 mg TID), and achieved near-complete radiographic resolution at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male patient had a dry cough, chest tightness after exercise, and shortness of breath for 1 week. He took oral cephalosporin for 3 days without any efficiency, and his symptoms got worse. On admission, leukoplakia in the mouth, little wet rales at the bottom of both lungs, and multiple swollen lymph nodes were found on clinical examination. His temperature was 37.6 C. His blood test results showed that the white blood cell count was 6.52*109/L, with an elevation in neutrophil ratio of 72.7%, high level of C-reactive protein (CRP) at 166 mg/L and serum amyloid protein A at 130 mg/L, low level of oxygen partial pressure at 87.5 mmHg and albumin at 30.3 g/L. Blood culture, antibody tests of Legionella pneumophila, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and PCR-based detection of SARS-CoV-2 were negative. Cryptococcal capsular antigen, 1-3-beta-D glucan detection, aspergillus galactomannan detection, and interferon-gamma release assays were negative. The viral load of HIV-RNA was 84,100 IU/ml. CD4+ T-cell count was 11 cells/mul. CT of the lung revealed multifocal bilateral ground-glass opacities (Figure 1). According to the clinical diagnosis of PCP, the patient was treated with four pills of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (sulfamethoxazole 1.2 g, trimethoprim 240 mg) three times a day.
After treatment for 2 days (on day 3), the symptoms of the patient were more severe, and his temperature got to 39.9 C. We performed a bronchoscopy on the patient, and it showed bronchial mucosa hyperemia and bronchial inflammatory changes. Nucleated cell counts of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were 20 * 106/L. Cryptococcal antigen, 1-3-beta-D glucan detection, and culture of BAL were negative. Hexamine silver staining of P. jiroveci and PCR-based detection of cytomegalovirus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were also negative. In addition, next-generation sequencing technologies (NGS) of BAL were carried out, the BAL was sent to a laboratory, and DNA was extracted for whole genomic sequencing, purified, and sonicated to a size of 100-150 bp. The DNA libraries were constructed followed by end repair, joint connection, no bias PCR amplification, and sequenced using the MGlseq-2000 platform after quality control. High-quality sequencing data were generated by removing low-quality reads. After removing human sequences, the remaining sequencing data were aligned to the bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoan databases.
After treatment for 5 days (on day 6), CT of the lung revealed that it was worse than before (Figure 2). Results of NGS reported 205,658 unique reads of P. jirovecii, with coverage of identified genes 1.70% and 115 unique reads of T. whipplei, with coverage of identified genes 1.00% in BAL. The P. jirovecii-specific SYBR Green quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) assay targeting a 301 bp fragment using a CFX96 Real-Time System was performed. The forward primer (pH207 5-ACAAATCGGACTAGGATATAGCTGGT-3) and the reverse primer pAZ102-E were used to detect the mtLSUrRNA gene, and the copy number of P. jiroveci was 4,787.36 copies/ml. For specific T. whipplei qPCR, the specimen was tested by using Twhi3F (5-TTGTGTATTTGGTATTAGATGAAACAG-3), Twhi3R (5-CCCTACAATATGAAACAGCCTTTG-3) primer pair, and the specific TaqMan probe Twhi3 (6-FAM-GGGATAGAGCAGGAGGTGTCTGTCTGG-TAMRA). When the specimen was positive in this assay, the result was confirmed by a second qPCR by using Twhi2F (5-TGAGGATGTATCTGTGTATGGGACA-3) andTwhi2R (5-TCCTGTTACAAGCAGTACAAAACAAA-3) primer set, and the Twhi2 probe (6-FAM-GAGAGATGGGGTGCAGGACAGGG-TAMRA). The copy number of T. whipplei was 11,717.3 copies/ml. Considering the progressed condition of the patient, meropenem 1 g q8h and caspofungin 70 mg per day were added for treating the infections of T. whipplei and P. jirovecii. Methylprednisolone 40 mg BID was added due to the severe symptoms. On day 12, there was a clinical improvement, and CT of the lungs showed obviously better than before (Figure 3), and the patient was discharged on day 16.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of dry cough, post-exercise chest tightness, and shortness of breath that worsened despite 3 days of oral cephalosporin therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a dry cough, exertional chest tightness, and dyspnea 1 week prior to admission. He took an oral cephalosporin for 3 days without relief, and his respiratory symptoms progressively worsened.
subjective.past_medical_history: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV infection on admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, post-exercise chest tightness, shortness of breath, oral leukoplakia, and low-grade fever (spiking to 39.9 °C on hospital day 3).

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Temperature 37.6 °C (rising to 39.9 °C on day 3), oral mucosal leukoplakia, multiple enlarged peripheral lymph nodes, and scant moist rales at both lung bases.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 6.52 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 72.7%), C-reactive protein (CRP) 166 mg/L, serum amyloid A (SAA) 130 mg/L, PaO2 87.5 mmHg, and serum albumin 30.3 g/L. Virological and microbiological screening: Positive HIV RNA viral load at 84,100 IU/mL; negative blood cultures, negative Legionella pneumophila, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibody tests, negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, negative cryptococcal capsular antigen, and negative interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA).
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological and fungal biomarkers: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with CD4 count of 11 cells/μL; serum and BAL 1,3-beta-D-glucan and Aspergillus galactomannan tests negative. Serial chest CT scans: Multifocal bilateral ground-glass opacities on admission that worsened on hospital day 6 before markedly resolving on day 12. Hospital day 3 bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) analysis: Bronchial mucosal hyperemia and inflammation; BAL nucleated cell count 20 x 10^6/L; negative BAL culture, cryptococcal antigen, 1,3-beta-D-glucan, hexamine silver (GMS) staining for P. jirovecii, and CMV/MTB PCRs.
