assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) confirmed via bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) in the setting of prolonged rituximab-induced B-cell depletion (0% peripheral B cells) and corticosteroid therapy for generalized myasthenia gravis and recurrent thymoma. Plan and clinical course: Treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 20 g daily for 5 days), oral sulfamethoxazole tablets, and reduction of oral prednisone to 20 mg and 5 mg every other day. Two months later, IgG was 7.86 g/L, IgM recovered to 0.65 g/L, and IgA remained low at 0.47 g/L. Downstream follow-up: In October 2021, she developed left eye CMV infectious retinitis with panhypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 6.86 g/L, IgM 0.43 g/L, IgA 0.51 g/L), treated with intravitreal ganciclovir, topical tobramycin/prednisone acetate, steroid discontinuation, and monthly-to-bimonthly IVIG (20 g), maintaining left visual acuity at 0.15. By May 2022, CD20+ B cells recovered to 11.65% (5.0–21%). In August 2022, she developed Coombs-positive erythroblastic anemia (minimum HGB 50 mg/dL) presenting with fatigue and dizziness, which responded to IVIG and prednisone 40 mg (HGB recovered to 94 mg/dL), followed by slow corticosteroid tapering and maintenance IVIG every 2–3 months.

raw_case_text:
A 6-month-old male infant was hospitalized in a local hospital with recurrent fever and cough for 1 month. The presence of E. coli was detected by using a blood culture test. After 14 days of ceftazidime treatment, his temperature returned to normal, and the blood culture test results turned negative. However, he soon developed high fever and cough again with shortness of breath and was transferred to the West China Second University Hospital of Sichuan University. It was found that the child had developed Klebsiella pneumoniae septicemia during the neonatal period and pneumonia at 2 months of age. The newborn screening test results of the child were negative, and there was no evidence of any abnormalities or anomalies in the family history of close members of the child, in birth history, or in environmental history. Upon admission, a physical examination revealed a high body temperature of 39.5 C, a pulse rate of 180 beats per minute, a respiration rate of 70 per minute, and a blood oxygen saturation rate of 70%. Moist rales and wheezing were found bilaterally.
The detailed timeline of this patient is shown in Figure 1. Upon admission, laboratory auxiliary blood routine examination revealed an increased white blood cell (WBC) count (16.9 x 109/L) and decreased lymphocyte absolute value (0.69 x 109/L), with an absolute value of monocytes of 0.30 x 109/L, absolute value of neutrophils of 15.24 x 109/L, C-reactive protein of 19 mg/dl, and procalcitonin (PCT) of 8.0 ng/mL. Cellular immune response revealed a lymphocyte absolute value of 0.34 x 109/L, absolute value of T lymphocytes of 0.02 x 109/L, absolute value of B lymphocytes of 0.28 x 109/L, and absolute value of NK lymphocytes of 0.02 x 109/L. The results of culture tests performed using blood, sputum, and cerebrospinal fluid were negative. The result of the PCR test for influenza A/B virus, parainfluenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, respiratory syncytial virus, metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, Bocavirus, adenovirus, and coronavirus was negative. The G test result for fungi was also negative. Lung computed tomography (CT) showed inflammation with decreased light transmittance, which was evident in the lower lobe of both lungs, as well as an exudation shadow and strip shadow (Figure 2). No thymus shadow was found (Figure 2). The results of sputum culture and two blood culture tests were also negative.
After admission, the patient received invasive ventilator therapy, anti-infective treatment with vancomycin (15 mg/kg, q6h) plus meropenem (40 mg/kg, q8h) and micafungin (4 mg/kg, qd), and gamma globulin infusion (1 g/kg). Considering the previous medical history (E. coli septicemia, K. pneumoniae septicemia, and pneumonia), lymphopenia, and the absence of thymus, congenital immunodeficiency, and opportunistic bacterial infection could not be ruled out. mNGS of blood was applied for rapid detection of pathogens. Meanwhile, whole-exome sequencing was performed in samples collected from the family members. The mNGS test results revealed 133 specific nucleic acid sequences of P. jirovecii, suggesting an infection with this pathogen (PCP). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was added to the treatment regimen. After 5 days of treatment, the patient's condition improved, but he still needed ventilator support. The patient's parents requested a discharge due to financial reasons and declined the provision of any further treatment for the child. A day after discharge, the child died of respiratory failure. The result of whole-exome sequencing suggested an X-linked immunodeficiency. A hemizygous mutation c.865c > t (p.r289*) was detected in the IL2RG gene, which was inherited from the mother (heterozygous state). The family also declined an autopsy for the child, and therefore, an anatomical diagnosis could not be obtained.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-month-old male infant presented with a 1-month history of recurrent high fever and cough complicated by acute shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant was initially hospitalized at a local hospital for 1 month of recurrent fever and cough, where blood cultures grew Escherichia coli. Following 14 days of ceftazidime therapy, his fever temporarily resolved and repeat blood cultures turned negative, but he rapidly relapsed with high fever, cough, and acute shortness of breath, prompting transfer to West China Second University Hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Neonatal Klebsiella pneumoniae septicemia; pneumonia at 2 months of age; negative newborn screening tests; unremarkable birth, environmental, and family histories.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent high fever, cough, and shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs on admission: Body temperature 39.5 °C, pulse rate 180 beats/min, respiratory rate 70 breaths/min, and blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) 70%. Chest auscultation: Bilateral moist rales and wheezing.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission complete blood count and inflammatory markers: Elevated WBC count 16.9 x 10^9/L, decreased absolute lymphocyte count 0.69 x 10^9/L, absolute monocyte count 0.30 x 10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 15.24 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 19 mg/dL, and procalcitonin (PCT) 8.0 ng/mL. Microbiological workup: Negative blood (two sets), sputum, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures; negative respiratory PCR panel for influenza A/B, parainfluenza, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, RSV, metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, bocavirus, adenovirus, and coronavirus.
objective.advanced_workup: Cellular immunity / lymphocyte subsets: Total absolute lymphocytes 0.34 x 10^9/L, T lymphocytes 0.02 x 10^9/L, B lymphocytes 0.28 x 10^9/L, and NK lymphocytes 0.02 x 10^9/L (T-B+NK- severe combined immunodeficiency phenotype). Fungal biomarker: Serum G test (1,3-beta-D-glucan) negative. Chest CT: Bilateral lower lobe predominant pulmonary inflammation with decreased light transmittance, exudative shadows, strip shadows, and complete absence of a thymus shadow. Peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Detected 133 specific nucleic acid sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii. Family trio whole-exome sequencing (WES): Identified a maternally inherited hemizygous nonsense mutation in the IL2RG gene, c.865C>T (p.Arg289*).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) confirmed by peripheral blood mNGS (133 P. jirovecii sequence reads) secondary to X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) caused by a hemizygous IL2RG mutation (c.865C>T, p.R289*). Plan and clinical course: Upon admission, the infant was intubated for invasive mechanical ventilation and treated empirically with intravenous vancomycin (15 mg/kg q6h), meropenem (40 mg/kg q8h), micafungin (4 mg/kg qd), and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1 g/kg). Following blood mNGS identification of P. jirovecii, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) was added. Despite clinical improvement after 5 days of targeted treatment, the infant remained ventilator-dependent; the parents requested discharge against medical advice due to financial constraints, and the child died of respiratory failure one day after discharge.

raw_case_text:
We report a case of an 87-year-old female patient with a long-standing history of RA. She was undergoing treatment with methotrexate 8 mg/week and monthly injections of the TNF inhibitor golimumab. The patient presented with chief complaints of dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and fatigue. A month before admission, she started experiencing dry coughing. Three days before presenting to our facility, she experienced a worsening of exertional dyspnea and increased fatigue. Upon initial examination at a local clinic, her oxygen saturation (SpO2) was found to be 70%. A chest X-ray revealed bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities. Due to these findings, she was referred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment.
Upon admission, her vital signs were as follows: pulse 75/min, blood pressure 137/72 mmHg, temperature 36.7 C, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 97% on 3 L/min of supplemental oxygen. Physical examination revealed inspiratory crackles in both lung fields, with no heart murmurs, edema, or joint pain. Her height was 146.0 cm, weight 45.1 kg, and BMI 21.16 kg/m2. In rapid testing, the influenza antigen, SARS-CoV-2 antigen, urinary pneumococcal antigen, and urinary Legionella antigen were all negative. Laboratory findings revealed a WBC count of 13,380/uL, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelet count 344x103/uL, CRP 20.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase level at 478 U/L, D-dimer at 6.6 microg/mL, and KL-6 397 U/mL (reference <500 U/mL). A high-resolution chest CT scan confirmed diffuse, unevenly distributed ground-glass opacities throughout both lungs (Figure 1).
The differential diagnosis included RA-related interstitial lung disease, MTX-induced pneumonitis, and opportunistic infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia, cytomegalovirus pneumonia, and bacterial pneumonia. Treatment was initiated with discontinuation of MTX, administration of steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone, or mPSL, 500 mg), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), antibiotics (levofloxacin 500 mg/day and ceftriaxone 2 g/day), and supplemental oxygen; 5000 units of Heparin Ca were administered due to elevated D-dimer levels (Figure 2).
On day 3, her respiratory status worsened, necessitating the initiation of high-flow oxygen therapy (Figure 2). On day 6, her serum beta-D-glucan levels on admission were found to be elevated (423 pg/mL). Cytomegalovirus antigen on admission was negative. Considering her clinical background, progression, and imaging findings, she was clinically diagnosed with PCP. Treatment was continued with TMP/SMX (three tablets/day), steroids, and ongoing oxygen supplementation, and antibiotics were discontinued.
On day 12, the patient developed trunk pruritus and rash, prompting a transition from TMP/SMX to atovaquone. On day 19, her chest CT showed complete resolution of the ground-glass opacities (Figure 3), and blood tests indicated decreased inflammatory markers. Steroid treatment was discontinued, and MTX was resumed at a half dose of 4 mg, which had been paused. On day 25, she showed no recurrence of pneumonia and was discharged home in a stable condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 87-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-month history of dry cough and a 3-day worsening of exertional dyspnea and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had a long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treated with weekly methotrexate (8 mg/week) and monthly golimumab injections, developed a dry cough 1 month prior to admission. Three days prior to hospital referral, her exertional dyspnea and fatigue markedly worsened. At a local clinic, her room-air SpO2 was 70% and a chest X-ray showed bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities, prompting urgent referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate (8 mg/week) and monthly golimumab (TNF-alpha inhibitor).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and fatigue; negative for arthralgias or peripheral edema. Home medications included methotrexate 8 mg/week and monthly golimumab.

objective.physical_examination: Anthropometrics: Height 146.0 cm, weight 45.1 kg, BMI 21.16 kg/m2. Admission vital signs: Pulse 75/min, blood pressure 137/72 mmHg, temperature 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 97% on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen (70% at the referring clinic). Chest and systemic exam: Bilateral inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation; no cardiac murmurs, peripheral edema, or joint pain.
objective.routine_investigations: Rapid infectious screening: Negative influenza antigen, SARS-CoV-2 antigen, urinary pneumococcal antigen, urinary Legionella antigen, and serum CMV antigen. Admission blood tests: WBC 13,380/μL, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelets 344 x 10^3/μL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 20.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 478 U/L, D-dimer 6.6 μg/mL, and KL-6 397 U/mL (reference <500 U/mL). Referring clinic chest X-ray: Bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) on admission: Diffuse, unevenly distributed ground-glass opacities (GGOs) throughout both lungs. Fungal biomarker (returned on hospital day 6 from admission sample): Markedly elevated serum beta-D-glucan at 423 pg/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) secondary to methotrexate and golimumab immunosuppression for rheumatoid arthritis, clinically confirmed by diffuse bilateral GGOs on HRCT, markedly elevated serum beta-D-glucan (423 pg/mL), elevated LDH (478 U/L), and negative CMV and bacterial antigen screens. Plan and clinical course: Upon admission, methotrexate was discontinued and empiric treatment was initiated with steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone 500 mg), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), ceftriaxone (2 g/day), levofloxacin (500 mg/day), supplemental oxygen, and subcutaneous heparin calcium (5,000 units for elevated D-dimer). On day 3, worsening hypoxemia required escalation to high-flow nasal cannula oxygen. On day 6, when elevated admission beta-D-glucan (423 pg/mL) and negative CMV antigen confirmed PCP, antibacterials were stopped and TMP/SMX (3 tablets/day) plus corticosteroids were continued. On day 12, she developed truncal pruritus and drug rash, prompting a switch from TMP/SMX to oral atovaquone. By day 19, repeat chest CT showed complete resolution of GGOs with normalized inflammatory markers; steroids were stopped, methotrexate was resumed at a reduced dose (4 mg/week), and she was discharged home in stable condition on day 25.

raw_case_text: A 25-year-old woman was admitted to a local hospital 2 years ago because of facial and lower limb edema. On admission, the patient had abnormal renal function with serum creatinine 150 mumol/L (normal range: 41.00-81.00 mumol/L) and 24-h urine protein excretion was 12.77 g. Laboratory examination showed positive ANA, anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), anti-Sm antibody, anti-U1RNP antibody, and mild reduction of complement C3. Renal histopathology indicated LN (class IV + V); the activity index was 9, and the chronic index was 1. Methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) pulse therapy was administered thrice. Subsequently, multitarget treatments were administered, including prednisone 30 mg/day, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1,000 mg/day, and tacrolimus 2 mg/day. After treatment for 4 months, anti-dsDNA and anti-ANA antibodies were negative, serum creatinine decreased from 150 mumol/L to 73 mumol/L, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased from 5,665 mg/gCr to 3,526 mg/gCr. Due to concerns about infection, MMF was stopped, and tacrolimus was adjusted to 4 mg/day, combined with hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) (200 mg/day). After 6 months of therapy, the patient's urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and serum albumin (ALB) were in a range of 3,834.33-8,590.89 mg/gCr and 22.7-32.8 g/L, respectively. In the seventh month of treatment, the patient developed fever and cough, procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels increased, and cytomegalovirus (CMV)-IgM was positive. Chest CT and blood next-generation sequencing results suggested that the patient had Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Tacrolimus and prednisone were discontinued and methylprednisolone (8 mg/day) was administered. The piperacillin-tazobactam (13.5 g/day), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (3.84 g/day), and ganciclovir (0.5 g/day) were given to treat the lung infection. After 2 months, the patient's lung infection was in remission. However, the patient's urine protein level was still within the nephrotic-range proteinuria. At the ninth month of treatment, the patient was treated with 160 mg per week telitacicept for 8 weeks. Telitacicept was administered in combination with MMF (500 mg/day), HCQ (200 mg/day), and prednisone (10 mg/day). After 8 weeks (eleventh month) of telitacicept treatment, the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio reduced from 5,600 to 3,856 mg/gCr. Serum ALB increased from 30.9 to 38.9 g/L and serum creatinine was stable. Level of immunoglobulin G decreased from 3.76 to 2.91 g/L. Then telitacicept reduced to 80 mg once per week. After 4 months (fifteenth month) of telitacicept therapy, the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio reduced significantly from 3,856 to 1,376 mg/gCr. Serum ALB improved from 38.9 to 42 g/L and level of immunoglobulin G increased from 2.91 to 4.21 g/L. After 6 months of telitacicept treatment (fifteenth month), the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio reduced significantly from 5,600 to 1,376 mg/gCr. During follow-up (from ninth to twenty-first month), the patient's renal function and proteinuria were stable, and there were no apparent manifestations of infection (Fig. 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old woman with biopsy-proven class IV+V lupus nephritis presented in the seventh month of immunosuppressive therapy with acute fever and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two years earlier, the patient had presented with facial and lower limb edema, renal insufficiency (serum creatinine 150 μmol/L), nephrotic-range proteinuria (24-h urine protein 12.77 g), hypocomplementemia (low C3), and positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, and anti-U1RNP antibodies; renal biopsy confirmed class IV+V lupus nephritis (activity index 9, chronicity index 1). She received three pulses of intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) followed by multitarget oral maintenance with prednisone (30 mg/day), mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 1,000 mg/day), and tacrolimus (2 mg/day). After 4 months, serum creatinine improved to 73 μmol/L and anti-dsDNA/ANA turned negative; MMF was stopped due to infection concerns, and she was maintained on tacrolimus (4 mg/day), hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/day), and prednisone, with persistent nephrotic proteinuria (UPCR 3,834.33–8,590.89 mg/gCr) and hypoalbuminemia (22.7–32.8 g/L) at month 6. In the seventh month of treatment, she developed acute fever and cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus with class IV+V lupus nephritis diagnosed 2 years prior, treated with pulse methylprednisolone, oral prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and hydroxychloroquine.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and cough at month 7; baseline history of facial and lower limb edema. Home medications at onset of pneumonia included tacrolimus (4 mg/day), hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/day), and prednisone.

objective.physical_examination: Initial baseline presentation 2 years prior notable for facial and lower limb edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline lupus nephritis workup: Serum creatinine 150 μmol/L (normal: 41.00–81.00 μmol/L), improving to 73 μmol/L at month 4; 24-h urine protein 12.77 g; UPCR 5,665 mg/gCr (3,834.33–8,590.89 mg/gCr at month 6); serum albumin 22.7–32.8 g/L; positive baseline ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, and anti-U1RNP with low C3. Month 7 pneumonia workup: Elevated procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP); positive serum cytomegalovirus (CMV)-IgM.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline renal biopsy: Class IV+V lupus nephritis (activity index 9, chronicity index 1). Month 7 chest CT and peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Demonstrated pulmonary infiltrates and Pneumocystis jirovecii sequences diagnostic of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by chest CT and peripheral blood next-generation sequencing) with concurrent cytomegalovirus (CMV-IgM positive) co-infection in a patient with class IV+V lupus nephritis on tacrolimus and prednisone. Plan and clinical course: Tacrolimus and oral prednisone were discontinued, and she was treated with low-dose methylprednisolone (8 mg/day), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (3.84 g/day), ganciclovir (0.5 g/day), and piperacillin-tazobactam (13.5 g/day). Her pulmonary infection achieved complete remission after 2 months. At month 9, to treat persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR 5,600 mg/gCr) safely after PJP recovery, subcutaneous telitacicept (160 mg weekly for 8 weeks, then 80 mg weekly) was added to low-dose MMF (500 mg/day), hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/day), and prednisone (10 mg/day), reducing her UPCR to 1,376 mg/gCr and normalizing serum albumin to 42 g/L by month 15 without any recurrent infections through 21 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Case 2 was a 49-year-old man from Fuzhou, Fujian Province. The patient developed a dry cough in April 2019 and developed a fever (up to 37.7 C) 3 days later, accompanied by post-activity asthma. After 2 days of fever, he was admitted to the Department of Organ Transplantation of our hospital. The patient had a history of hypertension and uremia, long-term peritoneal dialysis, and received renal transplantation in January 2019. The patient had a history of favism, was allergic to penicillin, and denied other medical histories.
On admission, the patient's blood pressure was 108/71 mmHg, respiratory rate was 20 times/min, pulse was 100 times/min, and body temperature was 37 C. Physical examination showed an abdominal renal transplantation scar, no tenderness and rebound pain, the transplanted kidney had no tenderness. Chest CT scan suggested bilateral lung infection, paraseptal emphysema of the upper lobe of both lungs, and a small amount of pericardial effusion ( Figures 3A, B ).
Laboratory tests after admission suggested that the patient had a deep fungal infection (G test of 325 pg/mL), anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hypoproteinemia, liver and kidney dysfunction, immunodeficiency (CD4 cells, 156/microL; and CD8 cells, 64/microL), and human cytomegalovirus infection (HCMV-DNA positive) ( Table 2 ). The biochemical examination results indicate a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level of 702.2 U/L. After admission, immunosuppressants (tacrolimus + mycophenolate mofetil) were discontinued, and anti-microbial drug (cefoperazone sodium and tazobactam sodium of 4 g q12h + micafungin sodium of 100 mg qd + ganciclovir of 75 mg qd), immunoglobulin infusion, gastric protection, red blood cell transfusion, cooling, and nutritional support were given. Two days later, a chest CT scan showed aggravation of bilateral lung infection ( Figures 3C, D ). A few days later, the patient developed severe asthma and fever (39 C). Respiratory pathogen detection (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid PCR) suggested Pneumocystis jiroveci. Therefore, the anti-infective regimen (caspofungin of 50 mg qd + imipenem cilastatin sodium of 500 mg q6h + moxifloxacin of 400 mg qd) was changed, and methylprednisolone sodium succinate (40 mg, once a day) and immunoenhancement therapy (thymopentin injection) were given. From day 5 to day 12, the patient's vital signs were stable without fever. During the period, the chest CT scan showed extensive exudative changes in both lungs and local infectious lesions ( Figures 3E, F ). On day 13, the patient developed a fever (38 C) again, and his asthma worsened. Clindamycin phosphate ester (1 g, q12h) was added, and the dose of methylprednisolone sodium succinate was increased (40 mg, twice daily). However, the patient developed persistent fever and dyspnea and was transferred to ICU on day 15.
Laboratory examination at the time of admission to ICU suggested that the patient's liver function improved, but the infection aggravated (G test of 1,493 pg/mL), anemia still existed, and coagulation dysfunction and cardiac insufficiency occurred ( Table 2 ). In ICU, the patient was given non-invasive ventilator-assisted breathing, continued anti-microbial drug (cefoperazone sodium and tazobactam sodium of 4 g q12h + clindamycin of 1 g q12h + caspofungin of 50 mg qd + sulfamethoxazole of 1 g q12h + ganciclovir of 75 mg qd), diuresis, hypoglycemic, and other treatments. On day 17, imipenem (500 mg, q6h) was added. From day 17 to day 20, the patient's vital signs were stable, but purpura appeared in the left forearm and gradually subsided after the improvement of coagulation function. On day 21, the patient developed a fever again (39 C), and a chest CT scan showed extensive exudative changes in both lungs with a bilateral lung infection, which was significantly more advanced than before ( Figures 3G, H ). Respiratory pathogen detection (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid PCR) showed Candida parapsilosis, the G test was 520.3 pg/mL, and GM test was positive. On day 24, the patient developed a fever again (38.1 C), and the patient's pulmonary infection was aggravated. Therefore, the dosage of sulfamethoxazole (2 g, three times a day) and caspofungin (70 mg, once a day) was increased, and human gamma globulin was added to enhance immunity. Clindamycin and ganciclovir were discontinued. One day later, urine culture returned Candida parapsilosis (50,000 CFU/mL); considering the patient's history of solid organ transplantation, prolonged use of antimicrobial agents, the presence of multiple indwelling catheters, and the failure of adequate antibacterial therapy, we point out that the patient had candidiasis. Four days later, blood culture returned T. marneffei. From day 29 to day 35, the patient's vital signs were stable, with occasional afternoon low fever, and the infection was better than before, but hyperkalemia, high urea nitrogen, diarrhea, and purpura were aggravated, and the coagulation function deteriorated ( Table 2 ). Renal replacement therapy and multiple transfusions of fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, platelets, and leukocyte-poor red blood cells were given. On day 36, the patient suddenly became irritable and could not tolerate a non-invasive ventilator. Tracheal intubation-assisted ventilation was performed, and a chest CT scan showed extensive exudative changes in both lungs, which progressed ( Figures 3I, J ). On day 37, the patient suffered sudden cardiac arrest and died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male renal transplant recipient presented in April 2019 with a 5-day history of dry cough and a 2-day history of fever (up to 37.7 °C) and exertional dyspnea/wheezing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a dry cough in April 2019, followed 3 days later by fever up to 37.7 °C and post-activity asthma/dyspnea, leading to hospital admission 2 days after fever onset. Three months earlier (January 2019), he had undergone allogeneic renal transplantation for uremia following long-term peritoneal dialysis and was maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, uremia treated with long-term peritoneal dialysis, and allogeneic renal transplantation in January 2019; history of favism (G6PD deficiency).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, fever, and exertional dyspnea/wheezing. Allergic to penicillin. Home medications included tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Blood pressure 108/71 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, pulse 100 beats/min, and body temperature 37.0 °C. Abdominal examination: Well-healed abdominal renal transplant scar without abdominal tenderness, rebound pain, or graft tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hypoproteinemia, hepatic and renal dysfunction, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) level 702.2 U/L, and positive human cytomegalovirus DNA (HCMV-DNA). Subsequent ICU labs (day 15 onward): Coagulation dysfunction, cardiac insufficiency, hyperkalemia, and elevated blood urea nitrogen; day 25 urine culture grew Candida parapsilosis (50,000 CFU/mL); day 29 blood culture grew Talaromyces marneffei.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission chest CT: Bilateral lung infection, bilateral upper lobe paraseptal emphysema, and small pericardial effusion (with progressive bilateral exudative consolidation on repeat CTs on days 2, 5–12, 21, and 36). Fungal biomarkers and lymphocyte subsets: Admission serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G test) elevated at 325 pg/mL (peaking at 1,493 pg/mL on day 15 and 520.3 pg/mL on day 21, with positive galactomannan [GM] test on day 21); severe T-cell lymphopenia with CD4+ count 156/μL and CD8+ count 64/μL. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) PCR assays: Initial BALF PCR confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii; repeat BALF PCR on day 21 detected Candida parapsilosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by BALF PCR and serum G test up to 1,493 pg/mL) complicated by polymicrobial opportunistic co-infections including cytomegalovirus (HCMV-DNAemia), invasive Candida parapsilosis pneumonia and candiduria (BALF PCR and urine culture), and disseminated Talaromyces marneffei fungemia (blood culture) in a renal transplant recipient. Plan and clinical course: Upon admission, tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil were stopped, and initial therapy with cefoperazone-tazobactam (4 g q12h), micafungin (100 mg qd), ganciclovir (75 mg qd), IVIG, and RBC transfusion was started. After BALF PCR confirmed P. jirovecii, the regimen was switched to caspofungin (50 mg qd), imipenem-cilastatin (500 mg q6h), moxifloxacin (400 mg qd), methylprednisolone (40 mg qd, increased to 40 mg bid on day 13), thymopentin, and clindamycin (1 g q12h added day 13). Following ICU transfer on day 15 for refractory fever and respiratory failure, he received noninvasive ventilation, sulfamethoxazole (1 g q12h, escalated to 2 g TID on day 24), caspofungin (escalated to 70 mg qd on day 24), clindamycin, cefoperazone-tazobactam, imipenem, ganciclovir, IVIG, continuous renal replacement therapy, and blood product transfusions. On day 36, he required endotracheal intubation for worsening bilateral exudative pneumonia, and on day 37 he suffered sudden cardiac arrest and died.

raw_case_text:
A 70-year-old female patient diagnosed with Philadelphia-like CRLF2 overexpression B-cell precursor ALL was admitted to our hospital in 2021. She underwent induction chemotherapy of the VDLD regimen (vindesine, idarubicin, dexamethasone, and pegylated asparaginase) on August 1, 2021, and achieved complete remission. However, she experienced complications of chemotherapy-induced bone marrow suppression, febrile neutropenia, and bloodstream infection of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Treatment with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and meropenem led to complete recovery by August 21. Her past medical history included hypertension and steroid-induced diabetes, both of which recovered after induction chemotherapy. Additionally, she underwent cholecystectomy due to cholecystolithiasis and thyroid nodulectomy with normal thyroid function.
For consolidation therapy following prior induction chemotherapy, she received blinatumomab on September 10th (9 mug per day during the first week and 28 mug per day during the next 3 weeks) via continuous infusion. Her white blood cell (WBC) count was 9.84 x 109/L, and the lymphocyte count was 1.55 x 109/L on September 8th. On the second day of blinatumomab infusion, she presented with subfebrile fever, which was thought attributed to mild cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and managed with loxoprofen. The WBC and lymphocyte count were 10.9 x 109/L and 0.91 x 109/L on September 10, separately. However, on the 9th day after blinatumomab use, she experienced intermittent fever without obvious respiratory symptoms, and her WBC count increased to 18.1 x 109/L. Chest CT revealed subtle infiltrates and nodules. The patient received empiric treatment with piperacillin/tazobactam, acyclovir, and 160 mg trimethoprim (TMP)/800 mg sulfamethoxazole (SMX) daily for PCP infection prophylaxis. Despite treatment, the fever persisted, and loxoprofen was administered as needed.
On the 17th day of blinatumomab treatment, she developed obvious shortness of breath, and her pulse oxygen saturation decreased to 78%. Chest CT showed diffuse GGO with scattered small nodules (as shown in Fig. 1). Additionally, her lymphocyte count decreased to 0.59 x 109/L, C-reactive protein increased from 2.41 to 109.75 (reference <3) mg/L, LDH increased from 250 to 413 (reference <250) U/L, and beta-D-glucan assays showed 298.6 (reference <100.5) pg/mL, all indicative of possible PCP infection. The dry cough with no sputum prompted next-generation sequencing of peripheral blood, which tested positive for pneumocystis jirovecii without evidence of other pathogens. Consequently, the patient was diagnosed with PCP.
Therapeutic dosages of TMP-SMX (15 mg/kg/day of the TMP component) and dexamethasone (8 mg IV twice a day for 5 days, gradually tapered over 14 days) were administered, and the first cycle of blinatumomab had to be stopped. She ultimately achieved complete recovery, and an additional four cycles of blinatumomab with prophylaxis of PCP (160 mg TMP/800 mg SMX daily) were administered. As of now, MRD has consistently been negative during follow-ups.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 70-year-old female with Philadelphia-like B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia developed intermittent fever on day 9 and acute dyspnea with dry cough on day 17 of continuous blinatumomab consolidation therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed with Philadelphia-like CRLF2-overexpressing B-cell precursor ALL in 2021 and achieved complete remission following VDLD induction chemotherapy (vindesine, idarubicin, dexamethasone, pegylated asparaginase) started on August 1, 2021, which was complicated by febrile neutropenia and Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia that resolved with G-CSF and meropenem by August 21. On September 10, 2021, she started consolidation therapy with continuous intravenous blinatumomab (9 μg/day week 1, then 28 μg/day). She had a subfebrile temperature on day 2 attributed to mild cytokine release syndrome (managed with loxoprofen). On day 9 of blinatumomab, she developed intermittent fever without obvious respiratory symptoms that persisted despite empiric piperacillin/tazobactam, acyclovir, and prophylactic-dose TMP-SMX (160 mg/800 mg daily). On day 17 of blinatumomab, she developed acute shortness of breath and dry cough without sputum.
subjective.past_medical_history: Philadelphia-like CRLF2-overexpressing B-cell precursor ALL in first complete remission; prior chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and Pseudomonas aeruginosa bloodstream infection (August 2021); hypertension and steroid-induced diabetes (both resolved post-induction); status post cholecystectomy for cholecystolithiasis and thyroid nodulectomy (euthyroid).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever, acute shortness of breath, and non-productive dry cough.

objective.physical_examination: On day 17 of blinatumomab infusion: Obvious shortness of breath and severe hypoxemia with pulse oxygen saturation (SpO2) dropping to 78%.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial complete blood counts and inflammatory markers: Baseline pre-blinatumomab (September 8) WBC 9.84 x 10^9/L and lymphocytes 1.55 x 10^9/L; day 2 (September 10) WBC 10.9 x 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.91 x 10^9/L; day 9 WBC rose to 18.1 x 10^9/L; day 17 lymphocyte count fell to 0.59 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) surged from 2.41 to 109.75 mg/L (reference <3 mg/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) increased from 250 to 413 U/L (reference <250 U/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial chest CT scans: Day 9 chest CT showed subtle pulmonary infiltrates and nodules; day 17 chest CT demonstrated diffuse ground-glass opacities (GGO) with scattered small nodules. Fungal biomarker (day 17): Elevated serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan at 298.6 pg/mL (reference <100.5 pg/mL). Peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii with no other pathogens detected.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) during blinatumomab consolidation therapy for B-cell precursor ALL, definitively confirmed by peripheral blood next-generation sequencing (mNGS), elevated serum beta-D-glucan (298.6 pg/mL), elevated LDH (413 U/L), lymphopenia (0.59 x 10^9/L), and diffuse bilateral GGOs on chest CT. Plan and clinical course: The first cycle of blinatumomab was halted, and therapeutic-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, 15 mg/kg/day of the TMP component) plus intravenous dexamethasone (8 mg IV twice daily for 5 days, tapered over 14 days) were administered. The patient achieved complete clinical and radiographic recovery and subsequently completed four additional consolidation cycles of blinatumomab under daily TMP-SMX prophylaxis (160 mg/800 mg daily), maintaining persistent minimal residual disease (MRD)-negative remission on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
In May 2023, a 63-year-old man presented with a fever peaking at 38 C, chills, fatigue, and poor overall well-being. Laboratory results indicated erythrocytopenia, with red blood cell (RBC) count at 2.2x1012/L, hemoglobin (Hb) at 72g/L, and platelet count (PLT) at 80x109/L; reticulocyte percentage was notably high at 9.7%. Elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) at 63.6mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 80mm/h, ferritin at 1469ng/mL, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 1103U/L were observed (Table 1). The patient tested positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgM, with both urine occult blood and hemosiderin tests returning positive results. Ultrasonography revealed splenomegaly. A bone marrow biopsy indicated active hyperplasia, with a decreased granulocyte to nucleated erythrocyte ratio, and erythroid hyperplasia being predominant, featuring occasionally hemophagocytic cells. Initially treated for hemophagocytic syndrome induced by EBV infection, the patient received ciprofloxacin, cyclosporine, dexamethasone, and etoposide in local hospital. Despite some improvement, weakness persisted.
In July 2023, the patient was readmitted with a low-grade fever. Routine laboratory tests revealed the following: RBC count at 1.58x1012/L, Hb level at 61g/L, PLT count at 76x109/L, Reticulocyte percentage at 15.71%, CRP count at 19.6mg/L, ESR at 66mm/h, Serum total bilirubin at 35.0mumol/L, Serum direct total bilirubin at 22.4mumol/L, and blood EBV DNA at 5.26x103 copies /mL (Table 1). A chest CT scan identified scattered nodules across both lungs, with a notably larger one located in the lower right lung (Figure 1A). Bone marrow smear analysis indicated that phagocytic reticulum cells constituted 0.5%, while the bone marrow biopsy did not reveal any abnormal cells. PET-CT showed that the metabolism of Fluoro-Deoxy-Glucose (FDG) in bone marrow cavity was slightly increased, and the spleen was full with FDG metabolism. Although lymphoma could not be entirely ruled out based on the existing diagnostic evidence, the primary concern was hemolytic anemia in conjunction with the confirmed EBV infection. Consequently, the patient received treatment with dexamethasone and cyclosporine to manage the hemolytic condition, in addition to galiximab, before being discharged. 
In September 2023, the patient was rehospitalized due to an exacerbation of symptoms, including a severe cough with sputum production, chest tightness, and acute shortness of breath following physical activity. Laboratory investigations showed RBC count of 1.81x1012/L; Hb level at 63g/L; PLT count at 206x109/L; Reticulocyte percentage at 15.8%; CRP level at 76.2mg/L and ESR at 99mm/h (Table 1). A CT scan of the lungs revealed a new mass in the upper lobe of the right lung (Figure 1B). Tests for fungal and bacterial infections, including fungal culture, bacterial culture, TB smear, Cryptococcus neoformans capsular antigen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, respiratory virus screening, and fungal immunofluorescence staining, returned negative results. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of sputum identified Babesia microti, Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, Pneumocystis yersii, and human herpesvirus. Additional mNGS testing of alveolar lavage fluid and blood samples also detected Babesia microti (Figure 2). Examination of a peripheral blood Giemsa smear showed 27.9% parasitaemia with Babesia microti (Figure 3).  
Upon inquiring about the patient's history of exposure, it was discovered that the patient had been bitten on the neck by ticks six months earlier while working in a mountainous area, though no significant bite marks or lesions were observed, and no treatment had been administered at that time. Treatment was initiated with atovaquone 750 mg orally Q12h plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenous injection Q24h for Babesia, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Nocardia, along with human immunoglobulin to bolster immunity. Following this regimen, the chest CT scan in November 2023 and routine laboratory tests in January 2024 both showed that the patient had recovered.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old man treated with dexamethasone, cyclosporine, and etoposide for suspected EBV-associated hemophagocytic syndrome and hemolytic anemia presented in September 2023 with severe productive cough, chest tightness, and acute exertional shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In May 2023, the patient initially presented with fever up to 38 °C, chills, fatigue, hemolytic anemia (Hb 72 g/L, reticulocytes 9.7%), thrombocytopenia (80 x 10^9/L), hyperferritinemia (1,469 ng/mL), elevated LDH (1,103 U/L), splenomegaly, positive EBV IgM, and erythroid hyperplasia with occasional hemophagocytosis on bone marrow biopsy; he was treated at a local hospital for presumed EBV-induced hemophagocytic syndrome with ciprofloxacin, cyclosporine, dexamethasone, and etoposide. In July 2023, he was readmitted with low-grade fever, persistent hemolytic anemia (Hb 61 g/L, reticulocytes 15.71%, total bilirubin 35.0 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 22.4 μmol/L), EBV DNAemia (5.26 x 10^3 copies/mL), and scattered bilateral lung nodules on chest CT (largest in the right lower lobe), and received dexamethasone, cyclosporine, and galiximab. In September 2023, he was rehospitalized for acute exacerbation of severe productive cough, chest tightness, and exertional dyspnea. Retrospective exposure history revealed he had been bitten on the neck by ticks 6 months earlier while working in a mountainous area.
subjective.past_medical_history: Presumed EBV-associated hemophagocytic syndrome and Coombs/hemolytic anemia diagnosed in May 2023, treated with dexamethasone, cyclosporine, etoposide, and galiximab; occupational tick bite on the neck 6 months prior while working in a mountainous area.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, fatigue, severe cough with sputum production, chest tightness, and acute exertional dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Splenomegaly noted on baseline evaluation; febrile up to 38 °C at initial onset.
objective.routine_investigations: May 2023 labs: RBC 2.2 x 10^12/L, Hb 72 g/L, PLT 80 x 10^9/L, reticulocytes 9.7%, CRP 63.6 mg/L, ESR 80 mm/h, ferritin 1,469 ng/mL, LDH 1,103 U/L, positive EBV IgM, positive urine occult blood and hemosiderin; abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly. July 2023 labs: RBC 1.58 x 10^12/L, Hb 61 g/L, PLT 76 x 10^9/L, reticulocytes 15.71%, CRP 19.6 mg/L, ESR 66 mm/h, total bilirubin 35.0 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 22.4 μmol/L, blood EBV DNA 5.26 x 10^3 copies/mL. September 2023 admission labs: RBC 1.81 x 10^12/L, Hb 63 g/L, PLT 206 x 10^9/L, reticulocytes 15.8%, CRP 76.2 mg/L, ESR 99 mm/h; negative routine bacterial/fungal cultures, TB smear, MTB DNA, Cryptococcus capsular antigen, respiratory virus panel, and fungal immunofluorescence staining. Peripheral blood Giemsa-stained smear (September 2023): Intraerythrocytic Babesia microti parasites with 27.9% parasitemia.
objective.advanced_workup: May & July 2023 bone marrow biopsies and PET-CT: Active erythroid hyperplasia with occasional hemophagocytic cells (0.5% phagocytic reticulum cells) and increased bone marrow and splenic 18F-FDG uptake on PET-CT without overt lymphoma. Serial chest CT scans: Scattered bilateral pulmonary nodules with a larger right lower lobe nodule in July 2023, followed by a new mass in the right upper lobe in September 2023. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) in September 2023: Sputum mNGS identified Babesia microti, Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, Pneumocystis jirovecii ('Pneumocystis yersii'), and human herpesvirus; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and peripheral blood mNGS both confirmed Babesia microti.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe human babesiosis (Babesia microti with 27.9% parasitemia on Giemsa blood smear and positive blood/BALF/sputum mNGS—which had initially mimicked EBV-induced hemophagocytic syndrome and autoimmune hemolytic anemia following a mountain tick bite) complicated by immunosuppression-induced pulmonary co-infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii, Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, and human herpesvirus (confirmed by sputum mNGS and right upper lobe mass on chest CT). Plan and clinical course: Treated with oral atovaquone (750 mg q12h) plus intravenous azithromycin (500 mg q24h) for Babesia microti, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, and intravenous human immunoglobulin. Follow-up chest CT in November 2023 and routine hematologic/biochemical tests in January 2024 confirmed complete clinical, hematologic, and radiographic recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of mixed-phenotype acute leukemia was admitted as an inpatient in the Hemato-Oncology Unit of the Centro Hospitalar Universitario de Sao Joao for first-line consolidation treatment with intensive chemotherapy with fludarabine, cytarabine, filgrastim, and idarubicin (FLAG-Ida) and sorafenib.
She underwent induction treatment one month before with the same regimen, achieving complete remission. During that hospital stay, she had two separate episodes of febrile neutropenia. The patient initially spiked a fever on admission and was treated with piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin; no infectious sources were identified and temperature soon abated after the start of the antimicrobials. However, the fever recurred after the antimicrobials were stopped, and piperacillin/tazobactam was restarted. The patient remained febrile and a piperacillin/tazobactam-resistant strain of Klebsiella oxytoca (K. oxytoca) was identified in blood cultures, motivating escalation to meropenem. The patient improved and meropenem was discontinued after seven days of treatment and after new blood cultures were negative for the previously identified pathogen. She was discharged home while clinically well and after recovery from neutropenia.
Twelve days after discharge, the patient was readmited for consolidation treatment to a ward with positive air pressure and air flow control in the Hemato-Oncology Unit. As per hospital protocol, antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis were instituted with acyclovir and posaconazole, respectively; no routine prophylaxis is given for bacterial infections or for Pneumocystis jirovecii (P. jirovecii) pneumonia in our center.
Eleven days after the start of chemotherapy, the patient developed febrile neutropenia while hemodynamically stable. Piperacillin/tazobactam was started empirically, but blood cultures again showed a K. oxytoca bacteremia with a resistant strain. She was immediately changed to meropenem and responded well, and was later de-escalated to cefepime to complete seven days of treatment.
After this episode had resolved, 25 days after the start of chemotherapy and while the patient was profoundly neutropenic (white blood cell count 0.06x109/L), a new febrile syndrome developed. There were no other signs of a specific source for infection and she remained hemodynamically stable, and so blood (both peripheral and central venous catheter) and urine cultures were obtained while meropenem was initiated as empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy for febrile neutropenia, considering previous findings of a recurrent K. oxytoca resistant to piperacillin/tazobactam. Analytically, and comparing to routine blood work from the day before, a sudden drop in hemoglobin concentration from 8.6 to 6.8 g/dL (reference range 12.0-16.0) and a new-onset unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (5.54 mg/dL in total bilirubin, reference range <1.2 mg/dL) were noted. Remarkably, both potassium and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) concentrations were unreportable due to hemolysis.
A few hours later that day, the patient was agitated and presented general malaise. She was somnolent, complained of unspecific abdominal discomfort, and showed a decrease in oxygen saturation. The urine presented frank red discoloration. A new analytic study showed rapidly aggravating anemia (Hb 4.5 g/dL) and new-onset microcytosis (MCV {mean corpuscular volume} 76.4 fL, reference range 87.0-103.0, previously 88.9 fL), associated with metabolic acidosis (pH 7.14, reference range 7.35-7.45), marked increase in serum lactate (19.5 mmol/L, reference range <2.0) and acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.43 mg/dL, reference range 0.51-0.95, previously 0.66). Unfortunately, a peripheral blood smear was not obtained. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen was performed to exclude signs of internal bleeding, considering the findings of worsening anemia, transfusion-dependent thrombocytopenia, and red-colored urine. The scan was otherwise unremarkable except for an air-dense lesion on the right hepatic lobe, not typical of pneumobilia and without any apparent association with vascular structures (Figure 1). No abnormalities were reported in the urinary tract.
The patient was kept on aggressive hydration and multiple transfusions with packed red blood cell concentrates. She was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to progressive clinical and neurological deterioration and for supportive treatment of a neutropenic septic shock with respiratory, renal, hepatic, and neurological dysfunction, and vancomycin was added to meropenem for additional large-spectrum antibacterial coverage with close monitoring of vancomycin levels according to protocol; considering hospital epidemiology, broader coverage for Gram-negative bacteria was felt unnecessary. A urine sample was obtained after admission to the ICU, and erythrocyturia (79.3 cells/microL, reference range <27.0) was abnormally mild for a hematuria-like red discoloration. This information, together with a rapidly progressing acute microcytic anemia, the apparent absence of internal or external bleeding, and the presence of an air-dense hepatic lesion associated with fever, was suggestive of massive intravascular hemolysis with probable hemoglobinuria and a gas-forming liver abscess, pointing to a toxin-producing clostridial infection. A few days after ICU admission, the initial blood cultures allowed the identification of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-negative multidrug-sensible Escherichia coli (E. coli) and concomitant co-infection with Gram-positive rods of C. perfringens, a known alpha-toxin producing pathogen, confirming the clinical suspicion.
During her stay in the ICU, the patient was started on vasopressors for the sepsis-related cardiovascular dysfunction, and on continuous veno-venous hemofiltration for failing to improve her kidney function. Antibacterial treatment was initially effective and a reduction in hemolytic markers was seen, as the patient also reduced her red cell transfusion requirements. Despite rapidly weaning the vasopressors and transitioning to sustained low-efficiency dialysis with support from the Nephrology team, respiratory insufficiency aggravated with increasing oxygen demands, which prompted the ICU team to start high-flow nasal cannula therapy and to repeat a CT scan of the thorax. Due to the presence of bilateral consolidations with ground-glass appearance, the patient was empirically started on amphotericin B for a possible invasive fungal infection. In order to obtain microbiological evidence for this, a bronco-alveolar lavage was performed after discussion with the Pneumology team. Both fungal cultures and markers were negative, including galactomannan on the blood and on the lavage; beta-D-glucan quantification is not available at our center. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for P. jirovecii was found to be positive and, although the radiological image was not highly suggestive of this diagnosis, the patient was started on co-trimoxazol and on a course of corticosteroids after a multidisciplinary meeting between the Hematology, ICU, and Infectious Diseases teams. Meropenem was maintained for twelve days and vancomycin was later deescalated to penicillin G directed at the hepatic abscess likely caused by the gas-producing anaerobe, aiming to more efficiently control the source of infection. Indeed, considering the complexity of this case, a multidisciplinary approach was necessary to adjust treatments on an almost daily basis.
The patient indeed survived the clostridial septic shock and the febrile neutropenia resolved. She was transferred back to the ward still on co-trimoxazole but improving from the pneumocystosis and no longer requiring oxygen support. Although the hepatic air-dense lesion disappeared on imaging re-evaluation, hyperammonemia, and other hepatic parameters failed to normalize and the patient did not recover from multifactorial kidney injury, permanently requiring dialysis. Two months after starting chemotherapy and more than a month after the septic shock, she further developed a progressive decline in awareness and a multifactorial metabolic encephalopathy ensued. The patient eventually died without hematopoietic recovery despite no evidence of relapsed leukemia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old woman with mixed-phenotype acute leukemia developed profound febrile neutropenia, acute intravascular hemolysis, somnolence, abdominal discomfort, red-colored urine, and hypoxemia on day 25 of FLAG-Ida plus sorafenib consolidation chemotherapy, followed by worsening hypoxemic respiratory insufficiency in the ICU.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient achieved complete remission of mixed-phenotype acute leukemia 1 month earlier following FLAG-Ida (fludarabine, cytarabine, filgrastim, idarubicin) plus sorafenib induction, which had been complicated by piperacillin/tazobactam-resistant Klebsiella oxytoca bacteremia treated with meropenem. Twelve days post-discharge, she was readmitted for consolidation with the same FLAG-Ida plus sorafenib regimen under acyclovir and posaconazole prophylaxis (without routine bacterial or Pneumocystis prophylaxis). On day 11 of consolidation, she had recurrent piperacillin/tazobactam-resistant K. oxytoca febrile neutropenia that resolved with meropenem/cefepime. On day 25, while profoundly neutropenic (WBC 0.06 x 10^9/L), she developed a new febrile syndrome, rapidly followed within hours by agitation, malaise, somnolence, nonspecific abdominal discomfort, oxygen desaturation, and frank red discoloration of the urine. After surviving acute clostridial septic shock in the ICU, she subsequently developed worsening hypoxemic respiratory insufficiency with escalating oxygen requirements.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia in first complete remission (status post FLAG-Ida + sorafenib induction 1 month prior); two prior episodes of piperacillin/tazobactam-resistant Klebsiella oxytoca bacteremia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, agitation, malaise, somnolence, nonspecific abdominal discomfort, red-colored urine (hemoglobinuria), and progressive dyspnea/hypoxemia.

objective.physical_examination: On day 25 of consolidation: Febrile, agitated, somnolent, with frank red urine, hypoxemia, and rapid progression to septic shock with multiorgan (respiratory, renal, hepatic, and neurological) dysfunction.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 25 consolidation labs: Profound neutropenia (WBC 0.06 x 10^9/L); abrupt hemoglobin drop from 8.6 to 6.8 g/dL and then 4.5 g/dL within hours (reference: 12.0–16.0 g/dL) with new microcytosis (MCV 76.4 fL from 88.9 fL, reference: 87.0–103.0 fL); unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 5.54 mg/dL, reference <1.2 mg/dL); potassium and LDH unreportable due to massive intravascular hemolysis; severe lactic acidosis (pH 7.14, serum lactate 19.5 mmol/L, reference <2.0 mmol/L); acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.43 mg/dL from 0.66 mg/dL, reference: 0.51–0.95 mg/dL); urinalysis showed disproportionately mild erythrocyturia (79.3 cells/μL, reference <27.0) despite frank red hemoglobinuria. Blood cultures (day 25): Co-infection with ESBL-negative multidrug-susceptible Escherichia coli and alpha-toxin-producing Clostridium perfringens.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT on day 25: Air-dense lesion in the right hepatic lobe compatible with a gas-forming liver abscess, without active internal hemorrhage. Repeat thoracic CT in ICU (during secondary respiratory worsening): Bilateral pulmonary consolidations with ground-glass appearance. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) analysis: Negative fungal cultures and negative blood and BAL galactomannan; BAL PCR assay was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Clostridium perfringens and Escherichia coli septic shock with a gas-forming hepatic abscess and massive alpha-toxin-mediated intravascular hemolysis, subsequently complicated by Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by positive BAL P. jirovecii PCR and bilateral ground-glass consolidations on thoracic CT) during profound post-FLAG-Ida neutropenia. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the ICU with packed RBC transfusions, vasopressors, continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (later transitioned to sustained low-efficiency dialysis), meropenem (12 days), and vancomycin (later de-escalated to penicillin G to target the clostridial hepatic abscess). When respiratory insufficiency worsened with bilateral ground-glass consolidations, empiric amphotericin B was started and then switched to co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) plus systemic corticosteroids alongside high-flow nasal cannula oxygen after BAL PCR confirmed P. jirovecii. She survived septic shock, resolved her hepatic abscess and PCP (weaning off supplemental oxygen), and transferred back to the ward on co-trimoxazole, but remained dialysis-dependent with persistent hepatic dysfunction/hyperammonemia and died over a month later from multifactorial metabolic encephalopathy without hematopoietic recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with gradual onset dyspnea accompanied by cough and fever. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to smoking (20 packs/year) and HIV infection without any follow-up or treatment, diagnosed three years prior during hospitalization for pulmonary actinomycosis. He did not have any recollection of when the transmission occurred.
On admission, his vital signs included blood pressure of 110/56 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, and SpO2 of 82% (room air). He was conscious, with a Glasgow coma scale ranking of 15 (ocular response four points, verbal response five points, motor response six points), without changes in pupil size or shape. Other notable findings during the physical exam included white lesions on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx, compatible with oral candidiasis, and papular lesions in the healing phase in his back (Figure 1). No lymphadenopathy was noted. He was sarcopenic, weighing 50 kg. Lung auscultation revealed scattered crackles. The neurological exam was normal, and no meningeal signs were present.
Arterial blood gas (oxygen at two liters/minute) showed pH 7.45, PaO2 73 mmHg, PaCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, and lactate 1.1 mmol/L, with an alveolar-arterial O2 gradient of 77.9 mmHg. Admission's laboratory notable findings included leukocytes 4.5 x 103/microL (lymphocytes 0.6 x 103/microL), LDH 330 U/L, and C-reactive protein (CRP) 7.9 mg/dL (Table 1). The patient had 1 CD4+ cell/uL (normal 410-1590 cells/uL), a T-helper/suppressor ratio of 0, and an HIV viral load superior to 92,000 copies. Additional serologic studies for syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania, and Hepatitis B and C virus were negative. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella urine antigen tests were also negative.
A high-resolution chest CT scan revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities (Figure 2). Since the patient was a person living with HIV without any follow-up or treatment and the imaging studies were suggestive of PCP, empirical trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (250/1250 mg three times a day) and prednisolone (40 mg twice a day on the first five days, followed by 40 mg once a day in the next five days and 20 mg once a day on the following ten days) were started. BAL (Figure 3) fluid analysis was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (by PCR), Cryptococcus neoformans (by culture), and multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli (by culture). Additionally, liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg daily) plus flucytosine (1250 mg four times a day) and meropenem (1000 mg three times a day, directed to Escherichia coli) were added. Blood cultures collected were also positive for Cryptococcus neoformans.
Three days after admission, the patient started with headaches, nausea, vomiting, and lethargy, and a head CT scan was performed, showing hypodense areas in the left gangliocapsular region with mass effect (Figure 4A-4B). Cerebral MRI confirmed the presence of tumefactive lesions in the head of the right caudate nucleus and in the head and body of the left caudate nucleus, with hypersignal in T2. These lesions were compressing the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles (Figure 5A-5B) and were suggestive of cryptococcomas.
A lumbar puncture was performed (with an opening pressure of 21 cm H2O), yielding positive results for Cryptococcus neoformans, both antigen (titer >1:1024) and culture. Second and third lumbar punctures (opening pressure <20 cm H2O) were done on days 7 and 14 of treatment. Its results can be observed in Table 2.
Due to the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis, the initiation of ART was deferred due to the risk of IRIS. Liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine were administered for two weeks until the cultures were negative, followed by consolidation therapy with fluconazole (800 mg once a day). Regarding PCP, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was maintained for 21 days, followed by secondary prophylaxis (160/800 mg thrice a week).
In the fourth week of hospitalization, the patient experienced a decreased level of consciousness, with a Glasgow coma scale of 10 (ocular response of three points, verbal response of two points, and motor response of five points), accompanied by vomiting, dizziness, headaches, right hemiparesis, and mixed aphasia. Emergent cerebral CT showed left gangliocapsular hyperdensity, compatible with hemorrhagic transformation following ischemic stroke, with ipsilateral intraventricular bleeding and hydrocephalus (Figure 6A-6B). He was subsequently transferred to the neurosurgery unit, where his condition deteriorated, not having surgical conditions and ultimately culminating in the patient's demise.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man with untreated HIV infection and COPD presented to the emergency department with gradual-onset dyspnea, cough, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been diagnosed with HIV infection 3 years earlier during a hospitalization for pulmonary actinomycosis but never engaged in follow-up or antiretroviral therapy, presented to the emergency department with gradually progressive shortness of breath, cough, and fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Untreated HIV infection diagnosed 3 years prior; pulmonary actinomycosis 3 years prior; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) secondary to a 20-pack-year smoking history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for gradual-onset dyspnea, cough, fever, oral thrush, and weight loss/sarcopenia (subsequently developed headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy on day 3, and right hemiparesis/aphasia in week 4).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Blood pressure 110/56 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, SpO2 82% on room air; weight 50 kg (sarcopenic). Neurological status on admission: Conscious and alert with GCS 15 (E4V5M6), normal pupils, no focal deficits or meningeal signs (later declined to GCS 10 with right hemiparesis and mixed aphasia in week 4). Mucocutaneous and chest exam: White plaques on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx consistent with oral candidiasis; healing papular skin lesions over the back; no palpable lymphadenopathy; scattered crackles on lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas (on 2 L/min O2): pH 7.45, PaO2 73 mmHg, PaCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, lactate 1.1 mmol/L, and alveolar-arterial O2 gradient 77.9 mmHg. Admission blood tests: WBC 4.5 x 10^3/μL (lymphocytes 0.6 x 10^3/μL), LDH 330 U/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 7.9 mg/dL, and HIV viral load >92,000 copies/mL. Negative infectious screening: Syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania, HBV, HCV serologies, and urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigens all negative. Blood cultures: Positive for Cryptococcus neoformans.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subsets: Absolute CD4+ T-cell count 1 cell/μL (normal: 410–1,590 cells/μL) with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0. High-resolution chest CT: Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid analysis: Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by PCR, Cryptococcus neoformans by fungal culture, and multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli by bacterial culture. Neuroimaging and lumbar punctures (day 3 onward): Head CT showed left gangliocapsular hypodensities with mass effect; brain MRI confirmed T2-hyperintense tumefactive cryptococcomas in the right caudate head and left caudate head/body compressing the frontal horns; lumbar puncture (opening pressure 21 cmH2O) was positive for Cryptococcus neoformans antigen (titer >1:1,024) and culture. Week 4 emergent head CT: Left gangliocapsular hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke with ipsilateral intraventricular hemorrhage and hydrocephalus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by BAL PCR), disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans infection (cryptococcal meningitis with basal ganglia cryptococcomas, cryptococcemia, and pulmonary cryptococcosis confirmed by BAL, blood, and CSF cultures and CSF CrAg >1:1,024), and MDR Escherichia coli pneumonia in a profoundly immunocompromised patient with untreated HIV/AIDS (CD4+ count 1 cell/μL). Plan and clinical course: Empirically started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX 250/1,250 mg TID for 21 days, followed by secondary prophylaxis at 160/800 mg thrice weekly) and a 21-day prednisolone taper (40 mg BID x 5d, 40 mg qd x 5d, 20 mg qd x 10d). Following BAL, blood, and CSF results, liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day) plus flucytosine (1,250 mg QID) for 2 weeks (until CSF cultures cleared, then fluconazole 800 mg/day consolidation) and meropenem (1,000 mg TID) were added, while antiretroviral therapy was deferred to avoid CNS IRIS. In week 4, the patient suffered a fatal left gangliocapsular hemorrhagic stroke with intraventricular extension and hydrocephalus.

raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old male presented with history of fever and skin rash on the extremities for 1 week. Additionally, he complained of chronic diarrhea. There was no history of night sweats, cough, chest or joint pain, oral lesions, drug use, and tick bites. He lived on a farm and mowed his lawn regularly. He had recently travelled to Florida 1 month prior to admission. His past medical history was significant for previously diagnosed T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS). He had received multiple immunosuppressive agents in the past, and was taking tofacitinib and daily prednisone at the time of presentation, in addition to valganciclovir. On admission, he was febrile (temperature 39.6 C). Bilaterally symmetrical desquamative, erythematous skin rash was seen on his hands, thighs, and lower legs in the background of generalized pitting edema. The rest of his physical examination was unremarkable.
Initial laboratory data demonstrated normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dl); normal white blood cell count (WBC 5.6 k/ul) including differentials and normal serum chemistries. His C-Reactive protein (CRP) was elevated at 29.6 mg/dl (normal = 0-1). Other relevant tests included negative blood cultures, negative fungal antibody panel in blood, negative blood CMV DNA by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), negative Parvovirus B19 by serologies and PCR tests, and negative serum West Nile virus immunoglobulin G (IgG); and serum cryptococcal antigen, urinary histoplasma, and Legionella antigen. A subsequent computerized tomography (CT) scan of the chest demonstrated multifocal ground-glass and consolidative opacities with air bronchograms predominantly in the left upper lobe (LUL) [Figure 1a and Figure 1b]. The skin rash was biopsied; initial tissue cultures from the biopsy grew spherical unicellular yeast-like fungal organisms. On the second day of his hospital stay, the patient developed significant hypoxia and confusion, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. The patient underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the LUL and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy in the form of vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated. The final cultures from both the skin biopsies, taken from upper and lower extremities, as well as later blood cultures were positive for Prototheca wickerhamii, a rare opportunistic yeast-like alga. The BAL smear was also positive for yeast-like organisms morphologically similar to Prototheca wickerhamii. However, typical morula forms were not observed in BAL, so the likelihood of a fungal-mimic could not be ruled out. Prototheca wickerhamii is known to mimic yeast-like fungus on routine media. Given the patient's immunosuppressive state, lung lesions, and the sudden hypoxia with widened A-a gradient, the possibility of coinfection with. Pneumocystis jiroveci was entertained. The antimicrobial coverage was broadened to include amphotericin B and trimethoprin-sulfamethoxazole with prednisone. A PCR, performed on the BAL, confirmed the presence of Pneumocystis jirovecii. A long-term course of amphotericin B and trimethoprin-sulfamethoxazole was planned to treat the concomitant systemic protothecosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). Eventually, the patient succumbed to a bacterial ventilator-associated pneumonia, and the family decided to transition him to comfort care.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old immunosuppressed male with T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, Crohn's disease, and rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-week history of fever and bilateral extremity skin rash alongside chronic diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who was taking daily oral prednisone, tofacitinib, and valganciclovir following multiple prior immunosuppressive regimens, presented with 1 week of high fever and a symmetric erythematous desquamative rash over his upper and lower extremities, superimposed on chronic diarrhea. On hospital day 2, he developed acute severe hypoxemia and confusion requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: T-cell large granular lymphocytic (T-LGL) leukemia; Crohn's disease; rheumatoid arthritis; cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis; monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Social and epidemiological history: Lived on a farm, mowed his lawn regularly, and had traveled to Florida 1 month prior to admission; no illicit drug use or known tick bites.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, extremity skin rash, generalized edema, and chronic diarrhea (and acute hypoxia/confusion on day 2); negative for night sweats, cough, chest pain, arthralgia, or oral lesions. Home medications were tofacitinib, daily oral prednisone, and valganciclovir.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile with temperature 39.6 °C; bilaterally symmetrical desquamative, erythematous skin rash over the hands, thighs, and lower legs against a background of generalized pitting edema; remainder of initial exam unremarkable. On hospital day 2: Significant hypoxemia and confusion requiring intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normocytic, normochromic anemia with hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL; normal WBC count (5.6 K/μL) and differential; normal serum chemistries; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) at 29.6 mg/dL (normal: 0–1 mg/dL); widened alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient on day 2. Negative infectious screening: Negative serum fungal antibody panel, blood CMV DNA PCR, Parvovirus B19 serology/PCR, West Nile virus IgG, serum cryptococcal antigen, and urinary Histoplasma and Legionella antigens. Skin biopsy and blood cultures: Upper and lower extremity skin biopsies and subsequent blood cultures grew spherical unicellular yeast-like organisms definitively identified as the achlorophyllous alga Prototheca wickerhamii.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Multifocal ground-glass and consolidative opacities with air bronchograms, predominantly in the left upper lobe (LUL). Hospital day 2 bronchoscopy with left upper lobe bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): BAL smear showed yeast-like organisms morphologically similar to Prototheca wickerhamii (without classic morula forms); BAL polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Concomitant disseminated Prototheca wickerhamii infection (cutaneous, bloodstream, and pulmonary protothecosis confirmed by upper/lower extremity skin biopsy cultures, blood cultures, and BAL smear) and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by positive BAL PCR, left upper lobe ground-glass/consolidative opacities on chest CT, and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with widened A-a gradient) in a patient receiving tofacitinib and prednisone for T-LGL leukemia, Crohn's disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. Plan and clinical course: Intubated on hospital day 2 and initially started on empiric vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam, then broadened to intravenous amphotericin B (for systemic protothecosis) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone (for PJP). Despite targeted therapy, he subsequently developed a secondary bacterial ventilator-associated pneumonia, was transitioned to comfort care by his family, and died.

raw_case_text: We examined a 3-month-old infant with persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive. The male patient was born at term to healthy non-consanguineous Italian parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His umbilical separation was delayed. At admission, he had a temperature of 38  C, CRP concentration of 41 mg/L, white blood cell count of 34.6 x 103/mul, polymorphonuclear cell count of 14.11 x 103/mul, lymphocytic cell count of 15.43 x 103/mul, and hypereosinophilia (3.8 x 103/mul). Adenovirus was detected in his stool sample. Physical examination revealed mild dysmorphic features with frontal bossing, micrognathia, hypoplastic nasal wings, and flattened alveolar margins. He presented signs of anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with fine and sparse hair, absent eyebrows, thin translucent skin with dry eczema, and hyperkeratosis (Fig. 1(A)). The absence of sweat glands at skin biopsy confirmed this hypothesis. Radiologic evaluation was performed and the images showed "bone-in-bone appearance" of the femoral, iliac, and ischial bones bilaterally, consistent with a diagnosis of osteopetrosis (Fig. 1(B, B')). His general condition rapidly deteriorated with significant dyspnea, oliguria, and lethargy. He presented acute seizures. A head CT scan was negative. MRI was not performed. He was immediately admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit. On admission, he had leukocytosis (52.24 x 103/mul) and the signs of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia (Hb 6.9 g/dl), elevated ferritinemia (37,300 ng/ml), LDH (2105 U/L), low fibrinogen (93 mg/dl), and hypertriglyceridemia (700 mg/dl). Conventional respiratory and circulatory support with inotropes was necessary. A thoracic scan image was concordant with interstitial pneumonitis. Pneumocystis jirovecii and CMV DNA were identified in the bronchoalveolar lavage by PCR. The patient was successfully treated with meropenem, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and ganciclovir. The signs of concomitant macrophage activation syndrome were gradually normalized under systemic corticosteroid therapy. During his prolonged hospitalization, the patient also displayed a transient and inconstant lymphedema of the lower limbs. Immunological assay was performed at 4 months of life. The patient presented severe hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG (1.73 g/L with normal range 2.22-8.46 g/L), IgA (0.01 g/L with normal range 0.06-0.6 g/L), and IgM (0.04 g/L with normal range 0.28-0.39 g/L). TRECs and KRECs were normal. Flow cytometry immunophenotyping revealed low NK and B memory cell counts (Table 1). NK cell functional activity (CD107a expression) could not be determined due to the low number of NK cells. Proliferative T cell responses to mitogenic stimuli were normal (Table 1). We performed an analysis of the IKBKG sequence (NM_001099856.3) from both genomic DNA and cDNA and we identified a novel missense mutation c.1238A>G (p.H413R) within exon 10 on the zinc finger domain. The substituted histidine is highly conserved among different species (Fig. 2).
