Using a bioinformatic system (Polyphen and SIFT-Sort Intolerant From Tolerant), the new mutation is predicted to be damaging with a score of 0.99 (sensitivity 0.09; specificity 0.99) and to affect protein function with a score of 0.00 (intolerant), respectively. The CADD score was also elevated (22.9). We performed a careful dermatological examination of the patient's mother, we did not observe any of the nail, hair, dental, or skin findings typical of incontinentia pigmenti. Moreover, there was no history of dermatological problems in the family. Maternal sequencing on genomic and cDNA revealed the WT IKBKG on both alleles. We evaluated the patient's blood cells after activation with TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and other agonists of TLRs. The response of the patient's blood cells to IL-1beta, LPS (agonist of TLR-4), and SAC was abnormal, in terms of IL-6 production (Fig. 1(C)). Moreover, the response to TNF-alpha was impaired in terms of IL-10 production (Fig. 1(C')). IL-6 and IL-10 production was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) after 48 h of activation. For persistent bloody diarrhea, hypoproteinemia and feeding intolerance parenteral nutrition was necessary. Colon biopsy showed macroscopic signs of enterocolitis with diffuse eosinophilic infiltrates in the lamina propria of the colon. Despite IV antimicrobial prophylaxis and regular infusions of IV immunoglobulin, at 10 months of age, the patient was readmitted presenting a new episode of catheter-associated bacteremia from E. coli. At 13 months of age, the patient underwent a myeloablative conditioning regimen consisting of thiotepa, treosulfan, and fludarabine followed by haploidentical stem cell transplantation with TCR-alpha/beta and CD19 depletion. He received anti-thymocyte globulin and mycophenolate mofetil with a complete antimicrobial prophylaxis as a prevention of acute GVHD and infectious complications. He died unexpectedly from acute respiratory distress and sepsis due to multiresistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa 6 days post HSCT.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-month-old full-term Italian male infant presented with persistent diarrhea, failure to thrive, fever (38 °C), anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, and osteopetrosis, and rapidly deteriorated into acute dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, and seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born full-term to healthy non-consanguineous Italian parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy, the infant had delayed umbilical cord separation and presented at 3 months of age with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and fever (38 °C). Shortly after hospital admission, his condition rapidly deteriorated with severe dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, acute seizures, and hepatosplenomegaly, prompting urgent transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).
subjective.past_medical_history: Delayed umbilical cord separation; persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive; born full-term to non-consanguineous Italian parents with no family history of incontinentia pigmenti or immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent (later bloody) diarrhea, failure to thrive, fever, acute dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, acute seizures, and transient lower limb lymphedema.

objective.physical_examination: Admission temperature 38.0 °C; mild dysmorphic features (frontal bossing, micrognathia, hypoplastic nasal alae, flattened alveolar margins); signs of anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (fine sparse hair, absent eyebrows, thin translucent skin with dry eczema and hyperkeratosis); rapid progression to lethargy, seizures, severe dyspnea, oliguria, hepatosplenomegaly, and transient lower extremity lymphedema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 34.6 x 10^3/μL (PMNs 14.11 x 10^3/μL, lymphocytes 15.43 x 10^3/μL, hypereosinophilia 3.8 x 10^3/μL), C-reactive protein (CRP) 41 mg/L, and stool positive for adenovirus. PICU deterioration labs (secondary HLH/MAS): Marked leukocytosis (WBC 52.24 x 10^3/μL), severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL), extreme hyperferritinemia (37,300 ng/mL), elevated LDH (2,105 U/L), hypofibrinogenemia (93 mg/dL), and hypertriglyceridemia (700 mg/dL). Skeletal radiography: Bilateral 'bone-in-bone' appearance of the femoral, iliac, and ischial bones diagnostic of osteopetrosis. Head CT: Negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin and colon biopsies: Skin biopsy confirmed complete absence of eccrine sweat glands; colon biopsy demonstrated eosinophilic enterocolitis with diffuse lamina propria eosinophilic infiltrates. Thoracic scan and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) PCR: Interstitial pneumonitis on thoracic imaging; BAL PCR was positive for both Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA. Immunological and genetic workup (at 4 months): Severe panhypogammaglobulinemia with IgG 1.73 g/L (normal: 2.22–8.46 g/L), IgA 0.01 g/L (0.06–0.6 g/L), and IgM 0.04 g/L (0.28–0.39 g/L); normal TRECs, KRECs, and mitogen T-cell proliferation, but low NK-cell and memory B-cell counts on flow cytometry; impaired blood cell IL-6 response to IL-1beta, LPS, and SAC, and impaired IL-10 response to TNF-alpha on ELISA; genomic/cDNA sequencing of IKBKG (NEMO) identified a de novo hemizygous missense mutation c.1238A>G (p.His413Arg / p.H413R) in exon 10 (zinc finger domain).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: OL-EDA-ID syndrome (osteopetrosis, lymphedema, anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, and immunodeficiency) caused by a novel de novo hemizygous IKBKG (NEMO) zinc-finger mutation (c.1238A>G, p.H413R), complicated at 3 months of age by Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) interstitial pneumonia (confirmed by BAL PCR), secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis / macrophage activation syndrome (HLH/MAS), and eosinophilic colitis. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the PICU with mechanical ventilation, inotropic support, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, ganciclovir, meropenem, systemic corticosteroids (which resolved MAS), parenteral nutrition, and regular IVIG replacement. After a catheter-related E. coli bacteremia at 10 months, he underwent TCR-alpha/beta and CD19-depleted haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at 13 months (conditioned with thiotepa, treosulfan, fludarabine, ATG, and MMF), but died 6 days post-HSCT from multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis and acute respiratory distress.

raw_case_text:
A 78-year old male patient with RA treated with tofacitinib (10 mg p.o. daily), methotrexate (20 mg p.o. weekly) and low dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 5 mg p.o. daily), was admitted to hospital with a 2-week history of arthralgia, nausea and confusion (Additional file 1). RA was diagnosed 6 months ago, as the patient fulfilled the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria with bilateral symmetric swollen and tender joints (wrists, hands and feet; over 10 affected joints in total) and arthralgia for 3 years (negative anti-CCP antibody and negative rheumatoid factor IgM). No signs of erosions were found on X-ray (hands and feet). Therapy was initiated with prednisone (20 mg/day) and MTX 15 mg/week s.c. with increasing doses over time. Tofacitinib was initiated 2 months prior hospital admission due to lack of efficacy of MTX monotherapy (MTX was switched to p.o. at that time, as the patient disliked injections).
At time of admission the patient reported shortness of breath on exertion but not at rest.
Physical examination showed following vital signs: temperature (auricular): 36.5  C blood pressure: 178/95 mmHg, heart rate: 75 bpm, oxygen saturation: 88-90% at rest and on exercise 80% on room air. Wrists and ankles were swollen and tender bilaterally symmetric. There were normal findings on auscultation of heart and lungs without any other signs of venous congestion.
Laboratory findings on admission revealed hypercalcemia (albumin-corrected 3.12 mmol/l (normal range 2.0-2.6 mmol/l) and elevated 1,25- dihydroxyvitamin D levels (162 ng/l, normal range 22-111 ng/l). PTH was appropriately low at < 0.5 pmol/l (normal range < 1.3 pmol/l). Further laboratory findings are described in Table 1.
Further investigation of hypercalcemia included a whole body CT scan, which showed bilateral interstitial pneumonic infiltrates without pleural effusions (Fig. 1). The patient was referred from normal ward care to the ICU due to acute respiratory failure requiring non-invasive ventilation/ high-flow oxygen therapy. PCR from bronchoalveloar lavage (BAL) was positive for P. jirovecii and Rhinovirus A/B/C and a diagnosis of PJP was made with colonization of Rhinovirus. Adequate therapy with TMP/SMX i.v. (15 mg/kg/d) and prednisolone p.o. (1 mg/kg/d) was initiated. Treatment with TMP/SMX was stopped after 10 days because of severe hyponatremia (drop from 136 mmol/l to 119 mmol/l; normal range 136-144 mmol/l) and acutely worsening confusion, which was attributed most likely to acute hyponatremia or as a direct adverse drug reaction to TMP/SMX. As second line therapy we initiated clindamycin and primaquine. Confusion improved but thrombocytopenia developed (drop from 441 G/l to 83 G/l) 4 days later, which was felt to be due to primaquine and led to the discontinuation of clindamycin and primaquine.
Both the patient's clinical condition and hypercalcemia were improved after 17 days of antibiotic therapy. PJP- prophylaxis with monthly inhaled pentamidin (300 mg) was initiated.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old male with seronegative rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 2-week history of arthralgia, nausea, confusion, and exertional shortness of breath two months after adding tofacitinib to methotrexate and prednisolone.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 6 months earlier with seronegative, non-erosive rheumatoid arthritis (>10 swollen/tender joints across wrists, hands, and feet with a 3-year history of arthralgia), the patient was initially treated with oral prednisone (20 mg/day) and subcutaneous methotrexate (15 mg/week). Two months prior to admission, due to inadequate efficacy of methotrexate monotherapy and dislike of injections, he was switched to oral tofacitinib (10 mg daily), oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly), and low-dose oral prednisolone (5 mg daily). He presented to the hospital with a 2-week history of worsening arthralgia, nausea, confusion, and exertional dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Seronegative (RF-IgM negative, anti-CCP negative), non-erosive rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 6 months prior (3-year symptom history).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for arthralgia, nausea, confusion, and exertional dyspnea (no dyspnea at rest). Subsequent inpatient drug adverse reactions included severe hyponatremia/worsening confusion from IV TMP/SMX and severe thrombocytopenia from primaquine. Home medications were tofacitinib (10 mg PO daily), methotrexate (20 mg PO weekly), and prednisolone (5 mg PO daily).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Auricular temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 178/95 mmHg, heart rate 75 beats/min, and room-air SpO2 88%–90% at rest dropping to 80% on exertion. Musculoskeletal and cardiopulmonary exam: Bilateral symmetrical swelling and tenderness of the wrists and ankles; normal heart and lung auscultation without signs of venous congestion.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission endocrine and metabolic labs: Severe PTH-independent calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia with albumin-corrected serum calcium 3.12 mmol/L (normal: 2.0–2.6 mmol/L), elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D at 162 ng/L (normal: 22–111 ng/L), and appropriately suppressed intact PTH <0.5 pmol/L (normal <1.3 pmol/L). Inpatient adverse drug reaction labs: Day 10 severe hyponatremia on TMP/SMX (sodium dropped from 136 to 119 mmol/L, normal: 136–144 mmol/L); day 14 severe thrombocytopenia on primaquine/clindamycin (platelets dropped from 441 G/L to 83 G/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Whole-body CT scan: Bilateral interstitial pneumonic infiltrates without pleural effusions or malignancy. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) molecular testing: Positive PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Rhinovirus A/B/C.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by positive BAL PCR and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CT, with Rhinovirus A/B/C co-colonization) presenting with calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (corrected calcium 3.12 mmol/L, 1,25-(OH)2D 162 ng/L) in a rheumatoid arthritis patient receiving triple immunosuppression (tofacitinib, methotrexate, and prednisolone). Plan and clinical course: Managed in the ICU with noninvasive ventilation / high-flow oxygen, intravenous TMP/SMX (15 mg/kg/day), and oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). On day 10, severe hyponatremia (119 mmol/L) and worsening encephalopathy prompted switching from TMP/SMX to second-line clindamycin plus primaquine, which was stopped 4 days later due to primaquine-induced thrombocytopenia (platelets 83 G/L). After 17 days of antimicrobial therapy, both his respiratory failure and hypercalcemia resolved, and he was transitioned to secondary PJP prophylaxis with monthly inhaled pentamidine (300 mg).

raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old married female with a medical history of diabetes was sent to our hospital because of daily persistent headaches in August 2018. Without any positive physical neurological examinations, a contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain suggested multiple enhancing masses in the corpus callosum and around the ventricles (Figure 1A-C). To make an accurate diagnosis, an imaging-guided stereotactic needle biopsy was performed. Pathology (Figure 2) confirmed diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL; non-germinal center B cell (GCB)) after observing infiltrating neoplastic lymphoid cells that expressed CD45RO, CD20, PAX-5, MUM1, and Bcl-6 and that did not express CD3, CD10, CD30, cyclin D1, EBER (in situ hybridization), CD5, GFAP, CK-Pan and TdT (Ki-67+ approx. 70% of cells). 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) was carried out, and the results demonstrated that many peripheral lymph nodes and extranodal organs or sites other than her brain, such as axillary lymph nodes, inferior diaphragmatic lymph nodes, and lymph nodes around the kidney area, were involved. Moreover, the vertebral arch of L3, sacrum, left side of the acetabulum, left femoral head and right femoral neck also showed FDG uptake. Our patient had negative cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) test results and negative marrow tests based on morphology and flow cytometry. Her LDH level was above the upper limit of normal, and an HIV test was negative. The genetic features of biopsy samples suggested MGMT (O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase) promoter methylation and CD79B and MyD88 L265P mutations.
Considering the central nervous system (CNS) involvement of systemic DLBCL at the initial diagnosis and MGMT promoter methylation, we designed a methotrexate (MTX)-based immunochemotherapy regimen by referring to the MARIETTA trial (NCT02329080) which was sponsored by International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group (IELSG) and we decided to combine two standardized chemotherapy regimens, high dose methotrexate-based regimen (MT-R: methotrexate, temozolomide and rituximab) for intracranial lesions and traditional R-CHOP (rituximab, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, prednisone and anthracycline) immunochemotherapy regimen for extracranial lesions. Eventually, the details of the first cycle treatment for our patient were as follows: rituximab (375 mg/m2, day (d) 0); high-dose intravenous MTX (3.5 g/m2, d1) with leucovorin for rescue, as previously described; vincristine (2 mg, d3); cyclophosphamide (0.75 g/m2 once per day, d3-4); prednisone (60 mg, d3-7); and temozolomide (150 mg/m2 once per day, d3-7) for the first chemotherapy cycle (Figure 3, chemotherapy regimen A). Because anthracyclines cannot penetrate the blood-brain barrier and produce severe bone marrow suppression, which may affect the intracranial chemotherapy dose, we omitted the anthracyclines that were also adopted in the SCNSL1 trial in these treatment regimens. Essential supportive treatments were added, which included hydration and the alkalization of the urine before/after MTX infusion, ranitidine hydrochloride and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). In the second cycle of our patient's treatment, considering our patient suffered from diabetes which is a proven risk factor for high-dose methotrexate-associated AKI in lymphoma patients. Fotemustine, another alkylating agent, was also proved to be effective in glioma patients with MGMT promoter methylation compared to unmethylated MGMT. Meanwhile, fotemustine, teniposide and dexamethasone (FTD) regimen has been applied in central nervous system lymphoma and been verified with no difference in 3 years PFS and OS when compared to HD-MA regimen (high-dose methotrexate plus cytarabine) in treating newly diagnosed primary central nervous system lymphoma. Our patient strongly believed that the massive amount of fluid infusion related to HD-MTX can interfere with her quality of life and refused to continue the regimen we designed in first cycle. In order to find a more suitable regimen, we referred previous clinical trials and her genetic features. Finally, we designed a new combination called chemotherapy regimen B (Figure 3, chemotherapy regimen B). In this regimen, we replaced MTX and temozolomide with fotemustine (140 mg/m2, d3) and teniposide (65 mg/m2 once a day, d1-3) in the second cycle of chemotherapy as the proved effect by clinical trials and we also added ibrutinib (420 mg once per day) to our patient's daily treatment in view of the CD79B and MyD88 L265P mutations in the tumors. In the meantime, previous research has confirmed methotrexate is antagonistic to ibrutinib. The ibrutinib-containing clinical trial (NCT03964090) for aggressive B-cell Lymphomas with secondary involvement of the central nervous system was also omit methotrexate because of the antagonistic effect. In summary, we changed our protocol to ibrutinib (420 mg once per day); rituximab (375 mg/m2, d0); vincristine (2 mg, d3); cyclophosphamide (0.75 g/m2 once per day, d3-4); prednisone (60 mg, d3-7); fotemustine (140 mg/m2, d3) and teniposide (65 mg/m2 once a day, d1-3) (Figure 3, chemotherapy regimen B). An MRI scan was obtained before the third cycle of our new immunochemotherapy. The masses in her head were significantly reduced, which was judged as a PR (partial response) according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Lymphoma (RECIL) 2017 standards (Figure 1D-F), and she recovered from an unbearable headache. During the treatment period, our patient suffered from only Grade 1 fatigue and Grade 3 hematologic toxicity according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.
Unfortunately, after six cycles of treatment, our patient experienced severe myelosuppression and had an extremely low white cell count (300/mm3). Afterwards, she suffered from fulminant respiratory failure accompanied with low-grade fever and dry cough. Piperacillin-tazobactam treatment had no therapeutic efficacy, and she was arranged to be monitored and cared for in the intensive care unit (ICU). Her CT lung screening revealed pulmonary consolidation in the inferior lobes surrounded by a wide range of ground-glass opacity effusions on both sides (Figure 4). The beta-D-glucan assay test was positive and the sputum sample was negative for hyphae and spores. With the help of conventional mechanical ventilation, several broad-spectrum antibiotics, and antifungal therapy with voriconazole and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) were also added. Adjunctive dexamethasone (5 mg/d) was used to reduce the serious inflammatory conditions. We sent the patient's blood sample for the detection of potential pathogens by next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology as previous reported with her parents' permission. The results confirmed a PCP infection, and we increased the dose of TMP-SMX. A re-examination with chest CT after 10 days of treatment showed that the majority of the previous lesions had resolved, and her dyspnea improved without ventilatory support. Our patient recovered from PCP, and we rechecked her lymphoma status by PET/CT. There was no abnormal FDG uptake in the region that previously had high metabolic activity (Figure 5). Meanwhile, the lesions in the brain displayed the same metabolic signal as normal brain tissues. Bone marrow biopsy also confirmed complete remission after chemotherapy. We recommended that our patient receive another two cycles of rituximab injections. After finishing treatment, MRI was conducted again to evaluate the status in her head, and images revealed that the corpus callosum and ventricle lesions were much smaller than they were initially, and our patient was judged as complete response (Figure 1G-I) and our patient checked the MRI again after 30 months follow-up (Figure 1J-L). She refused further whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) or autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) for consolidation and continues to be followed. All the treatment procedures were shown in Figure 6.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old married female with diabetes mellitus and systemic non-GCB diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the central nervous system presented with low-grade fever, dry cough, and fulminant respiratory failure after six cycles of intensive immunochemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Originally admitted in August 2018 for persistent daily headaches, the patient was diagnosed via stereotactic brain biopsy and staging 18F-FDG PET/CT with systemic non-germinal center B-cell diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL; MGMT promoter methylated, CD79B and MYD88 L265P mutated) involving the corpus callosum, periventricular brain, axillary/infradiaphragmatic/perirenal lymph nodes, and multiple bones (L3, sacrum, pelvis, femurs). She received one cycle of Regimen A (rituximab, high-dose methotrexate 3.5 g/m2, temozolomide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, prednisone) and five subsequent cycles of Regimen B (daily ibrutinib 420 mg plus rituximab, fotemustine 140 mg/m2, teniposide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone), achieving headache resolution and partial neuroimaging response. After completing six total cycles, she developed severe grade 4 myelosuppression (WBC 300/mm3) followed by low-grade fever, dry cough, and fulminant hypoxemic respiratory failure refractory to piperacillin-tazobactam.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic non-GCB diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with secondary CNS (corpus callosum and periventricular) and skeletal involvement (diagnosed August 2018); diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for severe daily headaches; post-cycle 6 presentation positive for low-grade fever, dry cough, and fulminant dyspnea/respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Initial baseline neurological physical examination was normal; post-cycle 6 course marked by fulminant respiratory failure requiring ICU admission and conventional invasive mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline lymphoma workup: Elevated serum LDH, HIV negative, negative CSF cytology, and negative bone marrow morphology/flow cytometry. Post-cycle 6 hematology and microbiology: Profound leukopenia with WBC 300/mm3; sputum smear negative for fungal hyphae and spores.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline brain MRI, stereotactic brain biopsy, and staging PET/CT: Multiple enhancing masses in the corpus callosum and periventricular regions plus FDG-avid nodal and osseous lesions; stereotactic biopsy confirmed non-GCB DLBCL (CD20+, PAX-5+, MUM1+, Bcl-6+, CD45RO+, Ki-67 ~70%; negative for CD10, EBER, CD3, CD5) with MGMT promoter methylation and CD79B/MYD88 L265P mutations. Post-cycle 6 chest CT: Bilateral lower lobe pulmonary consolidations surrounded by extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities and pleural effusions. Fungal biomarker and peripheral blood mNGS: Positive serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan assay; peripheral blood next-generation sequencing (NGS) confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fulminant Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by peripheral blood next-generation sequencing, positive serum beta-D-glucan, and bilateral ground-glass opacities/lower lobe consolidations on chest CT) complicating grade 4 myelosuppression (WBC 300/mm3) after six cycles of ibrutinib/rituximab/fotemustine/teniposide-based immunochemotherapy for CNS-involved MYD88/CD79B-mutated DLBCL. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the ICU with conventional mechanical ventilation, escalated therapeutic-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), voriconazole, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and adjunctive intravenous dexamethasone (5 mg/day). Repeat chest CT after 10 days showed near-complete resolution of pulmonary infiltrates, and she was weaned from mechanical ventilation. Following PCP recovery, she completed two additional cycles of rituximab and achieved a sustained complete systemic and CNS remission on PET/CT, bone marrow biopsy, and 30-month follow-up brain MRI.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 17 year old boy with a history of a congenital vesicoureteral reflux and other congenital abnormalities of kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) which gradually caused nephrosclerosis, secondary hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD). In April, 2019 he started peritoneal dialysis (PD) because of CKD stage 5. In June, 2019 he received a deceased donor kidney transplant (from a 58 year old female, cause of death - intracerebral hemorrhage. CMV +, EBV +, hepatitis markers - negative, CMV donor + /recipient -). Before KTx induction therapy consisted of Basiliximab - interleukin 2 receptor antibody (IL2Ra) 20 mg IV, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 750 mg PO and tacrolimus 3 mg PO. Intraoperatively methylprednisolone 500 mg IV was administered. After KTx patient underwent maintenance therapy with tacrolimus 3 mg PO once daily (o.d.), MMF 750 mg PO twice daily, methylprednisolone 48 mg PO Prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) with valganciclovir 450 mg PO for 6 months as high risk and prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii TMPSMX 80/400 mg PO was given for 3 months (up to September, 2019). Additionally, patient received treatment with antihypertensives and anticoagulants.
The post-transplant period was mostly uncomplicated with good diuresis, patient had no rejection episodes. Tacrolimus, other immunosuppressant and antihypertensive treatment was tailored a few times in order to achieve either required drug serum concentrations or clinical efficacy, graft function was relatively stable, eGFR ranging from 44,1 to 51,4 mL/min/1.73m2. Darbopoetin alfa 20 mug once every two weeks s/c and folic acid was started due to secondary anemia and continued for 6 months. In July, 2019 the first graft biopsy was performed due to proteinuria and poorly controlled hypertension. Results showed focal mesangioproliferative changes without immunoreactant deposition. Immunosuppresive treatment with tacrolimus and antihypertensive treatment was intensified
In September, 2019 the patient was hospitalised due to leukopenia, neutropenia, diarrhea, loss of apetite. His blood tests showed elevated CMV viremia (up to 8811 copies/ml, while on previous outpatient visits no viremia was detected). MMF was discontinued and valgancivlovir dose was increased up to 450 mg twice daily, for 2 weeks until viral load became undetectable. Patient had fungal toenail infection, topical terbinafine and naftifine were prescribed. Valganciclocvir was discontinued in December, 2019, after completion of 6 months of post-KTx prophylaxis. The last outpatient visit was 12 days before the case of PCP. During the visit the patient had no complaints, his physical examination was unremarkable, graft function was stable with eGFR of 41,4 mL/min/1.73m2 and low CMV viremia of 25 copies/ml (which was below the significant threshold). His immunosuppressive regimen consisted of tacrolimus 6 mg PO o.d., methylprednisolone 8 mg PO o.d. and MMF 500 mg PO twice daily and were not tailored recently.
At the end of June, 2020 patient was admitted to the hospital due to the subfebrile temperature, dry cough, shortness of breath for about 1 week and general fatigue for more than 3 weeks during physical activity. Important to note that additional information about earlier onset of patient's complaints was explicated only after the patient was hospitalized, because at last outpatient visit they did not inform about complaints of fatigue. Patient also lost 4 kg down to 46 kg of weight in the last month. On physical examination the patient was tachycardic (HR - 128 bpm), oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 89% and a subfebrile temperature of 37.2oC. Patient required 2-3 L/min of oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation above 92%. Blood pressure (BP) was 124/80mmHg. There was a reddish, dry maculopapular rash on the upper side of the trunk and around the neck and signs of toenail fungus were seen. Lung auscultation was normal. PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 from nasopharyngeal swabs were negative twice. No other remarkable findings.
Initial laboratory tests showed decreasing eGFR down to 32 mL/min/1.73m2. C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated - 79.2 mg/l, tacrolimus concentration - 5.7 ng/ml. Complete blood count, albumin, liver enzymes and electrolytes were normal (laboratory tests are presented in Table 1). Tuberculosis was excluded with both negative Tuberculin skin test (TST) and Interferon-gamma release assay. Atypical bacterial infections were excluded with negative serological testing and negative nasopharyngeal swab PCR. Blood culture was taken. Both EBV and CMV blood tests for PGR were taken and CMV viremia was present at 51 copies/ml.
Chest radiograph (Figure 1) revealed fine bilateral interstitial infiltrates with interstitial edema.
Immunosupressive and antihypertensive treatment was initially unchanged. Topical antifungal treatment was prescribed for suspected fungal etiology of toenail and skin lesions while microbiological tests were ongoing. O2 flow through face mask of 2 l/min was continued.
Chest CT scan (Figure 2) showed bilateral ground glass opacities, pneumatoceles in basal segments and diffuse varying in size centrilobular and peribronchovascular consolidation foci.
On the second day of hospitalisation, while the workup was still in process and bronchoscopy for acquisition of BALF was in line, patient's condition deteriorated, resulting in increased breathing rate, dyspnea and supplemental oxygen demand of up to 12 l/min in order to keep SpO2 >=92%. It was followed by a decrease of kidney function down to eGFR of 27,1 mL/min/1.73m2. Patient was empirically started on TMP-SMX 320 mg IV o.d., Fluconasole 100 mg IV o.d., Sol. Ganciclovir 115mg IV o.d. MMF dose was reduced to 250 mg twice daily, which was later temporarily discontinued. A bronchoscopy was performed and a BALF sample tested positive for P. jirovecii. CMV (3575 copies/ml) and EBV (70000 copies/ml) were detected too. In addition, immunoglobulin G (IgG) was found to be significantly lower - 2,16 g/l, so an IV infusion of 20g IgG was administered.
Over the next days the patient's condition improved, with a reduction of O2 therapy (Figure 3) and a gradual resolution of symptoms - patient reported no fatigue, better general well-being and only occasional coughing. Slight improvement in kidney function was observed with eGFR of 30,9 mL/min/1.73m2 and patient was discharged 2 and a half weeks later after he received IV TMP-SMX for 18 days, and IV ganciclovir for 1 week. Later valganciclovir PO was continued for a total of 1 month and TMP-SMX at a lower dose of 480 mg PO was continued for 3 months in total.
At follow-up his condition has progressively improved, with no signs of infection or respiratory distress, with a markedly improved kidney function and normal inflammation markers as seen in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male deceased-donor kidney transplant recipient presented at the end of June 2020 (1 year post-transplant) with a 1-week history of subfebrile temperature, dry cough, and shortness of breath, a >3-week history of exertional fatigue, and a 4 kg weight loss over 1 month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient underwent deceased-donor kidney transplantation in June 2019 (CMV D+/R-, EBV D+) with basiliximab/methylprednisolone induction and tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and methylprednisolone maintenance. He completed 3 months of TMP-SMX prophylaxis (stopped September 2019) and 6 months of valganciclovir prophylaxis (stopped December 2019 after treating a September 2019 episode of neutropenic CMV viremia [8,811 copies/mL]). Maintained on tacrolimus (6 mg PO qd), methylprednisolone (8 mg PO qd), and MMF (500 mg PO bid) with baseline eGFR 41.4 mL/min/1.73m2 and low-level CMV viremia (25 copies/mL), he developed >3 weeks of unreported exertional fatigue, a 4 kg weight loss over 1 month (to 46 kg), and 1 week of subfebrile fever, dry cough, and dyspnea at the end of June 2020.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital vesicoureteral reflux and CAKUT leading to nephrosclerosis, secondary hypertension, and stage 5 CKD (brief peritoneal dialysis in April 2019, followed by deceased-donor kidney transplant in June 2019); focal mesangioproliferative graft changes on July 2019 biopsy; post-transplant CMV viremia in September 2019; onychomycosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for subfebrile fever, dry cough, shortness of breath, >3 weeks of exertional fatigue, 4 kg weight loss, upper truncal/neck maculopapular rash, and toenail onychomycosis. Home medications included tacrolimus (6 mg qd), mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg bid), methylprednisolone (8 mg qd), antihypertensives, and anticoagulants.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Weight 46 kg, heart rate 128 beats/min, subfebrile temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 124/80 mmHg, and room-air SpO2 89% (requiring 2–3 L/min O2 initially, escalating on hospital day 2 to tachypnea and 12 L/min O2 to keep SpO2 >=92%). Mucocutaneous and chest exam: Reddish dry maculopapular rash over the upper trunk and neck; toenail onychomycosis; normal baseline lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Acute-on-chronic graft dysfunction with eGFR dropping from 41.4 to 32 mL/min/1.73m2 (and 27.1 mL/min/1.73m2 on day 2), C-reactive protein (CRP) 79.2 mg/L, whole-blood tacrolimus trough 5.7 ng/mL, and severe hypogammaglobulinemia with serum IgG 2.16 g/L; normal CBC, serum albumin, liver enzymes, and electrolytes. Negative infectious screening: Two negative nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR swabs, negative tuberculin skin test and IGRA, negative atypical bacterial serologies/PCR, and negative blood cultures; low-level blood CMV PCR (51 copies/mL). Admission chest radiograph: Fine bilateral interstitial infiltrates with interstitial edema.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Bilateral ground-glass opacities, basilar pneumatoceles, and diffuse centrilobular and peribronchovascular consolidations of varying sizes. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis (day 2): Tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus (CMV; 3,575 copies/mL), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV; 70,000 copies/mL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Late-onset Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) with concurrent pulmonary cytomegalovirus (CMV; 3,575 copies/mL) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV; 70,000 copies/mL) reactivation and severe IgG hypogammaglobulinemia (2.16 g/L) occurring 1 year after pediatric kidney transplantation (9 months after completing 3-month TMP-SMX prophylaxis), definitively confirmed by BALF molecular testing and chest CT showing ground-glass opacities and basilar pneumatoceles. Plan and clinical course: On hospital day 2, MMF was reduced and temporarily held, and treatment was initiated with intravenous TMP-SMX (320 mg IV qd for 18 days), IV ganciclovir (115 mg IV qd for 1 week), IV fluconazole (100 mg IV qd), and intravenous immunoglobulin (20 g IgG infusion). Oxygen requirements and symptoms steadily resolved with eGFR recovering to 30.9 mL/min/1.73m2; he was discharged after 2.5 weeks on a 1-month course of oral valganciclovir and a 3-month course of oral TMP-SMX (480 mg daily), achieving complete clinical and renal recovery on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 3-year-and-8-month-old boy who had primary combined immunodeficiency [X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency in the 1L2RG gene (OMIM: 312863), and X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency highly associated mutation (OMIM: 300400)] and experienced interstitial pneumonia at 2 years of age was admitted to our hospital for fever, cough and difficulty breathing. He was also a full-term child, and there was no abnormality in his birth history. He had been admitted to local hospitals 11 times since his first admission for "interstitial pneumonia" in 2019. He was transferred to the PICU of our hospital with a diagnosis of severe pneumonia, respiratory failure and interstitial pneumonia. Nasopharyngeal swabs were collected the next day. Coarse breath sounds and moist rates were found in both lungs. Chest CT demonstrated diffuse parenchymal changes and small alveolar emphysema in both lungs ( Figure 1B ). Sputum specimen was positive for Pneumocystis. Other clinical results are shown in  Table 1 . Upon admission, cotrimoxazole and methylprednisolone were given immediately to control infection and relieve inflammation. Fourteen days later, fungal hyphae were found in the respiratory tract, and voriconazole was added. On Day 87, his dyspnoea increased, and mechanical ventilation was given. On the 98th day of admission, his transcutaneous oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure dropped severely, with spontaneous breathing and aorta pulsates disappearing. He finally died due to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome that developed from pneumonia.
Two complete genome sequences of 5,229 bp (BCH2008-1) and 5,228 bp (BCH2020_1) were identified after mapping 35,550 (29,374,647 reads in total; 0.12%) and 56,897 (37,864,592 reads in total; 0.15%) sequencing reads, respectively, against the 5,229-bp-long reference genome for WUPyV (GenBank accession no. NC_009539). The whole-genome sequences of two WUPyV strains have been deposited in GenBank under accession numbers MW338654 and MW338655. The alignment results of the two sequences with the reference sequence are shown in  Table 2 . For BCH2008-1, there was only one amino acid variant in the VP2 protein (Glu250Gly) alignment to NC_009539. For BCH2020_1, there were three variants separately located in VP1 (Ala82Thr), VP2 (Met324Ile), and large T antigen (Asn56Lys). All four variations were not unique for our cases. After summarizing all WUPyV complete sequences submitted to GenBank (149 in total), the incidence of variations found in our sequences is shown in  Table 2 .
Phylogenetic analyses were performed with 112 other WUPyV complete sequences submitted to GenBank, with all sequences derived from China (67 in total) and representative sequences from other countries (23 from Australia, 2 from Thailand, 5 from Germany, 3 from the Netherlands, 5 from Canada, 3 from Sweden, 3 from South Korea, and 1 from the USA). The results showed that three branches were formed, and the largest branch (I) was further divided into four clusters. The strains in Cluster Ib were mainly from Western countries, and strains from China were gathered in Cluster Ia, Cluster Ic, and Cluster IIIa. Our isolate BCH2020-1 grouped most closely with the strain in Cluster Ia: FZ18 (accession no. FJ890981.1), which was collected in 2013 from Fujian, China. BCH2008_1 grouped most closely with strain CQ5307 (accession no. KX034823.1), which was collected from Chongqing, China, in 2013 ( Figure 2 ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-and-8-month-old boy with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (IL2RG mutation) and 11 prior hospitalizations for interstitial pneumonia presented with fever, cough, and difficulty breathing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born full-term with an unremarkable birth history, the child had genetically confirmed X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (IL2RG mutation) and had been hospitalized 11 times at local hospitals since age 2 (2019) for recurrent interstitial pneumonia. He was transferred to our PICU with fever, cough, severe dyspnea, and acute respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID; IL2RG gene mutation, OMIM 312863 / 300400); 11 prior hospitalizations for interstitial pneumonia starting at 2 years of age; full-term birth.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, cough, and severe difficulty breathing.

objective.physical_examination: Coarse breath sounds and moist rales auscultated across both lungs; progressive respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation on hospital day 87, culminating in severe hypoxemia, bradycardia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest on day 98.
objective.routine_investigations: Sputum and respiratory tract microbiology: Admission sputum specimen positive for Pneumocystis; respiratory tract specimen on hospital day 14 positive for fungal hyphae.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Diffuse bilateral parenchymal infiltrates and small alveolar emphysema. Nasopharyngeal swab metagenomic sequencing and viral whole-genome assembly: Identified and assembled complete 5,228-bp genome sequences of WU polyomavirus (WUPyV strain BCH2020_1, GenBank MW338655; 56,897 reads, 0.15% of total reads, clustering in Chinese Cluster Ia with VP1 Ala82Thr, VP2 Met324Ile, and large T antigen Asn56Lys variants).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal Pneumocystis pneumonia (confirmed on sputum examination), secondary filamentous fungal respiratory infection (day 14), and persistent WU polyomavirus (WUPyV strain BCH2020_1, GenBank MW338655) co-infection leading to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in a 3-year-8-month-old boy with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (IL2RG mutation). Plan and clinical course: Immediately treated on PICU admission with co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) and methylprednisolone, with voriconazole added on day 14 after fungal hyphae were detected in the respiratory tract, and invasive mechanical ventilation initiated on day 87; despite therapy, he died of refractory ARDS on hospital day 98.

raw_case_text:
This is a fifty-one year old female patient with history of diabetes mellitus and systemic lupus erythematoses (SLE) complicated by lupus nephritis. Although we have included her case in our previous publication, we have not reported her clinical details at that time. She was put on prednisolone 30 mg and azathioprine 100 mg daily since end of June and mid-July 2002, respectively. She was admitted to Queen Mary Hospital on 11th August 2002 for investigation of jaundice. Investigations revealed deranged liver function tests with cholestatic pattern. A diagnosis of drug-induced hepatotoxicity was entertained, and azathioprine was stopped after admission. As her autoimmune disease was under control, her steroid dosage was reduced from 25 mg to 15 mg daily within the next 14 days. Her CXR taken on admission was normal.
Soon after her immunosuppressive therapy was tapered, she developed fever and non-productive cough. A repeat CXR performed on 9th Sept revealed new infiltrate over the left mid-zone, suggestive of pneumonia. She was started on intravenous ceftazidime 1 gram eight hourly and oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily. Serial CXR performed three days later showed increasing bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and worsening hypoxemia. There was an upsurge of total lymphocyte count from 0.7 x 109/L (total white cell count 7.2 x 109/L) at the time of admission to 5.6 x 109/L (total white cell count 10.8 x 109/L) at the time of clinical deterioration. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy performed on the same day revealed Pneumocystitis jiroveci by methenamine sliver stain. Workup for other opportunistic pathogens including cytomegalovirus and aspergillus was negative. She was commenced on intravenous pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day) and corticosteroids for severe PCP infection. Despite active treatment she developed progressive respiratory failure and required admission to intensive care unit. She subsequently recovered after a stormy hospital course, and upon discharge from hospital, her total lymphocyte count had returned to her baseline of 0.86 x 109/L.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus nephritis, and diabetes mellitus developed acute fever and nonproductive cough shortly after stopping azathioprine and tapering prednisolone for drug-induced cholestatic jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been started on oral prednisolone (30 mg daily at the end of June 2002) and azathioprine (100 mg daily in mid-July 2002) for SLE and lupus nephritis. On August 11, 2002, she was admitted to Queen Mary Hospital for cholestatic jaundice attributed to azathioprine hepatotoxicity; admission chest X-ray was normal, azathioprine was discontinued, and her prednisolone dose was tapered from 25 mg to 15 mg daily over 14 days. Shortly after this rapid tapering of immunosuppression (early September 2002), she developed acute fever and a nonproductive cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) complicated by lupus nephritis; diabetes mellitus; azathioprine-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity (August 2002).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission positive for jaundice; September 2002 inpatient course positive for fever, nonproductive cough, and progressive hypoxemic dyspnea. Recent medications were prednisolone (tapered from 30 mg to 15 mg daily) and azathioprine (100 mg daily, stopped on admission).

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission notable for clinical jaundice; subsequent September 2002 deterioration marked by fever and progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring ICU admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission liver profile: Cholestatic liver function test derangement. Serial leukocyte and lymphocyte counts: Admission WBC 7.2 x 10^9/L with baseline lymphopenia (total lymphocyte count 0.7 x 10^9/L), which surged sharply to a total lymphocyte count of 5.6 x 10^9/L (WBC 10.8 x 10^9/L) during acute PCP clinical deterioration before returning to 0.86 x 10^9/L at hospital discharge. Serial chest radiographs: Normal on August 11 admission; new left mid-zone infiltrate on September 9; rapidly progressive bilateral pulmonary infiltrates 3 days later.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy (September 12, 2002): Methenamine silver staining of transbronchial biopsy specimen identified Pneumocystis jirovecii; workup for cytomegalovirus (CMV), Aspergillus, and other opportunistic pathogens was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by methenamine silver staining on transbronchial lung biopsy) precipitated by immune reconstitution (marked by an 8-fold surge in peripheral lymphocytes from 0.7 to 5.6 x 10^9/L) following azathioprine withdrawal and rapid corticosteroid tapering in a patient with SLE and lupus nephritis. Plan and clinical course: After failing initial empiric IV ceftazidime (1 g q8h) and oral clarithromycin (500 mg BID), she was treated with intravenous pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day), systemic corticosteroids, and ICU supportive care for progressive respiratory failure, ultimately achieving full clinical recovery and discharge.

raw_case_text:
An 11-week-old female ex-premature infant (corrected gestational age 6 weeks) presented to a peripheral hospital with respiratory distress and a three-day history of cyanotic episodes, following three weeks of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms. The infant was born at 35 weeks' gestation, weighing 2489 g, and did not require resuscitation or respiratory support at birth. The newborn had a 5-day admission to the special care unit for feeding establishment and observation prior to being discharged home well on day 7 of life. The child's mother had received six cycles of R-CHOP for NHL between 17 and 33 weeks of gestation.
The infant was tachypneic and hypoxic, was commenced on high flow nasal cannula support, intravenous (IV) ampicillin and gentamicin, and managed at the peripheral hospital's critical care unit. Over the next two days, respiratory support was escalated to noninvasive ventilation, and antibiotics were changed to IV cefotaxime (D1-D8) and IV azithromycin (D3-D5).
Nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) was negative for eight respiratory viruses. Respiratory virus detection for influenza A, influenza B, parainfluenza 1, 2, and 3, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus was performed using an in-house respiratory virus multiplex real-time RT-PCR assay, while human metapneumovirus (HMPV) was tested with the in-house real-time RT-PCR assay utilising oligonucleotides. Testing for Pneumocystis jirovecii was also requested on the NPA specimen and performed using an in-house real-time RT-PCR assay. A synthetic reference standard was also utilised to enable quantification. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) serology was negative. A chest X-ray revealed diffuse bilateral ground glass changes (Figure 1).
As the hypoxic respiratory failure worsened, atypical infections and possible childhood interstitial lung disease (ChILD) were considered and pulse IV methylprednisolone was commenced. The NPA was subsequently positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA at 2.0 x 106 copies/mL. Oral co-trimoxazole 20 mg/kg/day (D4) was commenced and transitioned to IV co-trimoxazole (D8) due to clinical deterioration.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-week-old ex-35-week premature female infant born to a mother who received six cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy during pregnancy presented with acute respiratory distress and a 3-day history of cyanotic episodes following a 3-week upper respiratory prodrome.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born at 35 weeks' gestation (birth weight 2,489 g, discharged well on day 7 of life) to a mother who had been treated with six cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) for non-Hodgkin lymphoma between 17 and 33 weeks of gestation, the infant developed 3 weeks of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms followed by 3 days of cyanotic spells and acute respiratory distress at 11 weeks chronological age (6 weeks corrected gestational age).
subjective.past_medical_history: Preterm birth at 35 weeks' gestation (birth weight 2,489 g); in utero exposure to six cycles of maternal R-CHOP immunochemotherapy between 17 and 33 weeks' gestation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms, 3 days of cyanotic episodes, tachypnea, and severe respiratory distress.

objective.physical_examination: Tachypneic and hypoxemic on admission to the peripheral hospital critical care unit, requiring escalation from high-flow nasal cannula to noninvasive ventilation over 48 hours.
objective.routine_investigations: Virological and serological screening: HIV serology negative; nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) multiplex real-time RT-PCR negative for eight common respiratory viruses (influenza A/B, parainfluenza 1–3, RSV, adenovirus, and human metapneumovirus). Chest X-ray: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Quantitative Pneumocystis jirovecii real-time PCR on nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA): Strongly positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA at 2.0 x 10^6 copies/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe infantile Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by quantitative nasopharyngeal aspirate real-time PCR showing 2.0 x 10^6 copies/mL and diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest radiograph) associated with in utero exposure to maternal R-CHOP chemotherapy and secondary combined immunodeficiency. Plan and clinical course: Initially managed with high-flow nasal cannula, noninvasive ventilation, empiric IV ampicillin/gentamicin followed by IV cefotaxime (days 1–8), IV azithromycin (days 3–5), and pulse IV methylprednisolone. Upon quantitative PCR confirmation of P. jirovecii, oral co-trimoxazole (20 mg/kg/day on day 4) was initiated and escalated to intravenous co-trimoxazole on day 8 due to progressive clinical deterioration.

raw_case_text: Two days later, the sputum culture result was negative. Nevertheless, the mNGS results showed that PJ and CMV nucleic acid sequences were found in both sputum and venous blood, and the tests were performed by Genskey Medical Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) using the procedures described by Grumaz et al. The database referenced during analysis of the sequencing data contains 12,895 species of bacteria, 11,120 species of viruses, 1582 species of fungi, 312 species of parasites, 184 species of mycoplasma/chlamydia, and 177 species of mycobacteria. The other microorganisms detected by mNGS are listed in Table 1, which were mainly common bacteria and were not considered to be the cause of invasive lung infections. The genomic coverage depth map of the sequence obtained by mNGS is shown in Figures 3A-D. We also verified PJ infection by Sanger sequencing (Figure 3E). Using these results combined with other physical examination results, the patient was diagnosed with PJ and CMV caused multipathogenic pneumonia. The causative agent of pneumocystis is generally known to be unculturable in vitro. Although the NGS results showed the presence of other microbial sequences, multiple blood culture and sputum culture results were negative, At the same time, the number of DNA copies of CMV was less than 2000 copies/mL, and CR showed that there was still a large amount of exudation in the lungs (Figure 2B). TMP-SMX (120 mg/kg dose Q6H) combined with CAS (14.4 mg, QD) as well as MEM (100 mg Q8H) was continued for 11 days (Figure 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A critically ill pediatric patient with severe pneumonia and negative routine cultures underwent metagenomic next-generation sequencing of sputum and peripheral blood.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following hospital admission for severe pneumonia with negative routine sputum and blood cultures, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed on both sputum and venous blood samples 2 days later to identify the underlying respiratory pathogens.

objective.routine_investigations: Routine microbiology and virology: Multiple blood and sputum bacterial/fungal cultures negative; quantitative blood cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA <2,000 copies/mL. Chest radiograph (CR): Extensive bilateral pulmonary exudation.
objective.advanced_workup: Sputum and venous blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS; Genskey Medical Technology) and Sanger sequencing: Detected nucleic acid sequences of both Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJ) and human cytomegalovirus (CMV) in paired sputum and venous blood specimens, with P. jirovecii infection further verified by targeted Sanger sequencing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe multipathogenic pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) co-infection, definitively confirmed by paired sputum and venous blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and Sanger sequencing despite negative conventional sputum and blood cultures. Plan and clinical course: Treated with combined trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX 120 mg/kg q6h), intravenous caspofungin (14.4 mg QD), and meropenem (100 mg q8h) for 11 days.

raw_case_text: Eleven days after admission, the child's condition was not alleviated. The ECMO support time was quite long, while the lung infection remained serious. The G test value increased (2419.3 pg/mL). The patient underwent bronchoscopy with a collection of BALF for routine examination and mNGS experiment. The smear and culture results were negative, and the mNGS results showed that the level of Pneumocystis infection decreased but CMV levels increased (Table 1). CT showed that both lungs were white with pneumothorax and pleural effusion (Figure 2C and D). Anti-infective treatment with MEM (100 mg Q8H) and CAS (50 mg QOD) was continued to prevent infection. Cefoperazone sodium and sulbactam sodium were administered (SCF, 400 mg Q8H) combined with TMP-SMX tablets (150 mg Q6H). Given that the number of platelets and lymphocytes were low in the patient, acyclovir (10 mg/kg dose Q8H) and IVIG (2.5 g/day) antiviral therapy were added for 2 days. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood cells showed that the CD3+ T cells/lymphocyte level was 52.32% (normal range 58.4-81.56%), and the CD4+ T cells/CD8+ T cells level was 4.2 (normal range 0.80-2.60). The diagnosis of immunodeficiency could not be excluded. After the following few days of treatment, the child was still in critical condition, and the G test value increased more (4138.0 pg/mL). CR showed that the lungs were still exuding severely (Figure 2E and F). The treatment, including ECMO, was suspended upon the request of the family. The child was eventually discharged after consent was obtained. Unfortunately, according to the telephone follow-up one week later, the child died two days later after leaving the hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A critically ill pediatric patient on prolonged extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for severe Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus co-infected pneumonia remained in refractory respiratory failure on hospital day 11.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After 11 days of inpatient treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, caspofungin, meropenem, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for mNGS-confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus pneumonia, the child's severe pulmonary infection and ECMO dependency failed to improve.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus pneumonia on prolonged ECMO support; suspected underlying primary immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent critical respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Critical respiratory failure requiring prolonged ECMO support, complicated by pneumothorax and pleural effusion.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: Thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia. Chest radiograph (CR): Persistent severe bilateral pulmonary exudation ('white-out' lungs).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G test): Markedly elevated at 2,419.3 pg/mL on day 11, rising further to 4,138.0 pg/mL over the subsequent days. Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets (flow cytometry): Decreased CD3+ T-cell percentage at 52.32% (normal: 58.4%–81.56%) and elevated CD4+/CD8+ ratio at 4.2 (normal: 0.80–2.60), suggestive of underlying immunodeficiency. Day 11 chest CT: Bilateral 'white-out' lungs complicated by pneumothorax and pleural effusion. Day 11 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS: Routine BALF smears and cultures negative; repeat BALF mNGS demonstrated a decreased read count of Pneumocystis jirovecii alongside an increased read count of cytomegalovirus (CMV).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Refractory fatal Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia complicated by bilateral 'white-out' lungs, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and prolonged ECMO dependence (with serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan rising to 4,138.0 pg/mL and persistent P. jirovecii and rising CMV reads on day 11 BALF mNGS) in a child with suspected underlying T-cell immunodeficiency. Plan and clinical course: Continued on meropenem (100 mg q8h), caspofungin (50 mg QOD), cefoperazone-sulbactam (400 mg q8h), oral TMP-SMX (150 mg q6h), intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h), and IVIG (2.5 g/day for 2 days). Due to worsening refractory respiratory failure and rising beta-D-glucan (4,138.0 pg/mL), the family requested withdrawal of ECMO and discharge against medical advice, and the child died 2 days post-discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old man presented and was admitted to the hospital with fever for 3 days and dyspnea for 1 day. The patient had been diagnosed with malignant pemphigus vulgaris and put on prednisolone, methylprednisolone and other immunosuppressive drugs for the past 9 years. On admission, he experienced respiratory failure. The absolute count of regulatory T lymphocytes was 156.67 cells/uL. The lactate dehydrogenase increased to 457 IU/L. The chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple flaky, fuzzy, and high-density opacities in both lungs (Figure 1A). The patient had been on steroids for a long time. He had obvious hypoxia and had never had any other respiratory symptoms or other infections. On respiratory examination, the patient did not have many rales in the lungs. The lung CT scan showed interstitial changes. PCP, usually treated with sulfonamides, was considered a possible etiology because of his immunocompromised state. Caspofungin is a good treatment of choice for Aspergillus infection, which could not be excluded. For other atypical pathogens, moxifloxacin should be added. Thus he was given trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 tablets, twice daily for 3 weeks), caspofungin (loading dose, 70mg infused over 1 hour; maintenance dose, 50 mg daily infused over 1 hour for 2 weeks), steroids, and moxifloxacin. Consequently, his respiratory function improved, and his body temperature dropped. PCP was confirmed 4 days later when cysts were found in the sputum (Supplementary Material).
Curiously, the follow-up chest CT suggested an enlarged consolidation in the left upper lobe (Figure 1A-C). The patient was admitted to the hospital again due to cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever. Bronchoscopy was performed for 3 times. Smears and culture of the bronchial brush, tracheal secretions, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were performed. Lung tissue was taken for culture and pathological examination, and tuberculosis was diagnosed (Figure 2). Antituberculosis treatment (isoniazid 300 mg once daily, rifapentine 600 mg twice weekly, ethambutol 750 mg once daily, and pyrazinamide 500 mg thrice daily) was given for 2 months and later ethambutol and pyrazinamide were excluded. Antituberculosis treatment lasted for 1 year. Simultaneously, traditional Chinese medicine techniques were used to manage the patient's psychological well-being and improve mental state. After 3 years of follow-up, the clinical outcome was good (Figure 3). The patient's complete course is shown in Figure 4.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old man on a 9-year regimen of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants for pemphigus vulgaris presented initially with a 3-day history of fever and 1-day history of dyspnea, and was later readmitted with recurrent cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever accompanied by an enlarging left upper lobe consolidation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Treated for the past 9 years with oral prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and other immunosuppressants for pemphigus vulgaris, the patient initially presented with 3 days of fever, 1 day of severe dyspnea, and hypoxemic respiratory failure. Following 4 days of empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, caspofungin, moxifloxacin, and corticosteroids, sputum examination confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and his fever and hypoxemia resolved. However, follow-up chest CT showed an enlarging consolidation in the left upper lobe, and he was readmitted with cough, sputum expectoration, and intermittent fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pemphigus vulgaris treated for 9 years with long-term prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: First admission positive for 3 days of fever and 1 day of severe dyspnea; second admission positive for productive cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever. Home medications included long-term prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and immunosuppressants.

objective.physical_examination: First admission: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with scant pulmonary rales on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission laboratory test: Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 457 IU/L.
objective.advanced_workup: First admission lymphocyte subsets, chest CT, and sputum microscopy: Absolute regulatory T-lymphocyte count 156.67 cells/μL; chest CT showed bilateral multiple flaky, hazy high-density and interstitial opacities; sputum microscopy on day 4 identified Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts. Readmission chest CT, serial bronchoscopies (3 times with bronchial brushings, tracheal secretions, and BALF), and lung biopsy: Follow-up chest CT showed an enlarging left upper lobe consolidation; lung tissue culture and histopathology confirmed active pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis co-infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Sequential/concomitant opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by sputum cyst identification on day 4) and left upper lobe pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed by lung biopsy pathology and culture after three bronchoscopies) in a patient receiving 9 years of corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy for pemphigus vulgaris. Plan and clinical course: Initial PCP was successfully treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 tablets BID for 3 weeks), IV caspofungin (70 mg loading, 50 mg daily for 2 weeks), moxifloxacin, and corticosteroids. Upon confirmation of left upper lobe pulmonary tuberculosis, he completed a 1-year antituberculosis regimen (2 months of intensive isoniazid 300 mg QD, rifapentine 600 mg twice weekly, ethambutol 750 mg QD, and pyrazinamide 500 mg TID, followed by 10 months of isoniazid and rifapentine) plus supportive traditional Chinese medicine, achieving a favorable clinical and radiographic outcome at 3-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old man with a history of peripheral T-cell lymphoma treated with six cycles of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (CHOP) was referred for abnormal imaging. Initial imaging showed enlarged mediastinal lymphadenopathy, particularly within the right paratracheal and subcarinal regions, as well as prominent mesenteric, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy. A surveillance computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis performed two months after therapy showed dramatic improvement. However, a new 1.2 cm pulmonary nodule was seen in the superior-medial aspect of the right lower lobe just lateral to the distal bronchus intermedius (Figure 1). A subsequent positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) scan revealed this nodule to be hypermetabolic with a standardized uptake value (SUV) of 5.7, raising the suspicion for a possible primary pulmonary malignancy (Figure 2).
The patient underwent bronchoscopy with linear endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS). After passing the scope into the distal bronchus intermedius and rotating the probe to face the posterior wall, the pulmonary nodule was identified on ultrasound. A 22-guage needle was used to obtain tissue. Cytology showed no evidence of malignant cells, and flow cytometry showed no discrete clonal B-cell or atypical T-cell population. No tissue was sent for culture. The patient underwent follow-up CT imaging two months later, which showed an enlargement of the nodule to 1.8 cm and two new 1 cm nodules in the peripheral basal right lower lobe. A repeat EBUS was performed, and the area of interest was identified (Figure 3). A 22-guage needle was used to obtain tissue from the same site; this time, suction was used, and up to fifteen passes with the needle were taken with each aspiration. Rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) did not confirm the presence of lymphocytes. Cytology was again nondiagnostic. No tissue was sent for culture.
The patient was referred to thoracic surgery. He underwent a right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with successful resection of the dominant right hilar nodule and two smaller basilar nodules. Pathology from the dominant nodule revealed multiple necrotizing granulomas, some of which were surrounded by organizing pneumonia (Figure 4). Acid-fast bacilli stain was negative. Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated clusters of organisms compatible with Pneumocystis in the center of these granulomas (Figure 5). On follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic. He declined treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and elected to pursue serial CT scans to monitor for recurrence. A repeat CT chest 6 months later showed no evidence of recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old asymptomatic man in remission 2 months after completing six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy for peripheral T-cell lymphoma was referred for a new 1.2 cm hypermetabolic right lower lobe pulmonary nodule.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had completed six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) 2 months earlier for peripheral T-cell lymphoma (which had initially presented with extensive right paratracheal, subcarinal, mesenteric, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy). While restaging thoracoabdominopelvic CT showed dramatic nodal regression, a new 1.2 cm right lower lobe nodule was discovered that demonstrated hypermetabolism (SUV 5.7) on PET-CT, and enlarged to 1.8 cm alongside two new 1.0 cm basilar nodules on 2-month follow-up CT.
subjective.past_medical_history: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma treated with 6 cycles of CHOP chemotherapy completed 2 months prior to referral.
subjective.review_of_systems: Completely asymptomatic from a respiratory and constitutional standpoint.

objective.physical_examination: Asymptomatic on outpatient evaluation.
objective.advanced_workup: Surveillance CT and 18F-FDG PET-CT (2 months post-CHOP): Dramatic resolution of lymphoma-related mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy, but appearance of a new 1.2 cm nodule in the superior-medial right lower lobe lateral to the distal bronchus intermedius with FDG SUVmax of 5.7; repeat CT 2 months later showed growth of the dominant nodule to 1.8 cm plus two new 1.0 cm peripheral right lower lobe basilar nodules. Two sequential linear endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspirations (EBUS-TBNA, 22G needle): Both procedures yielded nondiagnostic cytology without malignant cells or clonal B/T-cell populations on flow cytometry (tissue was not sent for microbiological culture). Right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) wedge resection of the dominant right hilar nodule and two smaller basilar nodules: Histopathology demonstrated multiple necrotizing granulomas surrounded by organizing pneumonia, negative acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain, and clusters of Pneumocystis organisms within the necrotic granuloma centers on Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Asymptomatic FDG-avid necrotizing granulomatous Pneumocystis jirovecii pulmonary nodules (1.8 cm dominant right lower lobe nodule and two 1.0 cm basilar nodules; SUVmax 5.7) mimicking primary lung malignancy or lymphoma relapse after six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy for peripheral T-cell lymphoma, definitively diagnosed by VATS wedge resection and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) staining after two nondiagnostic EBUS-TBNA procedures. Plan and clinical course: Following complete VATS surgical resection of the nodules, the asymptomatic patient declined oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy in favor of active radiographic surveillance, and 6-month follow-up chest CT confirmed no recurrence.

raw_case_text: A 5-year-old boy with steroid dependent MCNS was admitted to our hospital. He has been treated with prednisone, cyclosporine and 9 consecutive intravenous pulses of cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2 monthly) in the past 3 years. However, the patient still relapsed frequently. Therefore, a single dose of rituximab (375 mg/m2) was given intravenously in the latest episode of relapse. Three days later, the number of CD20 positive B cell decreased to be 0.19%. The urine protein turned to be negative within 1 week. Unfortunately, the patient presented with high fever (39 C) and cough on Day 13 after rituximab treatment. The complete blood count (CBC) test showed that leukocytes 4.76 x 109/L, hemoglobin 136.0 g/L, platelets 333.0 x 109/L, neutrophil percentage 91%, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L. Serum albumin 36.65 g/L, globulin 18 g/L, sodium 140 g/L, potassium 4.5 g/L, calcium 2.06 g/L. Liver and renal function was normal. Urinalysis: urinary protein ++. The chest CT showed ground-glass opacities in both lungs (Figure 1C). mNGS showed there was pneumocystis carinii in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. However, it was negative in sputum culture at the same time. Anti-infective treatment with meropenem, amoxicillin clavulanate potassium, oral SMZ-TMP and caspofungin were given. Meanwhile, the patient received mechanical ventilation due to severe respiratory distress. After 20 days of the treatment, dyspnea disappeared and the sign of lung infection was greatly improved (Figure 1D). Two months after RTX treatment, prednisone was terminated. One week after anti-PCP treatment, urinary protein turned to be negative. Moreover, the patient achieved complete remission in the following 24 months. The percentage of CD20 positive B cells were 2.6%, 5.9%, 16.1%, 24.2% in the 3rd, 6th, 12th and 24th month respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy with frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome presented with high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress 13 days after receiving a single dose of intravenous rituximab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 3 years, the patient had been treated for steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) with oral prednisone, cyclosporine, and nine monthly pulses of intravenous cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2), but continued to relapse frequently. During his latest relapse, he received a single intravenous infusion of rituximab (375 mg/m2), which reduced his CD20+ B cells to 0.19% in 3 days and cleared his proteinuria within 1 week. On day 13 post-rituximab, he acutely developed high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) treated over 3 years with prednisone, cyclosporine, 9 monthly IV cyclophosphamide pulses, and a single dose of IV rituximab 13 days prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress/dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: High fever (39.0 °C) and severe respiratory distress requiring endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 13 post-rituximab laboratory tests: WBC 4.76 x 10^9/L (91% neutrophils), hemoglobin 136.0 g/L, platelets 333.0 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 6 mg/L, serum albumin 36.65 g/L, globulin 18 g/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, calcium 2.06 mmol/L, normal hepatic and renal function, and urinalysis showing 2+ proteinuria; sputum culture negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral B-cell monitoring: CD20+ B cells decreased to 0.19% on day 3 post-rituximab (recovering to 2.6%, 5.9%, 16.1%, and 24.2% at months 3, 6, 12, and 24). Chest CT (day 13 post-rituximab): Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Positive for Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage fluid mNGS and bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest CT despite negative sputum culture) presenting 13 days after single-dose rituximab in a 5-year-old boy with steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome. Plan and clinical course: Treated with invasive mechanical ventilation, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-TMP), intravenous caspofungin, meropenem, and amoxicillin-clavulanate for 20 days, resulting in complete resolution of dyspnea and radiographic infiltrates. Urine protein turned negative 1 week after anti-PCP therapy, oral prednisone was discontinued 2 months post-rituximab, and he maintained complete nephrotic remission over 24 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 3-year-old boy with PNS was transferred to our hospital because of edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Initially, he responded well to steroid treatment. However, SDNS was developed eventually. The renal biopsy was performed 11 months after the onset of the disease. MCNS was the renal pathological change. Therefore, he was treated with a single dose of RTX (375 mg/m2). Three days later, the number of CD19 positive B cell decreased to be less than 0.5%. Complete remission was achieved in 1 week. However, he presented with cough and shortness of breath 6 weeks after RTX treatment. CBC test: leukocytes 8.83 x 109/L, hemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 465 x 109/L, neutrophil percentage 64.2%, C-reactive protein <=5 mg/L. Blood biochemical test: alanine aminotransferase 15 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, total protein 52.37 g/L, albumin 26.67 g/L, serum creatinine 36 ummol/L. The 24 h urinary protein was 1100.0 mg/m2. The chest CT showed diffuse exudation with interstitial changes in both lungs (Figure 1E). mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid revealed pneumocystis infection. He received high-flow of oxygen therapy. After 4 weeks of oral SMZ-TMP, caspofungin, meropenem and minocycline treatment, the symptoms of lung infection disappeared and complete resolution of inflammation was found in chest CT images (Figure 1F). Twenty-four hour urinary protein turned to be normal. Moreover, the patient achieved complete remission in the following 12 months. The percentage of CD20 positive B cells were 3.5%, 6.3%, 17.8% in the 3rd, 6th and 12th month respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old boy with biopsy-proven steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome presented with cough and shortness of breath 6 weeks after receiving a single dose of intravenous rituximab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially transferred with edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia, the patient developed steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (SDNS) with minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) confirmed on renal biopsy 11 months after disease onset. He received a single intravenous dose of rituximab (375 mg/m2), which depleted his CD19+ B cells to <0.5% in 3 days and induced complete remission within 1 week. Six weeks post-rituximab, he presented with acute cough and shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Biopsy-proven steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) treated with single-dose IV rituximab 6 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough and shortness of breath at 6 weeks post-rituximab.
