objective.physical_examination: Tachypneic and dyspneic at 6 weeks post-rituximab, requiring high-flow oxygen therapy.
objective.routine_investigations: Six-week post-rituximab laboratory tests: WBC 8.83 x 10^9/L (64.2% neutrophils), hemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 465 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) <=5 mg/L, ALT 15 U/L, AST 22 U/L, total protein 52.37 g/L, serum albumin 26.67 g/L, serum creatinine 36 μmol/L, and 24-hour urinary protein 1,100.0 mg/m2.
objective.advanced_workup: Renal biopsy (at 11 months of disease): Minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). Peripheral B-cell monitoring: CD19+ B cells <0.5% at day 3 post-rituximab (CD20+ B cells recovering to 3.5%, 6.3%, and 17.8% at months 3, 6, and 12). Chest CT (6 weeks post-rituximab): Diffuse bilateral pulmonary exudation and interstitial changes. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Confirmed Pneumocystis infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage fluid mNGS and diffuse bilateral exudative/interstitial changes on chest CT) occurring 6 weeks after single-dose rituximab therapy in a 3-year-old boy with steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome. Plan and clinical course: Managed with high-flow oxygen therapy and a 4-week regimen of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-TMP), caspofungin, meropenem, and minocycline, achieving complete clinical and chest CT resolution, normalization of 24-hour urinary protein, and sustained complete nephrotic remission over 12 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
At 6-month-old baby girl, born to non-consanguineous parents of Swedish descent (Caucasians), was admitted to a Swedish hospital due to severe pneumonia. Previous medical records showed failure-to-thrive and thrombocytosis. She received respiratory support, corticosteroids, and antibiotics at the intensive care unit. Rhino- and bocavirus were detected in nasal swabs, and radiology suggested a bacterial infection. Due to halting recovery after a week, extended testing was performed, revealing unmeasurable immunoglobulin levels and a nasopharyngeal swab PCR positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCJ). Radiology and further microbiologic testing confirmed PCJ pneumonia. This raised a suspicion of SCID, and antimicrobial therapy was adjusted and intravenous immunoglobulin substitution initiated. The patient was transferred to a tertiary pediatric hospital for intensive care and immunologic workup and treatment. Candida parapsiolosis was found in the feces. The necessity of allogenic HCT was evident; thus, it was carried out. The timeline is depicted in  Figure 1 .
Upon clinical diagnosis, we retrieved the patient's NBS sample and ran an SCID NBS assay analyzing both TRECs and KRECs: the TREC copy number was 110 copies/well [recall threshold <=5, population mean 79, IQR 55, 110 ] and KRECs were not measurable. Lymphocyte phenotyping in peripheral blood showed prevalent T lymphocytes of which the majority were CD4+ T lymphocytes, with a smaller fraction of CD8+ T lymphocytes. Both CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes had a uniform, atypical surface phenotype expressing intermediate levels of the naive cell marker CD45RA but high levels of the recent thymic emigrant marker CD31 ( Table 1 ). Analysis of the T lymphocyte receptor (TCR) Vbeta repertoire by flow cytometry revealed an essentially normal distribution in both CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes, but an elevated level of CD4+ Vbeta2+ T lymphocytes (19%, upper normal limit 13%). B lymphocytes were severely reduced in numbers (0.02 x 109/L) and were all found to be naive (93% with no plasmablasts and switched memory cells,  Table 1 ). No specific antibodies to previous vaccinations were detected. Lymphocyte proliferation showed adequate response to mitogens, except for pokeweed mitogen (PWM) in B lymphocytes and concavalin A (ConA) in CD8+ T lymphocytes. Conversely, a lymphocyte response was not evoked to either tetanus or pneumococcus despite previous vaccinations, or candida despite positive cultures ( Table 1 ). Assessment of the myeloid compartment (e.g., erythro-, mono-, and neutrophil granulocytes) was normal, besides absent eosinophil granulocytes and thrombocytosis ( Table 1 ). Whole genome sequencing with an in silico filter for IEI showed a heterozygous sequence variant in IKZF1 (c.476A>G, p.Asn159Ser). Confirmatory Sanger sequencing of the patient and parents showed the mutation to be de novo.
At 10 months of age, our patient underwent allogeneic HCT with an unrelated 10/10 HLA-matched donor, the timeline is depicted in  Figure 1 . The PCJ pneumonia and respiratory viruses were cleared before admission. HCT conditioning consisted of fludarabine, treosulfan, and anti-thymocyte globulin. The HCT was performed with neutrophil and thrombocyte engraftment at days +36 and +24, respectively, without complications. Ciclosporin A and methotrexate were used as graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis. Six weeks after the procedure, cutaneous and gastrointestinal GVHD grade 1 occurred and was treated with prednisolone. Thereafter, CMV viremia occurred, with good response to pre-emptive therapy with valganciclovir. Because of mixed chimerism with low counts of T and B lymphocytes, an evaluating bone marrow biopsy was performed approximately +4 months post-HCT. It revealed near total CD34+ autologous reconstitution, i.e., graft failure/rejection. Hence, re-HCT was performed with repeated conditioning (i.e., same as in first HCT with the addition of thiotepa) and the same donor and GVHD prophylaxis. Neutrophil and thrombocyte engraftment were seen at days +19 and +20, respectively. The re-HCT was without significant complications.
Six months after re-HCT, the patient displayed full donor chimerism. An additional 12 months later, our patient experienced several uncomplicated upper airway infections, with spontaneous recovery. Twenty-seven months after re-HCT, the patient is alive and well, without any continuous treatment. She has a full numeric immune recovery (lymphocytes and immunoglobulins), responded adequately to vaccinations, is developing as expected, and is now in preschool.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-month-old Caucasian female infant of Swedish descent was admitted with severe pneumonia and a prior history of failure to thrive.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant was admitted at 6 months of age to a Swedish hospital with severe pneumonia requiring intensive care unit respiratory support, corticosteroids, and empiric antibiotics. Initial nasal swabs detected rhinovirus and bocavirus, and chest imaging suggested bacterial pneumonia, but her clinical recovery halted after 1 week of therapy, prompting an extended immunological and microbiological evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Failure to thrive and persistent thrombocytosis documented in prior medical records; born to non-consanguineous Caucasian parents of Swedish descent; previously immunized according to schedule.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe respiratory distress/pneumonia and failure to thrive.

objective.physical_examination: Severe pneumonia requiring pediatric ICU respiratory support; failure to thrive.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial microbiology: Nasal swabs positive for rhinovirus and bocavirus; fecal culture positive for Candida parapsilosis. Extended baseline immunology and hematology: Unmeasurable serum immunoglobulin levels and complete absence of specific antibodies to prior vaccinations (tetanus, pneumococcus); normal myeloid compartment (erythrocytes, monocytes, neutrophils) except for absent eosinophils and persistent thrombocytosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Opportunistic pathogen testing: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR and confirmatory microbiological/radiological testing positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCJ) pneumonia. Newborn screening (NBS) card retrospective SCID assay: Normal TREC copy number at 110 copies/well (recall threshold <=5, population mean 79) but unmeasurable KRECs. Peripheral blood lymphocyte phenotyping and function: Prevalent T cells (predominantly CD4+ over CD8+) with a uniform atypical surface phenotype expressing intermediate CD45RA and high CD31 (recent thymic emigrants); TCR Vbeta repertoire largely normal except elevated CD4+ Vbeta2+ T cells (19%, upper normal limit 13%); severely reduced B lymphocytes (0.02 x 10^9/L), 93% naive without plasmablasts or switched memory B cells; impaired lymphocyte proliferation to pokeweed mitogen (PWM) in B cells, concanavalin A (ConA) in CD8+ T cells, and specific antigens (tetanus, pneumococcus, Candida). Whole-genome sequencing (IEI filter) and confirmatory trio Sanger sequencing: Identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in IKZF1, c.476A>G (p.Asn159Ser).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCJ, confirmed by nasopharyngeal swab PCR and radiology) and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by a de novo heterozygous IKZF1 mutation (c.476A>G, p.Asn159Ser), accompanied by rhinovirus/bocavirus co-infection and fecal Candida parapsilosis colonization. Plan and clinical course: Treated in the tertiary pediatric ICU with targeted anti-Pneumocystis antimicrobial therapy and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement, clearing PCJ pneumonia and respiratory viruses prior to transplantation. At 10 months of age, she underwent allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) from a 10/10 HLA-matched unrelated donor (conditioned with fludarabine, treosulfan, and anti-thymocyte globulin; GVHD prophylaxis with cyclosporine A and methotrexate), complicated by grade 1 cutaneous/GI GVHD (treated with prednisolone), CMV viremia (treated with valganciclovir), and autologous CD34+ graft rejection at +4 months. A second HCT using the same donor with added thiotepa conditioning achieved neutrophil/platelet engraftment by days +19/+20 and full donor chimerism at 6 months. At 27 months post-re-HCT, she is alive and well off all therapy with full numerical and functional immune reconstitution.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 2-year-old Caucasian male, ex-33-week premature infant with fetal alcohol syndrome who was diagnosed with early onset sJIA at 13 months of age after he presented with persistent quotidian fevers, evanescent rash, lymphadenopathy, and arthritis. Initial treatment included anakinra 100 mg subcutaneously daily. He had five prior hospitalizations for bouts of MAS, requiring treatment with high-dose intravenous (IV) corticosteroids and IV anakinra. His most recent admission, reported here, was prompted by persistent fevers, rash, laboratory values concerning for MAS flare, and chest x-ray suggestive of multifocal pneumonia. His home regimen prior to admission was 8 mg/kg/day of subcutaneous (SC) anakinra and 0.17 mg/kg/day of tacrolimus (with trough level of 7-9). It was initially unclear whether this episode was a continuation of a previous weeks-long MAS flare or constituted a new flare until results of infectious evaluation revealed extreme adenoviremia.
During his admission, which lasted for a total of 105 days, he was initially given pulse IV methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg/day) and was continued on high-dose steroids with inability to taper for weeks. On hospital day (HD) 2, anakinra was increased (25 mg/kg/day IV in divided doses) in the setting of worsening MAS labs. His oral tacrolimus was switched to IV cyclosporine from HD 10-38; however, due to persistently subtherapeutic levels, he was later switched back to oral tacrolimus after developing hypertension. Anakinra 25 mg/kg/day was discontinued on HD 11 to initiate emergent use of low-dose emapalumab 1 mg/kg twice weekly, given worsening MAS labs and fever despite high dose IV anakinra. However, unanticipated issues with IV access delayed his emapalumab infusion and he began to experience spiking fevers as a result. Biweekly emapalumab was added on HD 12 (1 mg/kg) with subsequent weekly dose escalation (3 mg/kg HD 13, 6 mg/kg HD 15, 10 mg/kg HD 19, and 10 mg/kg HD 22 and thereafter). On HD 13, his hyperferritinemia worsened to 67,000 ng/ml, AST/ALT > 1,000 IU/L, LDH >10,000 IU/L, and persistently down-trending platelets, hemoglobin, and leukocyte count. This laboratory trend in conjunction with persistent fevers and worsening respiratory status necessitated increased oxygen supplementation and prompted a transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) from HD 13 to 15. Very high dose anakinra was resumed in the PICU (37.5 mg/kg/day IV in divided doses on HD 13). His respiratory deterioration improved after receiving furosemide for interstitial pulmonary edema. He was switched to IV dexamethasone 1.5 mg/kg/day on HD 15. However, owing to worsening MAS labs, his IV anakinra dose was increased further (46 mg/kg/day IV in divided doses from HD 13 to 58). Etoposide (150 mg/m2 weekly for 8 doses) was added on HD 26 per pHLH protocol as recommended by pediatric hematology/oncology based on his severe refractory course despite aggressive treatment for sHLH. Of note, he did not have a pathogenic mutation in genes responsible for pHLH. He eventually stabilized after nearly 3 months of this combination therapy plus cidofovir for his adenoviremia, facilitating slow taper of high-dose IV steroids as well as anakinra from 46 mg/kg/day to 2 mg/kg/day over the course of 37 days (HD 59-96). Anakinra was eventually discontinued on HD 101. At discharge (HD 105), he was prescribed prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day, hydrocortisone 5 mg twice daily, emapalumab 10 mg/kg twice weekly, tacrolimus 0.2 mg twice daily (0.03 mg/kg/day) (Figure 1), as well as maintenance cidofovir.
As noted above, evaluation for pHLH was negative by genotyping of blood and bone marrow. Invitae  primary immunodeficiency genetic panel, quantitative immunoglobulins, and lymphocyte subsets were normal and did not indicate an underlying immunodeficiency. Bone marrow biopsies (at initial diagnosis and with current MAS flare) did not demonstrate malignancy and comprehensive infectious evaluation was entirely negative other than adenoviremia (>10,000,000 copies/ml). He was treated with weekly IV cidofovir, which was continued after discharge home, and five doses of IV immunoglobulin G (IVIG) to provide passive immunity. Chest computed tomography (CT) confirmed multifocal pneumonia and excluded interstitial lung disease. He was treated with voriconazole for presumed Aspergillus because of abnormal galactomannan from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), which was converted to posaconazole at discharge. However, there remains a debate whether he in fact actually had fungal pneumonia given that only one BAL galactomoannan was abnormal with a negative result on repeat BAL. Repeat BAL universal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) revealed Pneumocystis jiroveci (PJP) despite prophylaxis with nebulized pentamidine, which was treated with atovaquone (Table 1).
Now 24 months post hospital discharge, he has not had recurrence of MAS off steroids, anakinra, and emapalumab, remaining only on low dose tacrolimus and methotrexate for treatment of his sJIA. He receives monthly inhaled pentamidine for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis. He continues to be followed by Pediatric Rheumatology/Immunology for further management.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-year-old Caucasian male with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and recurrent macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) presented with persistent fevers and rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, an ex-33-week premature infant with fetal alcohol syndrome diagnosed with early-onset sJIA at 13 months of age (presenting with quotidian fevers, evanescent rash, lymphadenopathy, and arthritis), had five prior hospitalizations for MAS flares treated with high-dose IV corticosteroids and IV anakinra. Prior to this admission, he was maintained on subcutaneous anakinra (8 mg/kg/day), oral tacrolimus (0.17 mg/kg/day, trough 7–9), and nebulized pentamidine for PJP prophylaxis. He was readmitted for persistent fevers, rash, worsening MAS laboratory markers, and multifocal pneumonia on chest radiograph.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ex-33-week premature infant; fetal alcohol syndrome; early-onset systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) diagnosed at 13 months of age; five prior hospitalizations for macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent fevers and rash on admission, followed by worsening respiratory distress in the hospital. Home medications included subcutaneous anakinra (8 mg/kg/day), oral tacrolimus (0.17 mg/kg/day), and prophylactic nebulized pentamidine.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with rash on admission; developed worsening respiratory distress requiring escalated oxygen supplementation and PICU transfer on hospital days 13–15, as well as tacrolimus/cyclosporine-associated hypertension.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission chest X-ray: Suggestive of multifocal pneumonia. Hospital day 13 laboratory peak during MAS flare: Severe hyperferritinemia (67,000 ng/mL), AST and ALT >1,000 IU/L, LDH >10,000 IU/L, and progressively downtrending platelets, hemoglobin, and leukocyte counts. Virological testing: Extreme peripheral blood adenoviremia (>10,000,000 copies/mL); remainder of routine infectious screening negative. Immunological workup: Normal quantitative immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets.
objective.advanced_workup: Genetic and bone marrow workup: Primary HLH (pHLH) genotyping of blood and bone marrow negative for pathogenic mutations; Invitae primary immunodeficiency genetic panel normal; serial bone marrow biopsies negative for malignancy. Chest CT: Confirmed multifocal pneumonia and excluded interstitial lung disease. Bronchoscopy and serial bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Initial BAL showed abnormal galactomannan (which was negative on repeat BAL); repeat BAL universal PCR was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJP) despite prior nebulized pentamidine prophylaxis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Breakthrough Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by repeat BAL universal PCR), severe disseminated adenoviremia (>10,000,000 copies/mL), and presumed pulmonary aspergillosis complicating life-threatening refractory macrophage activation syndrome (MAS / secondary HLH) in a 2-year-old boy with sJIA. Plan and clinical course: Over a 105-day hospitalization, refractory MAS was managed with pulse IV methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg/day) switched to IV dexamethasone (1.5 mg/kg/day on HD 15), ultra-high-dose IV anakinra (escalated up to 46 mg/kg/day on HD 13–58, tapered HD 59–96, stopped HD 101), calcineurin inhibition (IV cyclosporine HD 10–38, then back to oral tacrolimus), biweekly IV emapalumab (escalated from 1 mg/kg on HD 12 to 10 mg/kg twice weekly from HD 19), and weekly etoposide (150 mg/m2 for 8 doses starting HD 26), plus furosemide for interstitial pulmonary edema in the PICU. Concurrent infections were treated with weekly IV cidofovir and five doses of IVIG for adenoviremia, voriconazole (transitioned to posaconazole at discharge) for abnormal BAL galactomannan, and oral atovaquone for breakthrough PJP. He was discharged on HD 105 on prednisolone, hydrocortisone, emapalumab, tacrolimus, and maintenance cidofovir; at 24 months post-discharge, he remains in MAS remission off steroids, anakinra, and emapalumab, maintained on low-dose tacrolimus, methotrexate, and monthly inhaled pentamidine prophylaxis.

raw_case_text:
Herein, we report the case of a 53-year-old man, followed since early 2020 for a grade III, well-differentiated, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with synchronous bone, nodal, liver, and lung metastases. His past medical history mainly includes hereditary polyneuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) without clinical invalidity. The patient successively received standard systemic treatments such as gemcitabine-oxaliplatin, capecitabine-temozolomide, carboplatin-etoposide (VP-16), and sunitinib from January 2020 to June 2022. The objective response rate with previous systemic therapy ranged from partial response to stable disease. Oncologic treatments were discontinued for progressive diseases and there was no arrest due to toxicity. Agnostic tumoral NGS (TSO500 panel) performed after progression under sunitinib treatments identified a CCDC6-RET fusion. The patient was enrolled in a tumor-agnostic platform clinical trial and received pralsetinib at a dose of 400 mg/day from 27th September 2022 as the fifth-line treatment. Notably, this patient had neither experienced any infectious events or complications during his oncologic history before pralsetinib initiation nor presented lymphopenia or neutropenia, which would suggest some types of immunosuppression. The patient had no corticosteroid treatment at pralsetinib initiation.
One month after pralsetinib initiation (5 November 2022), he developed symptomatic Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia (wild-type phenotype) complicated with lung septic embolisms and concomitant grade III cervical spondylodiscitis involving the 5th and 6th cervical vertebrae and para-vertebral C2 to C5 abscess. Pralsetinib was immediately discontinued, and the patient was successfully treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and ciprofloxacin antibiotic therapy for 14 days, followed by ciprofloxacin monotherapy for 4 more weeks. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) excluded infective endocarditis. Notably, the computational tomodensitometry (CT) performed to diagnose septic embolisms also reported a tumor partial response (PR), according to RECIST (Figure 1). After 3 weeks of ciprofloxacin monotherapy and resuming without pralsetinib (as of 5th December 2022), the patient was diagnosed with a second infectious episode of grade II pneumonia, for which he received 7 days of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. After 1 month of pralsetinib discontinuation due to these two infectious events, a full CT-scan re-evaluation was performed, which revealed new secondary lesions with pleural effusion, peritoneal carcinosis, and lytic bone lesions. Pralsetinib was then resumed on 23rd December 2022 at a standard dose of 400 mg per day, with rapid clinical benefits. After 3 weeks of reintroduction (12th January 2023), the patient experienced a third infectious episode with grade III pneumonia requiring hospitalization due to grade II neutropenia. This was successfully treated with 7 days of piperacillin-tazobactam. After 1 week of reintroduction, the patient presented with febrile back pain and a 4/5 motor deficit in the right leg. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified typical spondylodiscitis involving 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae. Considering the recurrent infectious events, an extensive infectious immune workout was performed. The vertebral biopsy identified the presence of P. aeruginosa, and the histology did not show the presence of bone tuberculosis or tumor progression. Repeated blood culture (bacterial and fungal) was performed and remained negative, and transesophageal echocardiography (TEO) was normal. Grade I lymphopenia was identified without concomitant neutropenia. Lymphocyte immunophenotyping did not reveal any imbalance between CD4 and CD8 sub-populations, B lymphopenia, and natural killer (NK) deficiency. However, plasmatic protein electrophoresis identified deep hypogammaglobulinemia with specific IgG deficiency without a decrease in IgA and IgM. Broad-spectrum serology, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis B and C, was negative. This fourth infectious episode was considered as a grade III lumbar spondylodiscitis, which required 2-week hospitalization, and was successfully treated with tobramycin and ciprofloxacin for 48 h followed by a high dose of piperacilline-tazobactam (16 g per day) and ciprofloxacin for 2 weeks, as well as monotherapy with ciprofloxacin for another 2 months. Pralsetinib was continued at 300 mg, and the patient experienced a new partial response in May 2023. Later, on 15th June 2023, in the context of persistent lymphopenia and febrile hypoxemia, a thoracic CT scan was performed and showed disseminated, poorly delimitated pulmonary lesions, which were first interpreted as disease progression. However, pulmonary secretion was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii. The final diagnosis was a symptomatic pneumocystis, which was treated with high-dose trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Pralsetinib was discontinued after the fifth episode. Finally, the patient presented with liver progression on 30 June 2023, and pralsetinib was definitively discontinued (Figure 1). The patient died in the palliative care unit in September 2023, 3 years after diagnosis, including 9 months of oncologic clinical treatment with pralsetinib.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old man with metastatic CCDC6-RET fusion-positive grade III pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor presented in June 2023 with febrile hypoxemia after 9 months of fifth-line pralsetinib therapy complicated by recurrent severe bacterial infections.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, followed since early 2020 for a grade III well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor metastatic to bone, lymph nodes, liver, and lungs, progressed through four prior lines of therapy (gemcitabine-oxaliplatin, capecitabine-temozolomide, carboplatin-etoposide, and sunitinib) without any prior infectious complications or cytopenias. After TSO500 tumor NGS identified a CCDC6-RET fusion, he initiated fifth-line pralsetinib (400 mg/day) on September 27, 2022. His course on pralsetinib was marked by four sequential infectious episodes: (1) November 5, 2022: wild-type Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia with septic pulmonary emboli and C5–C6 cervical spondylodiscitis/C2–C5 paravertebral abscess (treated with 2 weeks piperacillin-tazobactam + ciprofloxacin, then 4 weeks ciprofloxacin); (2) December 5, 2022 (off pralsetinib): grade II pneumonia (treated with 7 days amoxicillin-clavulanic acid); after CT showed tumor progression, pralsetinib 400 mg/day was resumed on December 23, 2022; (3) January 12, 2023: grade III pneumonia with grade II neutropenia (treated with 7 days piperacillin-tazobactam); (4) 1 week after reintroduction: febrile back pain and 4/5 right leg motor deficit from L1–L3 P. aeruginosa lumbar spondylodiscitis with newly identified grade I lymphopenia and deep IgG hypogammaglobulinemia (treated with tobramycin + ciprofloxacin for 48 h, high-dose piperacillin-tazobactam 16 g/day + ciprofloxacin for 2 weeks, and ciprofloxacin for 2 months while continuing reduced-dose pralsetinib 300 mg/day). On June 15, 2023, in the setting of persistent lymphopenia, he presented with a fifth infectious episode characterized by febrile hypoxemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Grade III well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with synchronous bone, nodal, liver, and lung metastases (diagnosed early 2020, harboring a CCDC6-RET fusion); hereditary polyneuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) without clinical disability.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and hypoxemia in June 2023; prior episodes of febrile neck/back pain and 4/5 right leg motor weakness.

objective.physical_examination: During the fourth infectious episode (January 2023): Febrile back pain with a 4/5 motor deficit in the right lower extremity. During the fifth infectious episode (June 15, 2023): Febrile hypoxemia.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial microbiological and immunological workup during pralsetinib therapy: Blood cultures positive for wild-type Pseudomonas aeruginosa in November 2022 (negative on repeat in January 2023); normal transthoracic (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE); transient grade II neutropenia (January 2023) and persistent grade I lymphopenia; serum protein electrophoresis showed deep hypogammaglobulinemia with selective IgG deficiency and normal IgA and IgM; HIV, HBV, and HCV serologies negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Cervical and lumbar spine MRI and L1–L3 vertebral biopsy: C5–C6 spondylodiscitis with C2–C5 abscess (November 2022) and L1–L3 spondylodiscitis (January 2023; biopsy culture positive for P. aeruginosa, negative for tuberculosis or tumor). Lymphocyte immunophenotyping (January 2023): Balanced CD4 and CD8 subpopulations without B-cell lymphopenia or NK-cell deficiency. Thoracic CT (June 15, 2023): Disseminated, poorly delineated bilateral pulmonary lesions initially mimicking tumor progression. Pulmonary secretion microbiological testing (June 2023): Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Symptomatic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by positive pulmonary secretion testing and disseminated poorly delineated pulmonary lesions on thoracic CT) and acquired selective IgG hypogammaglobulinemia/lymphopenia with recurrent invasive Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections (bacteremia, septic pulmonary emboli, C5–C6 and L1–L3 spondylodiscitis) induced by selective RET inhibition with pralsetinib. Plan and clinical course: Treated for PCP with high-dose trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and discontinuation of pralsetinib after the fifth infectious episode. On June 30, 2023, CT demonstrated hepatic tumor progression, leading to permanent discontinuation of pralsetinib, and the patient died in the palliative care unit in September 2023.

raw_case_text: These two patients were siblings. Case 1 was the elder brother, a full-term boy with a birth weight of 2.8 kg and congenital heart defects (coarctation of the aorta, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus). He underwent a cardiac operation at the age of 1 month and also developed neonatal jaundice. He presented with recurrent cough, wheezing, and tachypnea beginning at 2 months. He has also experienced developmental delay, recurrent diarrhea, feeding problems, and poor weight gain from the age of 2 months. During illness, he needed nasogastric feeding but was fed orally after discharge. He had two episodes of respiratory exacerbations accompanied by respiratory failure, leading to hospitalizations at the ages of 3 and 8 months. During his first hospitalization at 3 months, a physical examination revealed crackles, wheezing, retractions, funnel chest, hypotonia, and poor visual contact. His respiratory rate was 60-90 times/min, and his oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 80%-92%, requiring oxygen supplementation. He was anemic (hemoglobin 73 g/L), and his liver function indicators were slightly elevated [alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 53 U/L, total bilirubin (TBIL) 22 mumol/L]. His white blood cell count, C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), renal function, and thyroid function tests were within normal ranges. Pneumocystis jirovecii were found in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Immunological work-up showed a mild decrease in IgG and IgA levels, while lymphocyte subtypes remained normal. A chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs) and consolidations at the age of 3 months (Figure 1A). He developed respiratory failure necessitating invasive ventilation for 6 days and received anti-infection treatment for 1 month, with multiple antibiotics including trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole for P. jirovecii and antifungal drugs. He also received prednisone at a daily dose of 0.75 mg/kg for 20 days. After 1 month, repeated chest CT showed little improvement. After discharge, his cough improved, but tachypnea and oxygen desaturation persisted (respiratory rate 50-60 times/min, SpO2 94%). At the age of 8 months, he presented with a short-term fever followed by another episode of respiratory failure. Multiple pathogens were found in the aspiration of sputum obtained from the oropharynx, nasal cavity, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid during the second hospitalization, including Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, Candida parapsilosis, rhinovirus, and human metapneumovirus. The repeated chest CT indicated GGOs in the same area as before and increased consolidations (Figure 1B). Unfortunately, despite anti-infection treatment, he died of respiratory failure at the age of 8 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-month-old full-term male infant with repaired congenital heart disease presented with recurrent cough, wheezing, and tachypnea since 2 months of age that progressed to acute respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born full-term (birth weight 2.8 kg) with complex congenital heart defects surgically repaired at 1 month of age, the infant developed persistent cough, wheezing, tachypnea, developmental delay, recurrent diarrhea, feeding difficulties requiring intermittent nasogastric tube feeding, and poor weight gain starting at 2 months of age. He suffered two severe respiratory exacerbations with acute respiratory failure requiring hospitalization at 3 months and 8 months of age.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital heart defects (coarctation of the aorta, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus) status post surgical repair at 1 month of age; neonatal jaundice; developmental delay, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, recurrent diarrhea, and failure to thrive since 2 months of age. Sibling (younger brother, Case 2 in family) affected by the same genetic syndrome.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent cough, wheezing, tachypnea, dyspnea/retractions, poor visual contact, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, recurrent diarrhea, and poor weight gain.

objective.physical_examination: At 3-month hospitalization: Tachypnea with respiratory rate 60–90 breaths/min, hypoxemia with SpO2 80%–92% (persisting at RR 50–60/min and SpO2 94% post-discharge), chest retractions, pectus excavatum (funnel chest), bilateral pulmonary crackles and wheezing, generalized hypotonia, and poor visual contact.
objective.routine_investigations: At 3-month hospitalization: Anemia with hemoglobin 73 g/L; mildly elevated liver enzymes with ALT 53 U/L and total bilirubin 22 μmol/L; normal WBC count, C-reactive protein (CRP), ESR, renal function, and thyroid function; mild decrease in serum IgG and IgA levels. At 8-month hospitalization: Oropharyngeal, nasal, and BAL fluid aspirates detected Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, Candida parapsilosis, rhinovirus, and human metapneumovirus.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological phenotyping: Normal peripheral lymphocyte subsets. Chest CT at 3 months: Bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs) and consolidations (which showed minimal improvement after 1 month of therapy and worsened consolidation at 8 months). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) examination at 3 months: Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed in BALF at 3 months of age) and chronic childhood interstitial lung disease / syndromic immunodeficiency with developmental delay, hypotonia, and congenital heart defects, complicated at 8 months of age by polymicrobial respiratory infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, Candida parapsilosis, rhinovirus, and human metapneumovirus). Plan and clinical course: During his first hospitalization at 3 months, he required invasive mechanical ventilation for 6 days, 1 month of antimicrobial therapy including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and antifungals, and oral prednisone (0.75 mg/kg/day for 20 days). Although his cough improved and he was discharged, baseline tachypnea (50–60 breaths/min), hypoxemia (SpO2 94%), and bilateral GGOs persisted. At 8 months of age, he was readmitted with fever, polymicrobial pneumonia, and progressive consolidation on chest CT, and died of refractory respiratory failure.

raw_case_text:
A 5-months-old boy was admitted to the intensive care unit of a tertiary pediatric hospital in Lisbon for respiratory insufficiency following three days of fever, cough, and worsening respiratory distress. He presented with oral thrush, bilateral pulmonary rales, and hepatosplenomegaly. He had been vaccinated at birth with BCG (Danish strain 1331) and had had recurrent infections (conjunctivitis, otitis media, and persistent oral thrush). 
There was no consanguinity. Two maternal uncles died of pneumonia in infancy. 
The chest X-ray revealed absence of a thymus and showed bilateral areas of opacities (Figure 1). The immunologic panel confirmed the hypothesis of SCID (Table 1), later genetically characterized (missense mutation in exon 5, codon 226 CGC CAC, leading to an arginine 226 substitution by histidine; common cytokine receptor gamma chain of IL-2:IL2RG gene). This mutation has previously been described as causing human X-linked SCID. 
Although being asymptomatic, chimerism studies were performed to assess the presence of exogenous maternal lymphocytes, which can be important for an early diagnosis and for the choice of the conditioning regimen if bone marrow transplantation is considered. The results confirmed that 75% of total lymphocyte count was maternal.
The bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for Candida albicans, Pneumocystis jiroveci, and acid-fast bacilli. An ultrasound evaluation showed an enlarged spleen with nodules. The BCG primer-specific polymerase chain reaction quickly identified the infection by BCG (amplification of pncA gene1 and a multiplex PCR that targets the RD1 region for BCG), and presumptive diagnosis of disseminated BCG was made.
He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a four-tuberculostatic drug regimen, comprised of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin, according to laboratory data regarding BCG strain susceptibility. The infant started antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis and immunoglobulin replacement therapy.
Splenectomy was performed aiming for a reduction in BCG load which could worsen the prognosis following immune reconstitution. Spleen analysis revealed severe BCG infiltration (Figure 2), thus establishing the definitive diagnosis of disseminated BCG disease. Four and a half months after the start of tuberculostatic therapy, T-cell depleted bone marrow transplantation (BMT) from an unrelated 10/10 HLA matched donor following reduced intensity conditioning with treosulfan, fludarabine and campath was performed (graft contained 12,5 x 106/kilograms CD34+ stem cells). To enhance immune reconstitution, donor lymphocytes were administered at d + 31, d + 61, and d + 88 containing 5, 15, and 50 x 104 CD3+ T cells per kilograms, respectively. The transplant course was uneventful with the exception of repeated periods of fever that, in the absence of other reported infections, were probably related to active BCG infection, treated continuously by isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. Haematological reconstitution occurred within normal time frame, and there were no signs of graft-versus-host disease. About three months after transplantation, relevant numbers of T cells become detectable. During this phase of immunological reconstitution, signs of BCG infection augmented with prominent nodules at the BCG inoculation site (Figure 3), enlarged thoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, fever, leukocytosis, and massive elevation of C-reactive protein. Linezolid was added to other antituberculous drugs, and some short courses of steroids were administered. The child remained in good clinical condition and is alive and well to date.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-month-old boy presented to the pediatric ICU with acute respiratory insufficiency following a 3-day history of fever, cough, and worsening respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant, who had been vaccinated at birth with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG Danish strain 1331) and suffered recurrent infancy infections (conjunctivitis, otitis media, and persistent oral thrush), developed 3 days of fever, cough, and escalating respiratory distress culminating in acute respiratory insufficiency and pediatric ICU admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Vaccinated at birth with BCG (Danish strain 1331); history of recurrent conjunctivitis, otitis media, and persistent oral candidiasis. Born to non-consanguineous parents; family history notable for two maternal uncles who died of pneumonia in infancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, cough, severe respiratory distress, and persistent oral thrush.

objective.physical_examination: Oral thrush, bilateral pulmonary rales on auscultation, and hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray: Bilateral pulmonary opacities and complete absence of a thymic shadow. Abdominal ultrasound: Splenomegaly with multiple splenic nodules.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological, genetic, and chimerism studies: Confirmed X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) caused by a hemizygous missense mutation in exon 5, codon 226 (CGC>CAC, p.Arg226His) of the IL2RG gene; maternal chimerism analysis demonstrated that 75% of circulating peripheral lymphocytes were of maternal origin. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) microbiology and PCR: Positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, Candida albicans, and acid-fast bacilli; BCG-specific PCR (amplifying the pncA gene and RD1 region multiplex PCR) confirmed Mycobacterium bovis BCG strain. Splenectomy histopathology: Severe splenic infiltration by acid-fast BCG bacilli confirming disseminated BCG disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID; IL2RG exon 5 p.Arg226His mutation with 75% maternal lymphocyte engraftment) complicated by Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed on BAL), pulmonary/oral Candida albicans infection, and disseminated Mycobacterium bovis BCG infection (confirmed by BAL BCG-specific PCR and splenectomy pathology). Plan and clinical course: Treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for P. jirovecii, a four-drug anti-BCG regimen (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin), antibacterial/antifungal prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement, and therapeutic splenectomy to debulk disseminated BCG load prior to transplant. Four and a half months after starting anti-BCG therapy, he underwent a 10/10 HLA-matched unrelated T-cell-depleted bone marrow transplant (12.5 x 10^6/kg CD34+ cells; reduced-intensity conditioning with treosulfan, fludarabine, and alemtuzumab/Campath) followed by escalating donor lymphocyte infusions at days +31, +61, and +88. Three months post-BMT, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) at the BCG site and thoracoabdominal lymph nodes was successfully managed by adding linezolid and short courses of corticosteroids, and the child remains alive and well with full immune reconstitution.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old Japanese man who had been diagnosed with RA for 8 years according to the 1987 American Rheumatism Association classification criteria for RA was admitted with polyarthritis. He complained of pain and swelling in the wrists, fingers, and knees and had difficulty walking without assistance. He claimed to have morning stiffness lasting about 3 hours. Past medical history included a left total knee arthroplasty complicated by a traumatic fracture of the left distal femur postoperatively and a cerebral infarction with residual right hemiparesis. His medication regimen included sulfasalazine (1000 mg/day), bucillamine (300 mg/day), mizoribine (150 mg/day), and prednisolone (10 mg/day). The Steinbrocker stage was IV and functional class was 4. He was unable to stand unassisted due to bilateral knee pain. Swelling and tenderness were present in the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands and fingers, as well as in the wrists and knees. Right-sided muscle weakness was observed. Laboratory findings were as follows: white blood cell count 8800/mm3 (75.6% neutrophils, 19.5% lymphocytes, 2.9% monocytes, 0.3% eosinophils, 0.2% basophils), hemoglobin 10.7 mg/dL, platelets 48.7 x 104/muL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 75 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 3.58 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor (RF) 219.6 IU/mL, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (ACPA) 189 IU/mL. Serum beta-D-glucan was negative. The purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. 
Treatment was initiated with subcutaneous injections of etanercept 25 mg twice a week. Blood samples were collected before the first dose (at baseline), 24 hours after the first injection (day 1), daily until day 8, and weekly thereafter. Specimens were centrifuged at 3000 rpm and the sera stored at -80 C until the assay was performed. TNF-alpha, TNFR-I and -II, IL-6, and IL-1 beta concentrations were measured using commercial ELISA kits.
After initiating etanercept, the patient's clinical condition improved markedly, with swelling and tenderness of the wrists and finger joints significantly better. He was able to stand with the aid of crutches despite residual hemiparesis. The duration of morning stiffness dropped to below 30 minutes. The 28-joint count Disease Activity Score (DAS28) dropped significantly within the first 4 weeks and continued to decrease (DAS28 = 8.09, 5.37, 4.73, and 4.60, at baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, and 12 weeks, resp.), achieving the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) moderate response criteria. The CRP dropped to below 0.30 mg/mL within the first 2 weeks of therapy. Subsequently, the oral immunosuppressive regimen of sulfasalazine, bucillamine, and mizoribine was discontinued after initiation of treatment. Prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg/day.
After 12 weeks of treatment with etanercept, the patient developed a nonproductive cough along with a fever of 38 C. Serum beta-D-glucan was found to be positive, and sputum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for pneumocystis (Figure 1). Etanercept was discontinued, and an antifungal regimen initiated.
Preceding etanercept therapy, the serum IL-6 levels were found to be elevated, correlating with the high CRP value and high clinical disease activity. Conversely, the serum level of TNF-alpha was nondetectable (<0.2 pg/mL); the sTNFR-I, -II, and IL-1 beta values were not found to be significantly elevated (Figure 2). After initiation of etanercept, there was a rapid decline in the IL-6 and CRP levels, whereas the levels of TNF-alpha and sTNFR-II increased significantly within 24 hours after administration of the first dose to a plateau after 2 weeks (range: 100 pg/mL to 170 pg/mL) and 6-7 weeks (range: 300 ng/mL to 700 ng/mL), respectively. The sTNFR-I and IL-1-beta levels remained relatively unchanged (sTNFR-I levels at baseline, 3.56 ng/mL; 4 weeks, 3.36 ng/mL; 8 weeks, 2.93 ng/mL; 12 weeks, 3.58 ng/mL). At week 12, concurrent to the patient developing clinical symptoms of PCP, the levels of IL-6, CRP, and TNF-alpha showed an acute peak, which tapered downward over the following 3 weeks with the institution of an appropriate antifungal regimen (Figures 3 and 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old Japanese man with an 8-year history of severe rheumatoid arthritis initially presented with disabling polyarthritis and 3-hour morning stiffness, and subsequently developed a nonproductive cough and fever (38 °C) after 12 weeks of etanercept therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted with severe polyarthritis (Steinbrocker stage IV, functional class 4, baseline DAS28 8.09) involving the wrists, fingers, and knees, rendering him unable to stand unassisted. Subcutaneous etanercept (25 mg twice weekly) was initiated, resulting in rapid improvement in joint swelling/tenderness, reduction of morning stiffness to <30 minutes, and decline in DAS28 to 5.37 (week 4), 4.73 (week 8), and 4.60 (week 12), which allowed discontinuation of sulfasalazine, bucillamine, and mizoribine and reduction of prednisolone from 10 mg/day to 5 mg/day. At week 12 of etanercept therapy, he acutely developed a nonproductive cough and fever of 38 °C.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 8 years prior (Steinbrocker stage IV, class 4); left total knee arthroplasty complicated by postoperative traumatic fracture of the left distal femur; cerebral infarction with residual right hemiparesis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Baseline positive for polyarthralgia, joint swelling, and 3-hour morning stiffness; week 12 positive for nonproductive cough and fever (38 °C). Baseline medications included sulfasalazine (1,000 mg/day), bucillamine (300 mg/day), mizoribine (150 mg/day), and prednisolone (10 mg/day, tapered to 5 mg/day after starting etanercept).

objective.physical_examination: Baseline examination: Swelling and tenderness of bilateral PIP, MCP, wrist, and knee joints; inability to stand unassisted; residual right-sided hemiparesis. At week 12 of etanercept therapy: Febrile at 38.0 °C with nonproductive cough.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline pre-etanercept laboratory tests: WBC 8,800/mm3 (75.6% neutrophils, 19.5% lymphocytes, 2.9% monocytes, 0.3% eosinophils, 0.2% basophils), hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, platelets 48.7 x 10^4/μL, ESR 75 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 3.58 mg/dL (dropping to <0.30 mg/dL by week 2 before spiking at week 12), rheumatoid factor (RF) 219.6 IU/mL, anti-CCP antibody (ACPA) 189 IU/mL, and negative tuberculin PPD skin test.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial cytokine profiling (ELISA): Baseline elevated serum IL-6 with undetectable TNF-alpha (<0.2 pg/mL) and unremarkable sTNFR-I (3.56 ng/mL), sTNFR-II, and IL-1beta; following etanercept initiation, IL-6 and CRP fell rapidly while circulating TNF-alpha (100–170 pg/mL) and sTNFR-II (300–700 ng/mL) rose to a plateau, followed at week 12 (coinciding with PCP onset) by an acute surge in serum IL-6, CRP, and TNF-alpha. Fungal biomarker and molecular microbiology at week 12: Serum beta-D-glucan converted from negative at baseline to positive, and sputum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) developing 12 weeks after initiating etanercept therapy for rheumatoid arthritis, confirmed by positive sputum Pneumocystis PCR and seroconversion of serum beta-D-glucan, accompanied by a simultaneous acute spike in serum IL-6, CRP, and TNF-alpha. Plan and clinical course: Etanercept was immediately discontinued and targeted anti-Pneumocystis therapy was instituted, leading to clinical recovery and downward tapering of IL-6, CRP, and TNF-alpha levels over the subsequent 3 weeks.

raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old woman with a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred to the hematology service with bleeding after investigatory colonoscopy for symptomatic anemia. After colonoscopy she developed melena, hematuria, extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage, and a subsequent retroperitoneal hematoma. The severity of her bleeding required more than 30 packed red cell transfusions during her admission, FVIII concentrate, and tranexamic acid. There was no personal or family history of bruising or bleeding, and no underlying malignancy or autoimmune disorders were detected. HIV testing was negative.
The APTT was 79 seconds (reference range 25-37 seconds) with previously normal APTTs. Specific investigations demonstrated a strong FVIII inhibitor (234 BU) and residual FVIII activity of <1% (reference range: 50-150%). Initial management involved high-dose oral prednisone 50 mg daily and cyclophosphamide 100 mg daily. The prednisone was continued for 3 months and weaned to cessation over the fourth month. The cyclophosphamide was continued for 3 months and then ceased. No routine antimicrobial prophylaxis was concurrently given.
Three weeks following treatment initiation there was no improvement in APTT, FVIII inhibitor levels, or FVIII levels. Four cycles of RTX 375 mg/m2 weekly were initiated. Six weeks after commencement of RTX treatment, there was improvement of the APTT, FVIII inhibitor level, and FVIII levels (see Table 1). At 5 months after RTX treatment, the APTT and FVIII levels had normalised.
Two months after RTX treatment commenced and whilst receiving ongoing cyclophosphamide and prednisone, the patient required resuscitation for Pseudomonas aeruginosa septicemia. This was followed within a week by herpes simplex gingivostomatitis and pharyngotonsillitis and diarrhoea secondary to clostridium difficile infection. Pancytopenia developed with a neutrophil nadir of 0.9 x 109/L.
Two weeks later, pneumocystis jiroveci and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis were diagnosed on bronchoscopy washings and brushings. Clinical cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection was confirmed by positive CMV nucleic acid testing of lung biopsy and serum and urine PCR. The prednisone dose was weaned and ceased. Cyclophosphamide was also ceased. Multiple intensive care unit admissions with respiratory support were necessary to manage these complications, and multiple courses of antibiotics and antifungals were required. After a five-month admission requiring significant rehabilitation, the patient was discharged. The factor VIII inhibitor remains in remission.
At presentation to hospital the patient was found to have hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG level of 4.75 mg/dL, normal range 7-16 mg/dL). She received 3 doses of intravenous immunoglobulin 4 weeks apart. Interestingly, she was hypogammaglobulinemic prior to RTX and remains hypogammaglobulinemic 3 years after this episode. The cause of this is unknown; her IgA, IgG, and IgM are all below the reference range.
The patient was taking metformin 1 gram twice daily and gliclazide 160 mg twice daily at the time of admission. Her blood sugar level (BSL) control was poor prior to treatment with prednisone (range 7-20 mmol/L) and deteriorated further with steroids (range 13-24 mmol/L). Despite additional sliding-scale short- and intermediate-acting insulin, her BSL control remained unsatisfactory throughout her admission (range 4-20 mmol/L).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and idiopathic hypogammaglobulinemia treated with prednisone, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab for acquired factor VIII inhibitor developed sequential opportunistic infections culminating in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, and cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with life-threatening post-colonoscopy hemorrhage (melena, hematuria, extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage, and retroperitoneal hematoma requiring >30 packed RBC units, factor VIII concentrate, and tranexamic acid) and was diagnosed with acquired hemophilia A (APTT 79 s, factor VIII activity <1%, factor VIII inhibitor 234 BU) alongside baseline hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 4.75 mg/dL). She was started on oral prednisone (50 mg/day) and oral cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day) without antimicrobial prophylaxis, and at week 3 received four weekly cycles of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2). Two months after starting rituximab (while still taking cyclophosphamide and prednisone), she developed Pseudomonas aeruginosa septicemia, followed 1 week later by herpes simplex gingivostomatitis/pharyngotonsillitis, Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, and neutropenic pancytopenia (neutrophil nadir 0.9 x 10^9/L). Two weeks thereafter, she developed severe opportunistic pulmonary infection requiring multiple ICU admissions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled, baseline blood glucose 7–20 mmol/L); acquired factor VIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A); unexplained chronic panhypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG, IgA, and IgM preceding rituximab). No personal or family history of bleeding disorders, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for melena, hematuria, ecchymoses, and retroperitoneal pain/bleeding; post-immunosuppression course positive for febrile sepsis, painful oral/pharyngeal ulcers, diarrhea, and severe respiratory failure. Home medications at initial admission were metformin 1 g BID and gliclazide 160 mg BID.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation notable for extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage and retroperitoneal hematoma; subsequent immunosuppressive course marked by ulcerative herpes simplex gingivostomatitis/pharyngotonsillitis and respiratory failure requiring ICU ventilatory support.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline coagulation and immunology: Prolonged APTT 79 s (reference: 25–37 s), residual factor VIII activity <1% (reference: 50%–150%), factor VIII inhibitor titer 234 Bethesda units (normalizing 5 months post-rituximab); HIV negative; baseline hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG 4.75 mg/dL (normal: 7–16 mg/dL) and reduced IgA and IgM. Subsequent infectious and hematologic labs: Pancytopenia with neutrophil nadir 0.9 x 10^9/L; blood cultures positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa; stool positive for Clostridioides difficile; steroid-exacerbated hyperglycemia (13–24 mmol/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings, brushings, and lung biopsy (2.5 months post-rituximab): Bronchial washings and brushings diagnosed concomitant Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; lung biopsy, serum, and urine nucleic acid amplification (PCR) tests confirmed active cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis/infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Polymicrobial opportunistic pulmonary triad of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis (confirmed by bronchoscopic washings/brushings and lung biopsy/serum/urine CMV PCR), preceded by Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, HSV gingivostomatitis, and C. difficile colitis, complicating combined prednisone, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab therapy (without PJP prophylaxis) for acquired factor VIII inhibitor in a patient with baseline hypogammaglobulinemia. Plan and clinical course: Cyclophosphamide was stopped and prednisone was weaned and discontinued. She required multiple ICU admissions for respiratory support, prolonged antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral regimens, sliding-scale insulin, and three doses of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, 4 weeks apart). After a 5-month hospitalization and intensive rehabilitation, she was discharged home with her factor VIII inhibitor in sustained remission and persistent baseline panhypogammaglobulinemia at 3-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
The patient, a 68-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital because of "cough and sputum with breathlessness for 3 months". The patient presented with cough and sputum 3 months ago. Specifically, the patient had a paroxysmal cough with white mucous sputum, accompanied by chest distress, shortness of breath, and numbness of both lower limbs. He had a previous history of smoking for 50 years (20 cigarettes/day) but had quit smoking for 5 months. The rest of his past medical history was negative.
Physical examination: general condition was acceptable, superficial lymph nodes were not palpably enlarged, and the breath sounds of both lungs were rough without rhonchus and moist rales. No abnormalities were found on cardiac or abdominal examination.
The examinations undertaken are listed in Table 1. All images were taken by contrast-enhanced CT.
1. Chest CT plain scan and enhanced scan: (Figures 1A, B, 05 March 2022): a mixed-density mass measuring approximately 12.6 x 7.6 cm was found on the left upper lobe of the lung, with truncated bronchi in the upper lobe of the left lung, localized thinning of the left pulmonary artery, and multiple small patchy and nodular high-density shadows in the surrounding lung; multiple small nodules and small patchy high-density shadows were found in the lower lobe of the left lung.
2. Cranial MRI plain scan and enhanced scan (06 March 2022): abnormal lesion signal shadow was found in the anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle, which was presumed to be a cavernous hemangioma.
3. Tracheoscopy (09 March 2022): cauliflower-like neoplasm was found to block the orifice in the upper lobe of the left lung, and the opening of the lower lobe was slightly compressed and narrowed; no abnormalities were found in the bronchial tubes of the bilateral lobes.
4. Tumor markers (03 March 2022): carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 6mg/ml, CA125 was 88.18U/ml, section 19 of cytokeratin was 12.91ng/ml, and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) was 33.72ng/ml.
There were no abnormalities in the routine blood test, whole-body bone imaging, biochemistry analysis, blood clotting, echocardiography, and electrocardiogram.
Pathological findings: the moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma was revealed (through bronchoscopy biopsy of left upper lobe lung). Immunohistochemical findings: CK5/6 (+), CK7 (-), Ki-67 (+, 50%-60%), NapsinA (-), P40 (+), TTF-1 (-), and P63 (+). No abnormalities were found in etiological examinations for bacteria, fungus, M. tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii, Actinomyces, nocardiosis, and cytomegalovirus.
Final diagnosis: there was a malignant tumor (squamous cell carcinoma, cT4N3M0 IIIC) with obstructive pneumonia in the upper lobe of the left lung. Since the patient had no surgical indications, he was suggested for chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy and PD-L1 testing. Genetic testing showed negative results for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and PD-L1 expression.
Treatment:
Treatment course: a brief description of the treatment course is shown in Figure 2. After excluding contraindications, the first cycle of DP chemotherapy (docetaxel 120mg d1 + cisplatin 40mg d1-d3) was administered on 15 March 2022. Here, the chemotherapy went smoothly and the patient did not have any complaints. Then, the second cycle of chemotherapy was administered on 05 April 2022 with the same regimen as the first cycle. During chemotherapy, the patient had a severe gastrointestinal reaction and bone marrow suppression, with white blood cells falling to 1.3 x 109/L and neutrophils dropping to 0.23 x 109/L. Also, the patient was given symptomatic treatment such as leuke-raising injections but refused to accept another cycle of chemotherapy. After excluding contraindications, he was treated with 200 mg of camrelizumab for immunotherapy on 25 April 2022. On 21 May 2022, the patient began to cough up blood in phlegm with a volume of about 20 ml and he was reviewed using a chest CT on 22 May 2022 (Figures 3A, B), which showed that the lung cancer in the upper lobe of the left lung was less extensive than before, while multiple small nodules and small patchy high-density shadows in both lungs were more extensive than before, which could not exclude pneumonia or infection associated with ICIs. The patient was diagnosed with a tracheoscopy and a 13-item nucleic acid test for respiratory pathogens in the lavage fluid, which was positive for MTB. Moreover, the acid-fast bacillus stain test was positive. Therefore, the patient was considered to have active TB. Multidisciplinary oncology consultation suggested that the patient should stop immunotherapy and be treated with a four-drug anti-TB regimen of isoniazide, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. After 3 months of anti-TB treatment, the patient was reviewed using an enhanced CT scan on 19 August 2022, which showed that the primary focus of cancer in the right lung was stable and the nodular and small patchy high-density shadows in both lungs were less extensive than before (Figures 4A, B). Finally, the lung was stable, and no further ICIs were administered.The patient is currently in a relatively stable condition and is being followed up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of paroxysmal cough, white mucous sputum, and breathlessness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed paroxysmal cough productive of white mucous sputum 3 months prior to admission, accompanied by chest distress, shortness of breath, and numbness of both lower limbs.
subjective.past_medical_history: 50-year history of smoking (20 cigarettes/day), having quit 5 months prior to presentation. Remainder of past medical history was negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for paroxysmal cough, white mucous sputum, chest distress, shortness of breath, and bilateral lower limb numbness.

objective.physical_examination: General condition acceptable; superficial lymph nodes not palpably enlarged; bilateral lung breath sounds rough without rhonchi or moist rales; cardiac and abdominal examinations unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests, biochemistry analysis, blood coagulation profile, electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiography, and whole-body bone imaging showed no abnormalities. Tumor markers (03 March 2022): Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) 6 mg/mL, CA125 88.18 U/mL, cytokeratin fragment 19 (CYFRA 21-1) 12.91 ng/mL, and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) 33.72 ng/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced chest CT (05 March 2022): Mixed-density mass measuring approximately 12.6 x 7.6 cm in the left upper lobe with truncated left upper lobe bronchi, localized thinning of the left pulmonary artery, multiple surrounding small patchy and nodular high-density shadows, and multiple small nodules and patchy high-density shadows in the left lower lobe. Cranial MRI plain and enhanced scan (06 March 2022): Abnormal lesion signal shadow in the anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle, presumed cavernous hemangioma. Tracheoscopy (09 March 2022): Cauliflower-like neoplasm obstructing the left upper lobe bronchial orifice with slight compression and narrowing of the left lower lobe opening. Left upper lobe bronchoscopic biopsy pathology and immunohistochemistry: Moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma; CK5/6 (+), CK7 (-), Ki-67 (+, 50%–60%), NapsinA (-), P40 (+), TTF-1 (-), P63 (+); negative for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and PD-L1 expression. Baseline etiological workup was negative for bacteria, fungi, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii, Actinomyces, Nocardia, and cytomegalovirus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Initial diagnosis: Left upper lobe moderately differentiated lung squamous cell carcinoma (cT4N3M0, stage IIIC) with obstructive pneumonia (negative for Pneumocystis carinii and other baseline pathogens) and presumed left lateral ventricular cavernous hemangioma. Plan and clinical course: Treated with two cycles of DP chemotherapy (docetaxel 120 mg day 1 + cisplatin 40 mg days 1–3 on 15 March 2022 and 05 April 2022); the second cycle was complicated by severe gastrointestinal toxicity and grade 4 myelosuppression (WBC 1.3 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.23 x 10^9/L) treated with leukocyte-raising injections. After declining further chemotherapy, he received camrelizumab immunotherapy (200 mg on 25 April 2022). On 21 May 2022, he developed hemoptysis (~20 mL blood in phlegm); repeat chest CT (22 May 2022) showed shrinkage of the primary left upper lobe tumor but more extensive bilateral small nodules and patchy high-density shadows. Repeat tracheoscopy with a 13-item respiratory pathogen nucleic acid panel on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and acid-fast bacillus (AFB) staining confirmed active Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) infection rather than ICI-related pneumonitis or opportunistic fungal infection. Camrelizumab was discontinued and four-drug anti-TB therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) was administered for 3 months, resulting in regression of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and stable tumor status on follow-up CT (19 August 2022).

raw_case_text: A 52-year-old male was diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer, with multiple metastases to the lungs, liver, and peritoneum. Histology revealed well-to-moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, in which the KRAS and NRAS mutation tests were negative and microsatellite instability was stable, but the BRAF V600E mutation was positive. In his medical history, he had received an allogeneic BMT from his elder sister for severe aplastic anemia 33 years ago. As preparative therapy prior to BMT, the patient received total lymph node irradiation (7.5 Gy) and cyclosporine at 50 mg/kg for four days. Only the bilateral lung apices were involved in the irradiated field, but no pulmonary changes suggestive of radiation pneumonitis were noted thereafter. He experienced a grade 1 skin rash as an acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) symptom after BMT, which disappeared clinically without treatment; however, a skin biopsy performed several months later showed pathological findings suspicious of chronic GVHD. During follow-up, there was no worsening of GVHD at the skin or other sites, including interstitial pneumonia, and the patient received no immunosuppressive agents at the time of diagnosis of colon cancer. He had no history of smoking or known allergies. The patient had received two doses of COVID-19 vaccine manufactured by Moderna 9 and 10 months prior to the diagnosis of colorectal cancer and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for COVID-19 was negative multiple times during the DILD treatment. The vaccination history other than COVID-19 was unknown. He had type 2 diabetes and used long-acting insulin. Because the sigmoid colon tumor invaded the left ureter and lower gastrointestinal endoscope could not pass through the primary site, the patient underwent transverse colostomy for colon obstruction due to the tumor. Before receiving chemotherapy, the patient experienced a severe cough due to lung metastasis but had no respiratory distress, with a pulse oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 95% in room air. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed multiple pulmonary nodules, but no abnormal findings suggesting accumulative lung damage such as fibrosis ( Figure 1 ). All screening tests including blood cultures for bacterial infections and serological examinations for viral infections were negative. One month after surgery, 1st-line chemotherapy with FOLFIRI (5-fluorouracil [FU] bolus 400 mg/m2 + leucovorin 400 mg/m2 + irinotecan 150 mg/m2 followed by 5-FU 2400 mg/m2 in a 46-hour infusion) + bevacizumab (5 mg/kg) with palonosetron hydrochloride and dexamethasone as prophylactic anti-emetic therapy was started. He developed a fever without myelosuppression on day 6; however, the bacterial culture was negative, and there was no new lung infiltration on chest radiography. Naproxen (600 mg/day) was administered for the noninfectious fever, which quickly resolved. He was discharged from the hospital in a good general condition and received a second course of chemotherapy at our outpatient clinic with no severe adverse events. On day 15 of the second course of chemotherapy, the patient had no dyspnea. However, because his SpO2 was 92% in room air, the patient was admitted for oxygen demand. A CT scan showed no apparent tumor growth, but there were slight bilateral ground-glass shadows ( Figure 2 ). A bronchoscopy was performed on the same day. There were no abnormalities in the endotracheal lumen such as apparent redness, edema, or neoplastic lesions; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed in the middle lobe, and a biopsy of the peripheral lung was performed in the lower lobe of the right lung. The pathology showed that there was only fibrosis around the tumor as a tumor environment, and there was no obvious fibrosis in the background lungs consistent with the CT findings ( Supplementary Figure 1 ). Bacterial and fungal cultures and PCR tests for pneumocystis jirovecii DNA and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA of the BAL fluid were negative. Pathology of the lung biopsy showed pulmonary metastasis of the colon cancer and no apparent findings of inflammation. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and KL-6 levels were within the normal ranges, and the betaD-glucan test was negative. The white blood cell count was 2,740/muL, neutrophil count 1,140/muL, and lymphocyte count 880/muL. The interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative. Differential diagnoses were interstitial pneumonitis or atypical pneumonia. The clinical course after onset of DILD is summarized in the  Supplementary Figure 2 . There were no apparent clinical manifestations of chronic GVHD around the time of DILD. As his respiratory status was stable, the antimicrobial agent levofloxacin was initiated. Four days after admission, the patient's respiratory status was stable. However, at night on day 5, the cough and dyspnea worsened and the oxygen demand increased. CT examination revealed expanded bilateral interstitial infiltrations ( Figure 3 ). The white blood cell count was 6,260/muL, neutrophil count 5,440/muL, and lymphocyte count 720/muL, and the KL-6 level was mildly elevated (531 U/ml). On day 6, methylprednisolone (1 g/day) and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q6hr) were administered. Thereafter, the patient's respiratory condition improved rapidly, and the shadows in the bilateral lung fields disappeared on day 21 after starting steroid therapy ( Figure 4 ). The steroid dose was gradually decreased and steroid administration was switched to oral prednisolone 30 mg/day after day 22. The prednisolone dose was reduced to 20 mg/day on day 33 after starting steroid treatment, and the patient was scheduled to be discharged. Immediately before discharge on day 39, the patient complained of abdominal pain. Abdominal CT revealed a retroperitoneal hematoma and pseudoaneurysm in the anterior superior pancreatic duodenal artery. Because bleeding from the metastasis near the pancreatic head was suspected, the patient was transferred to a tertiary hospital, where intra-arterial embolization was performed. During the intervention, oral prednisolone was maintained at the same dose, and the patient returned to our hospital immediately after the intervention. On day 43, the lung infiltration reappeared. On day 44, steroid pulse therapy with methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q6hr) was resumed. The methylprednisolone dose was tapered to 125 mg/day on day 47. On day 49, nasal high-flow therapy was initiated because oxygen demand increased. On the same day, intravenous cyclosporine (150 mg/day) was started after consultation with a hematologist, and methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) was retried. On day 51, laboratory tests reported the levels of aspartate aminotransferase (32 U/L), alanine transaminase (53 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (351 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (236 U/L), and total bilirubin (3.0 mg/dL). Considering the possibility of exacerbation of sepsis, an antifungal agent, micafungin (100 mg/day), was administered to treat all infectious diseases. On day 53, because serum CMV antigenemia tested on day 51 was positive (Cytomegalovirus antigen positive cell count was 200-206 positive cells per two slides, CMV IgG was > 250 AU/mL, CMV IgM INDEX was 1.04, absolute lymphocyte count was 280/muL), ganciclovir (500 mg/day) was added in combination with other antibiotics. The measurements of the same blood sample showed that the white blood cell count was 22,740/muL, neutrophil count 22,060/muL, lymphocyte count 280/muL, LDH 654 U/L, creatinine kinase 22 U/L, CRP 3.89 mg/dL, and betaD-glucan test was negative. Unfortunately, the patient eventually died of respiratory and hepatic failure 56 days after starting the steroid therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male with metastatic BRAF V600E-mutant colorectal cancer presented on day 15 of his second cycle of FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab chemotherapy with asymptomatic hypoxemia (SpO2 92% on room air) following an earlier baseline severe cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed with advanced well-to-moderately differentiated colorectal adenocarcinoma (KRAS/NRAS wild-type, microsatellite stable, BRAF V600E-positive) metastatic to the lungs, liver, and peritoneum. Due to sigmoid colon tumor invasion of the left ureter and colonic obstruction impassable by lower endoscopy, he underwent a transverse colostomy. Prior to chemotherapy, he had a severe cough attributed to lung metastases without respiratory distress (SpO2 95% on room air). One month postoperatively, he began first-line FOLFIRI (5-FU bolus 400 mg/m2, leucovorin 400 mg/m2, irinotecan 150 mg/m2, and 46-hour continuous 5-FU 2,400 mg/m2) plus bevacizumab (5 mg/kg) with prophylactic palonosetron and dexamethasone. On day 6 of cycle 1, he had a noninfectious fever without myelosuppression or new radiographic infiltrates that resolved rapidly with naproxen (600 mg/day). He received cycle 2 as an outpatient without immediate adverse events, but on day 15 of cycle 2 he presented with an SpO2 of 92% on room air without subjective dyspnea, prompting hospital admission for supplemental oxygen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Metastatic sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma (BRAF V600E-mutant) status post transverse colostomy; severe aplastic anemia treated 33 years earlier with an allogeneic bone marrow transplant (BMT) from his elder sister (conditioned with 7.5 Gy total lymph node irradiation involving only the bilateral lung apices and cyclosporine 50 mg/kg for 4 days), complicated by self-resolving grade 1 acute skin GVHD and skin biopsy findings suspicious for chronic GVHD (inactive without immunosuppression at cancer diagnosis); type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with long-acting insulin; received two doses of Moderna COVID-19 vaccine 9 and 10 months prior to colorectal cancer diagnosis. Never-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for baseline severe cough prior to chemotherapy; denied subjective dyspnea on admission at day 15 of cycle 2 (subsequently developed worsening cough and dyspnea on hospital day 5, and abdominal pain on day 39). No known drug allergies. Home medications included long-acting insulin.

objective.physical_examination: Pre-chemotherapy baseline: SpO2 95% on room air, no respiratory distress. Admission (day 15 of cycle 2): SpO2 92% on room air without dyspnea; no clinical manifestations of chronic GVHD.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-chemotherapy screening: Blood cultures and viral serologies negative. Admission (day 15 of cycle 2) laboratory tests: WBC 2,740/μL, neutrophil count 1,140/μL, lymphocyte count 880/μL; serum LDH and KL-6 within normal ranges; interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for tuberculosis negative; multiple SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests negative. Day 5 lab tests (upon respiratory worsening): WBC 6,260/μL, neutrophils 5,440/μL, lymphocytes 720/μL, KL-6 mildly elevated at 531 U/mL. Day 51–53 lab tests: AST 32 U/L, ALT 53 U/L, ALP 351 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, WBC 22,740/μL, neutrophils 22,060/μL, absolute lymphocyte count 280/μL, LDH 654 U/L, creatine kinase 22 U/L, CRP 3.89 mg/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Pre-chemotherapy chest CT: Multiple pulmonary nodules without background pulmonary fibrosis. Admission chest CT (day 15 of cycle 2): No apparent tumor growth, but slight bilateral ground-glass shadows. Admission bronchoscopy with middle lobe BAL and right lower lobe transbronchial lung biopsy: Normal endotracheal lumen; BAL fluid bacterial/fungal cultures, Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA PCR, and CMV DNA PCR were all negative; serum beta-D-glucan negative; lung biopsy pathology showed pulmonary metastasis of colon cancer with peritumoral fibrosis only and no background lung fibrosis or inflammation.
