subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening fevers, productive cough, and increased work of breathing; negative for cyanosis, clubbing, or peripheral edema.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: Temperature 37.9 °C, heart rate 156 beats/min, respiratory rate 50 breaths/min, blood pressure 115/61 mmHg, and SpO2 83% on room air (improving to 98% on 1 L/min nasal cannula oxygen). General and systemic exam: Mild respiratory distress with increased work of breathing; moderate frontal bossing with an open anterior fontanelle; grade II/IV systolic ejection murmur; diffuse bilateral rales without wheezing on lung auscultation; non-distended abdomen with hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpated 4 cm below the costal margin and spleen palpable to the level of the umbilicus); no clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema. Ophthalmologic exam (day 7): No signs of CMV retinitis.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission chest radiograph: Diffuse ground-glass alveolar infiltrates that were chronic when compared against a chest X-ray from 1 year earlier (minimal interval improvement on follow-up CXR 2 weeks post-discharge). Transthoracic echocardiogram (day 3): Patent foramen ovale without cardiomyopathy. Abdominal ultrasound (day 3): Confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. Routine blood, urine, and respiratory cultures: Negative. Virological serology and PCR (day 7): Serum CMV IgG and IgM antibodies positive by immunoassay; peripheral blood CMV DNA PCR negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL, day 4): Anatomically normal airways; cloudy BAL fluid with cell differential showing 68% macrophages, 12% PMNs, and 10% lymphocytes, and a lipid-laden macrophage (LLM) index of 120; negative for malignant cells; Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii; Ziehl-Neelsen stain negative for acid-fast bacilli; BAL bacterial, fungal, AFB, RSV, and influenza cultures negative; Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain was strongly positive for abundant intracellular and extracellular amorphous proteinaceous material diagnostic of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP); BAL indirect fluorescent antibody testing (returned day 7) was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV). Parents declined chest CT.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP; confirmed by abundant PAS-positive amorphous material within pulmonary macrophages and extracellular aggregates on BAL fluid, and re-confirmed on repeat BAL during a subsequent out-of-state admission) with concurrent cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis (confirmed by BAL indirect fluorescent antibody and positive serum CMV IgM/IgG) in a 23-month-old girl with congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II; Pneumocystis jirovecii was excluded by negative BAL GMS staining. Plan and clinical course: Empiric oral azithromycin and parenteral ceftriaxone were discontinued on hospital day 5 as work of breathing improved. Following day 7 BAL CMV confirmation, she completed a 2-week course of parenteral ganciclovir, weaned to room air on day 9, and was discharged; several months later, she was hospitalized in another state with acute respiratory failure requiring intubation, where repeat BAL re-confirmed PAP.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old Greek male patient was presented to the outpatient clinic of the Pulmonary Medicine Department of our hospital due to relapsing episodes of fever spikes (up to 38.7 C) accompanied by general fatigue and discomfort. He was initially treated with a course of oral antibiotics (b lactam plus macrolide) with poor clinical response. He was then transferred to our department for further evaluation. He reported a hospitalization 2 years ago due to fever of unknown origin, which subsided after a short course of high doses of corticosteroids. Nonetheless, he failed to recall any further details regarding the etiology of his hospitalization. He was a current light smoker (5 pack-years) and reported no exposure to illicit drugs, environmental, and occupational allergens or toxic fumes, chemicals, and dust. On physical examination, he was febrile with general fatigue and discomfort; however, he reported no dyspnea, tachypnea (respiratory rate 12 breaths/min), or palpitations (heart rate within normal range-70 bpm). He had no hypoxaemia (partial pressure ofoxygen 84 mm Hg) on arterial blood gas analysis. He had no clubbing, skin lesions, cervical lymphadenopathy, or joint swelling. Auscultation of the lungs mild end-inspiratory crackles in both lower lung zones. Cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological system examinations were unremarkable.
Laboratory tests were performed and divulged microcytic iron deficiency anaemia (Hct: 35.9%, Hgb: 11.9 g/dL, MCV: 69.7, Fe: 19 mg/dL). Ferritin, B12, and folic acid levels were within normal range. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm h-1. The rest of the physical examination and routine laboratory tests, including white blood cell count and differential, red blood cell count, liver and renal function, and serum C-reactive protein, were normal. Gross and microscopic urinary analysis revealed neither hematuria nor renal red blood cell casts, while his 24-hour urine protein levels were within normal range (60 mg/dl). His chest X-ray showed alveolar infiltrates in both lower lobes. Patient was then commenced on intravenous course of broad spectrum of antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam plus moxifloxacin) coupled with oseltamivir 75 mgr twice daily, which was discontinued three days after the sputum smear was negative for H1N1.
Laboratory tests for collagen vascular disease and vasculitis, including antinuclear (ANA), antiextractable nuclear antigens (ENA), antineutrophil cytoplasm (ANCA), and antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies, were also negative. The tuberculin skin test was negative. His HIV test was also negative, while his hepatitis B and C antibody titers were within normal range. The patient had a positive Mayer stool test for erythrocytes raising a suspicion for inflammatory bowel disease, but his further gastrointestinal workup (gastroscopy and colonoscopy) excluded any source of bleeding. In particular, gastroduodenal biopsies were performed and findings were inconsistent with both inflammatory bowel disease and malignancy as well as celiac disease. Regarding the latter specific antibodies against transglutaminase (ATA), both IgA and IgG isoforms were also negative. 
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) were performed and showed normal FVC (91%), FEV1 (92%), and FEV1/FVC ratio (84.1%) and a strikingly elevated DLCO (120% of the predicted normal value) indicative of alveolar hemorrhage. 
Patient was then subjected to high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showing diffuse bibasilar ground-glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage (Figure 1). Diagnosis of DAH was confirmed by BAL demonstrating increased numbers of hemosiderin-laden macrophages (>40% of total number of macrophages). BAL fluid specimens were negative for routine bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, and viral as well as Pneumocystis stains and cultures. Due to the patient's continuously worsening clinical condition (onset of dyspnoea, ESR and CRP increase to 187 mm/h and 15.91 mg/L, constant decrease of haemoglobin levels), a VATS biopsy from the right middle lobe was employed to address the cause of the alveolar haemorrhage. Extensive pathologic evaluation of the lung specimen divulged hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages and absence of any specific pathology such as granulomas or evidence of vasculitis/capillaritis. Immunofluorescence microscopy of frozen tissue samples, using a panel of antibodies against complement and immunoglobulins was without notice of immune complexes that would drive a diagnosis towards a specific cause. Taking into consideration the above data, we came up with the diagnosis of IPH.
Treatment with high doses of oral prednisone (0.75 mg/kg of weight) as a monotherapy was adopted for 6 weeks and gradually tapered to 0.5 mg/kr for another 6 weeks and 20 mgr for another 6 weeks leading to a profound improvement of symptoms (dyspnoea) as well as imaging and laboratory findings including complete resolution of bilateral areas of ground-glass opacities (Figure 3(b)) as well as a significant incline of his haemoglobin levels and decrease of his CRP and ESR titers, respectively. The patient is now followed for almost 3 months, on an outpatient basis, in good clinical condition, free of disease relapses, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable on 10 mgr/day of oral corticosteroids. Due to high incidence of relapses, the patient is under close monitoring.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old Greek male presented with relapsing episodes of fever spikes up to 38.7 °C, generalized fatigue, and malaise refractory to outpatient oral beta-lactam and macrolide antibiotics.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the outpatient pulmonary clinic with relapsing high-grade fevers (up to 38.7 °C), general fatigue, and discomfort that failed to respond to an outpatient course of oral beta-lactam and macrolide antibiotics, prompting inpatient admission for evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hospitalization 2 years earlier for fever of unknown origin that resolved after a short course of high-dose corticosteroids (specific etiology unknown to patient); current light smoker (5 pack-years) with no occupational, environmental, toxic fume, or illicit drug exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for relapsing fever spikes (up to 38.7 °C), general fatigue, and malaise on admission; initially negative for dyspnea, tachypnea, or palpitations (subsequently developed progressive dyspnea in the hospital).

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile with generalized fatigue, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, heart rate 70 beats/min; no digital clubbing, skin lesions, cervical lymphadenopathy, or joint swelling; mild end-inspiratory crackles in both lower lung zones on chest auscultation; cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological exams unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission arterial blood gas: Normoxemic with PaO2 84 mmHg. Hematology and biochemistry: Microcytic iron-deficiency anemia with hematocrit 35.9%, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL (which progressively declined during hospitalization), MCV 69.7 fL, and serum iron 19 μg/dL; normal ferritin, vitamin B12, folate, WBC count/differential, platelets, and hepatic/renal function; elevated ESR at 65 mm/h (later surging to 187 mm/h) and normal baseline CRP (later rising to 15.91 mg/L). Urinalysis: No hematuria or RBC casts; normal 24-hour urine protein (60 mg/dL). Autoimmune, infectious, and GI workup: Negative ANA, ENA, ANCA, anti-GBM, anti-tissue transglutaminase (IgA/IgG), tuberculin skin test, HIV, HBV/HCV, and sputum H1N1 smear; positive Mayer stool occult blood test, with normal upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and gastroduodenal biopsies (excluding IBD, celiac disease, and malignancy). Admission chest X-ray: Bilateral lower lobe alveolar infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Normal spirometry (FVC 91%, FEV1 92%, FEV1/FVC 84.1%) with a markedly elevated diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO 120% predicted) indicative of alveolar hemorrhage. High-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Diffuse bibasilar ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Abundant hemosiderin-laden macrophages (>40% of total alveolar macrophages) confirming diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH); negative BAL bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, viral, and Pneumocystis stains and cultures. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) right middle lobe lung biopsy: Intra-alveolar hemosiderin-laden macrophages without granulomas, necrotizing vasculitis, capillaritis, or immune complex/complement deposition on frozen-tissue immunofluorescence.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis (IPH) presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) and microcytic iron-deficiency anemia, definitively confirmed by elevated DLCO (120% predicted), >40% hemosiderin-laden macrophages on BAL, and pauci-immune alveolar hemorrhage without capillaritis/vasculitis on VATS right middle lobe biopsy after excluding autoimmune vasculitides, celiac disease, and Pneumocystis or other infections. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric IV piperacillin/tazobactam, moxifloxacin, and oseltamivir (75 mg BID for 3 days) were ineffective. Following VATS confirmation of IPH, high-dose oral prednisone monotherapy (0.75 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, tapered to 0.5 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, then 20 mg/day for 6 weeks) produced complete resolution of dyspnea and bilateral ground-glass opacities on HRCT along with normalization of hemoglobin, ESR, and CRP; at 3-month outpatient follow-up, he remained in clinical remission on prednisone 10 mg/day.

raw_case_text: A 67 years old male, a non-smoker, with history of ischaemic heart disease, status post:coronary artery bypass graft, and bronchiectasis was diagnosed to have angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AIBTCL), stage III B at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre (KFSH&RC) in Riyadh in late December 2004. He presented with: fever, skin rash, generalized external lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. The blood counts, blood film and bone marrow biopsy were all normal. The renal and hepatic profiles as well as the immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits. Serological tests for CMV, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), hepatitis C virus and HIV were negative. Computed tomography (CT) scans of chest, abdomen and pelvis showed numerous small lymph nodes in mediastinal, mesenteric and retroperitoneal areas in addition to splenomegaly with focal splenic lesions. Skin biopsy showed atypical lymphohistiocytic changes. A right axillary lymph node biopsy revealed diffuse infiltration with: immunoblasts, lymphocytes, polymorphs, plasma cells, histiocytes and eosinophils with considerable proliferation of small blood vessels. The immunohistochemical stains showed positive: CD1A, CD3, CD4, CD7, CD8, CD15, CD20, CD21, CD30, CD45, CD68 and S100. The gene rearrangement studies revealed a monoclonal T-cell population. The AIBTCL was treated with: prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil and subcutaneous alemtuzumab: 30 mg/month for 4 months. Thereafter the patient developed: CMV infection treated with IV ganciclovir and pulmonary embolism treated with IV heparin then oral warfarin. On 29/10/06, the patient was readmitted with two week history of: fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum and mild dyspnea. He denied any associated chest or abdominal pain, headache or bleeding from any site. Physical examination revealed an unwell elderly male who was in mild respiratory distress. The temperature was 38.7  C, blood pressure (BP): 112/68 mmHg, pulse rate: 92/minute, respiratory rate: 20/minute and oxygen saturation was 93% on room air. There was pallor but no cyanosis, leg oedema, jaundice or external lymphadenopathy. The inspiratory volume was decreased and coarse crackles were heard over mid and lower lung fields bilaterally. There was no abdominal distension, tenderness or palpable organomegaly. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations did not reveal any abnormality. Full blood count (FBC) showed: WBC: 1.83 x 109/L, Hb: 109 g/L and PLT: 315 x 109/L. Differential cell count (DCC) showed neutrophils of 1.1 and lymphocytes of 0.3. Renal and hepatic profiles were all within normal limits. Blood, urine, stool cultures and CMV antigen test were all negative. Chest radiography showed bronchiectatic changes involving both lower lobes and bilateral nodular infiltration consistent with severe pneumonia. The patient was commenced on IV tazobactam-piperacillin: 4.5 grams thrice daily and gentamicin 2 mg/kg IV twice daily in addition to oxygen via mask at 2-4 Liter/minute and IV fluids at rate of 50-80 cc/hour. Initially the patient had partial response then he started to have higher pyrexia and respiratory distress. On 6/11/2006, the patient was experiencing high grade fever and rigors and his BP dropped to 85/45 mmHg. Septic screens were repeated and the IV antibiotics were replaced by IV meropenem 1 gram thrice daily and IV vancomycin 1 gram twice daily. Later on, BP improved and fever started to subside. A repeat CT scan of the chest showed: bronchiectatic cavities involving the lower lobes of both lungs, bilateral nodular infiltration, areas of segmental consolidation and bilateral pleural thickening (Fig. 1). Echocardiogram showed no vegetations, pericardial effusions or valvular defects and brain CT scan showed no evidence of space occupying lesions. Bronchoscopy was performed and BAL fluid showed scattered lipid laden macrophages and gram positive rods identified later on as Nocardia asteroides (N. asteroides). Special stains for fungi were positive and the fungus was identified as Aspergillus niger (A. niger). BAL fluid was negative for acid fast bacilli, pneumocystis carinii, viral cytopathy and malignant cells. Meanwhile, the previously taken sputum cultures grew branching gram positive rods identified as N. asteroides. However, sputum cultures were negative for acid fast bacilli, candida and aspergillus. Aspergillus galactomannan test was positive. Consequently, the following management modifications were made: vancomycin was stopped and meropenem was continued, IV liposomal amphotericin-B (amBisome) 5 mg/kg/day was commenced in addition to oral trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ) 960 mg thrice daily as well as IV amikacin 15 mg/kg/day. Later on, the patient started to improve clinically and radiologically and oxygen requirements decreased gradually. One week later, the patient sustained his hemodynamic stability and his clinical improvement so IV meropenem was discontinued. On 20/11/2006, IV amikacin was stopped and IV amBisome was replaced by oral voriconazole. Two days later; the patient was totally asymptomatic and his physical examination showed few basal crackles with good air entry bilaterally. FBC showed WBC: 2.25 x 109/L with neutrophils of 1.4, Hb: 94 g/L and PLT: 147 x 109/L. Renal and hepatic profiles were normal. He was discharged on: voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily and TMP/SMZ 960 mg orally thrice daily for 6 weeks in addition to warfarin, omeprazole, prophylactic valganciclovir as well as ventolin and atrovent inhalers. Thereafter, the patient had regular follow up at the hematology outpatient clinic and he remained clinically stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old male with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma and bronchiectasis presented on October 29, 2006, with a 2-week history of fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum, and mild dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in late December 2004 with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AIBTCL; monoclonal T-cell population positive for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD21, CD30 on axillary node biopsy) after presenting with fever, rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, the patient had been treated with prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and subcutaneous alemtuzumab (30 mg/month for 4 months), complicated by CMV infection (treated with IV ganciclovir) and pulmonary embolism (treated with IV heparin and oral warfarin). On October 29, 2006, he was readmitted with 2 weeks of fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum, and mild shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (diagnosed December 2004, treated with prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and alemtuzumab); prior CMV infection; prior pulmonary embolism on oral warfarin; ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG); bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis. Lifetime nonsmoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, productive cough with yellowish sputum, and mild dyspnea; negative for chest pain, abdominal pain, headache, or bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs (October 29, 2006): Temperature 38.7 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg (dropping to 85/45 mmHg with high-grade fever and rigors on November 6, 2006), pulse rate 92/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 93% on room air. General and systemic exam: Unwell elderly male in mild respiratory distress with pallor; no cyanosis, leg edema, jaundice, or peripheral lymphadenopathy; decreased inspiratory volume with coarse crackles over the mid and lower lung fields bilaterally; normal abdominal, cardiovascular, and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission complete blood count and chemistry: Leukopenia and lymphopenia with WBC 1.83 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 1.1 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.3 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 109 g/L, platelets 315 x 10^9/L (discharge CBC: WBC 2.25 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.4 x 10^9/L, Hb 94 g/L, PLT 147 x 10^9/L); normal renal and hepatic profiles. Microbiology: Blood, urine, and stool cultures and CMV antigenemia test negative; sputum cultures grew branching Gram-positive rods identified as Nocardia asteroides (negative for AFB, Candida, and Aspergillus). Imaging: Admission chest radiograph showed bilateral lower lobe bronchiectatic changes and bilateral nodular infiltrates; echocardiogram normal; brain CT negative for space-occupying lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (November 2006): Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectatic cavities, bilateral nodular infiltrates, segmental consolidations, and bilateral pleural thickening. Fungal biomarker: Serum Aspergillus galactomannan test positive. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Scattered lipid-laden macrophages; Gram-positive branching rods identified as Nocardia asteroides; fungal stains and culture positive for Aspergillus niger; negative for acid-fast bacilli, Pneumocystis carinii, viral cytopathic effects, and malignant cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe pulmonary co-infection with Nocardia asteroides and invasive Aspergillus niger (confirmed by BAL fluid stains/cultures, sputum cultures, and positive Aspergillus galactomannan, with Pneumocystis carinii ruled out on BAL) in a profoundly lymphopenic patient with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma previously treated with alemtuzumab, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g TID) and gentamicin (2 mg/kg BID) failed, and on November 6, 2006, septic shock (BP 85/45 mmHg) prompted escalation to IV meropenem (1 g TID) and vancomycin (1 g BID). Following BAL identification of N. asteroides and A. niger, vancomycin was stopped and targeted therapy was instituted with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ 960 mg TID), IV amikacin (15 mg/kg/day), IV meropenem, and IV liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome 5 mg/kg/day). He rapidly stabilized, allowing discontinuation of meropenem after 1 week and transition on November 20, 2006, from IV amikacin and AmBisome to oral voriconazole (200 mg BID) plus oral TMP/SMZ (960 mg TID for 6 weeks) alongside warfarin and prophylactic valganciclovir.

raw_case_text:
A 64 year-old-man was evaluated because of a heart stroke. Restrictive cardiomyopathy and interstitial pneumopathy were discovered as incidental findings in the study. He had been asymptomatic before the stroke. The patient suffered from hyperlipidemia. He smoked twenty cigarettes a day and drank alcohol occasionally. His medications included omeprazol and atorvastatin. He had no known allergies to medications. The physical examination only revealed few rales in lungs basal segments through pulmonary auscultation. 
In the complementary studies, we found a light hypoproteinemia, a known hypercholesterolemia, and high levels of ACE (83 UI/L, normal until 55 UI/L). The rest of serum studies were normal including hemogram, renal, hepatic, and thyroid functions, protein immunoglobulins, serum light chains kappa-lambda, beta2 microglobulin, antinuclear antibodies, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Prolonged incubation blood cultures were made just as HIV, HBV, HCV, Brucella and syphilis serology. 
There were elevated levels of immunoglobulin light chains in urine, especially lambda light chain (2.8 mg/dL, being normal until 0.39 mg/dL). Chest X-ray showed a bilateral interstitial infiltrate with Kerley-B lines and some grade of precapillary pulmonary hypertension. This interstitial pattern was confirmed on a thorax high resolution computed tomography that suggested type III sarcoidosis or systemic amyloidosis like most plausible diagnoses. Echocardiography revealed left ventricle hypertrophy with a normal ejection fraction. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a restrictive pattern with diffuse infiltrative cardiomyopathy expressed by huge wall thickness of both ventricles with a predominant subendocardial distribution. 
As a systemic infiltrative disease was suspected, an abdominal subcutaneous flat biopsy was taken, being normal. Then, we decided to take a bronchial biopsy through a bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, which was stained and cultivated to exclude Pneumocystis jirovecii and mycobacterial infections. The pathologic study identified extracellular amyloid deposits by Congo red staining and viewing under polarized light where amyloid deposits produce a distinctive apple-green birefringence (Figure 2). The determination of para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) and AA amyloid in the specimen was negative. So, the diagnosis was systemic AL amyloidosis. 
An ASCT was carried out, previous conditioning with melphalan (140 mg/m2 in two doses one day), that was not effective enough (persistent elevated levels of immunoglobulin light chains in urine). The patient suffered a congestive heart failure (CHF) and a light mucositis as side effects, which were solved with pharmacologic treatment. 
Then, it was followed by treatment with bortezomib and prednisone, without melphalan. The patient has received six cycles of this treatment, obtaining complete response with disappearance of immunoglobulin light chains in urine. During these cycles, the patient has suffered multiple episodes of CHF, right predominantly, which have been treated with furosemide. Actually, the possibility of a heart transplantation is being evaluated, due to infiltrative cardiomyopathy with symptomatic CHF.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old man evaluated for an ischemic stroke was incidentally found to have restrictive cardiomyopathy and bilateral interstitial lung disease.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been cardiorespiratory-asymptomatic prior to presenting with an acute stroke, during the workup of which bilateral interstitial pneumopathy and restrictive infiltrative cardiomyopathy were discovered incidentally.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hyperlipidemia; active smoker (20 cigarettes/day) with occasional alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint prior to stroke evaluation. No known drug allergies. Home medications were omeprazole and atorvastatin.

objective.physical_examination: Chest auscultation revealed a few basilar pulmonary rales; remainder of general physical exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood and urine laboratory tests: Mild hypoproteinemia, known hypercholesterolemia, and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) at 83 IU/L (normal <=55 IU/L); normal CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, serum immunoglobulins, serum free kappa/lambda light chains, beta-2 microglobulin, ANA, and ESR; negative prolonged-incubation blood cultures and negative HIV, HBV, HCV, Brucella, and syphilis serologies. Urine protein studies: Markedly elevated urinary lambda immunoglobulin light chains at 2.8 mg/dL (normal <=0.39 mg/dL). Chest X-ray: Bilateral interstitial infiltrates with Kerley B lines and features of precapillary pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography: Left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Bilateral interstitial pattern suggestive of stage III sarcoidosis or systemic amyloidosis. Cardiac MRI: Restrictive infiltrative cardiomyopathy with severe biventricular wall thickening predominantly in a subendocardial distribution. Abdominal subcutaneous fat pad biopsy: Normal. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial/bronchial biopsy: BAL stains and cultures negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and mycobacterial infections; bronchial biopsy pathology demonstrated extracellular amyloid deposits with characteristic apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining under polarized light (negative for PAS and AA amyloid), confirming primary AL amyloidosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Systemic primary AL (lambda light-chain) amyloidosis presenting with cardiac amyloidosis (restrictive infiltrative cardiomyopathy) and pulmonary interstitial amyloidosis, definitively confirmed by Congo red apple-green birefringence on bronchial biopsy and elevated urinary lambda light chains (2.8 mg/dL), with Pneumocystis jirovecii and mycobacterial infections excluded by BAL stains and cultures. Plan and clinical course: Initial autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) conditioned with melphalan (140 mg/m2) failed to clear urinary lambda light chains and was complicated by congestive heart failure (CHF) and mild mucositis. Subsequent salvage therapy with six cycles of bortezomib plus prednisone achieved a complete hematologic response (complete disappearance of urinary light chains), and the patient was referred for heart transplantation evaluation due to recurrent right-predominant CHF managed with furosemide.

raw_case_text: We report a case of 55-year-old Guyanese female with the history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for 10 years and history of latent tuberculosis. Isoniazid treatment was not completed due to abnormal liver function tests and rifampin was completed at 4 months. Her RA was poorly responsive to methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, and chronic prednisone therapy between 10 and 20 mg daily. She had been tried on leflunomide to control her symptoms but experienced severe hair loss. She was started on adalimumab (Humira), but with no clinical improvement, and also she developed rash 7 years ago. Weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg was started after adalimumab with good disease control for 3 years in the absence of pulmonary or mediastinal abnormality on chest computed tomography; however it was stopped due to insurance issue 3 years ago. She started to develop cough and dyspnea. The blood analysis demonstrated ESR 40 mm/h, CRP 1.35 mg/dL, negative antinuclear antibody, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, white blood cell 10.3 K/mcl, platelet 296 K/mcl, and normal renal and hepatic functions. High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed ground glass opacities on bilateral lower lungs. Echocardiography was normal. Methotrexate was stopped. Her cough and shortness of breath improved. Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesion. The microbiological analysis of bronchial lavage, bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, and pneumocystis smear was negative. Cytologic analysis was negative for malignant, reactive bronchial epithelial, pneumocytes, and lymphocytes cell. Transbronchial biopsy showed focal emphysematous changes, mild interstitial pneumonitis. Due to active RA, prednisone was increased to 10 mg twice daily and weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg was started again. Her RA symptoms including synovitis subsequently improved and prednisone was able to slowly taper down to 5 mg every other day. After taking etanercept for 12 months, follow-up HRCT showed decreasing bilateral ground glass opacities. However mediastinal lymph nodes were increasing in size to 2.3 x 3.1 centimeters (Figure 1). Mediastinoscopy was done and showed enlarged right anterior lymph nodes. Tissue biopsy showed nonnecrotizing epithelioid granulomata (Figures 3 and 4). All infectious studies of lymph node tissues were negative. Etanercept was discontinued. Follow-up chest CT 12 months later showed resolution of mediastinal lymph nodes (Figure 2). The diagnosis of etanercept induced pulmonary sarcoidosis was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old Guyanese female with a 10-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis developed subacute cough and dyspnea while on methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisone, followed 12 months after restarting etanercept by progressive mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) poorly controlled on methotrexate (20 mg weekly), hydroxychloroquine (400 mg daily), and chronic prednisone (10–20 mg daily), with prior intolerance/failure of leflunomide (alopecia) and adalimumab (rash). She had previously achieved 3 years of good RA control on weekly subcutaneous etanercept (50 mg) with a normal chest CT, but stopped etanercept 3 years earlier due to insurance issues. While maintained on methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisone, she developed new cough and dyspnea. Discontinuation of methotrexate improved her respiratory symptoms, and after bronchoscopy ruled out infection, she was restarted on etanercept (50 mg SC weekly) and prednisone (10 mg BID tapered to 5 mg every other day), which controlled her synovitis but led to enlarging mediastinal lymphadenopathy on 12-month follow-up HRCT.
subjective.past_medical_history: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years; latent tuberculosis treated with 4 months of rifampin (isoniazid discontinued early due to hepatotoxicity).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, dyspnea, and active rheumatoid synovitis. History of drug-induced hepatotoxicity from isoniazid, severe hair loss from leflunomide, and skin rash from adalimumab. Home medications prior to workup were methotrexate 20 mg/week, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day, and prednisone 10–20 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Active rheumatoid synovitis prior to resuming etanercept.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests at onset of cough and dyspnea: ESR 40 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 1.35 mg/dL, negative ANA, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, WBC 10.3 K/μL, platelets 296 K/μL, and normal renal and hepatic function. Echocardiography: Normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial high-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Bilateral lower lung ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy: No endobronchial lesions; BAL bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures and Pneumocystis smear all negative; cytology negative for malignancy; transbronchial biopsy showed focal emphysematous changes and mild interstitial pneumonitis. Follow-up HRCT after 12 months of resumed etanercept: Decreasing bilateral ground-glass opacities but enlarging mediastinal lymphadenopathy measuring 2.3 x 3.1 cm. Mediastinoscopy and right anterior mediastinal lymph node biopsy: Non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas with negative infectious stains and cultures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Etanercept-induced pulmonary/mediastinal sarcoidosis (confirmed by non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas on mediastinoscopic right anterior lymph node biopsy with negative infectious studies) preceded by mild methotrexate-related interstitial pneumonitis (with Pneumocystis jirovecii, fungal, and mycobacterial infections excluded by negative BAL smears and cultures). Plan and clinical course: Initial cough and dyspnea resolved upon stopping methotrexate. When enlarging granulomatous mediastinal lymphadenopathy developed 12 months after restarting etanercept (50 mg weekly), etanercept was permanently discontinued, resulting in complete resolution of mediastinal lymphadenopathy on follow-up chest CT 12 months later.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old Hispanic male presented to our care with a sore throat and odynophagia to liquid and solids for 3 days. He denied any fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or shortness of breath. He claimed that he had frequent respiratory and gastrointestinal infections when he was a child. On a previous hospital admission 2 years ago, he was discovered to have a lung abscesses (Staphylococcus aureus) and oral candidiasis. The computed tomography (CT) of the chest on the previous admission revealed a large consolidation involving the right lung and posterior segment of the left lower lobe with an air fluid level. These bilateral lung abscesses were drained and he was treated for aspiration pneumonia with clindamycin 300 mg PO four times a day for one month upon discharge. The CT of the chest (Figure 1) after drainage of the abscess revealed residual 6 cm thin walled cyst in the posterior aspect of the of left midlung field. Other past medical problems included recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections. He had no family history of any immunodeficiency disorders. He admitted to smoking 1 pack of cigarettes per week for the last 9 years and social alcohol use. He denied any illicit drugs use.
Initial vital signs were significant for hypertension (blood pressure: 147/85), tachycardia (heart rate: 116), and tachypnea (respiratory rate: 25 breaths per minute). Physical examination revealed a cachectic individual with multiple eczematous lesions and folliculitis over his entire body. He had white lesions resembling thrush on his tongue, palate, and oropharynx. It was noted that he had retention of his primary teeth. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally on auscultation. He was tachycardic but without murmurs. He had a decreased muscle mass of all four extremities. The initial lab work-up (Table 1) was only significant for acute renal insufficiency (BUN 25 mg/dL and creatinine 2.2. mg/dL), hypocalcemia (calcium 7.9 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.8 g/dL), and hypoproteinemia (7.9 mmol/L). The chest radiograph (Figure 2) on admission revealed a left lung cyst.
Our initial impression was oral/esophageal candidiasis and the possibility of an immunodeficiency disorder. For the treatment of oral/esophageal candidiasis, he was started on fluconazole 100 mg IV daily. The HIV test was negative. Other lab work-ups (Table 2) was ordered to rule out various immunodeficiency disorders. All the immunoglobulins (Ig) were within normal range except that IgE was very elevated (>5000 IU/mL). The normal value of IgE was <114 IU/mL. Genetic mutation analysis revealed a novel mutation affecting the transactivation domain of the STAT3 gene at exon 22. This provided a definite diagnosis of autosomal dominant hyper IgE syndrome which correlates with the clinical presentation. These results confirmed our suspicion of hyper IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). No curative treatment is available for hyper IgE syndrome. We treated his multiple skin infections with mupirocin 2% ointment and started prophylactic treatment of recurrent skin and pulmonary infections with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160 mg tab every 12 hours to prevent recurrent staphylococcal infections.
Approximately one year after previous, he presented again with a productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, generalized weakness, eczema, chest pain, and shortness of breath for 4 days. On the day of admission he had 3 bouts of hemoptysis. The CT of the chest (Figure 3) revealed the same cavitation measuring 5.6 cm in the superior segment of the left lower lobe (LLL) that contained soft tissue density that was suggestive of a mycetoma. A bronchoscopy was performed on this admission with findings of hemoptysis and cavitation in the LLL. The analysis of the bronchoalveloar lavage fluid did not reveal any pneumocystis or fundal organisms. He was discharged on amoxicillin-sulbactum 500 mg tab every 12 hours and itraconazole 200 mg tab every 12 hours. Even though the patient had recurrent infections typical of hyper IgE as a child, he never received an immunodeficiency investigation. Partly because hyper IgE is a rare disease that can have a variety of presentations and not all physicians may consider it in their differential diagnosis, another reason as stated by the patient was that he was treated for the infection and then either lost to follow up or went to another hospital once another infection recurred. This case demonstrates the chronic debilitating course of a patient with hyper IgE.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old Hispanic male with a history of recurrent childhood infections and bilateral Staphylococcus aureus lung abscesses presented initially with a 3-day history of sore throat and odynophagia, and re-presented 1 year later with a 4-day history of productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 3 days of sore throat and odynophagia to solids and liquids without fever or respiratory symptoms, leading to a clinical and genetic diagnosis of autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). Despite initiation of prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160 mg PO q12h), he re-presented 1 year later with a 4-day history of productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, generalized weakness, worsening eczema, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and three episodes of frank hemoptysis on the day of readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Frequent childhood respiratory and gastrointestinal infections; bilateral Staphylococcus aureus lung abscesses ( drained 2 years prior and treated with 1 month of oral clindamycin 300 mg QID, leaving a residual 6 cm thin-walled cyst in the left mid-lung field) and oral candidiasis; recurrent S. aureus skin infections/folliculitis; retained primary dentition. Social history: Smoked 1 pack of cigarettes/week for 9 years, social alcohol use, no illicit drug use; negative family history of immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission positive for sore throat, odynophagia, oral thrush, and chronic eczematous/follicular skin lesions (negative for fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea); 1-year readmission positive for productive cough with green sputum, 3 bouts of hemoptysis, fever, chills, generalized weakness, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission vital signs: Blood pressure 147/85 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 25 breaths/min. Physical findings: Cachectic male with generalized muscle wasting across all four extremities; diffuse eczematous skin lesions and folliculitis over the entire body; white thrush plaques on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx; retained primary teeth; bilaterally decreased breath sounds on lung auscultation; regular tachycardia without cardiac murmurs.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission laboratory tests: BUN 25 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, calcium 7.9 mmol/L, serum albumin 2.8 g/dL, total protein 7.9 mmol/L; HIV test negative; normal serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels. Initial admission chest radiograph: Residual 6 cm thin-walled cyst in the left mid-lung field.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological and genetic workup: Markedly elevated serum IgE >5,000 IU/mL (normal <114 IU/mL); STAT3 gene sequencing identified a novel heterozygous mutation in exon 22 affecting the transactivation domain, confirming autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). One-year readmission chest CT: Persistent 5.6 cm cavity in the superior segment of the left lower lobe (LLL) containing an intracavitary soft-tissue density suggestive of a mycetoma. Readmission bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Active hemoptysis and cavitation in the LLL; BAL fluid analysis was negative for Pneumocystis and fungal organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome; confirmed by serum IgE >5,000 IU/mL, retained primary teeth, recurrent S. aureus skin/lung abscesses, and a novel exon 22 STAT3 transactivation domain mutation) complicated by oral/esophageal candidiasis and subsequent recurrent superinfection/suspected intracavitary mycetoma within a chronic 5.6 cm left lower lobe pneumatocele/cavity (with Pneumocystis excluded on BAL). Plan and clinical course: Initial oral/esophageal candidiasis and skin infections were treated with IV fluconazole (100 mg daily), topical mupirocin 2% ointment, and prophylactic oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160 mg q12h). Upon readmission 1 year later with hemoptysis and left lower lobe cavitary superinfection/mycetoma, he was stabilized and discharged on oral amoxicillin-sulbactam (500 mg q12h) and oral itraconazole (200 mg q12h).

raw_case_text:
In July 2010 a 43-year-old female presented with a 24-hour history of 30 mL of frank haemoptysis. There were no symptoms suggestive of a respiratory infection. She worked as an office manager and had no relevant occupational or environmental exposures. She had ceased smoking ten years previously having accumulated a ten-pack-year history. She had hypertension treated with amlodipine and perimenstrual migraines. Both parents and her brother were alive without any significant medical diseases.
On presentation peripheral arterial oxygen saturation was 85% on room air, respiratory rate was 24 per minute, blood pressure was 200/100, and temperature was 38.5 C. She remained afebrile thereafter. An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm, 100 beats per minute. A chest X-ray demonstrated bilateral perihilar infiltrates. A CTPA confirmed diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates (Figure 1). No vascular filling defects were identified. Haemoglobin was 99 g/L (115-160). MCV (mean cell volume) was 67 fL (81-96), and the film was suggestive of iron deficiency. White cell count was mildly elevated at 137/nL (3.5-11). Other inflammatory markers were also mildly elevated. ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) was 29 mm (<15). CRP (C-reactive protein) was 68.1 mgl/L (<8). Creatinine was 65 mumol/L (50-100). Urea was 48 mumol/L (2.7-7.8). Electrolytes were within normal limits. INR (international normalised ratio) was 1.1 (0 9-1.2). APTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) was 28 seconds (25-34). Testing for antiglomerular basement membrane, antiuclear cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA and pANCA), antinuclear antibodies, and extractable nuclear antigens (ENA) were all negative. Rheumatoid factor was <10 IU/mL (<30). Several sputum samples were sent. No pathogens were identified on standard bacterial and mycobacterial cultures. There was no cytological evidence of malignancy. Urinalysis was normal. Phase contrast microscopy was not performed as the red cell count on several specimens was within normal limits. Albumin/creatinine ratio was 17.7 g/mol creatinine (<3.5). The patient was treated with benzylpenicillin and doxycycline, and there was improved, but persisting haemoptysis. On the third day the patient proceeded to fibre optic bronchoscopy where no source of bleeding or endobronchial abnormality was identified. A surgical lung biopsy was subsequently performed. At the operation blood was noted within the pleural space, the surface of the lung was oozing fresh blood, and the parenchyma was boggy. A wedge biopsy was taken from the right middle lobe. Microscopy demonstrated a widespread interstitial inflammatory process centred on capillary sized vessels. There were associated interstitial haemorrhage and fibrin deposition. Occasional neutrophils and eosinophils were both observed. The disease process was variable in intensity with propensity for different expression on either side of an interlobular septum. No granulomata were identified. Special stains were negative for fungal hyphae and Pneumocystis species (Figures 2 and 3). A diagnosis of small vessel pulmonary vasculitis was made, thought to be most consistent with microscopic polyangiitis.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the surgical procedure and the haemoptysis appeared to rapidly spontaneously settle. Induction immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide and high dose prednisolone was discussed. However, the patient declined. The patient was therefore, discharged three days after the operation with close outpatient surveillance arranged. Repeated clinical reviews with an assessment of lung function, chest radiology, renal function, and urinalysis demonstrated continued complete resolution of pulmonary vasculitis. 12 months after her initial presentation she remained well.
Pulmonary vasculitis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of haemoptysis. Microscopic polyangiitis is a small vessel systemic vasculitis that usually manifests with glomerulonephritis. The lungs are involved in association in approximately 20% to 30% of cases, with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage in approximately 10% to 20%. It is associated with pANCA in 90% of the cases. It is rare for this disease to present with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage in isolation. Treatment recommendations are largely based on historical data demonstrating poor prognosis for patients with pauciimmune glomerulonephritis. No randomised controlled trials have been performed for patients with pulmonary haemorrhage. Many advocate aggressive immunosuppression in this clinical situation with a combination of cyclophosphamide and high dose of prednisolone, with or without plasma exchange. Owing to the toxic effects of this regimen, different strategies have been investigated, and promising disease modifying and biological alternatives continue to emerge, both for induction and maintenance immunosuppression.
Here we described the unusual case of small vessel pulmonary vasculitis with spontaneous remission. Whilst the histology is thought to favour a diagnosis of microscopic polyangiitis, it is possible that an alternate diagnosis was missed, for example, through sampling error. This case highlights the difficulties applying guidelines to rare diseases, particularly when presentations are atypical, as was the case of this patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old female office manager presented in July 2010 with a 24-hour history of 30 mL of frank hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of 30 mL of frank hemoptysis over the preceding 24 hours without any antecedent symptoms of respiratory tract infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension treated with amlodipine; perimenstrual migraines; former smoker (10-pack-year history, quit 10 years prior); worked as an office manager with no occupational or environmental exposures. Family history unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for frank hemoptysis (30 mL); negative for infectious prodrome. No known drug allergies. Home medication was amlodipine.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) 85% on room air, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, blood pressure 200/100 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and temperature 38.5 °C on presentation (remaining afebrile thereafter).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Microcytic anemia suggestive of iron deficiency with hemoglobin 99 g/L (reference: 115–160 g/L) and MCV 67 fL (reference: 81–96 fL); mildly elevated WBC count at 13.7 x 10^9/L (reported as 137/nL, reference: 3.5–11); ESR 29 mm/h (reference <15); C-reactive protein (CRP) 68.1 mg/L (reference <8); creatinine 65 μmol/L (50–100); urea 4.8 mmol/L (reported as 48 μmol/L, reference: 2.7–7.8); normal electrolytes; INR 1.1 (0.9–1.2); APTT 28 s (25–34 s). Autoimmune serology: Negative anti-GBM, cANCA, pANCA, ANA, and ENA; rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL (<30). Urinalysis: Normal microscopy without hematuria; urine albumin/creatinine ratio mildly elevated at 17.7 g/mol creatinine (<3.5). Sputum studies: Negative bacterial and mycobacterial cultures and negative cytology. Electrocardiogram (ECG): Sinus tachycardia at 100 beats/min. Chest X-ray: Bilateral perihilar infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA): Diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates without pulmonary arterial filling defects. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy (day 3): No endobronchial abnormality or localized bleeding point. Right middle lobe surgical wedge lung biopsy: Blood noted in the pleural space with boggy, oozing lung parenchyma; histopathology demonstrated widespread pulmonary capillaritis (interstitial inflammation centered on capillary-sized vessels with neutrophils and eosinophils), interstitial hemorrhage, and alveolar fibrin deposition without granulomas; special stains were negative for Pneumocystis species and fungal hyphae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Isolated ANCA-negative small-vessel pulmonary vasculitis (pulmonary capillaritis most consistent with microscopic polyangiitis) presenting as diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, definitively confirmed by right middle lobe surgical wedge biopsy (with Pneumocystis species and fungal infections ruled out by special stains). Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered on admission. Following surgical lung biopsy on day 3, her hemoptysis spontaneously resolved. The patient declined recommended induction immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide and high-dose prednisolone and was discharged 3 days postoperatively under close outpatient surveillance; serial follow-up over 12 months demonstrated sustained spontaneous clinical, functional, and radiographic remission.

raw_case_text: A 21-year-old male presented with fever, cough, anorexia and weight loss of 2 months duration. He was a student, did not smoke and did not report alcohol or substance abuse. He did not have any significant medical history and was immunized appropriately. He reported exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis as a caregiver to a sibling 18 months prior to this episode; his sister recovered completely with 6 months of antituberculosis treatment. Tuberculin testing or isoniazid prophylaxis was not offered to the index patient according to current practice in India. He did not raise pets and had stayed alone in a hostel for the last 4 months. Chest radiographs showed bilateral infiltrates and computed tomography [CT, Figure 1] showed findings suggestive of extensive pulmonary tuberculosis. Tuberculin skin testing was negative (6 mm with 5 TU at 72 h). Sputum smears were strongly positive for acid-fast bacilli by Zeihl-Neelsen's stain and supervised daily four-drug antituberculosis treatment (isoniazid 200 mg, rifampicin 450 mg, pyrazinamide 1000 mg, ethambutol 600 mg, pyridoxine 20 mg; weight 40 kg) was initiated and sputum cultures and drug susceptibility for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by multiple growth indicator technique (MGIT) was requested. Sputum for GeneXpert for M. tuberculosis did not show resistance to rifampicin. Nutrition counseling and four doses of 2-weekly Vitamin D 100,000 I.U were administered as per unit's protocol. He presented with fever, worsening breathlessness, weight loss and chest pain 4 weeks after starting treatment. On examination he was afebrile, normotensive with respiratory rate of 40 breaths/min and pulse rate of 130 beats/min. He was malnourished (body mass inde x 14 kg/m2, normal 19-25 kg/m2). Respiratory examination showed reduced right-sided movements and breath sound intensity with coarse left-sided crackles. Resting SpO2 was 80%. Chest radiography [Figure 1, left] confirmed the diagnosis of right-sided pneumothorax with increased bilateral infiltrates. He was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) with appropriate respiratory isolation; intercostal chest drain was inserted on the right side. There was evidence of air-leak (Cerfolio E) from the right lung with minimal subcutaneous emphysema. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) was started; no worsening of air-leak was noted. Repeat sputum smears showed downgrading of smears with scanty acid-fast bacilli by Zeihl-Neelsen's stain. Sputum cultures requested at treatment onset confirmed pan-sensitive M. tuberculosis. Repeat CT-chest [Figure 2] showed increase in cavitation, consolidation and ground-glass opacities bilaterally. Further investigations are summarized in Table 1. Fasting blood glucose was 87 mg/dL and human immunodeficiency virus ELISA was negative and there was no CD4 lymphocytopenia. Sputum smears for Pneumocystis jirovecii were negative. Urine microscopy was normal and negative for albuminuria. Arterial blood gas analysis showed corrected hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.42, PO2 78 mm Hg on FiO20.4, PCO228 mm Hg, HCO322 mEq/L). Quantiferon-TB GOLD in-tube assay was strongly positive. He was continued on four-drug antituberculosis treatment; further doses of Vitamin D were not administered. He developed contralateral pneumothorax on the 2nd day of admission and worsened hypoxemia needing mechanical ventilation. Urgent left intercostal tube drainage was performed and air-leak (Cerfolio I) was noticed on the left side also. Repeat MGIT tuberculosis cultures were reported negative by day 10 of ICU admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old male student with smear-positive, pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis presented 4 weeks after initiating four-drug antituberculosis therapy and high-dose vitamin D supplementation with fever, worsening breathlessness, weight loss, and acute chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with a 2-month history of fever, cough, anorexia, and weight loss 18 months after serving as caregiver to a sister with pulmonary tuberculosis. Baseline chest imaging showed extensive bilateral infiltrates, sputum Ziehl-Neelsen smears were strongly positive for acid-fast bacilli (GeneXpert rifampicin-susceptible), and he was started on supervised daily weight-based four-drug antituberculosis therapy (isoniazid 200 mg, rifampicin 450 mg, pyrazinamide 1,000 mg, ethambutol 600 mg, pyridoxine 20 mg; weight 40 kg) plus four biweekly oral doses of 100,000 IU vitamin D. Four weeks into treatment, he presented with recurrent fever, severe worsening breathlessness, chest pain, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Smear- and culture-positive pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed 4 weeks prior; household tuberculosis contact (cared for his sister with pulmonary TB 18 months earlier without receiving latent TB prophylaxis). Nonsmoker, student living in a hostel, no alcohol or substance abuse, immunized appropriately.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, worsening breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, anorexia, and severe weight loss. Home medications were isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, pyridoxine, and biweekly high-dose vitamin D (100,000 IU).

objective.physical_examination: At 4-week readmission: Afebrile and normotensive, severe malnutrition with weight 40 kg and BMI 14 kg/m2 (normal: 19–25 kg/m2), marked tachypnea (respiratory rate 40 breaths/min), tachycardia (pulse 130 beats/min), and severe resting hypoxemia (SpO2 80%). Chest examination: Reduced right-sided chest wall movement and diminished right breath sounds with coarse left-sided crackles (followed on ICU day 2 by contralateral left-sided pneumothorax).
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas (on FiO2 0.40): pH 7.42, PaO2 78 mmHg, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L. Laboratory tests: Fasting blood glucose 87 mg/dL, HIV ELISA negative, normal urinalysis without albuminuria; baseline tuberculin skin test anergic (6 mm at 72 h), while QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube assay at readmission was strongly positive. Sputum studies: Baseline strongly AFB-positive sputum downgraded at 4 weeks to scanty AFB; baseline MGIT culture confirmed pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and repeat MGIT cultures turned negative by ICU day 10; sputum smears for Pneumocystis jirovecii were negative. Chest radiographs: Right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax with increased bilateral infiltrates on readmission, followed by contralateral left-sided pneumothorax on ICU day 2.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological workup: Normal CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (no CD4 lymphocytopenia). Repeat chest CT at 4-week readmission: Marked paradoxical progression of bilateral cavitation, consolidation, and ground-glass opacities compared to baseline.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Paradoxical tuberculous immune reconstitution / paradoxical reaction (potentiated by high-dose vitamin D supplementation and manifested by conversion from tuberculin anergy to a strongly positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay, worsening bilateral cavitary/ground-glass infiltrates, and sequential bilateral life-threatening spontaneous pneumothoraces) in an HIV-negative young adult with pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis; Pneumocystis jirovecii co-infection was excluded by negative sputum smears and normal CD4 counts. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the ICU with right intercostal tube drainage (for Cerfolio grade E air leak) and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, followed on ICU day 2 by urgent left intercostal tube drainage (for Cerfolio grade I air leak) and invasive mechanical ventilation. Further doses of vitamin D were discontinued while standard four-drug antituberculosis therapy was continued, achieving negative MGIT sputum cultures by ICU day 10.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old woman was transferred from Inukjuak, a first nation community in Northern Quebec, to the Montreal General Hospital in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Her respiratory symptoms included dry cough and dyspnea II/V on Medical Research Council dyspnea scale. She also complained of severe middle back pain radiating to her left ribs that began two months before admission. She smoked a mean of 20 cigarettes per day for 20 years and denied alcohol or drug abuse. Her past medical history was limited to a remote exposure to tuberculosis that did not required treatment. Prior to onset of symptoms, the patient was not taking any medication but began using acetaminophen in the four weeks before admission.
Physical examination was only significant for paraspinal tenderness between T7 and T9 vertebrae. Neurological examination did not reveal motor or sensory dysfunction. Chest auscultation identified normal breath sounds with no adventitious sounds in the absence of cyanosis or clubbing. Laboratory results were within normal values and showed no evidence of hyponatremia, elevated white blood count, or increased LDH. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation were normal. Chest X-ray showed a diffuse bilateral nodular interstitial pattern. A computed tomodensitometry (CT) in contrast to the chest was performed and revealed bilateral reticular-nodular disease in the lungs with the presence of cystic lesions that speared the lung bases (Figure 1(a)). As shown in Figure 1, no lymph node enlargement or pleural effusions were observed. The bone image on the same CT showed a solitary osteolytic lesion at T8 vertebral body and right pedicle, with a two-millimeter margin between the lesion and the spinal cord (Figure 2).
Pulmonary function tests (PFT) demonstrated a restrictive and a marked reduction in diffusing capacity (DLCO 63.5%). A bronchoscopy was performed to identify the cause of the diffuse micronodular lesions in the lungs. Results were negative for bacterial, viral, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains and grocott stains were negative for tuberculosis and pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, respectively. A transbronchial biopsy was performed and demonstrated eosinophilic granuloma with the presence of numerous bean-shaped cells with lobulated nuclei. These cells were aggregately stained and were immunohistochemically positive for S100, langerin, and CD1 consistent with the diagnosis of LCH.
To eliminate a neoplastic condition in T8 vertebra, an echo-guided bone biopsy was performed. Pathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of LCH in the body of the vertebra. Based on the absence of both bone collapse and neurological deficits, orthopedic decompression/fixation surgery was not undertaken. Conservative management with smoking cessation and close follow-up was proposed to the patient.
After three months, the dyspnea was reduced to an I/V level on the MRC breathlessness scale, and the diffuse interstitial lesions were no longer present on chest X-ray. The patient reported decreased use of acetaminophen for the back pain, which started to improve four weeks following smoking cessation.
After an 18-month follow-up, the patient experienced a complete resolution of all her symptoms. A repeated CT scan of the chest showed significant decrease of the multiple lung nodules and the bone view revealed an 80% bone regeneration at the site of the initial osteolytic lesion (Figures 1 and 2). Lastly, her lung function completely normalized. Following a final remote interview with the patient four years after this episode, the patient did not resume smoking and remains symptom-free.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old First Nations woman from Northern Quebec presented with a 2-month history of severe mid-thoracic back pain radiating to the left ribs, dry cough, and MRC grade II/V exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was transferred from Inukjuak, Northern Quebec, to Montreal General Hospital for evaluation of severe middle back pain radiating to her left ribs that started 2 months prior to admission, accompanied by a dry cough and Medical Research Council (MRC) grade II/V dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Remote exposure to tuberculosis not requiring treatment; 20-pack-year active cigarette smoking history (20 cigarettes/day for 20 years); denied alcohol or illicit drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, MRC grade II/V dyspnea, and severe mid-back pain radiating to the left ribs. Home medication was acetaminophen started 4 weeks prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: Localized paraspinal tenderness between the T7 and T9 vertebrae; intact motor and sensory neurological examination; normal bilateral vesicular breath sounds without adventitious sounds, cyanosis, or digital clubbing.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood and protein studies: Normal complete blood count (no leukocytosis), normal serum sodium (no hyponatremia) and LDH, and normal serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation. Chest X-ray: Diffuse bilateral nodular interstitial pattern. Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Restrictive ventilatory defect with markedly reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO 63.5% predicted).
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced chest and thoracic spine CT: Bilateral reticular-nodular lung disease with multiple pulmonary cysts sparing the lung bases, without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion; solitary osteolytic bone lesion in the T8 vertebral body and right pedicle with a 2-mm margin from the spinal cord. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy: BAL bacterial, viral, Ziehl-Neelsen (tuberculosis), and Grocott (Pneumocystis jirovecii) stains/cultures were all negative; transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated eosinophilic granuloma composed of aggregates of bean-shaped histiocytes with grooved/lobulated nuclei staining strongly positive for S100, langerin (CD207), and CD1a. Ultrasound-guided T8 vertebral biopsy: Confirmed Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Multisystem adult Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) involving the lungs and T8 vertebra, definitively confirmed by S100-, langerin-, and CD1a-positive Langerhans cells on transbronchial lung biopsy and ultrasound-guided T8 vertebral bone biopsy (with tuberculosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia ruled out by negative Ziehl-Neelsen and Grocott stains on BAL). Plan and clinical course: Because there was no vertebral collapse or neurological deficit, orthopedic surgery and systemic chemotherapy were deferred in favor of strict smoking cessation and close observation. Her back pain began improving within 4 weeks of quitting smoking; by 3 months, her dyspnea improved to MRC grade I/V with clearance of interstitial lesions on chest X-ray; and by 18-month follow-up, repeat chest/spine CT and PFTs demonstrated complete symptom resolution, normalization of lung function, regression of lung nodules, and 80% osseous regeneration of the T8 vertebral body (remaining abstinent from smoking and symptom-free at 4-year follow-up).

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old woman, previously healthy, Colombian, was admitted to the Department of Rheumatology at Hospital Militar Central, with a fever of 39 C, generalised arthralgia involving the elbows, wrists, proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints, knees and ankles, and fatigue. She had been in her usual state of good health until 2 weeks before admission and these symptoms starting shortly after the patient had a sore throat for 7 days.
Examination revealed angioneurotic edema detected on soles, palms and tongue (Figure 1a) and widespread red, urticated plaques in a symmetrical distribution affecting the arms, dorsal hands, upper and lower chest and back (Figure 1b). The rest of the examination was unremarkable. These lesions were present for less than 10 h per day and were not more pronounced at night with no associated bruising. She was diagnosed as having infection-associated-urticaria in a peripheral hospital and was treated with antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) and antihistamines (loratadine) without diminishment of her symptoms. Followed 5 days later by fever, the patient presented dyspnea, cough and hypoxemia. A chest x-ray film showed a patchy right lower lobe infiltrate (Figure 2a) and computed tomography showed unilateral consolidation and pleural effusion (Figure 2b).
An early bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was indicated revealing hemorrhagic lavage and pathological examination showed hemosiderin-containing macrophages in 80%. Bronchoalveolar lavage specimen was sent for routine bacterial cultures, fungal, viral and Pneumocystis carinii; all of the results were negative. A skin biopsy demonstrated dermal oedema, and a marked perivascular and neutrophilic infiltrate with no evidence of structural vasculitis. These features were consistent with neutrophilic urticaria (Figure 3). Other investigations revealed a normocytic anaemia Hb 11.5 g/dL erythrocyte mean corpuscolar volume 86 fl platelet count 408.000/mm3, a marked white blood cell count (WBC) 67.200 mm3 with 91% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes, 1% eosinophils, 3% monocytes and markedly elevated acute phase reactants: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 49 mm in the first hour, C-reactive protein 11,43 mg/dl and ferritin 1650 mug/L, alanine aminotransferase was mildly elevated at 74 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1200 IU/L and serum albumin reduced at 3,4 g/L. Antinuclear antibodies (immunofluorescence-Hep-2 cells), rheumatoid factor (nephelometry), antistreptolysin O, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins and serum electrophoresis were unremarkable. There was no serological evidence for active or recent infection with the following organisms: Toxoplasma gondii, group B streptococci, hepatitis A, B or C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, tuberculosis and syphilis. Blood cultures were negative. Ultrasound investigation of the liver and biliary tract was normal. In the bone marrow aspiration, we found remarkable hyperplasia and granulocytes of each mature state, without an increase of myeloblasts, the neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score was high, Ph chromose was negative. Immunophenotyping showed mature neutrophils expressing surface antigens CD13 and CD15 at a level higher than 95% and negative for CD34 and HLA-DR.
She was diagnosed with AOSD and methylprednisolone (mini-boluses of 125 mg/ day per 3 days) was initiated as prednisone sparing therapy. The patient's pulmonary symptoms improved with the doses of pulsed corticosteroids. After 3 days of pulsed methylprednisolone, therapy was maintained with 0.5 mg/kg of prednisone orally. Treatment with NSAIDs and prednisone controlled the rash, fever, arthritis, angioedema and significantly reduced the serum ferritin levels and all markers of activity disease. Two weeks after the pulse treatment, the chest radiography became normal. Methotrexate was prescribed for long term control of the disease at a dose of 7,5 mg/week. One month later prednisone was slowly decreased to 12,5 mg/day and withdrawn over three months. No activation period was observed during the one-year follow-up period.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 40-year-old Colombian woman presented with a 2-week history of high fever (39 °C), generalized polyarthralgia, fatigue, palmoplantar/lingual angioedema, and widespread urticarial plaques following a 7-day sore throat, and developed acute cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia 5 days after admission.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In her usual state of good health until 2 weeks before admission, the patient experienced a 7-day sore throat followed immediately by high fever (39 °C), severe fatigue, symmetrical polyarthralgia (elbows, wrists, MCPs, PIPs, DIPs, MTPs, knees, and ankles), angioedema of the palms, soles, and tongue, and transient symmetrical red urticarial plaques (<10 hours/day) over the trunk and upper extremities. She was initially treated at a peripheral hospital for presumed infection-associated urticaria with ciprofloxacin and loratadine without improvement. Five days after rheumatology admission, she acutely developed persistent fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for antecedent 7-day sore throat, high fever (39 °C), fatigue, generalized polyarthralgia, palmoplantar and lingual angioedema, evanescent urticarial rash, and subsequent cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile at 39 °C; angioneurotic edema involving the palms, soles, and tongue; symmetrical widespread erythematous urticarial plaques over the arms, dorsal hands, chest, and back (lasting <10 h/day without bruising); generalized polyarthralgia/arthritis; acute hypoxemia and tachypnea on hospital day 5.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology, biochemistry, and acute-phase reactants: Normocytic anemia (Hb 11.5 g/dL, MCV 86 fL), platelets 408,000/mm3, extreme leukemoid-like leukocytosis with WBC 67,200/mm3 (91% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, 1% eosinophils), ESR 49 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 11.43 mg/dL, marked hyperferritinemia at 1,650 μg/L, mildly elevated ALT (74 IU/L), elevated LDH (1,200 IU/L), and hypoalbuminemia (3.4 g/dL). Negative autoimmune and infectious workup: Negative ANA, RF, ASO titer, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, and normal serum protein electrophoresis; negative blood cultures and negative serologies/testing for Toxoplasma gondii, group B streptococci, HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV, CMV, tuberculosis, and syphilis. Hepatobiliary ultrasound: Normal. Day 5 chest X-ray: Patchy right lower lobe infiltrate.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 5 chest CT: Unilateral right lower lobe consolidation and pleural effusion. Early bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Grossly hemorrhagic lavage fluid with 80% hemosiderin-laden macrophages diagnostic of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH); BAL bacterial, fungal, viral, and Pneumocystis carinii cultures/stains all negative. Skin biopsy: Dermal edema with a marked perivascular and interstitial neutrophilic infiltrate without structural vasculitis, consistent with neutrophilic urticaria. Bone marrow aspirate and flow cytometry: Marked granulocytic hyperplasia across all maturation stages without excess myeloblasts, high neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (NAP) score, negative Philadelphia chromosome, and >95% mature CD13+/CD15+ neutrophils (CD34-/HLA-DR-).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) presenting with atypical neutrophilic urticaria, palmoplantar/lingual angioedema, extreme neutrophilic leukocytosis (67,200/mm3), hyperferritinemia (1,650 μg/L), and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (confirmed by hemorrhagic BAL with 80% hemosiderin-laden macrophages and negative BAL studies for Pneumocystis carinii, bacteria, fungi, and viruses). Plan and clinical course: Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone mini-pulses (125 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day), NSAIDs, and weekly methotrexate (7.5 mg/week). Her pulmonary hemorrhage, rash, angioedema, fever, and arthritis rapidly resolved, her chest X-ray normalized within 2 weeks, and prednisone was tapered off over 4 months without relapse during 1 year of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 65-year-old female, never smoker, with a history of hypertension, was diagnosed with colon cancer metastatic to the liver in June 2007. The patient commenced chemotherapy treatment according to the FOLFIRI protocol (bevacizumab/5-fluorouracil/irinotecan). From July 2007 to July 2009, she received 19 cycles of therapy with good response. Then she underwent liver metastasectomy and, in October 2009, she started chemotherapy according to the FOLFOX protocol (bevacizumab/5-fluorouracil/oxaliplatin). No treatment related side effects were noted and the patient was in very good performance status (WHO 1) until the 6th cycle of chemotherapy. On day 15 of the 6th cycle, she developed dyspnea and fever immediately after the treatment with oxaliplatin. She was treated with intravenous corticosteroids and promethazine with symptomatic improvement of the dyspnea. The following day her dyspnea worsened, with several episodes of near-syncope. Her saturation without oxygen was measured as low as 73%, and blood pressure was as low as 100/50 mm/Hg, but no tachycardia was observed. On physical examination, the patient was dyspneic, rales were heard on auscultation to the lungs, and mild pitting edema was noticed on the lower limbs. Initial blood tests revealed respiratory alkalosis, moderate acute-on-chronic renal failure, and hyponatremia of 122 mEq/L. Troponin and brain natriuretic peptide levels, as well as echocardiography, did not show cardiac failure or ischemia. Chest X-ray showed no pulmonary congestion (following treatment with loop diuretics) or infection. Chest CT scan showed diffused bilateral ground glass infiltrates and no pulmonary emboli (Figure 1). After ruling out cardiac and thromboembolic etiology of the dyspnea, diagnostic bronchoscopy was performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis, along with blood cultures, revealed no sign of bacterial, viral, or Pneumocystis carinii infection, and no eosinophilia. Candida infection was present in fungal cultures. Pulmonary biopsy showed organizing diffuse alveolar damage. A diagnosis of interstitial pneumonitis was concluded, most probably drug-induced. The patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids and wide ranging antibiotics, until the diagnosis of bacterial infection was ruled out, antifungal drugs, and loop diuretics. She received respiratory support with oxygen and continuous positive airway pressure. The patient's respiratory failure did not improve with treatment and she died 15 days following initial presentation.
