subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old female with metastatic colon cancer developed acute dyspnea and fever immediately after receiving her sixth cycle of FOLFOX plus bevacizumab chemotherapy, followed the next day by severe hypoxemia and near-syncope.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in June 2007 with colon cancer metastatic to the liver, the patient received 19 cycles of FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab (July 2007 – July 2009) with good response, underwent hepatic metastasectomy, and started FOLFOX (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin) plus bevacizumab in October 2009. She maintained a WHO performance status of 1 without side effects through five cycles, but on day 15 of the 6th cycle she developed acute dyspnea and fever immediately after oxaliplatin infusion. Despite transient symptomatic relief with IV corticosteroids and promethazine, her dyspnea markedly worsened the next day with recurrent episodes of near-syncope.
subjective.past_medical_history: Colon adenocarcinoma with liver metastases (diagnosed June 2007, status post 19 cycles of FOLFIRI + bevacizumab and liver metastasectomy); hypertension; lifetime never-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute fever, severe progressive dyspnea, and near-syncope.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Dyspneic, room-air oxygen saturation (SpO2) as low as 73%, blood pressure as low as 100/50 mmHg without tachycardia; pulmonary rales on chest auscultation; mild bilateral lower extremity pitting edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Respiratory alkalosis, moderate acute-on-chronic renal failure, and severe hyponatremia (serum sodium 122 mEq/L); normal cardiac troponin and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels; negative blood cultures. Echocardiography: No cardiac failure or ischemia. Chest X-ray: No pulmonary congestion (after loop diuretics) or focal infection.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass infiltrates without pulmonary embolism. Diagnostic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and lung biopsy: BAL negative for bacterial, viral, and Pneumocystis carinii infection and negative for eosinophilia (fungal cultures grew Candida); lung biopsy histopathology demonstrated organizing diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal oxaliplatin/FOLFOX-induced acute interstitial pneumonitis (organizing diffuse alveolar damage confirmed by lung biopsy; cardiac, thromboembolic, bacterial, viral, and Pneumocystis carinii etiologies excluded by echocardiography, chest CT, blood cultures, and BAL). Plan and clinical course: Managed with supplemental oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), high-dose systemic corticosteroids, broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics, antifungal therapy (for BAL Candida), and loop diuretics. Despite intensive respiratory and anti-inflammatory support, her respiratory failure proved refractory and she died 15 days after initial presentation.

raw_case_text: An 80-year-old male, never smoker, with a history of hypertension was diagnosed in September 2005 with adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage IIIB. He received standard neoadjuvant treatment of a combination of radiation therapy and 5-fluorouracil and then underwent total mesorectal excision. In July 2006, the patient had local recurrence of the rectal cancer confirmed by rectoscopy, and biopsy from the rectum and inguinal lymph node revealed well-differentiated adenocarcinoma of the rectum, with bilateral inguinal lymph node involvement, a nonresectable disease. CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was normal except for the rectal mass and enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. The patient started treatment with chemotherapy for metastatic disease, the FOLFIRI protocol (bevacizumab/5-fluorouracil/irinotecan) for two cycles. Due to the severe side effects of diarrhea, the treatment was changed to FOLFOX protocol (bevacizumab/5-fluorouracil/oxaliplatin). The patient was treated with this protocol for nine months with no side effects reported. Following the 17th treatment cycle, he was hospitalized due to fever, cough, and dyspnea. Physical examination revealed mild dyspnea, and blood tests showed mild respiratory acidosis and acute-on-chronic renal failure. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. CT scan showed a picture consistent with diffuse alveolar damage without pulmonary fibrosis, with a differential diagnosis of atypical infection or drug-induced pneumonitis (Figure 2). These findings did not appear on the previous CT scan taken three months earlier. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Bronchoscopy including bronchoalveolar lavage was performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis as well as blood cultures revealed no sign of bacterial, viral, or Pneumocystis carinii, Legionella, and Aspergillus infection and no eosinophilia. Candida infection was present on lavage analysis. There was no sign of malignancy on bronchial cytology. The patient was treated with wide spectrum empiric antibiotics, glucocorticosteroids, and oxygen, with continuous clinical deterioration and respiratory failure. He died 27 days following his initial presentation.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 80-year-old never-smoking male with locally recurrent and metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma presented with fever, cough, and dyspnea following his 17th cycle of FOLFOX plus bevacizumab chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed in September 2005 with stage IIIB rectal adenocarcinoma and underwent neoadjuvant 5-fluorouracil chemoradiotherapy followed by total mesorectal excision. In July 2006, he developed unresectable local pelvic recurrence with bilateral inguinal lymph node metastases. He received two cycles of FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab (stopped due to severe diarrhea) and was switched to FOLFOX (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin) plus bevacizumab, which he tolerated well for 9 months. Following his 17th cycle of FOLFOX plus bevacizumab, he was hospitalized with acute fever, cough, and dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage IIIB rectal adenocarcinoma (diagnosed September 2005, status post neoadjuvant 5-FU chemoradiation and total mesorectal excision, with unresectable local and bilateral inguinal nodal recurrence in July 2006); hypertension; lifetime never-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, cough, and dyspnea; prior history of chemotherapy-induced severe diarrhea on FOLFIRI.

objective.physical_examination: Mild dyspnea on admission physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Mild respiratory acidosis and acute-on-chronic renal failure; negative blood and urine cultures. Admission chest X-ray: Diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: New diffuse bilateral changes consistent with diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) without pre-existing pulmonary fibrosis (absent on a chest CT performed 3 months earlier). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative for bacterial, viral, Pneumocystis carinii, Legionella, and Aspergillus infections; no BAL eosinophilia and no malignant cells on bronchial cytology (Candida species isolated on BAL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal FOLFOX/oxaliplatin-induced acute interstitial pneumonitis / diffuse alveolar damage (confirmed by chest CT and exclusion of Pneumocystis carinii, Legionella, Aspergillus, bacterial, viral, and malignant etiologies via bronchoalveolar lavage). Plan and clinical course: Treated with supplemental oxygen, high-dose glucocorticosteroids, and broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. His respiratory failure progressively worsened despite treatment, and he died 27 days after hospital presentation.

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old Caucasian female with ulcerative colitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and cirrhosis presented with fever, chills, shortness of breath, dry cough, and chest pain for five days after being started on prednisone 40 mg daily and azathioprine 50 mg daily for autoimmune hepatitis two months earlier. She was born and raised in New York state and only travelled to Vermont and Florida. During the prior two weeks, she traveled to a hunting shack in northern New York and had been there twice before becoming ill. She had no personal or family history of tuberculosis and has had several prior negative PPDs during nursing school. On presentation, she was febrile to 102 F, pulse of 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 96/58 mmHg and required 2 liters oxygen to keep her saturation above 90%. Initial exam was benign with clear lungs. After blood and urine cultures were obtained, vancomycin and meropenem were started empirically. A paracentesis was not performed due to small ascitic fluid pockets. Initial chest X-ray showed trace left-sided pleural effusion without any evidence of infiltrates. Initial lab work showed ALT 62 U/L, AST 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 158 U/L, total bilirubin 13.2 mg/dL, INR of 2.9, WBC of 16,000/ul with 14,400/uL neutrophils, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, and platelets of 167,000/uL. After a CT chest revealed small bilateral cavitary nodules the following day, vancomycin and meropenem were continued along with amphotericin being started with concern for a fungal infection (Figure 1).
Without clinical improvement, a CT guided biopsy of the necrotic pulmonary nodules was performed by interventional radiology three days after admission. The CT chest of the biopsy showed a new right upper lobe lesion (Figure 1) despite being on meropenem, vancomycin, and amphotericin. A bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed the following day and Gram stain, fungal stain, and extensive cultures were all negative. With continued deterioration six days after the biopsy, a repeat CT chest showed increasing size and number of pulmonary nodules with ground glass opacities despite treatment with meropenem, vancomycin, and amphotericin. On day eleven of admission, cultures from the CT guided biopsy turned positive for Legionella. The antimicrobials were stopped and levofloxacin was started and continued for 3 weeks with resolution of symptoms. The culture was sent to the New York State Department of Health in Albany, NY, and identified as L. micdadei. Negative tests included normal transthoracic echo, normal head CT, and normal neck ultrasound. Five blood cultures, respiratory viral panel, urine Legionella antigen, Pneumocystis DNA PCR, Legionella culture from BAL, bacterial culture, fungal culture, Aspergillus antigen, and Histoplasma antigen were negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old Caucasian female with autoimmune hepatitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, cirrhosis, and ulcerative colitis presented with a 5-day history of fever, chills, shortness of breath, dry cough, and chest pain two months after starting prednisone and azathioprine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to admission, the patient was started on oral prednisone (40 mg daily) and azathioprine (50 mg daily) for autoimmune hepatitis. During the 2 weeks before presentation, she visited a hunting shack in northern New York twice. Five days prior to hospital admission, she developed high fever, chills, shortness of breath, dry cough, and pleuritic chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Autoimmune hepatitis (started on prednisone 40 mg/day and azathioprine 50 mg/day 2 months prior); ulcerative colitis; primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC); cirrhosis. Epidemiological history: Born and raised in New York state, recent visits to a hunting shack in northern New York, prior travel limited to Vermont and Florida; several negative tuberculin PPD skin tests during nursing school; no family history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, shortness of breath, dry cough, and chest pain. Home medications included prednisone 40 mg daily and azathioprine 50 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Temperature 102 °F, pulse 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, requiring 2 L/min supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >90%. Initial chest auscultation and systemic exam were benign with clear lungs.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 16,000/μL (neutrophils 14,400/μL), hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, platelets 167,000/μL, ALT 62 U/L, AST 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 158 U/L, total bilirubin 13.2 mg/dL, and INR 2.9. Negative microbiological screening: Five blood cultures, urine cultures, respiratory viral panel, and urinary Legionella antigen all negative. Imaging: Initial chest X-ray showed a trace left pleural effusion without focal infiltrates; transthoracic echocardiogram, head CT, and neck ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial chest CT scans: Day 2 chest CT revealed small bilateral cavitary pulmonary nodules; day 4 CT (at biopsy) showed a new right upper lobe lesion; day 10 CT showed increasing size and number of cavitary pulmonary nodules with surrounding ground-glass opacities despite broad-spectrum therapy. Day 5 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative Gram stain, fungal stain, bacterial/fungal/Legionella BAL cultures, Pneumocystis DNA PCR, Aspergillus antigen, and Histoplasma antigen. Day 4 CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of necrotic pulmonary nodules: Culture grew Legionella species on hospital day 11, definitively speciated by the New York State Department of Health (Albany, NY) as Legionella micdadei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Cavitary necrotizing Legionella micdadei pneumonia in an immunosuppressed patient on prednisone and azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis/PSC/cirrhosis, definitively confirmed by CT-guided lung biopsy culture and reference laboratory speciation after negative urinary Legionella antigen, negative BAL cultures, and negative Pneumocystis DNA PCR. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric vancomycin, meropenem, and amphotericin B failed to prevent radiographic progression of cavitary nodules. On hospital day 11, upon isolation of L. micdadei from the lung biopsy culture, meropenem, vancomycin, and amphotericin B were discontinued and targeted oral/IV levofloxacin was administered for 3 weeks, resulting in complete resolution of symptoms.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old never-smoking male of Danish origin, without any medical history, was referred acutely to our emergency department with abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice. He denied alcohol use and had no predisposition to cancer, pulmonary, or gastrointestinal (GI) diseases. As a gardener, he had no relevant occupational exposures. During the last 4 weeks, he had suffered from a lack of appetite, dull pain in the right upper abdominal quadrant, and had an unintended weight loss of 10 kg. He denied any respiratory symptoms, change in bowel habits, melena, or fever.
At physical examination, he was chronically ill with a body mass index of 18, jaundice and abdominal pain on palpation of the upper abdominal quadrant. Pulmonary and cardiac auscultation was normal and no exanthema was present.
Laboratory tests showed leucopenia of 2.50x109/L (3.50-8.80x109/L) and increased liver enzymes tests with alanine transaminase of 441 IU/L (10-70 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase of 194 IU/L (35-105 IU/L), bilirubin of 196 micromol/l (5-25 micromol/L), and lactate dehydrogenase of 218 U/L (105-205 U/L). Pancreas amylase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, C-reactive protein, haemoglobin, thrombocyte concentration, calcium, and creatinine were within normal limits. Because of the liver involvement, hepatitis was suspected, but serology test for Hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, and Leptospirosis were negative. There were normal immunoglobulin subgroups and autoimmunological tests, including anti-nuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, which were negative. However, an increased blood angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) above 88 U/L (8-53 U/L) was observed.
Lung function tests showed normal ventilation and diffusion parameters with forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 4.4l, corresponding to 102% of predicted; forced vital capacity (FVC) of 5.7l, corresponding to 105% of predicted; and lung diffusion of carbon monoxide (DLCO) corresponding to 85% of predicted. Total lung capacity was not measured.
Because of the biochemical signs of hepatitis, an abdominal sonography was performed, uncovering lymphadenopathy in the lever hilus. The patient underwent computer tomography (CT) of thorax and abdomen, which revealed lesions in the pancreas, bilateral pulmonary nodular infiltrates, as well as mediastinal and intraabdominal lymphadenopathy (Figs. 1-3).
As metastatic cancer was suspected, a whole-body 18 flour-deoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18-FDG PET) scanning was performed, presenting multiple pathological lesions in lungs, pancreas, lymph nodes, and bones (Fig. 4).
A sonography-guided lever biopsy showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. The patient underwent further invasive procedures: bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy (TBB), bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with flowcytometry, endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) with transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNAB) biopsy, and a bone marrow biopsy. None of the pathological tests revealed any malignant findings. Bronchoscopy was without any macroscopic abnormalities. BAL flowcytometry uncovered an overall lymphocytic inflammation with a proportion of 51%, an increased CD4/CD8 ratio of 5.4 without any eosinofilia or neutrofilia. Pathological evaluation of the samples from the TBBs demonstrated non-caseating granulomas and EBUS-TBNAB from the mediastinal lymph nodes showed unspecific fibrosis. Microbiological tests from the bronchoscopy specimens did not reveal any respiratory infection (no growth of bacteria in cultivation, negative tuberculosis tests including cultivation, negative PCR tests concerning Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumonia, Chlamydia psittaci et pneumoniae, and Pneumocystis jirovecii).
We considered the following differential diagnoses: metastatic malignancy with unknown primary tumour, liver diseases (hepatitis, both infectious and autoimmune, biliary cirrhosis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis), infectious diseases (leptospirosis, AIDS, and tuberculosis), and autoimmune systemic diseases.
Based on the composite findings (increased blood ACE, various FDG metabolic active lesions in the PET-scanning, non-caseating inflammation in liver biopsy and TBBs, lymphocytic inflammation with increased CD4/CD8 ratio in BAL) and exclusion of other diseases capable of producing a similar pathological and clinical picture, a diagnosis of systemic sarcoidosis was well established.
The patient was treated with systemic prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day=37.5 mg/day), slowly tapering every third week (25 mg/day for 3 weeks, then 12.5 mg for 3 weeks), until a fixed dose of 7.5 mg prednisolone/day was reached. Three weeks into the treatment, blood tests showed normalised ACE and liver function parameters. At present we follow him in our respiratory outpatient clinic and plan to fully taper steroids according to the disease activity.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 45-year-old never-smoking Danish male gardener presented acutely with abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, and a 10 kg weight loss over 4 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 4 weeks preceding acute emergency department referral, the patient experienced loss of appetite, dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and an unintentional 10 kg weight loss, culminating in acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and frank jaundice without fever or respiratory complaints.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable; never-smoker, gardener with no occupational exposures, denied alcohol use, and had no family predisposition to cancer, pulmonary, or gastrointestinal disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper quadrant abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, and 10 kg weight loss; negative for respiratory symptoms, fever, melena, or change in bowel habits.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically ill appearance with BMI 18 kg/m2, frank jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness on palpation; normal pulmonary and cardiac auscultation; no skin exanthema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Leukopenia with WBC 2.50 x 10^9/L (reference: 3.50–8.80 x 10^9/L); cholestatic and hepatocellular liver injury with ALT 441 IU/L (10–70 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase 194 IU/L (35–105 IU/L), total bilirubin 196 μmol/L (5–25 μmol/L), and LDH 218 U/L (105–205 U/L); normal pancreatic amylase, GGT, CRP, hemoglobin, platelets, serum calcium, and creatinine. Negative infectious and autoimmune screening: Negative HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV, and Leptospirosis serologies; normal immunoglobulin subclasses; negative ANA and ANCA. Sarcoidosis biomarker: Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) >88 U/L (reference: 8–53 U/L). Pulmonary function tests: Normal spirometry and diffusion (FEV1 4.4 L [102% predicted], FVC 5.7 L [105% predicted], DLCO 85% predicted). Abdominal ultrasound: Enlarged lymph nodes in the hepatic hilum.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracoabdominal CT and whole-body 18F-FDG PET-CT: Multiple FDG-avid lesions involving the pancreas, bilateral nodular lung infiltrates, mediastinal and intra-abdominal lymph nodes, and bones (initially mimicking disseminated metastatic pancreatic cancer). Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, bronchoscopy with BAL flow cytometry, transbronchial biopsy (TBB), EBUS-TBNA, and bone marrow biopsy: Liver biopsy and TBB demonstrated non-caseating epithelioid granulomas; EBUS-TBNA of mediastinal nodes showed nonspecific fibrosis; bone marrow biopsy and all tissue specimens were negative for malignancy; BAL flow cytometry revealed lymphocytic alveolitis (51% lymphocytes) with an elevated CD4/CD8 ratio of 5.4; bronchoscopic microbiological cultures and PCRs were negative for bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci/pneumoniae, and Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Multisystem extrapulmonary and pulmonary sarcoidosis (involving the liver, pancreas, lungs, lymph nodes, and bone) masquerading as metastatic pancreatic cancer, definitively confirmed by non-caseating granulomas on liver and transbronchial biopsies, lymphocytic BAL (51% lymphocytes, CD4/CD8 ratio 5.4), and elevated serum ACE (>88 U/L) after excluding malignancy, tuberculosis, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Plan and clinical course: Treated with systemic oral prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day = 37.5 mg/day, tapered every 3 weeks to 25 mg/day, 12.5 mg/day, and maintenance 7.5 mg/day). Within 3 weeks of initiating corticosteroid therapy, his serum ACE and liver function tests completely normalized.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 77 year-old Hispanic male who initially presented to the emergency room with a 6-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, cough productive of yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, worsening fatigue and weight loss of 10 lbs. On admission, he denied fever, chills, chest pain, sick contacts, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure and history. His past medical history was significant for Non-Hodgkin follicular B cell lymphoma (NHL) diagnosed in 1997, treated with Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin and Prednisone (RCHOP) three times. Last treatment was completed 1 year prior to presentation. He also had biopsy-confirmed cutaneous Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS), identified within the same year of presentation, treated with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 20 mg/m 2 once every 21 days for two cycles.
On admission, he had a low grade fever and was tachycardic. His physical exam was remarkable for a 2 cm firm, non-tender, mobile right submandibular lymph node. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. He was grossly anasarcic with 4 (+) pitting edema of the lower extremities. He also had multiple violet, non-tender skin lesions localized to the lower extremities, mainly around the medial aspect of his ankles and anterior thighs bilaterally.
His labs revealed a normal cardiac panel, a white blood cell (WBC) count of 8,100/mm 3 with no leukocytosis. Manual differentiation of the white blood cells showed 28% neutrophils, 48% lymphocytes, 17% monocytes and 5% eosinophils. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative for infections. Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. 
A chest X-ray done on admission showed a right lung consolidation consistent with pneumonia thus the patient was started on empiric vancomycin 1gm every 12 hours and piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5gm every 8 hours for a duration of 8 days. A computerized axial tomographic (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, showed numerous nodular opacities throughout each lung which were suspected to be consistent with KS as well as small pleural effusions in both lungs ( Figure 1).
Despite completing a course of antibiotics for pneumonia, his symptoms did not improve. A follow-up CT scan of the chest demonstrated that the bilateral pleural effusions had worsened ( Figure 2). Patient underwent a thoracentesis of the larger effusion in the right lung which showed a sero-sanguineous and exudative fluid based on chemistry analysis. Histopathology failed to demonstrate malignant cells.
A bronchoscopy was also performed, revealing diffusely hyperemic and edematous mucosa of the lower airways with mucopurulent secretions ( Figure 3). Biopsy was not performed at this time given concern for endobronchial bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) stains and cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi or acid fast bacilli. Pneumocystis jiroveci PCR and fluid cytology were also negative but PCR for HHV-8 showed 5800 DNA copies/mL. The patient had a HIV p24 rapid antigen test done which was negative.
After two weeks of supportive treatment, the patient's symptoms began to improve. He continued to have numerous indurated confluent lesions on his body and face consistent with KS. His pulmonary symptoms were thought to be due to disseminated KS. Following significant discussions with the patient and his family regarding the poor prognosis of his disease, he decided not to undergo any further antineoplastic treatments and eventually was discharged home with hospice.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 77-year-old Hispanic male with a history of follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma and cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma presented with a 6-week history of progressive exertional dyspnea, productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, fatigue, and a 10-pound weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department after 6 weeks of progressive shortness of breath on exertion, cough productive of yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, worsening fatigue, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss. He had completed his third course of R-CHOP chemotherapy for follicular B-cell lymphoma 1 year prior and had received two cycles of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (20 mg/m2 q21d) within the past year for biopsy-proven cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (diagnosed 1997, treated with three courses of R-CHOP, last completed 1 year prior); biopsy-confirmed cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma (diagnosed within the past year, treated with two cycles of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive exertional dyspnea, productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent hemoptysis, fatigue, 10-pound weight loss, generalized edema, and violaceous lower extremity skin lesions; negative for subjective fever, chills, chest pain, sick contacts, recent travel, or TB exposure.

objective.physical_examination: Low-grade fever and tachycardia on admission; a 2 cm firm, non-tender, mobile right submandibular lymph node; clear lungs to auscultation bilaterally; gross anasarca with 4+ bilateral lower extremity pitting edema; multiple non-tender violaceous indurated skin plaques and nodules over the medial ankles, anterior thighs, trunk, and face.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 8,100/mm3 (manual differential: 28% neutrophils, 48% lymphocytes, 17% monocytes, 5% eosinophils); normal cardiac panel; negative urinalysis and urine culture; negative HIV p24 rapid antigen test. Blood cultures: Positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Admission chest X-ray: Right lung consolidation. Right thoracentesis fluid analysis: Serosanguineous exudative pleural fluid negative for malignant cells.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans: Numerous bilateral pulmonary nodular opacities and bilateral pleural effusions that worsened despite 8 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Diffusely hyperemic, edematous lower airway mucosa with mucopurulent secretions (endobronchial biopsy deferred due to bleeding risk); BAL stains, cultures, and cytology were negative for bacteria, fungi, acid-fast bacilli, malignancy, and Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR, whereas BAL quantitative PCR for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) was strongly positive at 5,800 DNA copies/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated HIV-negative pulmonary and cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma (confirmed by characteristic violaceous mucocutaneous lesions, diffuse hyperemic airways, bilateral pulmonary nodules, and 5,800 HHV-8 DNA copies/mL on BAL PCR, with Pneumocystis jirovecii excluded by negative BAL PCR) complicated by concurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia/pneumonia in a patient previously treated with R-CHOP for follicular lymphoma. Plan and clinical course: Treated with an 8-day course of intravenous vancomycin (1 g q12h) and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q8h), therapeutic right thoracentesis, and 2 weeks of supportive care with symptomatic improvement; following goals-of-care discussions regarding the poor prognosis of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma, the patient declined further chemotherapy and was discharged home with hospice.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with a 3-day history of fever up to 39 C, non-productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Dyspnea worsened 12 h before admission. The patient had no relevant occupational exposure, known allergies, travel history, or previous lung disease. She was a smoker (10 pack-year) and her medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, depression, and recurrent UTIs which were treated with nitrofurantoin, 100 mg/day, for the previous 23 days.
On the day of admission, the patient was afebrile, blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, pulse rate was 120/min and respiratory rate was 28/min. Auscultation of the chest revealed fine inspiratory crackles on the middle and lower lung zones bilaterally. The rest of physical examination did not reveal noteworthy findings. Arterial blood gas (ABG) on room air showed type I acute respiratory failure (pH = 7.46, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) = 26 mmHg, partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) = 49 mmHg, bicarbonate (HCO3 -) = 21 mEq/L), while the clinical indicator of hypoxemia, the ratio of partial pressure arterial oxygen, and fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) was 233 and the alveolar-arterial PO2 difference ([A-a]PO2) was 63. The electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia without any other abnormalities. Laboratory results showed increased leucocytes (15.500 K/muL) and eosinophils (2.260 K/muL), with mildly increased inflammatory markers. Chest X-ray showed reticular changes bilaterally on the mid and lower lung zones and bilateral pleural effusions (Fig. 1). High resolution computerized tomography (HRCT) scan of the chest showed bilateral inter and intralobular septal thickening mainly involving the mid and lower lung zones, centrilobular nodules bilaterally, bilateral small pleural effusions, and patchy ground glass opacities (Fig. 2). On the day of admission, computerized tomography-pulmonary angiogram ruled out pulmonary embolism and the echocardiogram showed no structural or functional abnormalities.
Differential diagnosis included diseases presenting with type I acute respiratory failure and reticulo-nodular opacities on HRCT, such as respiratory infections, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and interstitial lung diseases with rapid onset and worsening (acute interstitial pneumonia, acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, drug reaction, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, connective tissue disease and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage).
The patient was supported with supplemental oxygen. Treatment with ceftriaxone and macrolide was administered pending the results of the laboratory tests. Nitrofurantoin was suspected to be the cause and it was discontinued immediately.
The patient's condition rapidly improved within 24 h: she had no shortness of breath, auscultation of the chest revealed fine inspiratory crackles only on the lower lung zones, the chest X-ray improved with reticular shadowing on the lower lung zones and ABG's on room air showed pH = 7,42, PaCO2 = 36 mmHg, PaO2 = 73 mmHg, and HCO3 - = 24 mEq/L.
As part of the investigational process, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed and the results showed 12% eosinophilia and CD+ 4/CD+ 8 ratio of 1.26 (normal). Microscopic examination and cultures of BAL for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii, bacteria and fungi were negative. Polymerase chain reaction of BAL for influenza and P. jirovecii was negative. Cytology test of BAL and sputum showed no malignant cells. Cultures of sputum, blood, and urine were sterile. Nasopharyngeal swab specimen testing for influenza was negative. Urine antigens for Legionella pneumophila and S Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Serology tests for Human Immunodeficiency Virus, Hepatitis C virus, Hepatitis B virus, chlamydia, mycoplasma, rickettsia, aspergillus, and common viruses were also negative. Complement factors, quantitative immunoglobulin levels, thyroid hormones, and serum angiotensin converting enzyme were within normal limits. Mantoux test was 0 mm. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Total Immunoglobulin (Ig)E of the blood was increased (203.54 UI/mL). Microscopic examination of peripheral blood smear showed eosinophilia.
Five days after admission, pulmonary function tests were performed and showed the ratio Forced expiratory volume in 1 sec to Forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) = 81%, FEV1 = 2.31(99%), FVC = 2.86(104%), Total lung capacity = 4.27(89%), Residual volume = 1.19(67%), Diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) = 91%, DLCOadj = 99%.
The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary toxicity due to nitrofurantoin use.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old Caucasian female presented with a 3-day history of high fever up to 39 °C, nonproductive cough, and progressive shortness of breath that acutely worsened 12 hours before admission after taking nitrofurantoin for 23 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been taking oral nitrofurantoin (100 mg/day) for the preceding 23 days for recurrent urinary tract infections. Three days prior to hospital admission, she developed fever up to 39 °C, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea that markedly worsened 12 hours prior to presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent urinary tract infections (treated with nitrofurantoin 100 mg/day for 23 days); hypertension; hypothyroidism; depression; 10-pack-year smoking history; no prior lung disease, occupational exposures, or recent travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for antecedent fever up to 39 °C, nonproductive cough, and acute progressive dyspnea. No previously known drug allergies. Home medications included nitrofurantoin 100 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Afebrile on arrival, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats/min, and respiratory rate 28 breaths/min. Chest auscultation: Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles over the middle and lower lung zones; remainder of physical exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission room-air arterial blood gas: Acute type I respiratory failure with pH 7.46, PaCO2 26 mmHg, PaO2 49 mmHg, HCO3- 21 mEq/L, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 233, and alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-aDO2) 63 mmHg (improving within 24 hours of stopping nitrofurantoin to room-air pH 7.42, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 73 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L). Hematology and biochemistry: Leukocytosis with WBC 15,500/μL, marked peripheral eosinophilia with absolute eosinophils 2,260/μL (confirmed on blood smear), elevated total serum IgE (203.54 IU/mL), and mildly elevated inflammatory markers; normal complement, immunoglobulins, thyroid hormones, and serum ACE; negative RF, ANA, and Mantoux PPD (0 mm). Negative infectious workup: Sterile sputum, blood, and urine cultures; negative nasopharyngeal influenza swab; negative urinary Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae antigens; negative serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Rickettsia, Aspergillus, and respiratory viruses. ECG and echocardiography: Sinus tachycardia with normal cardiac structure and function. Chest X-ray: Bilateral mid- and lower-zone reticular changes and small pleural effusions.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography and high-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Ruled out pulmonary embolism; demonstrated bilateral interlobular and intralobular septal thickening (predominantly mid and lower zones), bilateral centrilobular nodules, patchy ground-glass opacities, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): BAL cell count showed 12% eosinophilia and a normal CD4+/CD8+ ratio of 1.26; BAL microscopy, cultures, and PCR were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, influenza, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, bacteria, fungi, and malignant cells. Day 5 pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Normal spirometry and diffusion (FEV1/FVC 81%, FEV1 2.31 L [99%], FVC 2.86 L [104%], TLC 4.27 L [89%], RV 1.19 L [67%], DLCO 91%, DLCOadj 99%).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary toxicity / eosinophilic hypersensitivity pneumonitis presenting with type I respiratory failure, peripheral eosinophilia (2,260/μL), BAL eosinophilia (12%), and elevated IgE (203.54 IU/mL), confirmed by rapid clinical, arterial blood gas (PaO2 rising from 49 to 73 mmHg on room air), and radiographic resolution within 24 hours of drug withdrawal and negative BAL PCR/cultures for Pneumocystis jirovecii and other pathogens. Plan and clinical course: Nitrofurantoin was immediately discontinued on admission and supplemental oxygen plus brief empiric ceftriaxone and macrolide therapy were provided; her dyspnea resolved within 24 hours and lung function completely normalized by hospital day 5.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old African American female presented at four-week gestation with a nonproductive cough and severe shortness of breath that began four days prior with progressive worsening. The patient reported no history of recent travel. Oxygen was administered via nasal cannula and was well tolerated.
On physical examination, the patient was tachycardic (126 bpm) and tachypneic (36 breaths/min); temperature was 36.9 C; blood pressure was 132/81 mm Hg; and peripheral oxygen saturation was 98%. Pulmonary auscultation revealed diffuse wheezing and diminished breathing sounds in bilateral lung bases.
Echocardiogram ruled out valvular disease and myocardial wall abnormalities. Laboratory tests at the time of admission revealed an arterial blood gas analysis within normal limits, anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 mg/dL, hematocrit 34.1), and a normal platelet count (339,000). Chest X-ray revealed bilateral lung opacities with relative sparing of the right upper lobe and left pleural effusions (Figure 1(a)).
Computed tomography (CT) scan showed multifocal, bilateral, predominantly peripheral airspace opacities (Figure 1(b)). A nonspecific differential for this pattern of distribution included eosinophilic lung disease, sarcoidosis, pulmonary infarction, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, and chronic interstitial lung disease with atelectatic components at the dependent regions of both lungs. No pulmonary emboli to the segmental arteries were found.
She was admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia and developed hemoptysis two days after admission, only completing four days of azithromycin and ceftriaxone. A bronchoscopy with lavage was performed. The bronchial cytology sample showed numerous macrophages, some with cytoplasmic vacuoles, and abundant blood, suggestive of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
She was subsequently transferred to the Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU) with a differential diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus, Wegener's granulomatosis, pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, and other autoimmune and infectious diseases. Autoimmune laboratory workup for anti-beta 2 glycoprotein, antistreptolysin, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anticardiolipin, anti-GMB, anti-smooth muscle Ab, Anti-Jo, ssA, ssB, RF, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA showed negative results, ruling out the aforementioned autoimmune etiologies.
The patient tested negative for HIV. An infectious disease panel performed on the bronchoalveolar lavage samples of right and left lower lobes testing for HSV, CMV, EBV, PCP, atypical pneumonia panel (M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, and L. pneumophila), viral panel (metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, influenza viruses A and B, RSV A and RSV B, parainfluenza viruses 1, 2, and 3, and adenovirus), Aspergillus galactomannan, and Legionella pneumophila showed negative results. Thus it decreased the likelihood of any previously mentioned infectious diagnosis.
A wedge biopsy tissue of the right lower lobe revealed intra-alveolar hemorrhage with dilated capillaries containing nonrefractile vacuole-like structures suggestive of deposition of lipoid material (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). The lining of the dilated capillaries was positive for CD31 immunostain. Lymphatic spaces were also positive for D2-40 immunostain. No venoocclusive disease or features of arterial pulmonary hypertension were seen on EVG stain. These pathological findings raised concern for silicone embolism.
After discussion of the histological findings with the primary team, the patient was reinterrogated and she stated that she underwent twelve cosmetic subcutaneous silicone injections in the buttocks in the past by unlicensed practitioners. Her most recent injection occurred two months prior to this admission.
Within two weeks, she reported symptomatic improvement after supportive treatment and was discharged. Then, the patient was lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old African American female at 4 weeks' gestation presented with a 4-day history of progressively worsening severe shortness of breath and nonproductive cough, followed 2 days after admission by frank hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented at 4 weeks of pregnancy with a 4-day history of nonproductive cough and rapidly worsening dyspnea, developing frank hemoptysis on hospital day 2. Upon targeted re-questioning after lung biopsy, she disclosed having undergone 12 illicit cosmetic subcutaneous silicone injections into her buttocks by unlicensed practitioners, with the most recent injection performed 2 months prior to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Early intrauterine pregnancy (4 weeks' gestation); 12 prior cosmetic subcutaneous gluteal silicone injections by unlicensed practitioners (most recent 2 months prior to admission); no recent travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nonproductive cough, severe progressive shortness of breath, and subsequent hemoptysis (day 2).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Heart rate 126 beats/min (tachycardic), respiratory rate 36 breaths/min (tachypneic), temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 132/81 mmHg, and SpO2 98% on nasal cannula oxygen. Chest auscultation: Diffuse wheezing and diminished breath sounds at both lung bases.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normal arterial blood gas analysis, mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, hematocrit 34.1%), and normal platelets (339,000/μL). Autoimmune and infectious serologies: Negative HIV test; negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-GBM, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, RF, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Sm, anti-Jo-1, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein, and ASO titers. Admission chest X-ray: Bilateral pulmonary opacities (relatively sparing the right upper lobe) and a left pleural effusion. Echocardiogram: Normal valves and myocardial wall motion.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Multifocal, bilateral, predominantly peripheral airspace opacities without segmental pulmonary embolism. Bronchoscopy with bilateral lower lobe bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Grossly bloody lavage fluid with numerous vacuolated macrophages diagnostic of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH); comprehensive BAL infectious panel was completely negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP), HSV, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, respiratory viruses (influenza A/B, RSV A/B, parainfluenza 1–3, metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, adenovirus), and Aspergillus galactomannan. Right lower lobe surgical wedge lung biopsy: Intra-alveolar hemorrhage with dilated CD31-positive capillaries and D2-40-positive lymphatics containing nonrefractile vacuole-like lipoid/silicone globules (without veno-occlusive disease on EVG stain), diagnostic of pulmonary silicone embolism.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Delayed-onset pulmonary silicone embolism syndrome presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) during early pregnancy (2 months after illicit subcutaneous gluteal silicone injections), definitively confirmed by nonrefractile intravascular/lymphatic silicone vacuoles and intra-alveolar hemorrhage on right lower lobe wedge biopsy after excluding autoimmune vasculitis and Pneumocystis jirovecii or viral/bacterial infections via BAL. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin were stopped after 4 days; she was managed in the MICU with supplemental oxygen and supportive care, achieving symptomatic recovery and hospital discharge within 2 weeks.

raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old African American man with AIDS presented with complaints of pleuritic chest pain, exertional shortness of breath, and hemoptysis of 3-week duration. He reported 10-pound weight loss in 6 months, drenching night sweats, and fever. He denied tobacco use but admitted using marijuana in the past. He denied neurological, gastrointestinal, or dermatological symptoms and had no recent travel. He was being treated with dapsone and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir but was poorly compliant.
Of note, he was admitted 3 months earlier for similar complaints and was diagnosed with atypical pneumonia. A CT scan of the chest done on that admission showed diffuse fine noncalcified nodular densities in both lungs and small to moderate bilateral axillary, mediastinal, and hilar adenopathy. Bronchoscopy was unrevealing for endobronchial lesions. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid fast bacilli, or fungal infection.
On index presentation, he had bilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy with signs of right lower lung zone consolidation on chest examination. There were no lesions on the skin or mucosa. Complete blood count was significant for normocytic anemia and metabolic panel was within normal limits. Absolute CD4 cell count is of 102 cells mu/L (17%). A repeat CT scan of the chest showed significant worsening of fibronodular infiltrates with consolidation in the right middle and lower lobes and left upper and lower lobes with bilateral axillary, supraclavicular, mediastinal, and hilar lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). Subsequent bronchoscopy revealed erythematous lesions on the proximal and distal part of the trachea and right middle lobe (Figure 2). Left main stem had vascular markings with dilated veins. These findings were consistent with endobronchial KS. Transbronchial biopsy was done and pathology was positive for atypical spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, and extravasated red blood cells (Figure 3). Nuclear HHV8 immunostain was expressed in atypical cells consistent with Kaposi Sarcoma.
He was started on a different HAART regimen: abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine after consultation with the infectious disease team. The patient tolerated the new medication and was discharged with appropriate follow-up. However he was readmitted twice: once with Immune Reconstitution Syndrome and the second time with massive hemoptysis. He developed acute respiratory failure, which unfortunately led to his death.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old African American man with AIDS presented with a 3-week history of pleuritic chest pain, exertional shortness of breath, and hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been hospitalized 3 months earlier for similar symptoms diagnosed as atypical pneumonia (with diffuse fine noncalcified pulmonary nodules and negative BAL for Pneumocystis jirovecii, AFB, and fungi), re-presented with 3 weeks of pleuritic chest pain, exertional dyspnea, and hemoptysis, accompanied by fever, drenching night sweats, and a 10-pound weight loss over 6 months. He was prescribed dapsone and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir for HIV/AIDS but was poorly compliant.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS with medication noncompliance; hospitalized 3 months prior for presumed atypical pneumonia. Social history: Never smoked tobacco, past marijuana use, no recent travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pleuritic chest pain, exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, fever, drenching night sweats, and 10-pound weight loss; negative for neurological, gastrointestinal, or dermatological symptoms. Prescribed home medications (noncompliant) were dapsone and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir.

objective.physical_examination: Bilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy; physical signs of right lower lung zone consolidation on chest examination; no mucocutaneous lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and chemistry: Normocytic anemia with normal comprehensive metabolic panel.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Absolute CD4+ T-cell count 102 cells/μL (17%). Prior admission chest CT and bronchoscopy (3 months earlier): Diffuse fine noncalcified bilateral pulmonary nodules and bilateral axillary/mediastinal/hilar adenopathy; no endobronchial lesions; BAL negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi. Index admission repeat chest CT: Marked progression of bilateral fibronodular infiltrates with consolidation in the right middle/lower lobes and left upper/lower lobes plus bilateral axillary, supraclavicular, mediastinal, and hilar lymphadenopathy. Index bronchoscopy and transbronchial lung biopsy: Erythematous endobronchial lesions in the proximal and distal trachea and right middle lobe with prominent dilated vascular markings in the left mainstem bronchus; transbronchial biopsy pathology demonstrated atypical spindle-cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, extravasated erythrocytes, and positive nuclear HHV-8 immunostaining diagnostic of pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary endobronchial and parenchymal pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma without mucocutaneous involvement in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 102 cells/μL), definitively confirmed by HHV-8-positive atypical spindle-cell proliferation on transbronchial lung biopsy (with Pneumocystis jirovecii, mycobacteria, and fungi excluded on BAL). Plan and clinical course: Antiretroviral therapy was switched to abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine, which he tolerated well at discharge; however, he required two subsequent readmissions—first for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) and second for massive hemoptysis and fatal acute respiratory failure.

raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old woman with an 18-year history of ASS and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) overlap complicated by 5 years of nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) presented to the emergency department with 2 weeks of progressively worsening dyspnea and cough. The patient was diagnosed with polymyositis via muscle biopsy approximately 20 years prior. At 38 years of age, she developed progressively worsening exertional dyspnea. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive, confirming a diagnosis of ASS. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral subpleural ground glass reticulation and fibrosis, consistent with NSIP. A transbronchial lung biopsy also confirmed NSIP. Current immunosuppressive regimen included tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine for ASS.
Initial blood pressure was 149/59 mm Hg, heart rate of 103/minute, respiratory rate of 26/minute, temperature 38.2 C, and pulse oximetry (SpO2) 79% on room air. The patient appeared to be in mild to moderate respiratory distress and had coarse bi-basilar crackles. Admission chest radiography showed new diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities (Figure 1). Initial laboratory data showed a white blood cell count of 24 500/mm3 (38% neutrophils and 54% lymphocytes), a hemoglobin of 12.2 g/dL, platelet count of 268 000, blood urea nitrogen 26, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, and potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Initial differential diagnoses included the adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) from infection versus an acute exacerbation of ILD.
She was admitted to the intensive care unit and initially supported with high-flow oxygen via nasal cannula. Empiric antimicrobials targeting health care-associated pathogens and influenza were started for a working diagnosis of infectious pneumonia-induced ARDS in an immunocompromised host.
Urine Streptococcus, Legionella, Histoplasma, and Blastomycosis antigens were negative. Sputum gram stain and culture, sputum fungal culture, respiratory influenza nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), respiratory viral NAAT, serum cytomegalovirus NAAT, Pneumocystis jiroveci direct fluorescent antibody, and serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen were all negative.
On hospital day 2, chest CT revealed bilateral patchy consolidation and multiple enlarged axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes (Figure 2). On hospital day 3, her hypoxemia and clinical condition continued to decline necessitating endotracheal intubation. Bronchoscopy for airway examination was unremarkable. Bronchoalveolar lavage for infectious testing was also negative. On hospital day 5, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsies were taken from the right middle and lower lobes. Histopathology revealed peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS; Figure 3A and B). Staging workup revealed stage 4 disease. On hospital day 10, a chemotherapeutic regimen of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone was started. Chest CT revealed interval improvement in pulmonary infiltrates and patchy consolidation (Figure 4), and the patient was extubated on hospital day 13 and discharged home on hospital day 28 with 3 liters per minute oxygen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old woman with an 18-year history of antisynthetase syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis overlap complicated by nonspecific interstitial pneumonia presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening dyspnea and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with biopsy-proven polymyositis ~20 years earlier, anti-Jo-1-positive antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) and rheumatoid arthritis overlap 18 years earlier, and transbronchial biopsy-proven nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) at age 38 (5 years prior), the patient was maintained on tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine. She presented to the emergency department after 2 weeks of progressively worsening shortness of breath and cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Polymyositis (diagnosed 20 years prior); anti-Jo-1-positive antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) overlap (18 years); biopsy-proven nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP, 5 years).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressively worsening dyspnea, cough, and fever. Home medications were tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: Blood pressure 149/59 mmHg, heart rate 103 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, temperature 38.2 °C, and SpO2 79% on room air. Physical exam: Mild-to-moderate respiratory distress with coarse bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Leukocytosis with WBC 24,500/mm3 (38% neutrophils, 54% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 268,000/mm3, BUN 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, and potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Negative microbiological workup: Negative urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella, Histoplasma, and Blastomyces antigens; negative sputum Gram stain, bacterial/fungal cultures, respiratory viral and influenza NAATs, serum CMV NAAT, Pneumocystis jirovecii direct fluorescent antibody (DFA), and serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen. Admission chest radiograph: New diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Hospital day 2 chest CT: Bilateral patchy consolidations and multiple enlarged axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes superimposed on chronic subpleural ground-glass reticulation/fibrosis. Hospital day 3 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Unremarkable airway inspection and negative BAL infectious studies. Hospital day 5 video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) lung biopsies of the right middle and lower lobes: Histopathology and staging workup established stage IV peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Stage IV pulmonary peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS; confirmed by VATS right middle and lower lobe lung biopsies) masquerading as acute ARDS or interstitial lung disease exacerbation in a patient with antisynthetase syndrome/RA overlap on tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and other opportunistic infections excluded by negative DFA, BAL, and cultures. Plan and clinical course: Supported initially with high-flow nasal cannula oxygen and empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobials, then intubated on hospital day 3 for progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure. Following VATS confirmation of PTCL-NOS, CHOP chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) was initiated on hospital day 10, leading to rapid improvement of pulmonary consolidations on repeat chest CT, extubation on hospital day 13, and discharge home on hospital day 28 on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen.

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old Caucasian woman recently diagnosed with CMML presented to our rheumatology office for evaluation of an abnormal chest computed tomography (CT) showing inflammation surrounding the entire thoracic and abdominal aorta. She was experiencing shortness of breath, fatigue, fevers, and night sweats for about four months previously. She additionally had an unintentional weight loss of 35 pounds over the past 2 years which was initially attributed to Nissen fundoplication procedure for gastroesophageal reflux. She denied any headaches, vision changes, scalp tenderness, jaw pain, dysphagia, joint pain, joint swelling, muscle pain, or photosensitivity.
For the past eight months, she had been undergoing hematological workup of abnormal blood counts. Her white blood cell (WBC) counts were elevated with monocytosis and varying degrees of neutrophilia over the past 3 years. She had thrombocytosis. Her initial evaluation was negative for BCR-ABL PCR testing, Janus kinase-2, calreticulin, and MPL mutations. There was no hepatosplenomegaly on imaging. After these tests returned negative, she was planned for a bone marrow biopsy for further evaluation of monocytosis but opted to wait as she was asymptomatic. However, she presented back with a nontender, erythematous lesion on her left breast. About two weeks later, similar scattered pink small dermal papulonodules were present on the posterior neck, left shoulder, abdomen, and left thigh. Left breast punch biopsy described a dense dermal infiltrate with small lymphocytes with cytologic atypia. There was no significant epidermal involvement. The lymphocytes were positive for CD4 and CD43, myeloperoxidase, and lysozyme. The overall morphologic and immunohistochemical findings were those of a malignant neoplasm. Although this was originally thought to be a possible T cell lymphoma, case was discussed at the hematopathology conference and the overall presentation correlated with more systemic process, such as CMML.
Subsequent bone marrow biopsy and aspiration showed pieces of hypercellular bone marrow with overall cellularity of 50%, trilineage hematopoiesis, hypogranular myeloid cells, and increase of monocytoid cells with somewhat immature appearing features. Increased monocytosis (20%) with oval-shaped, slightly irregular nuclei was present. There was no evidence of fibrosis on reticulin staining. Adequate megakaryopoiesis and erythropoiesis without dysplastic changes was noted. The myeloid-to-erythroid ratio was mildly increased. Cytogenetic evaluation exhibited a normal karyotype (46, XX). Flow cytometry revealed CD14+/CD16- monocytes that are characteristic of CMML. CMML diagnosis was made based on the above findings, persistent peripheral blood monocytosis >= 1 x 109/L, with monocytes accounting for >=10% of the WBC count, no evidence of PDGFRA/PDGFRB, <20% blasts in the blood and bone marrow, not meeting WHO criteria for BCR-ABL1 positive chronic myeloid leukemia, primary myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, or essential thrombocytosis and all other causes of monocytosis excluded. For staging, she underwent positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) scans and both imaging studies showed soft tissue density surrounding the entirety of the thoracic and abdominal aorta, consistent with large-vessel vasculitis (see Figures 1 and 2).
Laboratory studies were positive for antinuclear antibody (ANA) with a titer of 1 : 640 in a nucleolar and speckled pattern as well as elevated RNP antibody (ab) at 1.1. Her inflammatory markers were elevated: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 36 mm/hr and C-reactive protein (CRP) 35.3 mg/L. The negative serologies included an anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic ab, anti-proteinase 3 ab, anti-myeloperoxidase ab, SS-A/SS-B ab, anti-Smith ab, anti-dsDNA ab, anti-smooth muscle ab, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide ab, and hepatitis panel.
For symptomatic aortitis, we started treatment with prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. Within a week, patient had significant improvement. Her shortness of breath subsided and she felt strong and energetic. Objectively, while on steroid therapy, her WBC count initially dropped. Since the aortitis related symptoms were improving, the hematology team planned to start her on treatment with a hypomethylating agent:azacitidine.
Steroid therapy was slowly tapered given her good response to initial high-dose steroids. However, two months later, she developed steroid-induced myopathy and prednisone was tapered more quickly. Within two weeks, she became more dyspneic and hypoxic. Her respiratory status deteriorated quickly, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. She was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for possible infectious etiology. CT chest demonstrated stable aortitis but increased diffuse ground-glass opacity throughout both lungs and bilateral pulmonary consolidation. These findings were attributed to paraneoplastic infiltrates from leukemia and less likely to be infectious. Cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage and Pneumocystis jirovecii testing were negative. Coincidentally, prior to this admission, she had a stable WBC count of 18,600/muL that now has progressed to WBC count of 77,000/muL, despite negative infectious workup, aortitis being asymptomatic and stable on CT imaging study.
Given her clinical deterioration from leukemia, in her final days she received her first treatment of CMML with hydroxyurea, then underwent leukapheresis, and received one dose of chemotherapy with decitabine one day prior to expiration. Unfortunately, she continued to deteriorate and was placed on hospice. Her family refused an autopsy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old Caucasian woman newly diagnosed with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) and paraneoplastic large-vessel aortitis presented with a 4-month history of shortness of breath, fatigue, fevers, and night sweats, and 2.5 months after starting prednisone developed acute severe hypoxemic respiratory failure during a rapid steroid taper.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over 4 months prior to rheumatology evaluation, the patient experienced dyspnea, fatigue, fevers, night sweats, and a 35-pound weight loss over 2 years, along with a 3-year history of persistent monocytosis/neutrophilia and recent leukemia cutis papulonodules (on the left breast, neck, shoulder, abdomen, and thigh). Staging PET/CT and bone marrow biopsy established chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) complicated by pan-thoracoabdominal large-vessel aortitis. High-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) produced rapid resolution of her dyspnea and aortitis symptoms within 1 week. However, 2 months later she developed steroid-induced myopathy, prompting an accelerated prednisone taper; within 2 weeks of rapid tapering, she developed acute severe dyspnea and hypoxemia requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) with leukemia cutis; gastroesophageal reflux disease status post Nissen fundoplication; 35-pound weight loss over 2 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for shortness of breath, fatigue, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, scattered pink dermal papulonodules, and subsequent steroid-induced myopathy; negative for headache, visual changes, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, dysphagia, arthralgias, myalgias, or photosensitivity.

objective.physical_examination: Initial skin exam showed a nontender erythematous lesion on the left breast followed by scattered small pink dermal papulonodules on the posterior neck, left shoulder, abdomen, and left thigh; late course marked by proximal muscle weakness (steroid myopathy) and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology and molecular workup: Persistent peripheral monocytosis (>=1 x 10^9/L, >=10% of WBCs), neutrophilia, and thrombocytosis, with WBC surging from 18,600/μL to 77,000/μL during her final respiratory decompensation; negative BCR-ABL1 PCR, JAK2, CALR, MPL, and PDGFRA/PDGFRB rearrangements. Autoimmune and inflammatory markers: Elevated ESR (36 mm/h) and CRP (35.3 mg/L); positive ANA (1:640 nucleolar/speckled) and anti-RNP antibody (1.1); negative ANCA, anti-PR3, anti-MPO, anti-SSA/SSB, anti-Sm, anti-dsDNA, anti-smooth muscle, RF, anti-CCP, and viral hepatitis panel.
objective.advanced_workup: Left breast punch biopsy: Dense dermal infiltrate of atypical small monocytoid/lymphoid cells positive for CD4, CD43, myeloperoxidase, and lysozyme (leukemia cutis). Bone marrow biopsy, cytogenetics, and flow cytometry: Hypercellular marrow (50% cellularity) with 20% immature monocytoid cells, <20% blasts, normal 46,XX karyotype, and characteristic CD14+/CD16- classical monocytes confirming CMML. Staging PET/CT: Circumferential hypermetabolic soft-tissue cuffing surrounding the entire thoracic and abdominal aorta diagnostic of large-vessel aortitis. Chest CT and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) during acute respiratory failure: Stable aortitis with new diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and bilateral pulmonary consolidations; BAL cultures and Pneumocystis jirovecii testing were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) presenting with leukemia cutis and paraneoplastic large-vessel thoracoabdominal aortitis, culminating in fatal leukemic pulmonary infiltration (diffuse ground-glass opacities and consolidations with hyperleukocytosis of 77,000/μL) following rapid corticosteroid tapering; infectious pneumonia including Pneumocystis jirovecii was excluded by negative BAL cultures and P. jirovecii assays. Plan and clinical course: Paraneoplastic aortitis initially responded dramatically to prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. When rapid steroid tapering for myopathy precipitated hyperleukocytosis (WBC 77,000/μL) and intubated respiratory failure, she received broad-spectrum antibiotics, cytoreduction with hydroxyurea, leukapheresis, and one dose of decitabine, but continued to deteriorate, was transitioned to hospice care, and died.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with complaints of increasing lethargy and fatigue over the course of several weeks, along with a one-day history of shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations. Past medical history was significant for HIV, anemia, and septoplasty. She was intubated on admission for airway protection due to concern for impending respiratory failure. On exam she was found to be febrile with Tmax of 39.9C, heart rate of 122 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 91/57 mmHg, saturating at 97% on 35% FiO2. Complete blood count revealed white blood cells of 3 x 103 cells/mL with 73% segs and 15% bands, hemoglobin of 4.5 g/dL, hematocrit of 17.7%, and platelets of 4,000 cells/mL. Ferritin was significantly elevated at 19,406 ng/mL and triglycerides were 412 mg/dL. HIV viral load was 1,842,730 copies/mL and CD4 count was 4 cells/mL. Physical exam revealed hepatosplenomegaly which was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound. The patient was diagnosed with HLH based on meeting the required five of eight criteria set forth in HLH-2004 guidelines (fever > 38.5C, splenomegaly, bicytopenia with hemoglobin < 9 g/dL and platelets < 100,000 cells/mL, triglycerides > 265 mg/dL, and ferritin > 500 ng/mL). The other three criteria (NK cell activity, CD25 level, and pathological evidence of hemophagocytosis) were not evaluated due to unavailability of labs and thrombocytopenia precluding bone marrow biopsy.
The patient was placed on empirical antibiotics (levofloxacin and vancomycin) for sepsis while investigation for infectious source was conducted. She was also started on methylprednisolone for respiratory failure at admission, which was continued for three days. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Sputum culture grew normal flora. Tests were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid fast bacilli, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, cryptococcus, histoplasmosis, syphilis, and influenza A. The only positive finding was antibody for influenza B, which was attributed to a mild upper respiratory infection that had resolved on its own with supportive measures two weeks prior to admission.
Despite aggressive transfusions, significant anemia and thrombocytopenia persisted. At this point, the most likely trigger of the HLH was determined to be an uncontrolled HIV infection. Given the patient's clinical instability and unresponsiveness to supportive treatment, ART was empirically initiated with tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir. Within one week of initiation of ART, the patient improved clinically and was able to be extubated, and her laboratory parameters began to normalize (Figure 1). By the time the patient was discharged three weeks after ART initiation, hemoglobin had risen to 10.5 g/dL and platelets to 169,000 cells/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old Caucasian female with untreated HIV infection presented with several weeks of increasing lethargy and fatigue and a 1-day history of shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced progressively worsening lethargy and fatigue over several weeks, followed 1 day prior to emergency department presentation by acute shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations. She had also had a mild self-resolving upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks prior to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection (untreated); anemia; prior septoplasty; mild self-limited upper respiratory infection 2 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive lethargy, fatigue, acute shortness of breath, hematemesis, palpitations, and high fever.

objective.physical_examination: Intubated on admission for airway protection and impending respiratory failure. Vital signs: Tmax 39.9 °C, heart rate 122 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 91/57 mmHg, and SpO2 97% on 35% FiO2. Abdominal examination: Hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission hematology and biochemistry: Severe pancytopenia with WBC 3 x 10^3 cells/mL (73% segmented neutrophils, 15% bands), hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL, hematocrit 17.7%, and platelets 4,000 cells/mL; severe hyperferritinemia at 19,406 ng/mL; hypertriglyceridemia at 412 mg/dL. Virological and microbiological studies: Plasma HIV viral load 1,842,730 copies/mL; negative blood and urine cultures; sputum culture grew normal flora; positive influenza B antibody (attributed to resolved URI 2 weeks prior); negative testing for influenza A, CMV, parvovirus, EBV, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, syphilis, and acid-fast bacilli. Abdominal ultrasound: Confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with CD4 count of 4 cells/mL. Opportunistic pathogen evaluation: Negative testing for Pneumocystis jirovecii (bone marrow biopsy, soluble CD25, and NK-cell activity were deferred due to severe thrombocytopenia of 4,000/mL and laboratory availability, as the patient already fulfilled 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; fulfilling 5 of 8 HLH-2004 criteria: fever 39.9 °C, hepatosplenomegaly, Hb 4.5 g/dL and platelets 4,000/mL, triglycerides 412 mg/dL, and ferritin 19,406 ng/mL) driven directly by uncontrolled advanced HIV viremia (viral load 1,842,730 copies/mL, CD4 4 cells/mL), with opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii, mycobacteria, fungi, and herpesviruses ruled out. Plan and clinical course: Intubated and initially treated with empiric vancomycin, levofloxacin, a 3-day course of methylprednisolone, and blood product transfusions without hematologic recovery. Upon identifying uncontrolled HIV as the primary HLH trigger, antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir) was initiated, leading to clinical stabilization and extubation within 1 week and hospital discharge after 3 weeks with hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL and platelets 169,000/mL.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male presented to an outlying hospital with a one-month history of productive cough, shortness of breath, and intermittent fevers, and a syncopal episode one week before. His past medical history was significant for hypertension, prostatic adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, atrial fibrillation, and bilateral pulmonary embolism. The prostatic adenocarcinoma was diagnosed 11 months before, and he developed the bilateral pulmonary embolism approximately 8 months before. He completed 40 cycles of radiation, and medications included Zytiga in conjunction with prednisone, Lupron, and Eliquis. He was a former smoker and smoked a maximum of 5 cigarettes daily for 35 years. His social history was otherwise negative for high-risk sexual behavior, intravenous (IV) drug use, recent travel, and occupational exposure. He was subsequently admitted with a diagnosis of anemia with hemoglobin of 7.1 g/dL and sepsis secondary to presumed pneumonia.
On admission, the patient received 4 units of packed red blood cells for anemia. The patient was also noted to have thrombocytopenia with platelet count of 48,000/mcL; thus, Eliquis was held. Chest X-ray revealed a 7.4 cm opacity in the right lung base as well as multiple right pulmonary nodules (Figure 1). A CT chest showed similar findings with the addition of extensive bone metastasis. The patient was started on vancomycin and Zosyn for sepsis while awaiting blood culture results. Infectious workup was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus IgG, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen (Ag), Histoplasma Ag, Fungitell, and Blastomyces antibody (Ab). Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), and influenza A and B serologies were negative. Blood cultures were negative for viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Infectious diseases were consulted. The patient subsequently underwent a bronchoscopy, with lavage specimens returning positive for Aspergillus Ag but negative for pneumocystis pneumonia, HSV, bacteria, fungus including Histoplasma, and malignant cells. The patient was then diagnosed with presumed subacute invasive pulmonary aspergillus. Antibiotics were then discontinued, and the patient was discharged with voriconazole for a 6-week duration.
Two days after discharge, he was admitted for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was performed and showed a highly mobile 5 cm mass involving the tricuspid valve with variable involvement of the right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 2). The ejection fraction was preserved. Infectious diseases and oncology were then consulted. The patient remained on voriconazole, and Zytiga was discontinued as his prostate cancer was castration sensitive, per oncology. CT surgery was consulted and performed sternotomy with resection of the mass, portions of the right atrium and ventricle, and tricuspid valve on day 2 of admission. The excised mass was pale yellow and pink, irregularly shaped, fragmented, bulky, and approximately 3 x 2 x 1.3 cm (Figure 3). Pathology from the mass and tricuspid valve showed necrotic debris with acute inflammation and abundant fungal hyphae (Figure 4). Cultures obtained from tissue in the operating room were positive for Aspergillus fumigatus and negative for bacteria and viruses.
The patient did well postoperatively. He was extubated to nasal cannula within 12 hours; however, he remained on pressor support. Voriconazole was continued. On day 4 of admission, he developed septic shock, renal failure with oliguria and acidosis, and shock liver requiring increased pressor support. He continued to deteriorate the next day requiring endotracheal intubation and ventilator support. On day 5 of admission, the patient developed ventricular tachycardia followed by pulseless electrical activity. Shortly thereafter, he was pronounced dead.
