The cause of death was invasive aspergillosis-induced septic shock with multiorgan failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male with metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma on abiraterone and prednisone presented with a 1-month history of productive cough, shortness of breath, and intermittent fevers, and a syncopal episode 1 week prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 11 months earlier with bone-metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma (treated with 40 fractions of radiotherapy, leuprolide [Lupron], abiraterone [Zytiga], and daily prednisone) and 8 months earlier with bilateral pulmonary embolism (on apixaban [Eliquis]), the patient presented to an outlying hospital after 1 month of productive cough, dyspnea, and intermittent fevers plus a syncopal episode 1 week prior. Two days after being discharged on oral voriconazole for presumed invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, he was readmitted with rapid atrial fibrillation and found to have a large Aspergillus fumigatus tricuspid valve vegetation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prostate adenocarcinoma with extensive bone metastases (diagnosed 11 months prior); bilateral pulmonary embolism (8 months prior); atrial fibrillation; hypertension. Social history: Former smoker (up to 5 cigarettes/day for 35 years); negative for IV drug use, recent travel, or occupational exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1 month of productive cough, shortness of breath, intermittent fevers, syncope, and subsequent rapid palpitations/atrial fibrillation. Home medications were abiraterone (Zytiga), prednisone, leuprolide (Lupron), and apixaban (Eliquis).

objective.physical_examination: Readmitted 2 days post-initial discharge in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, subsequently progressing on postoperative day 2 (hospital day 4) to oliguric septic shock.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission laboratory tests: Severe anemia with hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL (transfused 4 units PRBCs) and thrombocytopenia with platelets 48,000/μL; negative blood cultures; negative HIV, HSV, and influenza A/B serologies. Chest X-ray and chest CT: 7.4 cm consolidation/opacity in the right lung base, multiple right pulmonary nodules, and extensive osteoblastic bone metastases.
objective.advanced_workup: Fungal serologies and biomarkers: Positive serum Aspergillus fumigatus IgG, serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, 1,3-beta-D-glucan (Fungitell), Histoplasma antigen, and Blastomyces antibody (cross-reactive). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Positive BAL Aspergillus galactomannan antigen; negative for Pneumocystis pneumonia, HSV, bacteria, Histoplasma, and malignant cells. Readmission transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): Preserved LVEF with a highly mobile 5 cm mass on the tricuspid valve extending into the right atrium and right ventricle. Median sternotomy and tricuspid valve/cardiac mass resection pathology and culture: Bulky 3 x 2 x 1.3 cm pale yellow-pink friable mass showing necrotic debris, acute inflammation, and abundant septate fungal hyphae; intraoperative cardiac tissue cultures grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis complicated by fatal Aspergillus fumigatus tricuspid valve endocarditis (confirmed by positive serum/BAL galactomannan, Fungitell, and surgical pathology and culture of the resected 5 cm tricuspid valve mass, with Pneumocystis pneumonia ruled out on BAL) in a patient receiving prednisone and abiraterone for metastatic prostate cancer. Plan and clinical course: Apixaban and abiraterone were discontinued, and after initial empiric vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, oral/IV voriconazole was initiated and he underwent median sternotomy with resection of the tricuspid valve and right atrial/ventricular fungal mass on readmission day 2. Although extubated within 12 hours postoperatively, he developed refractory septic shock, oliguric renal failure, metabolic acidosis, shock liver, and fatal ventricular tachycardia / pulseless electrical activity arrest on hospital day 5.

raw_case_text:
This 31-year-old woman, with documented HIV infection for 8 years, presented with a four-day history of intermittent episodes of confusion associated with headache, fever, productive cough, and dyspnoea. Of note, the patient had declined treatment for HIV following her initial diagnosis and had not attended the outpatient department for several years.
On admission, she was moderately confused but had no focal neurological deficits or altered consciousness levels. Baseline laboratory tests revealed a very low CD4 cell count (14 cells/mm3 at 4%) and an HIV viral load of 206,548 copies/mL, indicating that the patient was significantly immunosuppressed and at risk for opportunistic infection. Other routine blood tests showed moderately raised inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR) with normal white cells and neutrophils. The patient's initial chest X-ray demonstrated patchy lower lobe infiltrates and she was commenced on treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for suspected pneumocystis pneumonia. Subsequent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was negative for pneumocystis jirovecii and treatment for this infection was stopped with the patient receiving seven-day antibiotic treatment.
Computerised tomography (CT) brain scan was performed on admission to investigate the cause of acute confusion and revealed a left basal ganglia lesion with mass effect. Differentials included toxoplasmosis and primary CNS lymphoma. MRI of brain confirmed a single left basal ganglia mass measuring 2.5 cm with alternating concentric T2 hypointense and hyperintense rims (Figure 1(a)) and postcontrast focal eccentric enhancing nodule that measured 1 cm (Figure 1(b)). These are considered both the "concentric" and "eccentric" target signs, which demonstrate specificity in the setting of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Biopsy of the lesion was performed and histopathological analysis confirmed toxoplasma cysts (Figure 2(a)) confirmed on immunohistochemistry (Figure 2(b)). There was no histological evidence of lymphoma. Further diagnostic testing such as serology and lumbar puncture was not required following detection of toxoplasmosis on biopsy.
The patient was commenced on treatment for toxoplasmosis, which involves a six-week course of antimicrobial therapy including sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid. She responded well to treatment and her confusion resolved. Of note, while awaiting BAL results, the patient also completed a seven-day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for suspected pneumocystis pneumonia, which is an alternative treatment choice for CNS toxoplasmosis. She was commenced on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and was counselled by the genitourinary service regarding the importance of compliance to her HIV treatment in the future.
CT brain scan was performed two days after biopsy and showed stable focal lesion with decreased vasogenic oedema. Repeat chest X-ray after two weeks showed complete resolution of infiltrate. She was eventually discharged from hospital four weeks after her initial presentation with outpatient follow-up arranged in the HIV clinic, at which point her CD4 count was noted to have risen to 129 cells/mm3 and 10% and her HIV viral load had reduced to 129 copies/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old woman with untreated HIV infection presented with a 4-day history of intermittent confusion, headache, fever, productive cough, and dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV infection 8 years prior, the patient had declined antiretroviral therapy and been lost to outpatient follow-up for several years. She presented to the hospital with a 4-day history of intermittent acute confusion accompanied by headache, fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Documented HIV infection for 8 years, untreated and lost to follow-up.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent confusion, headache, fever, productive cough, and dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Moderately confused on admission without focal neurological deficits or depressed level of consciousness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Plasma HIV viral load 206,548 copies/mL; moderately elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) with normal total white blood cell and neutrophil counts. Admission chest X-ray: Patchy lower lobe pulmonary infiltrates (which completely resolved on repeat CXR at 2 weeks).
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline lymphocyte subsets: Severe immunosuppression with absolute CD4+ T-cell count of 14 cells/mm3 (4%). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii. Neuroimaging (head CT and brain MRI): Single 2.5 cm left basal ganglia mass with surrounding vasogenic edema, mass effect, alternating concentric T2 hypointense/hyperintense rims ('concentric target sign'), and a 1 cm post-contrast focal eccentric enhancing nodule ('eccentric target sign'). Stereotactic brain biopsy: Histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoite cysts without evidence of primary CNS lymphoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Cerebral toxoplasmosis (confirmed by concentric/eccentric target signs on brain MRI and Toxoplasma cysts on left basal ganglia biopsy histopathology and immunohistochemistry) and concurrent lower lobe bacterial pneumonia (with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia ruled out by negative bronchoalveolar lavage) in a patient with untreated advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 14 cells/mm3). Plan and clinical course: Empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole started on admission for suspected PCP was discontinued after 7 days upon negative BAL results (providing early activity against toxoplasmosis), and she completed a definitive 6-week regimen of sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid alongside initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Her confusion and chest X-ray infiltrates resolved completely, and she was discharged at 4 weeks with an improved CD4 count of 129 cells/mm3 (10%) and HIV viral load reduced to 129 copies/mL.

raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old man with a history of RA presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He also reported having a nonproductive cough, fatigue, and one month of night sweats.
His therapy for RA comprised weekly methotrexate, daily hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine. His symptoms were well-controlled on this regimen. He also gave a history of receipt of rituximab for a year prior to presentation.
Our patient is originally from Mexico but has lived in the United States for over forty years. Prior to moving to Colorado, he gave a history of residence in Ohio. He works as a truck driver and his route involves the Midwest states. He also gave a history of travel to California nearly a year ago. About one month before admission, he unloaded his truck in Kansas City during a rainstorm and shortly thereafter began having night sweats and a nonproductive cough. No known history of exposure to tuberculosis.
On admission, he was afebrile but was found to have an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air and required 2-3 liters/minute of supplemental oxygen. Initial laboratory studies revealed a normal white blood cell count. Liver enzymes were elevated above his baseline (AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L). An abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly, and a chest X-ray showed a diffuse reticulonodular density with hilar lymphadenopathy. He received one dose of intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone and azithromycin and was started on empiric treatment with IV ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for community-acquired pneumonia. Additional negative studies included a respiratory viral PCR, Histoplasma urine antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Legionella urine antigen, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) 4th generation antibody/antigen assay, acute hepatitis panel, serum herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR, serum cytomegalovirus (CMV PCR), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) quantiferon gold, and sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) direct fluorescent antibody (DFA). Rheumatology recommended continuing hydroxychloroquine and stopping methotrexate and sulfasalazine in the setting of possible infection.
A CT chest interstitial lung disease (ILD) showed diffuse micronodularity in all five pulmonary lobes in a perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution and few scattered calcified granulomas that suggested disseminated infection. The CT chest scan also showed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy as well as splenomegaly (Figure 1). Diffuse micronodules had not been seen on previous CT chest scans six years prior and one month prior to presentation. His imaging findings suggested a miliary pattern. This combined with his clinical symptoms and environmental exposure history was concerning for an invasive fungal infection or tuberculosis (TB). Three sputum AFB cultures were collected and were smear negative. An MTB complex nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) was performed on one of his AFB sputum samples and was not detectable.
He underwent bronchoscopy and findings were notable for endobronchial nodules and plaques in the left upper lobe. Multiple biopsies were done and sent for standard aerobic, AFB and fungal cultures. An Aspergillus galactomannan antigen and PJP DFA in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BAL) were negative. Since all cultures remained negative, his antibiotics were stopped after 3 days. Infectious Diseases was consulted and recommended starting empiric anidulafungin and posaconazole combination therapy given concern for a fungal infection. Empiric combination therapy with an azole + echinocandin was chosen to cover possible endemic fungi and invasive aspergillosis. Posaconazole was chosen over voriconazole for the addition of Mucorales coverage. Assays for serum Histoplasma antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA), urine Histoplasma galactomannan antigen quantitative EIA, serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and serum Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii antigen were negative. T-SPOT interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated at 13.03 U/mL. Pathology from bronchoscopy biopsy showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation suggestive of infectious etiology. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stains were negative. Periodic acid- Schiff (PAS) stain and hematoxylin and eosin (HE) stain were not done. Five days after bronchoscopy, Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation (CF) assay returned positive at 1 : 8, Coccidioides IgM by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was positive, and Coccidioides IgG by ELISA was negative. Coccidioides immitis antibody by immunodiffusion (ID) demonstrated a partial identity reaction indicating the presence of two different types of antibodies. One antibody was identical to the positive control, and the other antibody was unrelated and could be a cross-reactive antibody due to infection with other systemic fungi. His Coccidioides immitis antibody was repeated three days later and was reported as detectable. This pattern of serological data suggested active coccidioidomycosis. He was started on liposomal amphotericin B. Posaconazole and anidulafungin were discontinued. After one week of liposomal amphotericin B treatment, he was transitioned to oral fluconazole 400 mg daily. His hypoxia resolved, and he was discharged home.
Nine days after discharge, our microbiology lab reported growth of mold from fungal lung tissue cultures. The isolate was preliminarily identified as Histoplasma capsulatum based on morphology (Figure 2) and was sent to a reference laboratory where it tested positive for Histoplasma capsulatum by DNA probe. A Histoplasma capsulatum DNA probe sent from his left upper lobe tissue culture was positive. On follow-up visit in the Infectious Diseases clinic, he was switched from fluconazole to itraconazole for the treatment of pulmonary histoplasmosis. A repeat chest CT showed improvement in the size and number of bilateral lung micronodules. One month after discharge, he reported resolution of shortness of breath. However, he described worsening of pain from RA in his shoulders, knees, wrists, and ankles. He was restarted on sulfasalazine and methotrexate after he had been on treatment for histoplasmosis for more than two months. Approximately eight months after presentation, his CT imaging continued to display multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Histoplasma antibodies by CF were checked and were negative (<1 : 8). He has been continued on his oral itraconazole treatment with plans to treat for at least one year.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male truck driver with rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-month history of night sweats and nonproductive cough and a 1-week history of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, shortly after unloading his truck in Kansas City during a rainstorm, the patient developed night sweats, fatigue, and a nonproductive cough. One week prior to emergency department presentation, his illness acutely worsened with fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis well controlled on weekly methotrexate, daily hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine, with a history of rituximab therapy for 1 year prior to presentation. Epidemiological/occupational history: Born in Mexico, lived in the US >40 years (previously in Ohio, currently in Colorado), worked as a Midwest long-haul truck driver (unloaded in Kansas City 1 month prior; traveled to California ~1 year prior); no known TB exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1 month of night sweats, nonproductive cough, and fatigue, and 1 week of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (and post-discharge RA polyarthralgia flare in shoulders, knees, wrists, and ankles). Home medications were methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile on admission with room-air oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 85%, requiring 2–3 L/min of supplemental oxygen.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normal WBC count; elevated liver enzymes above baseline with AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L. Negative routine infectious screening: Negative respiratory viral PCR, urinary Histoplasma antigen (and quantitative EIA), urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigens, 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab, acute hepatitis panel, serum HSV and CMV PCRs, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB, three AFB sputum smears/cultures, sputum MTB NAAT, and sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii direct fluorescent antibody (DFA). Fungal serologies: Elevated Aspergillus fumigatus IgG (13.03 U/mL); negative serum Aspergillus galactomannan and Cryptococcus antigen; cross-reactive Coccidioides serology (CF 1:8, ELISA IgM positive/IgG negative, immunodiffusion partial identity reaction). Imaging: Chest X-ray showed diffuse reticulonodular density with hilar lymphadenopathy; abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT: New diffuse miliary micronodularity across all five lobes in a perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution, scattered calcified granulomas, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and left upper lobe endobronchial/transbronchial biopsies: Endobronchial nodules and plaques in the left upper lobe; BAL negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii DFA and Aspergillus galactomannan; biopsy histopathology showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with negative AFB and GMS stains; fungal culture of left upper lobe biopsy tissue grew mold 9 days post-discharge that was definitively confirmed as Histoplasma capsulatum by reference laboratory DNA probe.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated/miliary pulmonary histoplasmosis in a Midwest truck driver with rheumatoid arthritis treated with rituximab, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, definitively confirmed by growth of Histoplasma capsulatum from left upper lobe bronchoscopic tissue culture and positive Histoplasma capsulatum DNA probe (after initial false-negative Histoplasma urinary/serum antigens and cross-reactive Coccidioides serologies, and negative sputum/BAL Pneumocystis jirovecii DFA). Plan and clinical course: Methotrexate and sulfasalazine were held on admission while hydroxychloroquine was continued. After failing 3 days of empiric antibacterials, he received empiric posaconazole plus anidulafungin, followed by 1 week of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and step-down to oral fluconazole (400 mg daily) when cross-reactive Coccidioides serology returned positive. Once lung biopsy cultures and DNA probe confirmed Histoplasma capsulatum 9 days post-discharge, therapy was switched to oral itraconazole (planned for >=1 year), achieving resolution of dyspnea, regression of pulmonary micronodules on repeat chest CT, and safe resumption of methotrexate and sulfasalazine after 2 months of antifungal therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old Caucasian man, nonsmoker, had recto-sigmoid carcinoma in September 2015. Initial investigations showed the cancer was T3, N2 and M0 (grade II adenocarcinoma). He received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy with Capecitabine and radiotherapy (50Gy in 25 fractions) which was completed in December 2015.
Post chemo-radiotherapy, computed tomography (CT) scan and positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed favourable rectal tumour response, but there were six small new liver lesions on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). He was started on Modified De Gramont regimen plus Oxaliplatin in March 2016, Panitumumab was added in May 2016 as K-RAS was wild-type. Reassessment CT scan, MRI and PET scans in September 2016 showed a very good response in the liver and rectal primary lesions with no evidence of extra-hepatic disease. Only two lesions had been identified in the liver MRI while the rest of the lesions disappeared (Figure 1). He underwent resection of the rectal disease with loop ileostomy by end of January 2017. The postoperative pathology showed a complete response. After recovery from bowel surgery, he continued on systemic chemotherapy and Panitumumab early March 2017 for three more cycles.
In May 2017, he was admitted with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, progressive shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. SpO2 was reduced at 88%. The total number of Panitumumab treatment cycles the patient received prior to this acute admission was 18.
Serial chest X-rays (Figures 2 and 3) showed diffuse reticulonodular shadowing. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) (Figure 4) showed nonspecific interstitial pneumonia.
Septic screen including blood culture, sputum culture, urine culture, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test, methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Pneumocystis Jirovecii PCR were all negative. In addition, autoimmune disorders were also excluded as antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) were negative. Unfortunately, the patient was clinically unfit for bronchoscopy to exclude possible lymphangitis carcinomatosis although it is rare in colorectal cancer and the patient refused further invasive procedures.
Pneumocystis jerovicii pneumonia.
Lymphangitis carcinomatosis.
Pulmonary oedema.
Oxaliplatin-induced ILD.
Differential diagnosis

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old nonsmoking Caucasian man with metastatic KRAS wild-type rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma presented in May 2017 with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, progressive shortness of breath, and reduced exercise tolerance after 18 cycles of panitumumab-containing therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in September 2015 with T3N2M0 rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma, the patient completed neoadjuvant capecitabine chemoradiotherapy (50 Gy in 25 fractions) in December 2015, developed six small liver metastases, and began modified de Gramont 5-FU plus oxaliplatin in March 2016 with panitumumab added in May 2016. Following an excellent hepatic and primary response, he underwent rectal resection with loop ileostomy in late January 2017 (pathologic complete response) and resumed systemic chemotherapy plus panitumumab in early March 2017. In May 2017, after a cumulative total of 18 panitumumab cycles, he was admitted with 3 days of fever, dry cough, progressive dyspnea, and decreased exercise tolerance.
subjective.past_medical_history: Grade II rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma (initially T3N2M0 in September 2015, later metastatic to the liver) status post neoadjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation, anterior rectal resection with loop ileostomy (January 2017), and 18 cycles of oxaliplatin/5-FU/panitumumab; lifetime nonsmoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, dry cough, progressive shortness of breath, and decreased exercise tolerance.

objective.physical_examination: Hypoxemic on admission with peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) reduced to 88%.
objective.routine_investigations: Microbiological and autoimmune screening: Negative blood, sputum, and urine cultures; negative HIV test; negative MRSA PCR; negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and rheumatoid factor (RF). Serial chest X-rays: Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular shadowing.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Bilateral changes consistent with nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). Molecular microbiology: Negative Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR (patient was clinically unfit for and declined diagnostic bronchoscopy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Panitumumab/oxaliplatin-induced interstitial lung disease (nonspecific interstitial pneumonia pattern on HRCT), established after excluding infectious pneumonia (including Pneumocystis jirovecii via negative PCR, MRSA, HIV, and bacterial cultures) and autoimmune disorders (negative ANA, ANCA, and RF).

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department with a cough, dyspnea, fevers, chills, night sweats, and fatigue.
She had never experienced pulmonary symptoms two weeks before presentation when she developed a cough and fever and was prescribed oral levofloxacin for pneumonia by her primary care physician. Completing a 7-day course of antibiotics, with unabating symptoms and worsening dyspnea, she presented to the emergency department for further treatment.
The examination was remarkable for tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 30/min, hypoxemia with an oxygen saturation of 87% in room air, and diffuse bilateral crackles, without jugular venous distension, or lower extremity edema.
Blood test was significant for white blood cell count of 30,000/microL, lactic acid of 5 mEq/L, and a normal metabolic panel. Arterial blood gas revealed a pH of 7.17, PaCO2 of 50 mmHg, HCO3 of 19 mmol/L, PaO2 of 65.3 mmHg, and SaO2 of 87%.
A CT-PE of the chest showed bilateral extensive multifocal infiltrates with significant hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no evidence of pulmonary embolism.
She was intubated for respiratory distress and admitted to the medical intensive care unit, with a tentative diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
A parasite smear and initial blood cultures were negative.
Bronchoscopy done on the day of admission showed mild diffuse erythema without hemorrhage. Given the patient's repeated desaturation during the procedure, transbronchial biopsies were not performed and the procedure terminated early. Lavage was sent for cytology, bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal stain, and culture.
An echocardiogram showed a hyperdynamic left ventricle with an estimated ejection fraction of 70% with severe right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesis. Right ventricular systolic pressure was estimated at 80 mmHg with a tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) of 1.3.
She continued to worsen, with worsening hypoxia and difficulty with mechanical ventilation, ultimately requiring airway pressure release ventilation and inhaled epoprostenol. Bronchoalveolar lavage remained negative, for bacteria, fungi, or Pneumocystis jirovecii sp.
Workup was expanded to include fungal blood cultures, histoplasma and coccidioides serology, and viral respiratory panel. Respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) were negative. Leptospira and pertussis remained negative. Noninfectious workup along autoimmune lines including antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP), and anti-Smith, anti-SCL70, anti-myeloperoxidase (anti-MPO), anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP), and anti-PR3 antibodies all returned negative, with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels on the high end of normal.
She continued to worsen, requiring hemodynamic support with norepinephrine, epinephrine, and vasopressin, with worsening hepatic function and oliguric renal failure.
On the third hospital day, she continued to be febrile. Morning ABG showed a pH of 6.99, PaCO2 of 47.4 mmHg, HCO3 of 10 mmol/L, PaO2 of 88.2 mmHg, SO2 of 83.2%, and lactic acid level of 9 mEq/L; after prompt discussion with the family, the decision was made to start the patient on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support.
However, the patient developed pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest before CRRT could begin, with the eventual demise of the patient.
An autopsy revealed noncaseating granulomata in hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary, splenic, and hepatic parenchyma. Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, and special stains were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic organisms.
Acid-fast bacillary and fungal cultures remained negative. No crystals were seen on polarized microscopy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 41-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of cough, fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and progressively worsening dyspnea refractory to a 7-day outpatient course of oral levofloxacin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having never experienced prior pulmonary symptoms, the patient developed acute cough and fever 2 weeks prior to admission and completed a 7-day course of oral levofloxacin prescribed by her primary care physician for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. Due to persistent fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath, she presented to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior history of pulmonary disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, severe dyspnea, fevers, chills, night sweats, and fatigue.

objective.physical_examination: Admission examination: Tachypnea with respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, hypoxemia with room-air SpO2 87%, and diffuse bilateral crackles on lung auscultation; no jugular venous distension or lower extremity edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests and arterial blood gas: Marked leukocytosis with WBC 30,000/μL, elevated lactic acid of 5 mEq/L, and normal baseline metabolic panel; admission ABG showed severe mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis with pH 7.17, PaCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mmol/L, PaO2 65.3 mmHg, and SaO2 87% (deteriorating on hospital day 3 to pH 6.99, PaCO2 47.4 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mmol/L, PaO2 88.2 mmHg, SO2 83.2%, and lactate 9 mEq/L alongside acute hepatic and oliguric renal failure). Negative infectious and autoimmune screening: Negative blood and fungal cultures, parasite blood smear, respiratory viral panel (RSV, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus), HIV, EBV, CMV, Histoplasma and Coccidioides serologies, Leptospira, and Bordetella pertussis; negative ANA, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Sm, anti-Scl-70, anti-MPO, anti-RNP, and anti-PR3 antibodies, with high-normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Transthoracic echocardiogram: Hyperdynamic LV (EF 70%) with severe right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesis, RVSP 80 mmHg, and reduced TAPSE (1.3 cm) indicative of acute cor pulmonale / severe pulmonary hypertension.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PE): Extensive bilateral multifocal pulmonary infiltrates and prominent hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without pulmonary embolism. Admission bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Mild diffuse mucosal erythema without hemorrhage (transbronchial biopsies aborted due to desaturation); BAL stains and cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Post-mortem autopsy histopathology: Widespread non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and throughout the pulmonary, splenic, and hepatic parenchyma, with negative Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, fungal, parasitic stains/cultures, and negative polarized microscopy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fulminant, fatal systemic and pulmonary sarcoidosis complicated by severe pulmonary hypertension / acute cor pulmonale (RVSP 80 mmHg), refractory hypoxemic/hypercapnic respiratory failure, and multiorgan shock, definitively diagnosed at autopsy by widespread non-caseating granulomas in the lungs, hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and spleen after comprehensive exclusion of Pneumocystis jirovecii, mycobacterial, fungal, viral, and autoimmune etiologies. Plan and clinical course: Intubated on admission and managed in the MICU with broad-spectrum antibiotics, airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), inhaled epoprostenol, and triple vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin). On hospital day 3, before planned continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and ECMO could be initiated, she suffered a fatal pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest.

raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old male with a long standing history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) presented with upper respiratory symptoms including mild productive cough and dyspnea. An outpatient chest CT showed innumerable bilateral ill-defined solid pulmonary nodules in a peribronchovascular distribution, which were new from a prior scan 6 months earlier (Figure 1). Many of the lesions had a peripheral ground-glass halo. Nonenlarged mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes were suspected to be related to the patient's history of CLL. The pulmonary nodules were not a typical manifestation of CLL and other etiologies were considered such as atypical pulmonary infection, sarcoidosis, Kaposi sarcoma, and metastasis, even though patient had no other known malignancy. He was treated with antibiotics and steroids for his symptoms; however there was progressive clinical decline over several weeks and thus the patient was admitted for further work-up.
At the time of admission, vital signs showed exertional hypoxia, mild tachycardia in the low 100's, and a fever up to 102.4, which raised the concern for an infection and septic emboli. However, there were no significant pulmonary findings on exam. Skin examination revealed erythematous/purple skin papules on both lower extremities which broadened the differential to also include autoimmune and vascular etiologies.
Aside from normocytic anemia (Hb 11.6 mg/dL), initial laboratory evaluation with CBC and BMP showed no significant abnormalities. IgG levels were low. Blood and sputum cultures were negative. QuantiFERON was negative for tuberculosis. Serologies for aspergillus, blastomycosis, coccidioides, cryptococcus, histoplasma, HIV, and toxoplasma were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for acid-fast bacilli, fungal organisms, and pneumocystis.
Immunologic evaluation was negative for ANCA, proteinase 3, and myeloperoxidase antibodies. This excluded granulomatosis with polyangiitis as a differential diagnosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for cytology.
Punch biopsy of one of the skin lesions demonstrated poorly circumscribed granulomas surrounding blood vessels and skin appendages, mild lymphocytic infiltration with no features to suggest cutaneous lymphoma, and no evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Stains for fungal and acid-fast bacilli were negative.
Left upper and lower lobe wedge biopsies of the nodules were taken through video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) as the diagnosis was still unclear. The biopsies revealed EBV-positive DLBCL with features of LG grade 3 (Figure 2). The features that favor LG over DLBCL include a background that consisted predominantly of inflammatory cells with a minority of large B-cells and vascular invasion. In addition, lung involvement and EBV positivity are not exclusive to LG, but are almost always present in LG. Flow cytometry did not detect the large B-cells which are sometimes too fragile to survive flow cytometric processing, but did detect rare, small monoclonal B-cells with a CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) phenotype. The flow cytometric findings are compatible with the morphology as no significant CLL/SLL population could be identified with CD5 and CD23 immunostaining (Figure 3). In this case, the source of rare CLL cells is likely peripheral blood, either physiologically through the inflammatory response or contamination during resection. Features of secondary organizing pneumonia were also present.
The patient underwent PET-CT 4 weeks following the initial chest CT (Figure 4). This showed significant progression and confluence of bilateral peribronchovascular lung opacities. The lung opacities had diffuse FDG uptake with a maximum SUV of 22.3. The PET/CT also demonstrated intense uptake in the cutaneous lesions of the lower extremities.
Bone marrow biopsy was consistent with hypercellular marrow with 20-30% marrow involvement by CLL/SLL cells. The patient was started on R-CHOP chemotherapy with Neupogen support. IVIG was also given for hypogammaglobulinemia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male with chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with mild productive cough, exertional dyspnea, high fever up to 102.4 °F, and violaceous lower extremity skin papules accompanied by new bilateral halo-sign pulmonary nodules refractory to outpatient antibiotics and corticosteroids.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had a long-standing history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), initially developed upper respiratory symptoms, mild productive cough, and dyspnea; an outpatient chest CT revealed innumerable new bilateral peribronchovascular pulmonary nodules with ground-glass halos. After experiencing progressive clinical decline over several weeks despite outpatient antibiotics and corticosteroids, he was hospitalized with exertional hypoxemia, tachycardia, fever up to 102.4 °F, and erythematous-to-purple lower extremity skin papules.
subjective.past_medical_history: Long-standing chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL); no other known prior malignancies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mild productive cough, exertional dyspnea, high fever (up to 102.4 °F), and bilateral lower extremity erythematous/purple skin papules.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Fever up to 102.4 °F, mild tachycardia (low 100s beats/min), and exertional hypoxemia. Physical exam: Unremarkable lung auscultation; multiple erythematous-to-violaceous skin papules on both lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL) with otherwise unremarkable CBC and basic metabolic panel; hypogammaglobulinemia with low serum IgG. Negative infectious and autoimmune workup: Negative blood and sputum cultures; negative QuantiFERON-TB assay; negative serologies for Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, HIV, and Toxoplasma; negative ANCA, anti-PR3, and anti-MPO antibodies.
objective.advanced_workup: Outpatient chest CT and 4-week follow-up 18F-FDG PET/CT: Innumerable new bilateral ill-defined peribronchovascular solid pulmonary nodules with peripheral ground-glass halos and mild mediastinal/axillary adenopathy, which progressed on 4-week PET/CT to confluent bilateral peribronchovascular opacities with intense FDG avidity (SUVmax 22.3) alongside intensely FDG-avid lower extremity cutaneous lesions. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative for acid-fast bacilli, fungi, Pneumocystis, and malignant cytology. Lower extremity skin punch biopsy: Poorly circumscribed perivascular/periadnexal granulomas and mild lymphocytic infiltrate without leukocytoclastic vasculitis, cutaneous lymphoma, or organisms on fungal/AFB stains. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) left upper and lower lobe wedge biopsies and bone marrow biopsy: Lung wedge biopsies established Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with features of grade 3 lymphomatoid granulomatosis (angiocentric/angiodestructive T-cell-rich inflammatory background with large EBV+ B cells and secondary organizing pneumonia, plus trace background CD5+/CD23+ CLL cells); bone marrow biopsy showed 20%–30% involvement by CLL/SLL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with features of grade 3 lymphomatoid granulomatosis (Richter-like transformation / immunocompromised EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder involving the lungs and lower extremity skin) in a patient with underlying chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL/SLL) and hypogammaglobulinemia, definitively diagnosed by VATS left lung wedge biopsies after excluding Pneumocystis, fungal, mycobacterial, and ANCA-vasculitic etiologies. Plan and clinical course: Initiated on R-CHOP immunochemotherapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) with pegfilgrastim/filgrastim (Neupogen) support and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old female with history of end stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy, who underwent a living related kidney transplantation in 1995, presented to our hospital with generalized malaise, dyspnea on exertion, and cough which started 6 months prior. Her other past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney allograft dysfunction due to recurrent IgA nephropathy. Immunosuppressive regimen included cyclosporine 100 mg every 12 hours, azathioprine 50 mg daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily. On arrival to the hospital, the patient was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 75/48 mmHg and febrile with a temperature of 100.6 F. Norepinephrine drip and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, although a source of infection was not obvious at that time. Laboratory testing was notable for anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and C-reactive protein (CRP). CMV viral load was positive with a titer of 3.6 log10 IU/ml and valganciclovir therapy was initiated as a result. Morning cortisol level was substantially suppressed at 0.6mcg/dL, and, due to concern for adrenal insufficiency, stress dose hydrocortisone was administered, followed by conversion to prednisone taper. Patient's hypotension and fever resolved within 24 hours from the initial presentation, and she was subsequently discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of CMV infection, on appropriate dose of valganciclovir with plan for follow-up as an outpatient. Unfortunately, the patient was rehospitalized 4 times in the subsequent 2 months with fever, shock, and fatigue. During each admission she received stress dose hydrocortisone and vasopressor with or without empiric antibiotics. Every time, her symptoms resolved rapidly (within 24 hours of initiation of therapy) without a clear diagnosis. Initially CMV was considered to be the cause of recurrent fever and hematologic abnormalities, but she had recurrent severe symptoms despite resolution of CMV viremia in the setting of valganciclovir treatment (summary in Table 1).
On the 5th admission, she presented again with hypotension and fever. The remainder of a review of symptoms was negative. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 7,200/mm3, persistent anemia with a hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dl, and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 83,000/mm3. LDH and CRP were yet again elevated (410 IU/L and 153.0 mg/L, respectively). Alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were mildly elevated at 50 IU/L and 41 IU/L, respectively. The patient's serum triglyceride level was 547 mg/dl (normal range 0-149 mg/dl) and ferritin level was remarkably elevated at 3311 ng/ml (normal range 13-150 ng/ml). As outlined above, CMV viral load was undetectable. Vasopressor and stress dose hydrocortisone were administered. As patient's hypotension resolved, vasopressor was discontinued within 24 hours from the time of admission. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed patchy ground glass opacities at the lung apices bilaterally. Bronchoscopy with broncho-alveolar lavage was performed, though it did not reveal any evidence of infection, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Further testing was performed to exclude rheumatologic disease, macrophage activation syndrome, malignancy, and autoinflammatory syndromes. Complement levels were within normal limits; antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor resulted as negative. Serum protein electrophoresis test showed normal levels of all immunoglobulins and no monoclonal component. EBV viral load was negative. Patient inevitably underwent a bone marrow biopsy, which revealed histiocytes with engulfed red cells, platelets, and neutrophils (Figure 1), suggesting HLH. High dose intravenous methylprednisolone was started at 1 gram intravenously daily and continued for 5 days, after which she was continued on oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day. Soluble Interleukin 2 receptor (sIL-2R) was elevated (15490 pg/ml, normal range <1033). Based on this, patient was diagnosed with HLH and discharged on high dose oral prednisone.
She remained afebrile, but suffered from severe persistent weakness. Subsequent outpatient laboratory testing revealed reduction of the platelet count and increased ferritin, indicating ongoing macrophage activation. Patient underwent thorough and extensive genetic testing, which was not consistent with familial HLH. Torso imaging was repeated to rule out an underlying malignancy, with positron emission tomography, and a magnetic resonance imaging did not reveal any suspicious neoplastic lesion. Given clinical and laboratory signs concerning for HLH exacerbation, chemotherapy with etoposide was started. She received four doses of etoposide in combination with daily dexamethasone. Unfortunately, patient developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure due to aspiration pneumonia in the setting of progressive encephalopathy, combined with Enterococcal and Neisseria bacteremia, and ultimately passed away within 3 months of her initial presentation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old female kidney transplant recipient presented with a 6-month history of generalized malaise, exertional dyspnea, and cough, accompanied by recurrent episodes of febrile hypotensive shock.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had undergone a living-related kidney transplant in 1995 for IgA nephropathy and was maintained on cyclosporine (100 mg q12h), azathioprine (50 mg daily), and prednisone (5 mg daily), presented with 6 months of malaise, exertional dyspnea, and cough, and arrived in febrile hypotensive shock (BP 75/48 mmHg, T 100.6 °F). Initial workup revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH/CRP, suppressed morning cortisol (0.6 μg/dL), and CMV viremia (3.6 log10 IU/mL); she stabilized within 24 hours on norepinephrine, stress-dose hydrocortisone, and valganciclovir. Over the next 2 months, however, she required four additional readmissions for recurrent febrile shock and fatigue despite clearance of CMV viremia, culminating in a 5th admission for febrile shock and hematologic deterioration.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy status post living-related kidney transplantation in 1995; chronic kidney allograft dysfunction due to recurrent IgA nephropathy; type 2 diabetes mellitus; secondary adrenal insufficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for 6 months of generalized malaise, exertional dyspnea, cough, fever, and hypotension; 5th admission positive for recurrent fever, hypotension, and severe weakness. Home medications were cyclosporine (100 mg q12h), azathioprine (50 mg daily), prednisone (5 mg daily), and valganciclovir.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission vital signs: Hypotensive with blood pressure 75/48 mmHg and febrile with temperature 100.6 °F. Fifth admission: Febrile and hypotensive with an otherwise unremarkable physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs: Anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and CRP, suppressed morning serum cortisol (0.6 μg/dL), and positive plasma CMV viral load (3.6 log10 IU/mL). Fifth admission labs: WBC 7,200/mm3, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelets 83,000/mm3, LDH 410 IU/L, CRP 153.0 mg/L, ALT 50 IU/L, AST 41 IU/L, hypertriglyceridemia at 547 mg/dL (normal: 0–149 mg/dL), and marked hyperferritinemia at 3,311 ng/mL (normal: 13–150 ng/mL); undetectable plasma CMV and EBV viral loads; normal complement levels and serum protein electrophoresis; negative ANA and rheumatoid factor.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT (5th admission): Patchy bilateral apical ground-glass opacities without lymphadenopathy or mass; subsequent whole-body PET and MRI negative for underlying malignancy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative for all infectious agents, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Bone marrow biopsy and HLH biomarkers: Demonstrated prominent hemophagocytosis (histiocytes engulfing erythrocytes, platelets, and neutrophils) and markedly elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) at 15,490 pg/mL (normal <1,033 pg/mL); familial HLH genetic panel negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; confirmed by bone marrow hemophagocytosis, sIL-2R 15,490 pg/mL, ferritin 3,311 ng/mL, triglycerides 547 mg/dL, bicytopenia, and recurrent febrile shock) initially triggered by cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation in a long-term renal transplant recipient, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and underlying lymphoma excluded by BAL and PET/MRI. Plan and clinical course: Treated on the 5th admission with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) followed by oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), and subsequently escalated for persistent outpatient macrophage activation to four doses of etoposide plus daily dexamethasone. Despite chemotherapy, she developed progressive encephalopathy, aspiration pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, and Enterococcus and Neisseria bacteremia, and died within 3 months of initial presentation.

raw_case_text:
A 13-year-old girl diagnosed the previous year with CVID in the setting of pneumonia, low serum immunoglobulin levels, and absent antibody responses to immunizations, presented with worsening dyspnea. Whole exome sequencing did not reveal an underlying genetic explanation for the immune deficiency. A chest CT scan at the time of CVID diagnosis revealed only mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She was placed on monthly IgG replacement therapy and did well until she reported gradual worsening of dyspnea over 3 months. The dyspnea first manifested during competitive sports and progressed to an inability to walk up a single flight of stairs. Pulmonary function testing results (Table 1) showed a restrictive pattern, and she was unable to complete the maneuvers for diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). A follow-up chest CT scan revealed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, peripheral interlobular septal thickening, peripheral consolidation, and ground glass opacities (Figure 1). Bronchoalveolar lavage obtained by bronchoscopy did not show any evidence of infection. Specific testing included bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral cultures along with PCR assays for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpes virus-8, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. She underwent a right lower lobe wedge resection biopsy via thoracoscopy. The biopsy (Figure 2) showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with aggregates of small lymphocytes, scattered multinucleated giant cells, scattered foci of organizing pneumonia, interstitial fibrosis focally in the subpleural space but not prominent or diffuse, and airway luminal compromise from adjacent lymphoid hyperplasia, confirming the diagnosis of GLILD.
She was treated with 4 doses of rituximab 375 mg/m2 given 4-6 months apart, based on clinical symptoms and pulmonary function testing, and azathioprine 50 mg daily for 18 months as IgG replacement therapy was continued. She responded well to the new therapy regimen with complete resolution of exercise intolerance and normalization of pulmonary function testing parameters (Table 1). She also had remarkable improvement of the CT scan abnormalities (Figure 1) with the follow up CT scan after completion of therapy demonstrating resolution of all abnormalities.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-year-old girl with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) on monthly immunoglobulin replacement therapy presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 1 year earlier with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID; low serum immunoglobulins, absent vaccine antibody responses, negative whole-exome sequencing, and isolated mediastinal lymphadenopathy on baseline chest CT), the patient had initially done well on monthly intravenous/subcutaneous IgG replacement therapy. Over the 3 months preceding presentation, she developed progressive exertional dyspnea that first appeared during competitive sports and worsened until she was unable to climb a single flight of stairs.
subjective.past_medical_history: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) diagnosed at age 12 following pneumonia; negative whole-exome sequencing for monogenic immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive exertional dyspnea and severe exercise intolerance over 3 months. Home medication was monthly IgG replacement therapy.

objective.physical_examination: Severe exercise intolerance (unable to walk up one flight of stairs).
objective.routine_investigations: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Restrictive ventilatory defect (unable to complete DLCO maneuvers at baseline; PFTs completely normalized following combination therapy).
objective.advanced_workup: Follow-up chest CT scan: Mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, peripheral interlobular septal thickening, peripheral consolidations, and ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral cultures, and negative PCR assays for Pneumocystis jirovecii, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, CMV, EBV, and HHV-8. Thoracoscopic right lower lobe wedge biopsy: Non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with aggregates of small lymphocytes, scattered multinucleated giant cells, focal organizing pneumonia, focal subpleural interstitial fibrosis, and peribronchiolar lymphoid hyperplasia compromising airway lumina, confirming granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD) complicating common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), definitively confirmed by thoracoscopic right lower lobe wedge biopsy after excluding Pneumocystis jirovecii, viral, fungal, and mycobacterial infections on BAL. Plan and clinical course: Treated with four doses of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2 administered every 4–6 months) combined with daily oral azathioprine (50 mg/day for 18 months) while continuing monthly IgG replacement therapy, resulting in complete resolution of exercise intolerance, normalization of pulmonary function tests, and complete clearance of CT abnormalities.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old African American male with medical history of AIDS presented with progressively worsening cough, shortness of breath, intermittent fever, and night sweats for about 10 months. He also reported 60-pound weight loss during that time. However, he was on a liquid diet because of difficulty of swallowing due to extensive oral lesions and odynophagia. The patient reported that he was off from HAART therapy for approximately one year but restarted treatment 14 months ago. He was on cobicistat, elvitegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir. However, he was noncompliant with his treatment. He had a biopsy of oral lesions done prior to the admission, showing KS.
Physical examination was significant for diffuse dark purple patches and plaques involving the face, back, arms, legs as well as hard palate and gums (Figures 1and 2). On chest examination, he had decreased air entry in the right lower lung fields.
Complete blood count was significant for normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The patient's absolute CD4 count was 27 cells/microliter. Chest x-ray (Figure 3) and subsequent chest computed tomography (Figure 4), showed moderate right lung pleural effusion with scattered bilateral diffuse infiltrates and mild mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
Immediately after the admission, the patient continued to deteriorate with worsening hypoxemia, requiring 15-liter oxygen with nonrebreather mask and transferred to the ICU for acute respiratory failure. He underwent thoracentesis which revealed hemorrhagic pleural fluid, negative for infection or malignancy. Infectious etiology has been excluded after blood culture and sputum culture were found to be negative for bacterial, viral, or fungal infections. Pulmonary tuberculosis, Coccidioidomycosis, pneumocystis jiroveci, and syphilis were also ruled out. Other malignancies which can involve lung and pleura in patient with AIDS (such as pulmonary lymphoma and lung cancer) were less likely as CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvic did not show any lymphadenopathy and pleural effusion cytology found to be negative for any malignant cells.
After exclusion of Infectious etiologies, and other malignancies, the patient was diagnosed with poor risk and extensive KS (T1I1S1). He was immediately started on chemotherapy with paclitaxel along with HAART. Dexamethasone 10 mg was also added at the time of chemotherapy administration for prevention of hypersensitivity reaction. Since receiving the chemotherapy, his condition has significantly improved with near complete resolution of the pleural effusion, oral and skin lesions. The patient was able to tolerate oral diet and has regained 30-pound weight. He completed total six cycle of chemotherapy with paclitaxel 190 mg with no significant side effects.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old African American male with advanced HIV/AIDS and biopsy-proven oral Kaposi sarcoma presented with a 10-month history of progressively worsening cough, shortness of breath, intermittent fever, night sweats, severe odynophagia, and a 60-pound weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 10 months of progressive cough, dyspnea, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and a 60-pound weight loss while restricted to a liquid diet due to painful, extensive oral Kaposi sarcoma lesions. He had previously been off antiretroviral therapy for 1 year and was noncompliant after restarting elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir 14 months prior to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS with medication noncompliance; biopsy-proven oral Kaposi sarcoma diagnosed prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic cough, progressive shortness of breath, intermittent fever, night sweats, 60-pound weight loss, odynophagia, dysphagia to solids, and extensive violaceous oral and cutaneous lesions. Prescribed home medication (noncompliant) was elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir.

objective.physical_examination: Mucocutaneous examination: Diffuse dark purple patches and plaques over the face, back, arms, and legs, as well as the hard palate and gingiva. Chest examination: Decreased air entry over the right lower lung field; rapidly developed severe hypoxemia after admission requiring 15 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask and ICU transfer.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Microbiological and infectious workup: Negative blood and sputum cultures for bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens; negative workup for pulmonary tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and syphilis. Chest X-ray: Moderate right pleural effusion with scattered bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Thoracentesis fluid analysis: Hemorrhagic pleural effusion with negative infectious cultures and negative malignant cytology.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Severe immunosuppression with absolute CD4+ T-cell count of 27 cells/μL. Chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT: Moderate right pleural effusion, scattered bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and mild mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Prior oral mucosal biopsy: Confirmed Kaposi sarcoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Poor-risk disseminated mucocutaneous, pulmonary, and pleural AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma (stage T1I1S1; confirmed by oral biopsy, hemorrhagic pleural effusion, diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and exclusion of Pneumocystis jirovecii, tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, and lymphoma) in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 27 cells/μL). Plan and clinical course: Initiated in the ICU on systemic paclitaxel chemotherapy (190 mg for 6 cycles, with dexamethasone 10 mg premedication) alongside resumption of HAART, resulting in near-complete resolution of the hemorrhagic pleural effusion, oral, and cutaneous lesions, restoration of a solid oral diet, and a 30-pound weight gain.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 3-year-old girl, the only child of Lebanese parents without direct consanguinity, with early onset of severe, recurrent pulmonary infections. Her first clinical manifestation occurred at 3 months of life, when she presented with fever without localizing signs. At that time, she was treated with intramuscular ceftriaxone for 3 days until she was admitted at an Intensive Care Unit due to bilateral pneumonia and pleural effusion. Then, she was submitted to pleural drainage and treatment with polymyxin, meropenem, vancomycin, and linezolid for 14 days. No etiological agents were identified in blood cultures and pleural fluids. At discharge, cefuroxime was prescribed for 10 days due to the persistent infection that was identified by radiological images.
At 4 months of age, she presented with oral moniliasis and Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) scar suppuration with slow healing. She was hospitalized for the second time at 6 months of age when she was diagnosed with bronchiolitis, with identification of Haemophilus parainfluenzae biotype I. She developed bilateral pneumonia, which did not respond adequately to ceftriaxone treatment and evolved to necrotizing pneumonia (Figure 1A). At that time, the patient was transferred to our hospital for evaluation by pulmonologists and immunologists. The patient was diagnosed with necrotizing pneumonia; left lung abscess; anemia, most likely secondary to infection; and stomatitis. She received a transfusion of red blood cell concentrate and was treated with ceftriaxone and linezolid and subsequently treated with meropenem and amphotericin B. Culture of material collected from bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no growth of aerobic or anaerobic bacteria.
At this time, the patient was submitted to an immunological investigation, which revealed normal immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subset numbers, and complement system. Nevertheless, a dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test showed that the patient's stimulated granulocytes presented abnormal ROS production, a characteristic of CGD patients (Figure 1B). Thus, CGD prophylaxis was initiated with the administration of Bactrim, itraconazole, and IFNgamma.
Despite prophylactic treatment, the patient continued to need hospitalization for pneumonia at 8 and 11 months of age that required systemic antibiotics. The first genetic analysis was performed on one of these occasions, although Sanger sequencing revealed no mutations in the NCF1 gene (data not shown). At this time, the patient's mother reported that one of the patient's female cousin had received two transplants for an unidentified immunological problem.
At 23 months of age, the patient presented with adenitis and cervical abscess, which were treated with ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and surgical drainage. She was discharged with cefuroxima treatment; however, 1 week later, she required medical assistance after developing right lobe pneumonia and atelectasis. These last conditions were treated with cefepime and prednisolone.
Whole-exome sequencing was performed to confirm or discard a CGD diagnosis, and sequence analysis revealed a mutation (c.256_257+2delAAGT NM_000433) in the NCF2 gene that leads to a K86Ifs*2 residue change in the p67-phox protein, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1C). Sanger analysis also showed that the parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The sequence data were analyzed using the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) and Ensembl SNP (www.ensembl.org) databases, confirming this novel mutation in NCF2.
Prophylactic medications were maintained during patient follow-up. However, at 2 years and 7 months of age, she was readmitted with pneumonia that was treated with ceftazidima. Thorax computed tomography revealed pulmonary consolidation in the upper segment of the right lower lobe and areas of retractable stretch marks, with a bilateral sparse sequential aspect that was more evident in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe, the middle lobe, and the lingula (Figure 1D). Bronchoscopy showed non-purulent laryngotracheobronchitis, with negative results for acid-alcohol resistant bacilli, fungi, cytomegalovirus or Pneumocystis jirovecii, as well as normal serum galactomannan levels.
At 3 years and 5 months of age, the child was hospitalized with jugal abscess arising from a dental procedure. The abscess was drained, and she received ceftriaxone, clindamycin and oral steroids for 5 days. Once she presented an anaphylactic reaction to ceftriaxone, the patient received epinephrine and continued treatment with clindamycin and steroids for an additional 3 days. Thereafter, she was discharged under treatment with sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old Lebanese girl with autosomal recessive p67-phox (NCF2) chronic granulomatous disease presented with a history of severe, recurrent sinopulmonary, mucocutaneous, and deep-tissue infections since 3 months of age.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born to non-consanguineous Lebanese parents, the child experienced recurrent life-threatening infections beginning in infancy: (1) 3 months of age: ICU admission for bilateral pneumonia and pleural effusion requiring chest drainage and 14 days of polymyxin, meropenem, vancomycin, and linezolid; (2) 4 months: oral candidiasis and slow-healing suppurative BCG scar; (3) 6 months: Haemophilus parainfluenzae biotype I bronchiolitis progressing to bilateral necrotizing pneumonia and a left lung abscess requiring PRBC transfusion, ceftriaxone, linezolid, meropenem, and amphotericin B, at which time an abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) assay established chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) and prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim), itraconazole, and interferon-gamma was started; (4) 8 and 11 months: breakthrough pneumonias; (5) 23 months: cervical lymphadenitis/abscess requiring surgical drainage followed 1 week later by right lobe pneumonia/atelectasis; (6) 2 years 7 months: readmission for right lower lobe pneumonia; and (7) 3 years 5 months: jugal (cheek) abscess following a dental procedure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) due to a homozygous NCF2 frameshift mutation; recurrent necrotizing pneumonia, left lung abscess, suppurative BCGitis, cervical abscess, and post-dental jugal abscess. Family history: Non-consanguineous Lebanese parents; female cousin underwent two hematopoietic stem cell transplants for an unspecified primary immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fevers, cough, necrotizing pneumonias, oral stomatitis/thrush, BCG scar suppuration, cervical abscess, and jugal abscess. Experienced an acute anaphylactic reaction to ceftriaxone at age 3 years 5 months. Prophylactic home medications were trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim), itraconazole, and interferon-gamma.

objective.physical_examination: Suppurative BCG scar and oral moniliasis/stomatitis in infancy; cervical lymphadenitis/abscess at 23 months; jugal abscess and acute ceftriaxone-induced anaphylaxis (treated with epinephrine) at 3 years 5 months.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline immunological screening (at 6 months): Normal serum immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subset counts, and complement activity; anemia secondary to severe infection. Microbiological and fungal studies: Identification of Haemophilus parainfluenzae biotype I at 6 months; negative blood, pleural fluid, and BAL aerobic/anaerobic bacterial cultures; normal serum galactomannan at 2 years 7 months.
objective.advanced_workup: Granulocyte oxidative burst and genetic testing: Dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) flow cytometry assay demonstrated absent/ severely impaired granulocyte reactive oxygen species (ROS) production; after negative NCF1 Sanger sequencing, whole-exome sequencing and confirmatory trio Sanger sequencing identified a novel homozygous splice/frameshift deletion in NCF2 (NM_000433: c.256_257+2delAAGT, p.Lys86Ilefs*2 in p67-phox, with heterozygous carrier parents). Thoracic CT and bronchoscopy at 2 years 7 months: Right lower lobe superior segment consolidation with bilateral fibrotic/retractile bands in the right upper lobe posterior segment, right middle lobe, and lingula; bronchoscopy showed non-purulent laryngotracheobronchitis with negative BAL testing for acid-fast bacilli, fungi, cytomegalovirus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Autosomal recessive p67-phox-deficient chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) caused by a novel homozygous NCF2 mutation (c.256_257+2delAAGT, p.K86Ifs*2), confirmed by abnormal DHR granulocyte oxidative burst and WES/Sanger sequencing, complicated by recurrent necrotizing pneumonias, lung/cervical/jugal abscesses, and BCG scar suppuration (with Pneumocystis jirovecii, CMV, fungi, and mycobacteria excluded on bronchoscopy at 2 years 7 months). Plan and clinical course: Maintained on long-term CGD prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, itraconazole, and interferon-gamma, with acute episodes managed via targeted intravenous antibiotics and surgical abscess drainage (switching from ceftriaxone to clindamycin, corticosteroids, and intramuscular epinephrine when ceftriaxone anaphylaxis occurred at age 3 years 5 months).

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man presented to the Accident and Emergency Department with a 2-month history of dyspnoea (acutely worsening over 2 days preceding admission), cough productive of purulent sputum, fever and weight loss. He was known to be HIV-positive (genotype-2, diagnosed 1991) but had been non-compliant with antiretroviral medication (Truvada, Darunavir and Ritonavir) for 2 years. Additional background included a history of depression, subdural haematoma, recurrent bacterial chest infections and drug abuse (daily heroin smoker).
On examination, he was unkempt, cachectic and dehydrated. He was septic but maintaining normal oxygen saturations on room air. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations were unremarkable. He was tachypnoeic and crepitations were auscultated at the right lung base. His abdomen was non-tender with palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Right-sided anterior cervical and right-sided inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpated.
Blood tests revealed microcytic iron-deficient anaemia, lymphopaenia with white cell count 2.6 x 109/L, C-reactive protein 198 mg/L, normal electrolytes and renal function, raised alkaline phosphatase level (1664 iU/L), hypoalbuminaemia (22 g/L) and deranged clotting. Lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 515 iU/L. Serology demonstrated serum Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) DNA PCR of 26 900 and positive Hepatitis B core-antigen (e-Antigen negative). HIV-2 viral load was 720 and CD4 count was 28 cells/muL (3%).
A chest radiograph demonstrated right basal opacification. Computerised tomography of the chest abdomen and pelvis (CT-CAP) revealed patchy air space opacification at the left oblique fissure, left lower and right lower lobes, paraseptal and central lobular emphysema and bibasal atelectasis (Figures 1 and 2). Hepatosplenomegaly was confirmed and free fluid was evident throughout the abdomen and pelvis (Figure 3). Multiple enlarged lymph nodes (up to 1.8 cm diameter) were visualised throughout the thorax, abdomen and pelvis (Figures 4 and 5).
Sputum cultures identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa; acid alcohol fast bacilli (AAFB) smears were negative. Tests for respiratory viruses, atypical organisms and Pneumocystis jirovecii were negative. Urine and blood cultures were negative, with no growth on mycobacterial blood cultures up to that point. Optimised antiretroviral therapy was restarted alongside intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam.
On multi-disciplinary team meeting, the clinical case was deemed to be in keeping with a diagnosis of respiratory tuberculosis. Alternative differentials included atypical lower respiratory tract infection (including MAC infection) or lymphoma. The patient subsequently underwent supraclavicular lymph node biopsy, which revealed classical HL. A positron emission tomography CT (PET-CT) scan diagnosed 'Stage 3B' but suggested that some lymphadenopathy may have been secondary to concurrent HIV-related lymphadenopathy or infection. A staging CT head excluded cerebral metastases. He was consequently initiated on a regimen of Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine and Dacarbazine (ABVD) chemotherapy.
Notably, one sputum culture subsequently grew Mycobacterium intracellulare; following this, another sputum culture grew Mycobacterium mucogenicum. Neither organism was grown on subsequent sputum samples. Neither of two mycobacterial blood cultures nor a lymph node mycobacterial culture showed any growth on final reporting. At least two sputum cultures positive for the same organism or one positive culture from a 'sterile' site (such as blood, lymph nodes or bone marrow) are required to diagnose atypical mycobacterial infection. The positive sputum cultures were therefore not considered significant.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man with untreated HIV-2 infection presented with a 2-month history of dyspnea (acutely worsening over 2 days), cough productive of purulent sputum, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV-2 in 1991, the patient had been noncompliant with his prescribed antiretroviral regimen (Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir) for the preceding 2 years. He presented to the emergency department with 2 months of shortness of breath that acutely worsened 2 days before admission, accompanied by a cough productive of purulent sputum, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-2 infection diagnosed in 1991 (nonadherent to ART for 2 years); recurrent bacterial chest infections; prior subdural hematoma; depression. Social history: Daily heroin smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea, productive cough with purulent sputum, fever, and weight loss. Prescribed home medications (nonadherent) were emtricitabine/tenofovir (Truvada), darunavir, and ritonavir.

objective.physical_examination: Unkempt, cachectic, dehydrated, and septic in appearance, with tachypnea but normal oxygen saturation on room air; right basilar crepitations on lung auscultation; soft, non-tender abdomen with palpable hepatosplenomegaly; palpable right anterior cervical and right inguinal lymphadenopathy; normal cardiovascular and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Microcytic iron-deficiency anemia, leukopenia/lymphopenia with WBC 2.6 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 198 mg/L, normal electrolytes and renal function, markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (1,664 IU/L), hypoalbuminemia (22 g/L), coagulopathy, and elevated LDH (515 IU/L). Virological serology and PCR: Plasma HIV-2 viral load 720 copies/mL; serum EBV DNA PCR positive at 26,900 copies/mL; hepatitis B core antibody positive (HBeAg negative). Microbiology: Sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa; sputum AFB smears, respiratory viral panel, atypical pneumonia screen, and Pneumocystis jirovecii testing were all negative; blood, urine, and mycobacterial blood/lymph node cultures were negative (single isolated sputum cultures later grew non-significant Mycobacterium intracellulare and Mycobacterium mucogenicum). Chest X-ray: Right basilar opacification.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Severe CD4+ T-cell depletion with CD4 count of 28 cells/μL (3%). Contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (CT-CAP): Patchy airspace opacification in the left oblique fissure and bilateral lower lobes, paraseptal and centrilobular emphysema, bibasilar atelectasis, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse abdominopelvic ascites, and widespread thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy (up to 1.8 cm). Supraclavicular lymph node excisional biopsy and staging PET-CT / head CT: Biopsy histopathology established classical Hodgkin lymphoma; PET-CT confirmed stage IIIB disease (head CT negative for brain metastases).
