On the basis of these findings a bronchoscopy was executed with transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) of mediastinal affected lymph nodes, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and bronchoaspiration for cytological and microbiological examination, including M. Tuberculosis and other mycobacterium species; pulmonary CD4/CD8 ratio was less than 3,5.
Biopsies of finger nodules and perimalleolar plaque were performed for pathologic and microbiological tests, including amplification of microbial DNA by PCR technique. The results confirmed the same granulomatous aspect of nodules previously removed, without any evidence of microbial presence.
Given the clinic and laboratory results, the patient was treated with prednisone per os at the dose of 0.5 mg/kg/die for one month, reducing the dose to 0.35 mg/Kg/die after one month, and finally to 0.2 mg/Kg/die in the third month. After one month of therapy, a reduction of inflammation was observed, the nodules seemed to be brighter and much less painful; whereas in the third month, we found a total healing, with scar formation. After six months from the beginning of therapy, blood tests were normal; a new PET/CT revealed the 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the region of mediastinum with a maximum SUV of 3.8 with a SUV lower than first PET/CT in the fingers of his hands; chest HRCT was unmodified. The patient is still in clinical, functional and radiological follow up, and currently in stable conditions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old Moroccan man living in Italy presented with progressive dyspnea since 2008, chronic chest pain, diffuse arthralgias, a chronic left perimalleolar plaque, and recurrent ulcerating digital nodules requiring multiple finger and toe amputations.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Since 2008, the patient experienced worsening exertional dyspnea, diffuse arthralgias, a persistent painless rubbery plaque in the left perimalleolar region, and painful ulcerating nodules over the distal phalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of his hands and feet. Between 2008 and 2012, severe pain and functional loss led to amputations of the left third toe distal phalanx, right second, third, and fourth finger distal phalanges, and right great toe distal phalanx—each showing necrotizing/non-necrotizing granulomatous pan-tissue inflammation—followed by recurrence in remaining digits and proximal MCP joints alongside chronic chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born in Morocco, resided in Italy for ~30 years as a peddler with sporadic trips to Morocco; never-smoker; history of multiple digital amputations (2008-2012).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic dyspnea, chest pain, diffuse arthralgias, painful ulcerating digital nodules, and a painless left perimalleolar plaque.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous and musculoskeletal examination revealed prior distal phalangeal amputations of the right index, middle, and ring fingers and bilateral toes, recurrent ulcerating nodules over the digits and proximal MCP joints, and a rubbery, non-erythematous, painless plaque in the left perimalleolar region. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were normal except for mildly elevated CA 19-9 (53 U/mL; normal <39 U/mL). ECG, arterial blood gases, 6-minute walk test, and spirometry with DLCO were normal; echocardiography showed trivial tricuspid regurgitation with estimated PASP of 25 mmHg. Chest X-ray showed a faint right supradiaphragmatic opacity. Mantoux tuberculin skin test and Elispot-TB IGRA were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution and contrast-enhanced chest CT showed normal lung parenchyma with enlarged, conglutinated, partially calcified mediastinal lymph nodes. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic uptake in the right upper lung lobe (SUVmax 4.01), mediastinal lymph nodes (SUVmax 6.70), and multiple upper/lower limb bones and MCP/MTP joints. Bronchoscopy with mediastinal TBNA, BAL, and bronchoaspiration showed a BAL CD4/CD8 ratio <3.5 and negative cytology and mycobacterial/microbial cultures. Repeat biopsies of the digital nodules and perimalleolar plaque with broad microbial PCR amplification were performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Biopsies of the digital nodules and perimalleolar plaque confirmed chronic epithelioid and giant-cell granulomatous inflammation extending from bone to skin with negative mycobacterial cultures and negative microbial PCRs, establishing multisystemic osseous, articular, cutaneous, and mediastinal sarcoidosis (ruling out tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteriosis, and Hansen's disease). Treatment with oral prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day for 1 month, tapered to 0.35 mg/kg/day in month 2 and 0.2 mg/kg/day in month 3) produced marked pain and nodule reduction by 1 month, complete scar healing of digital lesions by 3 months, and reduced mediastinal (SUVmax 3.8) and digital FDG uptake with normal blood tests at 6 months.

raw_case_text:
We experienced a case of diffuse-CL. The patient was a 24-year-old male (Fig. 2a, b) and was born and grew up in a small village near the Pacific coast of Ecuador, San Ignacio, Muisne, Esmeraldas province, a rural and mountainous area, located at 20 m above sea level (a.s.l.) (Fig. 1 (1)). In our epidemiological survey in the area, none of the patient's family members and neighboring people revealed diffuse-CL cases (Hashiguchi et al., unpublished data). When the patient was 16 years old, papules appeared on his left knee and right cheek. The eruption gradually increased in size and number. For about 2 years, he received various medications without confirmed diagnosis. Then, he was diagnosed clinically with leprosy and received the specific medication (multidrug treatment: dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine) for 1 month. After precise clinical and laboratory examinations, he was finally diagnosed with a diffuse-CL at the Department of Parasitology, National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, Guayaquil city, Ecuador, with positive smears for Leishmania parasites. Montenegro (Leishmanin) skin test was negative, but tuberculin, candidine, and trichophytin skin tests revealed positive reactions, demonstrating the existence of specific anergy against Leishmania antigen. On the other hand, the rK39 kit test revealed a strong positive reaction, suggesting the high-level function of humoral immune system of the diffuse-CL patient.
Physical examinations revealed pea- to rice-grain-sized reddish papules on both the ear lobes and the auricles. Induration of the lesions was palpable. Miliary to pea-sized reddish papules were observed on the face. The papules and nodules were also observed on the left shoulder. Many miliary to hen-egg-sized papule, nodule, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish-colored freckles were observed on the upper extremities. The surfaces of some of the nodules were scaly and crusted. Rice-grain to thumb-sized reddish papules grouped on the brownish-colored freckle lesion on the lower back were observed. Miliary-sized papules were scattered showing satellite lesions around the plaque-like lesions. Thumb- to palm-sized erythema was observed on the thigh. No loss of sensation was recognized. Various types of eruptions, such as papules, nodules, infiltrated erythema, and brownish-colored freckles, were observed on the lower extremities. There were no eruptions on the hands, the feet, the scalp, and the axillary, epigastric, inguinal, perineal, and anal regions, except a few verruca vulgaris lesions on the dorsal aspect of the left hand. There was no sensory loss on all over the body surface and no hypertrophy of the peripheral nerve. Numerous Leishmania amastigotes were observed in the stained smears from the skin lesion, though no acid-fast bacilli were observed in the slit-skin smear materials with Ziehl-Neelsen staining. The parasite was identified as L. (L.) mexicana by PCR analysis (Fig. 3).
Histological findings of the specimen taken from nodules on the thigh showed hyperkeratosis and mild acanthosis of the dermis. There was dense cellular infiltration in the dermis. Proliferations of blood vessels were also visible. In the foamy cells, innumerable Leishmania amastigotes were observed. No epithelioid cell granuloma was observed as seen in leprosy. No acid-fast bacilli were observed in the dermis. The patient was treated with meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime ) at a dose of 10 mg/kg/day and sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam ) at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day for 28 days with each drug; partial resolution of skin lesion was observed but relapsed soon after discontinuation of the treatment. In these treatments, the density of parasite on smear specimens was significantly reduced immediately after the beginning of each treatment but never disappeared completely. Thus, relapses were followed by 5- or 6-month intervals after each of the slight clinical improvements. Therefore, the patient had to receive repeatedly the intramuscular injection of Glucantime  after each relapse. Following this antimonial treatment, the patient received also pentamidine (3-4 mg/kg intramuscularly once or twice for a week) but had to be discontinued because of severe adverse reactions such as hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms, and syncope, without revealing a marked clinical and parasitological healing. Subsequently, the patient was treated with oral itraconazole (200 mg/day for 3 months), mefloquine (4.2 mg/kg/day for 6 days, repeated with a 3-week interval), and artesunate (6.7 mg/kg/day for 3 days, repeated with a 2-week interval), but compete healing was not obtained by any of these drugs. These mixed and alternative treatments were performed one after another because of the lack of any effective drugs for this diffuse-CL patient. The patient was also treated with oral miltefosine. The drug (Impavido ) was started at a dose of 2.5 mg/kg/day and continued for 5 months. However, 2 months after discontinuing miltefosine, small papular lesions appeared and the slit-skin smears and aspirates of lesions had become positive for Leishmania parasites. Miltefosine was re-started at the same dose, but no clinical or parasitological response was observed even after 2 months of re-treatment, and skin lesions continued to grow and spread over the entire body. No specific and efficient drug is available for the diffuse-CL in the world at the moment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male from rural coastal Esmeraldas Province, Ecuador, presented with an 8-year history of progressively disseminating papular, nodular, and plaque-like skin lesions across his face, ears, trunk, and extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At age 16 years, the patient developed papules on his left knee and right cheek that progressively multiplied and spread across his body over 8 years. After 2 years of ineffective empirical treatments, he was clinically misdiagnosed with leprosy and treated with WHO multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine) for 1 month before referral to the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in Guayaquil.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born and raised in San Ignacio, Muisne, Esmeraldas Province, Ecuador (20 m above sea level); local epidemiological survey showed no family or neighborhood cases of similar disease; prior 1-month course of anti-leprosy MDT.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for cutaneous sensory loss.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed widespread, indurated, miliary-to-hen-egg-sized erythematous papules, scaly/crusted nodules, infiltrated erythematous plaques with satellite papules, and brownish macules involving the bilateral earlobes and auricles, face, left shoulder, upper and lower extremities, thighs, and lower back, while sparing the scalp, palms, soles, axillae, epigastrium, groin, and perineum (except for a few dorsal left hand verruca vulgaris lesions). Cutaneous sensation was intact over the entire body and peripheral nerves were not enlarged.
objective.routine_investigations: rK39 immunochromatographic dipstick test was strongly positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Intradermal Montenegro (leishmanin) skin test was negative whereas tuberculin, candidin, and trichophytin skin tests were positive, confirming parasite-specific cell-mediated anergy. Slit-skin smears stained with Ziehl-Neelsen were negative for acid-fast bacilli, while Giemsa-stained lesion smears, thigh nodule biopsy, and species-specific PCR were performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Lesional skin smears and thigh nodule histopathology (showing epidermal hyperkeratosis/acanthosis, dermal neovascularization, and dense infiltrates of foamy macrophages packed with innumerable amastigotes without epithelioid granulomas or AFB) combined with PCR identification of Leishmania (Leishmania) mexicana confirmed anergic diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL), excluding lepromatous leprosy. Sequential treatment courses—including intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (10 mg/kg/day for 28 days), sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 28 days), intramuscular pentamidine (3-4 mg/kg 1-2x/week, stopped due to hypotension, GI toxicity, and syncope), oral itraconazole (200 mg/day for 3 months), mefloquine (4.2 mg/kg/day for 6 days x2), artesunate (6.7 mg/kg/day for 3 days x2), and oral miltefosine (2.5 mg/kg/day for 5 months followed by 2-month retreatment)—produced only transient partial regressions followed by clinical and parasitological relapse.

raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old male presented with single, painful, non-healing ulcer on the right sole with multiple, pink verrucous nodules at the lateral margin of the ulcer, involving the right lateral malleolus and lateral border of the right sole since two years. On detailed history taking, it was revealed that two years ago, patient had a traumatic injury on his right sole for which he did not consult any registered medical practitioner and applied some homemade chemicals on the wound. Surgical intervention was done to debride the wound by local, untrained, nonmedical personnel without proper antibiotic coverage, which led to secondary infections and nonhealing ulceration. Within the next 6 months, after developing a fully-formed ulcer, multiple small pinkish nodular lesions appeared at the lateral margin of the ulcer, which increased in size with time, coalesced with other nodular lesions, and became verrucous. On local cutaneous examination, a deep seated ulcer of 6 cm x 4 cm x 2 cm size was seen over the right sole, whose floor was clean (because of previous antiseptic cleaning) and the margin was hyperkeratotic and macerated [Figure 1]. Along the lateral border and on the lateral malleolus of right foot, multiple, coalescing, firm, pink-coloured verrucous nodules of varying sizes (largest measuring 3 cm x 2.5 cm) in a "Streusel-bread"-like appearance were present [Figure 2]. The size of the whole coalescing multinodular lesion was 9 cm x 6 cm. There was no regional lymphadenopathy, no loss of sensation, nerve thickening, or any other cutaneous signs of leprosy. There was no clinical or radiological evidence of osteomyelitis. The family history, past medical history, routine laboratory investigations, and systemic examinations were non-contributory.
To reach a final diagnosis, a wedge-shaped incisional biopsy was performed and the sample was sent for histopathological evaluation, which demonstrated vertically oriented, multiple, thin, anastomosing strands centred around the acrosyringium [Figures 3 and 4] forming a lattice of double-layered acrosyringeal ductal structures embedded in delicate fibrovascular stroma, extending into the reticular dermis [Figure 5].
On the basis of detailed history, clinical presentations, and distinct histopathological features, diagnosis of ESFA was made, and it was considered to be reactive in nature due to the traumatic nonhealing ulcer.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of a painful non-healing ulcer on his right sole bordered laterally by coalescing pink verrucous nodules.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two years prior to presentation, the patient sustained a traumatic wound on his right sole, applied homemade chemical concoctions, and underwent unsterile debridement by untrained nonmedical personnel without antibiotics, resulting in secondary infection and a chronic non-healing plantar ulcer. Six months after ulcer formation, small pink nodules appeared along the lateral ulcer margin and progressively enlarged and coalesced over 18 months into a verrucous multinodular mass extending to the right lateral malleolus.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of right plantar trauma and unsterile local debridement 2 years prior; otherwise non-contributory medical and family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic right plantar ulcer pain; negative for sensory loss or systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Local cutaneous examination revealed a deep 6 x 4 x 2 cm ulcer on the right sole with a clean floor and macerated, hyperkeratotic margins, bordered along the lateral sole and right lateral malleolus by a 9 x 6 cm coalescing plaque of firm, pink verrucous nodules (largest 3 x 2.5 cm) with a 'Streusel-bread'-like appearance. Cutaneous sensation was intact, peripheral nerves were not thickened, regional lymph nodes were not enlarged, and systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological and biochemical investigations and foot radiographs (showing no osteomyelitis) were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: A wedge-shaped incisional biopsy of the verrucous marginal lesion was performed for histopathological evaluation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathology demonstrated multiple thin, vertically oriented, anastomosing epithelial strands centered around the acrosyringium forming a lattice of double-layered acrosyringeal ductal structures within a delicate fibrovascular stroma extending into the reticular dermis, confirming reactive eccrine syringofibroadenoma (ESFA) secondary to a chronic traumatic plantar ulcer (and excluding leprosy and squamous cell carcinoma).

raw_case_text:
35-year-old female presented with a hyperkeratotic plaque on the left side of forehead. Lesion started as a small papule after 3 months following a roadside fall 2 years back, gradually increased in size, and spread in an annular fashion to form a plaque with warty surface [Figure 1], which started showing ulceration in last 3 months. Lupus vulgaris and leprosy were kept as the differential diagnosis. A detailed history and clinical examination were not in favour of leprosy. She had no history of visit to/residence in known endemic areas for leprosy, no family history of leprosy, no hypo/anaesthesia, tingling, or numbness of hands or feet, and no reduced sweating, loss of hair, dryness of eyes, or epistaxis. On clinical examination an erythematous annular hyperkeratotic plaque with a warty surface measuring 4 x 5 cm was present on the left side of forehead. The lesion showed some crusting and a small scar at the periphery. There was no lymphadenopathy. On clinical examination there were no hypopigmented lesions on body, there was no loss of sensations, and there was no nerve enlargement. Systemic examination also did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine investigations and X-ray chest were normal. Tuberculin skin test was positive with an induration of 20 mm.
A punch biopsy from the lesion showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis, acanthosis [Figure 2(a), H and E (40x), and Figure 2(b), H and E (400x)], and dense inflammatory infiltrates with epithelioid cells and giant cells in the dermis with few acid fast bacilli (AFB) [Figure 2(c), H and E (400x), and Figure 2(d), ZN Staining (1000x)]. PAS staining was not performed.
A small scar was evident in the plaque, possibly secondary to an earlier biopsy. Also the histopathology was more in favour of TBVC than lupus vulgaris. A diagnosis of tuberculosis verrucosa cutis was made, and the patient was started on category 1 treatment as per Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) with which the lesions improved.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of a progressively enlarging annular warty hyperkeratotic plaque on the left forehead that ulcerated over the preceding 3 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months after sustaining a roadside fall 2 years prior to presentation, the patient developed a small papule on the left side of her forehead that gradually expanded centrifugally into a verrucous, hyperkeratotic plaque and developed focal ulceration over the last 3 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of roadside forehead trauma 2 years prior; no residence in or travel to leprosy-endemic areas, and no family history of leprosy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for hypoesthesia, acral tingling or numbness, anhidrosis, madarosis/alopecia, dry eyes, or epistaxis.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed a 4 x 5 cm erythematous, annular, hyperkeratotic plaque with a verrucous surface, focal crusting, and a small peripheral scar on the left forehead. There were no hypopigmented skin lesions elsewhere, cutaneous sensation was intact, peripheral nerves were not thickened, regional lymphadenopathy was absent, and systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood investigations and chest radiograph were normal. Mantoux tuberculin skin test was strongly positive with 20 mm of induration.
objective.advanced_workup: Forehead punch biopsy was performed for H&E and Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) staining.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Punch biopsy histopathology revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and dense dermal epithelioid and Langhans giant-cell granulomatous infiltrates with sparse acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining (1000x), confirming tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (TBVC) and ruling out leprosy and lupus vulgaris. The patient was treated with Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) Category 1 anti-tubercular therapy with marked clinical improvement of the forehead plaque.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old dark-skinned male patient, hypertensive, reported the appearance of erythematous-brown, edematous and itchy plaques on the abdomen in the beginning of 2013, with inconclusive histopathology and immunohistochemistry. He remained under follow-up and presented to the outpatient dermatology clinic in February 2015 with an ulcerated tumor on the skin of the nose and worsening of the previous lesions. On clinical examination, he had brown and edematous plaques on the frontal region, associated with alopecia of the eyebrows and hairline, in addition to a deforming tumor on the nose (Figure 1). ENT assessment demonstrated an infiltrative lesion, with total obstruction of the right nostril and partial of the left nostril, with associated mucoid discharge. No lesions on the palate or jugal mucosa were seen. Slightly lichenified brown plaques were seen on the upper and lower limbs, predominantly on the trunk and ulcerated tumors on the upper limbs (Figure 2).
There was no lymphadenopathy. The suspicion was of paracoccidioidomycosis, leishmaniasis, syphilis, leprosy, sarcoidosis, mycosis fungoides, and lethal midline granuloma. Blood samples were collected, and microscopy, Montenegro's test, tuberculin test, bacilloscopy, serology for hepatitis, HIV and syphilis were all performed, and all were negative. Chest radiograph and abdomen ultrasound were unremarkable. New biopsies were taken, with unspecific findings. The patient's follow-up was then irregular, with long intervals between appointments, with worsening of the tumor on the nose. In July 2015 three new biopsies from different skin lesions were taken and the histopathology of the abdominal plaque revealed a dense atypical mononuclear infiltrate, involving the remaining follicular sheath and eccrine glands associated to psoriasiform hyperplasia of the epidermis and granulomatous reaction (Figure 3). Immunohistochemistry favored the diagnostic interpretation of non-Hodgkin epidermotropic and folliculotropic T-cell cutaneous lymphoma, CD4 and CD30 positive (Figures 4 and 5). The patient was seen by the hematology team and chemotherapy with gemcitabine and interferon, associated to phototherapy were scheduled.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old hypertensive male presented in February 2015 with a deforming, ulcerated nasal tumor and worsening pruritic erythematous-brown plaques and ulcerated tumors over his forehead, trunk, and extremities of 2 years' duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In early 2013, the patient developed pruritic, edematous erythematous-brown plaques on his abdomen with inconclusive initial biopsies. Following irregular follow-up, he returned in February 2015 and July 2015 with progressive worsening of the truncal and limb lesions and a deforming, ulcerated tumor on his nose causing bilateral nasal obstruction and mucoid discharge.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of systemic hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cutaneous pruritus, nasal obstruction, and mucoid nasal discharge.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed edematous brown plaques on the forehead with eyebrow and anterior hairline alopecia, a deforming ulcerated tumor on the external nose, slightly lichenified brown plaques over the trunk and upper/lower extremities, and ulcerated tumors on the upper limbs, without palpable lymphadenopathy. Otolaryngological (ENT) examination showed an infiltrative endonasal mass causing total right nostril and partial left nostril obstruction with mucoid discharge, while the palate and buccal mucosa were spared.
objective.routine_investigations: Direct microscopy, slit-skin smear bacilloscopy, Montenegro skin test, tuberculin skin test, and serologies for hepatitis, HIV, and syphilis were all negative. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Three repeat skin biopsies obtained in July 2015 (including from the abdominal plaque) demonstrated psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, a granulomatous reaction, and a dense atypical mononuclear infiltrate with epidermotropism and infiltration of hair follicle sheaths (folliculotropism) and eccrine glands; immunohistochemistry was positive for CD4 and CD30.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed CD4+, CD30+ epidermotropic and folliculotropic cutaneous T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (granulomatous/folliculotropic mycosis fungoides with large-cell transformation), ruling out leprosy, leishmaniasis, paracoccidioidomycosis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, and extranodal NK/T-cell nasal-type lymphoma. The patient was referred to hematology and scheduled for systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine and interferon combined with phototherapy.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man, presented to the Dermatology clinic with a history of a pruritic rash that started on his upper chest and spread to his head in a photodistributed pattern. He also had severe bone pain, unexplained recurrent fevers, right upper quadrant pain, muscle aches, ankle joint pain, mild subjective exertional dyspnea and drenching night sweats that began 9-10 months after the onset of the rash. He reported that the eruption was exacerbated by sun exposure. Previous treatment included two, 2-week courses of 50 mg of prednisone. Partial improvement of the rash, occurred each time. Multiple courses of topical permethrin to treat suspected scabies did not help. Past medical history was remarkable only for alcohol-induced cirrhosis and psoriasis. His medications were venlafaxine, naproxen, and pantoprazole. He did not have any industrial chemical or radiation exposures, and his family history did not include any autoimmune diseases.
On presentation, he had photodistributed well-defined red-brown, annular and ovoid non-scaly plaques mainly involving the head, neck, shoulders, and upper chest (Figure 1(a)). There were also subtle well-defined, non-scaly red-brown macules on the abdomen and thighs. The tibia and ulna were tender to palpation bilaterally. There was no overt joint inflammation and no adventitial breath sounds. The differential diagnosis included granuloma annulare, subacute cutaneous lupus, infectious granulomas including leprosy, actinic granuloma, and mycosis fungoides.
Notable laboratory findings included a negative antinuclear antibody test, diffuse reactive hypergammaglobulinemia with no monoclonal bands and mild transaminitis with elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase. It was felt his abnormal liver enzyme tests were most likely secondary to his alcohol use. Skin biopsy of the lesions revealed superficial and deep non-necrotizing granulomatous dermatitis with scattering accompanying lymphocytes. There were no atypical lymphocytes, diffuse neutrophilic/lymphocytic infiltrates, dermal edema, mucin, or epidermal change (Figure 1(b)). The skin biopsy (Figure 1(c)) and a blood smear were negative for leprosy. A tuberculosis skin test was non-reactive. On imaging, a computed tomography (CT) of his chest and abdomen showed non-calcified pulmonary granulomas, while a bone scan demonstrated cortical uptake in the tibia suggestive of osseous sarcoidosis. Further testing of pulmonary function excluded restrictive lung disease. An echocardiogram and ophthalmological exam were unremarkable.
In light of his investigations, he was diagnosed with systemic sarcoidosis with photodistributed cutaneous involvement. Prednisone 40 mg daily with a slow taper and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily were started. Resolution of his cutaneous involvement, arthralgias, and bone pain occurred over 3 months. He is followed by a general internist to monitor for progression of his pulmonary disease and his other systemic manifestations. He has not had any adverse side effects and has had a sustained remission on antimalarial monotherapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old man presented with a chronic photodistributed pruritic rash over his upper chest, neck, and head accompanied 9-10 months later by severe bone pain, recurrent fevers, drenching night sweats, right upper quadrant pain, myalgias, ankle arthralgia, and mild exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a sun-exacerbated pruritic eruption starting on his upper chest and spreading to his head, neck, and shoulders, followed 9-10 months later by severe tibial/ulnar bone pain, unexplained recurrent fevers, drenching night sweats, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, myalgias, ankle pain, and mild exertional dyspnea. Two prior 2-week courses of oral prednisone (50 mg/day) produced transient partial improvement of the rash, whereas multiple courses of topical permethrin for suspected scabies were ineffective.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of alcohol-induced liver cirrhosis and psoriasis. Home medications were venlafaxine, naproxen, and pantoprazole. Negative for industrial chemical or radiation exposure or family history of autoimmune disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for photosensitive pruritic rash, severe bone pain, recurrent fevers, drenching night sweats, RUQ pain, myalgias, ankle arthralgia, and mild subjective exertional dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed well-defined red-brown annular and ovoid non-scaly plaques in a photodistributed pattern over the head, neck, shoulders, and upper chest, along with subtle well-defined non-scaly red-brown macules on the abdomen and thighs. Musculoskeletal and chest examination showed bilateral tibial and ulnar tenderness to palpation without overt joint synovitis and clear lung fields.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests demonstrated mild transaminitis with elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (attributed to alcohol use) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia without monoclonal bands. Tuberculin skin test and peripheral blood smear for leprosy were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) was negative. Pulmonary function tests, echocardiography, and ophthalmologic examination were normal. Chest and abdominal CT revealed non-calcified pulmonary granulomas, and technetium bone scintigraphy demonstrated bilateral tibial cortical uptake suggestive of osseous sarcoidosis. Skin biopsy was performed for H&E and acid-fast staining.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Skin biopsy revealed superficial and deep non-necrotizing granulomatous dermatitis with scattered lymphocytes, no epidermotropism or mucin, and negative staining for Mycobacterium leprae, which together with non-calcified pulmonary granulomas on chest CT and tibial cortical uptake on bone scan confirmed systemic sarcoidosis with photodistributed cutaneous and osseous involvement (ruling out leprosy, subacute cutaneous lupus, granuloma annulare, actinic granuloma, and mycosis fungoides). Treatment with tapering oral prednisone (starting at 40 mg daily) and hydroxychloroquine (200 mg twice daily) resolved his skin lesions, arthralgias, and bone pain within 3 months, with sustained remission on hydroxychloroquine monotherapy.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old right-handed Hispanic male presented initially to an another hospital after a new-onset generalized seizure while driving. He emigrated from Mexico 15 years prior to presentation and has not returned for 6 years. He traveled to many states around the US for work, including Texas, Louisiana, Virginia, Florida, and Nebraska, but has lived in Alabama for the last 11 years. On admission to an outside hospital, he underwent CT head and subsequent MRI brain, which revealed a multi-lobulated cystic lesion of the left fronto-temporal region. A lumbar puncture was performed with cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) labs, culture, cytology, and flow cytometry; all of which were unremarkable. He was evaluated by an outside neurologist and started on oral phenytoin for seizure control. He was subsequently discharged with follow-up at our facility for further management.
Upon evaluation in clinic, he had no focal deficits on neurological examination. Imaging from the another hospital was reviewed. The CT head non-contrast showed a large left fronto-temporal multi-lobulated cystic lesion ~6.5 cm x 4.5 cm x 4 cm in size and primarily centered around the sylvian fissure, causing significant mass effect and 0.5 cm midline shift. Calcifications were present in the central confluence of the cysts. The largest cyst cavity was in the left temporal lobe and did not appear to communicate with the temporal horn. The MRI brain, with and without contrast with T2-weighted sequences, revealed high intensity within the cyst, similar to CSF [Figure 1]. FLAIR sequences showed minimal increased signal in the cyst walls. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences showed no increased diffusion restriction. Contrast-enhanced imaging showed no peripheral enhancement of the lesion. Serology for serum cysticercosis IgG antibodies was positive.
The patient was treated with dexamethasone 8 mg intravenously every 8 hours on the day prior to surgery and his home phenytoin dose was continued. The CT of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast were obtained to rule out other possible diagnoses on the differential, including metastatic disease and hydatid cysts; this was unremarkable. The patient was taken to the operating room the following day for surgery and pre-treated with 10 mg of dexamethasone intravenously. A large left pterional craniotomy was performed to sufficiently expose portions of the left frontal and temporal lobes, as well as the sylvian fissure (see supplemental video). Upon opening the dura, discoloration was noted in the superficial pia and arachnoid layers, consistent with chronic inflammation. Stealth navigation was used to plan a trajectory into the anterior and inferior portion or the large temporal cyst and a Touhey needle was inserted through the middle temporal gyrus to aspirate cyst contents, of which 6 mL of clear fluid was obtained. This was performed prior to further dissection to allow for relaxation of the brain. A sylvian dissection was performed, during which the cyst began to evaginate on its own [Figure 2a and b]. Gentle traction was applied to the cyst, which resulted in intra-operative rupture, spilling the cyst contents within the subarachnoid space [Figure 2c]. Copious irrigation was used to clear the cyst fluid and the patient was administered a second dose of 6 mg dexamethasone intravenously. With completion of the sylvian dissection, the cyst complex was removed en bloc with no intra-operative evidence of residual lesion [Figure 2d]. A post-operative neurological exam revealed no neurologic or speech deficits. Non-contrast CT head and MRI brain with and without contrast were obtained on post-operative day 1, which showed expected encephalomalacia surrounding the resection cavity, with no evidence of residual lesion [Figure 3].
Post-operatively, the patient was started on a 14-day course of oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily. He was discharged from the hospital on post-operative day 5 without complications. He was treated with dexamethasone while undergoing oral anti-parasitic therapy and discharged on a slow steroid taper. He remained on his admission dose of phenytoin at discharge. On scheduled outpatient follow-up, he felt well. Surveillance CT head revealed stable left fronto-temporal encephalomalacia and no evidence of recurrence [Figure 4].
Neuropathology was consistent with neurocysticercosis in racemose cyst formation [Figure 5]. Grossly, the specimen consisted of tan-white membranous tissue measuring 3.7 cm x 2.5 cm x 0.6 cm. Microscopic examination demonstrated a cyst structure larger than a classic cysticercus cyst, exhibiting multiple convolutions and foldings with rounded protusions at the surface of the tegument. The surface lining exhibited relatively well-preserved microtriches resembling microvilli. Within the inner reticular layer, several small oval or circular calcified bodies (calcareous corpuscles) were present. Scolices and rostellum (hooklets) were not present within this specimen, which is consistent with the racemose cyst variant.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old right-handed Hispanic man presented for neurosurgical evaluation after experiencing a new-onset generalized seizure while driving.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient suffered a new-onset generalized seizure while driving and was initially evaluated at an outside hospital, where neuroimaging revealed a large left frontotemporal cystic mass and normal CSF studies; he was started on oral phenytoin and referred to the neurosurgery clinic.
subjective.past_medical_history: Emigrated from Mexico to the United States 15 years prior to presentation and had not returned to Mexico for 6 years. He had lived in Alabama for 11 years while traveling for work to Texas, Louisiana, Virginia, Florida, and Nebraska.
subjective.review_of_systems: Taking oral phenytoin at the time of clinic evaluation.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination in clinic and postoperatively revealed no focal neurological or speech deficits.
objective.advanced_workup: Outside lumbar puncture CSF cell count, chemistry, culture, cytology, and flow cytometry were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was negative for metastatic or hydatid disease. Noncontrast head CT and contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated a giant ~6.5 x 4.5 x 4 cm multilobulated cystic lesion centered in the left frontotemporal Sylvian fissure (largest cavity in the left temporal lobe) with central calcifications, CSF-like T2 hyperintensity, minimal FLAIR wall signal, no diffusion restriction, no peripheral contrast enhancement, significant mass effect, and 0.5 cm midline shift.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum cysticercosis IgG antibody serology was positive. Following preoperative IV dexamethasone, he underwent a left pterional craniotomy with stereotactic needle aspiration (6 mL clear fluid) and en bloc microsurgical Sylvian dissection of the giant cyst complex (with copious irrigation and supplemental IV dexamethasone following intraoperative cyst rupture). Histopathology confirmed racemose neurocysticercosis, showing a 3.7 x 2.5 x 0.6 cm folded membranous cyst lined by microtriches and calcareous corpuscles in the reticular layer without a scolex or hooklets. He completed a 14-day postoperative course of oral albendazole (400 mg twice daily) with a corticosteroid taper while continuing phenytoin, and remained asymptomatic with no recurrence on follow-up head CT.

raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old right-handed male, from Estado de Mexico, presented with deficient hygiene and dietary habits. He was hypertense since 5 months prior to presentation which was controlled with losartan (40 mg once daily). Two days before admission, he experienced holocraneal headache 7/10 in the visual analogue scale, intermittent, with no response to any medication, sudden worsening of pain to 10/10, nausea, and vomit. On physical examination, he presented with 14 points in the Glasgow coma scale (M6, O4, V4), pupils were 3 mm, adequate light-reflex response, and bilateral papilledema. The cranial nerves did not have other pathological responses, extremities had adequate strength 5/5, and normal reflexes (++/++) were noted. He presented with gait disturbance with lateralization to the right side [Figure 1].
We describe our surgical decision and rationale for this management. The patient had classical clinical symptoms of intracranial hypertension such as headache, nausea and vomiting. The computed tomography (CT) scans showed tetraventricular hydrocephalus and important dilatation of the fourth ventricle, due to this finding and because of the high prevalence of neurocysticercosis in our country, we decided to perform a fourth ventricle exploration with the Hopkins II rigid endoscope (Karl Storz, Germany) . In this case, we considered that the described approach for the exploration of the fourth ventricle through a prefrontal burr-hole with flexible endoscopy could be riskier than approaching just the fourth ventricle with one suboccipital burr hole because the third ventricle and cerebral aqueduct were not dilated enough to allow our endoscope to go through. The patient was placed in a Concorde position, with a soft head paddle, taking care of the pressure points to avoid any complication, and then adequate antisepsis of the region was performed with iodine solution. A single burr hole approach was made, which was planned 3 cm from the midline to the right side and 2 cm down from the inion. The burr hole was planned with craneometric points in the preoperative images, as shown, we did not use any image-guided system. The skin was approached in the standard manner until the suboccipital bone was reached. Then we performed the burr hole with a midas rex system and adequate hemostasis was made. The dura was opened in a cruciate form and then we performed a 1 cm cortisectomy with bipolar forceps. The rigid endoscope was inserted directly through the cerebellar cortical surface in the right hemisphere with a freehand approach. Just as soon as the endoscope passed through to the fourth ventricle, a cystic lesion was found, which was compatible with a neurocysti; as shown in the image it was not adherent to any of the fourth ventricle structures. We were able to remove the entire cystic lesion, and then we performed a fourth ventricle exploration, showing that the aqueduct and both Luschka foramina were permeable, as well as the obex. Surgical time was 40 minutes with no complications. The fourth ventricle ependymal showed no macroscopycal findings of ependymitis, and due to the surgical procedure the cerebrospinal fluid flow was restored. Postoperatively, the patient did well and was discharged home 48 hours later, with oral standard neurocysticercosis treatment with albendazole 15 mg/kg and corticosteroids [Figures 2 and 3].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old right-handed Mexican man presented with a 2-day history of intermittent holocranial headache that acutely worsened to 10/10 intensity with nausea and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two days prior to admission, the patient developed an intermittent holocranial headache (7/10 on the visual analogue scale) unresponsive to medication, which suddenly intensified to 10/10 pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in Estado de Mexico with poor hygiene and dietary habits. Diagnosed with hypertension 5 months prior to presentation, controlled with losartan 40 mg once daily.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe headache, nausea, and vomiting; taking losartan 40 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14 (E4V4M6), pupils were 3 mm and reactive to light, and fundoscopy revealed bilateral papilledema. Cranial nerves were otherwise intact, limb motor strength was 5/5 with normal (++/++) reflexes, and gait examination showed ataxia with rightward lateralization.
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT demonstrated tetraventricular hydrocephalus with marked dilatation of the fourth ventricle.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: The patient underwent a freehand right suboccipital burr-hole transcerebellar rigid endoscopic exploration (Hopkins II endoscope) of the fourth ventricle, identifying and completely removing a non-adherent fourth-ventricular neurocysticercosis cyst without ependymitis and restoring CSF flow through the cerebral aqueduct, foramina of Luschka, and obex without shunt placement. He had an uncomplicated postoperative course and was discharged home after 48 hours on oral albendazole (15 mg/kg) and corticosteroids.

raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old female was referred to our emergency room by her homeland local hospital in Cape Verde (West Africa), with complaints of headaches and diminished vision over the last 4 months. On neurological examination, she had impaired visual acuity (right eye: 6/10; left eye: 7/10) and bilateral papilledema. No other neurological signs were observed. The brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hydrocephalus apparently caused by a well-defined cystic lesion in the fourth ventricle. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI sequences and had a peripheral millimetric solid component hyperintense on both sequences [Figure 1]. Another MRI was done 8 hours later due to a temporary malfunction of the gadolinium injector. In this second exam, the lesion showed no contrast enhancement but had changed its location to the contralateral side within the fourth ventricle [Figure 2], revealing its mobile nature. The FLAIR sequences showed cerebellar edema surrounding the cyst.
A surgical plan was elaborated to solve both problems - the hydrocephalus and the intraventricular cyst - at the same surgical time. Initially, an uneventful ETV was performed and intraventricular CSF was collected for further laboratorial analyses. No external drainage was left in place. The patient was then placed in prone position and underwent a suboccipital median craniotomy. Using microsurgical technique, a telovelar approach to the fourth ventricle was performed. The cyst microdissection was particularly challenging due to its thin wall and partial adherence to the surrounding ependyma, which contributed to an intraventricular cyst rupture by the end of its total removal. Extensive irrigation of the ventricle space with Ringer's solution was performed to avoid intraventricular dissemination.
The patient had an uneventful postoperative course. The CSF analysis showed no alterations. Postop MRI showed a total removal of the cyst lesion and reduction of the ventricle dimensions [Figure 3]. The pathology report confirmed the cyst to be a T. solium larva in its vesicular stage as had already been suspected [Figure 4]. It was decided not to initiate antiparasitic medication given the lack of evidence of a positive effect in intraventricular single neurocysticercosis cyst. The patient was discharged asymptomatic seven days later with a prescription to a progressive corticosteroids' weaning of.
Five weeks after discharge, she presented back, complaining of headaches and worsening of vision again. A significant pseudomeningocele with no CSF leak was visible underneath the frontal surgical wound. A bilateral papilledema was evident in the ophthalmological examination. The MRI showed hydrocephalus recurrence with no evidence of CSF flow through the previous ventriculostomy stoma [Figure 5]. A second endoscopic approach was performed to collect CSF and to reopen the ventriculostomy stoma, using the same burr hole and parenchyma trajectory. Intraoperatively, we visualized a transparent CSF plenty of floating debris [Figure 6]. In the histopathological examination, these were found to be fragments of brain parenchyma with granulation tissue foci, lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrates, with histiocytes, few neutrophils, and multiple calcifications. The CSF analysis showed no cells and normal glucose and proteins' levels. The patient did well postoperatively and was discharged 5 days later with no neurological deficits.
She has been followed up for 5 months now, remaining asymptomatic, with clearly defined optic discs on fundoscopy and has fully recovered visual acuity. The 5-month postop MRI ruled out hydrocephalus or any recurrent lesion [Figure 7].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old woman from Cape Verde presented with a 4-month history of progressive headaches and diminished vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred from Cape Verde with 4 months of persistent headaches and visual decline. Five weeks after initial surgical treatment and discharge, she re-presented with recurrent headaches and worsening vision.
subjective.past_medical_history: Referred from Cape Verde (West Africa).

objective.physical_examination: On initial neurological and ophthalmic examination, she had reduced visual acuity (6/10 right eye, 7/10 left eye) and bilateral papilledema without other focal neurological deficits. At readmission 5 weeks postoperatively, she had a frontal subgaleal pseudomeningocele without CSF leak and recurrent bilateral papilledema.
objective.advanced_workup: Two preoperative brain MRIs performed 8 hours apart demonstrated obstructive hydrocephalus, surrounding cerebellar FLAIR edema, and a well-defined, non-enhancing T1/T2-hypointense cystic lesion containing a millimetric hyperintense peripheral mural nodule (scolex) that migrated to the contralateral side within the fourth ventricle between scans. Intraoperative CSF analysis was normal. At 5-week readmission, repeat brain MRI showed recurrent hydrocephalus with absence of CSF flow through the prior third ventriculostomy stoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: The patient initially underwent simultaneous endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) and median suboccipital telovelar microsurgical excision of the fourth-ventricular cyst (with copious Ringer's lactate irrigation after terminal cyst rupture); histopathology confirmed a vesicular-stage Taenia solium larva (fourth-ventricular neurocysticercosis), and antiparasitic drugs were withheld while corticosteroids were tapered. When obstructive hydrocephalus recurred 5 weeks later due to ETV stoma occlusion by inflammatory/granulation tissue debris with calcifications, repeat endoscopic exploration and stoma reopening restored CSF flow, resulting in complete visual recovery, resolution of papilledema, and no recurrence on 5-month follow-up MRI.

raw_case_text:
Our patient is a 36-year-old female with a history of adult onset seizures. She was born and raised in Mexico and emigrated to the United States at the age of 8. Since arriving to the United States, she had never returned to Mexico. She had her first seizure about 10 years before presentation, at which point she was placed on anti-epileptic medications that were subsequently weaned off without any further seizure activity in the past several years. No prior imaging was available for our review, but the patient denied report of any intracranial lesions that could be identified as the culprit of the adult onset seizures.
She initially presented to an outside institution with progressively worsening bilateral headaches over the past year that were associated with vertigo and intermittent nausea. The headaches were worse at night and on waking up in the morning, and they improved throughout the day. A computerized tomography (CT) scan demonstrated ventriculomegaly and transependymal flow, with evidence of obstruction at the level of the fourth ventricle. She was referred to our clinic by our neurology colleagues, where she was found to have no neurologic deficits on examination. Outpatient magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated obstructed hydrocephalus secondary to a lobulated cystic mass within the fourth ventricle, with a streak of internal linear enhancement most consistent with racemose NCC. A worm was easily identified within the cyst on the MRI [Figure 1].
Given the chronic nature of the lesion and her benign clinical examination, she was scheduled for elective surgery a few weeks later. She underwent right frontal burr hole for endoscopic third ventriculostomy and placement of external ventricular drain (EVD), then she was positioned prone and underwent suboccipital craniotomy for resection of the fourth ventricular cystic mass followed by duraplasty. The cyst was removed as a single en bloc specimen, although during the process of removal, a small portion of the cyst ruptured into the ventricle - this was quickly suctioned and extensively irrigated. Gross examination [Figure 2] and pathology [Figure 3] demonstrated a mature T. solium plerocercoid larvae measuring 1.2 x 0.5 x 0.2 cm encased in a tan, gelatinous, cystic membrane.
Postoperatively, she had no neurologic deficits. Her EVD was quickly weaned with minimal drainage and low intracranial pressure, so it was removed on postoperative day 2. She underwent ophthalmologic examination, demonstrating no evidence of an active ocular infection or involvement of NCC, but concern for a chronic, inactive choroidal inflammatory process. Our infectious disease colleagues were consulted and found no other risk factors for NCC aside from living in Mexico until the age of 8, and she was negative for tuberculosis infection. Given her longstanding history of seizures, but recent presentation with an active lesion, it was felt that she may have been auto-infecting. She underwent a 21-day course of albendazole with a 14-day dexamethasone taper for protection against aseptic meningitis. She was also prescribed a single dose of praziquantel at the end of her therapy given concerns for possible auto-infection from her gastrointestinal system. On discharge, her headaches, vertigo, and nausea had completely resolved.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old Mexican-born woman presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening bilateral nocturnal and morning headaches accompanied by vertigo and intermittent nausea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the year preceding presentation, the patient experienced progressively worsening bilateral headaches that were most severe at night and upon awakening in the morning and improved during the day, associated with vertigo and intermittent nausea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born and raised in Mexico until immigrating to the United States at age 8, with no subsequent return travel to Mexico. She had a history of adult-onset seizures beginning 10 years earlier, had been weaned off antiepileptic medications several years prior without seizure recurrence, and denied prior neuroimaging showing intracranial lesions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache, vertigo, and nausea; currently off antiepileptic drugs.

objective.physical_examination: Preoperative and postoperative neurological examinations revealed no focal neurological deficits. Postoperative ophthalmologic examination showed no active ocular cysticercosis, noting only a chronic inactive choroidal inflammatory process.
objective.routine_investigations: Tuberculosis screening was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Outside head CT demonstrated ventriculomegaly and transependymal CSF flow with obstruction at the fourth ventricle. Outpatient brain MRI confirmed obstructive hydrocephalus caused by a lobulated fourth-ventricular cystic mass exhibiting internal linear enhancement and a visible intraluminal worm.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: The patient underwent right frontal endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), external ventricular drain (EVD) placement, and prone suboccipital craniotomy with en bloc resection of the fourth-ventricular cyst (with immediate suction and irrigation following minor intraoperative cyst rupture) and duraplasty. Gross and histopathological analysis identified a mature 1.2 x 0.5 x 0.2 cm Taenia solium larva encased in a tan gelatinous cystic membrane, confirming fourth-ventricular neurocysticercosis. The EVD was removed on postoperative day 2, and she completed a 21-day course of albendazole, a 14-day dexamethasone taper, and a single dose of praziquantel (to eradicate potential intestinal tapeworm carriage/autoinfection), with complete resolution of her headaches, vertigo, and nausea at discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old female, married Hindu graduate, resident of Uttar Pradesh, with no family history of mental illness, presented with manic symptoms of overtalkativeness, overcheerfulness, grandiose idea that she is a goddess, ideas of persecution against family members, decreased need for sleep, increased psychomotor activity, muttering to self, followed by two generalised tonic-clonic seizure episodes in April 2018. The patient first had seizures at the age of 13. She had been treated with antiepileptics since then until the age of 20 when she got married in the year 2016. The patient got pregnant in February 2017, and in September 2017, at the 8th month of pregnancy, the patient had a mood of sadness, irritability, crying spells, hopelessness, suicidal ideations and social withdrawal, and she was started on desvenlafaxine 100 mg that was continued until 2 months post partum until January 2018 after complete resolution of the episode.
In April 2018, at the onset of her manic symptoms, she was started on steroids dexamethasone 8 mg and antiepileptics (phenytoin 200 mg), and she was referred to higher centre for further investigations and treatment.
Her blood tests including red cell count, packed cell volume, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, urea, sugar and liver function test, thyroid profile and electrocardiogram (ECG) were unremarkable except for white cell count, which was raised to 13.1 x 109/L, suggestive of infection. Serum Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test and stool examination were negative for T. solium. In addition, examination of the fundus did not show any sign of raised intracranial pressure or deposits of cysticerci. X-rays of the skull, cervical spine, chest, forearm and upper arm did not show any calcification. Electroencephalogram was within normal limits. Nerve conduction study showed no sign of peripheral neuropathy. On mental status examination, the patient showed increased psychomotor activity, elated inappropriate affect, increased speech productivity and decreased reaction time with elementary auditory hallucinations, grandiose idea of being a goddess, impaired attention and concentration, impaired immediate and recent memory, impaired judgement and insight. However, abstraction was intact. Psychological testing, that is, Rorschach testing and Bender Gestalt revealed evidence of organic aetiology.
The patient was advised for a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain in April 2018 (figure 1). The MRI showed multiple T2 hyperintense round-to-oval-shaped lesions with surrounding hyperintense signals on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere and cerebellar hemisphere as depicted in figure 1. Some of the lesions were showing eccentric nodules. No post-contrast enhancement was seen suggestive of the colloidal vesicular stage of neurocysticercosis.
In July 2018, when manic symptoms were resolved, computed tomography (CT) scan showed multiple diffusely scattered tiny calcified lesions in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere as depicted in figure 2. Similar lesions were also present in occipital lobes and external capsules (not shown). No appreciable perilesional oedema was seen on non-contrast CT suggestive of the calcified nodular stage of neurocysticercosis. Another MRI in 2020 was done to look for the resolution of the disease, which showed multiple lesions as calcified (including the right temporal lobe lesion) and some of them were showing surrounding perilesional oedema but no enhancement suggestive of granular nodular stage and some of them were in the colloidal vesicular stage, which were showing enhancement and perilesional edema as depicted in figure 3.
Hence, the possibilities of tuberculoma, neurosyphilis and space-occupying lesion in the brain were excluded by imaging and blood tests.
At the higher centre, considering her symptoms, the patient was started on risperidone built up to 6 mg for the management of psychotic symptoms, and for epilepsy, tablet carbamazepine was started to use its additional action as a mood stabiliser. The patient showed improvement within 4 months and it was planned to give her steroids along with antihelmintics. The patient continued taking antiepileptics carbamazepine 600 mg and risperidone tapered down and stopped slowly over 2 years, and most of the lesions seemed to have calcified in subsequent radiological scans. The patient still had occasional headaches and dysmorphopsia probably owing to perilesional oedema in a few of the lesions and was started on dexamethasone 10 mg and albendazole 1200 mg. The patient reported improvement in these symptoms. She has been advised to continue the treatment and regular follow-up. In addition, it is planned to do a detailed neurological examination to find out any sign suggestive of reactivation of lesions in every follow-up visit and radiological investigations if required.
After 2 years of follow-up, in August 2020, the patient's radiological findings were multiple lesions in bilateral cerebral lobes, basal ganglia and left cerebellar parenchyma, a few of which are showing eccentric scolex and a few of which are calcified with mild perilesional oedema suggestive of multiple neurocysticerci in different stages of development. The current mental status examination of the patient was not suggestive of any other cognitive impairment except difficulty in sustaining attention. Figure 4 shows the chronology of events in summary.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh presented in April 2018 with acute manic and psychotic symptoms followed by two generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute mania characterized by overtalkativeness, overcheerfulness, grandiose delusions of being a goddess, persecutory delusions against family members, decreased need for sleep, increased psychomotor activity, and self-muttering, followed by two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She was initially started on dexamethasone 8 mg and phenytoin 200 mg before referral to a tertiary center.
subjective.past_medical_history: Married Hindu graduate from Uttar Pradesh with a history of epilepsy from age 13 to age 20 (treated with antiepileptics until her marriage in 2016) and an episode of antenatal/postpartum depression with suicidal ideation in the 8th month of pregnancy (September 2017) that resolved completely with desvenlafaxine 100 mg (discontinued in January 2018). Family history was negative for psychiatric illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Received dexamethasone 8 mg and phenytoin 200 mg prior to tertiary referral; later reported occasional headaches and dysmorphopsia during follow-up.

objective.physical_examination: Fundoscopic examination was normal with no papilledema or intraocular cysticerci. Mental status examination revealed increased psychomotor activity, elated inappropriate affect, pressured speech, decreased reaction time, elementary auditory hallucinations, grandiose delusions of being a goddess, persecutory delusions, and impaired attention, concentration, immediate and recent memory, insight, and judgment, with preserved abstraction.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count was elevated at 13.1 x 10^9/L, while red cell count, packed cell volume, ESR, blood urea, blood glucose, liver function tests, thyroid profile, and ECG were normal. Serum VDRL and stool examination for Taenia solium were negative. Radiographs of the skull, cervical spine, chest, forearm, and upper arm showed no soft-tissue or bony calcifications.
objective.advanced_workup: EEG and nerve conduction studies were normal, while Rorschach and Bender-Gestalt psychological tests indicated an organic brain syndrome. Brain MRI (April 2018) revealed multiple bilateral cerebral and cerebellar T2-hyperintense round-to-oval lesions with surrounding FLAIR edema, eccentric nodules (scolices), and no contrast enhancement (colloidal vesicular stage). Follow-up noncontrast head CT (July 2018) showed multiple scattered calcified lesions without edema (calcified nodular stage), and 2020 brain MRIs demonstrated multiple lesions across bilateral cerebral lobes, basal ganglia, and left cerebellum in multiple developmental stages (vesicular with eccentric scolex, colloidal vesicular, granular nodular, and calcified with mild perilesional edema).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Parenchymal neurocysticercosis in multiple developmental stages presenting with organic bipolar mania and epilepsy was confirmed by characteristic serial MRI/CT findings (including eccentric scolices) after excluding tuberculoma and neurosyphilis. She was treated with risperidone (titrated up to 6 mg/day and tapered off over 2 years) and carbamazepine (titrated to 600 mg/day), followed by dexamethasone (10 mg) and albendazole (1200 mg/day) for persistent symptomatic perilesional edema (headache and dysmorphopsia). Her mania, psychosis, and seizures resolved completely, leaving only mild difficulty sustaining attention at 2-year follow-up in August 2020.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old Indian male presented to the emergency services of our institute with an alleged history of a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient's Glasgow Coma scoring was E2V3M4. The patient was intubated. Noncontrast computed tomography revealed multiple well-defined cystic lesions in the cortical and juxtacortical regions. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed multiple ring lesions with enhancing protoscolex which was suggestive of neurocysticercosis (NCC) [Figure 1]. The optic nerve was free of any cysts. An ophthalmology consult was sought before starting anti-helminthic drugs. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable, and pupils were reacting normally to light. Fundoscopy showed clear media and discrete yellow-white placoid subretinal lesions nasal to the optic disc and in the macular area of 0.25 1 DD size in the right eye [Figure 2a]. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) scan through the lesion showed a hyperreflective cystic lesion with backscattering [Figure 2b]. B-scan ultrasound showed an anechoic cystic lesion in the coats of the eye with a hyperechoic scolex [Figure 2c]. The classical imaging findings of multiple cysts with scolex on the MRI head are an absolute criterion for diagnosis of definitive NCC. The ocular ultrasound, OCT, and epidemiology further supported the diagnosis of NCC with multiple subretinal cysticerci; however, the patient had no ocular complaint. The parasite appeared to be in the vesicular stage in both locations, and there was no surrounding inflammation.
Identification of serum antibodies with standard enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay techniques was negative which is a validated test with <70% positivity for intraocular cysticercosis. The stool tests for 3 days did not reveal any parasitic disease.
The patient was started on injectable steroids (dexamethasone 6 mg) followed by albendazole 15 mg/kg. The patient was initially followed up for 2 weeks till his discharge from the hospital. There was an improvement in the Glasgow Coma scores during this period. There were no episodes of fever and seizures. However, there was no resolution of the placoid lesions. Transpupillary thermotherapy was done for the persistent subretinal cysts using a large spot-size diode laser 810 nm [Figure 2d]. Chorioretinal scarring was noted at a week's follow-up visit in the retina clinic after laser treatment, and the patient's vision was documented as 20/20 OU. Unfortunately, no subsequent follow-up is available.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old Indian man presented to the emergency department with depressed consciousness following an alleged road traffic accident.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was brought to emergency services after an alleged road traffic accident and required intubation due to a low Glasgow Coma Scale score. He had no prior ocular complaints.
subjective.review_of_systems: He had no ocular complaints prior to presentation.

objective.physical_examination: On presentation, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was E2V3M4, and he was intubated. Ophthalmic examination revealed a normal anterior segment and normally reactive pupils. Fundoscopy showed clear media with discrete yellow-white placoid subretinal lesions measuring 0.25 to 1 disc diameter located nasal to the optic disc and in the macular region of the right eye.
objective.routine_investigations: Three consecutive daily stool examinations were negative for parasites. Ocular B-scan ultrasound demonstrated an anechoic cystic lesion in the coats of the right eye containing a hyperechoic scolex, and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed a hyperreflective cystic lesion with backscattering.
objective.advanced_workup: Noncontrast head CT demonstrated multiple well-defined cortical and juxtacortical cystic lesions. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed multiple vesicular-stage ring lesions with enhancing protoscolices and no surrounding inflammation, while the optic nerves were free of cysts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive vesicular-stage parenchymal and subretinal neurocysticercosis (NCC) was diagnosed based on the absolute diagnostic criterion of multiple cysts with scolices on brain MRI together with characteristic B-scan ultrasound and SD-OCT findings, despite negative serum anticysticercal antibody ELISA. He was treated with injectable dexamethasone (6 mg) followed by oral albendazole (15 mg/kg). Over a 2-week hospitalization, his GCS improved with no fever or seizures, but the subretinal placoid lesions persisted. Transpupillary thermotherapy using a large spot-size 810 nm diode laser was performed on the persistent subretinal cysts, resulting in chorioretinal scarring and documented visual acuity of 20/20 OU at 1-week follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 64-year-old man was admitted to our institute with a history of severe headache, an unsteady gait, and occasional urinary incontinence. These symptoms began 2 days prior to admission, and the patient had previously been healthy without medical concerns. He denied a previous history of consuming raw pork meat. On examination, the patient was alert but disoriented with respect to time and place. No significant pathological reflex was detected, and papilledema was absent. His lower extremities were hypotonic, and the strength of both legs, particularly in the proximal musculature, was diminished. A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the brain showed marked ventricular dilatation but no intraparenchymal lesions or intraventricular cysticercal lesions (Figure 1). In addition, no subcutaneous nodules were found. The peripheral blood findings revealed a leukocyte count of 8700/mm3 (eosinophils 3%) and a hemoglobin level of 12.8 mg/dL, although the hematological findings were unremarkable. Motor examination showed normal strength in both upper extremities but reduced strength in both lower extremities (Grade 4/5 on the Medical Research Council [MRC] scale). Under a diagnosis of acute hydrocephalus, lumbar tapping was attempted repeatedly, but cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was not obtained despite adequate lumbar puncture. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoraco-lumbar spine revealed multiple cystic contrast-enhancing intraspinal lesions extending from C7 to S1 (Figure 2). Ventriculoperitoneal shunting and microsurgical removal of the lesions following laminectomy from T12 to L1 and L3 to L4 were performed under general anesthesia. During surgery, lesions of a mixed solid and cystic nature were detected. Subsequent pathological findings showed fibrosis, local calcification, and chronic inflammation associated with the cysticercosis cyst walls.
Postoperatively, an anticysticercal agent (Albendazole, Zentel  400 mg, manufactured by Smith Kline Beecham Pharmaceuticals) and an oral steroid were administered for 6 weeks. During the early postoperative period, the patient remained awake, alert, and oriented, although his muscle strength and occasional urinary incontinence were not improved. After the 6-month follow-up period, these symptoms remained, and the patient was unable to ambulate without assistance despite improvements in ventricular dilation (Figure 3).

subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two days prior to admission, the previously healthy patient acutely developed severe headache, gait unsteadiness, bilateral lower limb weakness, and occasional urinary incontinence.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; denied any history of consuming raw pork.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for urinary incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: The patient was alert but disoriented to time and place. Papilledema, pathological reflexes, and subcutaneous nodules were absent. Motor examination showed normal upper extremity strength (5/5) but hypotonia and reduced strength (MRC grade 4/5, predominantly proximal) in both lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Peripheral blood count showed WBC 8,700/mm3 with 3% eosinophils and hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT demonstrated marked ventricular dilatation without intraparenchymal or intraventricular lesions. Repeated lumbar punctures failed to yield CSF ('dry taps'). Thoracolumbar spine MRI revealed multiple contrast-enhancing intraspinal cystic lesions extending from C7 to S1.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: The patient underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunting and T12-L1 and L3-L4 laminectomies with microsurgical excision of mixed solid and cystic intraspinal lesions; histopathology confirmed spinal neurocysticercosis (fibrosis, focal calcification, and chronic inflammation of cysticercal cyst walls). He completed a 6-week postoperative course of oral albendazole (400 mg) and corticosteroids. At 6-month follow-up, ventricular dilation had resolved on CT and his sensorium was normal, though paraparesis (requiring assistance to ambulate) and occasional urinary incontinence persisted.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old female patient presented with progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation and hyper nasal speech for 5 months duration. She had 4 episodes of partial seizures involving the right upper and the lower limb for the past 5 months and was not on any medications. There was weakness of the left upper limb for the past 15 days duration but there was no headache, vomiting or blurring of vision. She had emotional instability in the form of inappropriate crying. Neurological examination showed exaggerated jaw jerks and gag reflex with spastic dysarthria. She had both proximal and distal weakness in the left upper limb with power of 3/5. All the deep tendon reflexes were brisk with plantar response mute bilaterally and cortical sensory loss in the left upper limb. There was no atrophy or fasciculation of the affected muscles. The fundus and other system examination were normal.
Laboratory examination revealed positive neurocysticercosis serology. The peripheral smear was normal. The renal and liver function tests were normal. The MRI brain showed multiple small cysts with scolex in both the cerebral hemispheres and a giant intraparenchymal cyst measuring 5 x 4.3 cms in the right cerebral hemisphere [Figure 1a and b].
Our patient presented with pseudobulbar palsy, partial seizures and weakness of the left upper limb. Her NCC serology was positive and diagnosis confirmed by MRI, which showed multiple cysts with scolex (in vesicular stage). She received the treatment with albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day along with steroids (for two weeks). She also received phenytoin for seizures. The patient remained seizure free and there were no significant events during her hospital stay. On follow-up six weeks after the completion of albendazole therapy she reported no recurrence of seizures and her right upper limb weakness recovered partially with power of 4/5. There was also improvement in her speech, emotional instability and was able to take food without nasal regurgitation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, hypernasal speech, emotional lability, and right-sided focal seizures, followed by 15 days of left upper limb weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 5 months, the patient experienced progressive bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, hypernasal speech), emotional instability with inappropriate crying, and four episodes of partial seizures involving the right upper and lower limbs. Fifteen days prior to admission, she developed progressive weakness of the left upper limb, without headache, vomiting, or blurred vision.
subjective.past_medical_history: She was not taking any prior medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for headache, vomiting, or visual blurring; positive for inappropriate crying.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination demonstrated pseudobulbar palsy with spastic dysarthria and exaggerated jaw jerk and gag reflexes. She had proximal and distal left upper limb weakness (power 3/5) without muscle atrophy or fasciculations, diffusely brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilaterally mute plantar responses, and cortical sensory loss in the left upper limb. Fundoscopy and systemic examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Peripheral blood smear, renal function tests, and liver function tests were normal.
